66186276B48953429733047.name: Idaho
66186276B48953429733047.summary:
A trans visitor to Idaho stands under the United States federal framework in every respect concerning documents and entry. Executive Order 14168 of January 2025 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department has stopped processing the X marker, new passports are issued only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already carrying an X remain valid until expiry. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court in November 2025 allowed the changed treatment of trans passports to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992.

Idaho's own statute is the sharper exposure on the ground. House Bill 752 was signed by the governor and takes effect on 1 July 2026. It makes it a crime for a trans person to use a restroom or changing room that does not match their sex in government buildings and in public-facing private businesses, including gas stations, restaurants, entertainment venues and hospitals. A first offence is a misdemeanour carrying up to a year in jail.

According to the ACLU, House Bill 752 is the only state law in the country extending bathroom criminalisation to private businesses, and it carries steeper penalties than other states' bans. Six transgender Idahoans filed suit on 30 April 2026, before the 1 July effect date, arguing that the measure is unconstitutional. The ACLU's filing asserts due-process, equal-protection and privacy violations and notes that the law targets no actual criminal conduct. National wire reporting covered the legislature's passage of the ban and the jail penalties it carries, along with a lawsuit that has partially blocked it.

A July 2026 national risk assessment flagged Idaho as the latest "Do Not Travel" state for trans people, bringing the total to four states so flagged, and reported that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights while federal policies drove nationwide trends.

66186276B48953429733047.tangentialFactors:
Idaho's statute sits inside a national pattern rather than standing alone. A Movement Advancement Project tally counts state bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine states and one territory, with outright state bans on facility use per gender identity in additional states; 29 states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban, and some states make trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances.

Enforcement under comparable laws has produced arrests. In April 2025 a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol, which civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under that state's bathroom-restriction law.

Facilities exposure compounds at the federal layer. Executive Order 14168 barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, so a visitor may face both Idaho's criminal rule in state buildings and the federal restriction in federally funded settings.

Entry screening carries an outing risk independent of Idaho law. TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that are invasive of privacy. Several foreign governments responded to US document and data rules: in April 2025 CNN reported that several countries issued advisories about trans people travelling to the United States, and Axios reported in March 2025 that at least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the US.

Visa screening carries its own exposure. In February 2025 the State Department announced a ban on trans athletes entering the US to compete in women's sports, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking and treating applicants who list a gender other than their assigned sex as grounds for a permanent ban on grounds of fraud.

Care access is constrained for visitors who need it. Executive Order 14187 of January 2025 described gender-affirming care for minors as "chemical and surgical mutilation of children," some hospitals paused care, and in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed over 20 hospitals for records of patients under 19. In July 2025 the federal government shut down specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, and October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. Gender-affirming care for children is already banned in 27 states. Several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court.

66186276B41335105066757.name: Louisiana
66186276B41335105066757.summary:
Louisiana stands under the United States national framework on travel documents and entry. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, and prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The State Department has stopped processing the X marker and any marker inconsistent with sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. The Supreme Court allowed these restrictions to take effect in November 2025, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992, and the American Civil Liberties Union's suit on behalf of seven plaintiffs remains in federal court. By March 2025 trans and nonbinary travellers reported passports being confiscated or blocked at processing, with some left stranded abroad.

Entry screening carries separate exposure. Since 25 February 2025 the State Department has flagged visa applicants with an internal marking, treating as fraud, with a permanent bar, any applicant listing a gender other than the one assigned at birth, in the context of barring trans athletes from entering the United States to compete in women's sports. Separately, Transportation Security Administration checkpoint procedures involve secondary screening, hand-held devices and pat-downs that can be invasive of privacy and risk outing a trans traveller.

Louisiana records the highest per-capita killing rate of trans women of any state in the country: 24.7 per 100,000 people per year reported, on 19 recorded victims, against 23.5 for the state ranked safest. The count rests on a base of 428 victims recorded across the United States between 2008 and 2025, and every figure in that base is an undercount floor. A national analysis drawing on that data cautions that rankings built on legal risk do not sort physical safety: the states holding the worst law carry the highest rate.

Violence in Louisiana has also produced prosecutions of the people attacked. In August 2026 a mob beat trans couple Aurora Rush and Shae Sanders over restroom use at Cypress Black Bayou Park in Benton. Sanders, who has a pre-existing spinal injury, and Rush, who suffered a concussion and blood pooling, were both charged with disturbing the peace while no attacker was arrested, and the Sheriff's Office reported no other arrests that day. Rush was denied hospital care, jailed in a men's facility and searched by a male guard despite a 'female' marker on her driver's licence. The plea deal offered to the victims was not signed.

The same municipality simultaneously voted one of the country's most severe anti-trans restroom ordinances, placing local restroom access for trans residents and visitors on a restrictive footing at the time of the attack.

Custody is a documented site of harm. On 2 April 2024 Yella (Robert) Clark Jr., a 45-year-old Black trans woman serving a life sentence at Angola prison, was killed in a fight with several inmates. She was at least the 16th trans or gender-expansive person killed that year and the fifth in April alone, and such deaths are systematically under- or mis-reported.

66186276B52324970173776.name: Tennessee
66186276B52324970173776.summary:
Trans visitors to Tennessee stand under the United States federal framework as well as state law. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary; the State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth, and new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed these restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992. Passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until expiry, while trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. TSA screening can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that are invasive of privacy, and several foreign governments have issued advisories about trans people travelling to the United States over identity-document and data rules.

Tennessee's Adult Entertainment Act of 2023 (SB 3/HB 9) criminalises "adult cabaret entertainment", a definition that expressly includes "male or female impersonators", performed on public property or anywhere a child could see it. A first offence is a Class A misdemeanour carrying up to 11 months 29 days and a $2,500 fine; a second violation is a Class E felony carrying 1 to 6 years and fines to $3,000. A trans visitor who performs, or who is perceived as performing, within that definition faces repeat-offence felony exposure after a single prior conviction.

The Act survived federal challenge on procedural grounds, and in 2026 the Supreme Court refused to hear challenges to it, leaving the appeals-court ruling upholding the 2023 statute in place. A separate suit over the law remains ongoing.

Violence risk is documented at a level well above the national picture. A July 2026 national analysis using TGEU and Williams Institute data records Tennessee's killing rate of trans women at 7.8 per 100,000 per year, based on 10 recorded deaths between 2008 and 2025 and treated as an undercount floor rather than a total. The same analysis places Tennessee in the "Worst Laws Passed" tier of states.

Custody is hazardous. In April 2024 the Tennessee State Legislature passed a bill banning gender-affirming care for Tennessee inmates. Under the 2026 Riley Gaines Women's Safety and Protection Act, transgender inmates are to be placed in prisons according to sex assigned at birth, and the same Act bans trans women from women's shelters, removing an access point for a visitor who has no other accommodation.

Kansas sits within a wider national pattern rather than standing alone. A Movement Advancement Project tally counts state bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine states and one territory, with outright state bans on facility use per gender identity in additional states, while 29 states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban and some states make trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances. Gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states.

A July 2026 national risk assessment flagged Idaho as the latest Do Not Travel state for trans people, bringing the total to four, and reported that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights while federal policies drove nationwide trends. Kansas was the first state added to that tier in a year, in February 2026.

Enforcement patterns elsewhere show what facility laws can produce. In April 2025 a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol, which civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under that state's bathroom-restriction law. Rights groups have called the Kansas statute a template for other states, with further targeting bills pending in state legislatures.

Foreign governments have responded to the federal document and data rules. In April 2025 several countries issued advisories about trans people travelling to the United States over identity-document and data rules, and in March 2025 at least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the country.

Federal custody is a separate and documented harm, relevant to anyone facing detention. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted Florida-based policies mandating conversion therapy for transgender inmates, including cutting hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy and drugs; the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025. In immigration custody, transgender men were reportedly subjected to forced-labour programmes with refusals met by beatings, solitary confinement and reports of severe sexual abuse. In December 2025 the Attorney General instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists described as promoting radical gender ideology, and a May 2026 White House counterterrorism strategy stated that activities would prioritise groups whose ideology is anti-American, radically pro-transgender and anarchist. Advocates have compared these actions to the early stages of genocide.

66186276B69138566591314.name: Mississippi
66186276B69138566591314.summary:
Mississippi stands under the United States national framework on travel documents and entry, and that framework is the first exposure a trans visitor faces. Executive Order 14168 of January 2025 defined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary and barred self-selection of gender on passports and visas; the State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth, so new passports are issued only as M or F on supporting documents, while passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until expiry. The Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect in November 2025. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad; the ACLU is suing the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records. Screening at US checkpoints adds an outing risk through secondary screening, devices and pat-downs, and several foreign governments, including at least eight European countries, adjusted their travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the United States during 2025.

Facilities access inside Mississippi is restricted by state law. The Movement Advancement Project's equality map records bans on transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity in nine states and one territory, with additional states imposing outright facility-use bans; Mississippi enacted such bans across 2024 and 2025 and defines sex by birth in statute. Some states make trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances, and a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol in April 2025, which civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under that state's law.

The Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map's July 2026 update places Mississippi in its 'Worst Laws Passed' category, among states the assessment describes as having legislatively erased transgender people, on a five-year legislation-tracking methodology with a scoring rubric. A July 2026 national risk assessment separately flagged four states as 'Do Not Travel' for trans people and reported that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights. Mississippi's own 2024 session shows the legislative direction: the SAFER Act, which would have restricted trans people's use of public bathrooms, locker rooms and public university dormitories, and the 'Women's Bill of Rights,' which would have codified a binary definition of sex determined at birth and curtailed legal recognition of trans identities, both died on 29 April 2024 after lawmakers failed to agree compromise versions.

Court treatment of gender-transition recognition is documented. On 17 April 2025 the Mississippi Supreme Court ruled 8-1 that a transgender teen undergoing gender transition cannot change his name, denying a petition filed nearly two years earlier by a then-16-year-old whose parents both consented; Justice James D. Maxwell II's majority opinion referred to the trans boy as a 'minor female' and cited the 2023 REAP Act, which bans surgical and non-surgical treatments for transgender minors, as Mississippi's express public policy against children receiving gender-transition assistance. The 2023 statute is the state-level care restriction; nationally, gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states, and federal measures including Executive Order 14187, Department of Justice subpoenas to over 20 hospitals for records of patients under 19, the removal of specialised LGBTQ youth services from the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, and proposed Medicaid reimbursement bars for transgender patients under 18 constrain care, several of them blocked or enjoined in court.

Violence risk is measurable and federal prosecution has followed. The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Mississippi reported that Joshua Brandon Vallum was sentenced to 49 years in federal prison for the bias-motivated murder of a transgender woman in Lucedale. A July 2026 state-by-state analysis of killings of trans women, adjusted for undercounting across 2008-2025, records 6.6 such killings per 100,000 trans women annually in Mississippi, above the 6.0 per 100,000 US general-population homicide rate printed alongside it, and finds that legal tier does not sort violence, with both worst-law and safest-law states carrying high rates. Federal custody adds further documented harm: from 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted policies mandating conversion therapy for transgender inmates, the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025, and in December 2025 the Attorney General instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists characterised as promoting "radical gender ideology."

66186276B83300161667341.name: Oklahoma
66186276B83300161667341.summary:
Oklahoma is a state within the United States, so a visitor stands under the federal framework first. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed the attorney general to "correct the misapplication" of Bostock v. Clayton County (2020). The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. The Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect in November 2025, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992, and a civil-liberties union has sued the department on behalf of seven plaintiffs. By March 2025 trans and nonbinary travellers reported passports being confiscated or blocked at processing, with some left stranded abroad.

Entry screening carries a second exposure. The State Department announced on 25 February 2025 that it would bar trans athletes from entering the United States to compete in women's sports, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking and treating as fraud, with a permanent bar, any applicant listing a gender other than the one assigned at birth; the announcement followed an executive order titled "Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports" issued on 5 February 2025. Separately, Transportation Security Administration checkpoint procedures involve secondary screening, hand-held devices and pat-downs that can be invasive of privacy and risk outing a trans traveller.

State facilities rules are where Oklahoma itself appears in the national picture. The Movement Advancement Project's national tracker, in its 25 March 2026 edition, lists Oklahoma under bans on transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity, specifically covering K-12 school facilities, with enactments in 2022 and again in 2025. Nationally, school and government-building bans of this kind apply in 9 states and 1 territory, and some states make trans use of facilities a criminal offence in certain circumstances, while 29 states, 4 territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. In April 2025 a trans student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol after declaring an intention to break the law, and civil-rights attorneys described it as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law.

Identity documents are the active legislative front in Oklahoma. On 6 May 2026 House Bill 1225, requiring a male or female designation on Oklahoma birth certificates and prohibiting changes with very little exception, passed its most recent vote 70-17 and headed to Governor Kevin Stitt's desk. Its authors said the bill is designed to strengthen the existing law being challenged in federal court by transgender plaintiffs including Tulsa resident Rowan Fowler, and the state Attorney General's office confirmed that the bill clarifies Oklahoma never permitted gender birth-certificate changes; critics called it further discrimination. The bill was still pending the governor's signature when last reported. Comparable closure is documented elsewhere: Kansas enacted a law in March 2026 invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not match sex assigned at birth and barring trans people from sex-segregated facilities, which rights groups call a template for other state legislatures.

Care for trans people is restricted federally and applies in Oklahoma. Executive Order 14187 of 28 January 2025 described gender-affirming care for minors as mutilation and some hospitals paused care; in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed more than 20 hospitals for full records of patients under 19, including names, social security numbers and doctors' notes. Gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states, proposed health-department rules in October 2025 would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18, and in July 2025 the federal government shut down specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline.

Custody and enforcement machinery round out the federal layer. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted Florida-based policies for transgender inmates mandating short hair, withdrawal of hormone medication and substitution of psychiatric therapy and psychiatric drugs; imprisoned transgender people reported denied care, and the Bureau of Prisons stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners it holds from 2025. In immigration detention, transgender men were subjected to forced-labour programmes with guards justifying them by saying they would treat them "like a man," and those who refused faced beatings and solitary confinement, with severe sexual abuse also widely reported. In December 2025 the attorney general instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists promoting what she called radical gender ideology, describing such activists as domestic terrorist groups, and a May 2026 national counterterrorism strategy stated that activity would prioritise the rapid identification and neutralisation of groups whose ideology is described as anti-American, radically pro-transgender and anarchist.

Other federal measures in force or in litigation include the military purge under Executive Order 14183, the women's sports ban under Executive Order 14201, a January 2025 federal funding freeze, and an October 2025 rule blocking student loan forgiveness for public workers who provide gender-affirming care to transgender youth. Several of these orders have been blocked or enjoined in court, so the operative position on any given measure should be checked before travel.

Indiana is a state within the United States, and a visitor to Indiana stands under the national framework on travel documents and entry. Executive Order 14168 of January 2025 redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, and directed that federal identity documents reflect sex assigned at birth.

Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, the ACLU is suing the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and in November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992.

Visa screening carries separate exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged under the internal code SWS25 and an application listing a gender other than sex assigned at birth treated as grounds for a permanent fraud-based ban. 66186276B31593004124297.name: Utah
66186276B31593004124297.summary:
Travel documents are the sharpest exposure for a trans visitor to Utah. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary and barred self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The State Department has stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents. Passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU is suing the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and in November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in force since 1992.

Entry screening carries an outing risk that begins before arrival. TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs invasive of privacy, and multiple foreign governments responded: several countries issued advisories about trans people travelling to the United States in April 2025, and at least eight European countries adjusted guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the country. The State Department announced in February 2025 that applicants listing a gender other than their assigned sex could be treated as grounds for a permanent ban on fraud grounds, and flagged visa applicants with an internal marking when seeking to enter to compete in women's sports.

Facilities access inside Utah is governed by HB 257, 'Sex-based Designations for Privacy, Anti-bullying, and Women's Opportunities', introduced 11 January 2024 and signed by Governor Spencer Cox on 30 January 2024. The law requires people to use restrooms and locker rooms in public schools and government-owned buildings that match their sex assigned at birth. Transgender people can defend themselves against a complaint by producing documentation of gender-affirming care, and newly constructed government buildings must include single-occupant bathrooms. The Utah Legislature's own bill page records the signing on 30 January 2024 after several substitute versions cleared committee and floor stages.

Enforcement runs through a public reporting mechanism. The state operates a form on which residents can report transgender people in what the statute calls privacy spaces, including changing rooms and restrooms; complainants choose whether their names are included, and the state investigates each reported violation. The ACLU of Utah opposed HB 257 on the ground that it risked discriminatory enforcement.

Utah did not act alone. By January 2024 at least ten other states had passed laws regulating bathroom access for transgender people, and a national tally counted state bathroom bans reaching K-12 schools and some government buildings across nine states and one territory, with outright bans on facility use per gender identity in further states.

66186276B22881275445497.name: North Dakota
66186276B22881275445497.summary:
North Dakota stands under the United States national framework in every respect that governs a trans visitor's documents, screening and entry. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, and prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The 2023 statute tracked by the Movement Advancement Project bans all gender marker changes on birth certificates, with a narrow exception for individuals who have had genital surgery. The tracker marks North Dakota a negative law state, and a stricter and more explicit surgical requirement than applies in many other states. A July 2026 national anti-trans legal-risk assessment built from five years of daily legislative tracking places North Dakota among the worst states for legislation targeting transgender adults and among the states that prohibit any changes to birth certificates, a rule that forces trans people to out themselves when showing documents. 66186276B64762166704956.name: West Virginia
66186276B64762166704956.summary:
Every visitor to West Virginia stands first under the federal travel-document regime. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, and prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. The Supreme Court in November 2025 allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992. A trans or nonbinary visitor can therefore arrive holding papers that do not match their presentation, with airport screening and visa decisions following the same national rules, including the February 2025 State Department policy refusing visas to trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sporting events and treating applicants who list a gender other than their assigned sex as grounds for a permanent ban for fraud.

West Virginia's own facility restriction is statutory. Governor Patrick Morrisey signed Senate Bill 456, the 'Riley Gaines Act,' on 12 March 2025, after the state Senate passed it on 3 March and the House of Delegates passed it on 6 March. The statute defines 'woman' as an adult human of the female sex and 'man' as an adult human of the male sex and aims to preserve women's single-sex spaces, covering locker rooms, bathrooms, rape crisis centers, dormitories, prisons, and domestic violence shelters. At the signing, Morrisey said bathrooms, locker rooms, domestic violence shelters and rape crisis centers 'should be kept private for women only.' The Movement Advancement Project equality map cataloguing state bans on transgender people's use of public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity is the source for West Virginia's facility-ban enumeration.

National risk gradings place West Virginia near the top of the risk scale. Idaho was promoted to 'Do Not Travel' as the fourth such state after its felony bathroom ban, which carries up to 5 years and is partially court-blocked but in force wherever no gender-neutral option exists.

Kim Reynolds signed two bills on March 22, 2023: Senate File 538 bars doctors from administering gender-affirming care to anyone under 18 (covering puberty blockers, hormone therapy and transition-related surgeries), and Senate File 482 prevents transgender students from entering school bathrooms or changing rooms that correspond with their gender identities. The restroom restriction applies to multiperson restrooms and locker rooms at public and private elementary and secondary schools and took effect immediately, with single-person facilities available to trans students who obtain written consent from legal guardians.

sources.title: Iowa Supreme Court Says Medicaid Must Cover Care for Transgender People | American Civil Liberties Union
sources.summary: On March 8, 2019 the Iowa Supreme Court ruled unanimously in Good v. Iowa Dept. of Human Services that the state discriminated against two transgender women by denying their Medicaid claims for transition-related surgery, holding that excluding Medicaid coverage for gender-affirming surgery violates the Iowa Civil Rights Act.

sources.title: A Timeline of Litigation for Coverage of Gender-Affirming Transgender Surgery in Iowa - ACLU of Iowa
sources.summary: ACLU of Iowa's litigation timeline for coverage of gender-affirming transgender surgery in the state, from the lawsuit filed on behalf of Mika Covington and Aiden Vasquez over Iowa Medicaid's refusal to cover medically necessary gender-affirming surgery, through the March 2019 Iowa Supreme Court ruling and the litigation that followed. Tracks the state-court path that kept Medicaid surgery coverage available to transgender adults in Iowa.

sources.title: Iowa schools are scrambling to comply with new transgender bathroom law - KTVZ
sources.summary: KCCI (Des Moines) reporting syndicated by KTVZ: Gov. Kim Reynolds signed SF 482 into law on March 22, 2023, requiring anyone in an Iowa school, including students, staff, parents and visitors, to use only restrooms and other changing areas that correspond with the biological sex listed on their birth certificate, and Iowa school districts are scrambling to comply as the restriction takes effect. States the exact statute and subject scope (everyone on school grounds) behind Iowa's public-facility-use law.

A trans visitor to the state/province stands under the national framework on travel documents and screening. An executive order signed 20 January 2025 redefined sex for national purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, and prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The national passport authority stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. The country's highest court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect in November 2025, superseding a passport policy in place since 1992. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad; a national civil-liberties organisation has sued the passport authority on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and a national legal-advocacy group maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with national records.

Screening at national checkpoints carries an outing risk. Transport-security procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that are invasive of privacy, and multiple foreign governments have responded: in April 2025 several governments issued advisories about trans people travelling to the country over identity-document and data rules, and in March 2025 at least eight governments in one region, including two neighbouring jurisdictions, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the country. In the state/province itself, the sharpest facility rule applies to schools. One bill, signed by the governor on 22 March 2023, requires anyone on school grounds, including students, staff, parents and visitors, to use only restrooms and changing areas corresponding with the biological sex listed on a birth certificate. The restriction covers multiperson restrooms and locker rooms at public and private elementary and secondary schools and took effect immediately. A visitor entering a school building is therefore bound by it. Single-person facilities remain available to trans students who obtain written consent from legal guardians.

The state/province also bars gender-affirming care for minors. 66186276B79689460185872.name: South Carolina
66186276B79689460185872.summary:
A trans visitor to South Carolina enters under the United States federal document and screening regime before state law applies. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department has stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth, issuing new passports only as M or F, while previously issued X-marker passports remain valid until expiry. The Supreme Court allowed those restrictions to take effect in November 2025, and trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at processing, with some left stranded abroad.

Entry screening adds exposure. The State Department announced on 25 February 2025 that it would bar trans athletes from entering the United States to compete in women's sports, flags visa applicants with an internal marking, and treats a declared gender other than the one assigned at birth as fraud carrying a permanent bar. Transportation Security Administration checkpoint procedures can involve secondary screening, hand-held devices and pat-downs that risk outing a trans traveller.

Facilities are the sharpest South Carolina-specific exposure. Governor Henry McMaster signed House Bill 4756 into law on 15 May 2026, requiring transgender students in South Carolina public schools, colleges and universities to use restrooms matching their sex assigned at birth. The Senate amended the bill before passage, and the ACLU of South Carolina issued a response on 18 May 2026 framing it as discrimination against trans students in both K-12 and higher education.

The measure extends a pre-existing restriction on school restrooms into campus settings. A July 2026 anti-trans national legal risk assessment, which ranks states on the severity of adult and youth law by reading bills, places South Carolina among the escalating states rather than in the harshest tier.

Custody carries a further state-layer restriction: South Carolina operates a "freeze-frame" policy limiting the treatments transgender inmates may receive while incarcerated. Federal custody is separately affected by the Bureau of Prisons adoption of Florida-based policies for transgender inmates from 2026, which mandate short haircuts, withdrawal of hormone medication and substitution of psychiatric therapy and psychiatric drugs, and by the Bureau's cessation of reporting the number of transgender prisoners it holds from 2025.

66186276B65591139260314.name: Florida
66186276B65591139260314.summary:
Florida stands under the United States national framework, which sets the sharpest documentary risk for a trans visitor. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary and barred self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The State Department stopped processing the X marker; new passports are issued only as M or F on the supporting documents submitted, and passports already carrying an X remain valid until expiry. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and in November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the department's restrictions to take effect, superseding a policy in place since 1992.

Entry adds a second exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement banning trans athletes from entering the United States to compete in women's sporting events, with visa applicants flagged by an internal marking; applicants who list a gender other than sex assigned at birth are treated as grounds for a permanent ban for fraud. Several foreign governments responded, with advisories issued in April 2025 about trans people travelling to the United States and at least eight European states adjusting their guidance for trans and nonbinary citizens in March 2025.

Florida's own restrictions operate through Fla. Stat. 553.865, the 2023 restroom and changing-facility law. It applies only to buildings owned or leased by state or local government: state offices, courthouses, legislative offices, prisons and jails, local immigration detention, state parks and toll-road plazas. The statute purports to cover all schools, public and private. Refusing to leave a sex-segregated restroom or changing facility within its scope can be charged as criminal trespass. Private businesses fall outside its scope, and the ACLU advises fact-specific judgment and legal counsel in borderline settings.

The law produced its first known arrest on 19 March 2025, when Marcy Rheintgen, a 20-year-old transgender college student, washed her hands in a women's restroom at the Florida State Capitol after police were alerted in advance. She had announced publicly that she was there to break the law. The misdemeanor trespass charge carried up to 60 days in jail. On 20 June 2025 Leon County Judge Lashawn Riggans dismissed the case, holding that as a defendant charged under the statute she had no standing to argue that the law itself was illegitimate, so its substance was never tested in court. At least 14 states have adopted comparable laws barring trans women from women's bathrooms at schools and some government buildings.

Florida scores 8.0 on the national anti-trans law scale and is labelled Do Not Travel for trans people, with 3.7 trans women murdered per 100,000 per year. A national analysis of 2008–2025 data found that state law severity does not correlate with killing rates across the 26 states with data, the trendline nearly flat. Legal climate and street-level violence are separate visitor risks, and a permissive legal environment should not be read as a signal of personal safety.

Visitors who are detained face documented harm. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted Florida-based policies mandating conversion therapy for transgender inmates, including cutting hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy and drugs; the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025. In immigration custody, transgender men were reportedly subjected to forced-labour programmes with refusals met by beatings, solitary confinement and reports of severe sexual abuse.

Equality Florida took the unprecedented step on 12 April 2023 of issuing a travel advisory warning of risks to the health, safety and freedom of people considering short or long-term travel or relocation to Florida, citing hostile LGBTQ laws alongside reproductive-health restrictions, gun-safety rollbacks and book bans. The organisation reports cancellations of events and conferences and notes the US military considering redeployment for service members' families.

66186276B73402293045483.name: Nebraska
66186276B73402293045483.summary:
Nebraska is a state within the United States, and the national framework sets the first layer of exposure for a trans visitor. Executive Order 14168 of January 2025 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department has stopped processing the X marker, new passports are issued only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports carrying an X remain valid until expiry. The Supreme Court allowed those restrictions to take effect in November 2025, and the ACLU is litigating the policy on behalf of seven plaintiffs, with separate guidance available from Lambda Legal on how name and gender changes interact with federal records.

State policy reinforces the federal line. Executive Order 23-16, signed by Governor Jim Pillen on 30 August 2023 and titled a Women's Bill of Rights, defines sex, female, male, woman, girl, man, boy, mother and father for use by state agencies, and commits the state to sex-based segregation in athletics, bathrooms and changing rooms on the stated basis of biological differences in athletic ability and safety. A visitor dealing with Nebraska state agencies, state buildings or state-run sporting venues should expect to be classified by sex assigned at birth.

Entry and screening follow national rather than state procedure. In February 2025 the State Department announced it would refuse visas to transgender athletes seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sporting events, flagging applicants with an internal marking and treating a declared gender other than sex assigned at birth as grounds for a permanent ban for fraud. TSA screening at airports can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that carry an outing risk for visitors whose presentation does not match their documents.

Custody is a documented site of harm in Nebraska. Federal courts held in August 2022 that Nebraska prison officials were not liable for their treatment of a transgender inmate identified as Jane Doe, who was housed by sex assigned at birth in a men's prison, diagnosed with gender dysphoria and placed in a cell with a convicted male sex offender who assaulted her. District Judge Brian C. Buescher dismissed her failure-to-treat, denial-of-surgery and failure-to-protect claims, writing that without medical evidence no reasonable jury could find deliberate indifference to her medical need and that she had not plausibly alleged more than de minimis injuries from the assault. National prison policy is aligned with that placement: the Federal Bureau of Prisons rescinded its 2017 guidance permitting transfer to facilities matching gender identity in May 2018, and from 2026 has adopted policies mandating conversion-therapy-style measures for transgender inmates, including hair cutting, hormone withdrawal and substitution of psychiatric medication, while ceasing to report how many transgender prisoners it holds.

66186276B6801956407400.summary:
North Carolina is a state within the United States, and a trans visitor stands under the federal framework before any state rule applies. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed the attorney general to "correct the misapplication" of Bostock v. Clayton County (2020). The same order required federal agencies to use "sex" rather than "gender," mandated removal of materials promoting what the order calls gender ideology, and rescinded policies requiring use of names and pronouns consistent with a person's gender identity in federal workplaces. The facilities bar reaches federal buildings in North Carolina.

The State Department has stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until expiry. The X marker had been available since 2022. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992, and the restriction remains challenged in federal courts. The ACLU sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and by March 2025 trans and nonbinary travellers reported passports being confiscated or blocked at processing, with some left stranded abroad.

Entry screening carries its own exposure. An executive order titled "Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports" was issued on 5 February 2025, and on 25 February 2025 the State Department announced it would bar trans athletes from entering the United States to compete in women's sports, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking and treating as fraud, with a permanent bar, any applicant listing a gender other than the one assigned at birth. The Transportation Security Administration's checkpoint procedures involve secondary screening, hand-held devices and pat-downs that can be invasive of privacy and risk outing a trans traveller.

Gender-affirming care is restricted on several fronts. Executive Order 14187 of 28 January 2025 described such care for minors as mutilation and some hospitals paused care; in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed more than 20 hospitals for full records of patients under 19, including names, social security numbers and doctors' notes. Gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states, and in October 2025 proposed health-department rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. In July 2025 the federal government shut down specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline.

Custody is a documented site of harm. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted Florida-based policies for transgender inmates that mandate cutting their hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy and psychiatric drugs; imprisoned transgender people reported being denied care, and the Bureau of Prisons stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners it holds from 2025. In immigration detention, transgender men were subjected to forced-labour programmes with guards justifying them by saying they would treat them "like a man," and those who refused faced beatings and solitary confinement; severe sexual abuse was also widely reported.

Official hostility extends to enforcement machinery. In December 2025 the attorney general instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists promoting what she called radical gender ideology, describing such activists as domestic terrorist groups. A May 2026 national counterterrorism strategy stated that counterterrorism activity would prioritise the rapid identification and neutralisation of groups whose ideology is described as anti-American, radically pro-transgender and anarchist.

Other federal measures in force or in litigation include the military purge under Executive Order 14183, the women's sports ban under Executive Order 14201, a January 2025 federal funding freeze, and an October 2025 rule blocking student loan forgiveness for public workers who provide gender-affirming care to transgender youth. Several of these orders have been blocked or enjoined in court, so the operative position on any given measure should be checked before travel.

At state level, facility rules are the defining North Carolina question. After the Charlotte city council passed an ordinance in March 2016 allowing transgender people to use bathrooms matching their gender identity, the North Carolina General Assembly met in emergency session and passed House Bill 2, which barred cities from passing anti-discrimination ordinances protecting gay and transgender people and required people to use public bathrooms corresponding with the sex listed on their birth certificate. The law drew global backlash, with companies including Google and Disney pledging to pull back business, and the U.S. Justice Department called it "state-sponsored discrimination" and sued, while North Carolina filed its own suit. Legislators repealed House Bill 2 on 30 March 2017 in the face of the boycotts.

Facility use remains an active legislative subject in North Carolina. In the 2025 session Republican lawmakers were again pushing a transgender bathroom bill, years after the HB 2 boycotts forced the repeal, so a visitor should expect facilities access to be contested rather than settled.

Lethal violence against trans people in North Carolina does not track the state's protective posture. A July 2026 investigative data analysis comparing legal-risk tiers with Trans Murder Monitoring records found that protective statutes do not predict lower lethal risk for trans women; its state rate chart places North Carolina at 3.0 killings per 100,000 trans women, on a recorded base of three or more victims that the analysis acknowledges is an undercount, and characterises the state as moderate-risk. That rating describes recorded killings and should not be read as an assurance of safety for an individual visitor.

Clayton County (2020). The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992.

Travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and Lambda Legal maintains guidance on what documentation to consider and how name and gender changes interact with federal records. A visitor's documents may therefore mismatch presentation at the border or at checkpoints.

Screening carries an outing risk. TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that are invasive of privacy. Several foreign governments responded: in April 2025 CNN reported that multiple countries issued advisories about trans people travelling to the United States over identity-document and data rules, and Axios reported in March 2025 that at least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the country.

The state has passed laws that would normally place it among the worst states for trans people, but Montana's courts have repeatedly blocked or enjoined those laws under the state constitution. Adult restrictions that were enacted have consequently not taken full effect, and that court record improved Montana's standing in the July 2026 anti-trans national legal risk assessment. Montana was the only state to improve in the 2026 rankings.

66186276B13694661525286.name: Missouri
66186276B13694661525286.summary:
A visitor to Missouri stands under the national framework of the United States in every setting. Executive Order 14168 of January 2025 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth, the State Department has stopped processing the X marker, and new passports are issued only as M or F, so a trans visitor's documents may not match their presentation. Airport screening and visa decisions follow the same national rules, including the State Department's February 2025 announcement that trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas and flagged internally under the code 'SWS25', with a declaration of a gender other than sex assigned at birth capable of being treated as fraud and a permanent bar.

Missouri prohibits gender-affirming medical care for minors. The Save Adolescents from Experimentation (SAFE) Act, Senate Bill 49, took effect on 28 August 2023 after a St Louis judge denied a preliminary injunction against it on 29 August 2023. The statute bars hormones and puberty blockers for under-18s unless the patient was already in treatment, and prohibits all transition-related surgery for minors.

The SAFE Act also bars MO HealthNet Medicaid coverage of the prohibited care, restricts treatment access in prisons, jails and correctional centres, and exposes violating providers to licence revocation. CNN reports that the law additionally bars Missouri Medicaid from paying for gender-affirming care for a patient of any age, and that doctors who breach the ban can lose their state medical licence and be sued by patients up to 15 years after treatment.

Litigation over the ban has failed at every stage so far. Lambda Legal, the ACLU of Missouri and Bryan Cave Leighton Paisner filed suit on 25 July 2023 in Cole County Circuit Court on behalf of three families of transgender young people, medical providers, PFLAG National and GLMA, seeking to block Senate Bill 49 before its 28 August 2023 effective date. A Missouri judge upheld the law on 25 November 2024, and on 13 January 2026 the Missouri Supreme Court unanimously upheld the ban on gender-transition surgeries, cross-sex hormones and other gender-affirming care for minors, quoting the 2025 United States Supreme Court ruling that upheld Tennessee's similar ban. Counsel for the plaintiffs said they would appeal. The ban has been in force since 28 August 2023 and remains in force.

The statute carries a 2027 sunset enacted as a Republican-Democrat concession, but lawmakers have moved to make it permanent, and a November 2026 ballot initiative also seeks to ban such care indefinitely. The plaintiffs continue toward trial on the merits.

Correctional custody carries its own care exclusion. Governor Mike Kehoe signed an appropriations law, effective 2 July 2026, barring state funds from paying for cross-sex hormones or gender-transition surgery for transgender people in Missouri prisons, with no taper plan for inmates already receiving care. Missouri thereby became the seventh state, and the second in 2026 after Oklahoma, to ban gender-affirming care for inmates; Florida, Kentucky and North Carolina have near-identical laws, while similar Idaho and Georgia measures were blocked by federal courts.

A trans visitor to Missouri is unlikely to encounter the SAFE Act unless accompanying a minor who needs medical care, but anyone detained in a Missouri jail, prison or correctional centre loses access to state-funded hormone therapy and transition surgery under both the SAFE Act and the 2026 appropriations law.

Georgia stands under the national framework that governs every state. Since January 2025, Executive Order 14168 has required federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department has stopped processing the X marker, new passports are issued only as M or F from supporting documents, and passports already carrying an X remain valid until expiry. The ACLU is suing the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and the Supreme Court in November 2025 allowed the department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports. A visitor whose documents no longer match their presentation should expect that mismatch to surface at federal checkpoints, where TSA secondary screening, devices and pat-downs can compound the exposure.

Entry and screening follow national rules rather than Georgia law. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sports would be flagged with an internal marking, and applicants who list a gender other than their assigned sex can be treated as grounds for a permanent ban on fraud grounds. Several foreign governments, including at least eight European states, adjusted their travel guidance for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the United States during 2025.

Georgia's own law restricts care rather than entry. Governor Brian Kemp signed Senate Bill 140 on 23 March 2023, barring licensed medical professionals from providing hormone therapy or gender-transition surgery to patients under 18, with licence revocation as a possible penalty; the ban took effect 1 July 2023, and minors who began hormone replacement therapy before that date may continue. The ACLU of Georgia said it would sue. Georgia's public-employee State Health Benefit Plan, by contrast, was required under an October 2023 settlement reached in Atlanta federal court to pay for medically necessary gender-affirming care for employees, spouses and dependents, following a December 2022 discrimination lawsuit; the settlement means the plan could be obliged to cover care for minors outside Georgia even though it is prohibited inside the state.

Adult care access in Georgia has contracted under federal funding pressure. On 13 February 2025 Memorial Health University Medical Center in Savannah cancelled all gender-affirming surgeries, including a pre-approved double mastectomy for a 24-year-old transgender man, citing a responsibility to follow state and federal laws in what appears to reference the 28 January 2025 federal executive order denying Medicare and Medicaid funding to providers of youth gender-transition care. The Current reports the Savannah Pride Center said at least two other area residents were also denied care.

Violence risk is documented and concentrated. Atlanta police said in April 2023 they were actively investigating three violent crimes against transgender women in the city that year, after two Black transgender women were fatally shot a week apart, with a January 2023 shooting that left a transgender woman in critical condition also remaining open; the Atlanta Police Department acknowledged the epidemic-level violence Black and Brown transgender women face in America. Georgia's recorded killing rate for trans women is 4.8 per 100,000 per year, a figure drawn from an undercounted monitoring project and therefore an acknowledged floor rather than a full measure.

66186276B86627915353587.name: New Hampshire
66186276B86627915353587.summary:
Visitors to New Hampshire stand under the United States national framework in every respect that touches identity documents and entry. Executive Order 14168, in force since January 2025, requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department no longer processes the X marker, and passports are issued only as M or F on the supporting documents submitted. Passports already carrying an X marker remain valid until expiry, but trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application. The Supreme Court has allowed the State Department to continue this treatment, and the ACLU litigation on behalf of seven plaintiffs is pending.

Entry rules add a separate exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged internally under the code 'SWS25', and an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently.

Within that national regime, New Hampshire carries an unusually high recorded incident load. GLAAD's 2025 national census documents 72 anti-LGBTQ incidents in New Hampshire during 2025, the second-highest count of any state after California's 198, and ahead of Texas at 66, Ohio at 50 and Washington at 50. The figure exceeds counts recorded in states with several times New Hampshire's population, which is the strongest single indicator in the sourced material of what a trans visitor may encounter on the ground.

Against that, the state's courts have applied existing civil-rights machinery to a trans victim. On 17 July 2026 the Merrimack County Superior Court found that a Concord man violated the New Hampshire Civil Rights Act by striking a transgender woman. The case establishes that assault against a trans person in New Hampshire can be pursued as a civil-rights violation and adjudicated in state court, rather than going unremedied.

Checkpoint and screening exposure follows national procedure: the National Center for Transgender Equality describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can disclose a traveller's trans status to TSA officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request screening matching one's presentation. Multiple foreign governments, including at least eight European countries such as Finland and Denmark, have issued or adjusted travel advisories for trans and nonbinary citizens travelling to the United States.

66186276B89395128410123.name: Arizona
66186276B89395128410123.summary:
Arizona sits inside the United States federal framework, and that framework governs the documents a trans visitor carries. Executive Order 14168, in force since January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, and prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The State Department has stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992.

Documentation failures are documented rather than hypothetical. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and Lambda Legal maintains guidance on what documentation to consider and how name and gender changes interact with federal records.

Screening at United States checkpoints carries an outing risk. Transport Security Administration procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs invasive of privacy. Several governments have responded: in April 2025 multiple countries issued advisories about trans people travelling to the United States over identity-document and data rules, and in March 2025 at least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the country.

Visa screening carries separate exposure. In February 2025 the State Department announced a ban on trans athletes entering the country to compete in women's sports, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking and treating applicants who list a gender other than their assigned sex as grounds for a permanent ban on grounds of fraud.

Federal custody presents documented harm. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted Florida-based policies mandating conversion therapy for transgender inmates, including cutting hair short, withdrawing hormone medication, and substituting psychiatric therapy and drugs; imprisoned transgender people reported being denied care, and the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025. In immigration detention, transgender men were reportedly subjected to forced-labour programmes, with refusals met by beatings, solitary confinement and reports of severe sexual abuse. In December 2025 the Attorney General instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists described as promoting "radical gender ideology" and characterised as "domestic terrorist groups"; a May 2026 White House counterterrorism strategy stated that activities would prioritise the identification and neutralisation of groups whose ideology is "anti-American, radically pro-transgender, and anarchist." Advocates have compared these actions to the early stages of genocide.

Care access is constrained for visitors needing it. Executive Order 14187 (January 2025) described gender-affirming care for minors as "chemical and surgical mutilation of children," leading some hospitals to pause care; in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed over 20 hospitals for full records of patients under 19. In July 2025 the federal government shut down specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, and October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. Gender-affirming care for children is already banned in 27 states. Several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court.

Facilities access is restricted in a growing number of states. A Movement Advancement Project tally counts state bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine states and one territory, with outright state bans on facility use per gender identity in additional states; 29 states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban, and some states make trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances. In April 2025 a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol in what civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under that state's bathroom-restriction law. In February 2026 Kansas enacted a law preventing transgender people from changing markers on birth certificates and driver's licences and invalidating existing documents that do not match sex assigned at birth, and barring trans people from sex-segregated facilities; rights groups call it a template for other states.

Against that national backdrop, a July 2026 national legal risk assessment places Arizona in its Low-Risk States group, alongside Delaware, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Virginia, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia, describing these as jurisdictions that largely refrained from targeting transgender adults. Arizona is named alongside Virginia as a state that has enacted youth-targeting anti-trans policies judged unlikely to be extended to adults. The same assessment flagged Idaho as the latest "Do Not Travel" state for trans people, bringing the total to four states so flagged, and reported that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights while federal policies drove nationwide trends.

Prism (3 Jun 2026): Tucson Pride cancelled all 2026 events in January and effectively dissolved, citing a political and financial environment that made supporting queer events nearly impossible; Tucson grouped with Tampa FL and Arlington TX as affected cities.

66186276B78821008370123.name: Maine
66186276B78821008370123.summary:
Maine is a comparatively low-risk state for a transgender visitor within the United States. A July 2026 national anti-trans legal risk assessment places Maine in its Low-Risk States group. The sources reviewed attribute to Maine none of the state-level document restrictions, facility bans or care bans documented elsewhere: no state law blocking marker changes, no state bathroom restriction and no state ban on gender-affirming care is recorded against Maine in this inventory.

The federal layer nevertheless governs a visitor in Maine in full. Under Executive Order 14168 of January 2025, federal identity documents must reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department has stopped processing the X marker, new passport applications are decided as M or F on supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X remain valid only until expiry. In March 2025 the University of Maine System announced compliance with federal restrictions on transgender sports participation after the US Department of Agriculture suspended federal funding for research and programmes while investigating possible sex-based discrimination in federally funded education programmes. The July 2026 assessment separately flags Maine's risk as increased on that basis, the only factor cited against the state.

Andrea Balcer, a 27-year-old transgender woman convicted of two murders, was being held in the women's facility at the Maine Correctional Center in Windham for at least a year as of April 2026. Attorney Cynthia Dill filed the complaint. The placement is documented; the harassment and assault claims are allegations, and no ruling has been reported.

The Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted conversion-therapy-style policies for transgender inmates from 2026 and stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held in 2025; the Department of Justice subpoenaed records of patients under 19 from more than 20 hospitals in summer 2025; and October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. Several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court, with the outcome of individual cases unresolved.

66186276B31549545599635.name: Delaware
66186276B31549545599635.summary:
Delaware is a state within the United States, and the rules that govern entry, travel documents and identity screening are federal in every respect. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary and requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department has stopped processing the X marker; new passport applications are decided as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU is litigating on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and in November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992.

Visa screening carries its own exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 and the State Department announcement of 25 February 2025 refuse visas to transgender people seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sporting events, flag such applicants with an internal marking, and treat listing a gender other than the sex assigned at birth as grounds for a permanent ban on grounds of fraud.

Screening at United States checkpoints carries an outing risk. TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that are invasive of privacy. Several foreign governments have responded to these rules: in April 2025 CNN reported advisories issued about transgender people travelling to the United States over identity-document and data rules, and Axios reported in March 2025 that at least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the country.

The federal facility restriction reaches Delaware directly. Executive Order 14168 bars transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, which covers federal buildings a visitor may enter. Nationally, a Movement Advancement Project tally counts state bathroom bans applying to transgender people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine states and one territory, with outright state bans on facility use per gender identity in additional states, and some states making trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances. In April 2025 a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol, which civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under that state's bathroom-restriction law. Delaware records no such ban.

On state-level posture, a July 2026 national legal risk assessment lists Delaware within its Low-Risk States group, alongside Arizona, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Virginia, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia. The assessment characterises these jurisdictions as largely refraining from targeting transgender adults, while noting that none of them specialises in protecting them. Delaware's position therefore reflects the absence of state-level targeting rather than the presence of state-level protection, and it does not insulate a visitor from the federal measures above.

Federal health-care restrictions apply nationwide. Executive Order 14187 of January 2025 described gender-affirming care for minors as "chemical and surgical mutilation of children," leading some hospitals to pause care; in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed more than 20 hospitals for full records of patients under 19. In July 2025 the federal government shut down specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, and October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. Gender-affirming care for children is already banned in 27 states. Several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court.
