66186276B6628180846672.name: Pennsylvania
66186276B6628180846672.summary:
Travelers to Pennsylvania stand under the United States federal framework. Executive Order 14168 of January 2025 redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, and prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The State Department has stopped processing the X marker and issues passports only as M or F according to supporting documents; passports already carrying X remain valid until expiry. The Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect in November 2025, and the ACLU is suing the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs over the changed treatment of trans passport applicants.

Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 and a State Department announcement of 25 February 2025 bar visas for trans athletes entering the country to compete in women's sporting events; applicants are flagged under an internal marking, and a declared gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud carrying a permanent bar. Screening at checkpoints carries an outing risk through secondary screening, devices and pat-downs, and several foreign governments, including at least eight European states, adjusted travel guidance for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the country during 2025.

Pennsylvania itself sits in the low-risk tier of Erin Reed's anti-trans national legal risk assessment as updated in July 2026, which covers states that largely refrain from targeting trans adults without specially protecting them, while documenting continued national degradation of trans rights through the 2026 legislative season.

The live legislative risk in Pennsylvania concerns school and collegiate athletics rather than adult status, documents or public facilities. The Pennsylvania Senate passed Senate Bill 1293, the Save Women's Sports Act, on 22 April 2026, which would ban transgender female athletes from girls' and women's teams in the commonwealth; Governor Josh Shapiro called supportive lawmakers 'extremists', and it was unclear whether the House of Representatives would take the bill up. The Senate had already approved Senate Bill 9 on 6 May 2025, reserving women's-designated teams for 'biological females' in K-12 and collegiate sports and sending it to the House.

Pennsylvania has also declined an anti-trans measure of this kind: Governor Tom Wolf vetoed comparable legislation on 11 July 2022 that would have required public K-12 schools and colleges to designate sports as male, female or coed, with female-designated sports limited to athletes assigned female at birth. Both pending bills target youth sports participation rather than transgender adults or public-facility access, so a trans visitor to Pennsylvania faces no state-level restriction on restroom use, identity documents or medical care under the sources available here.

66186276B91272823970344.name: Wisconsin
66186276B91272823970344.summary:
Visitors to Wisconsin stand under the national framework of the United States. Executive Order 14168 of 20 January 2025 redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary and barred self-selection of gender on passports and visas; the State Department has stopped processing the X marker and issues new passports only as M or F from supporting documents, while passports already holding an X marker remain valid until expiry. The Supreme Court allowed those restrictions to take effect in November 2025, and by March 2025 trans and nonbinary travellers reported passports confiscated or blocked at processing, with some left stranded abroad.

Entry screening carries a separate exposure. An executive order of 5 February 2025 and a State Department announcement of 25 February 2025 provide for refusing visas to trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sports, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking and treating as fraud, with a permanent bar, any applicant listing a gender other than the one assigned at birth. Transportation Security Administration checkpoint procedures involve secondary screening, hand-held devices and pat-downs that can be invasive of privacy and risk outing a trans traveller.

At state level, Wisconsin is grouped among the low-risk states. A national legal-risk assessment of July 2026 placed Wisconsin in its 'Low-Risk States' group alongside Arizona, Delaware, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Virginia and the District of Columbia, describing such jurisdictions as having largely refrained from targeting transgender adults while not taking extraordinary steps to protect them. The second half of that formulation matters: the assessment records no Wisconsin statute restricting where trans people may be, and no state-level protection of comparable weight to the federal measures described above.

Wisconsin has no state ban on gender-affirming care for minors. Governor Tony Evers vetoed Assembly Bill 465 on 6 December 2023, blocking a measure that would have restricted such care; the Human Rights Campaign stated that the veto kept the restriction from taking effect in the state.

Wisconsin has no state ban on trans school athletes either. On 2 April 2024 Governor Evers vetoed a bill passed by the Republican-controlled Legislature that would have limited high school athletes to teams matching the sex assigned at birth. The bill's sponsor called the veto 'disgusting'; the Associated Press reported that Evers had promised the veto when the bill was introduced and that Democrats did not have the votes to stop its passage in the Legislature.

Care access is nonetheless constrained by federal funding pressure rather than state law. On 13 January 2026 UW Health and Children's Wisconsin each announced a pause on gender-affirming pharmacologic care for patients under 18, after the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services said it would deny Medicaid and Medicare payments to hospitals providing such care to minors. Mental and behavioural health services continued. Wisconsin Attorney General Josh Kaul joined a coalition of states seeking to block the HHS declaration.

Official hostility at federal level extends to enforcement machinery. In December 2025 the attorney general instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists promoting what she called radical gender ideology, describing such activists as domestic terrorist groups, and a May 2026 national counterterrorism strategy stated that counterterrorism activity would prioritise the rapid identification and neutralisation of groups whose ideology is described as anti-American, radically pro-transgender and anarchist.

Custody carries documented harm. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted Florida-based policies for transgender inmates that mandate cutting their hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy and psychiatric drugs; imprisoned transgender people reported being denied care, and the Bureau of Prisons stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners it holds from 2025. In immigration detention, transgender men were subjected to forced-labour programmes with guards justifying them by saying they would treat them 'like a man,' and those who refused faced beatings and solitary confinement, alongside widely reported severe sexual abuse.

66186276B37442548568489.name: Michigan
66186276B37442548568489.summary:
Michigan stands under the national framework of the United States. Executive Order 14168, in force since January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary and requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and issues new passports only as M or F on the supporting documents submitted. Passports already holding an X remain valid until expiry, but trans and nonbinary travellers report confiscation or blocked applications, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU is suing the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and in November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the department's passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a policy in place since 1992.

Entry carries a second exposure. On 25 February 2025 the State Department announced that it would refuse visas to trans athletes seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sporting events, flagging such applicants with an internal marking and treating a listed gender other than the one assigned at birth as grounds for a permanent ban for fraud. Screening at United States checkpoints can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that are invasive of privacy, and several foreign governments have issued advisories about trans people travelling to the United States over identity-document and data rules.

State law in Michigan runs in the opposite direction to the federal posture. Governor Gretchen Whitmer signed the first major expansion of the Elliott-Larsen Civil Rights Act on 8 March 2023, codifying sexual-orientation and gender-identity protections into state statute, after a July 2022 Michigan Supreme Court ruling had already made such discrimination unlawful. The legislature banned conversion therapy in 2023 and outlawed the gay and trans panic defense in 2024.

A July 2026 national anti-trans legal risk assessment places Michigan in its Low-Risk States tier, alongside Nevada, finding that both have enacted fairly robust non-discrimination policies but fall short in ensuring healthcare equity and in providing protections for incarcerated transgender individuals. The same assessment designates the United States overall as Do Not Travel for transgender people, so the state-level rating does not offset the federal entry, document and screening risks.

In March 2025 the Michigan House passed a non-binding resolution urging the Michigan High School Athletic Association to bar transgender athletes from girls' and women's sports. The measure is advisory only and does not change state law or the state's non-discrimination protections.

Care access is constrained nationally. Executive Order 14187 of January 2025 described gender-affirming care for minors as chemical and surgical mutilation of children, in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed over 20 hospitals for records of patients under 19, the federal government shut down specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline in July 2025, and October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. Gender-affirming care for children is already banned in 27 states, and several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court.

A federal judge denied civil-rights advocates' request to halt a neighbouring state's ban on gender-affirming medical care for minors. Hormones and puberty blockers are barred after 28 August, transition surgeries for minors are prohibited, and the law sunsets in 2027. The case indicates how regional courts have treated such care bans and is not evidence about Michigan law.

66186276B98615608994420.name: Nevada
66186276B98615608994420.summary:
Travellers entering Nevada are subject to the United States federal document regime. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, recognises only two sexes for federal purposes and directs agencies to implement that binary; the State Department suspended applications for passport gender-marker changes and ended the self-identified 'X' passport option on 22 January 2025. Passports issued before January 2025 carrying a marker other than sex assigned at birth remain valid until expiry, but new applications are processed only as M or F. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in force since 1992.

Entry rules add a separate exposure. Under Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 and the State Department announcement of 25 February 2025, trans athletes seeking to enter the country to compete in women's sporting events are refused visas, with applicants flagged under the internal code 'SWS25'; an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as having committed fraud and barred permanently. Screening at US checkpoints carries an outing risk, since TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs invasive of privacy. Several foreign governments have responded to these document and data rules: in April 2025 multiple countries issued advisories about trans people travelling to the United States, and in March 2025 at least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for their trans and nonbinary citizens.

Nevada's own framework is protective on identity documents and anti-discrimination. State law bars discrimination on the basis of gender identity and expression alongside sexual orientation. Since 2016 Nevada Vital Records has issued a corrected-gender birth certificate on two affidavits alone, with sex reassignment surgery not required, and comparable changes are available for driver's licences and state IDs. A law signed 22 June 2017 abolished the 1988 requirement that transgender people publish their names in newspapers before legal sex changes on government documents. Nevada has offered an 'X' third-gender designation on driver's licences, birth certificates and state IDs since 2019 with no medical documentation required, a state-level option that the federal passport suspension does not extend.

Care access inside Nevada is broader than the federal baseline but constrained at its edges. In March 2018 the state Medicaid agency announced it would cover sex-reassignment surgery, state law bans health insurers from discriminating against transgender patients, and a bill signed in June 2023 requiring insurers, including Medicaid, to cover all medically necessary gender-affirming treatments took effect 1 January 2024. In May 2023 the governor signed a law protecting transgender and intersex individuals in state correctional facilities, while the 2023 omnibus bill SB 302, which would have shielded gender-affirming care and abortion, was vetoed.

A July 2026 national legal risk assessment credits Nevada with fairly robust non-discrimination policies but finds it falls short on healthcare equity and on protections for incarcerated transgender people; Nevada sits in the assessment's Low-Risk group (Arizona, Delaware, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Virginia, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia), directly below the most-protective tier.

Federal measures continue to apply inside Nevada regardless of state policy. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted Florida-based policies mandating conversion therapy for transgender inmates, including cutting hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy and drugs, and the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025. In December 2025 the Attorney General instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists described as promoting "radical gender ideology"; a May 2026 White House counterterrorism strategy stated that activities would prioritise the identification and neutralisation of groups whose ideology is "anti-American, radically pro-transgender, and anarchist." Executive Order 14187 of January 2025 described gender-affirming care for minors as "chemical and surgical mutilation of children," the Department of Justice subpoenaed over 20 hospitals in summer 2025 for full records of patients under 19, specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline were shut down in July 2025, and October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. Several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court.

The Movement Advancement Project's Equality Map records state-by-state rules on whether transgender people may use public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity, and is the source used to situate Nevada within that comparison.

66186276B21291522594454.name: Maryland
66186276B21291522594454.summary:
Maryland stands under United States federal law on identity documents, and that layer is the sharpest document risk for a trans visitor. Executive Order 14168 of 20 January 2025 defines sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary and requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker inconsistent with sex assigned at birth, so new passports are issued as M or F on the supporting documents submitted, while passports already carrying an X remain valid until expiry. The Supreme Court allowed those restrictions to take effect in November 2025, superseding a State Department policy in force since 1992. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad, and the ACLU is in litigation with the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs. No Maryland instrument can alter a federal passport, so a visitor's document may fail to match their presentation for the duration of the trip.

Entry screening adds a separate exposure. In February 2025 the State Department announced that trans athletes entering to compete in women's sports would be refused, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking, and treating an applicant who lists a gender other than their assigned sex as grounds for a permanent ban for fraud. Several foreign governments responded: in April 2025 multiple countries issued advisories about trans people travelling to the United States over identity-document and data rules, and in March 2025 at least eight countries, among them Finland and Denmark, adjusted entry guidance for trans and nonbinary citizens. Inside Maryland, travellers still pass federal checkpoint procedures under which secondary screening, devices and pat-downs can be initiated, an outcome that outs a passenger to officers in public view.

Facilities rules are restrictive at the federal layer. The same executive order barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, which reaches federally funded settings in Maryland such as national park and federal building restrooms. The wider national tally is uneven: a Movement Advancement Project count records state bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine states and one territory, outright state bans on facility use by gender identity in additional states, and no such ban in 29 states, four territories and the District of Columbia, with some states making trans bathroom use a criminal offence in defined circumstances. In April 2025 a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol, which civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under that state's law.

Protective state law in Maryland has not removed documented violence against trans residents. On 11 September 2026 Sophie Lee, a 27-year-old Black trans woman, was found shot in Baltimore's Charles Village and died; it was the second killing of a Black trans woman shot to death in Baltimore within ten weeks. A July 2026 analysis plotting recorded anti-trans incidents against each state's law score placed Maryland in the 'Safest States' band with a law score of 23.5 and 11.1 recorded incidents, while Louisiana recorded the worst law score at 24.7 and the highest incident count at 11.6. The finding that a strong statutory floor does not by itself predict incident counts applies directly to how a visitor should read Maryland's reputation.

Detention carries documented harm under rules Maryland does not set. Federal policy on housing transgender prisoners moved in both directions between 2015 and 2018: a January 2015 immigration-detention memo directed that transgender detainees be housed according to gender identity, and 2016 Department of Justice guidelines forbade corrections agencies from assigning trans inmates to men's or women's units solely on birth anatomy, but the 2018 revision of the Federal Bureau of Prisons Transgender Offender Manual removed the commitment to recommend housing by gender identity and replaced it with case-by-case placement in which 'biological sex' is the initial determination and gender identity is used only in rare cases. From 2026 the Bureau adopted policies mandating conversion-therapy-style treatment for transgender inmates, including cutting hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy and drugs, and it stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025. Trans women held in men's facilities are subjected to what sources describe as V-coding, the assignment of trans women to aggressive cisgender male cellmates, characterised as a central part of a trans woman's sentence, and trans women who physically resist sexual assault are often charged with assault and placed in solitary confinement, with the charge used to extend the sentence and deny parole. A 2021 California study found 69% of surveyed trans women prisoners reported unwanted sexual acts, 58.5% reported violent sexual assault and 88% reported a marriage-like relationship. A visitor held in Maryland stands under these federal practices.

sources.summary: Federal policy on housing transgender prisoners moved in both directions between 2015 and 2018. A January 2015 ICE memo directed that transgender immigration detainees be housed according to gender identity, and in 2016 the US Department of Justice released guidelines forbidding corrections agencies from assigning trans inmates to men's or women's units solely on birth anatomy. 66186276B43071933723331.name: California
66186276B43071933723331.summary:
California is one of the states of the United States, and a trans visitor to California stands under the federal framework in every respect that touches documents, screening and admission. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, and prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992. A traveller's passport can therefore mismatch their presentation, and trans and nonbinary travellers have reported passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU is suing the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records.

Airport screening follows national rules. TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs that are invasive of privacy and can expose a traveller's trans status. Several foreign governments have responded to the document and data rules: in April 2025 multiple countries issued advisories about trans people travelling to the United States, and by March 2025 at least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, had adjusted travel guidelines for their trans and nonbinary citizens. Visa decisions follow national rules as well. In February 2025 the State Department announced a ban on trans athletes entering the country to compete in women's sports, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking, and treating an applicant who lists a gender other than sex assigned at birth as grounds for a permanent ban on grounds of fraud.

Federal custody and care measures apply inside California like every other state. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted policies mandating conversion therapy for transgender inmates, including cutting hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy and drugs; imprisoned transgender people have reported being denied care, and the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners it holds from 2025. In December 2025 the Attorney General instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists described as promoting "radical gender ideology" and characterised as "domestic terrorist groups". On care, Executive Order 14187 of January 2025 described gender-affirming care for minors as "chemical and surgical mutilation of children", the Department of Justice subpoenaed over 20 hospitals in summer 2025 for full records of patients under 19, specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline were shut down in July 2025, and October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. Several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court.

California's own law runs against that current. Governor Gavin Newsom signed SB 107 in September 2022, making California the first sanctuary state for transgender youth seeking medical care: out-of-state youth can obtain hormones and puberty blockers here, and the law shields families from child-abuse investigations or criminal prosecution for seeking gender-affirming care.

Recorded hostility in California is nonetheless the highest in the country. The GLAAD ALERT Desk documented more than 1,000 anti-LGBTQ incidents nationwide in 2025, and California recorded the most of any state at 198, ahead of New Hampshire (72), Texas (66), Ohio (50) and Washington (50). Law-enforcement data for Los Angeles shows a dramatic increase in anti-LGBTQ hate-crime reports over the same period, coinciding with Governor Newsom's platforming of anti-trans figures.

Detention conditions in the state differ from federal practice. As of January 2021 California is the one state that allows transgender people to be housed in prison according to their gender identity, with identity-based housing inside the general population and no trans-only separate facility documented; in 2015 it became the first state to fund gender-affirming surgeries for transgender prison inmates, and the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation issued operational guidelines for transgender inmates. Federal policy returned to placement by sex assigned at birth after the January 2017 federal guidance was rescinded.

66186276B10610315112087.name: Minnesota
66186276B10610315112087.summary:
Minnesota stands under the United States federal framework, which governs the identity documents a trans visitor carries and the screening they pass at checkpoints. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary and barred self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The State Department stopped processing the X marker; new passport applications are issued only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X remain valid until they expire. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992.

Visa exposure follows the same rule. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 and the State Department announcement of 25 February 2025 refuse visas to trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sporting events; applicants are flagged under the internal marking SWS25, and listing a gender other than sex assigned at birth can be treated as fraud warranting a permanent bar. Foreign governments have responded to these document and data rules: in April 2025 several countries issued advisories about trans people travelling to the United States, and by March 2025 at least eight European countries, among them Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the country.

Checkpoint screening carries an outing risk inside Minnesota as elsewhere in the United States. TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs that are invasive of privacy and can disclose a traveller's trans status to officers and to other passengers in the queue.

State law in Minnesota runs against the federal direction. Minnesota Session Law 2023 ch. 29 (HF 146) provides that gender-affirming health care as defined in the Act "is against the public policy of this state and must not be enforced or applied," and it amends the state's provisions on warrants, arrests and extraditions as they relate to out-of-state laws on gender-affirming health care. The practical effect for a visitor is that Minnesota will not enforce or give effect to another state's prohibition on that care, and will not process the arrest or return machinery such a prohibition would otherwise trigger here.

A national trans legal risk assessment published in July 2026 lists Minnesota among the most protective states, in a tier with California, Colorado, Connecticut, Hawaii, Illinois, Massachusetts, Maryland and New Jersey.

sources.title: CeCe McDonald (Wikipedia; Minnesota prisoner-placement case)
sources.summary: Documented Minnesota DOC placement practice, birth-sex determined: CeCe McDonald, a transgender woman, pleaded guilty to second-degree manslaughter and was sentenced on 4 June 2012 to 41 months; her attorneys acknowledged there was 'no way' she would be sent to a women's prison and 'really no history of transgender people being placed according to their gender identity'. 66186276B83663796884405.name: Connecticut
66186276B83663796884405.summary:
Connecticut is a state within the United States, and its laws stand under the national framework that governs a trans visitor's entry, identity documents and screening. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, and prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992.

Travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad, and the ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs. Screening at checkpoints carries an outing risk: TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that are invasive of privacy. Visa applicants who list a gender other than their assigned sex can be treated as committing fraud and barred permanently, and since February 2025 trans athletes have been barred from entering the country to compete in women's sports, with an internal marking applied to flagged applicants.

Care access for a visitor is constrained at the federal layer. Executive Order 14187 of January 2025 described gender-affirming care for minors as "chemical and surgical mutilation of children," leading some hospitals to pause care, and in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed over 20 hospitals for full records of patients under 19. In July 2025 the federal government shut down specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, and October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. Gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states, and several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court.

Against that national backdrop, Connecticut's own law runs in the opposite direction. A July 2026 national legal-risk ranking, built from a rubric applied to thousands of tracked anti-trans bills covering youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver-licence restrictions and the end of legal recognition, places Connecticut in a fifteen-state most-protective tier whose laws have gone above and beyond in safeguarding trans rights.

Connecticut also operates a shield or refuge law. The MAP Transgender Healthcare Equality Map, with data as of 27 September 2026, lists Connecticut as a state holding a shield law or executive order dating from 2022. The shield protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges where the care is legal in Connecticut but banned in the person's home state, which makes the state directly relevant to a visitor travelling from a state with a youth-care ban.

66186276B11383391196245.name: Illinois
66186276B11383391196245.summary:
Illinois stands under the national framework of the United States, where travel documents are the sharpest exposure for a trans visitor. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed federal agencies to use "sex" rather than "gender."

The State Department has stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are adjudicated only as M or F from supporting documents, while passports already issued with an X remain valid until expiry. The Supreme Court allowed the restriction to take effect in November 2025, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992. The ACLU is suing the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and by March 2025 trans and nonbinary travellers reported passports confiscated or blocked at processing, with some left stranded abroad.

Entry screening carries separate exposure. An executive order issued 5 February 2025 on women's sports was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes would be barred from entering the country to compete in women's sports; visa applicants are flagged with an internal marking, and an applicant listing a gender other than the one assigned at birth is treated as fraud carrying a permanent bar. Transportation Security Administration checkpoint procedures involve secondary screening, hand-held devices and pat-downs that can be invasive of privacy and risk outing a trans traveller.

Facilities rules at state level vary sharply. Bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools, and in some states to government buildings, cover 9 states and 1 territory, with trans use of facilities made a criminal offence in certain circumstances; 29 states, 4 territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. In April 2025 a trans student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol after declaring an intention to break the law, which civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law.

State-level identity documents are also being closed. In March 2026 Kansas enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not match sex assigned at birth and barring trans people from sex-segregated facilities, which rights groups call a template for other state legislatures. Equality-map research shows that the conditions for changing a gender marker on a licence or birth certificate differ state by state.

Custody is a documented site of harm. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted Florida-based policies for transgender inmates that mandate cutting their hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy and psychiatric drugs; imprisoned transgender people reported being denied care, and the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners it holds from 2025. In immigration detention, transgender men were subjected to forced-labour programmes with guards justifying them by saying they would treat them "like a man," and those who refused faced beatings and solitary confinement; severe sexual abuse was also widely reported.

Official hostility extends to enforcement machinery. In December 2025 the attorney general instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists promoting what she called radical gender ideology, describing such activists as domestic terrorist groups. A May 2026 national counterterrorism strategy stated that counterterrorism activity would prioritise the rapid identification and neutralisation of groups whose ideology is described as anti-American, radically pro-transgender and anarchist.

Care access is restricted on several fronts. Executive Order 14187 of 28 January 2025 described gender-affirming care for minors as mutilation and some hospitals paused care; in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed more than 20 hospitals for full records of patients under 19, including names, social security numbers and doctors' notes. Gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states, proposed health-department rules in October 2025 would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18, and in July 2025 the federal government shut down specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline.

Other federal measures in force or in litigation include the military purge under Executive Order 14183, the women's sports ban under Executive Order 14201, a January 2025 federal funding freeze and an October 2025 rule blocking student loan forgiveness for public workers who provide gender-affirming care to transgender youth. Several of these orders have been blocked or enjoined in court, so the operative position on each measure should be checked before travel.

Against that framework, Illinois sits at the protective end of state law. A July 2026 national legal-risk ranking built from a rubric over thousands of tracked anti-trans bills places Illinois in the fifteen-state "Most Protective" tier, whose laws are assessed as having gone above and beyond in safeguarding trans rights. The tier also includes California, Massachusetts, Minnesota, New York and Washington among its fourteen other members.

Illinois holds a shield or refuge law, recorded as "State has shield law or executive order 2023" on the Movement Advancement Project Transgender Healthcare Equality Map with data as of 27 September 2026. The law protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges where care that is legal in Illinois has been banned in the patient's home state, which bears directly on visitors travelling from ban states to receive care.

The shield position is a minority one nationally. Sixteen states and the District of Columbia, covering 38% of the trans population aged 13 and over, hold shields, while 32 states and 5 territories, covering 56%, hold none. A trans visitor to Illinois therefore reaches a jurisdiction with express statutory protection for care that a majority of states do not provide, while remaining subject to the federal document, entry and enforcement measures described above.

66186276B2592965416524.name: New Mexico
66186276B2592965416524.summary:
New Mexico stands under the national framework of the United States, and that framework is the first exposure a trans visitor faces. Since January 2025, Executive Order 14168 has required federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to the supporting documents submitted, while passports already issued with an X remain valid until they expire. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the State Department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports.

Entry and screening follow national rules regardless of which state the visitor lands in. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the country to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas and flagged internally under the code 'SWS25'; the same announcement states that an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently. At checkpoints, secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs can expose a traveller's trans status to officers and other passengers, according to the National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide, which sets out how to request screening matching one's presentation.

Facility use and identity documents are regulated state by state, so the rules encountered inside New Mexico differ from those in states that restrict them. State bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings are in force in nine states and one territory, with trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances in some jurisdictions, while twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. Enforcement has occurred: in April 2025 a trans student was arrested and handcuffed after using a women's restroom at a state capitol, identified by civil-rights attorneys as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law. Kansas has enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not bear sex assigned at birth and barring trans residents from changing those markers, described by rights groups as a template other legislatures are following. Multiple foreign governments, at least eight European countries including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for their trans and nonbinary citizens after the federal document and data rules, and a national legal risk assessment dated 13 July 2026 identifies four states now designated do-not-travel for trans people.

Within that national picture, New Mexico sits in the fifteen-state 'Most Protective' tier of the July 2026 national legal-risk ranking, alongside California, Colorado, Connecticut, Hawaii, Illinois, Massachusetts, Maryland, Minnesota, New Jersey, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont and Washington. The ranking is built from a rubric applied over thousands of tracked anti-trans bills covering youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver-licence restrictions and the end of legal recognition, and it records that the laws of the protective-tier states have gone above and beyond in safeguarding trans rights.

New Mexico also operates a shield or refuge law, listed by the Movement Advancement Project's Transgender Healthcare Equality Map as 'State has shield law or executive order 2023'. The law protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges when care that is legal in New Mexico has been banned in the home state of the person travelling for it. That protection is directly relevant to a visitor arriving from a state with a care ban, and it applies alongside, not instead of, the federal document and entry rules.

66186276B43575054209436.name: New York
66186276B43575054209436.summary:
New York stands under the United States federal framework, and that framework sets the sharper exposures for a trans visitor regardless of state protections. Executive Order 14168 of January 2025 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth, the State Department no longer processes the X marker, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid only until expiry. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement refusing visas to trans athletes seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sporting events, with applicants flagged under the code 'SWS25' and a declared gender other than sex assigned at birth treated as possible fraud carrying a permanent bar.

Checkpoint screening under these national rules can force disclosure: secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs can expose a traveller's trans status to officers, and multiple foreign governments have issued advisories on exactly this point, several European states adjusting their travel guidance for trans and nonbinary citizens in March 2025.

Against that federal backdrop, New York sits in the fifteen-state 'Most Protective' tier of a July 2026 national legal-risk ranking built from a rubric over thousands of tracked anti-trans bills covering youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver-licence restrictions, and the end of legal recognition. The ranking places New York alongside California, Colorado, Connecticut, Hawaii, Illinois, Massachusetts, Maryland, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont and Washington as states whose laws have, in the assessment's terms, gone above and beyond in safeguarding trans rights. The contrast tier is severe: the worst-law states carry up to five-year prison terms in Idaho, and Florida operates an arrest policy for gender-identity bathroom use.

Care access is the clearest area where New York's own law changes what a visitor faces. The state operates a shield or refuge law, listed by the Movement Advancement Project as a state shield law or executive order from 2023, which protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges where care that is legal in New York was banned in the patient's home state. This is directly relevant to visitors travelling from ban states: gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states nationally, and the shield architecture exists precisely for cross-border care.

The national shield picture remains partial. As of 27 September 2026 the MAP dataset records shields in 16 states and the District of Columbia, covering 38% of the trans population aged 13 and over, while 32 states and five territories, covering 56%, hold none. Some youth-care bans are tracked as permanently blocked in court, while several federal measures, including parts of the executive-order regime, have been enjoined or blocked at various points.

Two federal exposures do not stop at the state line. The Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted policies from 2026 mandating conversion therapy for transgender inmates, including cutting hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy, and stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025; in December 2025 the Attorney General instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists, and a May 2026 White House counterterrorism strategy named groups whose ideology is 'anti-American, radically pro-transgender, and anarchist' as a priority for identification and neutralisation. A visitor detained federally in New York falls under these regimes, not under state protective law.

66186276B97229519707655.name: Oregon
66186276B97229519707655.summary:
Visitors to Oregon enter under a United States federal framework that applies in every state. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, defined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed the attorney general to correct what it called the misapplication of the 2020 Bostock ruling. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed these passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy that had run since 1992.

Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The American Civil Liberties Union is suing the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and Lambda Legal maintains guidance on what documentation to consider and how name and gender changes interact with federal records.

Other federal measures reach the visitor directly. Screening at United States checkpoints carries an outing risk, because TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that are invasive of privacy; several foreign governments responded by issuing advisories about trans people travelling to the United States over identity-document and data rules, and at least eight European countries adjusted their entry guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens in March 2025. Federal custody records are adverse: from 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted policies mandating conversion therapy for transgender inmates, including cutting hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy and drugs, and the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners it holds from 2025. In immigration custody, transgender men have reportedly been subjected to forced-labour programmes with refusals met by beatings, solitary confinement and reports of severe sexual abuse. Care access is constrained: Executive Order 14187 of January 2025 described gender-affirming care for minors as chemical and surgical mutilation of children, the Department of Justice subpoenaed over 20 hospitals in summer 2025 for full records of patients under 19, the specialised LGBTQ youth service on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline was shut down in July 2025, and October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. Several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court.

Against that federal background, Oregon sits in the fifteen-state Most Protective tier of a July 2026 national legal-risk assessment built from a rubric covering thousands of tracked anti-trans bills, including youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver-licence restrictions and the end of legal recognition. The assessment records that Oregon's laws have gone above and beyond in safeguarding trans rights, and it contrasts this with the worst-law states, where penalties reach up to five years in prison or an arrest policy for gender-identity bathroom use.

The Movement Advancement Project's Transgender Healthcare Equality Map, with data as of 27 September 2026, lists Oregon as a state holding a shield law or executive order from 2023. That shield protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges when the care provided is legal in Oregon but banned in the patient's home state, which is directly material for visitors travelling in from states with youth-care bans.

The national picture behind that entry is uneven: 16 states and the District of Columbia, covering 38 per cent of the transgender population aged 13 and over, hold healthcare shields, while 32 states and five territories, covering 56 per cent, hold none. Youth-care bans are tracked on the same map and some have been permanently blocked in court.

66186276B98073251815399.name: Rhode Island
66186276B98073251815399.summary:
Travel documents are the sharpest risk for a trans visitor to Rhode Island, because they are issued under national rules rather than state ones. Executive Order 14168 of January 2025 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker inconsistent with sex assigned at birth, new passport applications are processed only as M or F on the supporting documents submitted, and passports already issued with an X remain valid until they expire. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the State Department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports.

Entry and screening follow the same national layer. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025, titled 'Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports', was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the country to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas and flagged internally under the code 'SWS25'; the same announcement states that an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently. Airport screening carries a separate exposure: the National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can reveal a traveller's trans status to TSA officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request screening of the type matching one's presentation.

Against that background, Rhode Island is listed among the 'Most Protective' states in the anti-trans legal risk assessment published on 13 July 2026, in the gender-identity non-discrimination tier, and the assessment also places Rhode Island among jurisdictions whose shield protections are enforceable against out-of-state action. The same assessment reports erosion at the federal layer and concludes that the top tier can no longer be considered most protective nationwide, so a visitor's protection at the state level coexists with the document, visa and screening rules described above. No Rhode Island-specific restriction on identity documents, facility use or care appears in the source inventory.

66186276B98555229882405.name: Washington
66186276B98555229882405.summary:
Washington stands under the United States national framework on travel documents and entry screening, which applies in every state. An executive order of 20 January 2025 redefined sex for national purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed the national justice department to "correct the misapplication" of a 2020 Supreme Court employment ruling. The national foreign-affairs department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, while X-marker passports issued before the change remain valid until expiry. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a departmental policy in place since 1992; the policy remains challenged in the federal courts, and trans and nonbinary travellers reported passports confiscated or blocked at processing by March 2025, some stranded abroad.

Entry screening carries its own exposure nationwide. Following an executive order of 5 February 2025 on women's sports, the foreign-affairs department announced on 25 February 2025 that it would bar trans athletes from entering the country to compete in women's sports, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking and treating as fraud, with a permanent bar, any applicant listing a gender other than the one assigned at birth. Transport-security checkpoint procedures involve secondary screening, hand-held devices and pat-downs that can be invasive of privacy and risk outing a trans traveller.

Against that national backdrop, a July 2026 legal risk assessment names Washington among the most protective states in the country. The same assessment groups Washington with Colorado, Hawaii and Maryland as states holding comprehensive health-insurance laws that cover facial hair removal and an expanded range of gender-affirming procedures, and records refugee protections for people fleeing hostile states.

Two ballot initiatives scheduled for November, I-001 and I-638, are flagged by that assessment as targeting transgender residents. They are proposals rather than enacted law at the time of assessment, and the sources do not record a result.

Custody in Washington has produced documented harm. In October 2023 Washington state prisons were legally required, under court order and rulings, to provide gender-affirming healthcare and/or sexual-reassignment surgery to inmates. In July 2024 a trans woman prisoner was transferred from a women's prison back to a men's prison as punishment for consensual sex with a cisgender inmate of the women's prison, so birth-sex housing was used as a sanction.

64170238B96397749018979.name: Monaco
64170238B96397749018979.summary:
Same-sex intimacy has been legal in Monaco since the 18th century, and the age of consent is 15 for same-sex and opposite-sex relationships alike. Hate-motivated conduct on the basis of sexual orientation is criminalised across several statutes. Loi n° 1.299 of 15 July 2005 on public freedom of expression bans hate speech and incitement to hatred and violence on that ground.

Article 234-2 of the Civil Code, amended by Loi n° 1.435 of 8 November 2016, punishes threats based on sexual orientation with 2 to 5 years' imprisonment and related offences with 6 months to 3 years. Law n° 1.478 of 12 November 2019 inserted sexual orientation into Civil Code articles 238-1, 239 and 421, covering violent acts not causing total incapacity (6 months to 1 year), attacks on a partner or co-resident (10 years), and unprovoked attacks on a person or group (five years).

A Monegasque court applied this framework in July 2010, sentencing a man to five days' imprisonment and a €5,000 fine for openly homophobic rhetoric against a gay man. It is the only documented prosecution in the sources.

Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned by law; Outright International reports such discrimination as rare but describes protections as very limited. Monaco does not recognise same-sex marriage and same-sex couples have no right to adopt children. Since 27 June 2020 same-sex couples may sign a contrat de vie commune, a cohabitation agreement signed before a notary and deposited at a public registry.

Transgender people cannot alter their legal gender in Monaco. LGBTIQ visibility is limited: roughly ten people are reported to dare to be openly out, no gay Pride is held anywhere in the principality, and there are no official gay bars, clubs or events. Visitors are directed to France or Italy for Pride.

Monaco is not an EU member, so EU LGBT-rights protections do not bind it, though it maintains close cultural and economic ties with France. France handles defence, and its armed forces allow openly gay, lesbian, bisexual and transgender people to serve; Monaco itself maintains only a National Guard.

sources.summary: Outright International country overview (last updated 12 March 2026): same-sex intimacy legal but very few protections — hate crimes and hate speech on sexual orientation are penalised, while discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned (reported discrimination is described as rare); same-sex couples have no marriage or adoption, and LGBTIQ visibility in the principality is limited.

French gay travel guide Monaco page: no gay Pride is held anywhere in Monaco (visitors are sent to France or Italy for one); the ~200-hectare state is pitched as a luxury/relaxation destination with an LGBTQ+-welcoming accommodation directory but no discernible local scene.

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report for Monaco: no significant changes; significant issues limited to libel and lèse-majesté laws (not enforced); no torture, arbitrary detention or other abuses reported.

Nice-Matin via Monaco Haut Commissariat (March 2025, French): homosexuality decriminalised since the 18th century, yet Monaco ranks near the bottom of European LGBT-rights rankings — no equal succession, survivor pensions or parental leave for same-sex partners; roughly 10 people dare to be openly out; Council of Europe rapporteur Béatrice Fresko-Rolfo: "C’est le triste bilan de Monaco".

Queer In The World Monaco guide (updated 3 December 2023): homosexuality legal and SOGI discrimination illegal only in certain contexts — limited protections with room for improvement; advises visitors to stay current with local laws and customs.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Hate-speech protection rests on Loi n° 1.299 of 15 July 2005 on public freedom of expression, which bans hate speech and incitement to hatred and violence based on sexual orientation. Article 234-2 of the Civil Code, amended by Loi n° 1.435 of 8 November 2016 (technological crime law), punishes threats based on sexual orientation with 2–5 years' imprisonment and related offences with 6 months–3 years. In July 2010 a Monegasque court jailed a man for 5 days and fined him €5,000 for openly homophobic rhetoric against a gay man. Law n° 1.478 of 12 November 2019 added 'sexual orientation' to Civil Code articles 238-1 (6 months–1 year for violent acts not causing total incapacity), 239 (10 years for attacking a partner or co-resident) and 421 (5 years' probation for unprovoked attacks on a person or group). Monaco does not recognize same-sex marriage, and ILGA-Europe's 2019 ranking (45th of 49 European countries) notes that transgender people cannot alter their legal gender. Since 27 June 2020 same-sex couples may sign a cohabitation agreement (contrat de vie commune), introduced in Parliament on 16 April 2018, unanimously approved by the National Council on 4 December 2019 and in force six months after publication in the Journal de Monaco; it is signed before a notary and deposited at a public registry. Cohabiting couples are treated like siblings for inheritance tax, not like married couples, and the arrangement is also open to siblings and parents/children. Same-sex couples have no right to adopt children. The LGBT community supports some gay-friendly establishments inside Monaco, but there are no official gay bars, clubs or events in the country, unlike nearby French cities Marseille, Nice and Lyon. Monaco is not an EU member, so EU LGBT-rights protections do not bind it, though it has strong cultural and economic ties with France. Monaco has no armed forces, only a National Guard; France handles defence and allows openly gay, lesbian, bisexual and transgender people to serve. The age of consent is 15 for both same-sex and opposite-sex relationships. The 2011 anti-discrimination bill's article 44 would have required a school programme every year of primary and secondary cycles to sensitise against racism and all article 1 discriminations (including sexual orientation), but the Council of Government did not approve the bill and its 18 December 2012 replacement dropped the sexual-orientation provisions. Same-sex couples' inability to adopt children directly affects family formation for youth, and most Monegasques affiliate with the Catholic Church, which regards homosexuality and transgender identity as immoral.

64170238B96397749018979.tangentialFactors:
Monaco ranks near the bottom of European LGBT-rights rankings. ILGA-Europe's 2019 assessment placed the principality 45th of 49 European countries. Council of Europe rapporteur Béatrice Fresko-Rolfo summarised the position as "C'est le triste bilan de Monaco".

Same-sex partners have no access to equal succession rights, survivor pensions or parental leave. Cohabiting couples are treated like siblings for inheritance tax purposes rather than like married couples, and the cohabitation agreement is equally open to siblings and to parents and children.

A 2011 anti-discrimination bill would have required an annual school programme across primary and secondary cycles to sensitise pupils against racism and all discrimination covered by its article 1, including sexual orientation. The Council of Government did not approve the bill, and its replacement of 18 December 2012 dropped the sexual-orientation provisions.

The 2023 US State Department Human Rights Report recorded no significant changes for Monaco and limited its significant issues to libel and lèse-majesté laws, which it described as not enforced; no torture, arbitrary detention or similar abuses were reported.

Most Monegasques affiliate with the Catholic Church, which treats homosexuality and transgender identity as immoral. The gay travel guide Gay Voyageur pitches the roughly 200-hectare state as a luxury and relaxation destination with an LGBTQ+-welcoming accommodation directory but no discernible local scene, and points visitors to Marseille, Nice and Lyon for gay nightlife and events.
64170238B96397749018979.localsOnly:
The contrat de vie commune entered Parliament on 16 April 2018, was approved unanimously by the National Council on 4 December 2019, and took effect six months after publication in the Journal de Monaco, on 27 June 2020. The agreement is executed before a notary and lodged with a public registry.

Residents have no statutory route to change legal gender, and no anti-discrimination statute covers sexual orientation or gender identity in employment, housing, education or services. Reported discrimination is described as rare, but there is no complaint mechanism to test that.

The 2012 replacement anti-discrimination bill left residents without the school sensitisation programme contemplated in 2011. Employment and public-accommodation protection on sexual-orientation grounds remains unenacted.

Monaco's only military formation is the National Guard; defence rests with France, whose forces accept openly LGBT service members.
64170238B96397749018979.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory reports a prosecution under Loi n° 1.299 of 15 July 2005 or under Law n° 1.478 of 12 November 2019, so enforcement of those provisions beyond the July 2010 case is unresolved.

No source addresses entry, visa or border-screening practice, customs questioning, or the treatment of gender markers on foreign passports at Monegasque borders. Nothing in the inventory indicates whether a visitor's documents are inspected for sex or gender inconsistencies.

Facilities, healthcare access, and any rule on restroom or single-sex-space use for transgender visitors are not sourced here. Neither are hate-crime statistics, police reporting practices, or the operation of the protection machinery for LGBTIQ visitors.

Outright International's characterisation of discrimination as rare is self-reported and carries no underlying data in the inventory; the absence of a statutory ban means official statistics on complaints cannot exist.

The July 2010 judgment is described only in secondary coverage; the court, the exact provision applied and any appeal outcome are not available from these sources.

SYN-ABW.name: Aruba
SYN-ABW.summary:
Aruba is a constituent territory within the Kingdom of the Netherlands. It applies its own Criminal Code (Wetboek van Strafrecht / Kódigo Penal), enacted in 2012, which carries its anti-discrimination provisions; decisions of its Appeals Court in sexual-orientation cases have been reviewed by the Supreme Court of the Netherlands.

Same-sex sexual activity is legal for both male and female forms. The age of consent is 16 and is equal for heterosexual and homosexual intercourse.

Article 1:221 of the Criminal Code defines discrimination as any form of discrimination, exclusion, restriction or preference that has the purpose or effect of affecting recognition, enjoyment or the exercise of human rights and fundamental liberties in political, economic, social or cultural fields or in other areas of social life. Articles 2:61 and 2:62 provide penalties ranging from fines to one year of imprisonment. The enumerated grounds cover sexual orientation only; gender identity and gender expression are not addressed anywhere in the provision. A trans visitor therefore has no statutory ground of protection against discrimination.

On 12 July 2024 the Supreme Court of the Netherlands upheld the Appeals Court decision barring discrimination based on sexual orientation, in the ruling that made same-sex marriage legal in Aruba.

On 8 September 2016 the Staten of Aruba passed a civil-code amendment opening registered unions to same-sex couples by 11 votes to 5, with four abstentions, after a 2.5-year campaign sponsored by openly gay MP Desirée de Sousa-Croes and an Igualdad Aruba petition of nearly 20,000 signatures. The amendment extends the marriage articles of the civil code to those registered unions and grants spousal pension succession and emergency medical decision-making rights. Aruba's own news service reported the vote as making the island the first in the Caribbean to act.

Marriages performed in the Netherlands were already recognised throughout the Kingdom, and the bill's sponsor had used exactly that route. The Associated Press reported that religious and cultural opposition to the measure was strong, and that neither Sint Maarten nor Curaçao allowed such unions at the time.

Charlene and Esther Oduber-Lamer reported frequent harassment and having rocks thrown at them during their court challenge of 2004 to 2007, which forced Aruba and the other Dutch Caribbean islands to recognise same-sex marriage. The Aruban government was particularly vocal in opposing same-sex marriage during that court challenge, and the Roman Catholic Church, the island's largest denomination, contributed to mainstream societal opposition.

The official Aruba tourism board markets the island as an established LGBT destination, positioning feeling safe, secure and welcome as the foundation of the offering and quoting a repeat visitor of nearly 20 years who reports never encountering mistreatment or discrimination based on sexual orientation. This is the destination's own marketer speaking, not independent evidence, but it documents mainstream tourism positioning.

GlobalGayz describes Aruba as tolerant and mostly open with a smaller, quieter out-and-proud LGBT population than Curaçao, and notes that same-sex adoption is legal. Several gay bars and clubs operate in the capital city of Oranjestad, and various venues, hotels and restaurants cater to or advertise as LGBT-friendly. Numerous LGBT associations operate, including Equality Aruba (Igualdad Aruba), Equal Rights Aruba and Alternative Lifestyle Federation Aruba; the last is quoted: 'Aruba has always been accepting, as long as it's not in their face. People are out, but discreetly out. There has never been anything official.'

Self-description by the destination's own marketer, not independent evidence, but it documents mainstream tourism positioning.

Aruba's own news site (Sep 9, 2016): parliament passed the civil-law amendment granting civil partnerships to same-sex couples by 11 votes to 5 on Sep 8, 2016, making Aruba the first island in the Caribbean; the campaign ran 2.5 years, with openly-gay MP Desiree de Sousa-Croes as sponsor and an Igualdad Aruba petition at nearly 20,000 signatures.

GlobalGayz cultural report (edited Jan 2017): Aruba described as tolerant and mostly open with a smaller, quieter out-and-proud LGBT population than Curacao; notes the government initially declared same-sex unions illegal until challenged by a lesbian couple legally married in the Netherlands, and that same-sex adoption is legal; Catholic influence noted as the main brake.

SYN-ABW.localsOnly:
Residents are covered by Articles 2:61 and 2:62 of the Criminal Code, which provide penalties ranging from fines to one year of imprisonment for discrimination on the enumerated grounds, and by Article 1:221's definition of discrimination. The enumerated grounds cover sexual orientation only.

The 2016 civil-code amendment confers spousal pension succession and emergency medical decision-making rights on registered same-sex unions, and same-sex adoption is legal. Openly gay MP Desirée de Sousa-Croes publicly introduced the registered partnership bill in August 2016, following a 2.5-year campaign and an Igualdad Aruba petition of nearly 20,000 signatures.

SYN-ABW.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether any Aruban instrument addresses gender identity, gender expression, legal gender recognition, or access to gender-affirming care is unresolved in the sources reviewed; the inventory states only that gender identity and gender expression are not addressed in the Criminal Code's discrimination provisions.

Entry, visa and border-screening rules for trans travellers, including any inspection of documents whose gender marker does not match presentation, are not sourced here. The parent-framework statement that Aruba stands under the Netherlands's document rules as they apply here has not been verified against a specific instrument in this inventory.

Enforcement of Articles 2:61 and 2:62 is unresolved: no case, prosecution or penalty under these articles is recorded in the sources reviewed. Whether the 2024 Supreme Court ruling's non-discrimination holding extends beyond sexual orientation to gender identity is also unresolved.

The claim that same-sex adoption is legal rests on a single cultural report (GlobalGayz, edited January 2017) and has not been corroborated against Aruban statute in this inventory.

SYN-AIA.name: Anguilla
SYN-AIA.summary:
Anguilla is a British Overseas Territory whose law is local law: the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not automatically extend to the island, and they can be applied there only by Order in Council.

Sex between men in private is legal, but the repeal was imposed from London rather than enacted by Anguilla's own legislature. On 5 January 2001 the Privy Council ordered decriminalisation of private consensual same-sex conduct in five Caribbean territories: Anguilla, the Cayman Islands, the British Virgin Islands, Montserrat and the Turks and Caicos Islands. The order was issued unilaterally after the local legislatures refused to repeal their statutes, and religious leaders protested the decision. Anguilla had never carried the prohibition in exactly the same statutory form as those other territories.

Anguillian law provides no legislative protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. The Constitution outlaws discrimination only on grounds of race, political opinions, colour, creed, sex or place of origin, so gender identity sits outside the protected categories entirely. A trans visitor therefore has no statutory non-discrimination footing in local law.

The age of consent is set at 18 for homosexual conduct and 16 for heterosexual conduct. The differential exposes same-sex couples to legal risk that different-sex couples do not face.

The Marriage Act defines marriage as the union of a man and a woman as husband and wife. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legal, and Anguilla is one of the British overseas territories that has not legislated for civil partnerships. A commercial destination-wedding service marketing ceremonies on the island states plainly that same-sex marriage is not recognised under Anguillan law, which means only symbolic, non-legal ceremonies are available to same-sex couples; non-legal ceremonies of same-sex couples have taken place.

Public LGBT life is extremely constrained. A subdued and subtle climate of homophobia has pushed local LGBT people toward secrecy. The island has no pride events, gay organisations, venues, bars or clubs and no community infrastructure, which the source attributes to the small population of roughly 15,000 residents. The only recorded public event is a small protest on 17 May 2011 in The Valley marking the International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia.

Visiting same-sex couples have described the island as gay-friendly and reported that nobody was discriminatory in any way, though the source cautions that the situation for locals may differ. A 2023 first-person account by a queer family likewise found gay sex legal through the British decriminalisation order but a muted, not out-and-proud scene, rooted in the imposed colonial legacy rather than local choice.
