Visiting same-sex couples have described the island as 'gay-friendly' and reported that 'nobody was discriminatory in any way', though the source cautions that the situation for locals may differ.

SYN-AIA.tangentialFactors:
Anguilla's decriminalisation forms part of a single act of regional legal change. The Privy Council ruling of 5 January 2001 covered five territories at once, and in each of them the repeal followed the same pattern: local legislatures declined to act, and the United Kingdom's highest court ordered the change instead. Religious leaders across the region protested, and the resulting legal position is widely understood locally as externally imposed rather than chosen.

Comparison with the other British overseas territories is instructive on relationship recognition. Several of them, including some covered by the same 2001 order, have since legislated for civil partnerships or same-sex marriage. Anguilla has not, and the practical confirmation comes from an unusual direction: a commercial wedding vendor selling island venues tells prospective same-sex clients that only symbolic ceremonies are possible, which is consistent with the statutory position in the Marriage Act.

The social picture is shaped by scale. With roughly 15,000 residents, there is no market or population base for dedicated LGBT venues or organisations, and the absence of such infrastructure means no visible point of contact for a visitor seeking community. Travellers' own accounts describe low friction in practice, while a 2023 first-person piece attributes the quietness to a colonial legal legacy rather than to acceptance.
SYN-AIA.localsOnly:
Anguillan residents live under a Constitution that names race, political opinions, colour, creed, sex and place of origin as the protected grounds of non-discrimination. Sexual orientation and gender identity appear nowhere in that list, and no separate statute fills the gap. Residents who experience discrimination on these grounds have no local legislative basis for a claim.

The age-of-consent differential is a matter of local criminal law. Sexual conduct between persons of the same sex is subject to a minimum age of 18, while the age for different-sex conduct is 16, so same-sex couples carry exposure that different-sex couples do not.

For LGBT residents the environment is described as a subdued and subtle climate of homophobia that has pushed people toward secrecy. There are no pride events, no gay organisations, no venues, bars or clubs and no community infrastructure of any kind. The single recorded public action was a small protest held on 17 May 2011 in The Valley for the International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia. Non-legal ceremonies for same-sex couples have nonetheless taken place.

The 2001 decriminalisation carries a particular character locally. It was ordered by the Privy Council after Anguilla's own legislature declined to repeal, and religious leaders protested the change, so the legal permission on the books is not matched by a locally enacted settlement.
SYN-AIA.outOfScopeNotes:
None of the material addresses legal gender recognition, the rules for changing gender markers on passports or other identity documents, or airport and border screening practice in Anguilla. Whether a trans visitor's documents attract scrutiny on arrival is unresolved on this evidence.

Also unsourced: any provision on hate-crime aggravation for offences motivated by gender identity or sexual orientation, any restriction or safeguard on gender-affirming healthcare, and any law or policy on access to sex-separated facilities such as bathrooms, changing rooms or shelters. The extension of the United Kingdom's 2025 single-sex-services code to Anguilla is stated to require an Order in Council, and whether such an order has been made is unresolved.

The sources disagree on the year of decriminalisation. The Associated Press report and the legal histories place the Privy Council order at 5 January 2001, while the 2023 travel account gives 2000. The 2001 date is the better attested of the two.

The characterisation of the island as gay-friendly rests on self-reported accounts by visiting same-sex couples, not on documented enforcement or complaint data, and one of the sources itself cautions that the experience of residents may not match that of tourists. The GlobalGayz country report dates from 2012 and may not reflect conditions now.

SYN-BES.name: Bonaire Sint Eustatius and Saba
SYN-BES.summary:
Caribbean Netherlands comprises Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba, three special municipalities within the Kingdom of the Netherlands. Dutch national law on civil status, marriage and anti-discrimination extends to the islands, and the statutory framework operating in the European Netherlands applies here in the same form.

That protection covers visitors as well as residents. Travel-facing coverage published by GayCities on 14 December 2022 and updated 1 September 2023 ranks Bonaire fifth among destinations in the Caribbean and Latin America that celebrate marriage equality, on the stated basis that as a territory of the Netherlands its citizens and visitors are covered by strict anti-discrimination laws and that same-sex couples are warmly welcomed.

Same-sex unions have been registrable since 2012. On 4 December 2012 the Census Office in Saba recorded the Caribbean Netherlands' first: Cedeno Xiomar Gonzalez, an Aruban national aged 26, wed Israel Ernesto Ruiz Pinto, a Venezuelan national aged 27. Neither man was resident on the island; both were visiting, which establishes a local record of performing same-sex unions for people who are only passing through.

Ceremonies on Saba run routinely through the island registry. The official weddings page of Saba Tourism identifies the Court Room in the Administrative Building as the simplest venue for an efficient civil ceremony and documents registrar Julieta Woods as flexible with couples' wishes, alongside a full destination-wedding supply chain of caterers, florists and accommodation.

No source in the current inventory addresses gender-marker rules on identity documents, entry screening practice, access to gender-affirming care, or facilities and harassment exposure for trans visitors specifically; the findings above rest on marriage and anti-discrimination provisions rather than trans-specific legal text.

For this record: travel-facing evidence that the island markets itself as equality-friendly with statutory protection behind it.

For this record: same-sex unions have been registrable in the islands since 2012, and the territory has a track record of performing them for visitors.

SYN-BES.tangentialFactors:
The strongest positive indicator in the inventory is a ranking rather than a legal instrument: GayCities places Bonaire fifth in a regional top ten, an assessment made by a travel publication on the strength of Dutch anti-discrimination law and marriage equality, not a finding of a court or ministry.

The equality-friendly reputation documented for Bonaire rests on provisions that protect on the basis of sexual orientation and status generally. Nothing in the inventory shows how those provisions are applied when a trans person is the complainant, or whether enforcement bodies treat gender identity as a protected ground in practice on the islands.

The 2012 Saba registration and the Saba Tourism wedding material both concern same-sex couples. They evidence an administrative willingness to process unions for people who are not resident, which is a useful indicator of registry openness, but they say nothing about how registry staff handle a applicant whose presentation differs from the sex recorded on their documents.

SYN-BLM.name: Saint Barthélemy
SYN-BLM.summary:
Saint Barthélemy stands under France's national law as in the metropole: identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as they do in France proper.

No provision of that framework restricts a trans or same-sex visitor. Same-sex marriage has been available since 2013, legal gender-marker change requires neither surgery nor sterilisation, gender-affirming hormone therapy and surgery have been available under French law since 1975, the statute covering discrimination on grounds of gender identity is in force, and the French ban on conversion practices adopted in 2023 applies.

Two limits sit alongside that coverage. Non-binary identity is not recognised in French law, so a visitor whose documents record a non-binary status has no legal counterpart on arrival. Gender-affirming care is delivered on an island of about 8 square miles with roughly 10,000 residents, and the single red flag recorded against Saint Barthélemy in an aggregate travel-safety rating is limited healthcare access; prescriptions and ongoing treatment cannot be assumed to be available locally.

Detention carries the sharpest documented risk. French prison administration policy recognises only biological sex for placement, and trans detainees, overwhelmingly women, are held under birth sex; a 2011 case in Nantes placed a trans woman in a men's prison. Detainees held in Saint Barthélemy fall under that same system. The controller-general of detention places, in an opinion of 25 May 2021 drawing on about 40 referrals received since 2010, found that serious violations of fundamental rights persist across places of detention, with recommendations that also cover intersex and non-binary persons.

An aggregate index rates the collectivity 7.7 out of 10, counting nine positive rights against the one healthcare red flag.

Socially the territory is discreet rather than permissive. It has no LGBTQ venues, no Pride events and no visible scene; same-sex couples attract no attention, crime is low, and the sources record no hostility toward gay or trans visitors.

sources.summary: French prison-system reporting: the controller-general of detention places finds trans detainees — overwhelmingly women held under birth-sex placement — suffer the most in prison; administration policy recognises only biological sex (a 2011 Nantes case placed a trans woman in a men's prison). BLM detainees fall under this French system.

France's Contrôleur général des lieux de privation de liberté opinion of 25 May 2021 on transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty draws on about 40 referrals since 2010. It finds serious violations of fundamental rights persist across places of detention, with recommendations applicable also to intersex and non-binary persons.

The French framework applies in Saint Barthélemy: legal gender-marker change without surgery or sterilisation, hormone therapy and surgery available since 1975, anti-discrimination coverage; non-binary recognition limited.

Full equality under French law applies across about 8 square miles and about 10,000 residents. The luxury-yacht economy has long welcomed gay couples, with no visible scene; discretion is the norm and same-sex couples attract no attention.

Aggregate rating 7.7/10, with 9 positive rights and 1 red flag: legal gender change without surgery, anti-discrimination law in place but limited healthcare access. No government LGBT+ travel advice exists; FCDO shows no warnings. No trans-specific visitor tips have been submitted.

Low crime, an open and accepting culture, no Pride-specific events, and staff trained for diverse guests. Visitors are high-end and discreet; there are no LGBTQ venues or scene, and no hostility is noted.

No government travel advice addressing LGBT+ visitors exists for Saint Barthélemy, and the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office records no warnings for the destination. Absence of official advice is an information gap rather than an assessment of safety.

No trans-specific visitor tips have been submitted to the aggregate index, so the rating rests on legal and structural data instead of first-hand accounts from trans travellers.

The framework is national, so no local ordinance in Saint Barthélemy narrows or widens the protections a visitor encounters; there is no sub-national variation to account for on the ground.

The luxury-yacht economy has long welcomed gay couples, and hospitality staff are described as trained for diverse guests. Discretion is the prevailing norm among a high-end, transient clientele, which keeps any visible scene absent rather than suppressed.

Crime is recorded as low and no hostility toward gay or trans visitors appears in the sources, a context that sits beside rather than offsets the documented detention risk under French prison policy.

Ongoing prescriptions and continuity of treatment cannot be assumed to be filled locally.

SYN-BMU.name: Bermuda
SYN-BMU.summary:
Bermuda is a British Overseas Territory. Local legislation governs, and the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex services code do not automatically extend to Bermuda; United Kingdom measures could be applied only by Order in Council.

The House of Assembly voted 22–16 on 14 May 1994 to decriminalise consensual sex between adult men, striking two sections of the Criminal Code. The debate divided the island, with religious leaders split and the Christian Coalition staging marches against the change.

In July 2013 the Senate passed the Human Rights Amendment Act, which outlawed discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and, in the same instrument, on grounds of age. Same-sex marriage was not permitted at that point.

The Governor gave assent to the Domestic Partnership Act in February 2018. It replaced same-sex marriage with domestic partnerships open to both same-sex and opposite-sex couples, making Bermuda the first jurisdiction to revoke marriage equality. Recognition of a same-sex partner therefore rests on the partnership register rather than on marriage.

sources.summary: Bernews (Feb 2018): Bermuda's Governor gave assent to the Domestic Partnership Act 2017, replacing same-sex marriage with domestic partnerships for both same-sex and heterosexual couples - the reversal that made Bermuda the first jurisdiction to revoke marriage equality.

Bermuda's AME and other churches protested a gay cruise (Norwegian Dawn, New York–Bermuda, July 12) as 'incompatible with the word of God and the Christian moral fibre', an instance of organised religious hostility toward visible same-sex couples.

LGBTQ Nation/AP (July 2013): Bermuda's Senate passed the Human Rights Amendment Act outlawing discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation (also banning age discrimination); same-sex marriage not then permitted.

Royal Gazette (14 May 1994): the House of Assembly voted 22–16 to decriminalise consensual sex between adult men, removing two Criminal Code sections. The debate split the island, with religious leaders divided and the Christian Coalition staging marches against it.

In July churches including the African Methodist Episcopal congregation protested a gay cruise calling it incompatible with the word of God and the Christian moral fibre, an episode that indicates the reception a visible same-sex couple may meet in public rather than a legal penalty.

The 1994 decriminalisation vote split the island, with religious leaders divided among themselves and the Christian Coalition marching against the reform. That division is the social backdrop to the 2018 reversal of same-sex marriage, which was itself the first such revocation recorded for any jurisdiction.

Residents seeking recognised partnership status use the domestic partnership register established by the Domestic Partnership Act 2017, which is open to opposite-sex couples as well as same-sex couples. Marriage is not the route available to a same-sex couple.

The 1994 amendment removed two sections of the Criminal Code, so consensual sex between adult men is not an offence locally.

SYN-COK.name: Cook Islands
SYN-COK.summary:
The Cook Islands are self-governing in free association with New Zealand. New Zealand nationality and passport rules apply to Cook Islanders, while local criminal law governs conduct on the islands.

Parliament voted on Friday 14 April 2023 to strike the male-sex offences from the Crimes Act through the Crimes Amendment Bill, effective 1 June 2023. A note attached to the bill cited growing acceptance of LGBT people in the Cook Islands, and the same bill added protections for victims of sexual abuse and assault.

Sections 154 and 155 of the Cook Islands Crimes Act 1969 criminalised sexual activity between men and any indecent act with or upon another male, with consent explicitly not a defence. Reported maximum terms differ across sources: the 2017 coverage gives seven years for sex between men and five years for an indecent act, while reporting on the repeal cites exposure of up to ten years for indecent acts between males. All sources agree the offences were never enforced in living memory.

Same-sex marriage remains prohibited. The Marriage Amendment Act 2000 defines marriage as between a man and a woman, so a foreign same-sex marriage is not recognised locally and a trans visitor in a same-sex relationship has no spousal standing.

sources.summary: PinkNews (14 Apr 2023): Cook Islands parliament voted on Friday to remove the never-enforced 'indecent acts between males' law — exposure of up to 10 years under the 1969 Crimes Act — through the Crimes Amendment Bill, effective 1 June 2023; a note in the bill cited growing acceptance of LGBTQ+ people, and the bill also adds protections for victims of sexual abuse and assault. Same-sex marriage remains outlawed under the Marriage Amendment Act 2000.

PinkNews (1 Oct 2020): decriminalisation stalled again — MPs deferred the Crimes Bill report by three months. Traces the full path: colonial-era 1969 sections 154/155 (up to 7 years for sex between men) criminalise; a 2017 select committee recommended removing them and 'indecent acts between men'/sodomy were struck from the draft, but MPs later backtracked and the kick-down-the-road continued; notes colonisation introduced the taboo into a historically accepting society.

PinkNews (3 Aug 2017): draft Crimes Bill, written with New Zealand help, would remove sections 154/155 of the 1969 Crimes Act — up to 7 years for gay sex and 5 years for 'any indecent act with or upon any other male', with consent explicitly not a defence. Population 21,000; the country's only LGBTI community group, Te Tiare Association, welcomed the move (member Valentino Wichman quoted on the law's homophobia).

RNZ Pacific (10 Aug 2017): public submissions opened in parliament on the Cook Islands Crimes Bill intended to replace the widely considered outdated 1969 Crimes Act. The clerk of Parliament, John Tangi, confirmed a submission from the Te Tiare Association representing the country's LGBTI community was already before the select committee; at least three lawyers expected to speak on penalties and sentencing.

SYN-COK.tangentialFactors:
The repeal followed a protracted legislative path. A 2017 select committee recommended removing sections 154 and 155, and the provisions were struck from the draft Crimes Bill, drafted with New Zealand assistance; MPs subsequently backtracked. In October 2020 members again pushed the bill's report back, this time by three months, before the 2023 passage.

Reporting on the 2020 deferral attributes the taboo underlying sections 154 and 155 to colonisation, describing the society as historically accepting of same-sex relations before that period.

Public submissions on the Cook Islands Crimes Bill opened in Parliament on 10 August 2017, the bill being intended to replace the widely considered outdated 1969 Crimes Act.
SYN-COK.localsOnly:
Te Tiare Association, the country's only LGBTI community group, appeared before the select committee and welcomed the draft reform; a member publicly described the 1969 provisions as homophobic. At least three lawyers were expected to speak to the committee on penalties and sentencing.

The 1969 offences were never enforced against residents in living memory, so there is no record of prosecutions of local men under sections 154 and 155.

The marriage bar applies to residents as well as visitors: Cook Islanders cannot contract a same-sex marriage locally, and no local mechanism recognises one contracted abroad.
SYN-COK.outOfScopeNotes:
The penalty figures for the 1969 provisions remain unresolved across the sources: the 2017 coverage gives seven years and five years, and the 2023 repeal coverage gives up to ten years. The inventory does not settle which figures were correct in the statute as it stood before 1 June 2023.

SYN-CUW.name: Curaçao
SYN-CUW.summary:
Curaçao is an autonomous constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands. It stands under the Netherlands's national criminal law and document rules as they apply here, with full autonomy except in defence, foreign affairs and matters reserved to the Supreme Court of the Netherlands.

In April 2015 representatives of all Kingdom governments agreed that LGBT people on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten should receive equal rights without delay, and a package of rights wishes was delivered to ministers in The Hague. The agreement commits the Kingdom's governments to equal treatment; it does not establish a right that a visitor can invoke at a border or before a local court.

Senior Curaçao officials have publicly endorsed equal treatment. In April 2015 commissioner Marvelyne Wiels of Pueblo Soberano backed "equal rights for everyone" in the local press.

Enforcement practice has not consistently followed that rhetoric. Winifred Raveneau, a Pueblo Soberano party colleague of Wiels, opposed the rights push fiercely and used a last-minute, exceptionally strict permit requirement to force Curaçao's 2013 Gay Pride to relocate to a hotel premises. Public LGBT assembly on the island can be obstructed through administrative permitting at short notice.

Curaçao opened an LGBT "Pink House" centre in 2010 and, alongside Aruba and Sint Maarten, has acted as a driver of equal-rights moves across the Kingdom.

sources.summary: GlobalGayz (updated Jan 2017): profiles the ABC islands (Aruba, Bonaire, Curaçao) as 'quiet nests of gay-friendliness' inside the Kingdom of the Netherlands; Curaçao-specific findings: it opened an LGBT 'Pink House' centre in 2010, has full autonomy except defense/foreign affairs/Supreme Court alongside Aruba, and (with Sint Maarten and Aruba) acts as driver of equal-rights moves across the Kingdom. Aruba passed same-sex civil partnerships 8 Sept 2016 — comparator context, not Curaçao law.

Caribisch Netwerk (22 Apr 2015, Dutch): representatives of all Kingdom governments agreed LGBT people on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten should quickly receive equal rights; Curaçao's commissioner Marvelyne Wiels (Pueblo Soberano) publicly backed 'equal rights for everyone' despite party colleague Winifred Raveneau's fierce opposition — Raveneau had forced Curaçao's 2013 Gay Pride to relocate to a hotel via a last-minute exceptionally strict permit. Curaçao Gay Pride's Frank Holtslag cites Curaçao's IGLTA award as 'most gay welcoming in the region'; a rights wishes-package was delivered to ministers in The Hague.

SYN-CUW.tangentialFactors:
Curaçao's international reputation runs ahead of its permitting record. Frank Holtslag of Curaçao Gay Pride cites the island's IGLTA award as naming it the most gay-welcoming destination in the region, and a travel-press profile updated January 2017 describes the ABC islands as quiet nests of gay-friendliness. Both are promotional or editorial characterisations rather than assessments of legal exposure.

Regional comparison: Aruba, a sibling constituent country of the Kingdom, passed same-sex civil partnerships on 8 September 2016. That statute governs Aruba, not Curaçao, and nothing in these sources establishes an equivalent partner-recognition measure in Curaçao itself.

The 2015 equal-rights agreement was pursued through a package of wishes delivered to ministers in The Hague, a diplomatic route that carries no automatic effect in local courts or at the border.
SYN-CUW.localsOnly:
Residents organise through the Pink House centre, opened in 2010 as an LGBT hub and cited in travel-press coverage of the island.

Event approvals depend on party-level positions rather than settled administrative practice. Pueblo Soberano supplied both the commissioner who endorsed equal rights in 2015 and the party colleague whose fierce opposition produced a last-minute, exceptionally strict permit requirement that pushed the 2013 Gay Pride onto hotel premises.

Local officials and Pride organisers publicly frame Curaçao, Aruba and Sint Maarten as the drivers of equal-rights moves across the Kingdom, and invoke the island's IGLTA award in promotion of the destination.

The inventory does not state which specific offences under the extending Netherlands criminal law would be charged against trans or LGBT people here, the penalties attached, or any case in which they have been used against visitors. No enforcement or prosecution data is available in these sources.

SYN-CYM.name: Cayman Islands
SYN-CYM.summary:
The Cayman Islands stands under the United Kingdom's framework. Same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in 2001 through an Order in Council imposed from London after the local legislature declined to act, and the reform left an unequal age of consent in its wake.

No local route to same-sex marriage exists. In March 2019 Grand Court Chief Justice Anthony Smellie struck down the statutory prohibition on same-sex marriage; the Court of Appeal overturned that ruling in August 2019 and restored the ban.

Recognition survives at the level of immigration administration. In December 2020 immigration authorities recognised the overseas same-sex marriage of Paul Pearson and Randall Pinder, who had wed in Ireland, and the Court of Appeal held that refusing recognition would treat persons unequally on sexual-orientation grounds. An overseas marriage therefore carries immigration effects in the Cayman Islands even though no domestic route to marriage exists.

Public visibility in the tourist-facing environment is high. Around 600 people, including the premier, the governor, ministers and MLAs, joined the Cayman LGBTQ Foundation's first Pride parade on 7 August 2021, with broad official participation. Organisers asked participants to refrain from excessive displays of affection as a condition of the public-space route.

sources.summary: PinkNews (11 Aug 2009): UK MPs on the Foreign Affairs Committee criticised the Cayman Islands' draft constitution for deliberately excluding gay rights, calling the omission 'deplorable' and warning the drafting could leave Cayman courts affording citizens less protection than the European Convention on Human Rights Art 14 requires; the FCO countered that the discrimination-grounds list was open-ended. Early-dated evidence of London–local friction over LGBT protections that frames the later recognition rulings.

Cayman News Service (29 Jul 2021): around 600 people — including the premier, the governor, ministers and MLAs — joined the Cayman LGBTQ Foundation's first Pride parade (Sat 7 Aug 2021 debut), an historic turnout with broad official participation; participants were asked to refrain from excessive displays of affection (organisers' condition amid public-space sensitivities). Evidence of high official tolerance in the tourist-facing environment.

Washington Blade (30 Dec 2020): immigration authorities recognised the overseas same-sex marriage of Paul Pearson and Randall Pinder, who wed in Ireland. The Court of Appeal held that refusing recognition would treat persons unequally on sexual-orientation grounds. Grand Court Chief Justice Anthony Smellie had struck down the same-sex marriage ban in March 2019; that ruling was overturned on appeal in Aug 2019, while the recognition-for-immigration-effects line survived.

SYN-CYM.tangentialFactors:
London-local friction over the scope of protections is documented from August 2009, when the United Kingdom's Foreign Affairs Committee criticised the draft Cayman Islands constitution for deliberately excluding gay rights, calling the omission deplorable and warning that the drafting could leave the territory's courts affording citizens less protection than Article 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights requires. The Foreign and Commonwealth Office answered that the draft's list of discrimination grounds was open-ended.

Relationship recognition arrived through the courts and immigration administration rather than the statute book: the marriage ban was restored on appeal while the recognition-for-immigration-effects line survived. A visitor should not read the December 2020 ruling as a general marriage right.

The organisers' condition on displays of affection for the Pride route marks a public-space sensitivity that persists alongside the broad official participation recorded in 2021.
SYN-CYM.localsOnly:
Recognition of an overseas same-sex marriage in the Cayman Islands runs through immigration administration rather than a marriage statute, so its reach is tied to immigration status and the circumstances of the case before the Court of Appeal in December 2020.

The statutory ban on same-sex marriage was reinstated by the Court of Appeal in August 2019, reversing Chief Justice Smellie's March 2019 ruling, and no legislative route to marriage has been enacted since.

The constitutional list of discrimination grounds is described by the United Kingdom's foreign office as open-ended, a position taken in answer to the 2009 Foreign Affairs Committee criticism that the draft had deliberately excluded gay rights.

Unequal age of consent is a resident-facing feature of the criminal law as left by the 2001 decriminalising order.

Official participation in the August 2021 Pride parade included the premier, the governor, ministers and MLAs, indicating institutional tolerance in public visibility while organisers restricted displays of affection on the route.
SYN-CYM.outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory contains no information on legal gender recognition, the sex or gender marking on Cayman Islands identity documents, access to gender-affirming care, restroom or facility rules, or hate-crime provisions covering gender identity.

Whether the unequal age of consent left by the 2001 decriminalisation has since been harmonised is unresolved in the sources; they record the inheritance, not its current text.

Whether Article 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights operates as directly enforceable domestic law in the Cayman Islands is unresolved. The 2009 exchange records a committee warning about the draft's reach and a ministerial reply, not a ruling.

Enforcement data on violence against trans people, sentencing outcomes, and any trans-specific protection machinery are not sourced.

SYN-ESH.name: Western Sahara
SYN-ESH.summary:
Western Sahara is a disputed territory. Moroccan security services, courts and detention facilities operate across the parts of it under Moroccan control, and a visitor there stands under Moroccan law wherever those institutions act. Human Rights Watch recorded that authority in a dispatch of 9 December 2005, covering the trial of seven human-rights defenders from Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara on charges of fomenting illegal protests; the organisation called the charges dubious and demanded a fair trial.

Same-sex intimacy is criminalised under that framework and carries six months to three years of imprisonment. The broad discretion police hold in applying morality provisions is the instrument turned on visibly trans people.

The Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic, a partially recognised state and an African Union member since 2016, claims sovereignty over Western Sahara. Its own legal order is recorded by the Council for Global Equality, Equaldex and ILGA as punishing same-sex sexual activity for both males and females with up to three years of imprisonment, and a global legality roundup published in July 2017 lists the state as a jurisdiction where homosexuality is illegal for men and women, and illegal there for decades. Both claimed frameworks therefore record criminalisation.

Protection machinery is absent on both sides of the dispute. The Spanish Commission for Refugee Aid (CEAR) states that there is no type of protection for LGBTQ individuals in case of discrimination or violence, a conclusion it reaches in part from a 2010 statement by Ahmed Mulay Alli, the Sahrawi state's diplomatic representative in Mexico, that the constitution does not refer to homosexuality or any other sexual practice and does not punish it. The statement resolves nothing for a visitor: the conduct is recorded as criminalised, while the protective text a traveller might rely on does not exist.

A visitor should expect screening, questioning and detention to be carried out by Moroccan officials in the controlled areas, under a morality provision whose wording leaves the decision to arrest largely with the officer on the street. No trans-specific entry rule, gender-marker rule or documented incident of trans-specific violence in the territory is recorded in the available sources.

PinkNews global legality roundup (Jul 2017): lists the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic as a jurisdiction where homosexuality is illegal for men and women, and states that it has been illegal there for decades. The partially-recognised state, an African Union member since 2016, claims sovereignty over Western Sahara. The status recorded for July 2017 is criminalised.

SYN-FLK.name: Falkland Islands (Malvinas)
SYN-FLK.summary:
The Falkland Islands are a British Overseas Territory with their own Legislative Assembly, which legislates locally. Same-sex activity has been legal since 1989 and the age of consent has been equal since 2005.

Same-sex marriage and civil partnerships have been available since 29 April 2017. The Legislative Assembly passed the bill in March 2017 by 7 votes to 1, and the registrar general confirmed by reply in June 2017 that it is law. Civil partnerships are open to opposite-sex couples as well as same-sex couples. A public consultation ahead of the bill showed 90% support for same-sex marriage and 94% for civil partnerships in a territory of roughly 3,000 residents.

The Constitution Order 2008, at Article 16, bans discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. The provision covers sexual orientation only; the sources do not identify a gender-identity ground in the Constitution.

United Kingdom frameworks do not reach the Islands. The UK Equality Act 2010 and the Gender Recognition Act 2004 do not extend to the Falkland Islands, so protection and recognition depend on the territory's own ordinances.

Legal gender change has been possible since 2014. There is no self-identification route and no recognition of non-binary status, and holders of a UK Gender Recognition Certificate are recognised in their acquired gender under the CPE Ordinance 2014.

Three ordinances frame the criminal-justice treatment of bias. The Crimes Ordinance 2014 provides for hate-stirring on grounds of sexual orientation, the CPE Ordinance 2014 provides for sexual orientation as an aggravating factor in sentencing, and a Prisons Ordinance was enacted in 2017.

Stepchild and joint adoption have been available to same-sex couples since 2017.

The United Kingdom is responsible for the territory's defence.

Rob Salerno blog (22 Jun 2017): the Falklands registrar general confirmed by reply that the same-sex marriage and civil partnership bill passed in March is law, resolving the outstanding question of its assent; the same registrar confirmed that same-sex marriage is not legal in the South Georgia and South Sandwich Islands dependency.

SYN-FRO.name: Faroe Islands
SYN-FRO.summary:
Faroe Islands stands under Denmark's national criminal law and document rules as they apply here.

The Faroe Islands are a self-governing territory within the Realm of Denmark. Domestic equality and family law are set locally, beneath a Danish human-rights framework. Same-sex marriage arrived only in 2017, late for the Nordics, after friction between church and state.

In 2006 LGBT activists gathered around 20,000 online signatures in a population of about 47,000, demanding an end to discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and a registered-partnership law aligned with the rest of the Nordics. The territory had neither at that date. Surveys of the period found violence and discrimination against openly gay people not uncommon and legally unaddressed.

Religiously motivated opposition sits openly in Faroese politics. On 7 September 2010 Centre Party leader Jenis av Rana refused to attend a state banquet for visiting Icelandic prime minister Johanna Sigurdardóttir and her partner, citing his religion. The refusal concerned the presence of an openly gay head of government at an official table.

Opposition to public visibility continued. In July 2015, when av Rana demanded that Pride be banned from its position two days before the national holiday, singer Eivor Pálsdóttir publicly urged people to ignore him. His party remains formally opposed to homosexuality.

For a trans visitor the recorded hostility is political and rhetorical rather than physical. The named targets are openly gay public figures and a Pride event, and the actions on record are a refusal to sit at a banquet and a call for a ban. Violence risk appears low on the sourced material.

PinkNews (7 Sep 2010): Centre Party leader Jenis av Rana refused to attend a state banquet for visiting Icelandic PM Johanna Sigurdardottir and her partner, citing his religion — signals the prominence of religiously motivated opposition to openly gay public figures in Faroese politics.

Gay Iceland (Jul 2015): when Faroese MP Jenis av Rana demanded Pride be banned (held two days before the national holiday), singer Eivor Palsdottir publicly urged people to ignore him; his party remains formally opposed to homosexuality — documents anti-Pride pressure and organised public pushback.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in the Faroe Islands since 1933, when it was legalized across the Kingdom of Denmark; the age of consent was then set at 18 for male same-sex relations, and the Faroe Islands did not follow Denmark's 1977 move to a gender-neutral age of 15 until 1988. The only criminal penalties touching LGBTQ people in the text are under the anti-discrimination law: anyone who publicly makes a statement threatening, insulting or degrading a group on account of race, colour, national or ethnic origin, religion or sexual orientation is liable to a fine or up to two years' imprisonment. That provision took effect on 1 January 2007, making the Faroe Islands the last Northern European country to ban discrimination and harassment based on sexual orientation. Wikipedia country coverage: Expression has been a recurring flashpoint: the first gay pride march in 2005 provoked much controversy, and in June 2015 Løgting Speaker Jógvan á Lakjuni published a letter to the editor, 'Hvar eru vit á veg?', attacking national broadcaster Kringvarp Føroya for the space it gave LGBT Føroyar and condemning a drag show at the Nordic House as 'non-culture', asking whether 'these people do not feel any shame'. Centre Party leader Jenis av Rana repeatedly compared LGBT Føroyar to the Sea Shepherd whale-hunting protesters and suggested the Tórshavn pride parade be moved out of the centre. Public petitioning also figures: a petition against same-sex marriage gathered 1,262 signatures, while an internet petition after the 2006 assault on Rasmus Rasmussen collected 20,000 signatures and eight women in Tórshavn gathered a further 2,000 by email and in shops, tourist centres and gas stations. Wikipedia country coverage: In 2006 openly gay singer, songwriter and radio host Rasmus Rasmussen was severely beaten by five men in Tórshavn and hospitalised shortly after coming out, and he and his family then received threatening telephone calls; police refused to handle the case because no Faroese law banned discrimination against sexual minorities at the time. He was later moved to a psychiatric hospital with severe depression exacerbated by the beating, never recovered, became mentally ill and died by suicide in 2012. In 2005 the Norwegian drag group Great Garlic Girls had to run from a gang of young men intent on physically assaulting them in Tórshavn — nowhere else had the group been attacked. The 2007 law criminalises public threats, insults or degrading statements against LGBT people with a fine or up to two years' imprisonment.

Pride is scheduled two days before the national holiday, which supplies opponents a framing beyond homosexuality itself. Organised pushback came from a nationally prominent singer rather than from an institution.

The sources bear on sexual orientation. No gender-identity claim appears among them.

SYN-GGY.name: Guernsey
SYN-GGY.summary:
Guernsey is a self-governing Crown Dependency with its own parliament, the States of Guernsey, and its own statute book. The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and the single-sex-services code issued under it in 2025 do not apply here automatically. Local law governs, and United Kingdom measures reach Guernsey only by Order in Council.

Same-sex sexual activity is legal for men and women. Criminalisation ended before 1983, when the age of consent was set at 21 in line with the United Kingdom; the male same-sex age of consent fell to 18 in 2000 and was equalised at 16 by legislation approved in 2011 that took effect on 5 November 2012. Guernsey nonetheless retains specific male homosexual offences, including a ban on homosexual sexual acts not conducted in private, which can expose men to prosecution for conduct that is lawful elsewhere.

Transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 2007, including obtaining a new birth certificate. Guernsey law permits only the issue of a new birth certificate and does not amend or remove entries from the existing record, so prior gender markers remain visible on the original document. Visitors carrying both records, or documents issued at different times, should expect the earlier marker to remain on file.

On 10 December 2015 the States of Guernsey approved same-sex marriage by 37 votes to 7. Two alternatives were put and rejected as insufficient: a civil-partnership-only scheme, and a single secular status called Union Civile that would have applied to all couples alike. The enabling legislation was left to a separate bill, which commenced in 2018.

Family recognition moved earlier the same year. A review of the Adoption Law, recorded at page 1170 of the States of Guernsey Billet d'État of 24 June 2015, ended a fifty-year bar on unmarried couples adopting; the States agreed that same-sex couples may adopt, that civil partnerships are recognised in adoption proceedings, and that both partners hold equal parental responsibility.

Discrimination protections were built up in stages. A 2004 law enabled the States of Guernsey to pass Ordinances banning discrimination, and the Sex Discrimination (Employment) (Guernsey) Ordinance, 2005 prohibited discrimination based on gender identity in employment. As of 2020 no equivalent Ordinance had outlawed discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. Protections covering sexual orientation and gender identity existed in child welfare proceedings in Guernsey and Alderney since 2008 and in Sark since 2016. In September 2022 the States passed a comprehensive anti-discrimination bill unanimously, by 33 votes to 0, explicitly including sexual orientation and rejecting proposed exemptions for businesses of five employees or fewer and for religious affiliations. It took effect on 1 October 2023.

Guernsey adopted the United Kingdom's relaxed blood-donor rules on 23 September 2011, making gay and bisexual men eligible after a twelve-month deferral from around 7 November 2011, ending a local ban dating from the 1980s HIV era. Other donation restrictions were unchanged.

Custodial safeguards are undocumented. Guernsey's only prison, Les Nicolles, holds male, female and vulnerable prisoners of juvenile and adult ages across 11 wings. No rule on housing prisoners by birth sex versus gender identity, no separate unit for trans prisoners, and no solitary or segregation practice for them is recorded in the available sources, so a trans visitor has no sourced assurance about placement if detained.

SYN-GIB.name: Gibraltar
SYN-GIB.summary:
Gibraltar is a self-governing British Overseas Territory with its own Parliament and its own Supreme Court, which between them make and interpret its civil and criminal law. Measures enacted by the United Kingdom do not apply here of their own force: the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and the single-sex-services code issued in 2025 bind Gibraltar only if extended by Order in Council, and no such extension appears in the sourced material.

The principal legal gap facing a trans visitor is gender recognition. No process exists in Gibraltar for changing a legal gender marker, and the sourced material records that transgender persons are not permitted to change legal gender. A trans visitor therefore travels on a document whose marker cannot be altered by any local route, and can expect to be read at the border and in public under that marker.

Statutory discrimination protection covering gender reassignment, alongside sexual orientation, has been in place since 2007 under Gibraltar's own equality provisions.

Hate-crime coverage now extends to trans people. Parliament amended the Crimes Act in September 2013 to criminalise hatred and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation, with royal assent on 25 September and effect from 10 October 2013, and in July 2026 passed a bill amending hate crime and hate speech legislation to include protections for transgender identity.

In July 2026 Parliament also passed a bill making it an offence to offer or practise conversion therapy.

Partner and family recognition is established locally: civil partnerships since 2014, same-sex marriage since December 2016 after a bill passed unanimously, a Supreme Court ruling of 10 April 2013 that section 5(2) of the Adoption Act 1951 violated the Gibraltar Constitution, and an Adoption Act 2023 in full effect from 18 April 2024 that expressly allows same-sex couples to adopt without discrimination.

The age of consent for all sexual activity regardless of sexuality or gender is 16. The Supreme Court ruled on 8 April 2011 that the previous age of 18 for gay sex was unconstitutional, and the gender-neutral Crimes Act 2011, approved in August 2011, set the equal age of 16 with effect from 23 November 2012.

The House of Commons Foreign Affairs Committee's 2008 inquiry into overseas territories recommended that discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender status be made illegal in all overseas territories, and its Seventh Report of 2007-08 sets accountability and good-governance expectations applicable to Gibraltar.

sources.summary: The UK House of Commons Foreign Affairs Committee's Seventh Report (2007-08) on Overseas Territories sets accountability and good-governance expectations that apply to Gibraltar as an overseas territory; it also records corruption concerns raised in Turks and Caicos.

El País in English (15 Aug 2016): Gibraltar put a draft bill amending the Civil Marriage Act for same-sex marriage before Parliament after a December 2015 consultation that left Gibraltarians polarized; a government minister presided over an inter-ministerial committee weighing all viewpoints, with popular consultation and main parties suggesting support for the change.

Gibraltar Chronicle (22 Jul 2021): the Ministry for Justice and Equality said it would 'urgently' consider legislation to tackle 'disgusting lurking homophobia' following an incident of anti-gay abuse.

Wikiwand (Wikipedia mirror): LGBTQ rights in Gibraltar - legal since 1993, equal age of consent since 2012, adoption right by Supreme Court ruling 2013, civil partnerships since 2014, same-sex marriage since Dec 2016 (passed unanimously), discrimination protections for sexual orientation and 'gender reassignment' since 2007; transgender persons not allowed to change legal gender.

sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Gibraltar's Parliament passed a bill on 19 September 2013, given royal assent on 25 September and in force on 10 October, amending the Crimes Act 2011 to criminalise hatred and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation as a hate crime. In July 2021 the Justice Ministry began investigating a further proposal to make denigration of a person on the basis of sexual orientation a specific criminal offence, prompted by what Chief Minister Fabian Picardo called 'disgusting lurking homophobia' on social media during Pride month. In July 2026 Parliament passed a bill amending hate crime and hate speech legislation to include protections for 'transgender identity'. The Supreme Court of Gibraltar ruled on 10 April 2013 that section 5(2) of the Adoption Act 1951 violated the Gibraltar Constitution, de jure legalising LGBT adoption, after a long-term lesbian couple denied adoption for lack of legal recognition of their relationship challenged the law; the government amended the law through the 2014 civil partnership legislation. The Adoption Act 2023 took full effect on 18 April 2024 and explicitly allows same-sex couples to adopt children without discrimination. In February 2021 Gibraltar enacted a surrogacy law permitting non-commercial, altruistic surrogacy for married couples or civil partners unable to conceive, with automatic recognition of children of same-sex couples conceived through artificial insemination. In June 2017 the Gibraltar Health Authority approved an amendment to its in vitro fertilisation policy allowing lesbian couples to access assisted reproductive technology. In July 2026 Parliament passed a bill making it an offence to offer or practice conversion therapy. The age of consent for all sexual activity regardless of sexuality or gender was equalised at 16. The Supreme Court of Gibraltar ruled on 8 April 2011 that the higher age of 18 for gay sex was unconstitutional, and the gender-neutral Crimes Act 2011, approved in August 2011, set an equal age of consent of 16 that took effect on 23 November 2012. Before that, gay male minors faced a discriminatory age of 18, and a private member's bill to equalise consent was defeated in Parliament on 18 May 2009. The Foreign Affairs Committee's 2008 enquiry into overseas territories recommended making discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender status illegal in all overseas territories.

SYN-GIB.tangentialFactors:
Gibraltar's framework diverges from United Kingdom law on two points that matter to a trans visitor. The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 does not extend to Gibraltar of its own force, and the United Kingdom's 2025 code on single-sex services, which governs access to women-only spaces in the parent jurisdiction, binds Gibraltar only through an Order in Council that the sourced material does not record.

Official response to anti-LGB abuse has been rhetorical and investigative rather than adjudicated. In July 2021 the Ministry for Justice and Equality said it would urgently consider legislation against what the Chief Minister called disgusting lurking homophobia on social media during Pride month, and the Ministry began examining a proposal to make denigration on the basis of sexual orientation a specific criminal offence.

The trajectory of Gibraltar's own legislation runs toward wider coverage: sexual-orientation hate crime in 2013, transgender identity added to hate crime and hate speech in July 2026, and conversion therapy criminalised in the same month. No enforcement data accompanies any of these measures in the sourced material.

External oversight has been limited to recommendations. The Foreign Affairs Committee's 2008 inquiry urged that sexual orientation or gender status discrimination be outlawed across overseas territories; the Committee's Seventh Report of 2007-08 frames accountability and good-governance expectations rather than binding obligations.

Same-sex marriage was legislated after a December 2015 consultation that left Gibraltarians polarised; a government minister presided over an inter-ministerial committee weighing the viewpoints, and the amending bill for the Civil Marriage Act went to Parliament in August 2016 before passing unanimously in December 2016.

SYN-GLP.name: Guadeloupe
SYN-GLP.summary:
Guadeloupe stands under France's national framework: French criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute, the marriage regime and the rules on identity documents apply here as they do in the metropole. Same-sex relations were decriminalised in the Penal Code of 1791 and retained in the 1810 Code, though public morality provisions continued to be used against LGBTQ people. No legal penalty attaches to trans existence.

Legal gender recognition has followed the simplified French procedure since 1 January 2017 under a law signed on 18 November 2016. Surgery and medical diagnosis are no longer required, and the requirements for self-certification of gender and proof of medical treatment were dropped from the final bill. A change of first name can be handled at the registry office; a change of the gender marker still requires an appearance before a court. A 2017 bid to have the law recognise a 'neutral sex' classification was rejected by the Court of Cassation, and in 2022 a court of appeal ruled that a transgender woman should be regarded as the mother of a child she conceived before her sex change.

Discriminatory and violent conduct is prosecuted under the law of 31 December 2004, which made homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic comments criminal, with a maximum penalty of a €45,000 fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment, and amended the 1881 Freedom of the Press Law to cover injury, defamation, insult and incitement to hatred, violence or discrimination on grounds of gender, sexual orientation or disability. Christian Vanneste, a serving MP, became the first person convicted under it in January 2006, though the Court of Cassation later cancelled that conviction. A conversion therapy ban passed the Senate on 7 December 2020 and was published on 1 February 2022, carrying two years' imprisonment and/or a €30,000 fine. Reported homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults rose 36% in 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims against about 1,380 in 2018.

Access to gender-affirming care is constrained in practice. An ILGA-Europe report in 2022 found significant problems in that healthcare: lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access depending on location, recommending an informed-consent model. Gender dysphoria was declassified as a mental illness by decree in 2010, though French trans organisations said nothing changed beyond the announcement; transsexualism remains listed under ALD 31 with treatment funded by the Sécurité Sociale, and gender-affirming surgery has been legal domestically since 1979. The Académie Nationale de Médecine characterised the rise in trans people seeking treatment as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and 'a primarily social problem' and advised extreme caution on access, without changing practice.

Trans minors are a live legislative target. In March 2024 centre-right senators commissioned a report from the Little Mermaid Observatory, a body opposed to all gender transition for minors, which called transition a 'health scandal' and transness a 'social contagion'. A bill banning medical transition under 18 passed the Senate in May 2024, opposed by the Macron government, with no further update after 23 July 2024. In late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued the country's first trans youth guidelines, recommending puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2. In 2022 it emerged that the president of the scientific committee of DILCRAH, France's interministerial body against racism, anti-Semitism and anti-LGBT hatred, sat on the Little Mermaid Observatory; one member resigned and the president stepped away.

Custodial settings are the documented risk area. A BuzzFeed News report of January 2018 found that in French prisons, whose rules govern detention in Guadeloupe, the placement of trans women follows the legal gender recorded on the incarceration papers, which may not correspond to the person's presentation; in practice assignment is said to weigh the individual's best interests, with individual cells or placement in more welcoming wings used where possible. The national preventive mechanism (CGLPL) issued an opinion on 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty, finding that serious violations of fundamental rights persist across places of detention, drawing on some 40 referrals since 2010.

Practical support exists on the island. Guadeloupe's first LGBT+ centre, the Maison des Diversités et de l'Inclusion, opened on 24 April 2024, offering reception, support and orientation for people of diverse identity, sexual, bodily and gender diversities, driven by a federation of Guadeloupean associations; the opening was attended by the visiting national minister Aurore Bergé, who announced measures to strengthen the fight against gender-based violence and discrimination in Guadeloupe, with structures adapted for overseas territories. Community organisations including Secret's Out, Queer Gang and Lovo Nova partnered on a year of LGBT-friendly social events across Guadeloupe in 2025.

In education, the national Ministry of Education launched the campaign 'Tous égaux, tous alliés' in January 2019 to tackle anti-LGBTQ bullying, providing reporting services, a helpline and guidance requirements, with 17 May as a sensitisation day. In March 2019 the Higher Education Minister announced that all higher education institutions should use transgender people's preferred names, including on student cards and exam forms.

The Mirguet amendment of 1960 doubled penalties for indecent exposure in homosexual activity (art. 330, 2nd alinea), repealed in 1980. SYN-GUF.name: French Guiana
SYN-GUF.summary:
French Guiana is an overseas department of France and stands under the French national framework. Identity documents, the criminal code, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime operate there exactly as in metropolitan France, and there is no separate local legislation on gender identity.

Legal gender recognition has been available on a simplified administrative basis since 2017, by declaration before a civil-status officer, with no requirement of surgery, sterilisation or psychiatric diagnosis. Anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity has been in force since 2012, and hate-crime sentence enhancement provisions were added in 2017. Nothing in French law criminalises trans status or gender expression.

Same-sex relations and same-sex marriage are legal under French law, and Pride events are held in the territory. The visible scene is small and anchored in Cayenne, with no venues listed by the GayOut travel guide, which rates French Guiana "Very Safe for LGBTQ+". That rating rests on formal legality rather than on the detention and healthcare conditions described below.

The most serious documented risk is custodial. A BuzzFeed News feature of January 2018 found that trans women incarcerated in France on the basis of their legal gender occupy a legal gray area, with placement decided case by case and little consistent protection; that practice governs the prisons of French Guiana. The CGLPL, the national body responsible for places of deprivation of liberty, issued an opinion on 25 May 2021 finding that serious violations in the treatment of transgender detainees persist across French places of detention, a finding that extends to the territory.

Access to specialised transgender healthcare is limited by distance from mainland treatment centres, which adds travel cost and delay to any medical step in transition. Socially, transphobia and cultural taboos discourage visibility and make reporting of abuse less likely, including reporting to police.

SYN-GUF.tangentialFactors:
The published traveller rating and the documentary record point in opposite directions. GayOut grades the territory "Very Safe for LGBTQ+" on the strength of formal legality, while the CGLPL opinion of May 2021 and the reporting of January 2018 describe conditions in custody that such a rating does not capture.

The healthcare constraint is geographic rather than statutory. Specialised and gender-affirming care sits mainly in mainland centres, so a person in French Guiana absorbs flights, accommodation and waiting time that a patient treated in a large mainland city does not.

Local visibility is limited. No venues are listed for the territory by the travel guides consulted, and the scene that exists is concentrated in Cayenne, which narrows the options for meeting others and for informal safety networks.
SYN-GUF.localsOnly:
Residents pursue legal gender recognition through the same prefectural and tribunal machinery used in Bordeaux: a declaration before a civil-status officer, with no medical evidence demanded. The procedure is administrative and does not depend on residency conditions specific to the territory.

Placement of a transgender prisoner is decided case by case, so a resident entering custody has no guaranteed assignment to a facility matching their legal gender and no consistent protection attached to that placement. The CGLPL found in May 2021 that serious violations in the treatment of transgender detainees persist across French places of detention.

For residents, every medical step in a transition depends on travel to mainland centres, and the resulting cost and delay fall on them directly. Transphobia and cultural taboos in the territory discourage visibility and weigh against reporting abuse to police, which limits reliance on the anti-discrimination and hate-crime provisions that are in force.

SYN-IMN.name: Isle of Man
SYN-IMN.summary:
The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not automatically extend to the Isle of Man. Local law governs, and United Kingdom measures reach the island only by Order in Council.

The Isle of Man is a self-legislating Crown Dependency. Its parliament, Tynwald, frames these questions through its own bills rather than through inherited Westminster statute, so the island's record must be read on its own terms.

Partner recognition is established. Same-sex marriage took effect on the island after Royal Assent of the Marriage and Civil Partnership Act, reported on 28 July 2016, and the first conversion of a civil partnership into a marriage was completed within days of entry into force. Civil partnerships, legal since 2011, convert without a second ceremony, which indicates a routine registration process rather than discretionary approval.

The primary legislative record of that reform sits in Tynwald Hansard for 26 April 2016, which records the Legislative Council's Third Reading of the Marriage and Civil Partnership (Amendment) Bill 2016 alongside consideration of the Equality Bill 2016. The reform also had stated political sponsorship: on 9 June 2015 Chief Minister Allan Bell publicly backed same-sex marriage and said he would formulate a bill to repeal the island's marriage prohibition, a commitment that preceded the 2016 Act.

Non-discrimination protection on the island was first legislated in the employment sphere. On 30 November 2005 the House of Keys adopted an amendment to the Employment Bill, tabled by Onchan MHK Peter Karran, barring dismissal of gay and lesbian employees on sexual-orientation grounds and aligning the island with United Kingdom human-rights law.

Nothing in this inventory documents a gender-recognition procedure, identity-document marker rules, entry or visa screening that could disclose a trans visitor's status, hate-crime provisions covering gender identity, or facility access rules. Those questions are not evidenced here rather than shown to be absent from Manx law, and a visitor should treat them as open.

SYN-MSR.name: Montserrat
SYN-MSR.summary:
Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults in private has been lawful in Montserrat since 2001. The reform was made retrospectively by an Order in Council under Sections 3(1) and 3(7) of the Caribbean Territories (Criminal Law) Order, 2000, and formed part of a single British decision to scrap anti-gay statutes in five Caribbean territories, including Montserrat and Turks & Caicos, on the stated ground that the laws violated signed international human rights agreements. The order was imposed from London over the objections of local politicians and religious leaders rather than with their consent.

Residual criminal exposure remains and turns on the sex of the partners and the setting. Lesbian activity was never an offence in Montserrat. Group sex and sex in public remain criminal offences for everyone. The age of consent is 18 for homosexual activity against 16 for heterosexual activity, so conduct lawful between opposite-sex partners of the same age can be an offence between same-sex partners.

As a British Overseas Territory, Montserrat stands under the United Kingdom's framework and must comply with international human rights instruments, including the European Convention on Human Rights and its non-discrimination and equality obligations. Domestically, Article 16 of the Montserrat Constitution and Article 79 of the Labour Code prohibit discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation, with 'discriminatory' defined as affording different treatment on grounds such as sex, sexual orientation, race, colour, language, religion or other status.

Relationship recognition does not extend to same-sex couples. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legal, and Article 10(1) of the Constitution protects only opposite-sex marriage, providing that every man and woman of marriageable age has the right to marry a person of the opposite sex and to found a family.

A visitor should expect almost no visible organised LGBT social infrastructure. Montserrat has no gay bars, nightclubs or other dedicated venues. Several hotels on the island welcome gay tourists and operate non-discrimination policies, which is the main documented point of entry for a visitor seeking a welcoming environment.

SYN-MTQ.name: Martinique
SYN-MTQ.summary:
Martinique stands under France's national framework. Article 73 of the Constitution applies French law to the department in full, so identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime operate here as in the metropole. Same-sex conduct has been decriminalised since 1815, the 2013 marriage-equality law applies, and gender-marker change is available through the simplified judicial route introduced by the 2016-17 reforms.

Discrimination protection rests on several instruments that reach the island directly. Goods and services have been covered since Law No. 2001-1066 (Penal Code articles 225-1 and 225-2), employment since Labour Code article L1132-1 in 2008, and discrimination on grounds of gender identity since Article 4 of the 2012 sexual-harassment law, where the wording 'sexual identity' was replaced by 'gender identity' in 2016. The Rights in Exile (AsyLex) resource page for the department lists local support organisations, case law and country-of-origin experts alongside these provisions. No Martinique-specific enforcement or litigation record for any of these instruments is documented in the sources available for this entry.

Hostile public speech is a criminal offence. A National Assembly amendment approved on 31 December 2004 made homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic public comment illegal, carrying a maximum penalty of a €45,000 fine and up to 12 months' imprisonment, and amended the 1881 press-freedom law to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence, and discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation. The first conviction under the provision, of MP Christian Vanneste in January 2006, was cancelled by the Court of Cassation. Penalties for physical assault or murder rise where the offence is motivated by the victim's sexual orientation, and since 2017 transphobia has operated as an aggravating cause for all crimes punishable by prison.

Legal gender recognition operates on the island under the regime effective since 1 January 2017: no surgery and no medical diagnosis are required, but an application must still be made to a court to change the gender marker, while a first-name change can be handled at the registry office. The bill was signed on 18 November 2016 after passing the Senate on 6 November 2015 and the National Assembly; the Constitutional Council ruled it constitutional on 17 November 2016 while dropping the original self-certification provision. Before that reform, legal gender change had been banned for decades until the 1992 European Court of Human Rights case B. v. France.

Prison is the sharpest documented risk for trans visitors. Under Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code, placement follows the gender marker on the detainee's identity documents rather than anatomy, which puts most trans women into all-male facilities where other detainees threaten them ('we don't want any women here'). The department's establishments operate under this same framework. France's detention-places watchdog, the CGLPL, found on 25 May 2021 'the persistence of serious violations' of the fundamental rights of transgender detainees across all French places of deprivation of liberty, drawing on referrals since 2010 concerning some forty transgender people and on-site inspections in which eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse; its recommendations cover placement, isolation, safety and staff training.

Healthcare is covered but uneven. Gender-affirming treatment is reimbursed by the Sécurité Sociale under the long-term-illness scheme ALD 31, and a 2022 ILGA-Europe report nonetheless documented significant problems, including extended waiting times and access that varies with location. Trans youth care is contested nationally: a report commissioned in March 2024 by centre-right Republican senators fed legislation to ban medical transition under 18, which passed the Senate in May 2024, was opposed by the Macron government and has had no recorded movement since 23 July 2024; in late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued the country's first guidelines for trans youth, recommending puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2 with calcium and vitamin D. The Académie Nationale de Médecine has characterised the rise in people seeking treatment as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and a 'primarily social problem', advising extreme caution on access.

Conversion therapy was banned by a bill published on 1 February 2022. Recorded anti-LGB(T) violence rose nationally by 36% in 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims against about 1,380 in 2018, according to a report released on 16 May 2020. Community infrastructure exists on the island: JM Concept 972 runs information, meetings and services for Martinique's LGBT community, with events listed for 4 July, 15 August and 5 September 2025, and LGBTQ organisations listed for the overseas departments include AIDES Territoire Martinique, KAP Caraïbe, Tjenbé Rèd Prévention and SAFE SXM.

The French prison framework applies to the department's establishments as French law.

Opinion of the CGLPL, France's detention-places watchdog (25 May 2021): finds 'the persistence of serious violations' of the fundamental rights of transgender detainees across ALL French places of deprivation of liberty, based on referrals since 2010 concerning some forty transgender persons plus on-site inspections (eight trans women and one trans man interviewed at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse sites). L1132-1 (2008); gender-identity discrimination prohibited since Article 4 of the 2012 sexual-harassment law, with 'sexual identity' replaced by 'gender identity' in 2016. Also lists local support organisations, case law and country-of-origin experts.

Its active, dated operation evidences local community infrastructure on the island.

SYN-MYT.name: Mayotte
SYN-MYT.summary:
Mayotte stands under France's national framework. Identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as they do in metropolitan France, and the French prison rules bind the island's places of deprivation of liberty as French establishments.

Nothing in that framework criminalises being trans or being in a same-sex relationship. Same-sex marriage has been available on the island since Mayotte voted to remain part of France in 1975, and it is one of the few jurisdictions in Africa and the Muslim-majority world where such marriages can be performed. The National Assembly's vote simplifying legal gender change for trans people likewise extends to the department.

Placement in custody follows the gender marker carried on the identity document, under Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code. Trans women are therefore typically held in all-male facilities, where other detainees threaten them; anatomy does not decide where a person is placed.

The national detention-places watchdog CGLPL reported on 25 May 2021 a persistence of serious violations of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across all French places of deprivation of liberty. The finding rests on referrals made since 2010 concerning some forty transgender people and on site inspections at which eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed, at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse. Because these are French establishments, the same standards and the same documented failures govern any facility holding a trans person on Mayotte.

Formal entitlement and lived experience diverge on the island. A teacher at the university centre of Mayotte and his Malagasy partner married at Sada town hall in 2023 only after what reporting described as a long and complicated path, on a predominantly Muslim island where the law on paper is not the whole of what a couple faces.

Legal representation is thinly available locally. A French-language directory of LGBT-friendly lawyers returns no referenced practitioner for Mayotte's towns, including Mamoudzou, Koungou, Dzaoudzi and Sada, while listing a Paris-based lawyer admitted to the Conseil d'État and Cour de cassation, working in persons and family law, as available.

SYN-NCL.name: New Caledonia
SYN-NCL.summary:
New Caledonia is a French collectivity in which France retains responsibility for penal law, civil-status documents and the justice system, while New Caledonia legislates locally on many domestic matters. The protections a trans visitor would rely on are French national provisions that apply here as French law, and no source in this inventory records a local ordinance narrowing them. Nothing in the inventory criminalises trans people or same-sex relations.

Same-sex marriage has been available in New Caledonia since France's 2013 marriage-equality statute, which applies here as French law. CNN reported on 29 May 2013 on the first same-sex wedding solemnised in France under that law. PinkNews reported on 26 August 2012 that the French government would introduce its same-sex marriage and adoption bill into Parliament in October 2012, fulfilling President Hollande's campaign pledge.

Sexual identity became a ground of discrimination in the French Penal Code through the sexual-harassment legislation of 2012, which enabled prosecution of discrimination and of transphobia as discrimination. Yagg reported that change in July 2012; the provision was amended in 2016 to read gender identity. As French law, the provision reaches New Caledonia.

Placement of detainees follows the recorded legal gender marker rather than anatomy. Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code assigns incarcerated trans people according to their recorded sex, which in practice puts trans women in all-male facilities where they face threats of assault by other detainees. BuzzFeed News reported that practice on 12 January 2018. The French prison framework governs the collectivity's establishments in the same way.

France's detention-places watchdog, the CGLPL, issued an opinion on 25 May 2021 finding a persistence of serious violations of the rights of transgender detainees across all French places of deprivation of liberty. Its findings rest on referrals made since 2010 concerning some forty transgender people and on inspections at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse, where eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed. Because French law applies here, the opinion extends to establishments in New Caledonia.

The protections recorded for New Caledonia are inherited rather than locally enacted. Marriage equality and the discrimination ground reached the collectivity because France legislated them, not because New Caledonia's own legislature adopted them, so a visitor's recourse rests on French legal machinery rather than on local ordinances.

The detention evidence in this inventory is drawn entirely from mainland France. BuzzFeed News reporting and the CGLPL's 2021 opinion describe conditions at French facilities and in French places of deprivation of liberty; the inference that they govern New Caledonia rests on the extension of French prison law, not on inspection findings made in the collectivity.

The CGLPL opinion treats the mistreatment of transgender detainees as systemic rather than isolated, covering all French places of deprivation of liberty and drawing on referrals accumulated since 2010. That is a materially different posture from the civil-status side of the record, where the inventory shows recognition and marriage access without any recorded local restriction.

The wording of the anti-discrimination ground shifted in 2016 from sexual identity to gender identity, so documentation dated before that year may describe the protection in narrower terms than the provision now carries.
