SYN-PCN.name: Pitcairn Islands
SYN-PCN.summary:
The Pitcairn Islands stand under the United Kingdom's framework: defence and external affairs are reserved to the United Kingdom, and United Kingdom domestic measures such as the Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not apply here of their own force. Local law governs, and those measures could reach Pitcairn only by Order in Council. Military service is likewise a United Kingdom responsibility rather than a local one.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in the Pitcairn Islands since 2001, so a visitor faces no criminalisation exposure on that ground.

The Pitcairn Constitution Order 2010 prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, in force since 2010. The guarantee is constitutional rather than an offence provision and names sexual orientation, not gender identity.

Same-sex marriage has been legal since 14 May 2015. The Same Sex Marriage and Civil Partnerships Ordinance 2015 defines marriage as the union of two people regardless of sex, sexual orientation or gender identity. The Island Council approved the ordinance unanimously on 1 April 2015, Governor Jonathan Sinclair signed it on 5 May 2015, and it was published on 13 May 2015.

The same ordinance recognises civil partnerships performed outside Pitcairn, which supports recognition of a visitor's or resident's existing foreign partnership. Adoption has been legal since 2015 and is open to married, unmarried and single people.

Pitcairn's permanent population is roughly 50 residents, and none is known to be in a same-sex relationship. The territory has no reported record of trans-specific violence, and no sourced reporting documents hostility toward visitors on these grounds.

Military service falls under UK responsibility.

SYN-PCN.tangentialFactors:
Pitcairn's protections and family law sit alongside a resident population so small that social exposure is a structural fact rather than a matter of legal risk: anonymity is limited, and any relationship or gender presentation is likely to be common knowledge across the island.

The territory's legal framework distinguishes Pitcairn from the United Kingdom in both directions. United Kingdom equality legislation does not extend automatically, and the local constitution's non-discrimination guarantee covers sexual orientation without naming gender identity, leaving gender-identity protection a narrower question than in several comparable small jurisdictions.

The 2015 marriage ordinance's definition of marriage by reference to two people regardless of sex, sexual orientation or gender identity is broader in wording than the constitutional discrimination clause, which is limited to sexual orientation.

SYN-PYF.name: French Polynesia
SYN-PYF.summary:
French Polynesia is an overseas collectivity of France, and French law governs it in matters of justice and civil status. Trans visitors therefore enter a legal regime in which gender recognition, detention policy and the rights framework are set by Paris, while much of daily life is regulated by the territorial institutions in Papeete.

France's national treatment of trans detainees reaches French Polynesia. Detention follows the gender marked on an identity document, and Article D248 of the French Code of criminal procedure requires separate men's and women's establishments; a trans woman holding a male marker is consequently held with men. BuzzFeed News, reporting on the situation in France in January 2018, treated this as a legal grey area rather than a settled outcome.

The national preventive-mechanism for places of deprivation of liberty, the CGLPL, issued an opinion on 25 May 2021 finding that France's Law 2016-1547 removed the requirement for medical transition or surgery when changing the gender on civil status, but that no norms were ever added governing how detainees should be housed in line with that change. Serious violations were documented across French detention, and the CGLPL's framework applies to French Polynesia's prisons. A trans visitor who is detained in the territory is therefore exposed to housing arrangements that national regulators themselves have found incompatible with the country's own gender-recognition law.

Gender-diverse healthcare in French Polynesia is limited by the small number of specialists available locally. Some trans residents, including rae-rae, face rejection from their families and leave for mainland France to obtain specialised services that the territory cannot provide. The gap between the law on paper and the care actually reachable in the archipelago is the most concrete material constraint for a trans person staying any length of time.

A reform effort to narrow that gap failed. Under Vice-President Eliane Tevahitua, the territorial government tabled a social-security bill that would have fully reimbursed hormonal treatment with progesterone and testosterone, matching mainland France. After heated debate in the Territorial Assembly the bill did not obtain sufficient support and lapsed.

The cultural setting is unusually documented. The mahu role, a traditional Polynesian recognition of gender diversity in which individuals embody both male and female qualities and hold recognised standing, predates colonisation, and mahu and rae-rae are visible across the islands in daily life. The territory hosted its first international LGBTQIA+ rights colloquium in 2023, bringing territorial government and church representatives together with the University of French Polynesia. Reporting from OutTraveler in July 2025 described this openness as ingrained in the culture rather than secured by law, noting that a visiting gay couple checked online whether the destination was safe before travelling and found mainstream inclusivity and acceptance operating without pride flags or organised protest. The 118-island territory has no Pride movement to speak of, which visitors read either as reassurance or as evidence that visibility is tolerated rather than defended.

Concrete care-access reform failed.

sources.summary: French national law, drawn from Wikipedia country coverage, with no stated bearing on French Polynesia: sodomy provisions were repealed by the Penal Code of 1791 and the Penal Code of 1810 retained that silence; an indecent-exposure clause (article 330, 2nd alinea) inserted in 1960 by the Mirguet amendment doubled penalties where the act was homosexual and was repealed in 1980, and in March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a compensation bill for men arrested under it, with the Senate yet to vote. A Vichy law of 6 August 1942 set consent at 21 for homosexual relations against 15 for heterosexual ones, lowered to 18 in 1974 and equalised at 15 in 1982; LGBTQ people in Alsace and Lorraine were interned in Nazi camps after 1940. The law of 31 December 2004 made homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic comments illegal, punishable by up to €45,000 and/or 12 months' imprisonment, criticised by Reporters Without Borders and defended by the Chirac government; Christian Vanneste was convicted under it in January 2006 and that conviction was later cancelled by the Court of Cassation. Sexual orientation became a protected ground in employment and services in 1985, 'sexual identity' was added in July 2012, and on 18 November 2016 'gender identity' replaced it in article 225-1 of the Penal Code, with the Labour Code covering sexual orientation and gender identity in recruitment and training. Assaults motivated by the victim's sexual orientation attract heavier penalties, and in 2017 transphobia became an aggravating circumstance for all crimes punishable by prison. A report of 16 May 2020 recorded a 36% rise in homophobic and transphobic attacks in 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims against roughly 1,380 in 2018. The conversion-therapy ban passed the Senate on 7 December 2020 and took effect on 1 February 2022; Le Refuge estimated 3-4% of its helpline calls concerned conversion therapy. The Académie Nationale de Médecine described the rise in trans people seeking treatment as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and a 'primarily social problem'; a March 2024 report commissioned from The Little Mermaid Observatory called gender-affirming care a 'health scandal' and youth transness a 'social contagion', and a bill banning medical transition under 18 passed the Senate in May 2024 without National Assembly action since 23 July 2024. Late-2024 guidelines from the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology recommend puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2. Civil solidarity pacts (PACS) date from 1999; same-sex marriage passed the National Assembly 329-229 on 12 February 2013 and was signed on 18 May 2013, with joint adoption rare thereafter and assisted reproduction extended to lesbian couples from September 2021. Schools observe 17 May under the 2019 Tous égaux, tous alliés campaign, enrolment forms use 'parent 1' and 'parent 2', and since March 2019 higher education institutions should use trans students' preferred names. Mayotte reports frequent family rejection and discrimination, and in 2014 only about 20% of overseas residents viewed homosexuality as a sexuality like any other, against 77% in metropolitan France.

SYN-PYF.tangentialFactors:
The protection available to a trans visitor in French Polynesia rests on a national equality and anti-discrimination regime that France applies to the territory, while the everyday indicators a traveller can observe are cultural rather than institutional. The absence of visible protest or organised community signalling should not be read as absence of risk management; acceptance described by travellers is diffuse and social, and the underlying legal remedies run through French courts and national bodies rather than through territorial institutions.

Detention is where the mismatch between the national recognition framework and its application is sharpest. France has reformed who qualifies for a legal gender change without disturbing the rules that determine where a person is locked up, and the national preventive mechanism has recorded the resulting violations. A trans visitor whose documents carry a marker inconsistent with their presentation is the person most exposed to this, both at arrest and at any later stage of the process.

Healthcare capacity is a structural difference from mainland France, not a temporary shortage. Hormonal treatment available through reimbursement in Paris is not equally obtainable in Papeete, and the failed territorial bill confirms that the shortfall is recognised politically and left unresolved. Visitors who rely on continuity of treatment should plan around what is locally prescribed and compounded rather than around what the French social-security system covers on the continent.
SYN-PYF.localsOnly:
Residents are bound by the same French civil-status machinery that governs trans visitors: the gender on the civil registry determines identity documents, and the requirement for medical or surgical intervention was removed by Law 2016-1547. The CGLPL's finding that implementing norms for detention were never written applies to territorial prisons as much as to metropolitan facilities.

Reimbursement of progesterone and testosterone through the territorial social-security system was proposed and rejected after debate in the Territorial Assembly, so residents currently bear the cost of hormonal treatment that mainland France covers. Specialist services are concentrated abroad, and family rejection is recorded as a reason trans residents, including rae-rae, relocate to France.

The mahu role carries cultural standing within Polynesian society, and territorial institutions have engaged publicly with LGBTQIA+ questions through the 2023 colloquium involving the Vice-President, the territorial government, churches and the University of French Polynesia. That engagement concerns reflection and education rather than new territorial legislation.
SYN-PYF.outOfScopeNotes:
It is unresolved whether Article D248 and the gender-marker detention rule described in the 2018 BuzzFeed News report have been revised since that reporting; the inventory sources the position as it stood then and through the CGLPL's 2021 opinion, and does not document a later change.

The inventory does not state whether French Polynesia has any territory-specific anti-discrimination statute of its own, nor how the national protections are actually invoked in the territory. Travel-writer accounts of mainstream inclusivity are single-perspective and describe visitor experience rather than measured incidence; the absence of reported incidents in the sources is not evidence that none occur.

SYN-REU.name: Réunion
SYN-REU.summary:
Réunion is a department of France and stands under French national law without local variation: identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as they do in metropolitan France.

Same-sex marriage reached Réunion with the statute adopted in France in 2013, following the bill announced by Prime Minister Jean-Marc Ayrault in October 2012 for passage through the National Assembly and the Senate, which delivered President François Hollande's campaign pledge. Both houses had to approve the text.

Discrimination on the ground of 'identité sexuelle' has been prosecutable in France since the National Assembly amended Penal Code article L225-1 in July 2012, making transphobic harassment a criminal matter; deputies Sergio Coronado and Elisabeth Pochon intervened in that debate. The provision is in force in Réunion.

Legal gender change rests on the Civil Code section inserted by amendment 282, adopted by the National Assembly on 19 May 2016 after being tabled by roughly forty Socialist deputies. The government's three sub-amendments could limit the scope of that section.

Prison placement in France follows the sex recorded on the identity document under Article D248 of the criminal procedure code. Transgender women held in male prisons therefore fall into a legal grey area and are, in the account of a BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018, 'punished for a lot more than their alleged crimes'; the piece follows cases including a trans woman held at Lille in 2014 amid inmate threats. The placement rule is the framework that governs detainees in Réunion.

The French places-of-deprivation-of-liberty watchdog (CGLPL) found 'the persistence of serious violations' of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across French custody facilities in its opinion of 25 May 2021. The finding rests on referrals received since 2010 covering some forty transgender persons, interviews with associations and experts, and on-site and documentary inspections, and it carries recommendations addressed to the Interior, Justice and Health ministries. The opinion applies to the national framework covering Réunion.

Opposition to the 2013 marriage reform came from organised religion as well as politics: the Catholic Bishops Conference in France came out against the adoption provisions of the bill, the record that accompanied the statute reaching Réunion.

Harassment or discriminatory treatment grounded in 'identité sexuelle' is prosecutable for residents under Penal Code article L225-1, in force since July 2012.

Residents detained in Réunion are assigned to prison accommodation by the sex recorded on their identity document under Article D248 of the criminal procedure code, the rule the CGLPL examined in its 25 May 2021 opinion.

SYN-SHN.name: Saint Helena
SYN-SHN.summary:
The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 code of practice on single-sex services do not automatically extend to Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha. Local law governs the territory, and those United Kingdom measures can be applied only by Order in Council, so a visitor should expect the territory's own statutes and practices rather than the United Kingdom framework to determine how single-sex services, records and complaints are handled.

Consensual same-sex activity has been lawful in the territory since 2001, and the age of consent is equalised at 16 across Saint Helena, Ascension Island and Tristan da Cunha. The 2009 constitutional order imposed by the United Kingdom bans discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation territory-wide, and those protections have been in force since 2009.

Same-sex marriage was legislated island by island. The Ascension Island Council approved the marriage ordinance on 31 May 2016 by 5 votes to 0; it was signed and gazetted on 20 June 2016 and commenced on 1 January 2017. Tristan da Cunha followed on 4 August 2017 and Saint Helena on 20 December 2017.

Adoption by same-sex couples has been permitted since 2017. The territory is classified as an Overseas Country or Territory of the European Union, and the applicability of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights is recorded on that basis.

sources.summary: As of 25 Apr 2026, same-sex sexual activity is legal in the territory, discrimination protections have been in force since 2009, and same-sex marriage has been legal on Ascension Island since 2017 (Alchetron).

Consensual same-sex relations became lawful in 2001. The age of consent is equalised at 16 territory-wide. The territory is an Overseas Country or Territory of the EU, with EU Charter applicability (GayLawNet, accessed 23 Jun 2013, citing ILGA State-sponsored Homophobia).

Wikiwand (Wikipedia mirror): LGBTQ rights in Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha - discrimination banned territory-wide since 2009; same-sex marriage legal since 2017 (Ascension 1 Jan, Tristan da Cunha 4 Aug, Saint Helena 20 Dec); adoption since 2017; detailed vote records of the Ascension Island Council (5-0).

SYN-SHN.tangentialFactors:
Because the United Kingdom's 2025 single-sex-services code does not apply of its own force, provisions elsewhere in the British Islands that shape how toilets, changing rooms and shelters admit people are not a reliable guide to what a visitor will encounter on Saint Helena, Ascension or Tristan da Cunha.

Ascension Island carried the territory's marriage reform first, and by the largest margin on record for the measure, with the Ascension Island Council voting 5 to 0 on 31 May 2016. Saint Helena, the most populous island, legislated last, on 20 December 2017.

GayLawNet's account of the territory's status as an Overseas Country or Territory of the European Union and the resulting Charter applicability was accessed in June 2013 and rests on the classification as recorded at that time; the current operational reach of the Charter in the territory is not addressed in the sources reviewed.
SYN-SHN.localsOnly:
Residents are covered by the anti-discrimination clause of the 2009 constitutional order, which has been in force territory-wide since 2009 and names sexual orientation among the protected grounds.

Local councils legislate for their own islands on family law: the Ascension Island Council passed its marriage ordinance on 31 May 2016 by 5 votes to 0, and the instrument was signed and gazetted on 20 June 2016 before commencing on 1 January 2017. Tristan da Cunha legislated on 4 August 2017 and Saint Helena on 20 December 2017.

Adoption by same-sex couples has been available to residents since 2017. Residents' access to single-sex services and to remedies for discrimination remains a matter of local law, since the United Kingdom equality statute and its codes reach the islands only through an Order in Council.

SYN-TCA.name: Turks and Caicos Islands
SYN-TCA.summary:
The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 code of practice on single-sex services do not extend automatically to the Turks and Caicos Islands. Local ordinances and the territory's own constitution govern, and United Kingdom measures reach the territory only by Order in Council, so a visitor should expect the Turks and Caicos Islands' legislation rather than the United Kingdom's equality framework.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in the Turks and Caicos Islands since 2001, decriminalised through the United Kingdom-led Caribbean reform programme, and the constitution prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation.

The Court of Appeal ordered the Director of Immigration to issue a residence permit to Timothy Haymon as the same-sex spouse of Richard Sankar. Reading "spouse" in the Immigration Ordinance to include a same-sex spouse lawfully married in another jurisdiction, the court held that a refusal on sexual-orientation grounds contravened the equality, non-discrimination and private-and-family-life guarantees of the constitution, while leaving the statutory definition of marriage untouched. The ruling secures residence recognition for the same-sex partners of residents and visitors; it does not create a right to marry locally.

Transgender status is handled operationally through United Kingdom document channels rather than through a published local statute. The United Kingdom HM Passport Office knowledge-base profile for the Turks and Caicos Islands, official 2025 operational guidance covering nationality, legitimacy, adoption, gender recognition, civil partnerships and marriage, states that transgender citizens are recognised in the Turks and Caicos Islands and that the passport office processes gender-recognised documents for this jurisdiction. A visitor presenting a United Kingdom passport carrying a changed gender marker can therefore expect that document to be treated as valid here. The underlying local legal instrument, if one exists, is not documented in the available sources.

The social climate favours discretion over visibility. A resident account from May 2009 described virtually no public information about gay life in the territory, no visible social scene, and privacy as the everyday norm, attributing this partly to a population in which roughly two-thirds of residents are not originally from the islands and full-citizen Belongers are a demographic minority. That account should be read as dated and impressionistic rather than as a finding on violence risk.

The court left the definition of marriage untouched, so residence recognition and marital status remain separate questions here.

The 2025 United Kingdom single-sex-services code addresses access to sex-separated facilities, but it bears on the Turks and Caicos Islands only if adopted by Order in Council. No evidence in the available sources shows that it has been.

That composition shapes a low-visibility everyday environment for both residents and visitors, and the account is more than fifteen years old.
SYN-TCA.localsOnly:
The constitution's prohibition on discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation is a protection available to residents pursuing local remedies, and it was the basis on which the Court of Appeal compelled the residence permit for Timothy Haymon.

Adoption is legal in the Turks and Caicos Islands, according to the United Kingdom HM Passport Office's operational knowledge-base profile for the territory.

Gender recognition appears to operate through United Kingdom passport channels: the passport office's profile records that transgender citizens are recognised in the Turks and Caicos Islands and that gender-recognised documents are processed for this jurisdiction. No local gender-recognition procedure is documented in the available sources, so residents needing a local birth certificate, national identification card or marriage record carrying a changed marker face an unresolved position.

Same-sex couples cannot marry in the Turks and Caicos Islands; the Court of Appeal expressly declined to alter the statutory definition of marriage, limiting its ruling to residence recognition for spouses married abroad.

SYN-VAT.name: Holy See
SYN-VAT.summary:
Vatican City presents essentially no criminal-law exposure to a trans visitor. No documented criminal-law persecution of consensual homosexual conduct has occurred in the territory in modern times, and decriminalisation has nineteenth-century roots. Nothing about being trans is criminalised.

No legal recognition of gender exists in Vatican City. No anti-discrimination protection, facilities rule, or document-amendment mechanism covers a visitor or a resident.

Vatican City operates no prison system. It holds only a few cells for pre-trial detention, and anyone sentenced to imprisonment by Vatican City serves the term in Italian prisons at Vatican expense. Because no domestic prison system exists, there is no trans-specific prisoner-placement policy and no documented trans-prisoner placement case for this jurisdiction.

The Holy See's institutional posture against homosexuality and gender theory drives policy even where the city-state's own law imposes nothing. The Congregation for Catholic Education's 2019 document, Male and Female He Created Them, opposes what it calls gender theory, stating that it "denies the difference and reciprocity in nature of a man and a woman" and "eliminates the anthropological basis of the family." The legal baseline for a visitor is the city-state's own law, which is distinct from the Church's diplomatic and doctrinal positions.

sources.summary: PinkNews (2 Oct 2008): Catholic officials rejected France's first-choice candidate as ambassador to the Holy See because he is gay, forcing Paris to name a different envoy -- documented instance of the Vatican government refusing an LGBT person in diplomatic relations.

SYN-VAT.tangentialFactors:
In 2008 Catholic officials rejected France's first-choice candidate as ambassador to the Holy See because he is gay, forcing Paris to name a different envoy. It is a documented instance of the Vatican government refusing an LGBT person in diplomatic relations, and it indicates the institutional climate a visibly LGBT person may encounter around the Holy See's own organs rather than any rule applied to visitors.

The current Holy See posture on blessing same-sex couples is set by the DDF declaration Fiducia Supplicans, issued under Pope Francis on 20 March 2023, which permits spontaneous blessings for same-sex couples while forbidding any rite resembling marriage. A January 2024 DDF press release reiterated that blessings never extend to the unions themselves.

Both items concern sexual orientation and institutional diplomacy more directly than they concern trans visitors, but they establish the direction of official policy in a territory where doctrine and government are held by the same institution.
SYN-VAT.localsOnly:
Residents of Vatican City have no mechanism to amend gender markers on identity documents, no route to legal recognition of gender, and no anti-discrimination remedy on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation. The territory's small resident population stands under a civil code that contains no such provisions.

The 2019 Congregation for Catholic Education document is the reference point for education policy across the institutions the Holy See directs, framing gender identity as a question of anthropology to be corrected through dialogue rather than a matter of individual status.

Residents sentenced by Vatican City courts serve their sentences in Italian prisons, with the costs covered by Vatican City, because the territory has no prison of its own. Any resident serving a custodial sentence therefore leaves the jurisdiction's custody entirely, and no Vatican authority operates a placement policy inside the receiving facilities.

SYN-VGB.name: British Virgin Islands
SYN-VGB.summary:
Same-sex intimacy has not been a criminal offence in the British Virgin Islands since January 2001, when the United Kingdom's Privy Council ordered the repeal of the sodomy laws in the territory and four other remaining British Caribbean territories after the local legislatures declined to act. Local legislator Orlando Smith conceded the position publicly, stating that "there is nothing we can do." The decriminalisation arrived by order of the United Kingdom's highest court of appeal rather than by enactment of the local House of Assembly.

The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010, including its 2025 single-sex-services code, does not automatically apply in the British Virgin Islands. The territory stands under the United Kingdom's constitutional framework, and measures of the United Kingdom's Parliament extend to it only when brought into force by Order in Council. A trans visitor should not assume the Equality Act's discrimination and service-access protections are available there by default; any such protection must be traced to British Virgin Islands legislation or to a specific extension order.

Family status remains contested rather than settled. The case testing whether the United Kingdom same-sex marriage of Kinisha Forbes and Kirsten Lettsome is valid under British Virgin Islands law was still running when, on 29 July 2022, the BVI Christian Council lost its bid to appeal the case-management orders of Justice Adrian Jack, as reported by BVI News. That refusal cleared a procedural obstacle and left the proceedings in place; it is not itself a ruling on whether such a marriage is recognised in the territory.

sources.summary: Britain scrapped the homosexuality laws in its five remaining Caribbean territories, including the British Virgin Islands, by Privy Council order after local legislatures refused to act, according to an AP report of January 2001 republished by GLAPN. Local legislator Orlando Smith conceded, 'there is nothing we can do.'
GlobalGayz (Aug 2012/2017) rates the BVI among the more gay-welcoming islands in the Caribbean, while describing native homophobia as 'silent and invisible' and gay life there as lived in secret.

BVI News (29 Jul 2022): the BVI Christian Council lost its bid to appeal the case-management orders of Justice Adrian Jack in the case testing whether the UK same-sex marriage of Kinisha Forbes and Kirsten Lettsome is valid under BVI law.

SYN-VGB.tangentialFactors:
GlobalGayz (August 2012, updated 2017) rates the British Virgin Islands among the more gay-welcoming islands in the Caribbean, while describing native homophobia there as "silent and invisible" and gay life as lived in secret. That account describes social climate rather than law, and it suggests a gap between formal legality and everyday discretion that a trans visitor may also experience.

The decriminalisation of same-sex intimacy was imposed by the United Kingdom's Privy Council after the local House of Assembly declined to legislate, which indicates a local legislature less receptive than the imposed outcome might suggest. The Forbes-Lettsome marriage litigation, in which the BVI Christian Council intervened and sought to appeal, shows organised religious opposition actively contesting family recognition in the courts.
SYN-VGB.localsOnly:
Residents gained decriminalisation through an external judicial order rather than through their own representatives, and the public response of legislator Orlando Smith framed the change as having no local remedy. The BVI Christian Council's pursuit of appeals in the Forbes-Lettsome case indicates that local religious bodies continue to litigate against recognition of foreign same-sex marriages, with implications for residents' family formation.

Protection against discrimination for residents rests on British Virgin Islands legislation, not on the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010, unless a specific Order in Council extends it. Residents seeking to rely on United Kingdom equality protections must first establish whether such an extension order exists for the territory.
SYN-VGB.outOfScopeNotes:
The Forbes-Lettsome proceedings are recorded here only up to 29 July 2022, when the BVI Christian Council lost its bid to appeal Justice Adrian Jack's case-management orders. The subsequent course and outcome of the case, and whether any ruling on recognition of the United Kingdom same-sex marriage has since issued, are unresolved in the available sources.

No source in the inventory addresses legal gender recognition, marker changes on documents, screening or identification procedures at entry, access to gender-affirming care, or facilities and bathroom rules in the British Virgin Islands. Whether British Virgin Islands legislation provides any statutory protection against discrimination on grounds of gender identity is likewise not sourced here and should be verified against local statute.

Whether the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 has ever been extended to the British Virgin Islands by Order in Council, in whole or in part, is not established by the available sources; the inventory states only that it does not apply automatically.

SYN-WLF.name: Wallis and Futuna Islands
SYN-WLF.summary:
Wallis and Futuna is a territorial collectivity of the French Republic and stands under the French national framework: the civil and criminal codes of France apply locally unless a local measure overrides them. No law in force criminalises trans people or same-sex relations, and discrimination on grounds of gender identity has been prohibited since the 2012 statutory extension covering employment, housing and access to services.

Legal gender-marker change is available on the basis of the 2016-17 French reforms, which removed the requirement for surgery or a psychiatric diagnosis. A trans visitor whose documents already reflect their lived gender can present them without entering a separate local procedure. French law recognises no non-binary status, so a third-gender or X marker cannot be obtained.

Nothing in the sources indicates trans-specific screening at entry or in local administrative processing. Practical exposure to harm is concentrated in two areas: detention and everyday social conditions. Under the French prison framework that applies here, trans women whose legal gender is marked male, largely those without reassignment surgery, are held in all-male establishments, a situation described in reporting as a documented legal grey area; one such transfer to a men's facility in Lille took place in 2014.

sources.summary: BuzzFeed News (Jan 2018): trans women in France whose legal gender is marked male — largely those without sex-reassignment surgery — are incarcerated in all-male establishments, a documented legal grey area; example of a trans woman transferred to Lille's men's facility in 2014. Relevant as the French prison framework Wallis and Futuna inherits (French law applies unless locally overridden).

CGLPL (French national preventive mechanism) opinion of 25 May 2021 on transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty: serious violations of fundamental rights persist in French detention, based on referrals about ~40 transgender detainees since 2010 and interviews with associations/experts; extends a 30 June 2010 opinion on trans prisoners. This French detention framework applies in Wallis and Futuna as a French collectivity.

Grokipedia compilation on transgender rights in Wallis and Futuna: French civil-law gender-marker recognition available without surgery or diagnosis since the 2016-17 French reforms; gender-identity discrimination protections since 2012 (employment, housing, services); but ~11,000 population, isolation and dominant Catholic/Polynesian norms leave practical healthcare and acceptance barriers, with fakafafine-type roles coexisting alongside stigma/concealment.

As a French collectivity, Wallis and Futuna stands under that detention framework.

The statutory protections that apply here are national in origin rather than locally drafted, and the sources do not document how local authorities apply them. SYN-WLF.localsOnly:

72843720B863019116732.name: Centro
72843720B863019116732.summary:
Visitors in Centro stand under Italy's national framework. Outright International records same-sex relations as legal throughout Italy for men and women, and that baseline has not prevented recurring violence against LGBT people, in particular against transgender people. ILGA-Europe's 2026 Annual Review documents homophobic and transphobic violence continuing in 2025, including organised dating-app entrapment schemes in which groups lure victims and then assault or rob them. Progetto Gionata characterises transphobia as the most severe and most widespread discrimination confronting transgender people in Italy.

Progetto Gionata's region-by-region study of anti-LGBT hate-motivated violence, covering 2012 to 2025, distributes victims across the country and names six regions at the top of that distribution. Two of the six, Lazio and Toscana, lie inside Centro, alongside Lombardia and Piemonte in the north-west and Campania and Puglia in the south. High recorded victim counts in the region a visitor is entering are therefore part of a documented pattern rather than an inference from isolated incidents.

The most serious traveller-specific violence finding in the national record concerns trans visitors directly. ANSA reports that convictions for the sexual assault of young transgender tourists in Campania were upheld on appeal in April 2026. The outcome affirms accountability and simultaneously confirms that the assault occurred and that the victims were targeted while in Italy. The dating-app entrapment schemes ILGA-Europe records for gay men define a comparable risk surface for transgender visitors who use hookup applications, where victims are isolated before being attacked.

Police violence against transgender people is documented and has been prosecuted. On 5 July 2024 tgcom24 reported that a Milan traffic officer was sentenced to ten months in prison for stopping a transgender woman and beating her with batons. The sentence shows that such conduct reaches criminal sanction and that a trans person in Italy faces the risk of physical violence from the officers who stop them.

Two judicial decisions inside Centro address violence against transgender people, and both favour the trans party. On 24 January 2025 a first-instance court in Bologna recognised a transphobic motive in the punitive rape of a trans sex worker, sentenced the perpetrator, awarded damages to the victim and to the trans-movement association that helps sex workers, and for the first time admitted the Movimento Identita Trans as a civil party; the source records this as the strongest judicial recognition of transphobic aggravation in Italy. On 5 March 2026 the Court of Cassation confirmed the appeal-court acquittal of trans woman Pinheiro Reis Duarte Hudson, known as Patrizia, over the 27 April 2021 death of Samuele De Paoli in Perugia, finding that the death resulted from cardiac arrhythmia caused by accidental compression during a scuffle De Paoli started. That case, in the region's main university city, was a national anti-trans media flashpoint, and the definitive outcome acquitted the trans defendant.

Anti-trans public messaging can be restricted in the region's largest city. On 30 August 2025 Rome's municipal administration announced that the Consiglio di Stato, the country's highest administrative court, had upheld the city's 2022 removal of Pro Vita and Famiglia posters attacking 'gender' ideology in schools. The court found the images discriminatory, including one showing a boy being given a red hairbow, and held that public spaces may not carry messages that generate alarmism, fear or serious disturbance, particularly concerning minors. The campaign behind the posters had collected 105,000 online signatures before the removal was challenged and then sustained.

Transgender people who are detained are held in an institutional environment that monitors describe as lacking consistent gender-affirming provision. The Ludwig Boltzmann Institute national report of July 2025 sets out the legal and policy framework governing LGBTIQ detainees in Italy, the pathways available for gender affirmation in custody, and the treatment of same-sex relationships in prison. A 2026 study in Frontiers in Psychiatry, drawing on a thematic analysis of transgender identity and psychiatric care in Italian prisons, records systemic gaps and institutional challenges in the care provided to incarcerated trans people.

The political and institutional climate is openly hostile. ILGA-Europe reports that Italy's Education Ministry omitted LGBTI persecution from its Holocaust Remembrance Day circulars for a second consecutive year, and that a cardinal described homosexual acts as a mortal sin. Human Rights Watch's 2025 World Report chapter on Italy records sustained hostile political rhetoric about LGBT people as contributing to a hostile environment, within a wider account of rule-of-law and civil-society constraints.

This is the strongest judicial recognition of transphobic aggravation recorded in Italy.

Progetto Gionata's region-by-region study of anti-LGBT hate-motivated violence, covering 2012 to 2025, names the Italian regions with the highest victim counts, six regions ranking at the top. Lazio and Toscana, both in Centro, are two of the six highest-victim regions, alongside Lombardia, Piemonte (Nord-Ovest), Campania and Puglia (Sud). The study supplies the per-region distribution of violence.

72843720B99597932318450.name: Nord-Ovest
72843720B99597932318450.summary:
Visitors in Nord-Ovest stand under the Italian national framework. Outright International records same-sex relations as legal throughout Italy for men and women, a baseline that has not prevented recurring violence against LGBT people and in particular against transgender people. ILGA-Europe's 2026 Annual Review documents that homophobic and transphobic violence continued in 2025, including organised dating-app entrapment schemes in which groups lure victims and then assault or rob them. Progetto Gionata characterises transphobia as the most severe and most widespread discrimination confronting transgender people in Italy, which matches the pattern of violence recorded by monitors rather than isolated incidents.

The most serious traveller-specific finding is the sexual assault of young transgender tourists in Campania. ANSA reports that the convictions for the assault were upheld on appeal in April 2026, an outcome that affirms accountability for violence against trans visitors while confirming that the assault took place and that the victims were targeted while in Italy. Transgender visitors who use dating and hookup applications face the comparable risk surface that ILGA-Europe records for gay men, where victims are deliberately isolated before being attacked.

Police violence against transgender people is documented and has been prosecuted. On 5 July 2024 tgcom24 reported that a Milan traffic officer was sentenced to ten months in prison for stopping and then beating a transgender woman with batons. The conviction shows that such conduct reaches criminal sanction, and that transgender people in Italy face physical violence from the officers who stop them.

Detention is where the documented deficits are deepest. Transgender people held in Italy are kept in an institutional environment that monitor reports describe as lacking consistent gender-affirming provision. The Ludwig Boltzmann Institute national report of July 2025 sets out the legal and policy framework governing LGBTIQ detainees in Italy, the pathways available for gender affirmation in custody, and the treatment of same-sex relationships in prison. A 2026 study in Frontiers in Psychiatry, drawing on a thematic analysis of transgender identity and psychiatric care in Italian prisons, records systemic gaps and institutional challenges in the care provided to incarcerated trans people.

The political and institutional climate is openly hostile. ILGA-Europe reports that Italy's Education Ministry omitted LGBTI persecution from its Holocaust Remembrance Day circulars for a second consecutive year, and that a cardinal described homosexual acts as a mortal sin. Human Rights Watch's 2025 World Report chapter on Italy records sustained hostile political rhetoric about LGBT people as contributing to a hostile environment, within a wider account of rule-of-law and civil-society constraints. One judicial development points the other way: in March 2025 the Civil Court of Asti recognised, for the first time in that court, the physical and psychological harm caused by homophobic mistreatment, and the source does not establish that the recognition reaches beyond that court.

On identity documents, Milan inaugurated Italy's first gender registry, the registro di genere, letting transgender people use their chosen name on civic and municipal documents; LifeGate presents it as a milestone for transgender rights in the country. The registry is tied to a 2022 council motion by the country's first elected transgender councillor. Turin, also within this region, runs a parallel Identita Alias practice at municipality level and in its libraries.

The regional violence picture is adverse by national standards. Progetto Gionata's breakdown of aggressions by region and city covering 2012 to 2025 shows that two of Nord-Ovest's constituent regions rank among the country's six highest-victim regions for anti-LGBT hate-motivated violence.

Placement and treatment in custody track the legal sex marker rather than lived gender. La Repubblica's investigation of 28 August 2013 recorded 69 transsexual prisoners spread across ten Italian facilities: female hormones could not be prescribed to prisoners who, according to their identity card, count as men; trans women were held in men's sections; and prisoners who had already undergone sex-change surgery were destined for the women's sections. Where cells were lacking, trans prisoners were put in isolation, described in the report as the most inhumane way to preserve their safety. Protected sections, including the G8 section at Rebibbia in Rome and the protected section at Poggioreale in Naples, imposed limitations that extended to partner visits.

Two earlier decisions bear directly on what a trans person can expect in custody. In the 2011 Terni case the Spoleto surveillance magistrate ordered the local health authority to pay for a prisoner's hormone therapy to guarantee psychophysical integrity; the ruling was appealed and followed by a July 2012 appellate decision. In 2010 Italy announced plans for one of the world's first dedicated transgender prisons at Pozzale, near Florence, converting a nearly empty medium-security women's prison into a specially equipped centre for about 30 of Italy's roughly 60 transgender prisoners, most convicted of drug or prostitution offences, with gay-rights groups welcoming the dedicated space and its psychological support. Until then transgender prisoners had been located in women's prisons where they are often segregated for their own safety, the documented 2010 baseline for placement practice. Repubblica reported in 2013 that the Pozzale project was abandoned, and the 2013 investigation records the same project as shelved.

72843720B59566147937015.name: Nord-Est
72843720B59566147937015.summary:
Visitors in Nord-Est stand under the national framework of Italy. Same-sex relations are legal for men and women, the age of consent is 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation, and cross-dressing is not an offence. Legal gender recognition has been available since 1982 and has not required sterilisation or sex reassignment surgery since 21 May 2015. On 23 July 2024 the Constitutional Court, in judgment no. 143, recognised non-binary individuals as rights-holders under Articles 2, 3 and 32 but declined to add a third registry marker, holding that only Parliament can alter the male/female binary; the same judgment struck down judicial authorisation for gender-affirming surgery after a legal sex change. On 14 April 2025 the Supreme Court of Cassation ordered identity cards to use the gender-neutral term "genitori" rather than "mother" and "father" for children with same-sex parents.

Protection against discrimination remains sectoral. No Italian law explicitly bans transphobic discrimination, and ILGA-Europe's 2021 report noted the absence of nationwide coverage of goods and services, leaving transgender people exposed in housing, education and health care. Employment discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation has been illegal since July 2003 under Legislative Decree no. 216 of 2003, with the police, armed forces and rescue-service exemptions removed by Law no. 101 of 2008. A Rome court ruled on 15 January 2023 that dismissing a trans professor amounted to sex discrimination, and in March 2025 the Civil Court of Asti recognised, for the first time, physical and psychological harm resulting from homophobic mistreatment.

Official hostility is part of the environment. The Education Ministry omitted LGBTI persecution from its Holocaust Remembrance Day circulars for a second year, a cardinal publicly described homosexual acts as a mortal sin, and Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 records political rhetoric hostile to LGBT people as contributing to a hostile climate. In the Veneto regional council, the governing majority embedded that orientation in regional education policy: motion n.340, passed at the 178th public session in Venice on 3 July, sits alongside deliberation n.92 of 14 October 2014, which committed the regional government to a mandatory "Natural Family Day" observance on the last school day before Christmas and rejected the aims of gender-awareness content. The official regional government bulletin carries the primary text of that deliberation.

ILGA-Europe's 2026 Annual Review documents that homophobic and transphobic violence continued during 2025, including organised dating-app entrapment schemes in which groups lure victims and then assault or rob them. Progetto Gionata characterises transphobia as the most severe and most widespread discrimination confronting transgender people in Italy, consistent with a pattern recorded by monitors rather than isolated incidents. The most serious traveller-specific finding remains the sexual assault of young transgender tourists in Campania; ANSA reports that convictions for the assault were upheld on appeal in April 2026, an outcome that affirms accountability for violence against trans visitors rather than impunity. State-agent violence has also been prosecuted: in July 2024 a Milan traffic officer was sentenced to 10 months for beating a transgender woman with a baton.

Detention is the sharpest region-relevant risk. In January 2010 Italy announced plans for one of the world's first dedicated transgender prisons at Pozzale, near Florence, converting a nearly empty medium-security women's prison for about 30 of the roughly 60 transgender prisoners then held nationally, mostly convicted of drug or prostitution offences; gay-rights groups welcomed the dedicated space and its psychological support. Repubblica reported in 2013 that the project was abandoned. Before it, and afterwards, transgender prisoners had been held in women's prisons, where they were often segregated for their own safety.

Repubblica's investigative report of 28 August 2013, "La doppia sofferenza delle trans in carcere", counted 69 transsexual prisoners across ten Italian facilities. Placement tracked legal sex, so female hormones could not be prescribed to prisoners who, according to their identity card, counted as men. Trans women were held in men's sections, and those who had already undergone sex-change surgery were destined for the women's sections. Where cells were lacking, trans prisoners were put in isolation, described in the report as the most inhumane way of preserving their safety. Protected sections such as the G8 section at Rebibbia in Rome and the protected section at Poggioreale in Naples imposed limitations, including on partner visits. The 2011 Terni case produced a different line: the Spoleto surveillance magistrate ordered the local health authority to pay for a prisoner's hormone therapy to guarantee psychophysical integrity; the ruling was appealed and a July 2012 appellate decision followed.

Italy recognises persecution based on sexual orientation or gender identity as grounds for asylum under the 1951 Geneva Convention and the EU Qualification Directive 2011/95/EU, and Decree-Law No. 130/2020, in force 22 October 2020, simplified asylum procedures and reinforced protection for vulnerable groups including those persecuted on those grounds.

72843720B81376294924159.name: Isole
72843720B81376294924159.summary:
Isole is a region of Italy and stands under the national framework of Italy. Same-sex relations are legal throughout Italy for men and women, and the age of consent is 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation. Italy has no single comprehensive statute governing sexual orientation and gender identity; protection rests on court rulings and sectoral measures, and no Italian law explicitly bans transphobic discrimination. ILGA-Europe's 2021 report recorded the absence of nationwide protection covering goods and services, leaving transgender people exposed to discrimination in housing, education and health care.

Violence against LGBT people is documented within the region itself. On 26 April 2025 three young men were beaten at a fast-food restaurant in Catania because they were gay; the Procura etnea reconstructed a sequence of insults and threats preceding the physical assault, and video of the attack circulated publicly. A Catania-based outlet reported on 5 June 2026 that assaults and suicide cases continued across Sicilian towns, indicating that the 2025 pattern of attacks had not stopped. The reporting spans several towns rather than a single city.

Detention carries a specific document risk. Placement in Italian prisons follows the sex recorded on identity documents rather than gender identity, so a trans visitor held in custody may be confined in a men's section. la Repubblica's 2013 investigation documented trans women held in men's sections because their carta d'identità still listed them as male, female hormones refused to detainees whose documents said male, decisions passing between prison directors and doctors with no national guideline, and some facilities allowing hormone treatment only if the detainee paid for it.

No dedicated transgender prison exists. Italy announced in January 2010 that it would open one of the world's first such facilities at Pozzale, near Florence in Tuscany, converting an almost empty medium-security prison to house trans inmates convicted mainly of drug and prostitution offences; Italian gay-rights groups welcomed the plan, but it was never realized, and trans prisoners continue to be placed in ordinary facilities.

Legal gender recognition has been available in Italy since 1982, when the country became the sixth worldwide to permit it, and since 21 May 2015 neither sterilisation nor sex reassignment surgery has been required. On 23 July 2024 the Constitutional Court, in judgment no. 143, recognised non-binary individuals as rights-holders under Articles 2, 3 and 32 while declining to add a non-binary registry marker, holding that only Parliament can alter the male/female binary.

82249235B5553315981608.name: Alberta
82249235B5553315981608.summary:
Alberta is a province of Canada and stands under the national framework. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017, and courts have applied those protections consistently. No Canadian jurisdiction restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities, entry carries no trans-specific friction, and identity documents issued federally can carry an X marker. Canadian authorities have issued no alert specific to trans travellers.

Alberta's own legislation runs against that framework. A package of three measures affecting transgender people as a class passed its final legislative stage on 4 December 2024: the Education Amendment Act 2024, which requires parental opt-in for classroom instruction and sets rules on student pronouns and sport; a health-statutes act barring certain gender-affirming care for minors; and a sports policy restricting trans participation. Premier Danielle Smith announced the package on 12 February 2024. Egale Canada and the Skipping Stone Foundation announced constitutional litigation on the day of passage, calling the measures discriminatory.

The laws are in force and shielded from challenge. Bill 9, the Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, passed at the tail of the fall sitting and invokes the Charter's notwithstanding clause to insulate the three measures from legal challenge for years. Egale Canada, the Skipping Stone Foundation and five families say their court challenge to the underlying education act continues regardless, so the constitutional outcome remains unresolved while the statutes operate.

The package was scoped to exclude detention and certain facilities. The February 2024 announcement stated that the bans would not include women's shelters, women's prisons or public changing rooms, and no provincial rule placing trans prisoners by birth sex was enacted. For an adult trans visitor, the practical provincial exposure is therefore concentrated in schools, organised sport and access to gender-affirming care for minors accompanying them, rather than in custody or everyday facilities.

Custody inside Alberta runs on federal policy. Since 2018 the Correctional Service of Canada has accommodated offenders by gender identity rather than sex assigned at birth, and permits gender-diverse offenders to request placement or transfer to a men's or women's institution aligned with their gender identity or expression, regardless of anatomy or the sex or gender marker on identity documents; a request is refused only where the service finds unresolvable overriding health or safety concerns. As of 2025 the service reported 90 self-identified transgender women in federal institutions, 73 housed in men's institutions and 17 in women's. After Bill C-16, federal policy is that transgender prisoners are to be placed according to their gender identity, and prisoners held for more than 12 continuous months are to be considered for sex-reassignment surgery.

Correctional conditions remain the weakest point in the record. Lawyer Barbara findlay represented the transgender prisoner Synthia Kavanagh in litigation over gender-affirming medical treatment and placement in a women's institution. The Office of the Correctional Investigator called the 2022 gender-diversity policy an important change but flagged the absence of clear parameters for what counts as an overriding health or safety concern and the absence of a dedicated mechanism for gender-diverse prisoners to report abuse. A 2022 report alleged a pattern of abuse and discrimination against gender-diverse prisoners in Canadian jails and a higher likelihood of sexual assault; a 2022 study of Nova Scotia correctional officers found them generally mindful of trans-prisoner safety and security, with some concerns about risk to other prisoners. These concerns reach a trans visitor only if the visitor is detained.

Premier Danielle Smith's 12 February 2024 announcement covered a ban on gender-affirming care for minors, parental-consent rules for school pronouns and sexuality instruction, and a ban on trans women in women's sports, and stated the bans 'would not include a ban on women's shelters, women's prisons or women's changing rooms' (Wikipedia biography of Danielle Smith, citing CBC's Lily Dupuis, 12 April 2024, that Alberta's proposed transgender rules won't include public change rooms or jails). No provincial placement-by-birth-sex rule for trans prisoners was enacted, and no Alberta-specific trans-prisoner placement, special unit or segregation case is documented.

82249235B5553315981608.blindSummary:
The state/province stands under the parent nation's national framework. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the national human rights act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the national criminal code, both added by national legislation in 2017 that passed the upper chamber 67-11 in June of that year, and courts have applied those protections consistently. No jurisdiction in the parent nation restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities, entry carries no trans-specific friction, and identity documents issued nationally can carry an X marker. National authorities have issued no alert specific to trans travellers.

The state/province's own legislation runs against that framework. A package of three measures affecting transgender people as a class passed its final legislative stage on 4 December 2024: an education amendment act requiring parental opt-in for classroom instruction and setting rules on student pronouns and sport, a health-statutes act barring certain gender-affirming care for minors, and a sports policy restricting trans participation. The provincial premier announced the package on 12 February 2024. Two national advocacy organisations announced constitutional litigation on the day of passage, calling the measures discriminatory.

The laws are in force and shielded from challenge. A child-protection statutes amendment act passed at the tail of the fall sitting and invokes the constitution's notwithstanding clause to insulate the three measures from legal challenge for years. The two advocacy organisations and five families say their court challenge to the underlying education act continues regardless, so the constitutional outcome remains unresolved while the statutes operate.

The package was scoped to exclude detention and certain facilities. The February 2024 announcement stated that the bans would not include women's shelters, women's prisons or public changing rooms, and no provincial rule placing trans prisoners by birth sex was enacted. For an adult trans visitor, the practical provincial exposure is therefore concentrated in schools, organised sport and access to gender-affirming care for minors accompanying them, rather than in custody or everyday facilities.

Custody inside the state/province runs on national policy. Since 2018 the national corrections service has accommodated offenders by gender identity rather than sex assigned at birth, and permits gender-diverse offenders to request placement or transfer to a men's or women's institution aligned with their gender identity or expression, regardless of anatomy or the sex or gender marker on identity documents; a request is refused only where the service finds unresolvable overriding health or safety concerns. As of 2025 the service reported 90 self-identified transgender women in national institutions, 73 housed in men's institutions and 17 in women's. Under the 2017 legislation, policy is that transgender prisoners are to be placed according to their gender identity, and prisoners held for more than 12 continuous months are to be considered for sex-reassignment surgery.

Correctional conditions remain the weakest point in the record. A lawyer represented the transgender prisoner Synthia Kavanagh in litigation over gender-affirming medical treatment and placement in a women's institution. The national corrections ombudsman called the 2022 gender-diversity policy an important change but flagged the absence of clear parameters for what counts as an overriding health or safety concern and the absence of a dedicated mechanism for gender-diverse prisoners to report abuse. A 2022 report alleged a pattern of abuse and discrimination against gender-diverse prisoners in the parent nation's jails and a higher likelihood of sexual assault; a 2022 study of correctional officers in one province found them generally mindful of trans-prisoner safety and security, with some concerns about risk to other prisoners. These concerns reach a trans visitor only if the visitor is detained.

82249235B5553315981608.tangentialFactors:
Sub-provincial turbulence in Canada is concentrated in schools and sport and bears mainly on minors and residents. Saskatchewan's 2023 Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act invoked the notwithstanding clause to require parental consent for students under 16 who ask to use a gender-related preferred name or to disclose their gender identity at school; human rights groups called for repeal and litigation followed. Alberta reached for the same constitutional device in 2025, which places the two provinces at the front of a small group of jurisdictions using an override against equality litigation.

Legal gender recognition elsewhere in the country is comparatively light. Most provinces allow the gender marker on official documents to be changed by declaring one's identified gender, and Prince Edward Island's 2016 amendment to its Vital Statistics Act removed the prior surgery requirement in favour of a declaration supported by a doctor's letter. The contrast with Alberta's legislative direction on healthcare and sport is marked.

National hate-crime data gives a mixed picture rather than a trans-specific one. Statistics Canada reported 4,882 police-reported hate-crime incidents in 2024, a 1% rise after a 34% jump between 2022 and 2023; incidents targeting sexual orientation fell 26% to 658, down from a 2023 peak of 889 and ending three consecutive years of increases. The release breaks out sexual orientation as a motivation category rather than gender identity, so trans-specific volume is not established.

Ontario supplies a contrast in official protection machinery: the Ontario Human Rights Code expressly covers gender identity and gender expression, and the Ontario Human Rights Commission's published policy sets out the legislation, case law and complaint route, giving an explicit basis for lodging a discrimination complaint.

82249235B71336988791422.name: Saskatchewan
82249235B71336988791422.summary:
Saskatchewan stands under the framework of Canada, where gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code as amended by Bill C-16, passed by the Senate 67-11 in June 2017. Courts have applied those protections consistently, no Canadian jurisdiction restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities, legal gender recognition operates largely on self-declaration, most provinces permit a change of the gender marker on official documents by declaration, federal identity documents can carry an X marker, and entry carries no trans-specific friction.

Provincial policy in Saskatchewan runs against that current. Saskatchewan and Alberta are the two provinces that have enacted rollbacks affecting trans people, and Saskatchewan's is anchored in schools. On 22 August 2023 the Government of Saskatchewan's education ministry announced parental inclusion and consent policies requiring schools to obtain parent or guardian permission before changing the preferred name and pronouns of students under 16, to inform parents about the sexual-health curriculum, and pausing third-party school programs. The announcement prompted a court challenge that has now reached Canada's highest court, and no ruling on the merits has altered the policy: the parental-consent requirement has been in force since 2023.

The litigation has produced a split record. On 11 August 2025, in Saskatchewan (Minister of Education) v UR Pride Centre, 2025 SKCA 74, the Court of Appeal for Saskatchewan set aside the 2023 chambers decision, holding that courts lack jurisdiction to test sections 1 and 15 Charter breaches of the school pronoun-notice policy where section 33 was invoked, so the policy stands; in the same decision the court granted the province's appeal in part and held that a judge does have jurisdiction to determine whether the law limits Charter rights, allowing UR Pride's litigation to continue in the Court of King's Bench. Amnesty International Canada, an intervenor, called the ruling a meaningful victory for the protection of human rights, arguing that use of the override clause must align with Canada's international-law obligation to provide an effective remedy. On 6 November 2025 the Supreme Court of Canada said it would hear the appeals, with both the province and UR Pride seeking expedited hearings alongside a challenge to Quebec's Bill 21. The constitutionality of the shielded consent rule is now before the country's highest court.

Conditions in custody are the weakest point for a trans visitor who is detained. The Correctional Service of Canada has, since 2018, accommodated offenders on the basis of gender identity rather than sex assigned at birth and permits gender-diverse offenders to request placement in a men's or women's institution aligned with their gender identity or expression regardless of anatomy or the sex or gender marker on identity documents, refusing a request only where overriding health or safety concerns cannot be resolved. The reality lags the policy: as of 2025, of 90 self-identified transgender women in federal custody, 73 were housed in men's institutions and 17 in women's. The Office of the Correctional Investigator's 2022-23 report welcomed the 2022 gender-diversity policy but flagged the unclear parameters of the override and the absence of any dedicated mechanism for gender-diverse prisoners to report abuse.

sources.title: Supreme Court to weigh in on Saskatchewan's school pronoun case

Both the province and LGBTQ+ group UR Pride appealed the Court of Appeal decision that the challenge can continue, and asked for the hearing to be expedited alongside the challenge to Quebec's Bill 21. No merits ruling has changed the policy, and the constitutionality of the shielded consent rule is now before Canada's highest court.

82249235B4167839012994.name: New Brunswick
82249235B4167839012994.summary:
Visitors in New Brunswick stand under the Canadian national framework. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017. Courts have applied those protections consistently, no jurisdiction restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities, legal gender recognition operates largely on self-declaration, federally issued identity documents can carry an X marker, and Canadian authorities have neither issued nor received alerts concerning trans travellers.

Provincial education policy is the layer where New Brunswick differs from the rest of Canada. Policy 713 (Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity) of the Department of Education and Early Childhood Development took effect on 17 August 2020, was revised on 1 July and 23 August 2023, and was revised again effective 1 January 2025. Under the current text, students of any age may choose the names and pronouns used for them informally in school, with parental consent encouraged but not required; formal use of a chosen name in official records for a student under 16 still requires parental consent. The revision was made by the Holt government and goes beyond the recommendations of child advocate Kelly Lamrock.

The application clause of Policy 713 covers the school environment as a whole and names the people it binds: all students, school personnel, contract and casual employees, visiting professionals, student teachers, parents, volunteers and visitors. A non-resident present in a New Brunswick classroom, whether as a visiting professional, student teacher or volunteer, is therefore subject to the same name, pronoun and privacy rules as a pupil.

The 2023 revisions remain the reference point for what the province is capable of imposing. Changes taking effect on 1 July 2023 barred teachers from using the preferred names and pronouns of students under 16 without parental consent and dropped explicit wording permitting students to take part in extracurricular activities, including sports teams, in accordance with their gender identity. The Progressive Conservative government of Premier Blaine Higgs made the change without a legislative vote, citing complaints from parents and teachers; two ministers resigned in protest and two others were removed, eight party members including six cabinet ministers boycotted question period over the handling of the file, and dissidents called for a leadership review. The Holt government's 1 January 2025 revision undoes the 2023 consent rule, which had drawn protests outside the legislature and a constitutional challenge by the Canadian Civil Liberties Association.

Facilities are addressed by Policy 713 as originally written: the 2020 policy requires schools to provide gender-neutral bathrooms. Whether that requirement survives verbatim in the text revised on 1 January 2025 is not established by the sources.

In federal custody, the Correctional Service of Canada permits gender-diverse offenders to request placement or transfer to a men's or women's institution matching their gender identity or expression, regardless of anatomy or the sex marker on their identification documents. Requests are assessed individually and may be refused where an unresolved overriding health or safety concern exists under the service's 2022 gender-diversity policy. As of 2025 the service recorded 90 self-identified transgender women in federal custody, 73 housed in men's institutions and 17 in women's; between fiscal years 2017-18 and 2024-25 it received 129 requests from people assigned male at birth for placement in women's institutions, with 35 approved, 72 denied and 22 withdrawn. The Correctional Investigator has criticised the unclear health-or-safety override and the absence of a dedicated abuse-reporting mechanism. New Brunswick is the clearest Canadian case of a provincial government reversing course on trans rights inside a single election cycle, and reversing it back. The 2020 policy protected 2SLGBTQIA+ student privacy and inclusion, the 2023 amendments restricted it, and the December 2024 decision restored it effective 1 January 2025. A visitor encountering school-facing rules in the province is reading a policy with a documented history of being rewritten by order of the executive rather than by statute.

The 2023 episode drew sustained public and political contestation. About 350 people rallied at the New Brunswick legislature on 14 May 2023 to protest the review, at which Gail Costello of Pride in Education, who helped write the policy, said the policy saves lives and warned that removing it would cost children. Education Minister Bill Hogan confirmed the review. Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said trans kids in New Brunswick need to feel safe, not targeted by politicians. The Canadian Civil Liberties Association mounted a constitutional challenge to the 2023 consent rule.

Two provinces, Alberta and Saskatchewan, have enacted policy rollbacks affecting trans residents, including school-facing measures on names, pronouns and notification of parents. Those rules govern residents rather than visitors, but they place New Brunswick's 2023 episode inside a wider provincial direction running alongside the human-rights statutes.

The national hate-crime climate cuts against the statutory protections. Statistics Canada recorded 4,882 police-reported hate-crime incidents in 2024, up 1% after a 34% jump the previous year; over the longer arc police-reported hate crime has risen for six consecutive years and is up 169% since 2018, with offences motivated by gender identity and gender expression among the fastest-growing categories, and Egale Canada documents an increasingly organised anti-trans movement. No New Brunswick-specific hate-crime figures are in the sources.
