14339913B23556801435424.name: Scotland
14339913B23556801435424.summary:
Scotland stands under the United Kingdom's post-April 2025 regime, which now operates through statutory and quasi-statutory machinery rather than executive decree. In August 2026 the equality watchdog's code on single-sex spaces came into force, giving organisations compliance examples for restricting toilets, changing rooms and similar facilities to one sex. The daily consequence for a trans visitor in Scotland is that facilities designated by biological sex are the ones to be used, with organisations instructed on how lawfully to enforce that division.

Prison placement has been litigated to the same end. On 19 June 2026, in For Women Scotland v Scottish Ministers [2026] CSOH 59, Lady Ross of the Outer House, Court of Session, struck down the Scottish Prison Service's non-statutory trans-custody guidance as unlawful, holding that sex segregation in prisons must rest on a lawful basis. The guidance had allowed some trans prisoners to be held in jails matching their gender identity rather than their sex at birth. The competing arguments were aired in the same court on 5 February 2026, when it was argued that housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk, while government lawyers defended individual risk assessments as a flexible safeguard and For Women Scotland pressed its challenge to the policy of holding only biological females in the women's estate.

Searching and strip-searching policy follows the same principle. On 17 April 2025 British Transport Police amended its strip-searching policy after the Supreme Court ruling, adopting an interim position that trans women are strip-searched by officers of their sex at birth; the prior policy had permitted trans women staff to intimately search women holding a gender recognition certificate, and Sex Matters welcomed the change. On 25 June 2025 Police Scotland published interim guidance under which searches in custody and stop-and-search involving removal of more than a jacket, gloves, headgear or footwear are conducted on the basis of biological sex, with efforts made to provide an officer of the individual's lived gender on request where lived gender differs.

Gender recognition documents carry their own consequences. In December 2023 the UK government said it would no longer accept gender recognition certificates issued by 50 countries and U.S. states, including Sweden, New York State and Belgium, on the ground that those jurisdictions allowed people to transition too easily; people from those locations must apply for a new certificate under British law to change their gender in the UK. The Women and Equalities Minister, Kemi Badenoch, called the changes long overdue, while Shadow Equalities Minister Anneliese Dodds warned of diplomatic consequences because the list excluded Canada, the United States, Australia and New Zealand. Within the UK, a certificate will not be issued unless the applicant's spouse consents; where the spouse does not consent the marriage must be terminated, and transgender people seeking a certificate have historically been required to divorce or annul first.

Access to gender-affirming care is restricted for minors. NHS England said in March 2024 that gender identity clinics would stop prescribing puberty blockers to children and young people, a suspension renewed indefinitely in December 2024 and due to be reconsidered in 2027. In April 2025 it was reported that the NHS had issued no new prescriptions of gender-affirming hormones to minors in the year since the Cass Review, with some families turning to black-market or overseas hormones instead. The Cass Review of April 2024 also led NHS England to close the Tavistock GIDS in March 2024, with only two of eight planned regional centres opened and many 16- and 17-year-olds transferred to adult services. Bell v Tavistock (December 2020) had found that children under 16 could not independently consent to puberty blockers; that judgment was overturned on appeal in September 2021.

Restrictions reach schools and sport. The Girls' Day School Trust barred admissions for trans girls without a gender recognition certificate in January 2022, and in July 2022 the RFU and RFL implemented a single-sex policy for under-12s excluding trans girls from girls' teams. Transgender youth are otherwise covered by the Equality Act 2010. On 18 August 2026 UN human rights experts warned that UK revisions to the Equality Act 2010 risk discriminating against and excluding transgender people.

Scotland operates its own hate-crime machinery, and charges carrying a transgender-identity aggravation are rising. The Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service reported in Hate crime in Scotland, 2025-26, published 30 June 2026, that 7,115 hate-crime charges were brought in 2025-26, up 17 per cent on 2024-25 and the highest total since 2003-04. Transgender-identity aggravation accounted for 104 charges, a rise of 21 per cent from 86 and the highest level recorded since the Hate Crime and Public Order (Scotland) Act 2021 took effect. Sexual-orientation aggravation accounted for 2,062 charges, the second commonest category. A trans visitor therefore enters a jurisdiction where trans-motivated offences are actively charged under a dedicated statutory aggravator, at a level the prosecuting service describes as the highest since the provision began.

31927357B79016588373767.name: Distrito Federal
31927357B79016588373767.summary:
The Distrito Federal stands under the national framework of Mexican equality law, where legal gender recognition remains the central unfinished task. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that many of Mexico's states now operate administrative procedures for legal gender recognition, that implementation differs sharply from one state to another, and that the states without such procedures should adopt them. Where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

Lethal violence against trans people is documented at national scale. The annual report published in May 2025 by a Mexican LGBT+ news collective recorded 115 violent incidents against LGBT+ people across Mexico in 2024, of which 59 were killings. Transgender Europe's monitoring counts 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months, and AP reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City; the killings drew LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests.

Within that national pattern the Distrito Federal is a single data point, and in 2024 it was the largest one. For the first time Mexico City topped the national count with 17 LGBT+ homicides, 11 of them trans women, ahead of Nuevo León's 5. Part of the elevated count reflects the capital's superior reporting infrastructure rather than proportionally higher danger, but the raw figures remain a negative signal for a visitor.

The institutional response is the strongest of any Mexican state. Mexico City's congress approved transfeminicidio as a distinct crime in the local penal code on 19 July 2024, making the capital the second state to create the offence. The reform is known as the Ley Paola Buenrostro, after a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished, and activists describe the law as critical to their sense of safety. Article 148-Ter, added to the local code on 23 August 2024, typifies the killing of a trans woman or feminine-spectrum person by reason of her gender identity or expression.

Investigation practice has been reorganised around that offence. A dedicated Transfeminicide Investigation Unit was created in December 2024 to cover all violent deaths of trans women, and its investigators may no longer demand legal name or gender change or medical documentation from trans people, removing a documented route to outing and delay when a crime is reported. The prosecutor's instrument FGJCDMX/04/2025 sets initial-response protocol rules for transfeminicide alongside feminicide investigations, and on 25 August 2025 the mayor of Mexico City launched a new Gender Police with 30 patrol units to handle cases of violence against women and girls in the capital.

Enforcement remains the open question. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that all LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels. Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice, and cautions explicitly that the analysis must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

Partnership recognition is settled at the national level: same-sex marriage has been legal in Mexico since 2009, with Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction.

31927357B79016588373767.tangentialFactors:
Document barriers elsewhere in Mexico indicate what obstructed recognition looks like in practice. The Human Rights Watch report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" (6 March 2024) found that delays and refusals in name and gender recognition in Tabasco leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying everyday discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police; the same report set those barriers against killings, including a trans woman found dead in the Carrizal River in August 2023. A visitor whose papers do not match presentation can expect the same friction at checkpoints and counters.

The state-by-state comparison is uneven in both directions. Nuevo León's 5 LGBT+ homicides in 2024 against the capital's 17 shows how concentrated the recorded toll was, and the capital's reporting infrastructure inflates its relative position without negating the underlying level of violence. On the legislative side the Distrito Federal was the second state to typify transfeminicide, which means other states still lack the offence entirely and cases there are prosecuted, if at all, under ordinary homicide provisions.

Impunity is the recurring regional condition rather than a local exception. The Inter-American Commission's 2024 warning that impunity may have reached alarming levels, together with the unpunished 2016 murder that gave the Ley Paola Buenrostro its name, frames the practical value of the new offence as untested. Beer's LSE USAPP analysis makes the same point nationally: formal rights that are rarely enforced fairly or uniformly.

31927357B30741484985331.name: Nuevo Leon
31927357B30741484985331.summary:
Three trans women murdered in less than a week in July 2024 (one disappeared and found dead days later; one killed while sex work); four transfeminicides recorded in July 2024 alone and five for the year in the national NGO yearbook — second only to Mexico City. Activists reported six trans women killed in a short period and accused three levels of government of rights omissions. Nuevo León's penal code contains no transfeminicide offence, and its 2019 hate-crime provision covers sexual orientation but not gender identity — meaning a visitor assaulted in Monterrey faces a legal framework with no specific protective category. The state has an anti-conversion-practices law carrying 2-5 years, and the national observatory's verdict on such statutes is that transfeminicide 'advances in law but not in sentences.'

Legislative response has been refusal: an initiative filed by Colectivo Casa Trans was 'ignored and finally lapsed,' prompting a 50+-day protest encampment outside the state congress still ongoing in January 2026 (activists report harassment and lack of basic facilities at the camp). A PT deputy in 2026 could only ask the congress to 'unfreeze' the bill. There is no investigative unit, no protocol, and no named offence to invoke. The gap between nominal coverage and protection is documented in the observatory review 'transfeminicide advances in law but not in sentences.'

Context for comparison: Mexico City pairs a similar lethality record with a dedicated transfeminicide investigation unit (Dec 2024), mandatory-response protocols and a gender police force (Aug 2025); Nayarit was first in the country to typify the crime (March 2024). Nuevo León's explicit legislative refusal is the opposite signal.

Letra S 'Las dinámicas de la violencia por prejuicio — Homicidios de personas LGBT+ en México, 2024' (May 2025): the country's longest-running civil-society hate-crime observatory (since 1998) yearbook. Records CDMX as the state with the most LGBT+ killings in 2024 (17 homicides, 11 trans women) ahead of Nuevo León (5); notes the Mexican state has no official registry of bias-motivated violence, and documents under-counting where media accounts lack victim names and gender data.

Verificado (2024): Nuevo Leon recorded 7 attacks on LGBT people, 3 forced disappearances and 4 transfeminicides during the year, and transfeminicidio is not typified in the state penal code. 31927357B49073316106075.name: Michoacan de Ocampo
31927357B49073316106075.summary:
Michoacán has not typified the killing of LGBT people as a hate crime under state law, an absence acknowledged by the state's own welfare officials and by civil-society monitors. Attacks against the community concentrate geographically in Tierra Caliente, the zone of armed-group influence, so risk inside the state is uneven rather than uniform: Morelia, the state capital, records the largest absolute number of LGBT homicides, but enforcement of any protective framework is weak throughout.

Homicide against LGBT people in Michoacán is sustained and documented. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes contra Personas LGBT, presented by Raúl Martínez of Colectivo Michoacán es Diversidad, counted 46 LGBT homicides in the state between 2015 and 2024, distributed across Morelia (11), Lázaro Cárdenas (6), Apatzingán and Uruapan (5 each) and Zamora (4). The deadliest year was 2015, with 10 victims. Trans women accounted for 27 of the 46 homicides, and the 25 to 39 age bracket was the most affected. Thirteen disappearances of LGBT people were reported between 2022 and 2024, a figure whose investigation status the civil-society data does not resolve.

The pattern continued into 2026. Six homicide cases against LGBT people were identified in the state in the first four and a half months of that year, three in Morelia and one each in Uruapan, Ocampo and Maravatío. One of them was 'Daniela', a trans woman found beaten to death in a drainage channel in Morelia on 2 April 2026; a suspect was arrested, an outcome that stands out against the surrounding pattern of inaction. At least 56 aggressions against the community have been registered in Michoacán since 2014.

Impunity is the decisive variable for a visitor assessing protection. Of the 46 hate-crime cases recorded by civil society in the state since 2015, only one was moving toward judicial proceedings: the murder of Meredith Escarlet, a trans woman killed in Tarímbaro. The state prosecutor's office keeps no disaggregated data on these cases, and the victims commission, the state human rights commission and the state council against discrimination lack the capacity or budget to act. No public prevention policy for LGBT violence exists in the state.

31927357B5337219705256.name: Veracruz de Ignacio de la Llave
31927357B5337219705256.summary:
Veracruz de Ignacio de la Llave stands under the national framework of Mexico, where legal gender recognition remains the central unfinished task of equality law. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that many Mexican states now operate administrative recognition procedures while others lack them entirely, and that implementation differs sharply from one state to another. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2009.

Veracruz was among the last states to legislate. The Human Rights Watch state-by-state map shows that only in 2025 did the state's Congress reform the Civil Code to create an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, with no age requirement. The same page documents no prison-placement rule for Veracruz and no information on where trans prisoners are housed; its Veracruz content concerns civil registry and identity documents only.

The state's record on lethal violence is the worst in the national monitoring data. Letra S's report "Muertes violentas de personas LGBT+ en México — Informe 2021" (May 2022) found that Veracruz led the national count of violent deaths of LGBT+ people for the fourth consecutive year, with 10 recorded cases in 2021, against Guanajuato with 9, Estado de México with 7 and Chihuahua with 6; 19 of the 32 states recorded victims.

The 2025 figures show the same concentration. Letra S's annual impunity report of 7 May 2026 records 60 LGBT+ people murdered nationwide in 2025, of whom 35 (58.3 percent) were trans women, a national trans-women homicide rate of 23.7 per 100,000. The state ranking places Puebla first with 7 killings and Veracruz and Guanajuato second with 6 each; a Veracruz case in that count is the November 2025 killing in a motel in Oluta.

Diario de Xalapa reports that Veracruz closed 2025 with 15 recorded hate crimes against the LGBT community. Jornada Veracruz reports that the state prosecutor's office holds several open LGBT-murder files, according to activist Leonardo Ruiz of Orgullo Xalapa, among them Edhibaldo Presa Parra, a Universidad Veracruzana professor found dead on 7 January. Activists say suspicion of a hate crime rests on motive patterns, including prior harassment, aggravating factors and the victim's orientation, and attribute unresolved cases to impunity in the state prosecutor's office; data cited from 'Soy Humano' put Veracruz below the national average in 2024.

Recorded totals understate the harm. The Letra S 2021 report notes under-reporting: in a third of 2021 cases no victim name was published, and in 43 percent the recorded sex was male without attention to gender identity.

31927357B6525686063804.name: Oaxaca
31927357B6525686063804.summary:
Oaxaca is a state of Mexico and stands under the national framework in which legal gender recognition remains unfinished and uneven. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2024 and its state-by-state map of 11 and 31 March 2025 record that 21 of Mexico's 32 states permit administrative name and gender-marker changes on birth certificates, under standards set by a 2019 Supreme Court ruling and extended to adolescents and children in March 2022. Where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

Oaxaca has built the procedure. A 2019 reform of the state civil code created an administrative route to legal gender recognition, a 2021 decree extended it to people aged 12 and over, and a June 2023 Supreme Court ruling fully opened the procedure, including for children under 12. Oaxaca's only documented gender-identity law concerns identity documents; it does not govern where trans inmates are held.

Oaxaca is simultaneously reported as Mexico's fastest-growing tourist destination and its most dangerous state for the LGBT+ community. Trendencias (April 2025) reported violent incidents under investigation with possible municipal-police involvement in municipalities where armed groups operate, and listed among the murdered muxe Cristian Hernandez Cutino, aged 31, and stylist Zulma Hernandez Mendoza, aged 43. The state response described there has been stepped-up visitor security rather than institutional reform.

The state human-rights ombudsperson, the Defensoría, opened 34 investigations into attacks on LGBTIQ+ people between 2015 and 2022, El Universal reported on 27 September 2026. Violence against muxes persists: muxe teacher Marimar "Estrellita" Santiago was killed in 2022 on the road to Huilotepec in the Istmo de Tehuantepec, prompting community demands for justice.

Exclusion also reaches trans people through private event rules. The organising brotherhood of the Vela San Vicente Ferrer Goola "Lado Sur" festival in Juchitán circulated an invitation stating that "men dressed as women will not be admitted"; muxe activists, among them defender Felina Santiago, who has campaigned for three decades, filed a discrimination complaint with the national equality body over the exclusion. Three velas went ahead on 26 May 2024, with muxes affirming that they are part of local society and culture.

31927357B6525686063804.tangentialFactors:
Oaxaca's legal position is ahead of much of Mexico. Human Rights Watch records administrative name and gender-marker changes on birth certificates in only 21 of the country's 32 states, so Oaxaca's completed procedure places it in the minority of states where a visitor or resident can obtain documents matching their identity without litigation.

Formal availability and lived exposure diverge. Analysis by Caroline Beer published on the LSE USAPP blog (22 November 2024) found that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are rarely enjoyed in practice, and stated explicitly that her findings must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ people in Mexico are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

The national pattern of killings gives context to the Oaxaca cases. Transgender Europe monitoring recorded 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico from 2008 to September 2021 and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a total second only to Brazil's 100. The Associated Press reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening period of that year, including activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, which triggered street demonstrations.

Other jurisdictions have moved further on criminal law than Oaxaca. Mexico City's Congress approved the "Paola Buenrostro law" in July 2024, criminalising transfemicide and named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished; activists quoted at the time described the measure as critical to their feeling safe in the capital. No equivalent Oaxaca statute on transfemicide is documented in these sources.

Regional oversight bodies have pressed the authorities across the country. In 2024 the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded investigation of all LGBTI violations using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may reach alarming levels.

31927357B1137737933275.name: Puebla
31927357B1137737933275.summary:
Puebla stands within Mexico's national framework on legal gender recognition, which Human Rights Watch described on 31 March 2025 as unfinished and uneven. Many Mexican states now operate administrative procedures for recognition, but implementation differs sharply from state to state, and where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation. The organisation called on the states lacking such procedures to adopt them.

Puebla's own regime rests on a 2021 reform of the state civil code adopted by the Puebla State Congress, together with a corresponding implementing decree, recognising the right to legal gender recognition. Human Rights Watch records in its state-by-state survey of 11 March 2025 that Puebla's regime carries an 18-year minimum age requirement that a court has voided.

Puebla also recorded the highest number of LGBT+ homicides of any Mexican state in 2025. Quadratin reported on 16 June 2026 that 60 LGBT+ people were murdered across Mexico that year, of whom 35 were trans women, or 58.3 per cent, with victims in at least 17 states. Seven of the killings were recorded in Puebla.

1811400B57209440839078.name: Tripura
1811400B57209440839078.summary:
Tripura stands under India's national framework. India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, replacing the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist. The government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking; critics say it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. An estimated two million transgender people live in India.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which the Supreme Court has interpreted to cover gender identity. The Allahabad High Court extended that prohibition in 2021 to bar employment discrimination on sexual orientation grounds. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed legal safeguards that had protected trans persons from sexual violence, and trans people fear a rise in assaults because the new code omits the gender-identity-specific offences the old law carried.

Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction across India. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person asked to take a medical exam by passport authorities. In November 2024 Sakshi Jain, an openly transgender law student, was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at the station under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender persons arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.

Within Tripura, transgender travellers have themselves been the object of sustained checkpoint enforcement. Police apprehended 15 Bangladeshi nationals including 7 transgender individuals in separate incidents within 24 hours, searching a bus at the Panisagar checkpoint on the Assam-Agartala highway in North Tripura and finding detainees with fake Aadhaar and PAN cards travelling to Mumbai via Guwahati. On 2 August 2024 at the same Panisagar check post, officers detained 7 Bangladeshi nationals, 2 transgender individuals and 5 others described as disguised as third-gender, bound for Mumbai by bus. On 9 November 2024 a joint 24-hour operation detained 12 Bangladeshi nationals including minors and transgender people: a first group of 6, holding 3 transgender persons, was stopped after midnight en route to Mumbai, and a second group of 6, including 3 children from Khulna, was held at Udaipur Railway Station, with a local helper, Md Hafizur, arrested for facilitating movement. Tripura shares a 856-km porous border with Bangladesh, and the cases were framed as fraudulent-document and border-crossing offences rather than offences against the detainees' gender.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic, while victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities.

Tripura shares an 856-km porous border with Bangladesh.

1811400B32673734874058.name: West Bengal
1811400B32673734874058.summary:
West Bengal stands under India's national framework. Parliament's Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill of March 2026 replaced the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals, so trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist, while the government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018 and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, read to cover gender identity, but same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024: replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed gender-identity-specific sexual-violence offences that had protected trans persons, and trans people fear a rise in assaults as a result. Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person asked to take a medical exam by passport authorities; in November 2024 openly transgender law student Sakshi Jain was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card. In West Bengal itself, a group of trans women heading to RG Kar Medical College filed an FIR on 18 August 2024 alleging an RPF constable at Rabindra Sadan metro station groped one of them to check her gender and made inappropriate remarks; Metro Railway and the RPF denied the allegations and counter-filed an FIR against the group, while footage showed the trans woman in tears. Transgender persons arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic; victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities; bans from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating.

West Bengal registered 3 of the 7 Transgender Persons Act cases filed nationally in 2021, the highest count that year alongside Assam and Kerala, though national totals remain very small at 20 cases from 2019 to 2023, a figure the report attributes to police-registration bias rather than low incidence. A 2025 survey recorded prevalence of 27.2% physical violence and 22.3% sexual violence against trans people. South Dinajpur police arrested Bangladeshi transgender person Ali Mondal, also known as Bijli Mondal, from Sirajganj district, along with the e-rickshaw driver who brought her across the border, for allegedly infiltrating India, illustrating exposure to immigration enforcement for trans border-crossers.

Facilities and care access are largely set at state level. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha run transgender welfare boards coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions, and several states provide targeted welfare, housing and healthcare benefits for hijras. Nationally, the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community, and in August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries. West Bengal is one of the 12 states and union territories that notified a transgender welfare board, but its constituted board operates without a functioning policy framework; nationally, most boards have held fewer than one meeting per year since creation, and the 17 existing boards are mostly running rudderless without a policy framework, compliance mechanism or any power, with several functioning as non-transparent bodies that diffuse demands instead of serving trans people.

Intersex minors remain at risk: reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations, and the Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.

1811400B91946361694107.name: Punjab
1811400B91946361694107.summary:
Punjab has no statute of its own targeting transgender people. A trans visitor to Punjab stands under India's national framework. In March 2026 India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill, replacing the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist. The government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking, while critics say it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

The statute of record in Punjab is the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 (Act No. 40 of 2019). It was passed by the Lok Sabha on 5 August 2019 and the Rajya Sabha on 26 November 2019, received presidential assent on 5 December 2019, and has been in force since 10 January 2020. Following the Supreme Court's 2014 NALSA judgment, it grants transgender people the right to declare a self-perceived gender identity without undergoing sex reassignment surgery, bans discrimination in education, employment, healthcare and housing, creates a National Council for Transgender Persons, and prescribes imprisonment of not less than six months up to two years plus a fine for crimes against transgender people. Criticism holds that the Act omits mandatory reservations in jobs and education. On 27 January 2020 the Supreme Court issued notice in a petition challenging the Act's constitutionality.

Determinations that bind Punjab include the Supreme Court's judgment of 6 September 2018 in Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India, in which a five-judge bench ruled unanimously to strike down Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code insofar as it criminalised consensual same-sex acts, holding that discrimination based on sexual orientation violates the Constitution while preserving the provision for non-consensual acts. The 2014 NALSA judgment recognised a legal third gender and the right to self-identified gender identity. In July 2024 the Indian Penal Code was replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which omits Section 377 entirely; the replacement also removed gender-identity-specific sexual-violence offences that had protected trans persons under the old code, and trans people fear a rise in assaults as a result. Discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which courts have interpreted to cover gender identity. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership in India, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Punjab's clearest documented signal is institutional rather than criminal. Pride Amritsar cancelled the parade scheduled for 27 April 2025 at the Rose Garden after mounting resistance from Sikh religious organisations, including the Nihang Singh faction and the Akal Takht, with organisers citing religious-group opposition as the reason. The Washington Blade reported the cancellation on 23 April 2025. No state intervention to preserve the event is recorded in the audited sources, so organised religious opposition has compelled the disappearance of Punjab's annual public trans assembly.

Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction across India. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person who had been asked to take a medical exam by passport authorities. In November 2024 an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card for identity verification. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at the station under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender persons arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic, while victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. Bans on conversion therapy from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating.

Nationally the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community, and in August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries. Intersex minors remain at risk: reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations, and the Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.

1811400B45534780755480.name: Kerala
1811400B45534780755480.summary:
Kerala is a state within India and stands under the national transgender-rights framework, which Parliament narrowed in March 2026. The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill replaced the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist; the government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking, while critics say it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

The national baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court of India in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which courts have interpreted to cover gender identity: the Supreme Court has held that discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity falls within Article 15's prohibition of discrimination by sex, and the Allahabad High Court extended that in 2021 to bar employment discrimination on sexual orientation grounds. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed legal safeguards that had protected trans persons from sexual violence, and trans people fear a rise in assaults because the new code omits the gender-identity-specific offences the old law carried.

Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction across the country. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person who had been asked to take a medical exam by passport authorities. In November 2024 an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at the station under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender persons arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic; victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. Bans flowing from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating.

Kerala's own enforcement record under the national statute is among the highest sub-national totals in India. A crime-data report of 30 January 2026 records two of the seven national Transgender Persons Act cases in 2021 as arising in Kerala, and four of the eleven in 2023, a figure joint-highest with Tamil Nadu. The report cautions that national counts are tiny because of police-registration bias, so these totals measure recorded cases rather than incidence.

Facilities and care access are set largely at state level. The Union government told Parliament in December 2021 that Kerala is among twelve states and union territories reported to have constituted Transgender Welfare Boards under Section 10(1) of the 2019 Rules. Kerala's board operates alongside those of Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra and Odisha, coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions. Nationally, the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community, and in August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.

Intersex minors remain at risk. Reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations, and the Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.

1811400B11231190780494.name: Uttar Pradesh
1811400B11231190780494.summary:
Uttar Pradesh stands under India's national framework for transgender persons. India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, replacing the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist. The government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking; critics say it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which the Supreme Court has held covers sexual orientation and gender identity under Article 15; the Allahabad High Court extended that in 2021 to bar employment discrimination on sexual orientation grounds. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed legal safeguards that had protected trans persons from sexual violence, and trans people fear a rise in assaults because the new code omits the gender-identity-specific offences the old law carried.

Identity documents remain a live source of friction. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person who had been asked to take a medical exam by passport authorities, indicating that intrusive document screening has been applied to trans travellers in Uttar Pradesh and that the state's high court has intervened against it.

The most trans-visible public space in Uttar Pradesh is the Maha Kumbh gathering in Prayagraj. On 12 February 2025, at the fourth ceremonial bath of the 45-day fair, Pavitra Nandagiri, a Mahamandaleshwar of the Kinnar Akhada and one of the gathering's highest-ranking monks, led 15 transgender spiritual leaders in the ritual bathing, marching alongside Naga Sadhus and Aghori. The episode documents an institutionalised trans religious hierarchy operating openly in the state.

Trans-specific violence is documented. Kajal, a 25-year-old transgender woman in Kanpur, was killed in a home-invasion robbery; the record dates to 10 August 2025, a suspect was later arrested, and her 12-year-old adopted brother also died. The killing was logged in the 2025 international transgender day of remembrance list through local press reporting.

Protection machinery at state level is mandated but its Uttar Pradesh implementation is not established in the sources. The Ministry of Social Justice stated on 8 December 2021 that state governments must constitute Transgender Welfare Boards under section 10(1) of the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Rules, 2020, and all state governments were reminded on 9 October 2020 to act.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic; victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police.

14911670B7632012573600.name: Ceara
14911670B7632012573600.summary:
Ceará stands under Brazil's national framework for LGBTI people. The Constitution, the Penal Code and federal anti-discrimination provisions apply in the state, and no Ceará-specific statute distinguishes gender identity or expression. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change in 2018, the age of consent is equal regardless of sexual orientation, and an expat legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate across the country. A trans visitor's documents and family status are therefore handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry and in registry matters.

After the Supreme Court's 2019 ruling, constitutional and federal criminal provisions prohibit discrimination and hate crimes on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds, with transphobia punishable on the same footing as racism. Ceará is bound by those provisions like every other state, and there is no indication in the sources of a state law or state policy cutting back on them.

The violence record is the sharpest finding for a visitor. Reporting by G1/Globo on 28 January 2025, citing the ANTRA dossier, identifies Ceará as the Northeast state with the most killings of trans people in 2024: 11 killings, the third highest count in the country. The following year did not reverse the pattern. Igbá Agência reported on 26 January 2026, and SBT News the same day, that the ninth ANTRA dossier placed Ceará among the states with the most trans killings in 2025 with 8 cases, tied with Minas Gerais at the top of the state ranking.

National totals give those figures their scale. Brazil recorded 80 trans killings in 2025, an 18th consecutive year as the country with the highest number worldwide and a 34 per cent fall from 2024. Between 2017 and 2025 the count reached 1,261, an average near 140 a year. The victims are overwhelmingly racialised: of the 57 victims with race data in the 2025 dossier, 70 per cent were Black, against an average of 77 per cent across 2017 to 2025.

Detention in Ceará is governed by a specific national regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, fixes where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed. A person is recognised as LGBTI for these purposes by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing. On arrest the place of deprivation of liberty is set by a judge in a reasoned decision after the person has been consulted: the judge must list the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it the general population or a specific wing or cell. The declared preference is recorded, placement can be changed later, and transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

Practice does not reliably follow that framework anywhere in the country. A peer-reviewed census of travestis and transgender women in Rio de Janeiro state prisons, carried out between April and June 2021, interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates inside eleven units operated as masculine in the metropolitan region, documenting placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights. The study also records a 2015 Rio de Janeiro state law granting parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units, covering hair length, feminine clothing, accessories and cosmetics, and national norms from 2014 and 2020 permitting people to be housed where they choose, including in units denominated masculine. No equivalent census for Ceará's prisons is available in the sources.

14911670B91095571793858.name: Rio Granda do Norte
14911670B91095571793858.summary:
Rio Grande do Norte stands under Brazil's national framework. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change in 2018, the age of consent is equal regardless of sexual orientation, and since the Supreme Court's 2019 ruling constitutional and federal criminal provisions prohibit discrimination and hate crimes on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds, with transphobia punishable on the same footing as racism. An expat legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that marriage recognition, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate across the country, so a trans visitor's status and documents are handled like anyone else's at entry and in family matters. No state-level statutory restriction or unique legal finding applies in Rio Grande do Norte.

The dominant visitor-facing signal is lethal violence against trans people. ANTRA's dossier for 2024 recorded 122 trans and travesti killings nationally, 16 per cent below the 145 recorded in 2023 and close to the 125-per-year average for 2008 to 2024; five of the victims were human-rights defenders and 95.9 per cent were travestis or trans women. The same dossier documents systematic under-counting because official bodies do not record LGBTQIA+ victims properly, which is the basis on which Rio Grande do Norte appeared with zero recorded killings in 2024.

The ninth ANTRA dossier, covering 2025, records 80 trans killings nationwide, Brazil's eighteenth consecutive year at the top of the global tally. In the state ranking Ceará and Minas Gerais lead with eight each, while Paraíba and Rio Grande do Norte appear with four each. Against a population of roughly 3.5 million, four cases yield about 1.14 killings per million per year, the highest per-capita rate among all 27 units in 2025 and around three times the national figure of roughly 0.38 per million. The jump from zero in 2024 makes Rio Grande do Norte the sharpest deterioration in the dataset, and the dataset itself cautions against reading a single-year zero as evidence of safety.

Lethal violence against trans women in the state continued after both counted years. In the early hours of 4 May 2026, Emanuelle Samira Fernandes Neta, a 27-year-old transgender woman, was shot dead inside her rented home in the Dom Jaime Câmara neighbourhood of Mossoró after five men broke in and killed her while she slept; military police found the body on a routine patrol and one suspect was arrested with a pistol and booked for illegal firearms discharge and armed criminal association. In late February 2026 a transgender woman known as Naomi was found dead in her own home in Praia da Pipa, in the Tibau do Sul municipality, killed by stab wounds, with the Civil Police opening an investigation.

Detention, if it arises, is governed by national rather than state rules. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, requires that a person held as LGBTI be recognised by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing, and that placement be fixed by a reasoned judicial decision after the person has been consulted about their preference. Trans, travesti and intersex people must be asked whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit and within it the general population or a specific wing or cell; LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited. No Rio Grande do Norte placement policy is documented in the sources held, and practice elsewhere in the country has been found to diverge sharply from this framework.

14911670B97385369352280.name: Paraiba
14911670B97385369352280.summary:
Paraíba stands under Brazil's national framework: same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change in 2018, and after the Supreme Court's 2019 ruling constitutional and federal criminal provisions prohibit discrimination and hate crimes on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds, with transphobia punishable on the same footing as racism. An expat legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that gender-marker rules and spousal-visa equality operate nationwide, so a trans visitor's documents are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry.

The protective text does not describe what people encounter. Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records that LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination despite those provisions. The ANTRA 2025 dossier, reported by SBT News on 26 January 2026, recorded 4 trans killings in Paraíba during 2025, tied with Paraná, Rio Grande do Norte and São Paulo, against a national total of 80. CNN Brasil's 2024 dossier recorded 5 trans killings in Paraíba in 2024, while Rio Grande do Norte, Acre and Roraima recorded zero and Bahia, Mato Grosso and Pernambuco recorded 8 each. Brazil leads the world in killings of trans people, and Paraíba sits among the states with the highest counts in both years.

Prison placement for LGBTI people is governed nationally. A federal portaria issued by the Secretaria de Direitos Humanos da Presidência da República, reported by G1 on 17 April 2014, sets where LGBT prisoners are housed across Brazil's prison system and applies in Paraíba's state system: transsexual men and women must be forwarded to female prison units, gay and travesti prisoners held in male prisons must be offered specific conviviality spaces, LGBT inmates may use their social name (which must appear in the admission record) and choose male or female clothing. The portaria carries no sanction for non-compliance. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, further requires that a person is recognised as LGBTI for placement purposes by self-declaration before a judge, that placement is fixed by a reasoned judicial decision after consultation with the person about their preference among male, female and LGBTI-specific units, and that LGBTI-specific spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation. No Paraíba-specific implementation, wing, segregation practice or case is documented.

14911670B2612452665424.name: Pernambuco
14911670B2612452665424.summary:
Pernambuco recorded 7 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, the second-highest count of any Brazilian state in the ANTRA dossier released on 26 January 2026, behind only Ceará and Minas Gerais at 8 each, against a national total of 80. Valor Internacional reported the same state-level counts on 27 January 2026, and Diario de Pernambuco carried the state ranking on the same date.

The annual figure has fallen from 13 in 2022 to 9 in 2023, 8 in 2024 and 7 in 2025, so 2025 is the lowest count since 2022 while remaining among the highest in the country. Over six years Pernambuco recorded 83 violent deaths of trans people, sixth-most in the national ranking for that period, within a Northeast regional total of 349 killings from 2017 to 2025.

The danger is concentrated away from Recife. Most such killings occur in interior municipalities rather than the state capital, where monitoring, denunciation and access to public services are thinner. On 2 October 2025 a trans woman was shot dead inside her home in Belo Jardim, in the Agreste interior; the Civil Police opened an inquiry to identify the author and motive, and no arrests were reported at publication. The same report recalled the national ANTRA count of 122 trans people killed in Brazil in 2024.

Interior killings of Black trans women have a documented history in the state. Detention stands under the national framework rather than any Pernambuco-specific rule. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, as amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, gives LGBTI detainees placement by self-declaration before a judge, notification of available male, female and LGBTI-specific units, and prohibits using LGBTI living spaces as disciplinary isolation. 14911670B19428866735507.name: Bahia
14911670B19428866735507.summary:
Bahia is a state in north-east Brazil and stands under the national framework described above: the federal constitutional and criminal prohibitions on SOGI discrimination, the 2018 removal of the surgical requirement for legal gender change, equal age of consent, same-sex marriage and spousal-visa equality, and National Council of Justice Resolution 348/366 governing the placement of LGBTI detainees all extend to Bahia and to its prison system.

Bahia records one of the country's highest burdens of trans and travesti killings. The ANTRA 2025 dossier, reported by SBT News on 26 January 2026, counts 7 trans people killed in Bahia during 2025, behind only the states recording 8; on the same national reckoning, which counts 1,261 killings across Brazil from 2017 to 2025, Bahia ranks third with 97, after São Paulo at 151 and Ceará at 107. Valor Internacional recorded the same state-level counts on 27 January 2026, placing Bahia behind the Ceará and Minas Gerais pair.

The figure is persistent rather than a single-year outlier. The ANTRA dossier for 2022 ranked Bahia seventh among the Brazilian states, with 7 killings of travestis recorded in the state that year, putting Bahia in the top band of consecutive annual dossiers.

Individual cases show how the violence is charged and processed. On the weekend of 6–7 December 2025, Rhianna, an 18-year-old trans woman, was choked to death in Luís Eduardo Magalhães, in the west of Bahia. The suspect, a 19-year-old app driver, drove the victim's body to the police station himself, confessed, and claimed self-defence; he was released. The Civil Police confirmed that the case is being investigated as a feminicide, and the state police framed the killing as gender-based, so the killing of a trans woman in Bahia was classified as gender-based violence while the accused was initially set free.

For a trans visitor, the practical exposure is the violence risk and its investigative handling rather than any entry, document or visa rule: the national framework applies Bahia's entry and family-law treatment on the same footing as for anyone else, and no Bahia-specific rule governing where trans detainees are held was located in the sources reviewed.

14911670B85657526756793.name: Rio de Jeneiro
14911670B85657526756793.summary:
Rio de Janeiro state stands under Brazil's national framework. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change in 2018, and since the Supreme Court's 2019 ruling constitutional and federal criminal provisions prohibit discrimination and hate crimes on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds, with transphobia punishable on the same footing as racism. An expat legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide, so a trans visitor's status and documents are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry and in family matters.

Courts have applied the anti-discrimination provisions to commercial conduct. The 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing, affirming the compensation ordered at first instance in Barra Bonita.

Lethal violence against trans people in Rio de Janeiro state is low relative to the country as a whole. Three trans and travesti people were killed in the state in 2025, roughly 0.18 per million residents, below the national rate. ANTRA's ninth annual dossier, reported on 26 January 2026, records 80 trans and travesti people killed across Brazil in 2025, a fall of about 34 per cent year on year, with the country still first in world rankings; the victims were overwhelmingly travestis and trans women, killed with extreme violence.

Violence against trans people also reaches the state's courts as an enforcement matter. The Rio de Janeiro state court (TJ-RJ) decreed preventive detention of a man accused of exploiting trans women in Niterói, a former city-hall employee there until January 2026, with pre-trial custody confirmed in the extortion case.

Detention is governed nationally by National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021. A person is recognised as LGBTI for these purposes by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing; on arrest a judge fixes the place of deprivation of liberty in a reasoned decision after consulting the person about their preference among male, female and LGBTI-specific units, and within a unit whether the general population or a specific wing or cell. The declared preference is recorded, later changes of placement are possible, and transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

14911670B6484683145874.name: Goias
14911670B6484683145874.summary:
Goiás stands under Brazil's national framework. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change in 2018, federal anti-discrimination provisions cover sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds, and since the Supreme Court's 2019 ruling transphobia is punishable on the same footing as racism. Same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationally, so a trans visitor's status and documents are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry and in family matters.

Lethal violence against trans people remains a documented feature of the national picture. ANTRA's ninth annual dossier, reported by SBT News on 26 January 2026, recorded 80 trans and travesti people killed across Brazil in 2025, a fall of about 34% year-on-year, with Brazil ranked first in world rankings; the victims were overwhelmingly travestis and trans women, killed with extreme violence. Goiás accounted for 5 of those 80 national victims. Against a state population of roughly 7.2 million, that is a rate of about 0.69 per million per year, close to 1.8 times the national rate derived from the same year's figures.

The prior year's tally was higher: ANTRA's dossier for 2024, reported on 27 January 2025, recorded 122 trans and travesti killings nationally, 16% below 2023, with five of the victims rights defenders.

Detention carries a specific regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed in Brazil, including in Goiás. A person is recognised as LGBTI for these purposes by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing. On arrest the place of deprivation of liberty is fixed by a judge in a reasoned decision after the person has been consulted about their preference; the judge must set out the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it the general population or a specific wing or cell. The declared preference is recorded, a later change of placement is possible, and transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

Practice does not reliably follow that framework. A peer-reviewed census of travestis and transgender women held in Rio de Janeiro state prisons, carried out between April and June 2021, interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates inside eleven units treated as masculine in the metropolitan region. It documents that in that system travestis and trans women are housed in units operated as masculine, with some held in so-called neutral or security units, and treats placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights. The same study notes a 2015 Rio de Janeiro state law granting parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units, covering hair length, feminine clothing, accessories and cosmetics, and national norms from 2014 and 2020 that permit people to be housed where they choose, including in units denominated masculine.

Protection machinery has widened. An analysis of case law from 2022 records lower courts pressing the Superior Court of Justice toward unanimously extending the remedies of the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women, bringing trans people within the country's violence-prevention statutes. Courts have also applied anti-discrimination provisions to commercial conduct: the 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing, affirming the compensation ordered at first instance in Barra Bonita.

The protective text of the law does not describe what people routinely encounter. Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records that LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions. A May 2024 investigation documented 'boa noite, Cinderela' drink-spiking robberies in which LGBTQIA+ people are targeted in São Paulo nightlife. In the October 2024 municipal elections, close to 1,000 transgender candidates stood across every state of the country and received death threats and intimidation, while the number of trans officeholders tripled compared with the previous cycle.

sources.summary: Wikipedia's 'LGBT rights in Brazil' states in its Politics section that LGBTQ prisoners have a special place in Brazilian prisons, separate from other prisoners; that transsexuals have the right to be called by their social name rather than their birth name and to be forwarded to women's prisons; and that LGBTQ prisoners may choose male or female clothing. No instrument more recent than that portaria is cited for these rules.

sources.title: LGBTQ people in prison (Wikipedia) - Brazil section
sources.summary: Wikipedia overview article (fetched and read in full, 4 Oct 2026). Its Transgender issues > Brazil section contains no trans-prisoner placement rule - only discussion of social vulnerability, stigma and fragmented identity of travestis and transgender people during rehabilitation; international sections show placement norms elsewhere (e.g., Canada placing by gender identity, Italy's admission discretion). Negative evidence: this general overview documents no Brazil-specific trans-prisoner housing policy, special unit or segregation-for-placement practice.

14911670B2082355341666.name: Mato Grosso
14911670B2082355341666.summary:
Mato Grosso stands under the national framework of Brazil, where same-sex marriage has been legal since 2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change in 2018, and the 2019 ruling places transphobia on the same footing as racism under constitutional and federal criminal provisions. The age of consent is equal regardless of sexual orientation and a federal anti-discrimination framework covers sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds. Entry, visa and gender-marker rules operate on the same footing for trans visitors as for anyone else, a position confirmed by an expat legal guide updated in April 2026 covering same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules nationwide.

Detention carries a defined regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where arrested or imprisoned LGBTI people are housed. Recognition rests on self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing. The place of deprivation of liberty is fixed by a reasoned judicial decision after the person has been consulted about their preference; the judge must set out available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it the general population or a specific wing or cell. The declared preference is recorded, later change of placement is possible, and transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

Violence against trans and travesti people remains documented at national scale. ANTRA's ninth annual dossier, released on 26 January 2026, records 80 murders of trans and travesti people across Brazil in 2025, 34 per cent below 2024, alongside at least 75 attempted homicides marked by excessive violence. Mato Grosso accounted for 3 of those killings in 2025, placing the state 12th among Brazilian states, and has recorded 43 killings of travestis, trans women, trans men, transmasculine and non-binary people since 2017.

Within Mato Grosso, a jury has explicitly recognised the gender dimension of a trans woman's killing. On 16 April 2026, businessman Jorlan Cristiano Ferreira, 44, was sentenced to 13 years and six months in prison for the feminicide of trans woman Mayla, found dead with knife wounds in January 2024 on a farm beside the MT-485 highway in Sorriso, together with procedural fraud and corpse concealment. The jury held that the killing was motivated by gender-based contempt and discrimination.

10402087B89016843004490.name: Sachsen
10402087B89016843004490.summary:
Sachsen is a Land within Germany and stands under the national framework: federal constitutional and equality protections apply nationwide, national identity documents and marriage law are uniform, and no Land can remove the federal floor. Legal gender recognition in Sachsen therefore runs through the Self-Determination Act, in force since 1 November 2024, under which adults change their legal gender by self-determination with three months' notice; the 'divers' marker available on birth certificates, passports and driving licences since 1 January 2019 requires a doctor's statement confirming intersex status and does not extend to transgender people.

Prison placement is the sharpest documented exposure for a trans visitor detained in Sachsen. German prisons, including those in the Land, operate under statutory separation with a binary men and women housing model, and the Criminological Research Institute of Lower Saxony (KFN) reads § 170(2) of the Lower Saxony correctional act as the operating rule, reporting that placement corresponding to a prisoner's gender identity has been practised only in exceptional cases. The exception has produced opposite outcomes: in August 2025 the chief prosecutor for Halle stated that Marla-Svenja Liebich, whose gender entry was changed to female at the end of 2024, would serve an 18-month incitement sentence at Chemnitz women's prison with placement reviewed at intake, and DW reported on 16 July 2026 that she had been transferred to a men's prison despite being legally registered as a woman, authorities citing the safety of prisoners at the women's facility while critics characterised the gender change as an abuse of the self-determination law.

Sachsen, Sachsen-Anhalt and Thuringia jointly launched a Länder initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act after that case, with the stated aim of blocking misuse of self-ID. Sachsen is a co-sponsor of an organised multi-state push to roll back trans self-determination law, a documented legislative threat to trans people in the state.

Public visibility carries a documented far-right disruption risk. On 31 May 2025 thousands marched through Dresden for CSD while neo-Nazis mounted a counter-protest aimed at disrupting the march; the march proceeded. That far-right attempt to disrupt Pride in Dresden in 2025 is the basis for the elevated risk rating assigned to Sachsen.

Protection machinery applies in Sachsen on the national footing: discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity is prohibited in health services and in education under the General Act on Equal Treatment, in force since 18 August 2006, and a nationwide ban on conversion therapy for minors in force since May 2020 carries penalties of up to one year in prison and fines of €30,000 for offering, promoting or referring minors to such treatment. The German STOP the HATE campaign maintains a counselling finder, an LSBTIQ* crisis line and a hate-crime knowledge base covering underreporting, evidence preservation and reporting channels.
