25490228B14384488423733.name: Comunitat Valenciana
25490228B14384488423733.summary:
Comunitat Valenciana stands under two layers of law. The national layer is Ley 4/2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado on 28 February 2023, which establishes real and effective equality for trans persons and guarantees LGTBI rights: under Article 43 any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own civil registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, an administrative self-identification route that replaced the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis plus two years of medical treatment. Recognition is possible from age 12 under conditions, and the law regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16.

Other operative provisions of the same national statute include a ban on non-consensual normalising surgeries on intersex children, expanded assisted reproduction rules, parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, strengthened sexuality education, and anti-discrimination measures covering healthcare, employment and housing. Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have been in force across Spain since 2005, and legal gender change does not require surgery or sterilisation.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on legal gender self-determination rather than on biological sex, so the gender marker recorded in the civil registry is the operative basis for facility rules in Spain.

There is no free-standing criminal offence of gender-expression-based hate crime: the phrase 'gender expression' appears in no article of the Spanish Criminal Code. The hate-speech aggravating circumstance in Article 22.4 and the penalties of Article 510, one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months, derive from Organic Law 6/2022, while Ley 4/2023 itself reformed offences against sexual freedom, including Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.

Enforcement of the gender-identity aggravation is documented. In July 2026 the Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo applied the transfobia aggravating circumstance for the first time in a misdemeanour case concerning threats sent by WhatsApp to a trans woman, fining the author EUR 300. Within the Comunitat Valenciana, the Audiencia Provincial de Valencia, Section 5, sentenced a group over a June 2022 incident in a park in the Patraix district of Valencia, where an 18-year-old and several minors insulted, chased, filmed and mocked a trans woman because of her gender identity; the adult defendant accepted six months' prison, suspended on condition of committing no offence for two years, plus a EUR 720 fine and a EUR 1,000 moral-damages payment to the victim, and two minors were sentenced separately to supervision measures. The case was handled by the hate-crime prosecutor.

The regional layer adds two statutes of its own. Ley 8/2017, de 7 de abril, integral del reconocimiento del derecho a la identidad y a la expresión de género, published as BOE-A-2017-5118, makes its purpose the guarantee of an adequate normative framework for gender self-determination for people whose felt gender identity differs from the one assigned at birth; it obliges public bodies of the Comunitat Valenciana to treat people according to their felt gender identity, and its Title III provides for administrative documentation and an advice-and-support service for trans people and their families. Ley 23/2018, de 29 de noviembre, de igualdad de las personas LGTBI, published as BOE-A-2019-281, is the community's general equality statute: it covers non-discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity or expression, sets access and admission rights under Article 56, reverses the burden of proof under Article 57, and establishes a Title V regime of administrative infringements and sanctions under Articles 58 to 66 for discrimination against LGTBI people.

With administrative self-declaration at national level, Spain stands alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay.

Other communities in the same inventory carry a single statute, among them Cataluña (Ley 11/2014) and Aragón (Ley 4/2018).

LGTBI federation's 2025 radiography of public educational policies across Spain's autonomous communities, covering gender-identity protocols and education legislation in each, places the Comunidad Valenciana with Madrid, Extremadura, Murcia and Navarra among the leaders on educational policy coverage, and records that the Valencian parliament completed its gender legislation.

19177384B97722443848736.name: Buenos Aires
19177384B97722443848736.summary:
Buenos Aires province stands under Argentina's national framework, which remains among the most permissive in the world for legal gender recognition. Law 26.743, promulgated on 24 May 2012 after passage by the Chamber of Deputies by 167 votes to 17 and by the Senate by 55 votes to one abstention, allows a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval, and the United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region. The 2012 Gender Identity Law remains in force in the province.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action rather than repeal. A national DNU of December 2024 added consent and medical-judicial requirements for minors' gender-affirming care and is under litigation. In February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei issued a decree banning gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy for minors; legal experts called it illegal and unconstitutional and petitioned the courts, with the outcome not recorded in the sources available here.

The provincial Ombudsman's Gender Violence Office, created by Resolución Nº 100/10, documented in a submission to the UN Human Rights Committee for its June and July 2016 review that provincial police, or third parties acting under police cover, committed violence, persecution and harassment against trans and travesti people in Buenos Aires province.

Trans and travesti women in the province face indirect criminalisation through drug-offence and street-offence prosecutions. After Buenos Aires province assumed jurisdiction over drug-sale and possession offences in 2005, microtrafficking enforcement in La Plata's Zona Roja became the operative instrument of this practice, even though the 2012 Gender Identity Law formally decriminalised trans presence.

In February 2025 the national government banned housing trans women convicted of sexual crimes, human trafficking, or any violent crime against a woman in women's prisons. This policy is national; Buenos Aires province has no trans-specific placement rule of its own, and no separate trans housing unit is recorded.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina reached a documented high in 2025, with at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity recorded during the year, averaging one every 38 hours. On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence for Gabriel Marino's 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán but rejected attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance, so the gender-motivated-crime aggravator does not apply in the case as it now stands.

17162690B44985096553766.name: Subcarpathian Voivodeship
17162690B44985096553766.summary:
Subcarpathian Voivodeship stands under the national framework of Poland, where detention is the clearest documented risk to a trans visitor. In a case publicised by the Association for Legal Intervention on 13 March 2024, a regional court placed a transgender Vietnamese woman in a guarded centre for male foreign nationals; her hormone therapy was interrupted for three months because the centre would not supply the medication, and she was released only after NGO intervention prompted the Border Guard commander to order it. The same case documented her history of violence and sexual assault, indicating that trans women held in these facilities may be exposed to both untreated care needs and vulnerable placement.

Courts have proved willing to intervene. On 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights found that Polish prison authorities violated Article 8 of the Convention by denying a trans prisoner hormone replacement therapy, awarding EUR 8,000 in damages while rejecting the Article 3 claim. The ruling establishes that medication denial in Polish custody is litigable and winnable, though Poland operates no specialised trans prison section and placement decisions remain individual and unpredictable.

Entry itself is straightforward for many nationalities: Global Affairs Canada's travel advisory notes visa-free entry for tourists staying up to 90 days. The same advisory lists sexual orientation among reported motives for harassment in Poland, alongside physical appearance and foreigner status, and links general LGBTQ2+ travel guidance.

The local-authority hostility of the past decade has formally ended. The county of Łańcut in Subcarpathian Voivodeship repealed its anti-LGBT resolution at an extraordinary councillors' session on 27 April 2025, the last such measure in Poland; at the wave's peak about one third of the country's territory was covered by these documents. The voivodeship's own council had already repealed its 'LGBT-free' resolution on 20 September 2021, so a visitor arriving now encounters no standing regional declaration of that kind, although the resolutions were political statements rather than entry restrictions.

Recognition of same-sex relationships has moved materially. In June 2024 Justice Minister Bodnar revoked the directive issued by his predecessor Ziobro that had blocked recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad, and in September 2024 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Poland's absence of partnership recognition leaves couples in an illegal vacuum contrary to their rights, calling for a recognition framework.

The wider legal environment remains in transition. Human Rights Watch describes LGBT-rights reform under the Prime Minister Tusk government as slow and insufficient through 2024. Deputy Justice Minister Smiszek announced a hate-speech law extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation; a March draft Penal Code amendment raising penalties for anti-LGBTI hate speech and violence cleared the Government Legislation Centre in May before approval was postponed, and a second bill followed in late October 2024. The Prosecutor General established a special response team with new guidelines for law enforcement.

At the wave's peak about one third of Poland's territory was covered by such documents, per the Atlas of Hate mapping project. This sets the dated end-point for the county-level resolution era.

The Them (23 Sep 2021, updated 29 Sep): Podkarpackie's voivodeship council repealed its 'LGBT-free' resolution on Monday 20 September 2021, alongside Małopolska and Lubelskie, after the European Commission threatened to withhold regional development funds. Podkarpackie replaced its ordinance with a generic anti-discrimination statement.

17162690B86810837764805.name: Łódź Voivodeship
17162690B86810837764805.summary:
Łódź Voivodeship stands within Poland's national legal framework, and the clearest documented risk to a trans visitor in that framework is detention. In a case publicised by the Association for Legal Intervention on 13 March 2024, a regional court placed a transgender Vietnamese woman in a guarded centre for male foreign nationals. Her hormone therapy was interrupted for three months because the centre would not supply the medication, and she was released only after NGO intervention prompted the Border Guard commander to order it. The same case documented her history of violence and sexual assault, indicating that trans women held in these facilities may face both untreated care needs and vulnerable placement.

Polish courts and the European Court of Human Rights have proved willing to intervene on that exposure. On 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights found that Polish prison authorities violated Article 8 of the Convention by denying a trans prisoner hormone replacement therapy, awarding EUR 8,000 in damages while rejecting the Article 3 claim. The ruling establishes that medication denial in Polish custody is litigable and winnable, though Poland operates no specialised trans prison section and placement decisions remain individual and unpredictable.

Entry is straightforward for many nationalities. Global Affairs Canada's travel advisory notes visa-free entry for tourists staying up to 90 days, and lists sexual orientation among reported motives for harassment in Poland alongside physical appearance and foreigner status, linking general LGBTQ2+ travel guidance.

The national legal environment is in transition. Human Rights Watch describes LGBT-rights reform under the Prime Minister Tusk government as slow and insufficient through 2024. Deputy Justice Minister Smiszek announced a hate-speech law extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation; a March draft Penal Code amendment raising penalties for anti-LGBTI hate speech and violence cleared the Government Legislation Centre in May before approval was postponed, and a second bill followed in late October 2024. The Prosecutor General established a special response team with new guidelines for law enforcement. The status of these bills at the time of travel should be verified rather than assumed.

Recognition of same-sex relationships has moved materially. In June 2024 Justice Minister Bodnar revoked the directive issued by his predecessor Ziobro that had blocked recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad, and in September 2024 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Poland's absence of partnership recognition leaves couples in an illegal vacuum contrary to their rights, calling for a recognition framework.

At regional level, Łódź Voivodeship's own anti-LGBT resolution was revoked by the Supreme Administrative Court of Poland on 12 October 2023. It had been one of five voivodeships, with Lublin, Lesser Poland, Podkarpackie and Świętokrzyskie, written to by the European Commission on 2 June 2020 over such resolutions; the Świętokrzyskie council revoked its own on 22 September 2021. By 24 April 2025 every anti-LGBTQ resolution and every Local Government Family Rights Charter in Poland had been withdrawn or invalidated by court order.

Between 2019 and 2025 more than 100 Polish local governments adopted 'LGBT-free zone'-style resolutions which at their peak covered roughly a third of the country's land area. Administrative courts struck them down as unconstitutional under Article 32 on equal treatment, the European Commission linked EU development funds to their repeal, and the last remaining zone in Łańcut was abolished in 2025. The resolutions were symbolic and institutional rather than criminal: they created no new penalties and barred no one physically, but they signalled to local bureaucracies and schools which families and identities local leadership considered legitimate.

17162690B84565288021286.name: Masovian Voivodeship
17162690B84565288021286.summary:
Masovian Voivodeship stands under Poland's national framework. Detention is the clearest documented risk to a trans visitor to Poland. In a case publicised by the Association for Legal Intervention on 13 March 2024, a regional court placed a transgender Vietnamese woman in a guarded centre for male foreign nationals; her hormone therapy was interrupted for three months because the centre would not supply the medication, and she was released only after NGO intervention prompted the Border Guard commander to order it. The same case documented her history of violence and sexual assault, indicating that trans women held in these facilities may be exposed to both untreated care needs and vulnerable placement.

Courts have proved willing to intervene. On 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights found that Polish prison authorities violated Article 8 of the Convention by denying a trans prisoner hormone replacement therapy, awarding EUR 8,000 in damages while rejecting the Article 3 claim. The ruling establishes that medication denial in Polish custody is litigable and winnable, though Poland operates no specialised trans prison section and placement decisions remain individual and unpredictable.

Entry itself is straightforward for many nationalities: Global Affairs Canada's travel advisory notes visa-free entry for tourists staying up to 90 days. The same advisory lists sexual orientation among reported motives for harassment in Poland, alongside physical appearance and foreigner status, and links general LGBTQ2+ travel guidance.

Anti-LGBT local governance, once widespread, has been dismantled through the courts and through municipal withdrawal. By January 2020 a third of Poland's territory had passed anti-LGBT resolutions. On 6 February 2024 the Voivodeship Administrative Court in Warsaw, which sits in Masovian Voivodeship, repealed the last document 'against LGBT ideology' in Poland, and by 24 April 2025 every anti-LGBTQ resolution and Family Charter endorsement had been withdrawn or court-invalidated. No such resolution is currently in force in Masovian Voivodeship.

The capital's own position has run in the opposite direction since March 2019, when Warsaw Mayor Rafał Trzaskowski signed the city's pledge of equality, non-discrimination and hate-crime response. The declaration stands and no repeal is recorded, giving a visitor in Warsaw a documented municipal commitment that contrasts with the national picture.

The wider legal environment is in transition. Human Rights Watch describes LGBT-rights reform under the Prime Minister Donald Tusk government as slow and insufficient through 2024. Deputy Justice Minister Smiszek announced a hate-speech law extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation; a March draft Penal Code amendment raising penalties for anti-LGBTI hate speech and violence cleared the Government Legislation Centre in May before approval was postponed, and a second bill followed in late October 2024. The Prosecutor General established a special response team with new guidelines for law enforcement. The status of these bills at the time of travel should be verified rather than assumed.

Recognition of same-sex relationships has moved materially. In June 2024 Justice Minister Bodnar revoked the directive issued by his predecessor Ziobro that had blocked recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad, and in September 2024 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Poland's absence of partnership recognition leaves couples in an illegal vacuum contrary to their rights, calling for a recognition framework.

27671186B7584771598694.name: Bauchi
27671186B7584771598694.summary:
Visitors to Bauchi State stand under two overlapping criminal regimes. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies nationwide with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex conduct, cohabitation between same-sex partners, public displays of a same-sex relationship and the operation of gay organisations, and Human Rights Watch has documented police using it to justify torture and arbitrary arrest. On top of that, Bauchi's Sharia Penal Code remains in force: the UK Home Office country policy and information note of June 2025 confirms the religious penal codes of all twelve northern Nigerian states, Bauchi among them, and records male sodomy as carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

Bauchi is the one state where that capital ceiling has actually been pronounced for same-sex conduct. On 28 June 2022 a Sharia court sitting in Ningi local government area sentenced three men, one of them 70-year-old Malam Haruna, to death by stoning for homosexuality under Section 134 of the Bauchi State Penal Law of 2001. The prosecution was brought by members of the Hisbah Vanguard, who told the court the three were arrested at Gwada village on 14 June 2022. Reuters reported the case on 2 July 2022 as the first time the death penalty had been imposed for homosexuality in Nigeria. Presiding judge Munka'ilu Sabo-Ningi granted a 30-day appeal window, and relatives told Punch in July 2022 that the sentence had not been carried out at that point. The UK Home Office note adds that a stoning sentence cannot be carried out until ratified by the state governor, and records a further death-by-stoning sentence for homosexuality from a Bauchi Sharia court in May 2024.

Capital sentences for sodomy in Bauchi have a history of being overturned on appeal. Amnesty International's 2004 press release records that the Upper Sharia Court of Bauchi State quashed Jubrin Babaji's death-by-stoning sentence, handed down on 25 September 2003 under Section 133 of the Bauchi Sharia Penal Code Law 2001, on grounds of denial of counsel and a defective confession, following the quashing of Yunusa Rafin Chiyawa's conviction on 14 November 2003. Amnesty described a pattern of convictions and death sentences quashed on appeal.

Vigilante pressure accompanies the courts. In January 2014 an angry mob stormed Bauchi's Tudun Alkali Upper Sharia Court during a sodomy trial demanding a death sentence, as recorded by the UK Home Office.

Gender expression itself is a charged offence in Bauchi. State police arrested eighteen men and charged them with sodomy for dressing as women under the Sharia penal code; the charges were later reduced to vagrancy and the men were held in jail for several years awaiting trial, with the pre-trial detention dissolving by the end of 2011. Persons perceived as trans-feminine in Bauchi have been arrested and held under Sharia charges for years.

No source records where such detainees are housed inside custody, whether in a male or female wing, a special unit, or solitary confinement, and no trans-specific placement rule, facility or policy is documented for Bauchi. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.

27671186B50148357657004.name: Kano

Kano State stands under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies nationwide with penalties of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex conduct, reaches visitors as well as residents, and provides no legal protection for LGBT+ people. Operating over that national layer, Kano State runs its own religious penal code, the Sharia Penal Code Law 2000, which took effect on 26 November 2000.

The statutory ceiling in Kano is the harshest a trans visitor can face anywhere in the country. Under the Kano code, consensual same-sex activity draws 100 lashes and up to one year's imprisonment where the offender is unmarried, and stoning to death (rajm) where the offender is or has been married. 27671186B99510750195830.name: Sokoto
27671186B99510750195830.summary:
Visitors in Sokoto State stand under two penal regimes at once. Nigeria's Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies nationally and reaches beyond marriage: Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that it bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have invoked it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests. The UK Home Office country policy note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment.

On top of that national layer, Sokoto State operates its own Sharia Penal Code Laws, which took effect on 31 January 2001. Male same-sex activity is punished by stoning to death where the offender is or has been married, and by 100 lashes otherwise. Sexual acts between women, termed wsafa, draw ta'azir punishment of up to 100 lashes and/or imprisonment. These penalties sit inside a code that the UK Home Office records as applying across all twelve northern states, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

Capital sentences under the Sokoto code are not theoretical. On 9 October 2001 the Upper Sharia Court at Gwadabawa in Sokoto State convicted Safiyatu Hussaini Tungar Tudu of zina under sections 128-129 of the Sokoto State Sharia Penal Code and sentenced her to death by stoning, while her co-accused was discharged and acquitted. She appealed on 26 October 2001, and on 25 March 2002 the Sharia Court of Appeal of Sokoto State quashed the conviction and discharged and acquitted her. The case concerned zina rather than same-sex conduct, but it establishes that Sokoto's religious courts apply the state Sharia Penal Code in practice, including the capital-punishment framework the code carries for married men's same-sex acts.

Gender expression carries separate exposure. Sokoto is listed among the twelve northern states whose Sharia criminal codes apply to Muslims, alongside Bauchi, Kano and others, with maximum penalties of death for men and whipping and/or imprisonment for women for same-sex acts. Northern states also criminalise cross-dressing: Kano carries up to one year for men who dress or behave as women, and a northern Islamic court has imposed 10 lashes for cross-dressing. Whether Sokoto State itself has enacted a cross-dressing provision is not established by these sources; nationally, Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live under fear of such proposals, and their enactment is unsettled here.

No documented arrest, trial or custody case involving a trans person in Sokoto appears in these sources, and there is no record of where trans prisoners would be housed, no trans-specific unit, and no solitary or segregation practice. Where comparable cases exist elsewhere in Nigeria, placement is discretionary: press coverage of Bobrisky's 2024 imprisonment openly asked which prison the authorities would keep her in, and an October 2024 panel found that housing her in a maximum-security facility violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act.

Practical risk also comes from non-state actors. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states, which covers Sokoto directly.

27671186B69054806776702.name: Yobe
27671186B69054806776702.summary:
Yobe State stands under the national framework of Nigeria. Same-sex conduct is criminalised nationally under the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 (SSMPA), and the statute reaches far beyond marriage: Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests.

Criminal exposure attaches at entry. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (Version 4.0, June 2025, updated April 2026) records that same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and that Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions. Yobe is one of those twelve states. Human Rights Watch's 2004 report lists Yobe among the states that had adopted Shari'a into criminal legislation by 2002, the only states whose Shari'a courts try Muslim criminal cases beyond federal law.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Trans people in Nigeria face documented killing and official indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in the capital hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; the police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the capital's police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Police violence against perceived gay people is a routine feature of enforcement. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by police in Nigeria's largest city, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law producing a climate of hostility independent of its text.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the SSMPA reinforced colonial-era criminalisation. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice for Nigeria, as reported by Sahara Reporters, warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.

27671186B21163522287660.name: Zamfara
27671186B21163522287660.summary:
Zamfara State stands under two overlapping layers of criminal law. Nigeria's national framework, the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014, binds every person in the country including visitors; the UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex sex between men under secular law, and Human Rights Watch ('Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe', October 2016) documents that the Act reaches well beyond marriage, banning cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with 10 to 14 years' imprisonment. The same Human Rights Watch record shows police using the statute to justify torture and arbitrary arrest.

Zamfara is the jurisdiction where Nigeria's Sharia criminal-law wave began. Human Rights Watch (2004) records that Zamfara's governor was the first to act, introducing the Sharia Establishment Law on 27 October 1999, in force 27 January 2000; by 2002 twelve northern states had adopted some form of Sharia into their criminal legislation, and to date those twelve are the only states where Sharia courts hold jurisdiction to try criminal cases. A visitor in Zamfara is therefore subject to a religious criminal code that operates alongside, not instead of, the national Act.

Zamfara's own legal architecture is documented in the state's account of its adoption, set out by its then Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice, Alh. Ahmed Bello Mahmud, at a JNI-sponsored seminar on 6 July 2000. The enabling legislation, the Sharia Courts (Administration of Justice and Certain Consequential Changes) Law 1999, was enacted under section 6 of the 1999 Constitution and established Sharia courts with criminal jurisdiction in Islamic law, enabling the codification of a Sharia Penal Code; the Grand Kadi took over court administration on 29 June 2000. The governor had appointed a committee in June 1999 mandated to study implementation, including the full scope of Islamic criminal law, and the resulting codification of offences and punishments produced the penal-code architecture that the Sharia courts of all twelve states apply, a framework Zamfara pioneered across the northern bloc.

For an LGBT+ visitor the practical consequence of that framework is capital risk. The UK Home Office assesses that Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions. The latest UK FCDO travel advice for Nigeria, reported by Sahara Reporters in August 2026, warns of attacks, blackmail and intimidation against LGBT+ travellers, up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states. Zamfara is one of those states.

Enforcement nationally takes the form of mass arrests at social venues rather than isolated prosecutions, and the pattern reaches the north. Men arrested in Bauchi in August 2007 were held for several years awaiting a trial that had dissolved by end-2011, and 76 people were arrested at a party in Gombe state in October 2023. The same tactic has been used in the south, with 100-plus party-goers arrested at a hotel in Asaba, Delta State, in June 2018 and 57 young men at Egbeda, Lagos, in August 2018, alongside the 'Warri 67' in Warri, Delta State, in August 2023.

Appearance alone is treated as grounds for police action. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that a 24-year-old man, Okafor, was stopped by Lagos police, struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and freed only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for 'looking gay'; those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law creating a climate of hostility. Trans Nigerians face lethal violence with official misgendering and subsequent impunity: the beaten body of the Abuja trans TikToker 'Abuja Area Mama', a 33-year-old transgender woman, was found on a highway in Abuja in August 2024, hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend, and police said preliminary investigations showed 'a man fully dressed in female clothing'. Six months later, in February 2025, The Dial reported that no suspects had been charged.

Two further exposures apply directly to a visitor's conduct. Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents 'kito' gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and other apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing, and Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians fear proposals to criminalise cross-dressing as a discrete offence.

Imprisonment raises placement questions that remain unresolved. Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye) pleaded guilty to four counts of Naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine; she served the term in Kirikiri maximum-security prison, Lagos, and was released on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison would hold 'the crossdresser', reflecting discretionary placement, and an October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that placing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

Care access is chilled by arrest and extortion risk. Many LGBTQ Nigerians fear seeking medical care or reporting crimes, and activists say the Same-Sex Marriage Prohibition Act hampers access to HIV prevention services and forces LGBTQ people and allies to abandon community health and education work.

Borno is one of the twelve northern states that had adopted Sharia into its criminal legislation by 2002, with Sharia courts holding criminal jurisdiction over Muslims beyond federal law (Human Rights Watch, 2004). Borno's own statute deepens the exposure. Trans people in Nigeria face documented killing and official indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; the police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. 27671186B90305463766462.name: Gombe
27671186B90305463766462.summary:
Visitors in Gombe State stand under two overlapping criminal regimes. Nationally, Nigeria's Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 reaches all persons including tourists, carrying 10 to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex conduct, cohabitation between same-sex partners, public shows of a same-sex relationship and the operation of gay organisations; the UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment.

Gombe is one of the twelve northern states that had adopted Shari'a into its criminal legislation by 2002, as documented in Human Rights Watch's 2004 report, which also records that Shari'a courts hold criminal jurisdiction over Muslims beyond federal law. The state's Shari'a Penal Code Law 2001 was signed on 23 November 2001 and criminalises same-sex conduct by men and women on terms harsher than the federal code.

Under Gombe's 2001 statute, the sodomy offence punishes unmarried men with caning of 100 lashes plus one year's imprisonment and married men with stoning to death (rajm); the lesbianism offence carries up to 50 lashes and imprisonment of up to six months. Gombe defines gross indecency in its own formulation as any sexual offence against the normal or usual standards of behaviour, a formulation broad enough to reach gender non-conformity in public.

The UK Home Office note (June 2025) records that Islamic law applies to Muslims in the twelve northern states and criminalises same-sex acts both between men and between women. The maximum penalty for sodomy for men is death in all twelve states, and penalties for lesbianism range from death to flogging and imprisonment. The note carries a dedicated section on enforcement of Shari'a provisions and on the attitude of the hisbah, the religious morality police operating in northern states.

Enforcement in Gombe is documented at the incident level. In October 2023 the Gombe State Command of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps raided a gathering at Duwa Plaza along the Bauchi-Gombe Expressway that was preparing a same-sex wedding, arresting 76 people. State spokesperson Buhari Sa'ad told reporters that 59 males were detained, 21 of whom wilfully confessed to being homosexuals, and that 17 females were present, adding that the detainees would be charged to court for a crime of social vice in Gombe State.

The Guardian of 23 October 2023 independently confirmed the arrests after a tip-off about a same-sex birthday and planned marriage, with Gombe NSCDC Commandant Mohammed Muazu confirming the operation and spokesperson Buhari Saad stating that 21 of the 59 detained males were involved in gay activities while the remaining males and the 17 females were invited guests and onlookers. Officers voiced concern over the ages of participants. Two Lagos-based press accounts of the same raid establish that Gombe applies its moral-crimes layer on the ground rather than leaving it on paper.

No legal protection on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity exists at either level. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Shari'a law in northern states, which includes Gombe.

27671186B1226853346294.name: Jigawa
27671186B1226853346294.summary:
Jigawa stands under Nigeria's national framework as well as its own state code. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies nationwide; Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that it bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, carrying 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment.

Jigawa is one of twelve northern states in which Sharia has jurisdiction over criminal cases, and it is the only layer of criminal law that applies to Muslim residents for offences of this kind. Human Rights Watch (2004) traces the arrangement to Zamfara's governor, the first to extend Sharia to criminal law through the Sharia Establishment Law of 27 October 1999, in force 27 January 2000; by 2002 twelve northern states, Jigawa among them, had adopted some form of Sharia into their criminal legislation, and those twelve remain the only states where Sharia courts try criminal cases.

Jigawa's own instrument is the Sharia Penal Code Law 2000, Law No. 12 of 2000, signed into law on 18 December 2000 and brought into operation on 27 December 2000 (Jigawa State Gazette Vol. 1 No. 12). The UK Home Office (June 2025) lists Jigawa in its twelve-state Sharia penalties table under Sharia Penal Code (2000) and confirms that the Sharia penal layer remains the operative criminal frame for Muslims in Jigawa; the same note's section 8.2.20 sets out the Sharia codes in force in Kano, Borno, Kaduna and other states of the region.

The penalties Jigawa's code carries are severe and sex-specific. Married men face death by stoning; unmarried men face 100 lashes and imprisonment of up to one year; same-sex acts between women carry up to 50 lashes with imprisonment of up to six months. Jigawa is one of four states, with Gombe, Kano and Zamfara, whose sodomy offence sets out those same terms, and Jigawa's code includes an 'unnatural fusion of the female sexual organs' explanation of the offence. The state code reaches conduct the federal statute does not reach, including women's same-sex conduct.

Entry and travel advice reflect that exposure. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice for Nigeria warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states. Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people.

Enforcement in Nigeria generally is not limited to the statute's text. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police who was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying part of a 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing, a risk that follows dating-app use into any state.

27671186B1226853346294.tangentialFactors:
Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression carries exposure. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Trans people in Nigeria face documented killing and official indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; the police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

The only trans-specific imprisonment case in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

Jigawa's exposure differs from that of the southern states in one structural respect: a visitor who is Muslim faces both the federal statute and a state penal code written expressly for sexual offences, while a visitor who is not Muslim faces the federal statute alone. 27671186B54051914323789.name: Kaduna
27671186B54051914323789.summary:
Kaduna State stands under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies nationwide with up to 14 years' imprisonment and reaches well beyond marriage: it bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years. Human Rights Watch (October 2016), in 'Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe', records police torture and arbitrary arrests carried out under the Act.

Kaduna adds two further layers of its own on top of the federal statute. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) documents this two-layer criminalisation: Kaduna's secular Penal Code, adopted in 2017, punishes 'unnatural offences' including sodomy, lesbianism and bestiality under Section 259 with up to 21 years' imprisonment plus a fine, a ceiling above the federal 14-year maximum; alongside it, Kaduna's Sharia Penal Code Law 2002 applies to Muslims as a parallel criminal code.

Kaduna is one of twelve northern states where Sharia courts hold jurisdiction to try criminal cases, a bloc created when Zamfara's governor introduced the Sharia Establishment Law on 27 October 1999, in force 27 January 2000, and by 2002 twelve northern states had adopted some form of Sharia into their criminal legislation. Kaduna's own instrument is Law No. 4 of 2002, signed and brought into operation on 21 June 2002 (Kaduna State Gazette No. 17 Vol. 36, 4 July 2002, pp. A15-A108, bound with the Sharia Criminal Procedure Code). Its enacted text states that whoever commits the offence of sodomy shall be punished with stoning to death (rajm), with no unmarried or married graduation, and the corresponding offence between women is left to ta'azir, discretionary punishment at the discretion of the qadi. Kaduna is one of only three states whose enacted text carries that explicit capital sentence. The Home Office note's section 8.4.3 reproduces this Kaduna row: death by stoning as the maximum for liwat (sodomy).

Official foreign guidance aimed at LGBT+ visitors is explicit and current. The Home Office note records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalising same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions. Sahara Reporters (August 2026), reporting the latest UK FCDO travel advice for Nigeria, relays warnings of attacks, blackmail and intimidation against LGBT+ travellers, up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.

Trans visitors face lethal violence followed by official misgendering and impunity. The beaten body of the Abuja trans TikToker 'Abuja Area Mama', a 33-year-old transgender woman, was found on a highway in Abuja in August 2024, hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police said preliminary investigations showed 'a man fully dressed in female clothing', and the Abuja police chief ordered a 'thorough and discreet' investigation. Six months later, in February 2025, The Dial reported that no suspects had been charged.

Police use the national law against people for how they appear. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that a 24-year-old man, Okafor, was stopped by Lagos police, struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and freed only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for 'looking gay'. Those affected describe the Act as a weaponised law creating a climate of hostility.

Dating applications carry a specific entrapment risk. Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents 'kito' gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and other apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Enforcement takes the form of mass arrests at social venues across the country: men arrested in Bauchi in August 2007 were held for several years awaiting a trial that dissolved by end-2011; more than 100 party-goers were arrested at a hotel in Asaba, Delta State, in June 2018; 57 young men at Egbeda, Lagos, in August 2018; the 'Warri 67' in Warri, Delta State, in August 2023; and 76 people arrested at a party in Gombe state in October 2023. LGBTQ-friendly venues face closure: the House of Rainbow Metropolitan Church in Lagos cancelled conferences after members' names and addresses were published in four newspapers on 12 September 2008 and some were threatened, beaten and stoned.

Care access is chilled by arrest and extortion risk. Many LGBTQ Nigerians fear seeking medical care or reporting crimes, and activists say the Same-Sex Marriage Prohibition Act hampers access to HIV prevention services and forces LGBTQ people and allies to abandon community health and education work.

27671186B99661334382691.summary:

Katsina operates that religious layer through its own statute: the Sharia Penal Code Law 2001, Law No. 2 of 2001, coming into operation on 20 June 2001 and gazetted in Katsina State Gazette Vol. 12 No. 23 of 27 August 2001. Ostien's annotated volume records Katsina among the three states, with Kaduna and Kebbi, whose sodomy text reads: whoever commits the offence of sodomy shall be punished with stoning to death (rajm).

Sexual acts between women carry a death maximum here as well. A footnote in the same annotated volume shows that only Kano and Katsina reach stoning to death as the maximum punishment for the lesbianism offence, against the harmonised northern code's base of 50 lashes and up to six months' imprisonment. Katsina is therefore one of only two states whose law carries death as the maximum for same-sex acts between women as well as between men.

Trans identity itself is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public, and the sources available here do not settle whether those proposals have been enacted. The cross-dressing layer that is documented applies to men who dress or behave as women, who face prison or a fine; a Kano court sentenced a TikToker to one year in prison over a cross-dressing video on 20 June 2025. In the Sharia-governed northern states generally, punishments for same-sex conduct range from lashing or caning to capital punishment.

Violence against perceived trans people has gone unpunished. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing. Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice, as reported by Sahara Reporters, warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.

The clearest documented case of a trans prisoner's placement concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

The penalties apply to any person present in the country, including visitors.

Entry carries criminal exposure. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalising same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.

Kebbi is one of the twelve northern states that re-adopted criminal Sharia. Human Rights Watch (2004) records that Zamfara first re-adopted criminal Sharia with its Shari'a Establishment Law enacted 27 October 1999 and in force 27 January 2000, and that by 2002 twelve northern states, Kebbi among them, had Sharia criminal legislation and Sharia courts with criminal jurisdiction over Muslims — the only states with such jurisdiction. Sharia jurisdiction in Kebbi therefore turns on the defendant's religion, while the federal SSMPA applies regardless.

Kebbi enacted its own Sharia penal layer in that wave. The Kebbi State Penal Code (Amendment) Law (Law No. 21 of 2000) was signed into law and came into operation on 1 December 2000, published in the Kebbi State Gazette Vol. 2 No. 1, Supplement, 31 December 2000. The enacted text states that whoever commits the offence of sodomy shall be punished with stoning to death (rajm), and provides for lesbianism with up to 50 lashes and imprisonment of up to six months. The UK Home Office's June 2025 note carries Kebbi's own row in its twelve-state Sharia penalties table at section 8.4.3, confirming death by stoning for liwat (sodomy) and the 50-lash and six-month maximum for same-sex acts between women — the standard bloc penalty for women's conduct rather than the Kano or Katsina capital maximum. Kebbi's state code is thus broader in scope and harsher than the federal statute for Muslim defendants.

Ostien's annotated volume of northern Nigerian Sharia legislation lists Kebbi's Law No. 21 of 2000 and records Kebbi as one of three states, with Kaduna and Katsina, whose enacted text specifies stoning to death for sodomy.

Gender expression remains exposed, though no Kebbi-specific cross-dressing provision is sourced here. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public, and whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available. 27671186B79778155682183.summary:
Niger State stands under Nigeria's national framework, which reaches into every part of the state. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 criminalises same-sex conduct nationwide and extends well beyond marriage: Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (version 4.0, June 2025) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment.

A second, state-level layer applies in Niger State specifically. Human Rights Watch (2004) documents the wave of Sharia adoption across northern Nigeria and lists the twelve states concerned: Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara. The wave traces from Zamfara's Shari'a Establishment Law, promulgated 27 October 1999 and in force 27 January 2000, and the provisions remain in force. The UK Home Office note records Sharia law in all twelve states as criminalising same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

Niger State enacted its own statutory machinery for that layer. The Penal Code (Amendment) Law 2000 (HB.4/2000) was signed into law on 22 February 2000 and came into operation on 4 May 2000, gazetted as Niger State Gazette Vol. 25 No. 8 of 9 March 2000 (pp. B29-B36). It is a law to amend Penal Code Law Cap 94, Laws of Niger State, to review the punishments therein. The enactment defines adultery to include sodomy and inserts section 68A, under which a Muslim convicted of a listed offence and proved against him to the Islamic evidentiary standard receives the harsher punishment specified by Sharia, with amputation added to the caning paragraph of section 68; the ordinary Penal Code punishment otherwise applies.

The editor of Ostien's sourcebook notes that the 2000 enactment is not a complete Sharia Penal Code. It amends the Penal Code of 1960 so that certain sections, applied to Muslims, carry different burdens of proof and different punishments than when applied to non-Muslims, and the text is reproduced in full. The UK Home Office note sets out Nigeria's hybrid legal system, the twelve-state Sharia criminal layer and its coverage of women.

The consequence for a visitor is a parallel track that operates independently of federal law. A Muslim visitor who is outed in Niger State stands under a harsher legal frame than the national statute alone imposes, because religion and the standard of proof determine which punishment applies to the same conduct. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice for Nigeria, as reported by Sahara Reporters, warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.

27671186B8148656125930.name: Imo
27671186B8148656125930.summary:
Imo State stands under Nigeria's national framework: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 (SSMPA) applies in full and reaches well beyond marriage. Human Rights Watch records that it bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, carrying 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and documents police torture and arbitrary arrests carried out under it. The UK Home Office country policy and information note (June 2025, updated April 2026) assesses same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment. Sharia criminal law, under which male sodomy carries the death penalty in twelve northern states, does not extend to Imo, a southern state.

Enforcement in Imo is recent and active. On 19 February 2025 the Imo Police Command reported foiling a same-sex party at Graziella Hotels, Orogwe, in Owerri West, arresting what it described as many gay and lesbian suspects and placing attendees who fled on a police search list. The command gave no precise figure for those arrested, and no court outcome from that raid has been sourced.

Community vigilantism runs alongside state action. In April 2018 two men in Imo State were stripped, beaten and paraded through the streets accused of gay sex; a NoStringsNG inquiry found that the victims were themselves arrested by police and might need legal support. A crowd assault therefore ended in police processing of the men who had been attacked.

Dating applications are an identified entrapment channel nationwide. Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents 'kito' gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and other apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing. Official foreign guidance reflects the exposure: the UK FCDO travel advice warns of attacks, blackmail and intimidation against LGBT+ travellers, up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states (Sahara Reporters, August 2026).

Presentation alone can draw police attention. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for 'looking gay'; those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law creating a climate of hostility. Reuters (September 2022) records that transgender Nigerians fear proposals to criminalise cross-dressing, which would make appearance itself a discrete offence. Those proposals are not sourced as enacted law.

Lethal violence against a visibly transgender woman has gone unpunished. The beaten body of the Abuja trans TikToker 'Abuja Area Mama', a 33-year-old transgender woman, was found on a highway in August 2024 hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police described 'a man fully dressed in female clothing' and the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough investigation. In February 2025 The Dial reported that no suspects had been charged.

27671186B63712480376187.name: Edo
27671186B63712480376187.summary:
Visitors in Edo State stand under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies nationwide and reaches well beyond marriage: Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalising same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

Edo State is not among those twelve northern states, so the Sharia death-penalty provisions have no application there; the secular penalties of the 2014 Act and the wider criminal law govern. Official foreign guidance aimed at LGBT+ travellers remains current and explicit: the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office warns of attacks, blackmail and intimidation against LGBT+ visitors, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.

The documented violence in Edo State is lethal and community-led. The Nigerian Observer (May 2018) reports that in Ekpoma a mob lynched one of two men caught together and that the other escaped, the killing framed as an 'abominable act' under traditional heritage. On 10 June 2010 the same newspaper reported from Benin City, Oredo local government area, that a middle-aged man escaped being killed by a mob after he was caught in a same-sex act in his partner's rented apartment; a neighbour raised the alarm, he fled through the backyard, and the mob then 'unleashed terror' on the partner left behind. The report records no police intervention, no arrest and no prosecution, and his whereabouts were still unknown at filing.

Law enforcement in Edo has historically aligned with the mob rather than with the people targeted. The Nigerian Observer reported on 15 August 2008 that police declared a man wanted over 'gay practice' after he and his partner were caught together in a remote Edo community in February 2008; a mob beat both men for 'desecrating the community', one escaped before police arrived, and police arrested the other for interrogation. A community lynching attempt was answered with an arrest and a wanted declaration, not protection.

Care and help-seeking are chilled by the same dynamics. Many LGBTQ Nigerians fear seeking medical care or reporting crimes, and activists say the Same-Sex Marriage Prohibition Act hampers access to HIV prevention services and forces LGBTQ people and allies to abandon community health and education work. Dating applications carry a specific entrapment risk: Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents 'kito' gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and other apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

The Initiative for Equal Rights (TIERs) '2024 Human Rights Violations Report', published January 2025, records 556 violations affecting 850 victims based on real or perceived SOGIESC across Nigeria during the reporting period. The figures are national in scope, with no Edo-specific breakdown, and TIERs states they represent only a fraction of the true scale.

65028918B93184959873838.name: Aceh
65028918B93184959873838.summary:
Indonesia is a high-risk destination for trans visitors, and Aceh operates inside that national framework rather than alongside it. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national-level morality provisions. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors.

65028918B88589358118692.name: Lampung
65028918B88589358118692.summary:
Lampung province stands under Indonesia's national framework. The national penal code, signed in December 2022 and in force since 2 January 2026, punishes consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment; because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations, and reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. The same framework criminalises expression: the 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment, and website and app blocks covering LGBTQ-related content remain in place. No national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option, and legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery plus a judge's approval. A trans visitor whose documents do not match their presentation can therefore be questioned on identity grounds at any point where papers are checked.

Provincial and district authorities add a layer of their own. OutRight International's study of discriminatory regional regulations examines eight Indonesian provinces, Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatera, South Sulawesi, South Sumatera and Yogyakarta, at both province and district level, and Lampung is named among them. The study documents regulatory restriction rather than a provincial criminal code: the sources do not set out which Lampung ordinances apply to visitors or what penalties they carry.

Trans people in Lampung have been targeted directly by the province's own enforcement machinery. In November 2018 the Satpol PP, the regional morals-and-order force, raided three trans women, detained them at the Satpol PP office and hosed them down at the firefighter building while an officer recorded the incident. The detention of trans people by that force, and the recording of it, indicates that identification as trans is itself treated as an administrative violation by provincial officers.

That incident sits inside a documented national pattern. A human-rights review records trans women murdered in 2017 in Bone, Semarang and South Sulawesi, and lobbying for anti-LGBT bylaws during election cycles from 2016 onward. A survey of 1,520 Indonesians carried out in November 2016 found that 16.6% of respondents held LGBT people in hatred. More recent national reporting ties rising vigilante violence against trans people to official condemnation, including a presidential decree of October 2025 listing LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat, and police raids on private gatherings continue, most recently the arrest of 75 people at a rented villa near Bogor on 22 June 2025.

65028918B84835514626455.name: West Papua
65028918B84835514626455.summary:
West Papua stands under the national framework of Indonesia, which is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment; because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations, and reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, add their own criminalisation, but West Papua is not among them.

The dominant risk in this province is the conduct of the security forces rather than any trans-specific provision. A report of 22 July 2025 by the Asia-Pacific Solidarity Network records 138 acts of torture or other ill-treatment against people in detention by police and military in Maybrat and the Central Highlands areas of West Papua, covering the period through early 2025. Most victims were male and under 24; seven were female, seven were minors aged 15 to 17. The report's finding is near-total impunity, summarised as impunity, secrecy and silence. Any visitor held or questioned by officers in the province faces an accountability environment in which abuse is unlikely to be answered for.

Military activity in the province has intensified. The Papua human-rights monitor's quarterly report for the third quarter of 2025 records a notable increase in military deployments and operations in West Papua's highland regions since August 2025. Police in Sorong arrested more than a dozen protest participants in August 2025. On 27 September 2025 a military task force opened fire on civilians in Agats, Asmat Regency, alongside ongoing displacement and racial tension affecting indigenous Papuans.

No trans-specific finding is recorded for West Papua in these sources. The general security-force pattern nonetheless amplifies exposure for a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor, since stops, document checks and detention in the province are handled by units already documented committing ill-treatment with impunity.

65028918B37605681672150.name: North Sumatra
65028918B37605681672150.summary:
Indonesia is a high-risk destination for trans visitors, and North Sumatra stands under that national framework. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option, legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, and no national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

North Sumatra is one of eight focus provinces examined in OutRight Action International's mapping of national laws and discriminatory regional regulations affecting women and LGBTIQ people, alongside Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra and Yogyakarta. The study finds substantial overlap across the country but significant regional variation in dress codes, curfews and restrictions on where transgender people may appear, and states that its conclusions hold for provinces outside the focus set. A visitor to North Sumatra therefore faces both the national morality provisions and locally varying administrative restrictions on presentation and movement.

The only documented legal-recognition case for North Sumatra is favourable in outcome. Dimas Cahya, a transgender man from Medan, became the first transgender man in the city to change his name legally to match his identity; after a six-week process the Medan District Court granted the application. The judge warned that the change would 'erase my identity' but otherwise stayed out of LGBTI issues entirely, and the court process produced no enforcement action against him or his partner. Reporting frames Medan as conservative, with LGBTI people deemed 'immoral', and records that a Medan legal-aid organisation asked the couple invasive questions before the case was filed.

65028918B94007491868798.name: Southeast Sulawesi
65028918B94007491868798.summary:
Southeast Sulawesi stands under the national framework of Indonesia, a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Same-sex marriage is not permitted anywhere in Indonesia, so that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations, and reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national morality provisions. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors; two men were publicly caned there for a same-sex relationship in February 2025.

Physical risk is rising across the country. Vigilante mobs are attacking transgender people, and reporting in August 2026 ties the surge to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 that lists LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism. Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue: on 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International said the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him, which Indonesian police deny.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment. In March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words including Grindr, and a bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option. Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, and no national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

OutRight Action International's 2022 mapping of Indonesia's national laws and regional regulations examined discriminatory provisions in eight focus provinces: Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra and Yogyakarta. Southeast Sulawesi is not among them; the Sulawesi entry in that set is South Sulawesi. The study states that its findings apply to regions beyond the focus set.

A qualitative study by Universitas Halu Oleo researchers, published in Jurnal Budaya Etnika Vol. 8 No. 2 on 23 December 2024, describes gay life in Kendari, the capital of Southeast Sulawesi. Same-sex communities there live discreetly, and the article reports no enforcement incident, raid or local regulation.

sources.summary: OutRight Action International, 'Creeping Criminalisation: Mapping of Indonesia's National Laws and Regional Regulations That Violate Human Rights of Women and LGBTIQ People' (Katjasungkana & Wieringa; 2022 file copy) examines discriminatory national laws and regional regulations in eight focus provinces: Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra and Yogyakarta. It finds much overlap between those provinces alongside significant regional variation in dress codes, curfews and restrictions on where transgender people may appear, and states that the findings apply to regions beyond the focus set.
