65028918B6070530336190.name: Special Region of Yogyakarta
65028918B6070530336190.summary:
The Special Region of Yogyakarta stands under Indonesia's national framework, and that framework is hostile to transgender visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment; because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, the provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations, and reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. Yogyakarta is not among the two provinces where provincial criminalisation of same-sex sexual activity is recorded under regional religious law, so the provincial Sharia penalties imposed in Aceh and South Sumatra do not extend to this special region.

OutRight Action International's mapping of Indonesian national laws and discriminatory regional regulations (Katjasungkana and Wieringa, 2022 file copy) examined regional regulations across eight focus provinces, Yogyakarta among them, and found substantial overlap alongside significant regional variation in the content of those regulations, including dress codes, curfews and restrictions on where transgender people may appear. The study states that its findings hold for regions beyond the focus set, so a visitor should expect some form of locally enacted restriction on trans visibility here even where no provincial anti-trans statute exists.

The clearest enforcement-adjacent event on record in Yogyakarta concerned a trans institution rather than a visitor. On the night of 24 February 2016 the Pondok Pesantren Waria Al-Fatah, a religious school where trans women (waria) study Islam, was closed after the hardline Front Jihad Islam threatened to seal it. BBC reporting described rising hate speech against LGBT people, especially in Yogyakarta. The Banguntapan district head, Jati Bayubroto, justified the closure on the grounds that the pesantren lacked a permit, conflicted with Islamic values and had once had alcohol found on site; the founder, Shinta Ratri, said about 20 waria attended the weekly weekend classes, which taught ordinary Islamic instruction.

The closure meeting itself ran about two hours at the Jagalan ward office from around 20:00 on 24 February 2016, attended by ward and residents' officials, the lurah, the local military district commander, and, in an earlier session on 19 February, the Banguntapan camat and the local police sector chief. A waria witness said a Front Jihad Islam leader delivered fiery anti-LGBT remarks to shouts of 'Allahu Akbar' and vowed the group would keep hunting LGBTI people wherever they gather. The shutdown concluded on administrative and community grounds, with no provincial anti-trans statute cited. The Governor of the Special Region of Yogyakarta, Sultan Hamengku Buwono X, publicly urged restraint on both sides, described LGBT people as 'fellow children of the nation' and said the regional government would study the issue.

The Al-Fatah pesantren and the Yogyakarta waria community are operating again years after the 2016 closure. Reporting from June 2021 recorded an aromatherapy-candle making class held at the pesantren on 12 June 2021 with the local small business Malini.yk to teach new income skills, and noted that waria continued performing even when donors refused even masked performances. Economic and social marginalisation of trans people in the province persists.

On 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in a highland area near a major city after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman; an international human-rights organisation said the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 a foreign student on honeymoon was arrested at a national airport on drug charges; during a phone call his mother abroad was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him. National police denied that violence was used.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. A 2006 national statute against pornography and pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment. In March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words including a major dating application, and a bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Compared with one other state/province where two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025 under provincial religious law applying to anyone present including foreign visitors, this state/province carries no recorded provincial sexual-conduct penalty. The difference is one of legal layer, not of safety: the national code, the national expression offences and the vigilante environment apply here as everywhere in the country.

76434192B26311534340602.name: KwaZulu-Natal
76434192B26311534340602.summary:
KwaZulu-Natal is a province of the Republic of South Africa and stands under the national constitutional framework. The Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, prohibits unfair discrimination on the grounds of sex, gender and sexual orientation, and the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act (PEPUDA) of 2000 gives effect to that guarantee through the Equality Court, which also hears hate-speech and harassment complaints. Legal gender recognition has been available since the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act of 2003, same-sex marriage since the Civil Union Act of 2006, and the Prevention and Combating of Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act of 2024 names sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics as protected grounds. A visitor engages no consensual-conduct offence on the basis of gender identity or sexual orientation anywhere in the province.

The gap between that framework and conditions on the ground is the province's defining feature for a trans visitor. A 2024 Masters criminology thesis submitted to the University of KwaZulu-Natal in Durban, buthelezi Ayanda Nomfundo's study of queerphobic violence in KwaMashu Township, drew on in-depth interviews with 15 queer participants recruited through the Imvelo Yesizwe Organisation and reports significant victimisation of queer individuals in township settings, alongside questions about whether available support, interventions and safety strategies are adequate.

Hostility from the province's highest traditional authority is documented. In January 2012 remarks by Zulu King Goodwill Zwelithini at a harvest festival drew demands for an apology, police opened an investigation, and both the KwaZulu-Natal Premier and Contralesa publicly engaged the royal family's account.

Custody is where the province's national legal order has been most forcefully tested. Jade September, a transgender woman, was held in the male section of Pollsmoor Prison and won her 2019 Equality Court case against the Minister of Correctional Services, which held that barring her from expressing her gender identity was unfair discrimination. The resulting Department of Correctional Services standard operating procedure for LGBT+ prisoners requires a safety-risk assessment within the first six hours of admission, requires that transgender men and transgender women be detained or transported only with other transgender men and transgender women respectively, and sets rules on respectful searching and communication.

On 14 November 2025 the High Court sitting as an Equality Court ruled for the transgender inmate Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena against the Department of Correctional Services in case 2024/070075, delivered by the Gauteng Division of the High Court in Johannesburg on 10 November 2025. The court found unfair discrimination and harassment arising from the refusal to let her wear feminine attire and be addressed with she/her pronouns, and the failure to provide appropriate accommodation; it held that the constitutional right to adequate medical treatment includes gender-affirming hormone therapy at State expense, rejected the department's contrary argument, and ordered immediate implementation of accommodations, enforcement of the department's own standard operating procedures, and provision of the prescribed care. The South African Human Rights Commission, acting as National Preventive Mechanism under OPCAT since its designation on 4 December 2024, welcomed the judgment as an affirmation of the rights of transgender persons in correctional facilities.

Lawyers for Human Rights, which represented Mokoena, has separately litigated on behalf of 'NM', a transgender woman serving a long-term sentence at Johannesburg Correctional Centre, over gender-affirming healthcare, and rights organisations have raised continuing concern about whether the standard operating procedure is implemented in practice rather than merely on paper. Transgender prisoners are held inside the ordinary national corrections system, so placement and accommodation obligations rest on departmental procedures enforceable through litigation.

76434192B51294388644125.name: Nothern Cape
76434192B51294388644125.summary:
The Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, prohibits unfair discrimination on the grounds of sex, gender and sexual orientation, and the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act (PEPUDA) gives effect to that guarantee through the Equality Court. Sexual-orientation discrimination was banned in 1996, making South Africa the first country to do so; marriage equality followed with the Civil Union Act of 2006; legal gender recognition has been available since the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act of 2003; and the Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act of 2024 explicitly protects sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics. The Northern Cape province stands under that national framework, and no provincial statute narrowing it is documented.

The province recorded at least three LGBTIQ+ community members killed during 2024. On 14 May 2024 in Paballelo, Upington, Jo-Ann Isaks, a 27-year-old transgender woman, was found dead in her burning room with multiple stab wounds to the upper body; a family member noticed the flames at about 23:00. On 1 June 2024 in Kimberley, Karabelo Pudumo, an 18-year-old transgender Grade 10 learner at Pescodia High School, was stabbed more than 20 times, allegedly by a man she had been drinking with after he realised she was transgender. The third killing, in September 2024, was of Lazarus Ikaneng Thomas, a 50-year-old gay man.

The violence is severe in method and has drawn sustained community response: more than 300 children and community members attended a memorial for Karabelo Pudumo at her school, and the province's LGBTIQ+ district leader, Jenny Sambok, said the ZF Mgcawu region community was shaken after the Upington killing. Official handling has been uneven. Police in the ZF Mgcawu District opened a murder case in the Isaks matter, described the investigation as at a critical stage, and reported no arrests at that point; the same spokesperson publicly identified the victim by a birth name. An arrest was reported in the Pudumo case, but the reporting outlet could not verify it with authorities.

Everyday exposure outside violence turns largely on documents. The Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act requires medical evidence, a pathologising route that locks people out of legal gender recognition, and its binary sex classification excludes non-binary people altogether; reform toward self-determination is pending but not in force. Costs of affirming one's gender through the process are described as dauntingly high. Where identity documents do not match presentation, trans people face humiliation, denial of service and threats of arrest for alleged fraud. A 2024 Gender Dynamix report documents a trans woman met with police mockery and refused when she attempted to file a domestic-violence complaint after producing her identity document.

Access to gender-affirming care is uneven. Activists in East London delivered a memorandum to Frere Hospital over treatment delays running to a year. Academic analysis published in 2024 examining whether PEPUDA read with section 9 of the Constitution prohibits the exclusion of transgender and non-binary people from gender-segregated bathrooms concludes that trans people do not in practice experience equal protection in facility access, so restroom and changing-room disputes remain foreseeable for visitors.

Detention is a site of elevated risk. Jade September, a transgender woman held in the male section of Pollsmoor, won her 2019 Equality Court case against the Minister of Correctional Services, which held that not allowing her to express her gender identity was unfair discrimination. The Department of Correctional Services standard operating procedure that followed requires a safety-risk assessment within the first six hours of admission and stipulates that transgender men and transgender women are to be detained or transported only with other transgender men or transgender women respectively, alongside respectful-search and communication rules. On 10 November 2025 the Gauteng Division of the High Court, Johannesburg, sitting as an Equality Court, ruled for Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena against the Department in case 2024/070075, finding unfair discrimination and harassment over refusal of feminising attire, she/her pronouns and accommodation; the court held that the constitutional right to adequate medical treatment includes gender-affirming hormonal therapy at State expense, and ordered immediate implementation of accommodations, enforcement of the Department's own standard operating procedures, and provision of prescribed medical care. The South African Human Rights Commission, acting as the National Preventive Mechanism under OPCAT, welcomed the ruling on 14 November 2025. Reporting in August 2025 records that rights organisations doubt whether the procedure is implemented in practice.

Outside detention, national-level incidents indicate the surrounding risk environment: on 26 December 2024 Aobakwe Mahlobo, a 23-year-old trans woman and make-up artist, survived an unprovoked assault at a tavern in Tshwane that left severe facial injuries, with an arrest reported, and OUT LGBT Well-being's rights watch for December 2024 recorded five LGBTQIA+ murders that month. Violence disproportionately affects Black lesbian, trans and gender-nonconforming people in townships.

District police opened a murder case in the Isaks matter, described the investigation as at a critical stage, and reported no arrests at that point; the same spokesperson publicly identified the victim by a birth name. an arrest was reported in the Pudumo case, but the reporting outlet could not verify it with authorities.

The Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act requires medical evidence, a pathologising route that locks people out of legal gender recognition, and its binary sex classification excludes non-binary people altogether; reform toward self-determination is pending but not in force. Costs of affirming one's gender through the process are described as dauntingly high. Where identity documents do not match presentation, trans people face humiliation, denial of service and threats of arrest for alleged fraud. A 2024 Gender Dynamix report documents a trans woman met with police mockery and refused when she attempted to file a domestic-violence complaint after producing her identity document.

Access to gender-affirming care is uneven. Activists in East London delivered a memorandum to Frere Hospital over treatment delays running to a year. Academic analysis published in 2024 examining whether PEPUDA read with section 9 of the constitution prohibits the exclusion of transgender and non-binary people from gender-segregated bathrooms concludes that trans people do not in practice experience equal protection in facility access, so restroom and changing-room disputes remain foreseeable for visitors.

Jade September, a transgender woman held in the male section of Pollsmoor, won her 2019 Equality Court case against the Minister of Correctional Services, which held that not allowing her to express her gender identity was unfair discrimination. The national human rights commission, acting as the National Preventive Mechanism under OPCAT, welcomed the ruling on 14 November 2025. Reporting in August 2025 records that rights organisations doubt whether the procedure is implemented in practice.

Violence disproportionately affects Black lesbian, trans and gender-nonconforming people in townships.

76434192B92524600968894.name: Mpumalanga
76434192B92524600968894.summary:
Mpumalanga is a province of the Republic of South Africa and stands under the national framework: the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, prohibits unfair discrimination on the grounds of sex, gender and sexual orientation, and the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act (PEPUDA) of 2000 gives effect to that guarantee through the Equality Court, which also hears hate-speech and harassment complaints. Sodomy and the common-law 'unnatural sexual offence' were struck down by the Constitutional Court in 1998 and the gender-neutral age of consent was set at 16 in 2007, so no consensual-conduct offence engages a visitor on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation. Marriage equality dates from the Civil Union Act of 2006, and the Prevention and Combating of Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act signed in May 2024 names sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics as protected grounds.

Legal gender recognition has been available since the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act of 2003, which requires medical or surgical treatment including hormone therapy but not sex reassignment surgery, and issues identity documents and passports reflecting gender identity. Identity documents remain strictly binary, and mismatched documents remain a daily hazard: analyses by Gender Dynamix record trans people facing humiliation, denial of service and threats of arrest for fraud when presenting documents that do not match their presentation, and a 2024 report records a trans woman turned away from filing a domestic-violence case after showing her ID while police mocked her.

Provincial hostility from traditional leadership is documented on the record. After meeting at Hazyview in Mpumalanga in June 2010, the National House of Traditional Leaders and its Provincial Houses issued a letter stating that although they respected the Constitutional Court's same-sex marriage judgment they were disappointed that the practice had been given a lifeline by the courts, that they do not support legalisation of same-sex marriage, and that they warned of ostracism and violence while vowing a five-year campaign against it. In 2016 the same body asked Parliament to review the constitutional clause protecting people against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation.

Violence against lesbians and trans people is the principal physical risk, and Mpumalanga has recorded a killing with community mobilisation in response. Portia Mtsweni, a 25-year-old lesbian, was found dead near Zamani Primary School in Tweefontein in the early hours of Sunday 29 December 2019, half naked with stab wounds. On 2 January 2020 about 800 people marched in the Thembisile Hani Local Municipality in protest, organised by Lasiphumakhona LGBTI, the ANC Women's League and others, with mayor Nomsa Mtsweni calling on parents, leaders and churches to stand united against gender-based violence. Nationally, OUT LGBT Well-being's December 2024 rights watch recorded five LGBTQIA+ murders in that month alone, and a 23-year-old trans woman, Aobakwe Mahlobo, was attacked without provocation at a tavern in Tshwane on 26 December 2024 with an arrest reported.

Public LGBTIQ+ presence in the province is established and police-supported at organised events. Mpumalanga's first Pride march and celebration was held on Saturday 9 August 2014 in the provincial capital, Nelspruit (Mbombela), under the theme 'Moving Forward, Proud, Strong & United', with around 1,000 participants marching from the SABC offices to Nelspruit Plaza and a post-parade picnic at Oorwesig Garden Park. Organiser Joy Kunene said police were visible and supportive and supplied about 20 police and traffic officers, and the event launched the LGBTI Mpumalanga Movement, an umbrella group for the province's LGBTI organisations.

Police treatment of LGBTIQ+ people when reporting is nonetheless contested in the province. At a Pride Flag Tour held at the eMbalenhle Sasol Club on 18 August 2026, community members led by the Rainbow Seed Institute raised concerns about alleged discrimination and stigmatisation at government institutions, particularly police stations. Participants said they were ridiculed, questioned or treated unfairly when seeking assistance; one member alleged that after being sexually assaulted in eMbalenhle months earlier, an officer at eMbalenhle Police Station asked why she didn't fight back, and attendees said they fear reporting crimes because of stigmatisation.

Gender-affirming care is lawful and available but unevenly distributed: hormone therapy can be accessed from age 16 and surgery from 18, or younger with parental consent, with private care concentrated in the major cities and public systems facing long waits that push rural patients to travel to urban centres. On 14 November 2025 the Gauteng High Court, sitting as an Equality Court, ruled for a transgender inmate against the Department of Correctional Services, holding that refusing prescribed gender-affirming health care falls below the required standard of health care in custody and ordering treatment at state expense, gender-expressing clothing and cosmetics, and enforcement of the Department's standard operating procedures for transgender inmates.

76434192B37104984973577.summary:
The Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, prohibits unfair discrimination on the grounds of sex, gender and sexual orientation, and the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act (PEPUDA) of 2000 gives effect to that guarantee through the Equality Court, which also hears hate-speech and harassment complaints. Consensual same-sex conduct has not been an offence since the Constitutional Court's 1998 judgment striking down sodomy and the common-law unnatural sexual offence, marriage equality has been available under the Civil Union Act since 2006, legal gender recognition has been available under the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act since 2003, and the Prevention and Combating of Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act of 2024 names sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics as protected grounds.

Limpopo stands under that national framework, and no statute of the province or of the Republic criminalises a trans visitor's expression of gender identity. The province's distinctive exposure lies in customary jurisdiction over the former Bantustan areas that cover much of its rural territory. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 May 2012 that the Traditional Courts Bill then before parliament threatened LGBT South Africans by creating a parallel customary-law justice system covering people in those former homelands, and that the bill offered no opt-out from customary jurisdiction.

Human Rights Watch further reported that rural LGBT people already faced discrimination, violence and poor police cooperation, and that chiefs' courts punish lesbians in rural areas. Mamba Online, writing on 18 April 2012, reported that the Traditional Courts Bill under debate in provincial public hearings would re-criminalise gay and lesbian conduct in former-Bantustan areas through a separate customary system, that lesbians are reported punished at chiefs' homesteads and tribal offices with no opt-out, and that those who can are expected to leave rural areas. Traditional leaders were also reported to oppose the Civil Union Act of 2006.

A trans visitor therefore faces the national protective framework in Polokwane and other urban centres, and a materially different setting in areas under traditional authority, where a dispute or a complaint can be taken before chiefs' courts that apply customary norms rather than the Equality Court route. The relevant hazards are humiliation, punishment and refusal of protection rather than a statutory offence, compounded by the poor police cooperation HRW recorded for rural LGBT people.

The Traditional Courts Bill episode documents a structural tension rather than a single incident: South Africa's post-1994 equality framework operates alongside a parallel customary system covering the former Bantustans, and the two do not align on sexual orientation or gender identity. HRW's 2012 assessment was that the bill would have extended that customary system without providing an exit for the people it affects.

Resistance to national equality law is concentrated among traditional leadership. Mamba Online reported in 2012 that traditional leaders opposed the Civil Union Act as it was being settled nationally, which locates the source of friction in institutional authority in rural areas rather than in the national legislature.

Both sources date from 2012, and they describe a legislative proposal under debate at that time alongside conditions HRW reported as already present in rural areas: discrimination, violence, poor police cooperation and punishment of lesbians by chiefs' courts.

76434192B85643022077130.name: North West
76434192B85643022077130.summary:
The Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, prohibits unfair discrimination on the grounds of sex, gender and sexual orientation, and the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act (PEPUDA) gives effect to that guarantee through the Equality Court. Sexual-orientation discrimination was banned in 1996, making South Africa the first country to do so; marriage equality followed with the Civil Union Act of 2006; legal gender recognition has been available since the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act of 2003; and the Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act of 2024 explicitly protects sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics.

On 14 November 2025 the Gauteng High Court, sitting as an Equality Court, delivered judgment in Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre (case 2024/070075), a challenge brought against the Department of Correctional Services with the assistance of Lawyers for Human Rights. The court held that refusing a transgender inmate prescribed gender-affirming health care falls below the required standard of health care, and that refusing feminising clothing and accessories is likewise unlawful. Orders compelling the Department to provide hormone treatment at state expense, permit clothing and cosmetics expressing the inmate's gender identity, implement the accommodations required by its own standard operating procedure for transgender inmates, and deliver prescribed medical care were granted. The South African Human Rights Commission's National Preventive Mechanism welcomed the ruling the same day.

Correctional Services already had a standard operating procedure for transgender prisoners before the ruling; reporting in August 2025 recorded that rights organisations doubt whether it is implemented in practice. Detention therefore remains a site of elevated risk for trans visitors and residents despite the binding remedies now in place.

Outside prison, everyday exposure is shaped by documents. The Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act requires medical evidence, a pathologising route that locks people out of legal gender recognition, and its binary sex classification excludes non-binary people altogether; reform toward self-determination is pending but not in force. Costs of affirming one's gender through the process are described as dauntingly high. Where documents do not match presentation, trans people face humiliation, denial of service and threats of arrest for alleged fraud. A 2024 Gender Dynamix report documents a trans woman who was met with police mockery and refused when she attempted to file a domestic-violence complaint after producing her identity document.

Violence risk is documented and ongoing. On 26 December 2024 Aobakwe Mahlobo, a 23-year-old trans woman and make-up artist, survived an unprovoked hate-crime assault at a tavern in Tshwane that left her with severe facial injuries and lasting physical and emotional scars; she spoke out publicly and an arrest was reported. OUT LGBT Well-being's rights watch for December 2024 recorded five LGBTQIA+ murders that month. Violence disproportionately affects Black lesbian, trans and gender-nonconforming people in townships.

Access to gender-affirming care is uneven. Activists in East London delivered a memorandum to Frere Hospital over treatment delays running to a year. Academic analysis published in 2024 examining whether the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act read with section 9 of the Constitution prohibits the exclusion of transgender and non-binary people from gender-segregated bathrooms concludes that trans people do not in practice experience equal protection in facility access, so restroom and changing-room disputes remain foreseeable for visitors.

Within North West province, the principal sub-national legal divergence is the reach of traditional and customary courts. Human Rights Watch's analysis of the Traditional and Khoi-San Leadership Act identifies the former-Bantustan geography, which includes North West, as standing under a separate legal system; HRW's earlier reporting on the Traditional Courts Bill (29 May 2012) described a parallel customary-law justice system covering people in the former Bantustans, offered no opt-out from customary jurisdiction, and recorded that rural LGBT people already face discrimination, violence and poor police cooperation, with chiefs' courts punishing lesbians in rural areas. The Act was declared invalid in Mogale (2023) but suspended and extended, and the replacement Bill (TKLB) has been delayed. No province has religious criminal law, and no statute criminalises a visitor's expression here.

Healthcare access is the sharpest practical constraint on the ground. The trans community in North West cannot access hormone replacement therapy at any public health facility in the province; the North West Department of Health confirmed it has no facilities providing HRT for transgender people in response to a complaint lodged by Action for Social Justice International with the South African Human Rights Commission, and residents are forced to travel sometimes hundreds of kilometres to Soweto in Gauteng to obtain it. A visitor dependent on prescribed HRT should expect no provincial public provider and should carry a sufficient supply.

Hate-crime evidence for the province is thin but exists. The Love Not Hate campaign research conducted by OUT LGBT Well-being (2016) records that only three quantitative studies of hate crimes against LGBT people have been done in South Africa: the 2003 empowerment study covering Gauteng, KwaZulu-Natal and the Western Cape, a 2010 North West province study, and the national campaign study itself. North West is therefore one of only three provinces ever to have received its own representative hate-crime prevalence study.

sources.title: North West trans community desperate for hormone replacement services
sources.summary: The trans community in North West province cannot access hormone replacement therapy (HRT) at any public health facility in the province and residents are forced to travel sometimes hundreds of kilometres to Soweto in Gauteng to get it, MambaOnline reported on 21 February 2023. The North West Department of Health confirmed it has no facilities providing HRT for transgender people, in its response to a complaint lodged by Action for Social Justice International with the SA Human Rights Commission. Documents the province-level absence of trans-specific healthcare that a trans visitor reliant on prescribed HRT would confront on the ground.

sources.title: Lesbian pupil banned from school in North West
sources.summary: MambaOnline (23 March 2016, citing the Taung Daily News) reported that 18-year-old lesbian Zinzi Manini Molema of Maphoitsile village, North West, was barred from attending school for refusing to wear a skirt; the principal sent her home saying she must wear a skirt 'since I was a girl', and she stayed home for three weeks without attending any classes. Records a North West institution enforcing a gendered dress code against a gender-nonconforming pupil, illustrating the province's socially conservative enforcement climate.

sources.title: New Report on LGBT Community in North West
sources.summary: A report entitled 'Same-sex sexuality in North-West province', released in October 2010, presented the results of a survey conducted under the auspices of the UNISA Centre for Applied Psychology during 2009 and 2010, with OUT LGBT Well-being, OUT North-West and Gay Umbrella collaborating. It surveyed 319 LGBT people from a largely rural background in one of the country's poorest and most under-populated provinces, asking about openness about same-sex sexuality, how LGBT persons perceive their environment, and sexual abuse and discrimination.

76434192B98113213215773.name: Eastern Cape
76434192B98113213215773.summary:
The Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, prohibits unfair discrimination on the grounds of sex, gender and sexual orientation, and the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act (PEPUDA) gives effect to that guarantee through the Equality Court. Sexual-orientation discrimination was banned in 1996, marriage equality followed with the Civil Union Act of 2006, legal gender recognition has been available since the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act of 2003, and the Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act of 2024 explicitly protects sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics. The Eastern Cape has no separate provincial trans statute, ban or enforcement regime; visitors to the province are covered by these national instruments.

Detention in the province runs under a placement rule fixed nationally rather than locally. In Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre (case 2024/070075), delivered by the Gauteng High Court sitting as an Equality Court on 14 November 2025, the Department of Correctional Services conceded that the regulations to the Correctional Services Act on vulnerable inmates and its own Standard Operating Procedures require inmates to be housed in cells appropriate to their gender identity where feasible and safe, and that those Standard Operating Procedures prescribe single-cell accommodation for transgender inmates. The court ordered single-cell placement or placement with inmates of the same gender identity. That is the operative rule for transgender prisoners in Eastern Cape correctional centres, including St Albans, Mthatha and East London; no province-specific trans placement case is on record. The same judgment held that refusing prescribed gender-affirming health care and refusing feminising clothing and accessories are unlawful, with hormone treatment to be provided at state expense. Reporting in August 2025 recorded rights organisations' doubt that the Department's standard operating procedure is implemented in practice, so detention remains an elevated-risk setting.

Legal gender recognition under the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act requires medical evidence, a pathologising route that excludes non-binary people through its binary sex classification; reform toward self-determination is pending but not in force, and the cost of affirming one's gender through the process is described as dauntingly high. Where identity documents do not match presentation, trans people in the province face humiliation, denial of service and threats of arrest for alleged fraud. A 2024 Gender Dynamix report documents a trans woman met with police mockery and refused when she attempted to file a domestic-violence complaint after producing her identity document.

Access to gender-affirming care in the Eastern Cape is uneven. Activists in East London delivered a memorandum to Frere Hospital over treatment delays running to a year, a concrete service bottleneck for a visitor needing continuity of hormone therapy or other prescribed care.

Violence risk is documented and ongoing. On 26 December 2024 Aobakwe Mahlobo, a 23-year-old trans woman and make-up artist, survived an unprovoked hate-crime assault at a tavern in Tshwane that left her with severe facial injuries; she spoke out publicly and an arrest was reported. OUT LGBT Well-being's rights watch for December 2024 recorded five LGBTQIA+ murders that month nationally, and violence disproportionately affects Black lesbian, trans and gender-nonconforming people in townships, a pattern that holds in the Eastern Cape's township and rural areas. Within the province, Eastern Cape police arrested four suspects over the killings of two women in Gqeberha on 2 May 2025, in a case that drew public outrage and renewed calls to confront rising gender-based violence.

A further exposure is jurisdictional rather than statutory. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 May 2012 that the Traditional Courts Bill then before parliament threatened LGBT South Africans by creating a parallel customary-law justice system covering people in the former Bantustans, with no opt-out from customary jurisdiction; it reported that rural LGBT people already face discrimination, violence and poor police cooperation, and that chiefs' courts punish lesbians in rural areas. For a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor outside the metro civil-society belt, the practical forum is therefore as likely to be a chief's court as a magistrate's court.

Supports the province's framing of traditional-court rural jurisdiction as the defining risk factor for LGBT travellers off the main cities.

76434192B98113213215773.tangentialFactors:
The Eastern Cape's exposure profile is set less by provincial law than by the interaction of national protection machinery with rural customary jurisdiction and a thin service base. Academic analysis published in 2024 examining whether PEPUDA read with section 9 of the Constitution prohibits the exclusion of transgender and non-binary people from gender-segregated bathrooms concludes that trans people do not in practice experience equal protection in facility access, so restroom and changing-room disputes remain foreseeable at malls, hotels, gyms and workplaces throughout the province.

Gender-based violence provides the ambient crime backdrop. The Gqeberha arrests of four suspects over two women's killings in May 2025 illustrate a provincial pattern of lethal violence against women that is not trans-specific but shapes the risk environment for any visibly gender-nonconforming traveller, particularly after dark and in informal settings such as taverns. The December 2024 assault on Aobakwe Mahlobo in Tshwane is the clearest documented trans-specific hate crime in the recent record and establishes that targeted violence against trans women continues in social venues, with arrest following in that instance.

Comparison with the rest of the country is unhelpful in one respect and instructive in another: the binding remedies created by the Mokoena judgment bind the Department of Correctional Services nationwide, so trans prisoners in Eastern Cape centres hold the same orders as those in Gauteng, but the province has no litigation of its own pressing implementation, which may slow uptake.

76434192B69392740373411.name: Gauteng
76434192B69392740373411.summary:
Gauteng stands under the national constitutional framework of South Africa. The Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, prohibits unfair discrimination on the grounds of sex, gender and sexual orientation; the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act (PEPUDA) of 2000 gives effect to that guarantee through the Equality Court, which also hears hate-speech and harassment complaints; and the Prevention and Combating of Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act, signed in May 2024, explicitly names sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics as protected grounds. No consensual-conduct offence engages a visitor on the basis of gender identity or sexual orientation: sodomy and the common-law 'unnatural sexual offence' were struck down in 1998 with retroactive effect to 1994, and the residual disparity in the age of consent was equalised at a gender-neutral 16 by the 2007 statute, the old disparity being confirmed unconstitutional in Geldenhuys v NDPP in 2008.

Legal gender recognition has been available since the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act of 2003, which permits amendment of sex status in the population registry and the issue of identity documents and passports reflecting gender identity. The statute requires medical or surgical treatment, including hormone replacement therapy, but not sex reassignment surgery. Identity documents remain strictly binary, so non-binary people cannot be recognised, and the medical requirements lock some people out of recognition altogether. In October 2021 the Department of Home Affairs announced plans for gender-neutral identification on South African ID cards, an identity-management document estimating 530,000 non-binary residents, but officials confirmed the change would take a few years as it passes through consultation to legislation.

On 10 November 2025 the Gauteng Division of the High Court in Johannesburg, sitting as an Equality Court, delivered judgment in Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre and Others (Case No. 2024/070075). The court held that the Department of Correctional Services engaged in unfair discrimination and harassment of a transgender inmate by refusing to let her express her gender identity and by denying prescribed gender-affirming hormone therapy, and that the constitutional right to adequate medical treatment includes gender-affirming hormonal therapy at state expense. The orders require the Department to provide that treatment, to permit clothing and cosmetics expressing her gender identity, to implement the required accommodations, and to enforce its own standard operating procedures for transgender inmates. The South African Human Rights Commission's National Preventive Mechanism welcomed the ruling on 14 November 2025 as an affirmation of the rights of transgender persons in correctional facilities.

The judgment is also the only documented determination of where a trans prisoner is housed in Gauteng. Mokoena, a transgender woman serving a life sentence, was held at Johannesburg Correctional Centre: first in Medium A section, where she could express her gender identity through long hair, makeup and women's clothing, then transferred to Medium C section, and at the time of judgment housed in C Single Section, a segregated single-confinement unit. Despite requesting a single cell she was accommodated with cisgender male cellmates, first two cisgender gay men and then one cisgender male, the Department justifying this by overcrowding. The court found that the Department's own standard operating procedures prescribe accommodation appropriate to gender identity where feasible and safe, that no basis existed for refusing single accommodation, and ordered housing in a single cell or with inmates of the same gender identity.

Violence against visibly trans people remains the principal physical risk in the province. On 26 December 2024 Aobakwe Mahlobo, a 23-year-old transgender woman from Soshanguve living in Winterveld, was assaulted at a tavern in Tshwane at about 1:30 am after a man began saying gay and lesbian people 'don't deserve to live'; he smashed a bottle into her face as she lit a cigarette, saying 'I told you I'm gonna kill you', leaving deep cuts to her mouth, lips, nose, cheek and forehead that were stitched at Kgabo Clinic. She opened an assault case at Dube Police Station, which as of 6 January 2025 had shown no progress.

Nationally, OUT LGBT Well-being's December 2024 rights watch recorded five LGBTQIA+ murders in that month alone, and lesbians and trans people have been murdered, beaten and subjected to 'corrective rape', including among pupils, with activists accusing police of negligent handling of cases and ActionAid condemning impunity. Mismatched documents remain a daily hazard: an analysis published in January 2026 by Mikhail Petersen of Gender Dynamix describes trans people facing humiliation, denial of service and threats of arrest for 'fraud' when identity documents do not match presentation, and Gender Dynamix's 2024 report records a trans woman turned away from filing a domestic-violence case after showing her ID, with police mocking her. Facilities access is contested rather than settled: a 2024 analysis in PER/PELJ concludes that trans people do not in practice experience equal protection in facility access, so venue rules are expected to vary rather than rest on a single national rule. Gender-affirming care is lawful and available, from age 16 for hormone therapy and 18 for surgery or younger with parental consent, but private care is concentrated in the major cities and public systems face long waits. Partner and family recognition is broad, the Civil Union Act having been in force since 2006, with court decisions extending to same-sex couples covering immigration, employment and pension benefits and joint adoption.

sources.summary: 'Hate Crimes Against Gay and Lesbian People in Gauteng: Prevalence, Consequences and Contributing Factors' - Joint Working Group research initiative conducted by OUT LGBT Well-being with the UNISA Centre for Applied Psychology (authors Wells & Polders), the first representative quantitative provincial hate-crime study in South Africa (2003/04); partner roster includes Behind the Mask, Triangle Project, GALA and the Durban Lesbian & Gay Community & Health Centre.

Love Not Hate campaign research (GALA-hosted, conducted by OUT LGBT Well-being, 2016): the companion review of hate crimes against LGBT people in South Africa states that only three quantitative studies have ever been done - the 2003 empowerment study across Gauteng, KwaZulu-Natal and Western Cape; a 2010 North West province study; and this national campaign study - and measures levels of discrimination against LGBT people nationally.

She opened an assault case at Dube Police Station, which MambaOnline (6 January 2025) reported had shown no progress. The province's most recent documented trans-specific hate incident on record.

sources.title: Media Statement: National Preventive Mechanism welcomes the High Court ruling affirming the rights of transgender persons in correctional facilities

The court found the Department of Correctional Services engaged in unfair discrimination and harassment of the transgender inmate by refusing to allow her to express her gender identity and denying her prescribed gender-affirming hormone therapy, and held that the constitutional right to adequate medical treatment includes gender-affirming hormonal therapy at state expense, ordering the DCS to implement accommodations and enforce its own SOPs. 76434192B69392740373411.tangentialFactors:
The evidentiary base for hate-crime levels in Gauteng is thin. The first representative quantitative provincial study was 'Hate Crimes Against Gay and Lesbian People in Gauteng: Prevalence, Consequences and Contributing Factors', a Joint Working Group initiative conducted by OUT LGBT Well-being with the UNISA Centre for Applied Psychology (Wells and Polders) in 2003/04, with a partner roster including Behind the Mask, Triangle Project, GALA and the Durban Lesbian & Gay Community & Health Centre.

The companion national review accompanying the Love Not Hate campaign research (GALA-hosted, conducted by OUT LGBT Well-being, 2016) states that only three quantitative studies of LGBT hate crime have ever been done in South Africa: the 2003 study across Gauteng, KwaZulu-Natal and Western Cape, a 2010 North West province study, and the 2016 national campaign study. No province-wide quantitative update to the 2003/04 Gauteng findings appears in the inventory.

Human Rights Watch and other legal commentators warned before the May 2024 enactment that the hate-speech provisions are vague and burden free expression, though the statute converts protection into a defined offence framework rather than only a sentencing consideration.

Protection machinery exists at national level: a Department of Justice National Task Team from 2011, a National Intervention Strategy for LGBTI Communities from April 2014 with a rapid response team for unsolved cases, a Justice Ministry programme against gender-based and LGBTI violence launched in the 2010s, and the 2024 Hate Crimes Act. Enforcement records remain uneven against that machinery.

National campaign research review (2016, hosted by an LGBT archive): only three quantitative studies of anti-LGBT hate crime exist in this country — a 2003 multi-province survey including this province, a 2010 study of another province, and this campaign study; measures national levels of discrimination.

An international human rights organisation and other legal commentators warned before the May 2024 enactment that the hate-speech provisions are vague and burden free expression, though the statute converts protection into a defined offence framework rather than only a sentencing consideration.

Protection machinery exists at national level: a national task team within the justice department from 2011, a national intervention strategy for LGBTI communities from April 2014 with a rapid response team for unsolved cases, a justice ministry programme against gender-based and LGBTI violence launched in the 2010s, and the 2024 hate crimes statute. 76434192B56312278962278.name: Western Cape
76434192B56312278962278.summary:
The Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, prohibits unfair discrimination on the grounds of sex, gender and sexual orientation, and the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act (PEPUDA) gives effect to that guarantee through the Equality Court. Sexual-orientation discrimination was banned in 1996, making South Africa the first country to do so; marriage equality followed with the Civil Union Act of 2006; legal gender recognition has been available since the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act of 2003; and the Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act of 2024 explicitly protects sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics.

The Western Cape stands under that national framework. Nothing in the sourced material identifies a provincial statute, prohibition, enforcement action or official directive restricting trans people in the province, and no provincial rule conditions bathroom or changing-room use on sex assigned at birth or on legal gender status.

What the province supplies is an enforcement-and-response gap. On 19 February 2025 Taswald Ruiters, a transgender woman from Eerste River in Cape Town, was threatened with removal from Green Point Athletic Stadium after using the women's bathroom. A security guard told her "Look at you, you're a man", ordered her to use the men's bathroom and asserted that he had the final say. Police were called four times over nearly three hours and never arrived, MambaOnline reported on 28 February 2025.

The stadium is a public facility operated by the City of Cape Town; on the day of the incident the venue was rented by Western Province Athletics, which was responsible for contracting the security services. The incident therefore shows what a visibly trans visitor can meet in the province's best-resourced metro: a private guard enforcing a sex-segregated facility against a trans woman with no provincial authority behind him, and no police response to a reported intimidation. It aligns with the national finding that trans people do not in practice experience equal protection in facility access, so restroom and changing-room disputes remain foreseeable for visitors.

The Western Cape High Court appeal decision in 'Khoin v Jenkins in re: Observatory Civic Association v Trustees ... Facility access in practice is left to venue staff and security contractors, as the Green Point Athletic Stadium episode shows. Local advocacy reporting indicates that complaints of this kind are pursued through media and public statement rather than through an on-site provincial or municipal complaints mechanism; the City of Cape Town operates the stadium but the security on duty that day was contracted by the renting club.

Residents also carry the national document burden. 19338628B22645672383103.name: Île-de-France
19338628B22645672383103.summary:
Île-de-France stands under the French national framework: France's rules on identity documents, anti-discrimination law, criminal law and marriage apply uniformly across the region, and no separate regional regime governs transgender visitors.

The risks documented for transgender travellers in France concentrate in two settings, detention and the border. In everyday movement, accommodation and services, the country's own oversight bodies record persistent discrimination rather than legal prohibition.

Prison placement follows no statutory rule. Where a trans woman is held is decided by the gender inscribed on her identity documents, with each facility improvising through special units or isolation that restricts contact with other inmates. France's national custodial-inspection authority, the CGLPL, examined roughly 40 referrals from trans detainees since 2010 and issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 finding serious and persistent violations: placement by birth sex, isolation, exposure during strip searches. It recorded no marked improvement since its 2010 opinion despite the 2016 legal gender-recognition reform, and issued binding guidance for places of deprivation of liberty.

That practice remained current in 2025. Louna, a trans woman detained for opposing the A69 motorway works, has been held since mid-October 2024 in the Tarbes men's prison and kept in isolation since October. Her incarceration was put to the Keeper of the Seals in oral question no. 219 in the French National Assembly, arguing that the case exposes a prison system unable to guarantee conditions for trans detainees; placement remains under parliamentary scrutiny.

At entry points, trans women have faced questioning of their identity documents in public. Giovanna Rincon's first-person account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of questioning by French border police at the airport, in front of other travellers, documenting identity-document friction for trans travellers arriving in France.

The Défenseur des droits issued a new framework decision on trans rights confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony. It cites the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and sets out official guidance for service providers. Partner recognition rests on the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013; CNN reported France's first same-sex wedding on 29 May 2013, performed days after the law took effect.

Recorded anti-LGBT+ offences in France reached 4,800 in 2024, up 5% on 2023, with crimes and délits rising 14% a year since 2016, according to the interior ministry statistics service's Infraction rapide n°53 of May 2025. Only about 4% of victims file complaints. Acts concentrate in urban units of over 200,000 inhabitants, and Paris records 22 offences per 100,000 against a national rate of 7, a gap the note attributes in part to non-resident victims and commuters. Recorded victims are more than 70% men.

19338628B95725112529620.name: Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur
19338628B95725112529620.summary:
The risks documented for transgender travellers in France concentrate in two settings: detention and the border. In everyday movement, accommodation and services, the country's own oversight bodies record persistent discrimination rather than legal prohibition.

Prison placement follows no statutory rule. Where a trans woman is held is decided by the gender inscribed on her identity documents, with each facility improvising: special units, or isolation that restricts contact with other inmates. Treatment varies between establishments, and accounts collected in a BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 describe heightened assault vulnerability and suicide risk under those arrangements.

France's national custodial-inspection authority, the CGLPL, examined roughly 40 referrals from trans detainees since 2010 and issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 finding serious and persistent violations: placement by birth sex, isolation, and exposure during strip searches. It recorded no marked improvement since its 2010 opinion despite the 2016 legal gender-recognition reform, and issued binding guidance for places of deprivation of liberty.

The national preventive mechanism told the Association for the Prevention of Torture that a new opinion was needed precisely because the 2010 opinion produced no marked improvement, because the gender-recognition law and its terminology had changed, and because coverage now extends to intersex and non-binary detainees. Its findings rest on a decade of letters from detained trans people and identify structural problems in the isolation of vulnerable detainees and in suicide prevention.

That practice remained current in 2025. Louna, a trans woman detained for opposing the A69 motorway works, has been held since mid-October 2024 in the Tarbes men's prison and kept in isolation since October. Her incarceration was put to the Keeper of the Seals in oral question no. 219 in the French National Assembly, arguing that the case exposes a prison system unable to guarantee conditions for trans detainees; placement remains under parliamentary scrutiny.

At entry points, trans women have faced questioning of their identity documents in public. Giovanna Rincon's first-person account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of routine humiliation by French border police at the airport, questioned in front of other travellers.

The Défenseur des droits issued a new framework decision on trans rights, confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony. It cites the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and sets out official guidance for service providers.

For partner recognition, the legal baseline dates from the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013; CNN reported France's first same-sex wedding on 29 May 2013, performed days after the law took effect.

Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur stands under this national framework, and the region's own record adds one episode of appearance policing on public beaches. On 1 August 2023 the mayor of Fréjus issued an order prohibiting swimming while wearing 'covering and baggy clothing' on the commune's sea beaches, in force until 17 September 2023 and carrying a €135 fine.

The administrative tribunal of Toulon suspended that order on 5 August 2023, in freedom-of-relief order n° 2302537 brought by the Ligue des droits de l'homme, finding a grave and manifestly unlawful attack on fundamental freedoms: manifestation of religious conviction, freedom of movement, and freedom of dress in public space. It condemned the commune to pay €3,000.

Toulon's order followed the Conseil d'État's ruling of 17 July 2023 on an identical arrêté at Mandelieu-la-Napoule, where the Ligue des droits de l'homme had already contested the ban; observers noted that the Fréjus communiqué justified the prohibition on laïcité grounds while safety was cited publicly, framing religiously marked swimwear as the target. The order no longer operates, so the residual visitor-facing effect on this region's beaches is a signal that visible non-conformity in public dress can attract mayoral prohibition until a court stops it.

28173009B98838729156012.name: Chechnya
28173009B98838729156012.summary:
Chechnya is an autonomous republic of Russia, and visitors there stand under the federal framework that governs the country. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents took effect; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression that "justifies" gender transition. Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and the US State Department advises against all travel to Russia at Level 4, with warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

Chechnya's security services operate against LGBT people with a severity not documented elsewhere in Russia. Human Rights Watch (26 May 2017) established that a police purge began in February 2017: men believed to be gay were rounded up and held in unofficial detention facilities for days, humiliated, starved and tortured. Some were forcibly disappeared; others were returned to their families barely alive from beatings, with captors outing them to relatives and urging honour killings. The investigation found that top regional officials knew of the operation, despite the regional leader's public denial.

The purge was not a single episode. Novaya Gazeta (11 January 2019) reported renewed persecution of gay men in the republic, with warnings circulated through the administrators of LGBT groups on the VKontakte social network telling those still at large to leave; the regional leader's press secretary denied the reports. That reporting followed the paper's April 2017 investigation into the torture and killing of gay men, for which no criminal case was ever opened.

Detention has since been converted into coercion toward the war in Ukraine. The Insider (4 September 2024) reported that the monitoring group SK SOS documented Chechen security forces pressuring detained gay men into military service: at least seven were sent to the frontlines and at least one was already killed, and the methods predate the mobilisation order of 21 September 2022. In early September 2022, six men were detained on suspicion of homosexuality, threatened with fabricated charges and warned that they would be sent to the front.

The same machinery operates on the wider population. An investigation by the Memorial Human Rights Centre, reported by OC Media, found a mass wave of unlawful detentions in which people were taken in over minor pretexts such as missing insurance documents, held at police departments, subjected to psychological pressure and physical abuse, and forced to sign service contracts; in some cases a family had to produce two "volunteers" before a detained relative would be released.

The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) records systematic anti-LGBT campaigns across this republic and the wider North Caucasus from 2017 to 2024, involving abduction, torture and extrajudicial killing. It assesses that in the North Caucasus trans people and publicly active LGBT+ advocates are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, and notes that the 2023 designation of the international LGBT+ movement as an extremist organisation exposes support for it to 2 to 6 years' imprisonment and organising to 6 to 10 years, with violence spreading beyond the region.

28173009B75413689166101.name: Ingushetia
28173009B75413689166101.summary:
Ingushetia stands under the framework of Russia, where legal gender recognition is prohibited outright. The law signed by President Vladimir Putin in 2023 bans gender reassignment surgery and any change of gender marker on official documents, voids a marriage concluded by a trans person with someone of their same birth sex, and removes the right to adopt from people diagnosed with gender dysphoria. A 2024 law additionally bans adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that permit gender transitions, a rule that also bears on foreign visitors.

Public expression is constrained by the propaganda statutes. The 2013 law targeted material concerning minors; it was expanded in December 2022 to cover all age groups and now reaches content that promotes "non-traditional" sexual relationships, makes minors interested in gender transition, or gives minors a "desire to change their sex", including speech that justifies gender transition. More than 180 cases were brought under these provisions in 2023 alone, exceeding the total for 2013 to 2022 combined and producing roughly 26 million rubles in fines; cases have increased eighteenfold over the past decade, and fines brought over 60 million rubles (about $765,300) into the state budget in the two years to mid-2025.

Since the Supreme Court's November 2023 designation of a non-existent "international LGBT movement" as extremist, charges have been brought for displaying the rainbow flag or its colours. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in that movement or display of its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, with charges drawn from both the administrative and criminal codes. Between March and May 2026, nine LGBTQ organisations, among them the Russian LGBT Network, Coming Out and Centre T, were outlawed as extremist. Within 48 hours of the 2023 ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night; arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ life through 2025. In December 2024 a man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel business was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

For many transgender Russians emigration has become the only remaining means of living openly. The US State Department advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and includes language relevant to LGBT travellers, while the UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (version 2.0, June 2025) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention.

At the regional level the UK Home Office country policy note (June 2025) treats the North Caucasus, including Ingushetia, as the exception to its otherwise non-persecutory finding on Russia: trans people and public LGBT+ advocates in the region are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. The note documents systematic regional campaigns between 2017 and 2024, and states that the 2023 "extremist" designation exposes LGBT+ activity to 2 to 6 years' imprisonment, rising to 6 to 10 years for organising, with violence spreading beyond the region.

David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS, interviewed by Human Rights House Foundation, states that there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus and that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families. He attests that conditions in the region have deteriorated year on year.

Global Affairs Canada advises avoid all travel to Russia and lists Ingushetia among the republics with frequent terrorist attacks, alongside Chechnya, Dagestan and Stavropol Krai. The advisory notes surveillance of foreign nationals and states that 2SLGBTQI+ persons, their allies and their families have been attacked, harassed and abused; since January 2024, organisations advocating for 2SLGBTQI+ issues are treated as "extremist". The Ministry of Interior requires special permission to enter certain areas.

Public expression is constrained by the propaganda statutes. The 2013 law targeted material concerning minors, and was expanded in December 2022 to cover all age groups, reaching content that promotes "non-traditional" sexual relationships, makes minors interested in gender transition, or gives minors a "desire to change their sex"; the provisions reach speech that justifies gender transition. Enforcement has grown sharply: more than 180 cases were brought under these provisions in 2023 alone, exceeding the total for 2013 to 2022 combined and producing roughly 26 million rubles in fines, while fines brought over 60 million rubles (about $765,300) into the state budget in the two years to mid-2025.

Since the national supreme court's November 2023 designation of a non-existent "international LGBT movement" as extremist, charges have been brought for displaying the rainbow flag or its colours. A human rights organisation recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in that movement or display of its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, drawn from both the administrative and criminal codes. Between March and May 2026, nine LGBTQ organisations were outlawed as extremist. Within 48 hours of the 2023 ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in the capital; about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night. Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ life through 2025, and in December 2024 a man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel business was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Coercive conversion practice against trans people is documented. In summer 2021 a transgender woman was lured by relatives to a centre elsewhere in the country and held for nine months, forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour, escaping only after police responded to a phone she had found.

The country provides no anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, does not designate hate crimes as such, and does not treat gender-identity or sexual-orientation motivation as an aggravating factor in sentencing. Entry and onward-protection context carries explicit warnings for LGBT travellers. A foreign government's travel advisory for the country is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and includes language relevant to LGBT travellers. The country policy note of a neighbouring jurisdiction's asylum authority on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (version 2.0, June 2025) affirms that LGBT+ people in the country, including another state/province in the region, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention. A regional LGBTIQ+ advocate working in exile, interviewed by an international human rights organisation, states that there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the region and that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families; he attests to annual deterioration.

A visitor presenting documents whose marker does not match their presentation has no lawful route to resolve the discrepancy inside the country.

Public expression is constrained by the propaganda statutes. Enforcement has accelerated: more than 180 cases were brought under the provisions in 2023 alone, exceeding the total for 2013 to 2022 combined and producing roughly 26 million rubles in fines; cases have risen eighteenfold over the past decade, and fines brought over 60 million rubles into the state budget in the two years to mid-2025.

Since the Supreme Court's November 2023 designation of a non-existent "international LGBT movement" as extremist, displaying the rainbow flag or its colours has drawn charges. The North Caucasus, including Karachay-Cherkessia, is treated as worse than the national baseline. The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (version 2.0, June 2025) singles out the North Caucasus as the exception to its otherwise non-persecutory finding on Russia: trans people and public LGBT+ advocates there are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, with systematic regional campaigns documented across 2017 to 2024. The same note records that the 2023 extremist designation carries 2 to 6 years' imprisonment, rising to 6 to 10 years for organising. David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS, an on-the-ground defender now in exile, states that there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus and that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families; he reports year-on-year deterioration across the North Caucasus republics, which include Karachay-Cherkessia.

Coercive conversion practice against trans people is documented. 28173009B7235812138525.name: North Ossetia–Alania
28173009B7235812138525.summary:
North Ossetia–Alania stands under the legal framework of the Russian Federation, and that framework carries the heaviest anti-trans penalties in Europe. In July 2023 Russia enacted a law banning gender transition outright, prohibiting both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition on official documents; the federal 'propaganda' statute of 2013 was expanded in December 2022 to apply to people of all ages and to material that makes minors interested in gender transition; and in November 2023 the Russian Supreme Court designated the 'international LGBT public movement' an extremist organisation, which makes participation in LGBT activism a criminal offence. Foreigners who breach these statutes face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and the US State Department advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, with explicit warnings addressed to LGBT travellers.

The North Caucasus region, including this republic, is treated as a distinct and more dangerous category in the UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025). The note singles the region out as the exception to its otherwise non-persecutory finding on Russia: trans people and public LGBT+ advocates there are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. It records systematic regional campaigns against LGBT people running from 2017 to 2024, and notes that the 2023 extremist designation carries two to six years' imprisonment, rising to six to ten years for organising.

David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS, an on-the-ground defender speaking in exile, states that there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus and that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families; he describes year-on-year deterioration. His account covers the region including North Ossetia–Alania.

The federal laws apply to this republic without modification, which means visible LGBT activity a visitor brings into North Ossetia–Alania sits entirely outside federal legal protection. New laws effective 1 July 2023 further reclassify homosexuality as a mental illness. Enforcement nationally has escalated in both volume and severity: Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the designated movement or for displaying its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, and within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's designation, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, searching and photographing about 100 patrons at one venue.

28173009B89423349656391.name: Stavropol Krai
28173009B89423349656391.summary:
Stavropol Krai stands under the national framework of Russia, where legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care have been banned outright since 2023. The expanded "propaganda" statute criminalises public expression that, explicitly, justifies gender transition, and the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation. Foreign nationals who breach these provisions face arrest, detention of up to 15 days, and deportation. The US State Department carries a Level 4, Do Not Travel advisory for Russia with warnings directed at LGBT travellers, and Global Affairs Canada advises avoiding all travel to the country.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) identifies the North Caucasus as the exception to its otherwise non-persecutory assessment of Russia. Within this zone, trans people and public LGBT+ advocates are assessed as likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, with systematic regional campaigns recorded across 2017 to 2024. Charges following the 2023 extremist designation carry two to six years' imprisonment, rising to six to ten years for organising.

Movement into the neighbouring North Caucasus entities is restricted for visitors: Global Affairs Canada reports that Ministry of Interior special permission is required to enter Kabardino-Balkaria, including the Elbrus area, Karachai-Cherkessia and North Ossetia. The same advisory records that 2SLGBTQI+ persons and the families of their allies have been attacked, harassed and abused, that advocacy organisations have been treated as extremist since January 2024, and that foreign visitors are subject to surveillance.

David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS, speaking to the Human Rights House Foundation as a North Caucasus defender in exile, states that there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the region and that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families. He reports a year-on-year deterioration in conditions.
