28173009B19676032168465.name: Moscow
28173009B19676032168465.summary:
Visitors in Moscow stand under the national framework of the Russian Federation. The law signed by President Vladimir Putin in 2023 prohibits legal gender recognition outright: it bans gender-affirming surgery, removes any route to changing a gender marker on official documents, voids a marriage concluded by a trans person with someone of their same birth sex, and removes the right to adopt from people diagnosed with gender dysphoria.

Public expression is constrained by the propaganda statutes. The 2013 law targeted material concerning minors; it was expanded in December 2022 to cover all age groups and now reaches content that promotes "non-traditional" sexual relationships, makes minors interested in gender transition, or gives minors a "desire to change their sex". The provisions reach speech that justifies gender transition. More than 180 cases were brought under these provisions in 2023 alone, exceeding the total for 2013 to 2022 combined and producing roughly 26 million rubles in fines; fines brought over 60 million rubles (about $765,300) into the state budget in the two years to mid-2025.

Since the Supreme Court's November 2023 designation of a non-existent "international LGBT movement" as extremist, entered on the state's unified list of terrorist and extremist organisations on 22 March 2024, charges have been brought for displaying the rainbow flag or its colours. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in that movement or display of its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, with charges drawn from both the administrative and criminal codes. Between March and May 2026, nine LGBTQ organisations, among them the Russian LGBT Network, Coming Out and Centre T, were outlawed as extremist.

Moscow is where the designation has been applied most directly. Within 48 hours of the ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in the city; about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night. Kotov, the first person charged with creating an extremist organisation on LGBT grounds, was arrested in Moscow in late December 2024. In the same month, a man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel business was found dead in a pretrial detention facility. Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ life through 2025.

Proceedings have produced custodial terms. Russia's first prison sentence under the LGBT-extremism designation was reported in February 2025 and concerned organising, on the basis of a court ruling in Siberia reported in January 2025.

Russia provides no anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, does not designate hate crimes as such, does not treat gender-identity or sexual-orientation motivation as an aggravating factor in sentencing, and does not officially record hate crimes against the LGBTQ community. Moscow authorities have never approved a request to hold a gay pride rally.

Entry and onward-protection context carries an explicit warning for LGBT travellers. The US State Department advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and includes language relevant to LGBT travellers. The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (version 2.0, June 2025) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention.

28173009B76603557910928.name: Orenburg Oblast
28173009B76603557910928.summary:
Visitors in Orenburg Oblast stand under the national framework of the Russian Federation, which presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors and has deteriorated sharply since 2022. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded propaganda law criminalises any public expression, including anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention, and deportation, and official national government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers of this.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the designated "international LGBT movement" or for displaying its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, with charges brought under both the administrative and criminal codes, and called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

Enforcement is escalating in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding. Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025; The Moscow Times reported on 23 June 2025 a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation. In December 2024 a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian, on 27 July 2024, followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found. The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (v2.0, June 2025) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.

Orenburg Oblast is the jurisdiction in which that extremism designation first produced a criminal prosecution against a commercial leisure venue. The Central District Court of Orenburg registered materials in Russia's first criminal case under the "international LGBT movement" ban on 10 July 2025; the investigation into staff of the Pose club had been opened in March 2024 and the case was sent to court on 9 July 2025.

The proceedings concluded with Russia's first known "LGBT extremism" convictions. On 29 June 2026 Novaya Gazeta Europe reported that Pose club owner Vyacheslav Khasanov was sentenced to 7 years' imprisonment plus forfeiture of 1 million rubles, manager Diana Kamilyanova to 6 years and 3 months, and art director Alexander Klimov to 2 years and 3 months. A visitor present at a comparable venue in Orenburg Oblast therefore faces exposure to an extremism charge carrying a multi-year term, on top of the national propaganda, detention and deportation provisions.

36201628B69282955287113.name: NCR
36201628B69282955287113.summary:
National Capital Region stands under the national framework of the Philippines: same-sex relations and trans identity are not criminalised, and no national provision penalises a person for being transgender. A 2026 travel-risk assessment scores Manila at 69 of 100 for LGBTQ+ travellers overall, placing it in the 'Generally Safe' band, but 62 for trans travellers, which falls in 'Exercise Caution'; HIV-positive travellers score 81.

No administrative legal gender recognition process exists. The Clerical Error Law (RA 9048, 2001) bars an administrative birth-certificate sex change, leaving a court order as the only route, and the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery. Papers therefore carry the sex assigned at birth, and a mismatch between documents and presentation is settled by the birth-certificate entry.

No national SOGI anti-discrimination statute is in force. The SOGIE Equality Bill has been pending since 2000 without passage. Protections are instead a patchwork of local ordinances and sectoral statutes: the Magna Carta for Public Social Workers penalises SOGIE harassment with a fine of 20,000 to 40,000 pesos and/or up to one year's imprisonment, the Magna Carta of Women and the Safe Spaces Act punish transphobic and homophobic slurs with fines of 1,000 to 10,000 pesos, up to 30 days' penalty and a sensitivity seminar, and Republic Act 11166 prohibits discrimination tied to HIV status, sexual orientation, gender identity and expression.

Inside Metro Manila, Quezon City has enacted a gender-inclusive health ordinance introduced by Councilors Bernard Herrera and colleagues. All Quezon City public health facilities must offer gender-affirming consultations and counselling, mental health support, and medical guidance and referrals regardless of gender identity or expression; Mayor Joy Belmonte states the measure removes longstanding healthcare barriers for gender-diverse and transgender residents. This is a municipal-level guarantee, not a regional or national entitlement.

Violence is documented within the region. Shaina Bayabay, 29, was killed in Pasig City, Metro Manila, on 1 March 2024; the memorial record categorises the case as violence and the cause as strangulation, and the underlying report states she was killed during a drinking session. Nationally the pattern is recent: in June 2025 two trans women were killed within days, 18-year-old Kierra Apostol found dead in a Cagayan river on 23 June and a trans woman former journalist and activist shot inside a clinic in General Santos; the Commission on Human Rights has described that year's killings of trans people as a disturbing pattern of transfemicide.

Detention carries acute risk. Transgender women and gay men are held in ordinary male dormitories, including Manila City Jail, where head-shaving on arrival is mandatory for the male dorm and safety rests on inmate hierarchies rather than policy; there is no gender-matched placement. In Davao the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology instead transfers LGBT detainees in batches to the City Jail Annex alongside persons with disabilities, the sick and senior citizens.

Entry and documents at Manila's ports of entry follow the same framework: no legal gender recognition route means a trans visitor whose passport marker differs from presentation should expect screening questions tied to that mismatch, though nothing in the sources records a specific port-of-entry refusal.

Counterweights exist at the local and institutional level. Quezon City launched the country's first Right to Care Card in June 2023, letting registered LGBTQ couples make medical and health decisions for each other, initially in government-owned hospitals. Openly gay and bisexual people have served in the armed forces since 2009 and transgender people since 2017, with uniform policy following the birth-certificate gender; the lawyers' Code of Professional Responsibility was updated in 2023 to bar discrimination against clients on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity. Marriage equality does not exist.

36201628B47630810559445.name: Central Luzon
36201628B47630810559445.summary:
Central Luzon stands under the national framework of the Philippines, which does not criminalise same-sex relations or trans identity and contains no provision criminalising a person for being transgender. Same-sex relations have never been criminalised in the country. No administrative legal gender recognition process exists: the Clerical Error Law (RA 9048, 2001) bars an administrative birth-certificate sex change, and the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery, leaving a court order as the only route. No national SOGI anti-discrimination statute is in force, the SOGIE Equality Bill having been pending in Congress since 2000.

The clearest documented threat to a trans traveller in Central Luzon is trafficking and sexual exploitation in commercial sex venues, not any rule against being transgender. The United States government's Trafficking in Persons Report 2024 states that traffickers exploit victims in tourist destinations and urban areas across the Philippines. Within the region the operations on record cluster in one Pampanga city's bar district, where trans women are also concentrated in sex work.

On 17 June 2025 the National Bureau of Investigation announced that its Bataan District Office had arrested five people for human trafficking in Barangay Balibago, Angeles City: Alvin Baguio, registered owner of Field Sensation's Bar, together with Reden Roa, John Parro, Shirly Calilong and Marilyn Ferrer. The case began with a 19 May 2025 referral from Destiny Rescue Pilipinas Incorporated. Agents ran an entrapment and rescue operation on 1 June 2025 in which 'barfine' transactions ranged from P5,000 to P10,000, and 45 victims including 13 minors were rescued and turned over to the social welfare agency.

On 10 March 2025 the same NBI district office arrested foreign national Shin Ki Jung and accomplices in Angeles City for violations of R.A. No. 11862, the Expanded Anti-Trafficking in Persons Act of 2022, and R.A. No. 7610. A complaint from the husband of a trafficked victim alleged that women were recruited as Korea-bound performers as cover for work at a club in Angeles City; a subsequent rescue operation freed 12 victims including 5 minors. The arrested subjects were presented for inquest before the Office of the City Prosecutor of Angeles City.

Reporting by the Preda Foundation published on 21 November 2019, originally from The Fuller Project, found that hundreds of girls are supplied each year in Angeles City to meet demand from foreign men paying for sex, many of them American, in the city that hosted a former US military base. More than 150 women and girls interviewed by The Fuller Project said they wanted to leave prostitution but did not know how. City-regulated 'entertainers' must take weekly STD tests, a requirement activists criticised as marketing the sex industry as clean, and advocates warned that a new airport terminal on the city's outskirts could triple visitor numbers and expand sex trafficking.

36201628B13373758884154.name: Calabarzon
36201628B13373758884154.summary:
Calabarzon stands under the national framework of the Philippines. The Philippines does not criminalise same-sex relations or trans identity, and no provision of national law criminalises a person for being transgender. Same-sex relations have never been criminalised. A 2026 travel-risk assessment scores Manila at 69 of 100 for LGBTQ+ travellers overall, rated Generally Safe, and 62 for trans travellers, which falls in the Exercise Caution band; the same assessment scores HIV-positive travellers at 81. The scores are national and are not broken down by region, so nothing in them distinguishes Calabarzon from the capital.

No administrative legal gender recognition process exists anywhere in the country. The Clerical Error Law (RA 9048, 2001) bars an administrative birth-certificate sex change for trans people, leaving a court order as the only route, and the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery. A bill filed by trans Filipinos would permit applicants, including consenting minors, to choose markers other than male or female, such as X or non-binary; it had not been enacted as of the reports, and allies planned to endorse it to the 20th Congress on 28 July. The Commission on Human Rights has described that year's killings of trans people as a disturbing pattern of transfemicide.

No national SOGI anti-discrimination statute is in force. The SOGIE Equality Bill has been pending in Congress for roughly 25 years, since 2000, without passage, and in November 2022 the newly elected government rejected United Nations recommendations that included passage of the bill, describing them as unacceptable. The protections that exist form a patchwork: SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinances in eight provinces, including Albay, Agusan del Norte, Bataan, Batangas, Cavite, Dinagat Islands, Ilocos Sur and Iloilo, and in 32 cities and municipalities, alongside sectoral statutes. The Magna Carta for Public Social Workers penalises SOGIE harassment with a fine of 20,000 to 40,000 pesos and/or up to one year's imprisonment; the Magna Carta of Women and the Safe Spaces Act punish transphobic, homophobic and misogynistic slurs and ridicule with fines of 1,000 to 10,000 pesos, up to 30 days' penalty and a sensitivity seminar. Republic Act 11166 prohibits discrimination tied to HIV status, sexual orientation, gender identity and expression.

Two Calabarzon provinces sit among the eight with provincial ordinances. Cavite enacted its ordinance in 2014 and extended it in 2018 to cover gender identity; Batangas province followed in 2015. Two cities in the region have their own instruments, Batangas City in 2016 and Calamba in 2017. Within these areas a visitor can invoke an explicit local prohibition on discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity; in the rest of the region no such instrument is sourced.

Violence against trans people is documented and recent, and part of it occurred inside Calabarzon. In August 2025 an LGBTQ pageant winner was murdered in Lipa City, Batangas, sustaining 13 stab wounds days after her crowning, and the case is being worked as a homicide. In May 2025 a foreign national was arrested in Batangas for raping a trans woman. Nationally, two killings occurred within days in June 2025: 18-year-old trans woman Kierra Apostol was found dead in a Cagayan river on 23 June after being reported missing, and a trans woman former journalist and activist was shot by an unidentified gunman inside a clinic in General Santos the same day. In April 2024 the drag artist Taylor Sheesh was struck on stage by a man from the crowd at a concert in Bayambang, Pangasinan; she called the attack traumatic, and the town mayor publicly apologised to the LGBTQ+ community. Murders of transgender and gender-nonconforming persons have been reported in the Philippines since at least 2012. Bahaghari cited the June 2025 cases as an urgent reason to pass the SOGIE Equality Bill.

Detention carries acute risk. Transgender women and gay men are held in ordinary male dormitories in Philippine jails, including Manila City Jail, where head-shaving on arrival is mandatory for the male dorm and safety depends on inmate hierarchies rather than policy; informal same-sex pairings are used by gangs as a survival and protection strategy against abuse. There is no gender-matched placement. The Bureau of Jail Management and Penology in Davao instead transfers LGBT detainees in batches to the City Jail Annex, alongside persons with disabilities, the sick and senior citizens, to prevent abuse.

Local ordinances elsewhere in the country restrict presentation in public. Marawi City banned men from appearing in public in female attire, makeup or earrings in December 2004, and Kabacan in Cotabato prohibited cross-dressing and homosexual relations for Muslims in November 2019 under penalty of imprisonment. Gender-diverse people have been refused entry and service by establishments, and cross-dressers and transgender people may be excluded from private and public spaces with little or no legal consequence. After the 2017 Marawi siege, people perceived as LGBTQ were at times harassed in displacement camps. No comparable public-presentation ban is sourced for any part of Calabarzon.

Social visibility is high. Long-standing gender-diversity traditions with local names such as bakla and tomboy sit alongside prominent Pride events and nightlife and a substantial LGBTQ+ media presence. Openly gay and bisexual people have been permitted in the armed forces since 2009 and transgender people since 2017, with uniform policy following the legal gender recorded on the birth certificate. The lawyers' Code of Professional Responsibility was updated in 2023 to bar discrimination against clients on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity. Marriage equality does not exist; in June 2023 Quezon City, outside the region, launched the country's first Right to Care Card, letting registered LGBTQ couples make medical and health decisions for each other, initially in government-owned hospitals.

36201628B91065962446027.summary:
Western Visayas stands under the national framework of the Philippines, where same-sex relations and trans identity are not criminalised and no provision of national law punishes a person for being transgender. Same-sex relations have never been criminalised. There is no administrative legal gender recognition: the Clerical Error Law (RA 9048, 2001) forecloses an administrative birth-certificate sex change, a court order is the only route, and the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery.

No national SOGI anti-discrimination statute is in force. The SOGIE Equality Bill has been pending in Congress since 2000 without passage, and the protections available to a visitor rest on sub-national and sectoral law: SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinances in eight provinces and 32 cities and municipalities, the Magna Carta of Women, the Safe Spaces Act, and Republic Act 11166, which prohibits discrimination tied to HIV status, sexual orientation, gender identity and expression. Of the five provinces in this region, only Iloilo appears in the national inventory of provinces with a SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinance.

Institutional exclusion on gender-presentation grounds has occurred inside the region. In October 2022 Capiz State University issued a hair-and-uniform directive that excluded students perceived as trans women, and an advocacy campaign followed. A legal-NGO case study dated December 2025 examines that exclusion and its aftermath; the university's binary haircut rules shaped students' everyday conduct, and one graduate reported that cutting her hair in earlier years felt like a loss of self-confidence.

The exclusion did not end in institutional exclusion. At its 21st commencement exercises on 7 August 2025, Capiz State University produced its first openly trans woman to graduate summa cum laude, Khaz-JP Padilla, batch valedictorian of the social work class with the highest Latin honor; reporting attributes the outcome to the advocacy campaign that followed the October 2022 directive. Padilla has described carrying out her transition once pandemic-era online classes freed her from the haircut rule.

For a trans visitor the practical position is legality without a general remedy. Nothing in national law criminalises trans presence or presentation, and a 2026 travel-risk assessment scores Manila at 69 of 100, 'Generally Safe', for LGBTQ+ travellers overall and 62 for trans travellers, within the 'Exercise Caution' band, with 81 for HIV-positive travellers. Refusal of entry or service by establishments, and exclusion from private and public spaces, remains possible with little or no legal consequence where no local ordinance applies.

36201628B64564033926366.summary:
The Ilocos Region stands under the national framework of the Philippines, which does not criminalise same-sex relations or trans identity and contains no provision of national law criminalising a person for being transgender. It also has no national anti-discrimination statute covering sexual orientation and gender identity: the SOGIE Equality Bill has been filed and stalled in Congress for 25 years, a blockage campaigners cite as the direct reason two killings in June 2025 produced no legislative remedy. Protections are sub-national or sectoral, so what a visitor can invoke depends on the specific locality they are in.

Local instruments of that kind exist within the region. Ilocos Sur is one of eight provinces nationwide with a SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinance, and Bayambang in Pangasinan is among the 32 cities and municipalities carrying such an ordinance. Bayambang Municipal Ordinance No. 15, s-2023, dated 16 October 2023 and authored by Coun. Benjamin Francisco S. De Vera, protects lesbians, gays, bisexuals, transgenders, queers and intersex persons in the municipality against any and all forms of discrimination solely on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity, expression and sex characteristics, and provides penalties for violation.

The ordinance sets an escalating penalty ladder. A first offence carries a fine of at least PHP 1,000 or one month's imprisonment; a second, at least PHP 2,000 or one month and a day to six months; a third, at least PHP 2,500 or six months and a day to eight months; and later violations carry one year's imprisonment plus at least PHP 2,500. Violators must also complete mandatory human rights education. Complaints are filed through the barangay mechanism under the Katarungang Pambarangay provisions of R.A. 7160, the Local Government Code of 1991, giving a person discriminated against in the Pangasinan corridor a defined local complaint route.

The ordinance carries provincial endorsement. Pangasinan Sangguniang Panlalawigan Resolution No. 799-2024, adopted at the session of 19 August 2024 in Lingayen, declared Municipal Ordinance No. 15, s-2023 to conform with the Bill of Rights and with Section 16 of R.A. No. 7160, affirming the municipal instrument at provincial level.

Recourse is not uniform across the region. In the rural parts of two of its provinces, a customary-justice system maintained by Itneg elders, adopted and modified as the Bodong Indigenous Allied Group, operates as an alternative dispute-resolution body alongside Philippine courts and police, so the institution handling a dispute may not be a national court.

Trans-specific exposure remains national in character. There is no administrative legal gender recognition: the Clerical Error Law (R.A. 9048, 2001) forecloses an administrative birth-certificate sex change, a court order is the only route, and the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery. A pending bill would open recognition to applicants including consenting minors and allow markers beyond male and female. Transgender women are detained according to birth sex, and violence is documented and recent: in April 2024 the drag artist Taylor Sheesh was struck on stage by a man from the crowd during a concert in Bayambang, Pangasinan, and the town mayor publicly apologised to the LGBTQ+ community.

36201628B64564033926366.tangentialFactors:
A 2026 travel-risk assessment rates Manila 'Generally Safe' for LGBTQ+ travellers overall at 69 of 100 but scores trans travellers lower, at 62, in the 'Exercise Caution' band. That assessment covers the capital, not the Ilocos Region, and no equivalent regional score is sourced here.

Social visibility in the Philippines is high: gender-diversity traditions with local names such as bakla and tomboy are long-standing, Pride events and nightlife are prominent in the capital, and LGBTQ+ themes carry substantial media presence. High visibility coexists with the absence of a national SOGIE statute and with documented killings; the Commission on Human Rights has described the trans killings recorded in a single year as a disturbing pattern of transfemicide.

Other sectoral protections operate independently of local ordinances. The Magna Carta for Public Social Workers punishes SOGIE harassment with a fine of PHP 20,000 to 40,000 and up to one year's penalty, while the Magna Carta of Women and the Safe Spaces Act reach slurs and ridicule with fines of PHP 1,000 to 10,000, up to 30 days' penalty and a sensitivity seminar. The armed forces have permitted openly gay and bisexual personnel since 2009 and transgender personnel since 2017, with the uniform policy following the legal gender shown on the birth certificate, and the Code of Professional Responsibility was updated in 2023 to bar discrimination against clients on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity.

The Bayambang ordinance is narrower than a provincial statute: it binds one municipality, and its provincial endorsement is a conformity declaration rather than a region-wide rule. Elsewhere in the country, recourse has been absent after violence; campaigners cite the stalled SOGIE Equality Bill as the reason two killings in June 2025 produced no legislative remedy.

36201628B64564033926366.localsOnly:
Residents of Bayambang may file a SOGIESC discrimination complaint through the barangay under the Katarungang Pambarangay mechanism of R.A. 7160, with the penalty ladder running from a fine of at least PHP 1,000 or one month's imprisonment on a first offence to one year's imprisonment plus at least PHP 2,500 for later violations, and mandatory human rights education attached to violations.

Residents of Ilocos Sur are covered by one of the eight provincial SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinances in the country, while residents of the rural parts of two provinces in the region may have disputes handled by the bodong customary-justice body maintained by Itneg elders, operating alongside the courts and police.

For trans residents, birth-certificate sex governs detention placement and, in the armed forces, uniform policy. Transgender women are held with male inmates according to birth sex; at Manila City Jail arrivals to the male dormitory have their heads shaved, and survival against abuse is organised through inmate hierarchies and informal same-sex 'weddings' with male inmates rather than through policy. The Bureau of Jail Management and Penology's documented response at Davao City Jail is administrative segregation, transferring LGBT detainees in batches to the City Jail Annex 'to prevent abuse' alongside persons with disabilities, the sick and senior citizens, with three LGBT groupings housed there since the annex was established.

Legal gender recognition requires a court order, and Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) holds that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery. A pending bill would open recognition to applicants including consenting minors and allow markers such as X or nonbinary; its drafter links the absence of recognition to social exclusion, forced disclosure of trans status and violence, and allies have signalled endorsement of the bill to the 20th Congress.

Schools are a documented site of harm for gender-diverse young people: a 2017 Human Rights Watch investigation recorded bullying and discrimination against gender-diverse students across Philippine schools while noting that law offered few remedies at the time.

36201628B49646111072560.name: ARMM
36201628B49646111072560.summary:
The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao stands under the national framework of the Philippines, which does not criminalise same-sex relations or trans identity and contains no provision criminalising a person for being transgender; same-sex relations have never been criminalised there. No instrument reviewed for this record creates such an offence at regional level either. The visitor-facing risk in the region is structural rather than statutory: it arises from which forum hears a dispute and which body of personal law applies, not from any provision aimed at gender non-conformity.

Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 13, the Bangsamoro Administrative Code, whose drafting began on 29 March 2019, prescribes the structures and rules of governance of the autonomous region and guarantees religious freedom. Its justice-dispensation clause commits the region to adjudication "in consonance with the Constitution, Shari'ah, traditional or tribal laws", placing constitutional, religious and customary law side by side in the same adjudicative mandate.

On 14 July 2026 the Bangsamoro Parliament proposed a Shari'ah Justice System Code of 10 books that would extend Shari'ah jurisdiction beyond the personal-status field confined to it since Presidential Decree 1083 of 1977, into civil actions, Islamic commercial transactions, ta'tir offences and alternative dispute resolution. The proposal rests on the authority of the Bangsamoro Organic Law and on the 1977 Code of Personal and Family Relations. Whether it has been enacted is unresolved in the sources reviewed.

Marriage, divorce, succession and family relations for Muslim residents remain governed by Shari'ah forums, with written-opt-in clauses available to civil entities. This legal-pluralist marriage regime is the layer a visitor married to a Muslim spouse would encounter: the forum and the applicable personal law follow the religious status of the parties, not the visitor's own nationality.

In August 2024 President Marcos Jr. signed a law creating three new Shari'ah judicial districts and 12 circuit courts, expanding the Shari'ah court system beyond the Bangsamoro into majority-Christian northern Mindanao, provinces of the Davao region, parts of the Visayas, Luzon and Metro Manila; the Bangsamoro Parliament passed it unanimously. The measure carries the region's Shari'ah personal-law regime onto a national footing, so the forum questions above are no longer confined to Mindanao's autonomous area.

That contest concerns institutional jurisdiction rather than any provision addressing gender identity.

36201628B92932511992503.summary:
The Philippines does not criminalise same-sex relations or trans identity, and no provision of national law criminalises a person for being transgender. Same-sex relations have never been criminalised. A 2026 travel-risk assessment scores Manila at 69 of 100, 'Generally Safe', for LGBTQ+ travellers overall, but 62 for trans travellers, which falls in the 'Exercise Caution' band; the same assessment scores HIV-positive travellers at 81.

No administrative legal gender recognition process exists. The Clerical Error Law (RA 9048, 2001) bars an administrative birth-certificate sex change for trans people, leaving a court order as the only route, and the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery. A bill filed by trans Filipinos would permit applicants, including consenting minors, to choose markers other than male or female, such as X or non-binary; it had not been enacted as of the reports, which allies planned to endorse to the 20th Congress on 28 July. The Commission on Human Rights has described that year's killings of trans people as a disturbing pattern of transfemicide.

No national SOGI anti-discrimination statute is in force. The SOGIE Equality Bill has been pending in Congress for roughly 25 years, since 2000, without passage. The protections that do exist form a patchwork: SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinances in eight provinces, including Albay, Agusan del Norte, Bataan, Batangas, Cavite, Dinagat Islands, Ilocos Sur and Iloilo, and in 32 cities and municipalities, alongside sectoral statutes. The Magna Carta for Public Social Workers penalises SOGIE harassment with a fine of 20,000 to 40,000 pesos and/or up to one year's imprisonment; the Magna Carta of Women and the Safe Spaces Act punish transphobic, homophobic and misogynistic slurs and ridicule with fines of 1,000 to 10,000 pesos, up to 30 days' penalty and a sensitivity seminar. Republic Act 11166 prohibits discrimination tied to HIV status, sexual orientation, gender identity and expression.

Violence against trans people is documented and recent. In June 2025 two killings occurred within days: 18-year-old trans woman Kierra Apostol was found dead in a Cagayan river on 23 June after being reported missing, and a trans woman former journalist and activist was shot by an unidentified gunman inside a clinic in General Santos the same day. In May 2025 a foreign national was arrested for raping a trans woman in Batangas. In April 2024 the drag artist Taylor Sheesh was struck on stage by a man from the crowd at a concert in Bayambang, Pangasinan; she called the attack traumatic, and the town mayor publicly apologised to the LGBTQ+ community. Bahaghari cited the June 2025 cases as an urgent reason to pass the SOGIE Equality Bill.

Detention carries acute risk. Transgender women and gay men are held in ordinary male dormitories in Philippine jails, including Manila City Jail, where head-shaving on arrival is mandatory for the male dorm and safety depends on inmate hierarchies rather than policy; informal same-sex pairings are used by gangs as a survival and protection strategy against abuse. There is no gender-matched placement. Official practice instead takes the form of administrative segregation: the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology in Davao transfers LGBT detainees in batches to the City Jail Annex, alongside persons with disabilities, the sick and senior citizens, to prevent abuse.

Local ordinances restrict presentation in public. Marawi City banned men from appearing in public in female attire, makeup or earrings in December 2004, and Kabacan in Cotabato prohibited cross-dressing and homosexual relations for Muslims in November 2019 under penalty of imprisonment. Gender-diverse people have been refused entry and service by establishments, and cross-dressers and transgender people may be excluded from private and public spaces with little or no legal consequence. After the 2017 Marawi siege, people perceived as LGBTQ were at times harassed in displacement camps.

Social visibility is high. Long-standing gender-diversity traditions with local names such as bakla and tomboy sit alongside prominent Pride events and nightlife and substantial LGBTQ+ media presence. Openly gay and bisexual people have been permitted in the armed forces since 2009 and transgender people since 2017, with uniform policy following the legal gender recorded on the birth certificate. The lawyers' Code of Professional Responsibility was updated in 2023 to bar discrimination against clients on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity. Marriage equality does not exist; in June 2023 Quezon City launched the country's first Right to Care Card, letting registered LGBTQ couples make medical and health decisions for each other, initially in government-owned hospitals.

The Cordillera Administrative Region, created on 15 July 1987 and comprising Abra, Apayao, Benguet, Ifugao, Kalinga and Mountain Province centred on Baguio, is the country's only landlocked region and its least populated according to the 2020 Census of Population and Housing, with fewer residents than the national capital. It is home to numerous ethnic groups, including a majority-Igorot province, and a continuing Cordillera autonomy movement; the Cordillera People's Liberation Army ceasefire was secured by the Aquino government. Within this region, Kalinga province was formed out of Kalinga-Apayao on 8 May 1995 by Republic Act No. 7878 with Tabuk as capital.

In Kalinga, the inter-tribal customary justice system runs alongside the formal court system. Bodong and pagta holders resolve criminal and tribal offences, with Philippine National Police personnel, prosecutors and barangay officials participating in customary-law conflict resolution. This indigenous governance context developed against a history of resistance: Kalinga was a flashpoint between the Marcos martial-law government (declared September 1972) and its indigenous peoples over the Chico River Dam Project, which would have displaced about 100,000 indigenous people; the 24 April 1980 murder of tribal leader Macli-ing Dulag turned public opinion and made the dam dispute a landmark ancestral-domain case, and the September 1986 Mount Data Peace Accord created the Cordillera Autonomous Region, with later plebiscites failing to ratify autonomy.

68945753B94077674833362.name: Daegu
68945753B94077674833362.summary:
Daegu stands under the national framework of South Korea, where gender identity and gender expression are not criminalised in civilian life and consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal. The armed forces are the exception: Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, and the Constitutional Court upheld the provision in 2023. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether. Legal gender recognition is available, and on 8 May 2024 a court ruled that requiring sex-reassignment surgery as a condition of changing legal sex status violates physical integrity.

Daegu hosts the country's second-largest LGBT event, a pride parade and film programme running a week or two, usually in late June. The Daegu Queer Culture Festival has been held every year since June 2009 without interruption, most recently on central Daegu's Dongseong-ro.

Organised opposition is annual and recurrent, and it is contained by the courts rather than by the state declining to act. The Daegu Queer Opposition Countermeasure Committee sought injunctions against the festival in 2022, 2023, 2024 and again in 2025; the Daegu District Court dismissed each bid. An estimated 28 religious and right-wing groups form a standing countermeasure committee in Daegu to block LGBT events, and that opposition has kept the festival off an outdoor stage on a popular central street.

Police practice constrains the march itself. Officers again restricted the 2025 route to a single bus-only lane, and the Daegu District Court has found the police notice restricting the event legitimate on the ground that Jungang-ro is a key urban traffic artery and one lane must be secured for public welfare. In 2023, under then-Mayor Hong Joon-pyo, municipal officials physically blocked the road. Organisers framed the 2025 event as resistance to hate and discriminatory politics.

Mobilisation against the festival is large and well organised. A Daegu-Gyeongbuk conservative Protestant umbrella body convened its 17th annual 'National Assembly Against Queer' response in September 2025, gathering roughly 3,500 believers from about 1,600 churches at Banwoldang station and along a 450-metre stretch toward the Gyesan intersection under anti-homosexuality slogans.

Venue restriction remained live into the 2026 edition. The Daegu Queer Opposition Countermeasures Headquarters, comprising the Daegu-Gyeongbuk Parents' Alliance for Protecting the Next Generation, the Daegu Christian Council and the Dongseong-ro Merchants' Association, filed a collective petition with the National Human Rights Commission of Korea demanding a change of festival venue on public-welfare grounds, claiming about 34,000 signatures and describing that as unusually large for a single Commission petition. The petition answers a January filing by the festival committee against the National Police Agency Commissioner General and the National Assembly Speaker over Article 12(1) of the Assembly and Demonstration Act.

68945753B85435209225479.name: Daejeon
68945753B85435209225479.summary:
Daejeon stands under South Korea's national legal framework, in which gender identity and gender expression are not criminalised in civilian life and consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is lawful. The exception is the armed forces: Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, and the Constitutional Court upheld the provision in 2023. Enforcement has been punitive and targeted, most visibly in the 2017 military operation that Amnesty International described as a gay witch hunt, under which 32 personnel were criminally charged and one gay soldier received a six-month prison sentence for consensual sex. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

Daejeon is where the sharpest documented harm to a trans person in South Korean military service was litigated. Staff Sergeant Byun Hee-soo was compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after a military panel treated the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a physical or mental handicap. She died by suicide in March 2021. On 7 October 2021 the Daejeon District Court ordered cancellation of the Army's discharge in what is recorded as the first known legal case involving a transgender soldier, holding that the military should have recognised her as female following her legal sex change, that loss of genitalia was not valid grounds for dismissal, and that fitness review should weigh basic rights. The decision vindicated her posthumous appeal. In March 2024 the Defence Ministry recognised her death as in the line of duty.

Byun Hee-soo was buried at the National Cemetery in Daejeon on 24 June 2024, an official honour that did not settle the institutional question. About 60 activists attended and protested, arguing that the burial was marred by discriminatory treatment, and her case continues to be recorded against gender dysphoria classified as a mental disorder and a post-surgery physical-disability finding. Her state burial in Daejeon therefore coexists with an institutional stance that remains conservative.

Legal gender recognition is available in South Korean courts and the surgical condition is falling away. On 8 May 2024 a court ruled that mandating sex-reassignment surgery as a condition of changing legal sex status violates physical integrity, holding for five plaintiffs assigned male at birth who had been on hormone therapy for years, and finding that outdated judicial guidelines cannot ground dismissals. On 24 November 2022 the Supreme Court ruled en banc that transgender individuals with minor children can have their gender legally recognised provided they are not married, overturning an 11-year-old precedent that had uniformly denied recognition to trans parents of minors; a 2011 Supreme Court ruling had required persons seeking gender-affirming care to be over 20, single and without children.

South Korean national law does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, and same-sex couples cannot jointly adopt children. A 2024 Constitutional Court ruling on same-sex partners' healthcare rights is the main advance in that area. There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, though LGBTI organisations can register; an NGO won registration litigation at the Seoul Metropolitan Court in March 2017 and the government appealed onward, which Human Rights Watch described as years of bureaucratic obstruction.

Restroom access is a live problem in both judicial and school settings. On 2 July 2024 the Seoul Central District Court ruled final, with no appeal available, that police advice telling a trans plaintiff undergoing gender correction to avoid public restrooms for a period infringed personal rights, and ordered symbolic compensation of 300,000 won against the state. Research from the youth LGBTQ+ centre DDing Dong, presented on 20 March 2024, shows trans teenagers avoid school restrooms for fear of being outed; a 16-year-old trans girl at a boys' school reported holding it in and leaving school early, and researchers urged legal and institutional reform for safer school environments.

Healthcare carries an official blind spot identified from within the state machinery. In November 2023 the National Human Rights Commission of Korea flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation after the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, reasoning that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

Documented violence and hostility concentrate at public events and in everyday life. In Incheon a Pride event ended in violence when about 1,000 Christian protestors attacked participants, after which organisers filed charges against pastors and accused police of inaction; at Busan's 2018 Pride some 2,000 police were deployed to protect 15,000 attendees from violent anti-gay protesters. A 2014 finding recorded that 54% of LGBTQ Korean youths were harassed by classmates, 16.1% of outed LGBTQ people were recommended conversion therapy with 65.4% reporting harm and 94% psychological trauma, and a 2018 study found 51.5% of transgender adults faced harsh discrimination in the past year. During the May 2020 Itaewon COVID-19 cluster, contact tracing outed LGBTQ people, doxing and online harassment rose, and a trans-male bartender told NBC News he felt threatened walking on the street absent a nondiscrimination bill.

A peer-reviewed nationwide survey published on 27 June 2025 in Epidemiology and Health, covering 585 transgender and non-binary young adults, mapped milestones and stigmatisation across life stages and documented a pervasive discrimination burden at school, work and in transition-related care. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 describes an overall relatively positive record on free media and civil society alongside persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people.

68945753B85435209225479.tangentialFactors:
Daejeon's role in this record runs against the national grain in one respect and with it in another. The Daejeon District Court delivered the pro-recognition ruling that reversed a trans soldier's discharge, while the same city hosts the state cemetery where the military's treatment of her was formally contested by protesters at the burial. A visitor should not read the court ruling as evidence that the armed forces themselves have softened: article 92-6 stands, the Constitutional Court affirmed it in 2023, and transgender people remain outside military service by exclusion rather than by choice.

The trajectory of the Byun Hee-soo case is a reasonable proxy for how recognition advances in South Korea. It moved through discharge, death, posthumous judicial reversal, line-of-duty recognition by the Defence Ministry in March 2024, and burial with state honours in June 2024, with each step contested by activists who judged the treatment discriminatory. Recognition arrives case by case rather than through a general statute, which is also how gender recognition itself has moved: two Supreme Court and high-court rulings in 2022 and 2024 removed, respectively, the bar on trans parents and the surgical precondition.

Comparatively, the pattern in South Korea is protective machinery without a protective statute. There is a functioning National Human Rights Commission, active LGBTI organisations, a registry route for NGOs, and a Constitutional Court willing to grant partner healthcare rights, yet no comprehensive anti-discrimination law and repeated bureaucratic obstruction of registration litigation. Violence risk is concentrated and episodic: Pride events draw large counter-protests requiring thousands of police, and public-health contact tracing has previously produced outing on a mass scale.

68945753B59172752195743.name: North Chungcheong

North Chungcheong Province stands under the national framework of South Korea, where gender identity and gender expression are not criminalised in civilian life and consensual same-sex conduct between adults is legal. Enforcement has been punitive and targeted. In 2017 the military ran what Amnesty International described as a gay witch hunt, criminally charging 32 personnel, and a gay soldier received a six-month prison sentence for consensual sex. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

This province is the location of the gravest documented harm to a transgender service member in South Korea. Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su, the country's first openly transgender soldier, was found dead at her home in Cheongju on 3 March 2021, aged 23. She had been compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after a military panel classified the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a physical or mental handicap, and her challenge to that discharge was rejected in July 2020. Her death triggered national debate on the treatment of transgender troops. The Daejeon District Court later ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021, and in March 2024 the Ministry of National Defence recognised her death as in the line of duty.

Legal gender recognition is available in South Korea and the surgical precondition is falling away. National law does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, and same-sex couples cannot adopt children jointly. The 2024 Constitutional Court ruling on same-sex partners' healthcare rights is the main advance in that area. No comprehensive anti-discrimination law covers sexual orientation or gender identity: an anti-discrimination bill has been introduced eight times since 2007, the June 2020 draft included gender-identity provisions, and prosecutors and activists called for its passage after Byun Hee-soo's death. LGBTI organisations can register, though an NGO won registration litigation at the Seoul Metropolitan Court in March 2017 and the government appealed onward, part of what Human Rights Watch described as years of bureaucratic obstruction.

Restroom access is a documented problem in both judicial and school settings. On 2 July 2024 the Seoul Central District Court ruled final, with no appeal available, that police advice telling a transgender plaintiff undergoing gender correction to avoid public restrooms infringed personal rights, ordering symbolic compensation of 300,000 won against the state. Research from the youth LGBTQ+ centre DDing Dong, presented on 20 March 2024, shows transgender teenagers avoid school restrooms for fear of being outed; a 16-year-old trans girl at a boys' school reported holding it in and leaving school early, and researchers called for legal and institutional reform of school environments.

Healthcare carries an official blind spot identified from within the state itself. In November 2023 the National Human Rights Commission of Korea identified a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation after the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, reasoning that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

Documented violence concentrates at public events. In Incheon a Pride event ended in violence when roughly 1,000 Christian protestors attacked participants, after which organisers filed charges against pastors and accused police of inaction; at Busan's 2018 Pride some 2,000 police were deployed to protect 15,000 attendees from violent anti-gay protesters. During the May 2020 Itaewon COVID-19 cluster, contact tracing outed LGBTQ people, doxing and online harassment rose, and a trans-male bartender told NBC News he felt threatened walking on the street in the absence of a nondiscrimination bill.

Following Byun Hee-soo's death, the National Human Rights Commission honoured her and national pressure for protection grew, but no new law at provincial level followed; the protection gap is national, not local.

68945753B70752081047384.name: South Chungcheong
68945753B70752081047384.summary:
South Chungcheong Province stands under South Korea's national framework. South Korean law does not criminalise gender identity or gender expression in civilian life, and consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal. The criminalising instrument is the Military Criminal Act, article 92-6, which penalises consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment; the Constitutional Court upheld it in 2023, and enforcement has been punitive and targeted, with a 2017 military operation that Amnesty International called a gay witch hunt resulting in criminal charges against 32 personnel and a six-month prison sentence for a gay soldier over consensual sex. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

The sharpest documented harm concerns Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su, compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after a military panel treated the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a physical or mental handicap. She died by suicide in March 2021. The Daejeon District Court ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021, and in March 2024 the Defence Ministry recognised her death as in the line of duty.

Legal gender recognition exists and the surgical precondition is falling away. On 8 May 2024 a court refused to mandate sex-reassignment surgery as a condition of changing legal sex status, holding for five plaintiffs assigned male at birth who had undergone years of hormone therapy that demanding surgery violates physical integrity and that outdated judicial guidelines cannot ground dismissals. On 24 November 2022 the Supreme Court ruled en banc that transgender people with minor children may have their gender legally recognised provided they are not married, overturning an 11-year-old precedent that uniformly denied recognition to trans parents of minors; a 2011 Supreme Court ruling had required persons seeking gender-affirming care to be over 20, single and without children.

South Korean national law does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, and same-sex couples cannot jointly adopt children. A 2024 Constitutional Court ruling on same-sex partners' healthcare rights is the main advance in that area. There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, though LGBTI organisations can register: an NGO won registration litigation at the Seoul Metropolitan Court in March 2017 and the government appealed onward, part of what Human Rights Watch described as years of bureaucratic obstruction.

Restroom access is a documented problem in judicial and school settings. On 2 July 2024 the Seoul Central District Court ruled final, with no appeal, that police advice telling a trans plaintiff undergoing gender correction to avoid public restrooms for a period infringed personal rights, ordering symbolic compensation of 300,000 won against the state. Research from the youth LGBTQ+ centre DDing Dong, presented on 20 March 2024, shows trans teenagers avoid school restrooms for fear of being outed; a 16-year-old trans girl at a boys' school reported holding it in and leaving school early, and researchers urged legal and institutional reform for safer school environments.

Healthcare carries an official blind spot identified from within the state: in November 2023 the National Human Rights Commission of Korea flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation after the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, reasoning that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

Documented violence and hostility concentrate at public events and in everyday life. In Incheon a Pride event ended in violence when about 1,000 Christian protestors attacked participants, after which organisers filed charges against pastors and accused police of inaction; at Busan's 2018 Pride some 2,000 police protected 15,000 attendees from violent anti-gay protesters. A 2014 finding recorded that 54% of LGBTQ Korean youths were harassed by classmates and that 16.1% of outed LGBTQ people were recommended conversion therapy, with 65.4% reporting harm and 94% psychological trauma; a 2018 study found 51.5% of transgender adults faced harsh discrimination in the past year. During the May 2020 Itaewon COVID-19 cluster, contact tracing outed LGBTQ people, doxing and online harassment rose, and a trans-male bartender told NBC News he felt threatened walking on the street in the absence of a nondiscrimination bill.

A peer-reviewed nationwide survey published on 27 June 2025 in Epidemiology and Health, covering 585 transgender and non-binary young adults, mapped milestones and stigmatisation across life stages and documented a pervasive discrimination burden at school, work and in transition-related care. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 describes an overall relatively positive record on free media and civil society alongside persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people.

South Chungcheong Province has its own student human-rights ordinance, enacted on 10 July 2020, whose Article 15 covers gender identity and sexual orientation. The provincial council passed a repeal bill on 24 April 2024; the Chungcheongnam-do Office of Education challenged it before the Supreme Court on 13 May 2024 and obtained suspension of execution on 30 May 2024, so the ordinance remains in effect, and the Office of Education argues that repeal violates the Constitution and international human-rights treaties. The Republic of Korea's response of 21 February 2025 to the Joint Communication from UN Special Procedures (ref. OL KOR 3/2024) filed the Seoul Metropolitan Office of Education and the Chungcheongnam-do Office of Education as stakeholders enforcing authorities in the repeal dispute, recording the Seoul office's parallel 11 July 2024 petition and the Supreme Court's 23 July 2024 suspension.

The Chungnam section records: the provincial council passed a repeal bill on 24 April 2024 against the ordinance enacted 10 July 2020 (Article 15 covers gender identity and sexual orientation); the Office of Education challenged it before the Supreme Court on 13 May 2024 and obtained suspension of execution on 30 May 2024, so the ordinance remains in effect; it argues the repeal violates the Constitution and international human-rights treaties. The province stands under the national framework of the country. Gender identity and gender expression are not criminalised in civilian life, and consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal. The exception is the armed forces: the military criminal code criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, the constitutional court upheld the provision in 2023, and enforcement has been punitive and targeted. In 2017 the military ran what an international rights organisation described as a gay witch hunt, criminally charging 32 personnel, and a gay soldier received a six-month prison sentence for consensual sex. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

The sharpest documented harm to a transgender person concerns a staff sergeant compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after a military panel classified the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a physical or mental handicap. She died by suicide in March 2021. A district court ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021, and in March 2024 the defence ministry recognised her death as in the line of duty.

Legal gender recognition is available and the surgical condition is falling away. On 8 May 2024 a court ruled against mandating sex-reassignment surgery as a condition of changing legal sex status, holding for five plaintiffs assigned male at birth who had been on hormone therapy for years that demanding surgery violates physical integrity and that outdated judicial guidelines cannot ground dismissals. On 24 November 2022 the supreme court ruled en banc that transgender individuals with minor children can have their gender legally recognised provided they are not married, overturning an 11-year-old precedent that uniformly denied recognition to trans parents of minors; a 2011 supreme court ruling had required persons seeking gender-affirming care to be over 20, single and without children.

National law does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, and same-sex couples cannot jointly adopt children. A landmark 2024 constitutional court ruling on same-sex partners' healthcare rights is the main advance in that area. There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, though LGBTI organisations can register; an NGO won registration litigation at a metropolitan court in March 2017 and the government appealed onward, part of what an international rights organisation described as years of bureaucratic obstruction.

On 2 July 2024 a district court ruled final, with no appeal, that police advice telling a trans plaintiff undergoing gender correction to avoid public restrooms for a period infringed personal rights, ordering symbolic compensation of 300,000 won against the state. Healthcare carries an official blind spot flagged from within the state. 47653553B66835736668351.summary:
Región del Bío-Bío stands under Chile's national framework for trans people. Legal gender recognition has operated under Gender Identity Law 21,120 since 27 December 2019: adults change their registered name and sex on request to the Civil Registry with no therapy or surgery required, applicants aged 14 to 18 must apply to family courts with psychosocial and family-context antecedents, and people under 14 cannot use the law although the statute recognises them as transgender. On 9 April 2025 the Constitutional Court declared the 'over 14 years old' wording inapplicable as unconstitutional in a case brought by the mother of a 10-year-old trans girl, and that ruling applies only to that case.

The 2012 Zamudio Law prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, was extended to gender expression in 2018, and treats hate-crime motivation as an aggravating criminal circumstance. Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022, civil unions since 2015, and birth certificates offer a third sex option for intersex children.

Transphobic violence remains documented. A young trans man was murdered in 2023 in a killing covered up for 24 hours and described in national reporting as Chile's largest hate crime; the perpetrator, an acquaintance, confessed. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for close to an hour at a Santiago hotel, where the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim.

Detention carries specific rules. Gendarmería de Chile's national director signed a protocol guaranteeing the gender identity of trans detainees, providing placement by assumed gender, segmented housing and entry examinations, with a standing committee of Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives overseeing implementation, including access rules for trans visitors.

The public health system has funded sex reassignment surgery and hormone therapy since 2013, and a 2011 Ministry of Health circular obliges all care centres to register transgender patients by their social name. Circular 7 of June 2024 suggested deferring the initiation of new gonadotropin-releasing hormone blockers and cross-sex hormone therapy in adolescents until national guidelines are published; the Medical College noted that physicians may still prescribe. On 9 January 2025 the Constitutional Court, by seven votes to three, annulled section 46 of the 2025 Budget Law, which had barred the Ministry of Health from financing hormone therapies for trans children and adolescents. In November 2025 Congress defunded the Ministry of Social Development's Gender Identity Support Program through the 2026 Budget Law, but the Ministry of Health-run programme continues to provide support in medical centres; the Crece con Orgullo programme has operated since 2023 for children and adolescents aged 3 to 17.

Entry and removal rules reference gender identity. The Migration and Immigration Law of 11 April 2021 bans arbitrary discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity and offers protection to LGBT immigrants seeking asylum. Article 10 provides that recognised asylum seekers may be granted complementary protection, and no foreigner holding complementary protection may be expelled or returned to a country where their right to life, physical integrity or personal freedom is at risk on grounds including sexual orientation or gender identity.

Restrictive proposals are active but non-binding. On 15 May 2025 the Chamber of Deputies approved the CEI 57 commission report, 56 votes to 30 with 6 abstentions, a non-binding recommendation to eliminate the Gender Identity Support Program, restrict minors' progressive autonomy, ban hormonal treatment for minors and repeal the circular protecting gender identity in schools.

Within Chile, Región del Bío-Bío accounted for 5.89% of the national case total in 2024, the third-highest share of any region, and Concepción was among the cities recording the most documented incidents, with five. Care facilities in the region have been the subject of a formal discrimination complaint: on 14 October 2016 Movilh Chile reported that Movilh-Biobío had filed a complaint with the Seremi de Salud, Mauricio Careaga Lemus, concerning the Hospital Traumatológico de Concepción, where patient Hanna Jiménez Carrasco, interned from 28 September to 3 October 2016, was placed and treated as male despite public policy and the legal duty to use her chosen name and social sex. The complaint alleged brutal and illegal discriminatory acts by hospital staff.

47653553B84299910343297.summary:
La Araucanía is a region of Chile with no regional variant of the national rules, so a trans visitor's legal position there is set by Chilean statute, courts and administrative practice.

Legal gender recognition rests on Gender Identity Law 21,120, in force since 27 December 2019. Adults may change their registered name and sex on request to the Civil Registry without therapy or surgery. Applicants aged 14 to 18 must go to the family courts with psychosocial and family-context antecedents, and the statute does not provide for those under 14, although it recognises them as transgender. On 9 April 2025 the Constitutional Court declared the 'over 14 years old' wording inapplicable as unconstitutional in a case brought by the mother of a 10-year-old trans girl, and that ruling applies only to that case.

The 2012 Zamudio Law prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, was extended to gender expression in 2018, and treats hate-crime motivation as an aggravating criminal circumstance. Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022, civil unions since 2015, and birth certificates offer a third sex option for intersex children.

Recorded anti-trans and homophobic violence in La Araucanía is rising faster than anywhere else in Chile. Movilh's XXIV annual human-rights report, published in March 2026 on 2025 data, ranked the region first in year-on-year growth in recorded cases, up 150%, and put La Araucanía at 1.96% of the national case total. The same report recorded a national figure of 3,620 documented cases for 2025, 27.1% above 2024, with that single year accounting for 23% of all cases across the 24-year series.

Lethal and near-lethal transphobic violence is documented nationally. A young trans man was murdered in 2023 in a killing covered up for 24 hours and described in national reporting as Chile's largest hate crime; the perpetrator, an acquaintance, confessed. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for close to an hour at a hotel in Santiago, where the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim.

Detention carries specific rules. Gendarmería de Chile's national director signed a protocol guaranteeing the gender identity of trans detainees, providing placement by assumed gender, segmented housing and entry examinations, with a standing committee of Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives overseeing implementation, including access rules for trans visitors.

Care access has both protection and pressure on it. The public health system has funded sex reassignment surgery and hormone therapy since 2013, and a 2011 Ministry of Health circular obliges all care centres to register transgender patients by their social name. Circular 7 of June 2024 suggested deferring the initiation of new gonadotropin-releasing hormone blockers and cross-sex hormone therapy in adolescents until national guidelines are published, though the Medical College noted that physicians may still prescribe. On 9 January 2025 the Constitutional Court, by seven votes to three, annulled section 46 of the 2025 Budget Law, which had barred the Ministry of Health from financing hormone therapies for trans children and adolescents. In November 2025 Congress defunded the Ministry of Social Development's Gender Identity Support Program through the 2026 Budget Law, but the Ministry of Health-run programme continues to provide support in medical centres; the Crece con Orgullo programme has operated since 2023 for children and adolescents aged 3 to 17.

Entry and removal rules reference gender identity. The Migration and Immigration Law of 11 April 2021 bans arbitrary discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity and offers protection to LGBT immigrants seeking asylum. Article 10 provides that recognised asylum seekers may be granted complementary protection, and no foreigner holding complementary protection may be expelled or returned to a country where their right to life, physical integrity or personal freedom is at risk on grounds including sexual orientation or gender identity.

Restrictive proposals are active but non-binding. On 15 May 2025 the Chamber of Deputies approved the CEI 57 commission report, 56 votes to 30 with 6 abstentions, a non-binding recommendation to eliminate the Gender Identity Support Program, restrict minors' progressive autonomy, ban hormonal treatment for minors and repeal the circular protecting gender identity in schools.

47653553B78904739401519.name: RegiÃ³n Metropolitana de Santiago
47653553B78904739401519.summary:
Chile's Gender Identity Law 21,120, in force since 27 December 2019, applies in full to the Región Metropolitana de Santiago. Adults may change their registered name and sex on request to the Civil Registry, with no therapy or surgery required. People aged 14 to 18 must apply to family courts with psychosocial and family-context antecedents, and the statute's under-14 exclusion cannot stand as written: on 9 April 2025 the Constitutional Court declared the 'over 14 years old' wording inapplicable as unconstitutional in a case brought by the mother of a 10-year-old trans girl, a ruling that applies only to that case.

Non-discrimination and hate-crime rules also apply nationwide. The 2012 Zamudio Law prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, was extended to gender expression in 2018, and treats hate-crime motivation as an aggravating criminal circumstance. Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022, civil unions since 2015, and birth certificates offer a third sex option for intersex children.

Transphobic violence is documented in Santiago and elsewhere. A young trans man was murdered in 2023 in a killing covered up for 24 hours and described in national reporting as Chile's largest hate crime; the perpetrator, an acquaintance, confessed. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for close to an hour at a Santiago hotel, where the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim.

Detention carries specific rules. Gendarmería de Chile's national director signed a protocol guaranteeing the gender identity of trans detainees, providing placement by assumed gender, segmented housing and entry examinations, with a standing committee of Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives overseeing implementation, including access rules for trans visitors.

The public health system has funded sex reassignment surgery and hormone therapy since 2013, and a 2011 Ministry of Health circular obliges all care centres to register transgender patients by their social name. On 9 January 2025 the Constitutional Court, by seven votes to three, annulled section 46 of the 2025 Budget Law, which had barred the Ministry of Health from financing hormone therapies for trans children and adolescents. In November 2025 Congress defunded the Ministry of Social Development's Gender Identity Support Program through the 2026 Budget Law, while the Ministry of Health-run programme continues to provide support in medical centres; the Crece con Orgullo programme has operated since 2023 for children and adolescents aged 3 to 17.

Entry and removal rules reference gender identity. The Migration and Immigration Law of 11 April 2021 bans arbitrary discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity and offers protection to LGBT immigrants seeking asylum. Article 10 provides that recognised asylum seekers may be granted complementary protection, and no foreigner holding complementary protection may be expelled or returned to a country where their right to life, physical integrity or personal freedom is at risk on grounds including sexual orientation or gender identity.

Local authority practice across the capital's comunas diverges sharply, and a visitor's experience of municipal protection depends on which comuna they are in. On 15 April 2026 the Ñuñoa municipal council approved Chile's first anti-discrimination ordinance by nine votes to one; it bans hate speech, obliges non-discrimination clauses in municipal tenders and contracts, creates a communal good-practice seal and requires anti-exclusion notices in municipal buildings, and it was drafted by the comuna's Diversity and Non-Discrimination Department head María Fernanda Ulloa and endorsed by mayor Sebastián Sichel.

The refusal marks a municipal-level retreat in the capital's affluent comunas.
