10402087B60477050509260.name: Bayern
10402087B60477050509260.summary:
Visitors to Bayern stand under Germany's national legal framework. Identity documents, marriage law and anti-discrimination protections are set nationally and uniformly, and no German state can remove that floor.

Legal gender recognition has been available to adults since 1980. The Self-Determination Act, passed by the Bundestag on 12 April 2024 by 374 votes to 251, approved by the Bundesrat on 17 May 2024 and in force since 1 November 2024, allows adults to declare a change of first name and gender before the registry office with three months' notice, with a one-year lockout after a change. A 'divers' marker has been available on birth certificates, passports and driving licences since 1 January 2019 under the Third Gender Act, but it requires a doctor's statement confirming intersex status and does not extend to transgender people.

Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since 2017. Discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is prohibited nationwide in employment and in goods and services, and in health services and education under the General Act on Equal Treatment, in force since 18 August 2006.

Prison placement is the sharpest documented exposure. German prisons operate under statutory separation with a binary men and women housing model, and the Criminological Research Institute of Lower Saxony reports that placement corresponding to a prisoner's gender identity has been practised only in exceptional cases. The outcome has gone both ways. In July 2026 DW reported that Marla-Svenja Liebich, whose gender entry had been changed to female under the Self-Determination Act, was transferred to a men's prison after her extradition, with authorities citing the safety of prisoners at the women's facility. In the earlier Penelope Frank case in 2023, a climate activist with a legal male registration faced assignment to a men's prison if convicted, and the reporting described German prisons as offering few safe spaces for trans inmates.

Airport screening has produced a specific documented complaint. The DJ and producer BASHKKA filed a legal complaint under the General Act on Equal Treatment over a screening at Frankfurt Airport on 23 November 2024, alleging that officers deliberately disregarded her gender identity in a targeted, degrading act of transphobic harassment.

Bavaria's own measures cut against that national floor in two directions. Gender-inclusive German has been prohibited in Bavarian schools, universities and all state administration since 1 April 2024, so a visitor dealing with a Bavarian registry office, school or government counter should expect binary gender forms in official communication. Bavaria also joined Sachsen, Thüringen and Sachsen-Anhalt in a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act, an organised state-level attempt to make the nationwide self-ID law stricter.

Access to women-protected spaces is contested in the leisure sector. A Deutscher Sauna-Bund guideline issued in January 2025 restricted women's saunas to persons whose primary sex characteristics correspond, and reporting from Berlin on how saunas and similar venues handle trans women has followed months of argument over women-protected spaces and fears that the self-declaration route would be misused.

10402087B20892132820961.name: Berlin
10402087B20892132820961.summary:
Berlin is a Land of the Federal Republic of Germany. Federal constitutional and equality protections apply in every Land, national identity documents and marriage law are uniform, and no Land can remove that federal floor. Legal gender recognition is therefore governed nationally, not by the Berlin Senate.

The Self-Determination Act, passed in April 2024 by 374 votes to 251 and in force from 1 November 2024, replaced the 1980 Transsexuals Act, whose surgery and sterilisation requirements the Federal Constitutional Court struck down in January 2011. Transgender, intersex and non-binary adults can change their legal gender by self-determination with three months' notice. A 'divers' marker has been available on birth certificates, passports and driving licences since 1 January 2019 under the Third Gender Act, but it requires a doctor's statement confirming intersex status, and it was clarified in April 2019 as applying to intersex people only.

Custody is the sharpest documented exposure. German prisons operate under statutory separation with a binary men and women housing model. The Criminological Research Institute of Lower Saxony reads § 170(2) of the Lower Saxony correctional act as the operating rule and reports that placement corresponding to a prisoner's gender identity has been practised only in exceptional cases; it runs a research project on the situation of transgender people in prison. Several Länder have amended their prison statutes in recent years to accommodate legally recognised gender diversity, and a new § 17 of the Rhineland-Palatinate prison act took effect on 1 March 2026 with no press coverage.

Berlin's own prison service states that legislation has created a basis for considering trans, inter* and non-binary people held in custody, that its staff are responsible for taking each detainee's individual needs into account within the legal framework, and it sets out gender-segregated placement, intake procedures and counselling and support offers across the city's facilities, including JVA Moabit and JVA für Frauen Berlin. How the exception is applied in practice is unsettled, and outcomes have gone both ways. In August 2025 the chief prosecutor for Halle said Marla-Svenja Liebich, whose gender entry had been changed to female at the end of 2024, would serve an 18-month sentence for incitement at Chemnitz women's prison with placement reviewed at intake. After her extradition from Czechia, DW reported on 16 July 2026 that she had been transferred to a men's prison despite being legally registered as a woman, with authorities citing the safety of prisoners at the women's facility. In the Penelope Frank case, covered by DW in August 2023, a climate activist with a legal male registration faced assignment to a men's prison if convicted, and the reporting described German prisons as offering few safe spaces for trans inmates.

Recorded anti-LGBTI violence in Berlin is high by national standards. MANEO, the city's anti-violence documentation project, logged 723 LSBTIQ+-hostile incidents in Berlin in 2025, slightly fewer than the 738 documented in 2024, drawn from 1,014 new reports — a new high for reporting volume. Its 12 May 2026 release lists insults, threats and physical attacks on public transport, in parks and in streets, with Schöneberg, Neukölln, Kreuzberg, Friedrichshain and Tiergarten the most affected districts, plus 58 attacks on LSBTIQ+ venues, memorials and events. MANEO states the figures capture only part of reality because of a high dark figure, and reports that its own counselling centre was attacked several times in 2025.

At the 48th Berlin Christopher Street Day, MANEO reports that a vehicle drove into a crowd in the Tiergarten area, killing one woman, injuring several people and forcing the event to be cancelled. The project offers victim counselling and an anonymous reporting line on 030-2163336, staffed daily 17:00 to 19:00.

Nationally the picture is one of rising pressure on Pride events. The amadeu-antonio-stiftung counted 55 right-wing-extremist attacks on Pride events across Germany in 2024 and 30 so far in 2025 across roughly 120 parades, including an attack with boiling water, and runs a €100,000 CSD support fund focused on eastern Germany. Maneo, the Berlin anti-violence documentation project, states that big-city parades such as Berlin and Cologne were not specifically threatened and that smaller towns are hardest to police. Berlin CSD organisers have publicly urged vigilance with hundreds of thousands of attendees expected. A queer café owner in Berlin-Neukölln reported 45 police complaints over homophobic attacks in 18 months.

Airport screening has produced a specific documented complaint. The DJ and producer BASHKKA filed a legal complaint under the General Act on Equal Treatment over a screening at Frankfurt Airport on 23 November 2024. According to her account, reported by Resident Advisor in June 2025, officers deliberately disregarded her gender identity in what she called a targeted, degrading act of transphobic harassment; she provided the publication a copy of her statement to the airport.

Access to women-protected spaces has been contested in the leisure sector since the Self-Determination Act took effect on 1 January 2025. A Deutscher Sauna-Bund guideline issued in January 2025 restricting women's saunas to persons whose primary sex characteristics correspond set off a public debate about registered trans women's access, and reporting from Berlin on how saunas and similar venues handle trans women followed months of argument over women-protected spaces and fears that the self-declaration route would be misused.

Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity is prohibited in health services and education under the General Act on Equal Treatment, in force since 18 August 2006. The Federal Anti-Discrimination Office found that a July 2025 ban on gender-inclusive language imposed by the Education Minister in her own ministry contradicted constitutional equality protection. Since May 2020 a nationwide ban on conversion therapy for minors has carried penalties of up to one year in prison for practitioners and fines of €30,000 for offering, promoting or referring minors to such treatment.

Asylum and admission policy moved against LGBTI protection during 2025. In June the Federal Cabinet proposed designating Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia as safe countries of origin despite LGBTI people facing imprisonment there, and in August the governing coalition announced it would end humanitarian admission programmes, including the Afghanistan scheme for persecuted LGBTI people.

10402087B85226028911536.name: Hessen
10402087B85226028911536.summary:
Hessen stands under Germany's national framework. Federal constitutional and equality protections apply to visitors nationwide, national identity documents, marriage law and the Self-Determination Act are uniform across the Länder, and no Land can lower that floor.

Recorded anti-queer crime in Hessen has risen steeply. The Hessian Interior Ministry answered a Landtag small inquiry from three Grüne MPs in April 2025 with 33 police-registered queer-hostile offences in 2022, 83 in 2023 and 135 in 2024, an increase of 52 over the year before. The 2024 total comprised 16 cases of dangerous grievous bodily harm, seven of bodily harm, 13 of property damage and 26 of insult, with suspects identified in 46 proceedings and six convictions. Interior Minister Roman Poseck called the development alarming and attributed part of the responsibility to far-right forces. A further ministry answer reported on 17 May 2026 recorded 141 queer-hostile offences in 2025, a more than fourfold rise within four years, which Poseck described as only the tip of the iceberg given the assumed dark figure; he cited a January 2026 tram incident in Kassel in which a male couple was homophobically insulted, threatened and spat on.

The Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA) publishes a situation report on the security of LSBTIQ* people in Germany together with the Interior Ministry. It documents a multi-year rise in police-registered queer-hostile offences nationwide and a new federal reporting category that makes Land-by-Land comparison possible for the first time, while warning that changes in classification can inflate individual Land counts.

Airport screening is a documented exposure at Frankfurt. The DJ and producer BASHKKA filed a complaint under the General Act on Equal Treatment over screening at Frankfurt Airport on 23 November 2024, in which, according to her account reported by Resident Advisor on 20 June 2025, a male security officer refused her a search by a female officer and told her she was not a woman. Frankfurt Airport apologised by email, said the security service provider had been instructed to investigate, and promised training for security staff on dealing with transgender and gender non-conforming travellers.

10402087B23625801106445.name: Sachsen-Anhalt
10402087B23625801106445.summary:
Sachsen-Anhalt stands under the German national framework: federal constitutional and equality protections apply in every Land, identity documents and marriage law are uniform, and no Land can remove that floor. Custody placement is the sharpest documented exposure for a trans visitor. German prisons operate under statutory separation with a binary men and women housing model, and placement corresponding to a prisoner's gender identity has been practised only in exceptional cases; the Criminological Research Institute of Lower Saxony gives that reading of § 170(2) of the Lower Saxony correctional act as the operating rule and runs a research project on the situation of transgender people in prison. Several Länder have amended their prison statutes in recent years to accommodate legally recognised gender diversity, and a new § 17 of the Rhineland-Palatinate prison act took effect on 1 March 2026 without press coverage.

The case that now drives policy in this Land is Marla-Svenja Liebich's. In July 2023 the Halle District Court sentenced her to one year and six months' imprisonment without parole for incitement to hatred, defamation and insult. At the end of 2024 she changed her legal gender from male to female by declaration at a registry office under the federal Self-Determination Act, and the chief public prosecutor in Halle told MDR Sachsen-Anhalt that she would begin the term at Chemnitz women's prison. German outlets including Der Spiegel questioned the seriousness of the change.

Placement went the other way. DW reported on 16 July 2026 that Liebich, legally registered as a woman since 2025, was transferred to a men's prison at Zeithain in the Meissen district after her extradition from the Czech Republic, where she had been arrested in April 2026. Prison management said the decision prioritised the safety of women at the Chemnitz facility, while critics called the gender change an abuse of the self-determination law. A court has yet to decide whether the changes can be reversed, so the outcome of the central question is unresolved.

Sachsen-Anhalt is one of three Länder, with Sachsen and Thüringen, pressing a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act. The dpa report of 2 June 2026 describes a proposed abuse review mechanism allowing registry-office intervention on objective, documentable grounds, triggered by the Liebich case and backed by Union MPs, resisted by the SPD, while the federal family ministry runs a scheduled evaluation of the Act.

Legal gender recognition itself is straightforward on paper: adults change their legal gender by self-determination with three months' notice, a procedure in force since 1 November 2024 that replaced the Transsexuals Act of 1980. Entry and document checks are therefore unlikely to raise an issue for a visitor carrying consistent papers. A visitor who is arrested or held in Sachsen-Anhalt, by contrast, faces the same binary housing rule that produced the Zeithain transfer.

10402087B67217417145666.name: Thüringen
10402087B67217417145666.summary:
Thüringen stands under Germany's national framework. Federal constitutional and equality protections apply nationwide, national identity documents and marriage law are uniform, and the state government cannot remove that federal floor.

No trans-specific safety finding was documented for Thüringen. The sources record no prosecution, assault or enforcement action against a trans visitor in the state, so the risk picture there rests on political posture and on the exposures that apply across Germany.

In the state election of 1 September 2024, AfD Thüringen, classified by the state's Office for the Protection of the Constitution as right-wing extremist, took 32.8% of the vote, ahead of the CDU at 23.4%, the BSW at 15.8% in its first state election, Die Linke at 13.1% and the SPD at 6.1%. The CDU, BSW and SPD then formed the first 'Brombeerkoalition' under minister-president Mario Voigt, a minority cabinet without its own Landtag majority. Within that configuration the AfD fraction moved to have the existing ban on gender-inclusive language in Thuringian schools consistently enforced and proposed dismantling the state's equality machinery. Formal, multi-layered institutional hostility to gender policy in Thüringen rests on this parliamentary arithmetic.

On 2 June 2026 Thüringen co-signed an initiative from Sachsen and Sachsen-Anhalt to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act after the 'Liebich case', framing anti-abuse amendments alongside stronger recognition of trans and intersex people. Three state governments can call for federal change; they cannot enact it.

Custody is the sharpest documented exposure for a trans person anywhere in Germany, and it applies equally on Thuringian territory. German prisons operate under statutory separation with a binary men and women housing model, and placement corresponding to a prisoner's gender identity has been practised only in exceptional cases. The outcome has gone both ways in documented cases: in August 2025 the chief prosecutor for Halle stated that Marla-Svenja Liebich would serve an 18-month sentence at Chemnitz women's prison with placement reviewed at intake, and DW reported on 16 July 2026 that she had instead been transferred to a men's prison despite legal registration as a woman, authorities citing the safety of prisoners at the women's facility.

The DJ and producer BASHKKA filed a legal complaint under the General Act on Equal Treatment over a screening at Frankfurt Airport on 23 November 2024 in which, on her account reported by Resident Advisor in June 2025, officers deliberately disregarded her gender identity in what she called a targeted, degrading act of transphobic harassment. 14339913B89763821047858.name: Wales
14339913B89763821047858.summary:
Wales stands under the United Kingdom's post-April 2025 regime, which now operates through statutory and quasi-statutory machinery rather than executive decree. In August 2026 the Equality and Human Rights Commission's code on single-sex spaces came into force, giving organisations compliance examples for restricting toilets, changing rooms and similar facilities to one sex. A trans visitor in Wales uses facilities designated by biological sex, and organisations are instructed on how lawfully to enforce that division.

Prison placement follows the same rule across the United Kingdom. On 19 June 2026, in For Women Scotland v Scottish Ministers [2026] CSOH 59, Lady Ross of the Outer House, Court of Session, struck down the Scottish Prison Service's non-statutory trans-custody guidance as unlawful, holding that sex segregation in prisons must rest on a lawful basis. The Welsh Prison Service operates under the same national expectation that custody segregation rest on sex.

The Welsh Government's own LGBTQ+ Action Plan for Wales, announced by Deputy Minister Hannah Blythyn in the Senedd on 21 June 2022 and published in February 2023, set the objective of making Wales the most LGBTQ+ friendly nation in Europe. It was built on 61 recommendations from the Independent LGBTQ+ Expert Panel of March 2021 and a 12-week consultation drawing 1,328 responses, and it funds a Grassroots Pride Fund. The plan records the UK Government's blocking of the Gender Recognition Reform (Scotland) Bill in January 2023.

The action plan's machinery has been maintained and updated. A version for young people was posted in January 2026, and its update page answers the For Women Scotland judgment of 19 December 2025, the date of the UK Supreme Court ruling on the definition of sex in the Equality Act 2010. The Welsh Government separately pursued a Wales-specific ban on conversion practices, forming a Working Group on Banning Conversion Practices in December 2022 and publishing 'Banning conversion practices in Wales' in May 2024.

Schools in Wales carry statutory guidance. 'Rights, Respect, Equality', out for consultation in May 2025, obliges schools to challenge bullying and harassment on grounds of sex, gender reassignment and sexual orientation, to record and monitor incidents, and to provide a parental escalation route. Transgender pupils are therefore covered by anti-bullying duties in Welsh schools while the national Equality Act 2010 protections for transgender youth remain in force.

Legal gender recognition has been available in Wales since 2004 under the Gender Recognition Act, and discrimination protections cover gender identity as well as sexual orientation. Civil partnership rights date from 2005, same-sex marriage from 2014, and full adoption rights from 2005. Same-sex sexual activity was legalised in 1967, the age of consent was equalised in 2001 and remaining restrictions removed in 2003.

Healthcare access has a distinct Welsh history. Trans adults in Wales were referred to London clinics for transgender healthcare until the first Welsh gender identity clinic opened in September 2019. In March 2024 Welsh NHS commissioners stated they had no plans to develop a children's gender service, and parents of transgender children publicly called for more help that month. Minors across the United Kingdom cannot obtain puberty blockers from NHS gender clinics under the suspension first announced by NHS England in March 2024, renewed indefinitely in December 2024 and due for reconsideration in 2027.

14339913B6930312138089.name: Northern Ireland
14339913B6930312138089.summary:
Northern Ireland stands within the United Kingdom's post-April 2025 framework, in which the Supreme Court's ruling now operates through statutory and quasi-statutory machinery. In August 2026 the UK equality watchdog's code on single-sex spaces came into force, giving organisations compliance examples for restricting toilets, changing rooms and similar facilities to one sex. Trans visitors to Northern Ireland therefore use facilities designated by biological sex, and organisations are instructed on how lawfully to enforce that division.

Prison placement and searching follow the parent framework. On 19 June 2026, in For Women Scotland v Scottish Ministers [2026] CSOH 59, Lady Ross of the Outer House, Court of Session, struck down the Scottish Prison Service's non-statutory trans-custody guidance as unlawful, holding that sex segregation in prisons must rest on a lawful basis; the same argument had been aired in that court on 5 February 2026, where government lawyers defended individual risk assessments as a flexible safeguard. On 17 April 2025 British Transport Police amended its strip-searching policy to treat trans women as strip-searched by officers of their sex at birth, and on 25 June 2025 Police Scotland published interim guidance placing custody searches and stop-and-search involving removal beyond a jacket, gloves, headgear or footwear on biological sex, while endeavouring to provide an officer of the individual's lived gender on request.

Northern Ireland's own education authorities have moved against trans-inclusive practice. On 8 September 2025 BBC News reported that guidance supporting transgender pupils was withdrawn from the Northern Ireland Education Authority's website after Education Minister Paul Givan requested its removal, arguing that it conflicted with departmental policy and with the law in Northern Ireland. The withdrawn guidance had recommended that trans pupils be allowed to use changing rooms matching their gender identity, and teachers' representatives warned that its removal ignores the practical realities faced in schools.

Protection machinery in Northern Ireland remains incomplete. On 14 December 2025 BBC News reported that other Northern Ireland Executive parties blocked Justice Minister Naomi Long's plan to add transgender people as a protected characteristic in the region's new hate-crime legislation. Long had sought executive approval in early November 2025 with a response deadline in mid-November, against a bill that had held executive agreement since December 2024, and she cited Police Service of Northern Ireland statistics of close to 100 transgender-identity incidents or hate crimes.

Northern Ireland sits on equality legislation different from the Great Britain statute and is still assessing the impact of the Supreme Court ruling, so the precise reach of the single-sex provisions in local equality law is not yet settled by any Northern Ireland court.

Gender recognition documents carry entry and administrative consequences across the United Kingdom. In December 2023 the UK government said it would no longer accept gender recognition certificates issued by 50 countries and U.S. states, including Sweden, New York State and Belgium, on the ground that those jurisdictions allowed people to transition too easily; people from those locations must apply for a new certificate under British law to change their gender in the UK. Within the United Kingdom a certificate will not be issued unless the applicant's spouse consents, and if the spouse does not consent the marriage must be terminated.

Access to gender-affirming care for minors is restricted under the parent framework. NHS England stopped prescribing puberty blockers to children and young people in March 2024, renewed that suspension indefinitely in December 2024 with reconsideration due in 2027, and by April 2025 had issued no new prescriptions of gender-affirming hormones to minors in the year following the Cass Review of April 2024, which also led to the closure of the Tavistock GIDS in March 2024. Schools and sport carry parallel exclusions: the Girls' Day School Trust barred admissions for trans girls without a gender recognition certificate in January 2022, and in July 2022 the RFU and RFL implemented a single-sex policy for under-12s excluding trans girls from girls' teams, while transgender youth are otherwise covered by the Equality Act 2010.

82085004B70364588595557.name: Northern Territory
82085004B70364588595557.summary:
The Northern Territory stands under the Australian national framework. Gender identity has been a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act since 2013, and in August 2024 the Federal Court held in Tickle v Giggle that the protection extends to trans women as women. Federal hate-crime legislation passed in February 2025 (Act 1 of 2025, in force immediately) explicitly covers sex, sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex status, with penalties of up to seven years' imprisonment.

Vilification coverage across Australia is uneven, and the Northern Territory sits at the unprotected end. New South Wales, the ACT and Victoria cover only sexual orientation; South Australia, Tasmania and Queensland also cover gender identity; the Northern Territory and Western Australia cover neither. The territory's own hate-crime statute does not list sexual orientation or gender identity among its motives, so federal coverage of those motives dates only from 2025.

Within that frame, protection has been withdrawn rather than extended. The Anti-Discrimination Amendment Act 2025 (No. 27 of 2025, assented 30 October 2025; Part 3 commencing 27 July 2026) removes the civil provision that made it unlawful to offend, insult, humiliate or intimidate a person in public on the basis of a protected attribute, gender identity included, and to have a complaint heard by the NT Anti-Discrimination Commission. The Country Liberal Party government confirmed the repeal on 2 March 2025, three years after adding the provision; a bill followed in July 2025 and passed parliament on 17 October 2025, the government having earlier backtracked from scrapping the section outright. Attorney-General Marie-Clare Boothby framed the change as restoring freedom of speech and religion, including letting religious schools again hire only co-religionists. NT Anti-Discrimination Commissioner Jeswynn Yogaratnam publicly rebuked the move, warning the government may be 'opening the doors for a very dangerous stream of hate speech'.

Official hostility has reached beyond statute. The NT government banned rainbow pride flags in public hospitals in February 2025 and issued a policy directive in December 2025 banning gender-affirming healthcare for minors.

Entry, documents and facilities carry no trans-specific friction. No Australian jurisdiction confines bathrooms or changing facilities by gender identity, federal identity documents are issued uniformly across the country, and no border friction has been reported for trans travellers entering Australia. Birth-certificate sex-marker change in the Northern Territory has required clinical treatment since 2018. Marriage equality has applied nationwide since the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Act 2017 came into force on 9 December 2017 after a 61.6% Yes result nationally; the territory's own postal-survey Yes vote was 60.6%. Federal law has recognised same-sex couples as de facto partners since 2009 and recognises overseas same-sex marriages automatically.

82085004B60194602145168.name: Victoria
82085004B60194602145168.summary:
Victoria stands under Australia's national framework on gender identity. Gender identity has been a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act since 2013, and in August 2024 the Federal Court held in Tickle v Giggle that the protection extends to trans women as women, awarding damages against a female-only dating app that had excluded a trans woman member. Federal hate-crime legislation passed in February 2025 (Act 1 of 2025) explicitly covers sex, sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex status with penalties of up to seven years' imprisonment. No Victorian or Australian law confines bathrooms or changing facilities by gender identity, no border friction has been reported for trans travellers, and marriage equality has held since the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Act 2017 came into force on 9 December 2017.

Victoria's own anti-vilification machinery was rebuilt by the Justice Legislation Amendment (Anti-Vilification and Social Cohesion) Act 2025, passed in April 2025. It inserts civil vilification protections into the Equal Opportunity Act 2010 and criminal protections into the Crimes Act 1958 while repealing the Racial and Religious Tolerance Act, with the stated aims of equal participation and public safety. The Act carries gender identity as a ground but takes effect on 30 June 2026, and until that date Victoria's vilification coverage outside the federal layer extends only to sexual orientation. A visitor reporting gender-identity vilification in Victoria before 30 June 2026 therefore rests on the federal hate-crime offence rather than on state law.

Trans-specific mortality has been examined officially in the state. On 29 August 2024 ABC News reported that a Victorian coroner investigating the suicides of five young transgender women recommended urgent investment in health care for trans and gender-diverse people. The state government said it was reviewing the recommendations, and local advocacy groups said they would press for their implementation.

82085004B60194602145168.tangentialFactors:
Vilification coverage across Australia is uneven outside the federal layer: New South Wales, the ACT and Victoria cover only sexual orientation, South Australia, Tasmania and Queensland also cover gender identity, and the Northern Territory and Western Australia cover neither. Victoria's position is therefore middling until its 2025 Act commences, and Queensland strengthened discrimination and vilification protections for gender-diverse people in April 2024 while New South Wales passed the Equality Legislation Amendment (LGBTIQA+) Act 2024.

Restrictions on gender-related care sit in other Australian jurisdictions rather than in Victoria. In January 2025 the Queensland government paused new prescriptions of puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones for under-18s in public health services, exempting existing patients; the Queensland Supreme Court ruled the directive unlawful on 27 October 2025, a new ministerial directive reinstated substantially the same restrictions on 28 October 2025 pending reviews, and a legal challenge was filed in December 2025. A New South Wales independent review released in September 2024 found puberty blockers safe, effective and reversible while calling for more long-term research. A visitor passing through those states on a longer itinerary faces a different care environment from the one Victoria presents.

Detention practice elsewhere in Australia also differs from any assumption a visitor might carry. Queensland's inspection standards of August 2023, issued under the Inspector of Detention Services Act 2022, direct that transgender and intersex prisoners are generally admitted to facilities corresponding to their lived or experienced gender, but staff retain discretion at admission and transgender people who have undergone sexual reassignment surgery are excluded from that identity-based process; the 2009 Corrective Services procedure it replaced was assessed as largely ineffective.

The Queensland Human Rights Commission announcement of April 2024 is no longer reachable and the New South Wales Parliament bill document would not load, so those two items rest on the record held here rather than on a live page.

82085004B21656044714531.name: New South Wales
82085004B21656044714531.summary:
New South Wales stands under the Australian national framework. Gender identity has been a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act since 2013, and in August 2024 the Federal Court held in Tickle v Giggle that the protection extends to trans women as women, awarding damages against a female-only dating app that had excluded a trans woman member. Federal hate-crime legislation passed in February 2025 (Act 1 of 2025, effective immediately) explicitly covers sex, sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex status, with penalties of up to seven years' imprisonment.

State-level vilification coverage is narrower than in several other Australian jurisdictions. New South Wales, the Australian Capital Territory and Victoria cover only sexual orientation, while South Australia, Tasmania and Queensland also name gender identity and the Northern Territory and Western Australia name neither. A trans visitor in New South Wales therefore retains federal discrimination remedies, including the Tickle v Giggle precedent, but has no state vilification ground specific to gender identity.

The Conversion Practices Ban Act 2024 took effect on 4 April 2025. Practices causing substantial mental or physical harm are punishable by up to five years' imprisonment, taking a person out of New South Wales for conversion therapy carries up to three years, and Anti-Discrimination NSW can investigate complaints from 4 April 2025 with civil referral pathways available. The state's other principal recent instrument is the Equality Legislation Amendment (LGBTIQA+) Act 2024.

Trans visitors have been killed in the state. In July 2021 ABC Background Briefing reported the investigation into the killing of Mhelody Bruno, a 25-year-old transgender woman from the Philippines who was visiting Australia, in Wagga Wagga; the perpetrator's guilty plea to manslaughter drew a 22-month term, a custodial outcome far below a murder sentence.

The restrictive machinery reported elsewhere in Australia does not apply here: no law confines bathrooms or changing facilities by gender identity, no border friction has been reported for trans travellers entering New South Wales or Australia, and marriage equality has held since the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Act 2017 came into force on 9 December 2017. Federal law has recognised same-sex couples as de facto partners since 2009, and overseas same-sex marriages are recognised automatically.

Care access for young people rests on state-commissioned evidence: a New South Wales independent review released in September 2024 found puberty blockers safe, effective and reversible while calling for more long-term research. That review stands in contrast to the restrictions operating in Queensland public health services.

82085004B93533858076668.name: Western Australia
82085004B93533858076668.summary:
Australia treats gender identity as a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act, in force since 2013. In August 2024 the Federal Court held in Tickle v Giggle that gender-identity discrimination protection extends to trans women as women, and awarded compensation against a female-only dating app that had excluded a trans woman member. Visitors in every state, Western Australia included, stand under that national framework, and marriage and federal documents are uniform nationwide.

State protection in Western Australia runs through a narrower formulation. The Equal Opportunity Act 1984 protects the attribute 'gender history', defined by living, or seeking to live, as a member of the opposite sex, and the official WA Government guidance states that a person has gender history where they identify as a member of the opposite sex by living or seeking to live as such. Direct discrimination, including treating a person as their former sex, and indirect discrimination are both unlawful under the Act. The binary, medically-inflected wording means a non-binary or gender-nonconforming visitor may fall outside the state-law definition and would rely on federal coverage for a state-level complaint. Western Australia has no state anti-vilification offence, civil or criminal, and no statutory charter binding public authorities.

Complaint eligibility under the state attribute has historically been tied to recognition certificates or a registry change through the Births, Deaths and Marriages framework. On 16 April 2024 Premier Roger Cook and Attorney-General John Quigley announced the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Amendment (Sex or Gender Changes) Bill 2024, which repeals the Gender Reassignment Act 2000 and abolishes the Gender Reassignment Board, described by the ministers as the only remaining board of its kind in Australia. The Board's functions move to a streamlined administrative process within the Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages, and applicants are no longer required to undergo medical or surgical reassignment. A statement from a medical practitioner or psychologist certifying appropriate clinical treatment, which may include counselling, now suffices, and a 'non-binary' sex descriptor becomes available. Stricter rules apply to under-18s through parental consent or Family Court of WA permission, and the Act contains a statutory review clause after three years. The reform implements the WA Law Reform Commission's 2018 recommendations.

The registration reform reshapes the state discrimination attribute itself. The Equal Opportunity Commission's fact sheet records that the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Amendment (Sex or Gender Changes) Act 2024 amends section 4(1) of the Equal Opportunity Act 1984 by deleting the definition of 'gender reassigned person' and inserting a definition tied to recognition certificates under the Gender Reassignment Act 2000 or registration of sex or gender under the amended regime. The Act also repeals the Gender Reassignment Regulations 2001, does not operate retrospectively, and commences by proclamation; once it is in force, gender history complaints must comply with the new registration requirements.

Two complaint routes exist and only one may be used. A complaint may be lodged with the WA Commissioner of Equal Opportunity under the Equal Opportunity Act 1984 within 12 months, with acknowledgment of receipt within a week and a free conciliation conference to follow, or with the Australian Human Rights Commission under the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 within 24 months, reduced to 12 months for employment matters. Choosing one route forecloses the other.

Visitors encounter none of the restrictive machinery found elsewhere in the world: there are no laws confining bathrooms or changing facilities by gender identity in Western Australia, no border friction has been reported for trans travellers, and marriage equality has held nationally since 2017, which matters to same-sex couples arriving together.

Counterweights are documented. 82085004B40257551482390.summary:
Visitors in every state stand under the national framework: gender identity is a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act, and marriage and federal documents are uniform nationwide.

The territory's Human Rights Act 2004 requires public authorities to act compatibly with human rights and enables courts to issue declarations of inconsistency, giving a visitor who encounters discriminatory conduct by a police officer, public servant or public facility a legal review mechanism that common-law states without a charter lack. The territory is also one of four jurisdictions with an explicit self-identification basis for prison placement, reducing the risk of inappropriate custody for a detained gender-nonconforming visitor.

No region-specific incident series, enforcement pattern or institutional-failure finding was identified in the dossier for this territory; the absence of negative evidence, combined with the structural rights protection and the self-identification custody rule, places it modestly above the national average.

A conversion-practices ban has been in force since early 2021, with offending practices attracting up to a 12-month custodial term or a fine, alongside civil penalties giving a tribunal power to issue orders and order redress; practices supporting someone undergoing or considering a gender transition are explicitly not banned. No visitor documents or border-screening practice specific to this territory is recorded in the dossier.

The bill was amended before passage after the Association of Christian Schools and the ACT Law Society argued the definition of conversion practice was 'too broad and vague', while practices supporting someone undergoing or considering a gender transition were explicitly not banned. 25490228B8471183517505.name: Castilla y León
25490228B8471183517505.summary:
Castilla y León stands under Spain's national framework. Ley 4/2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado on 28 February 2023, establishes real and effective equality for trans persons and guarantees LGTBI rights. Under Article 43 any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own civil registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, an administrative self-identification route that replaced the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis plus two years of medical treatment. Recognition of the acquired gender is possible from age 12 under conditions, and the law regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16.

Other operative provisions of the same statute include a ban on non-consensual normalising surgeries on intersex children, expanded assisted reproduction rules, parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, strengthened sexuality education, and anti-discrimination measures covering healthcare, employment and housing. Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have been in force since 2005, and legal gender change does not require surgery or sterilisation.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on legal gender self-determination rather than on biological sex, so the gender marker recorded in the civil registry is the operative basis for facility rules in Castilla y León, in contrast to the stricter single-sex-space approach being adopted in the United Kingdom on biological-sex lines with restrictions applied case by case rather than as a blanket ban.

There is no free-standing criminal offence of gender-expression-based hate crime: the phrase 'gender expression' appears in no article of the Spanish Criminal Code. The hate-speech aggravating circumstance in Article 22.4 and the penalties of Article 510 (one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months) derive from Organic Law 6/2022, while Ley 4/2023 itself reformed offences against sexual freedom, including Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.

Enforcement of the gender-identity aggravation is documented at first-instance level. In July 2026 the Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo applied the transfobia aggravating circumstance for the first time in a misdemeanour case concerning threats sent by WhatsApp to a trans woman, fining the author EUR 300. In a separate case reported on 8 January 2026, a juvenile gang harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park in Valencia to mock them; the only adult defendant received six months' prison and two minors were judged separately.

Regional legislation is being built on top of the national floor. The PSOE parliamentary group registered a bill for real and effective equality of LGTBI+ people in Castilla y León on 20 December 2024, framed as an end to the "sexilio", the out-migration of LGBTI people from the region, with group leader Tudanca urging the fastest possible processing. On 11 June 2025 the Cortes de Castilla y León voted to take the bill, which runs to 76 articles, into consideration after the PP abstained and Vox opposed; the bill answers regional LGBTI+ collectives' long-standing demands, and advocates fear the process could stall in committee.

Comparatively, Spain's administrative self-declaration regime places it alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay. A 2016 23-country survey ranked Spain the most trans-supportive of the group surveyed and the only country where a majority supported unrestricted legal gender designation change, a dated baseline predating the 2023 law.

25490228B48808997991554.name: Ciudad Autónoma de Ceuta
25490228B48808997991554.summary:
Ceuta is an autonomous city of Spain with no LGTBI or gender-identity statute of its own. The legislative index at planlgtbi.es states expressly that Ceuta and Melilla have no regional LGTBI statutes and must instead apply the national equality framework together with central-government policies, so a trans visitor to Ceuta is dealing directly with Spanish law and Spanish institutions rather than with any local ordinance.

The statutory gap is documented rather than incidental. FELGTBI+'s September 2025 radiography of LGTBI+ public policy, prepared with the Universidad de Salamanca, identifies Asturias, Castilla y León, Ceuta and Melilla as the only Spanish territories still without a specific law promoting LGTBI+ rights. The same report records legislative progress in Castilla y León and Asturias in June 2025 and no equivalent step for Ceuta or Melilla. A 2020 precedent study had already placed Ceuta and Melilla at the bottom of the rankings for trans-student recognition and protection.

Ley 4/2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado on 28 February 2023, establishes real and effective equality for trans persons and guarantees LGTBI rights. Under Article 43 any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own civil registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, an administrative self-identification route that replaced the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis plus two years of medical treatment. Recognition is possible from age 12 under conditions, and the law regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16. Legal gender change does not require surgery or sterilisation.

Other operative provisions of the same statute reach the day-to-day conditions of a stay: a ban on non-consensual normalising surgeries on intersex children, expanded assisted reproduction rules, parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, strengthened sexuality education, and anti-discrimination measures covering healthcare, employment and housing. Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have been in force since 2005.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on legal gender self-determination rather than on biological sex, so the gender marker recorded in the civil registry is the operative basis for facility rules in Spain. This contrasts with the stricter single-sex-space approach being adopted in the United Kingdom on biological-sex lines, with restrictions applied case by case rather than as a blanket ban.

There is no free-standing criminal offence of gender-expression-based hate crime: the phrase 'gender expression' appears in no article of the Spanish Criminal Code. The hate-speech aggravating circumstance in Article 22.4 and the penalties of Article 510, one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months, derive from Organic Law 6/2022, while Ley 4/2023 itself reformed offences against sexual freedom, including Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.

Enforcement of the gender-identity aggravation is documented at first-instance level. In July 2026 the Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo applied the transfobia aggravating circumstance for the first time in a misdemeanour case concerning threats sent by WhatsApp to a trans woman, fining the author EUR 300. In a separate case reported on 8 January 2026, a juvenile gang harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park in Valencia to mock them; the only adult defendant received six months' prison and two minors were judged separately.

Ceuta's border position shapes protection needs for trans people held there. Europa Press reported on 17 September 2026 that the LGTBI+ association Arcópoli wrote to the Secretary of State for Migration, Pilar Cancela, demanding the urgent transfer to the peninsula of LGTBI+ migrants remaining in Ceuta after thousands entered irregularly on 30 and 31 July. Arcópoli called transfer the only effective measure to guarantee their protection and inclusion, cited the extreme vulnerability of people who flee criminalisation and persecution in countries including Morocco, and launched a free remote social, psychological and legal support service for those still in Ceuta.

Comparatively, Spain's administrative self-declaration regime places it alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay. A 2016 survey of 23 countries ranked Spain the most trans-supportive of the group surveyed and the only country where a majority supported unrestricted legal gender designation change, a dated baseline predating the 2023 law.

15666254B53975248776023.name: Kelantan
15666254B53975248776023.summary:
Kelantan stands under the national framework of Malaysia. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" for any person regardless of gender or consent, carrying a maximum of 20 years plus whipping; these provisions are not limited to Malaysians and apply to visitors. Sodomy was first criminalised in 1871.

Kelantan maintains Sharia enactments that criminalise cross-dressing or "a man posing as a woman", with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. These state offences reach Muslims only. Enforcement is carried out by the state Islamic religious department, and the law contains no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing.

The Federal Court struck down 16 provisions of the Kelantan Syariah Criminal Code Enactment 2019 in February 2024 on federalism grounds, leaving the federal Penal Code offences fully intact. The Kelantan state legislature responded by passing the Syariah Criminal Offences (Kelantan) Bill 2026 on 13 August 2026, which replaces those 16 struck provisions and legislates covering aurat, gender change, and safeguarding the modesty of private parts. Clause 15 requires Muslims to safeguard the sanctity and modesty of their private parts in accordance with Islamic law, and the state's legislative direction explicitly regulates gender-change matters under Islamic criminal law, with enforcement beginning in 2026.

The new provisions are in force and are being applied by the Kelantan Syariah courts. A case in February 2026, which preceded the bill, was the first Kelantan Syariah Court case involving gender change.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor, the Sharia cross-dressing and gender-change offences do not apply, but the Penal Code does. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted; the documented national pattern is raid-based arrest and public outing rather than individual stops. A High Court denied a request to declare the Sharia prohibition on cross-dressing unconstitutional, so the state layer remains legally contested rather than voided.

A constitutional challenge to the Sharia regime was pending as of late 2014 following the mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding on 8 June 2014.

15666254B71460903090065.name: Terengganu
15666254B71460903090065.summary:
Terengganu is one of the 13 states of Malaysia and stands under the national framework: sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" for any person regardless of gender or consent, with a maximum of 20 years plus whipping. Sodomy has been criminalised in Malaysian law since 1871. These provisions are not limited to Malaysian citizens, so a foreign visitor in Terengganu is exposed to them on the same terms as a resident.

The state layer adds a second offence that reaches only Muslims. Every one of the 13 states, Terengganu included, maintains a Sharia enactment criminalising cross-dressing or "a man posing as a woman", punishable by up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. Enforcement sits with the state Islamic religious department, and the enactments contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing. Litigation has narrowed this layer without loosening the federal one: the Federal Court struck down Selangor's cross-dressing provision in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds, while sections 377A and 377B remain fully intact. A non-Muslim foreign visitor therefore falls outside the Sharia offence but remains squarely covered by the Penal Code.

Official messaging in Terengganu is explicitly hostile. In May 2025 a Terengganu state executive councillor confirmed that warning signboards against homosexual practices installed at strategic locations across the state are intended to instil hatred of homosexual acts, and stated that the state wants people to regard those acts as dirty, wrong and to be avoided. This is state-level endorsement of anti-homosexual signage, and it sets the tone a gender-nonconforming visitor can expect from public authorities in the state.

Civil society has contested the campaign on the record. In May 2025 thirteen organisations including Justice for Sisters urged the Kuala Terengganu City Council to remove the anti-LGBT signboards, describing them as discriminatory and a violation of international human rights law, and criticising the executive councillor's defence of the boards as inciting hatred and discrimination. The pushback has not produced a documented removal.

Enforcement across Malaysia is conducted in public and produces outing as well as prosecution. Raid-based arrest of gender-nonconforming people by religious departments, mass arrests at venues, and lethal violence against trans women with impunity are documented nationally; tourists are rarely targeted individually, but a visitor who is visibly gender-nonconforming in Terengganu faces the same official hostility expressed in the state's signage campaign. There is no same-sex marriage and no anti-discrimination law anywhere in Malaysia.

15666254B71428205180864.name: Kedah
15666254B71428205180864.summary:
Malaysia criminalises both same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity at two levels, and Kedah stands under that national framework. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" for any person regardless of gender or consent, carrying a maximum of 20 years plus whipping; these provisions are not limited to Malaysians and apply to visitors. Every one of the 13 states and the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya additionally maintains a Sharia enactment criminalising cross-dressing or "a man posing as a woman", with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. Those state offences reach Muslims only.

Kedah's own instrument is the Syariah Criminal Offences (Kedah Darul Aman) Enactment 2014 (En.18/2014). 65028918B28366581005022.name: West Java
65028918B28366581005022.summary:
West Java stands under the national framework of Indonesia, which is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment; because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations, and reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Sub-national variation sits inside that framework. Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national-level morality provisions, and in Aceh two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025. Those provincial provisions apply to foreign visitors present in those provinces, not to West Java; West Java's own exposure comes from national law, national police action and street violence.

Police in West Java investigate and break up LGBT gatherings even where no offence is alleged. On 22 June 2025 the West Java Regional Police confirmed the detention of 75 people, 74 men and one woman, at a privately rented villa in Puncak in Bogor Regency, following a tip from local residents; police described the event as an LGBT family gathering held to avoid detection. Amnesty International, which said the gathering violated no law, called the operation a discriminatory raid and a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and demanded release and accountability.

Street violence against trans women is documented in the province. On 15 August 2026 reporting from Bogor recorded men dousing a trans woman on a public street with what appeared to be urine, one of a wave of attacks. Activists tied the violence to a 2025 presidential regulation classifying the spread of LGBTQ culture as a non-military threat and to discriminatory regional regulations, arguing that official language legitimises violence against trans women; a trans woman quoted in the report said that people who previously appeared in public now live in fear.

65028918B4119458748300.name: West Sumatra
65028918B4119458748300.summary:
West Sumatra stands under the national framework of Indonesia, a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations, and reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national-level morality provisions. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors; two men were publicly caned there for a same-sex relationship in February 2025.

West Sumatra carries no equivalent provincial religious criminal regime. The operative restrictions here are regional public-order bylaws made by city and regency authorities under Indonesia's regional-bylaw mechanism, and they bind anyone within the locality. Bukittinggi City adopted Regional Regulation (Perda) No. 2 of 2024 on Public Order, which targets LGBT people and is framed in the text as a response to local religious values and Minangkabau customs. In Limapuluh Kota regency, the regional legislature (DPRD) finalised on 13 May 2026 a draft anti-LGBT regional regulation folded into a Public Order and Tranquility (Trantibum) regulation, carrying administrative fines and rehabilitation for LGBT people.

Physical risk in Indonesia is rising. Vigilante mobs are attacking transgender people, and reporting in August 2026 ties the surge to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 that lists LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism. Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue: on 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International stated the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him. Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment. In March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words including Grindr, and a bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Document and status rules offer no cover. Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors with no third-gender or X option, legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, and no national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

65028918B6690755070061.name: Bali
65028918B6690755070061.summary:
Bali stands under Indonesia's national framework, and that framework is where the legal risk sits. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted anywhere in Indonesia, that provision reaches consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. Same-sex marriage remains unrecognised for visitors and residents alike.

The island's own environment is materially milder than the statute book. Travel guidance current to March 2026 describes a "live and let live" basis, records no criminal enforcement against foreign tourists, and names Seminyak (Eat Street and Batu Belig), Canggu and Ubud as the areas with the most consistently LGBTQ+-friendly venues. Public displays of affection warrant discretion. A separate traveller-facing guide rates Bali 6.3 out of 10 overall but only 2.0 for legal safety, warning that LGBTQ+ travellers face legal risk under Indonesian national law and advising visitors to keep affection quiet despite the island's tolerant reputation.

Peer-reviewed ethnography published in 2025 documents the transpuan (trans feminine) community in Bali across four case studies, describing lives marked by discrimination and misrecognition alongside informal resistance. The academic record confirms that Bali hosts a visible trans community living with real precarity.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller in Indonesia. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges and died in custody; his mother alleges police beat him, and Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option. Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval. No national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

For this record: academic ground-truth that Bali hosts a visible trans community living with precarity, discrimination, and informal resistance.

65028918B16658067687714.name: Papua
65028918B16658067687714.summary:
Papua stands under the national framework of Indonesia, a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual sexual activity outside marriage; because same-sex marriage is not recognised in Indonesia, the provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations. Prosecutions are reported as selective rather than systematic. Papua carries no equivalent provincial criminal provision in the sourced record, but customary laws may operate alongside the national code.

Detention in Papua is the province's dominant traveller risk, and it is documented rather than speculative. A TAPOL briefing of July 2025 records 138 acts of torture or ill-treatment in detention by police and military in Maybrat and the Central Highlands between September 2021 and the first quarter of 2025, with almost no consequences for perpetrators. Victims were predominantly males under 24, together with seven women and seven minors; arrests were largely made for alleged links to armed groups or for participation in demonstrations. Deaths during torture were documented in the operation areas, and the incidents are catalogued on the 'Papuans Behind Bars' database.

The Human Rights Monitor Papua quarterly report of 31 October 2025 records killings, arbitrary detentions, torture and arrests of protesters across West Papua as security forces expand their presence, alongside the failure of accountability mechanisms and a healthcare crisis under scrutiny. That report carries no trans or LGBTI findings; the risk it evidences is general detention risk, which compounds sharply for a trans detainee held in a facility with documented ill-treatment and no redress.

Identity documents are obtainable in Papua. Since June 2021 Indonesia's Ministry of Home Affairs has run an outreach programme issuing identification papers (KTP) to transgender Indonesians, and Papua is among the provinces where trans residents have received them, alongside Banten, West Java, Central Java, East Java, North Sumatra, South Sumatra, South Sulawesi and Lampung. Only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors are recognised, and the birth gender is printed on the document unless a court order for legal gender recognition has already been obtained.

Human Rights Monitor Papua Quarterly Report Q3 2025, dated 31 October 2025, covers West Papua and records killings, arbitrary detentions, torture, arrests of protesters and the failure of accountability mechanisms as security forces expand across the territory, alongside a healthcare crisis under scrutiny. These findings describe a high-violence, low-accountability security climate in West Papua that bears on overall traveller safety. The report carries no trans or LGBTI findings.

31927357B35339934753022.name: Baja California
31927357B35339934753022.summary:
Baja California is among the Mexican states that have legislated an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition. The state congress created the procedure through a 2022 reform to the Civil Code, initially limited to adults. In June 2023 the Supreme Court of Justice of the Nation invalidated the 18-years requirement, holding that the law failed to recognise the rights of transgender children and adolescents, and the state congress responded with a further reform in 2024 establishing a procedure for individuals under 18 and extending legal gender recognition to non-binary people.

No criminalisation of trans presence applies. The national framework, as Human Rights Watch set out on 31 March 2025, leaves legal gender recognition to the states and records a patchwork of procedures whose implementation differs sharply; where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation. Baja California sits on the reformed side of that patchwork, but the gap between statute and practice documented across Mexico applies here as elsewhere: Caroline Beer's analysis for LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly.

Lethal violence against women in the state is under-classified. Zeta Tijuana reported on 8 March 2025 that under Governor Marina del Pilar Ávila 1,179 women have been killed in Baja California while only 110 cases were typified as feminicide. The same reporting places female economic participation in the state at roughly 46-47%, 14th of 32 states.

Extradition machinery has been used in feminicide cases. Zeta Tijuana reported on 8 July 2023 that Brayan Rivera was presented on 6 July 2023 before US Judge Karen L. Stevenson in provisional detention for extradition, accused by Mexico of the feminicide of Ángela Carolina Acosta, killed on 24 January 2022 in room 404 of Hotel Cascadas beside Bar Hong Kong in Tijuana's tolerance zone. A US federal court determined probable cause on 29 June 2023; he was arrested at his parents' Downey, California home, where officers found the Hotel Cascadas rent receipt and rope and gloves. At a 7 July 2023 press conference the Baja California attorney general called the 30-year-old a serial perpetrator, said extradition could take from 15 days to two years, and that nearly a decade of open case files were being reviewed; the investigation had linked him to at least three feminicides: Ángela (January 2022), Elizabeth (14 February), and Karen, 28 (30 August 2021, Motel Hacienda Soler).

Partnership recognition is settled at the national level: same-sex marriage has been legal across Mexico since 2009.

31927357B84428150771724.name: Campeche
31927357B84428150771724.summary:
Campeche stands under Mexico's national framework for legal gender recognition, which remains incomplete. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of Mexico's 32 states now operate an administrative procedure for recognising a person's gender in official documents, and called on the states that lack such procedures to adopt them. The same dispatch warned that implementation differs sharply from one state to another, and that where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

Campeche's elected congress passed a 2024 reform to the Civil Code creating an administrative legal gender recognition procedure. A trans visitor or resident can therefore have identity documents aligned through an administrative route rather than through litigation, which is the single most consequential legal fact for anyone crossing borders or dealing with police, banking and health services on mismatched documents.

Formal rights and their enforcement diverge. Analysis published by Caroline Beer on the LSE USAPP blog (22 November 2024) found that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are rarely enjoyed in practice. Beer stated explicitly that her earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ people in Mexico are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

Delays and refusals in name and gender recognition in the neighbouring state of Tabasco leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying everyday discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police, the Human Rights Watch report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" (6 March 2024) found. That report set these findings against killings including a trans woman found dead in the Carrizal River in August 2023.

Killings of trans people continue and have drawn public protest. The Associated Press reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening period of that year, including activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, which triggered LGBTQ+ outrage and street demonstrations. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that violence against trans people and the murder of LGBTI+ defenders had increased over the previous year. Transgender Europe monitoring recorded 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico from 2008 to September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a total second only to Brazil's 100.

Mexico City's congress approved the "Paola Buenrostro law" in July 2024, criminalising transfemicide with up to 70 years' imprisonment, making it the second of Mexico's 32 states to do so. The law is named for Paola Buenrostro, a trans sex worker murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished; activists quoted at the time described the measure as critical to their feeling safe in the capital. It obliges the attorney-general's office to publish statistics on crimes against the LGBTQ+ community.

Regional oversight bodies have pressed the authorities. In 2024 the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded investigation of all LGBTI violations using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may reach alarming levels.

31927357B65177449444732.name: Chiapas
31927357B65177449444732.summary:
Chiapas operates within Mexico's national legal framework, and no Chiapas statute criminalises or restricts the presence, conduct or dress of trans visitors. A trans traveller to Chiapas commits no trans-specific offence under state law.

Legal gender recognition is the decisive legal gap. Human Rights Watch's state-by-state assessment of 31 March 2025 records that 22 of Mexico's 32 states now operate an administrative procedure for changing the name and gender marker on identity documents. Chiapas is not among them; as of March 2025 the state had not reformed its legislation to create such a procedure.

The practical consequence for a trans visitor is an identity document that cannot be corrected locally. Where no administrative route exists, recognition is available only through the courts, case by case, on a timeline that no short visit can accommodate. A trans person entering Chiapas on documents that do not match their presentation carries those documents through every interaction that requires identification, from hotel check-in to police stops.

What mismatched documents produce is documented in the neighbouring state of Tabasco. Human Rights Watch reported on 6 March 2024 that trans people there face document-mismatch discrimination in employment, health care, education and financial transactions, and recorded hospital staff calling out interviewees' legal names in waiting rooms. The report urged the state to adopt a simple self-identification procedure.

31927357B49801195703560.name: Chihuahua
31927357B49801195703560.summary:
Chihuahua stands under Mexico's national framework, in which legal gender recognition remains unfinished and uneven. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that many Mexican states now operate administrative procedures for legal gender recognition and called on those without them to adopt one, while warning that implementation differs sharply from state to state and that where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

Chihuahua grants recognition through an administrative procedure run by the state Civil Registry rather than through a statute of its own. The Supreme Court struck down the civil code's requirement of a judicial process in 2019, and the registry has conducted administrative recognitions on that basis since. As of March 2025 the Chihuahua state legislature had enacted no recognition reform.

Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of Mexico's 32 states operate an administrative legal-gender-recognition procedure, placing Chihuahua among the majority in practice while remaining outside the group that has codified recognition in state law. Because the procedure rests on registry practice rather than on state legislation, a visitor who moves between jurisdictions may meet a different procedure, a court-based route, or none at all.

Formal rights and their enforcement diverge across the country. Analysis published by Caroline Beer on the LSE USAPP blog (22 November 2024) found that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are rarely enjoyed in practice; Beer stated explicitly that her earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ people in Mexico are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture. In 2024 the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded investigation of all LGBTI violations using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may reach alarming levels.

Killings of trans people continue. The Associated Press reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening period of that year, including activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, which triggered LGBTQ+ outrage and street demonstrations. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that violence against trans people and the murder of LGBTI+ defenders had increased over the previous year. Transgender Europe monitoring recorded 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico from 2008 to September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a total second only to Brazil's 100.

One state has altered the penalty landscape. Mexico City's congress passed the "Paola Buenrostro law" on 24 July 2024, criminalising transfemicide with a sentence of up to 70 years and making Mexico City the second of Mexico's 32 states to do so. The law is named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished, and it obliges the attorney-general's office to publish statistics on crimes against the LGBTQ+ community. Transfemicide is therefore not a criminal offence in Chihuahua.

Partnership recognition is settled nationally: same-sex marriage is available across Mexico, so a trans visitor in a recognised partnership enters on the same footing as elsewhere in the country.
