31927357B32124965101143.name: Coahuila de Zaragoza
31927357B32124965101143.summary:
Coahuila de Zaragoza stands under the national framework of Mexico, where Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that most states now operate administrative procedures for legal gender recognition while warning that implementation differs sharply between them, and where same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2009.

Coahuila is one of the states that has legislated. The 2018 Law on the Civil Registry of the State of Coahuila, articles 124 to 128, established an administrative procedure for recognition of self-identified gender identity; the Human Rights Watch state-by-state tracker of March 2025 records it among the 32 states with such a procedure and links the official gazette text of the reform. The bill reached the plenary of the Congress of Coahuila through proposals from several parliamentary groups and an initiative by former governor Rubén Moreira, and the dictamen was approved unanimously. It reformed article 133 of the Ley para la Familia de Coahuila de Zaragoza and created the Civil Registry law, whose article 2, fraction XI, defines gender identity as the personal and internal conviction.

The procedure is in working use. Ricardo Malacara, director of Coahuila's Civil Registry, stated in March 2023 that roughly 1,500 people had completed the legal gender-identity change before the Civil Registry from early 2019 to March 2023, in both directions, male to female and female to male.

Recognition on paper does not settle the wider risk environment. Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021 and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, second only to Brazil's 100; a Guardian report of 24 July 2024 states that more than 95% of homicides nationally went unpunished in 2022. On 18 July 2024 the legislature of Mexico City made transfemicide a crime carrying sentences of up to 70 years under the Paola Buenrostro law, named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and state authorities in 2024 to prevent and punish violence against trans people, to investigate LGBTI violations using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.

Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP of 22 November 2024 concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice, and cautions that this must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence. No Coahuila-specific incident or enforcement pattern appears in the sources assembled here, so visitor-facing risk in the state tracks the national baseline rather than a documented local pattern.

31927357B75771156097737.name: Colima
31927357B75771156097737.summary:
Colima is a state of Mexico, and a trans visitor's exposure there is set by Mexico's national framework rather than by any Colima statute identified in the sources reviewed. Same-sex conduct is not criminalised anywhere in the country, same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2009 with Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction, and nothing in the inventory indicates that Colima has enacted a law targeting trans presence.

Legal gender recognition in Mexico is decided state by state. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that, as of March 2025, 22 of the country's 32 states had legislated an administrative recognition procedure, two further states operate one in practice without enactment, six legislatures have enacted nothing, and only seven states extend recognition to children. The Supreme Court of Justice of the Nation set binding guidelines for the states and extended the right to minors in 2022, and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights requires a simple, accessible procedure.

Where no procedure exists, the consequences are documented directly. HRW records identity-document mismatch driving discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, with incidents logged in Guanajuato and Tabasco. The HRW and Community Center for Inclusion report of 6 March 2024, written from Tabasco, found that without identity documents matching a trans person's gender, every document request or appearance scrutiny carries risk of violence, harassment and humiliation, and excludes trans people from employment, health services, education and financial transactions.

The violence context behind those findings is stated in the same reporting: trans woman Karina Gómez was murdered in Villahermosa in August 2023, and more than 95% of homicides in Mexico went unpunished in 2022, with transfemicide impunity thought to run higher still.

One legislative trend bears directly on lethal risk. Mexico City passed the Paola Buenrostro law in July 2024, criminalising transfemicide with penalties of up to 70 years, making it the second of Mexico's 32 states to create the offence after Nayarit, where the maximum is 60 years. Colima had not been identified in the sources as either recognising transfemicide as a crime or operating a legal gender-recognition procedure at the time of review.

31927357B5285092776894.name: Durango
31927357B5285092776894.summary:
Durango is one of Mexico's 32 states and stands under the national framework: legal gender recognition in Mexico is established state by state, and the vetted sources document no administrative recognition procedure enacted in Durango. Where a state has not legislated a procedure, the national and judicial layers are the operative rule for a trans person in Durango.

The national count is the working baseline. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of the 32 states had legislated an administrative recognition procedure, that two further states operate one in practice without enactment, and that six legislatures have enacted nothing; only seven states extend recognition to children.

Binding authority sits above that uneven layer. Mexico's Supreme Court set binding guidelines for the states and extended the right to minors in 2022, and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights requires a simple, accessible procedure across the federation. These rulings apply in Durango regardless of what its own legislature has done.

Human Rights Watch documents what follows where no procedure exists: identity-document mismatch driving discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, with incidents recorded in Guanajuato and Tabasco. The HRW and Community Center for Inclusion report of 6 March 2024, examining a Mexican state without a recognition procedure, found that every document request or appearance scrutiny carries a risk of violence, harassment and humiliation, and that mismatched documents exclude trans people from employment, health services, education and financial transactions.

The security context behind those findings is severe. The Tabasco material records the August 2023 murder of trans woman Karina Gomez in Villahermosa, and more than 95% of homicides nationally went unpunished in 2022. Transgender Europe monitoring recorded 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico from 2008 to September 2021 and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a total second only to Brazil's 100. The Associated Press reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening period of that year, including activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca shot in Mexico City, which triggered street demonstrations, and Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that violence against trans people and the murder of LGBTI+ defenders had risen over the previous year.

Transfemicide is being newly defined as a crime, but in few places. Mexico City's Congress passed the Paola Buenrostro law in July 2024, punishable by up to 70 years, making Mexico City the second of the 32 states to criminalise the offence after Nayarit, where the maximum is 60 years. The sources identify no equivalent offence in Durango, and note that transfemicide impunity is thought to exceed the already-high general figure.

Formal protection does not equal enforcement. Analysis published by Caroline Beer on the LSE USAPP blog on 22 November 2024 found that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, and stated that her earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ people in Mexico are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture. In 2024 the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded investigation of all LGBTI violations using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may reach alarming levels.

31927357B20618267715210.name: Guerrero
31927357B20618267715210.summary:
Guerrero stands under Mexico's national framework on legal gender recognition, and that framework is the only documented layer for this record. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that recognition is set state by state: 22 of Mexico's 32 states had legislated an administrative procedure, two more operated one in practice without enactment, six state legislatures had enacted nothing, and only seven states extended recognition to children.

Two higher authorities constrain what Guerrero may do. Mexico's Supreme Court set binding guidelines for the states in 2022 and extended the right to minors in the same year, and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights requires a simple, accessible procedure. Where a state has not enacted its own procedure, this national framework governs the visitor's expectations.

Human Rights Watch documents the practical consequence of an absent or obstructed procedure: identity-document mismatch drives discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, with incidents recorded in Guanajuato and Tabasco.

The Community Center for Inclusion's report of 6 March 2024 on Tabasco, a Mexican state with no legal gender-recognition procedure, records what that absence means at street level. Without identity documents matching a trans person's gender, every document request or appearance scrutiny carries risk of violence, harassment and humiliation, and trans people are excluded from employment, health services, education and financial transactions.

The same report sets those barriers against lethal violence and impunity. A trans woman, Karina Gómez, was murdered in Villahermosa in August 2023, and more than 95% of homicides nationally went unpunished in 2022.

The Mexican picture is uneven rather than uniform. Two thirds of the states had legislated a recognition procedure by March 2025, two more administered one without legislation, and six had neither, so a trans visitor's document position depends heavily on which state the paper is issued in. A trans person who is assaulted or killed can therefore expect little from the investigative process, and the Tabasco report places the murder of Karina Gómez in Villahermosa in August 2023 inside that context.

31927357B41082348713023.name: Mexico
31927357B41082348713023.summary:
Mexico has no national administrative procedure for legal gender recognition; the process is set state by state. As of March 2025, 22 of the 32 states had legislated an administrative recognition procedure, two more operated one in practice without legislative enactment, and six state legislatures had enacted none at all. Only seven states extend recognition to children.

In 2022 the Supreme Court set binding guidelines for the states and extended the right to minors, and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights requires a simple, accessible procedure. Where no procedure exists, trans people are left carrying identity documents that contradict their lived gender, and that mismatch drives discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, with incidents recorded in Guanajuato and Tabasco. Recognition therefore depends on the state a person is in.

Tabasco, documented jointly by Human Rights Watch and the Community Center for Inclusion on 6 March 2024, had no legal gender-recognition procedure. There, every document request or appearance scrutiny carries risk of violence, harassment and humiliation, and trans people are excluded from employment, health services, education and financial transactions.

The protective machinery is weak. More than 95% of homicides nationally went unpunished in 2022, and the Tabasco material includes the August 2023 murder of trans woman Karina Gomez in Villahermosa.

31927357B15886886594254.name: Nayarit
31927357B15886886594254.summary:
Nayarit stands within Mexico's federal legal framework, where legal gender recognition remains unfinished and uneven. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of Mexico's 32 states have legislated an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, that eight have none, and that two recognise it in practice without legislation. The same document records 2019 national Supreme Court guidelines on the subject and notes that only seven states extend recognition to children.

Nayarit is among the states with a statutory route. A 2017 reform of the state Civil Code established an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, allowing adults to change identity documents to match their gender identity. A trans visitor whose documents were issued in Nayarit therefore has a recognition mechanism on the books.

Nayarit is the first of Mexico's 32 states to criminalise transfemicide, introducing sentences of up to 60 years in 2024. Mexico City followed in July 2024 as the second, with up to 70 years under the Paola Buenrostro law, named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished.

The Nayarit measure also lets friends, not just relatives, identify and claim bodies and drive investigations. That provision carries weight in a country where families commonly disown trans relatives.

31927357B98648037880103.name: Queretaro de Arteaga
31927357B98648037880103.summary:
Querétaro de Arteaga stands under the national framework of Mexico, where legal gender recognition remains the central unfinished task of equality law. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of Mexico's 32 states had legislated a legal gender-recognition procedure, and its state-by-state table lists Querétaro among the six states that have never legislated any such procedure. A trans visitor to Querétaro therefore has no local administrative route to align identity documents with lived identity; the papers carried on arrival are the only identification available, and they cannot be corrected there.

Where recognition is absent, mismatched documents are the documented exposure. The Human Rights Watch report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" (6 March 2024) found that delays and refusals in Tabasco leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police, and it presents Tabasco as the clearest case among the six states whose legislatures still refuse any procedure. The same report set those barriers against killings, including a trans woman found dead in the Carrizal River in August 2023.

Querétaro's Penal Code cuts the other way on one specific point. The reform prohibiting Esfuerzos para Corregir la Orientación Sexual y la Identidad de Género (ECOSIG), commonly called conversion therapies, was published and is in force as of reporting on 20 September 2023, and it sets two to six years' imprisonment, a fine of 20 to 2,000 times the UMA and 50 to 100 hours of community service, treating such practices as discriminatory and torturous under articles 1 and 6 of the Inter-American Convention to Prevent and Punish Torture.

It sets a penalty of two to six years in prison, a fine of 20 to 2,000 times the UMA and 50 to 100 hours of community service, treating such practices as discriminatory and torturous under articles 1 and 6 of the Inter-American Convention to Prevent and Punish Torture. 31927357B22618747134228.name: San Luis Potosi
31927357B22618747134228.summary:
San Luis Potosí stands under the national framework of Mexico, where legal gender recognition remains unevenly implemented. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of Mexico's 32 states had legislated a legal gender-recognition procedure by that date, and set out a per-state compliance picture showing that implementation differs sharply from one state to another. Where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

San Luis Potosí is among the states that have acted. The state began authorising legal gender changes for transgender people on 17 May 2019, following a 2019 reform of the Civil Registry Law that created an administrative recognition procedure with implementing regulations issued by gubernatorial decree. The state is listed among the states that enacted a gender-identity law in 2019.

Partnership recognition is settled here as well. Same-sex marriage took effect in San Luis Potosí on 21 May 2019, after the state Congress voted 14-12 in favour on 16 May 2019, and joint adoption by same-sex couples has been legal in the state from the same month. Nationally, same-sex marriage has been legal since 2009, with Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction.

The state's hate-crime statutes recognise motivation by gender and sexual preference, which gives trans victims a route to aggravated treatment of an attack. Its local anti-discrimination law bans discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender but does not name gender identity, leaving a gap in the statutory protection a trans visitor would be able to invoke.

The distance between statute and practice is the recurring national finding. Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice, and cautions explicitly that the work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

Violence against trans people is documented at national scale. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that many states operate administrative recognition procedures while calling on those that lack them to adopt them. The Human Rights Watch report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" (6 March 2024) found that delays and refusals in name and gender recognition in Tabasco leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying everyday discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police, and set those barriers against killings, including a trans woman found dead in the Carrizal River in August 2023. AP reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, killings that drew LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months. Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100.

Two official responses frame what a trans visitor can expect from authorities. Mexico City's Congress approved the "Paola Buenrostro law" in July 2024, criminalising transfemicide, a statute named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished and which activists describe as critical to their sense of safety. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that all LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.

No region-specific incident, enforcement or ordinance evidence was found for San Luis Potosí, and no border-screening or document-procedure information specific to the state is recorded.

31927357B30231562725156.name: Sinaloa
31927357B30231562725156.summary:
Sinaloa stands under Mexico's national framework, where legal gender recognition remains unfinished and uneven across the country. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that many of Mexico's states now operate administrative procedures for legal gender recognition, while calling on the states that lack such procedures to adopt them and warning that implementation differs sharply from one state to another. Where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

Against that national picture, Human Rights Watch reported the same day that 22 of Mexico's 32 states had legislated a legal gender-recognition procedure by March 2025. Sinaloa's own legislative status is measured against that count, and one secondary account places the state on the other side of it: Wikipedia's Mexico-wide LGBT rights article lists Sinaloa among the states that enacted a gender-identity recognition law, dated there to 2022.

Sinaloa's relationship recognition framework is documented. The same article reports that the Mexican Supreme Court ordered the state to legalize same-sex marriage within 90 days on 15 May 2018, and that the Sinaloa Congress passed a same-sex marriage law on 15 June 2021. Civil unions, for both same-sex and opposite-sex couples, are performed in the state.

Wikipedia also lists Sinaloa among the Mexican states whose local law bans discrimination on grounds of both sexual orientation and gender identity, and among those with hate-crime statutes covering gender and sexual preference. A visitor to Sinaloa therefore faces a stated protective framework at state level whose real-world application sits inside the wider national pattern of uneven implementation described by Human Rights Watch.

31927357B37261891092938.name: Sonora
31927357B37261891092938.summary:
Sonora is a state of Mexico and stands under the national framework of Mexico, where legal gender recognition remains unevenly implemented. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of Mexico's 32 states had legislated a legal gender-recognition procedure by that date and named six legislatures that had enacted none. The same report warned that implementation differs sharply between states, and that where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

Sonora sits on the legislated side of that divide. The Hermosillo daily El Sol de Hermosillo reported on 1 October 2020 that Sonora's Congress approved the state's Gender Identity Law (Ley de Identidad de Género), under which people who identify with the opposite gender can modify their official documentation. Secondary legal reference material counts Sonora among the 25 Mexican states that have legislated a gender identity law, dated to 2020, giving trans people a statutory route to rectify gender on civil documents.

Sonora's hate-crime legislation recognises motivation by gender and sexual preference, and the state ratified the 2011 federal constitutional amendment prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. A visitor who is assaulted in Sonora therefore has a statutory aggravating-grounds provision available, though the sources assembled here do not document how state prosecutors have applied it in a trans case.

Partner recognition is settled at state level. By 31 December 2022 every Mexican state, including Sonora, had legalised same-sex marriage by legislation, executive order or judicial ruling.

The formal rights described above coexist with weak enforcement nationally. Analysis published by Caroline Beer on the LSE USAPP blog on 22 November 2024 found that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are rarely enjoyed in practice. Beer stated explicitly that her findings must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ people in Mexico are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

The Associated Press reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening period of that year, including activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, triggering street demonstrations. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that violence against trans people and the murder of LGBTI+ defenders had increased over the previous year. Transgender Europe monitoring recorded 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a total second only to Brazil's 100.

Legislative and oversight responses have followed. Mexico City's Congress approved the Paola Buenrostro law in July 2024, criminalising transfemicide, named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished. In 2024 the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded investigation of all LGBTI violations using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may reach alarming levels. The Human Rights Watch report of 6 March 2024, "I Just Want to Contribute to Society," found that delays and refusals in name and gender recognition in Tabasco leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police.

31927357B81008000569871.name: Tabasco
31927357B81008000569871.summary:
Tabasco stands under Mexico's national framework, where legal gender recognition remains unfinished and uneven. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that many of Mexico's states now operate administrative procedures for legal gender recognition and called on those that lack such procedures to adopt them, while warning that implementation differs sharply from one state to another and that where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

Tabasco is on the wrong side of that divide. The state has not reformed its legislation and operates no legal gender recognition procedure, one of eight Mexican states with none; two further states handle recognition in practice only, with no procedure in law.

The practical consequence is that documents and lived gender never line up. The Human Rights Watch report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" (6 March 2024), produced together with a local community centre for inclusion, found that trans residents of Tabasco carry identity documents that never match their gender, curtailing their rights across four socio-economic areas, among them banking, health care and dealings with police. Where no recognition route exists, mismatched documents invite police stops and institutional mistreatment.

Formal protections and their enforcement diverge across the country. Analysis published by Caroline Beer on the LSE USAPP blog (22 November 2024) found that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so rights exist formally but are rarely enjoyed in practice. Beer stated explicitly that her earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ people in Mexico are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

Trans people are killed in Tabasco as well as elsewhere in Mexico. The March 2024 report documented the murder of Karina Gómez, a trans woman, in Tabasco in August 2023.

An international human rights organisation reported on 31 March 2025 that many state/provinces now operate administrative procedures for legal gender recognition, called on those lacking such procedures to adopt them, and warned that implementation differs sharply from one state/province to another, and that where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

The state/province is on the wrong side of that divide. It has not reformed its legislation and operates no legal gender recognition procedure, one of eight state/provinces with none; two further state/provinces handle recognition in practice only, with no procedure in law.

The practical consequence is that documents and lived gender never line up. A human rights report of 6 March 2024, produced together with a local community centre for inclusion, found that trans residents carry identity documents that never match their gender, curtailing their rights across four socio-economic areas, among them banking, health care and dealings with police. Where no recognition route exists, mismatched documents invite police stops and institutional mistreatment.

Formal protections and their enforcement diverge across the country. Analysis published by a researcher on a university research blog (22 November 2024) found that the country's progressive LGBTQ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so rights exist formally but are rarely enjoyed in practice. The researcher stated explicitly that her earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ people in the country are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

Trans people are killed in the state/province as well as elsewhere in the country. The March 2024 report documented the murder of a trans woman in the state/province in August 2023.
31927357B81008000569871.localsOnly:

Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that the state has not reformed its legislation, leaving trans residents to carry documents that contradict their lived identity; the delays and refusals recorded in the state amplify everyday discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police.

The documentation of these conditions is local as well as international. The report of 6 March 2024 was produced together with a community centre for inclusion in Tabasco, which gathered on-the-ground accounts of the documentary mismatch and of its effects across four socio-economic areas.

The killing of Karina Gómez in Tabasco in August 2023 is part of the record the report sets against recognition failures, and her case has not been shown in the inventory as resolved.

Human Rights Watch has called explicitly on the states that lack a recognition procedure to adopt one, which places Tabasco's legislature among the bodies addressed by that demand.

31927357B81008000569871.tangentialFactors:
Transfemicide totals place Mexico among the highest in the world. Transgender Europe monitoring recorded 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico from 2008 to September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100.

Killings have drawn public protest. The Associated Press reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening period of that year, including activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, which triggered LGBTQ+ outrage and street demonstrations. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that violence against trans people and the murder of LGBTI+ defenders had increased over the previous year. The Human Rights Watch dispatch of 31 March 2025 also cited a trans woman found dead in the Carrizal River in August 2023 among the killings that frame its findings on document recognition.

One specific offence exists at sub-national level in Mexico. Mexico City's Congress approved the "Paola Buenrostro law" in July 2024, criminalising transfemicide; the law is named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished, and activists quoted at the time described the measure as critical to their feeling safe in the capital.

Regional oversight has been exercised directly. In 2024 the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded investigation of all LGBTI violations using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may reach alarming levels.

31927357B88239390016047.name: Tamaulipas
31927357B88239390016047.summary:
Legal gender recognition is unavailable in Tamaulipas. The Human Rights Watch state-by-state table of 31 March 2025 records that the state legislature has not reformed its legislation to create a legal gender recognition procedure for transgender people. The table places Tamaulipas among the eight Mexican states with no procedure at all, against 22 of 32 states that have legislated an administrative procedure, with two further states offering recognition in practice only. A trans person whose identity documents are issued in Tamaulipas therefore has no administrative route to change those documents to match their gender identity.

The gap persisted into 2026. On 4 February 2026 deputies of Tamaulipas's 66th legislature met LGBT+ civil-society groups, including Tamaulipas Diversidad, Vihda Trans A.C., Tendremos Alas A.C. and La Resistencia Trans, and agreed a joint agenda to push a Gender Identity Law alongside anti-discrimination and health reforms. The meeting recorded that these initiatives have been pending since June 2025 and that the absent law continues to limit trans people's access to health care, education and employment in the state.

Criminal law moves in the opposite direction to civil recognition. On 18 June 2025 the Tamaulipas state Congress unanimously approved reforms to the local Penal Code adding a chapter on crimes against sexual orientation, gender identity or gender expression. The reforms explicitly ban conversion therapies and carry prison terms of two to six years with fines of up to 2,000 UMA, rising by half where victims are minors, disabled or elderly, or where the conduct occurs in subordinate settings such as the family, medical care or the workplace.

31927357B22008724034476.name: Tlaxcala
31927357B22008724034476.summary:
Tlaxcala stands under Mexico's national framework and adds its own statute on top of it. The state congress's 2019 reform of the Civil Code (Decree D.113, dated 1 October 2019) created an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, and the decree text is published on the state congress's own site. The procedure requires no court proceeding, which is the legal basis a trans visitor would rely on to update identity documents in Tlaxcala.

Layered over that, the Supreme Court's ruling of 17 October 2018 makes a change of name and gender marker available through a simple administrative procedure founded on self-declaration. Document correction therefore does not depend on a judge's approval, on medical evidence, or on a surgical prerequisite.

Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of Mexico's 32 states had legislated a legal gender-recognition procedure, while six state legislatures had enacted none. Tabasco and Tamaulipas are among the states with no such procedure, so a visitor crossing a state boundary can move between a functioning administrative route and no route at all.

Other national protections apply within Tlaxcala: same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2022, and federal law has prohibited discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation since 2003.

Formal entitlements diverge from practice. Analysis published by Caroline Beer on the LSE USAPP blog on 22 November 2024 found that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, leaving rights that exist on paper largely unenjoyed. Beer stated explicitly that her earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ people in Mexico are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

Violence against trans people remains lethal and sustained. The Associated Press reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening period of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, which triggered LGBTQ+ outrage and street demonstrations. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that violence against trans people and the murder of LGBTI+ defenders had increased over the previous year.

Transgender Europe monitoring recorded 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a national total second only to Brazil's 100.

Responding to that record, Mexico City's Congress approved the Paola Buenrostro law in July 2024, criminalising transfemicide. The law is named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished, and activists quoted at the time described the measure as critical to their feeling safe in the capital. In 2024 the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded investigation of all LGBTI violations using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may reach alarming levels.

31927357B35199150741361.name: Yucatan
31927357B35199150741361.summary:
Yucatán offers an administrative route to legal gender recognition. A 2024 reform to the state's Civil Registry Law, published in the Diario Oficial of 26 April 2024, created a procedure through which transgender people can update the legal gender on their identity documents without a court order. Human Rights Watch's state-by-state rundown of 11 March 2025 carries Yucatán on that basis, and the procedure is the fact a trans visitor's document situation turns on when entering or being stopped in the state.

Yucatán stands under Mexico's unfinished national framework for recognition. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of Mexico's 32 states had legislated a legal gender-recognition procedure by that date and named six states whose legislatures had enacted none; Yucatán belongs to the 22. The same reporting warns that implementation differs sharply from one state to another, and that where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

Uneven implementation has concrete results. The Human Rights Watch report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" (6 March 2024) found that delays and refusals in name and gender recognition in Tabasco leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying everyday discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police. Those findings were set against killings including a trans woman found dead in the Carrizal River in August 2023.

Analysis published by Caroline Beer on the LSE USAPP blog (22 November 2024) found that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so rights exist formally but are rarely enjoyed in practice. Beer stated explicitly that her earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ people in Mexico are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

Trans-specific violence remains documented at scale. The Associated Press reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening period of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, which triggered LGBTQ+ outrage and street demonstrations. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that violence against trans people and the murder of LGBTI+ defenders had increased over the previous year. Transgender Europe monitoring recorded 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico from 2008 to September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a total second only to Brazil's 100.

Marriage equality in Yucatán is settled and has been for more than a decade. The Third District Court of the State of Yucatán ruled on 1 July 2013 that two petitioners were able to marry, and the first same-sex couple legally married in the state on 8 August 2013. The Yucatán Constitutional Court dismissed a challenge to the Civil Code's marriage provisions on 2 March 2015 and the federal Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on 31 May 2015. The Congress of Yucatán passed a constitutional amendment allowing same-sex marriage on 7 September 2021 and amended secondary legislation to permit it on 1 March 2022.

Regional oversight bodies have pressed the authorities. In 2024 the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded investigation of all LGBTI violations using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may reach alarming levels.

31927357B22408340646138.name: Zacatecas
31927357B22408340646138.summary:
Legal gender recognition is available across most of Mexico but not all of it. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of the country's 32 states had legislated a procedure for recognising a person's gender identity in official documents, and named six states whose legislatures had enacted none. Zacatecas is not among the six: it operates a legislated route to recognition.

Deputies of the 64th Legislature of Zacatecas approved a reform of the Family Code of Zacatecas on gender identity on 23 December 2022, by 14 votes in favour to 7 against, after the Justice Committee issued a positive opinion (dictamen). The reform establishes the possibility of issuing a new birth certificate recognising an applicant's gender identity, principally for the trans community.

The law has an administrative layer behind it. The Human Rights Watch state-by-state feature of March 2025 records that in 2023 the director of the state Civil Registry issued guidelines implementing the gender-recognition reform, and both the reform entry and the guidelines entry link to the official state gazette of Zacatecas.

Zacatecas's Penal Code also carries an explicit ban on practices aimed at changing gender identity. On 25 August 2021 the Congress of Zacatecas approved the prohibition and sanctioning of conversion therapies, or ECOSIG (Esfuerzos para Corregir la Orientación Sexual e Identidad de Género), by adding fraction VI to article 182 Bis of the Penal Code. Anyone who incites hatred or violence on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or who promotes such practices, faces one to three years' imprisonment or up to 300 days of community work. The same session typified hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity in the Penal Code.

Partnership recognition is settled at the national level: same-sex marriage has been legal across Mexico since 2009.

82249235B3191732862561.name: Prince Edward Island
82249235B3191732862561.summary:
Prince Edward Island stands under the national framework of Canada. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017, and courts have applied those protections consistently. Federal criminal law and human-rights protections apply in Prince Edward Island as they do across the country.

Legal gender recognition in Prince Edward Island carries no surgery requirement. A 2016 amendment to the Vital Statistics Act removed the prior surgery requirement and replaced it with a declaration of the gender the applicant identifies with, supported by a letter from a doctor. The regime has operated on that basis ever since. An adult born in the province may apply if resident there for at least three months; the application requires completed forms including a physician statement and a written statement by the applicant, signed before a commissioner of oaths at Vital Statistics.

Provincial photo ID can carry a non-binary or undisclosed marker. Since 4 December 2018 Islanders completing a driver's licence at Access PEI locations may select 'gender not listed', shown on the licence as X, or 'prefer not to say', shown as a blank, alongside male and female. The Government of Prince Edward Island stated that the province was the first jurisdiction in Canada to offer the 'prefer not to say' blank option.

National police-reported hate-crime data gives no Prince Edward Island figure. Statistics Canada reported 4,882 hate-crime incidents nationally in 2024, up 1% on 2023, at a rate of 12.1 per 100,000 population, down 2% in 2024 and up 142% since 2018, with eight provinces recording stable or declining rates. The release reports no Prince Edward Island-specific rate or incident count, and no provincially deviating pattern is documented for the province.

82249235B52639524229375.name: Quebec
82249235B52639524229375.summary:
Quebec is a province of Canada and stands under the national framework: gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017. Federal criminal law and the federal human-rights framework apply uniformly in Quebec. No jurisdiction restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities, federal identity documents can carry an X marker, and entry carries no trans-specific friction.

Provincial law adds a second layer. Quebec's Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms has listed gender identity and gender expression as prohibited grounds of discrimination since 2016, and the enforcement machinery produces outcomes: on 10 June 2024 the Quebec Human Rights Tribunal found that a Montreal bar discriminated against a trans woman in hiring on the basis of her gender identity and ordered the employer to pay $10,000 in moral damages, $4,000 in punitive damages and $118.40 for unpaid training. A trans visitor considering employment or service refusal in Quebec can point to a tribunal that has ruled this way in the recent past.

The province's rules on sex designation and identity documents were reshaped by litigation. After a two-month trial heard in front of 29 witnesses, the Quebec Superior Court held in 2021 QCCS 191 that provisions of the Civil Code of Quebec were invalid because they violated the fundamental rights of trans, intersex and non-binary people; the Quebec Court of Appeal largely upheld that decision in 2024 QCCA 348, and the ruling led to legislative reform of the Civil Code. Documents issued under the reformed regime should therefore reflect a visitor's stated sex designation, though the specific issuing practice in Quebec is not set out in the sources.

Correctional placement is the one area where Quebec has moved against the national direction. On 19 June 2025 CBC News reported that the Quebec public security minister announced that transgender inmates in the province will be incarcerated according to their anatomical sex rather than their gender identity, citing fairness and safety, in a directive issued just after trans woman Levana Ballouz sought a transfer to a women's prison following her conviction for murdering her partner and children. Advocates stated that the policy violates the Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms. This affects a transit visitor only in the event of detention, but it is a documented reversal of the previous practice of considering gender identity in correctional placement.

Manitoba stands under the national framework: Canada is among the safer large destinations for trans visitors, with gender identity and gender expression protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16 in 2017. Provincially, the Manitoba Human Rights Code already prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity. The NDP government has a bill before the Legislative Assembly to extend the Code to gender expression as well. Justice Minister Matt Wiebe says the change would align Manitoba with most other provinces and would cover preferred pronouns and outward presentation such as clothing. The bill was slated for debate later in 2025, and Charlie Eau, executive director of Trans Manitoba, welcomed it. Until it passes, gender expression is not itself a listed prohibited ground in Manitoba, though conduct based on gender identity remains covered.

Manitoba's recorded hate-crime exposure is low by national standards. Statistics Canada reported 4,882 police-reported hate-crime incidents nationally in 2024, a 1% rise on 2023, at a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000. Manitoba recorded a rate of 5.3 per 100,000, joint-lowest among the provinces with Newfoundland and Labrador, and no increase in 2024, placing it among the eight provinces whose rates were stable or declining. Federal criminal law and human-rights protections apply uniformly across the country, and police figures capture only incidents reported to and recorded by police. Egale Canada's 2024 hate-crime analysis report, an LGBTIQ+ organisation's reading of the same national police data, breaks out gender identity as a motivation alongside sexual orientation.

Oxenham said the day would show transgender, two-spirit and non-binary Manitobans that they are supported.

On 20 November 2023 the transgender flag was raised in Memorial Park in Winnipeg, an observance the province first held eight years earlier, with the flag raised by Logan Oxenham, the first openly trans man elected to the Manitoba legislature. Families minister Nahanni Fontaine and health minister Uzoma Asagwara said in a statement that the government supports and upholds the life-saving work of trans, two-spirit and gender-diverse Manitobans. Brandon advocate Anastasia Gibson said the day memorialises people murdered as a result of transphobia and that such violence shows no sign of slowing.

Sub-provincial policy turbulence in Canada is concentrated in schools and sport, and primarily affects minors and residents rather than visitors. Saskatchewan's 2023 Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act invoked the notwithstanding clause to require parental consent for students under 16 who ask to use a gender-related preferred name or to disclose their gender identity at school; human rights groups called for repeal and litigation followed. Alberta passed the Health Statutes Amendment Act, the Education Amendment Act and the Fairness and Safety in Sport Act in 2024, then shielded them from challenge through Bill 9, the Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025, again using the notwithstanding clause. Yukon's own record runs the other way, with its education minister publicly defending the territory's SOGI 123 school policy after an incident of flag vandalism.

Conditions inside correctional institutions are the weakest point in the Canadian record. Federal policy is that transgender prisoners are to be placed according to their gender identity, and prisoners held for more than 12 continuous months are to be considered for sex-reassignment surgery. Litigation has tested both placement and care: lawyer Barbara findlay represented the transgender prisoner Synthia Kavanagh in a case over gender-affirming medical treatment and placement in a women's institution. A 2022 report alleged that gender-diverse prisoners face a pattern of abuse and discrimination in Canadian jails and are more likely to be victims of sexual assault, while a 2022 study of Nova Scotia correctional officers found them generally mindful of trans-prisoner safety and security, with some concerns about risk to other prisoners. These concerns bear on transit visitors only if detained.

National hate-crime reporting is heavily urban-weighted, and the 2.5-fold gap between large-metropolitan and smaller-town rates suggests that recorded incidence in a small population such as Yukon's reflects reporting capacity as much as underlying victimisation.

82249235B23927232378620.name: Nunavut
82249235B23927232378620.summary:
Canada is among the safer large destinations for trans visitors, and Nunavut stands under that national framework. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017. Federal identity documents can carry an X marker, entry carries no trans-specific friction, and no jurisdiction in Canada restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities.

Nunavut layers its own statutory protection on top of that federal floor. In March 2017 Nunavut MLAs voted unanimously on third and final reading of Bill 31, amending the territory's Human Rights Act to add gender identity and gender expression alongside sexual orientation as protected grounds. Justice Minister Keith Peterson said the amendment would make clear that discrimination against transgender people is prohibited. At that point nine provinces and one territory listed gender identity or expression in their human-rights laws, which made Nunavut the first Canadian territory to do so.

Nunavut's Vital Statistics Act now carries a third sex designation on birth certificates. On 18 September 2025 MLAs voted 12-8 in committee of the whole to restore the non-binary option after the standing committee had struck it from Health Minister John Main's May 2025 bill; the bill then passed third reading. Sponsor Adam Arreak Lightstone said the Government of Nunavut now joins the rest of Canada in recognizing non-binary and transgender individuals.

The territorial government also funds transition-related care. From March 2022 Nunavut's Health Department funded breast augmentation, chest contouring, hysterectomy and vaginoplasty for transgender and non-binary residents under a partnership with the Metropolitan Centre of Surgery in Montreal. The local LGBTQ group Positive Space called the step overdue while flagging information gaps for residents outside the capital.

National hate-crime data sets the surrounding risk picture. Statistics Canada's release 'Police-reported hate crime in Canada, 2024', published 30 March 2026, records 4,882 police-reported hate-crime incidents, up 1% over the year and 169% since 2018, a rate of 11.9 per 100,000. Incidents motivated by gender identity or expression rose 8% to 139, a fourth consecutive annual increase and 184% above 2020. Sexual-orientation-motivated incidents fell 26% to 658, though June 2024 alone recorded 113 incidents against a monthly average near 50. Rates run roughly 2.5 times higher in metropolitan areas than in smaller towns, a gap that matters for a territory with no metropolitan reporting hub.

Egale Canada's 2024 hate-crime analysis report works through police-reported data including gender identity and expression motivations and supplies national 2SLGBTQ+ victimisation context rather than territorial figures.

82249235B23927232378620.tangentialFactors:
The correctional system is the weakest point in the Canadian record. Federal policy after Bill C-16 holds that transgender prisoners are to be placed according to their gender identity, and prisoners held for more than 12 continuous months are to be considered for sex-reassignment surgery. Lawyer Barbara findlay represented the transgender prisoner Synthia Kavanagh in litigation over gender-affirming medical treatment and placement in a women's institution. A 2022 report alleged a pattern of abuse and discrimination against gender-diverse prisoners and elevated risk of sexual assault, while a 2022 study of Nova Scotia correctional officers found them generally mindful of trans-prisoner safety with some concerns about risk to other prisoners. These conditions bear on a visitor only if detained.

Sub-provincial policy turbulence elsewhere in Canada is concentrated in schools and sport and falls mainly on minors and residents. Saskatchewan's 2023 Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act used the notwithstanding clause to require parental consent for students under 16 who ask to use a gender-related preferred name or their gender identity at school, drawing repeal calls and litigation. Alberta passed health, education and sport statutes in 2024 and shielded them through Bill 9, the Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025, again invoking the notwithstanding clause.

The pace of change in Nunavut contrasts with the 2017 baseline, when only nine provinces and one territory listed gender identity or expression in their human-rights laws; the territory now sits with the rest of Canada on non-binary recognition as well as on protected grounds.

The national statistics show divergent directions within the same year: gender identity and expression motivations climbed for a fourth consecutive year while sexual-orientation motivations fell, so an aggregate decline in hate crime does not describe the trans-specific trend.

14339913B95766344400054.name: England
14339913B95766344400054.summary:
England stands under the United Kingdom's national framework. Passport and document rules, entry and visa rules, marriage law and criminal law are uniform across the country, and the single-sex-services regime operates through the national equality legislation and the national equality watchdog, with no devolved layer between a visitor and those institutions. The United Kingdom Supreme Court sits in London and the Equality and Human Rights Commission's headquarters are in England, so the machinery that governs a trans visitor's day here is the machinery of the whole state.

The defining judgment is the unanimous ruling of the United Kingdom Supreme Court in For Women Scotland, handed down on 16 April 2025. The court held that "woman" and "sex" in the Equality Act 2010 mean biological woman and biological sex, and that a gender recognition certificate does not entitle a trans woman to the Act's sex-based protections. Lord Hodge said the ruling should not be read as reducing the Act's protection against discrimination for transgender people. Those definitions govern services, searches and detention allocation in England.

The Equality and Human Rights Commission, the body enforcing the Equality Act 2010 in England and Wales, updated its code of practice after the Supreme Court ruling. As reported on 20 May 2025, the code advises that services and businesses may ask a person for their birth certificate where there is "genuine concern" about biological sex, and that trans people may be excluded from single-sex sport "when necessary" for safety. This is the operative guidance a trans visitor meets at venues, on transport and in services from day to day.

Prison and custody allocation follows the same principle. On 19 June 2026 Lady Ross of the Outer House, Court of Session, struck down Scottish Prison Service guidance that had allowed some trans prisoners to be housed according to gender identity, holding that sex segregation in prisons must rest on a lawful basis in line with the April 2025 definition-of-a-woman ruling. The Supreme Court had already held that Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights confers no automatic right to accommodation with the opposite biological sex, and that UK-wide ruling governs England's prison and custody decisions. The first minister said the government will consider the judgment. A judicial review reported on 5 February 2026 tested how far the April 2025 ruling reaches into prison accommodation UK-wide: government lawyers argued that a blanket rule housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk, while For Women Scotland called the identity-based policy "Orwellian".

The Home Office's England-and-Wales hate-crime statistics, published 9 October 2025, record 115,990 police-recorded hate crimes in the year ending March 2025. The transgender strand fell 11% and the sexual-orientation strand fell 2% against the previous year. The bulletin cautions that recorded figures understate prevalence, with the Crime Survey estimating about 176,000 hate-crime incidents a year, and that a February 2024 Metropolitan Police recording-system change means earlier years over-counted. These are the official baseline figures for trans-hostile incidents in the jurisdiction where the national framework applies directly.

The first minister said the government will consider the judgment.

82085004B13995298844162.name: Queensland
82085004B13995298844162.summary:
Queensland is a state within Australia and stands under the national framework: the federal Sex Discrimination Act has protected gender identity since 2013. In August 2024 the Federal Court held in Tickle v Giggle that this protection extends to trans women as women and awarded damages against a female-only dating app that had excluded a trans woman member; Reuters reported the decision on 23 August 2024 as a national precedent on the exclusion of trans women from services under sex-discrimination law. The dispute arose out of organised exclusionary activism.

Federal hate-crime legislation (Act 1 of 2025) passed in February 2025 and took effect immediately, explicitly covering sex, sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex status with penalties of up to seven years' imprisonment. Vilification coverage at state level remains uneven across Australia: Queensland is one of the jurisdictions whose law covers gender identity, alongside South Australia and Tasmania, while New South Wales, the ACT and Victoria cover only sexual orientation and the Northern Territory and Western Australia cover neither.

Queensland's own discrimination law strengthened on 29 April 2024, when amendments commenced that moved serious vilification out of the Anti-Discrimination Act and into the Criminal Code, raising the maximum penalty from six months to three years' imprisonment. Those amendments explicitly extend protection to non-binary and gender-diverse people and broaden the definition of gender identity, as stated by the Queensland Human Rights Commission. The Commission has separately presented its account of the Anti-Discrimination Bill 2024 rewrite as a modernised gender identity attribute alongside revised vilification provisions.

Queensland was the first Australian state to criminalise conversion practices. The Health Legislation Amendment Bill 2019 passed the Queensland Parliament on 13 August 2020, criminalising electro-shock, drug and hypnotherapy practices aimed at changing a person's sexuality or gender identity, with fines and jail time for practitioners. Survivors told SBS the ban does not reach conversion practices in informal, non-healthcare settings.

Entry, facilities and relationship recognition carry no restriction: no Australian law confines bathrooms or changing facilities by gender identity, no border friction has been reported for trans travellers, and marriage equality has held since the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Act 2017 came into force on 9 December 2017 after a 61.6% Yes result in the national postal survey. Federal law has recognised same-sex couples as de facto partners since 2009, and overseas same-sex marriages are recognised automatically.

Care access for trans young people is the adverse measure in force for this visit window. In January 2025 Health Minister Tim Nicholls halted puberty blockers and hormone therapy for new public-system patients under 18 with gender dysphoria, formalised by a Queensland Health directive of 28 January 2025 that exempts patients already registered at the Queensland Children's Gender Service. The Queensland Supreme Court ruled the directive unlawful on 27 October 2025; a new ministerial directive reinstated substantially the same restrictions on 28 October 2025 pending reviews, and a legal challenge was filed in December 2025. Equality Australia has called Queensland an outlier state, and families affected by the pause report private treatment costs of hundreds of dollars per injection, approaching $2,000 in one case.

Detention runs on a stated rule with discretion attached. Queensland's inspection standards of August 2023, issued under the Inspector of Detention Services Act 2022, direct that transgender and intersex prisoners are generally admitted to facilities corresponding to their lived or experienced gender, but staff retain discretion at admission and transgender people who have undergone sexual reassignment surgery are excluded from that identity-based process. The 2009 Corrective Services procedure it replaced was assessed as largely ineffective.

82085004B14973555098025.name: South Australia
82085004B14973555098025.summary:
South Australia stands under the national framework: the federal Sex Discrimination Act has treated gender identity as a protected ground since 2013, and in August 2024 the Federal Court held in Tickle v Giggle that the protection extends to trans women as women, awarding damages against a female-only dating app that had excluded a trans woman member. The precedent binds service providers nationally, including in South Australia.

State law supplies a parallel remedy. The Equal Opportunity Act 1984 was amended in 2016 to protect gender identity and sexual orientation, so discrimination on that ground is actionable under South Australian statute as well as federal statute.

Identity documents are the clearest visitor-facing advantage. Since 23 May 2017, under the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration (Gender Identity) Amendment Act 2016 (royal assent 15 December 2016), a South Australian can change the sex descriptor on a birth certificate with appropriate clinical treatment, with no sex-reassignment surgery required and no forced divorce if married. Non-binary and 'indeterminate' sex descriptors are also available on state birth certificates. With the ACT, South Australia was one of the first two Australian jurisdictions to allow the sex recorded on a birth certificate to be changed without sex-reassignment surgery.

Hate-crime sentencing laws explicitly covering sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex characteristics passed and were implemented in November 2021, giving trans visitors protection at sentencing that some other Australian states lack.

Relationship recognition is settled: registered domestic relationships date from 1 August 2017, same-sex couples could adopt from 17 February 2017, and same-sex marriage has been legal since December 2017 under the federal Act, with the 2017 postal survey returning a 62.5% 'Yes' result in South Australia.

Criminal-law history runs in a protective direction. South Australia was the first Australian jurisdiction to decriminalise male homosexual activity, the law commencing 2 October 1975, and it was the last to abolish the gay-panic defence, doing so on 1 December 2020 with effect from 1 April 2021. The Conversion Practices Prohibition Act 2024 passed in October 2024 and is in legal effect from 1 April 2025.

Historical convictions are handled by a distinctive scheme: South Australia is the only Australian jurisdiction whose approach to historical gay convictions is 'spent' rather than expunged, under the Spent Convictions (Decriminalised Offences) Amendment Act 2013, in force 22 December 2013.

82085004B70793016411369.name: Tasmania
82085004B70793016411369.summary:
Tasmania stands under the Australian national framework. The federal Sex Discrimination Act has treated gender identity as a protected ground since 2013, and in August 2024 the Federal Court held in Tickle v Giggle that the protection extends to trans women as women, awarding damages against a female-only dating app that had excluded a trans woman member. A trans visitor to Tasmania can invoke that federal protection directly, and Tasmania is among the Australian jurisdictions whose vilification law also names gender identity as a protected ground. Federal hate-crime legislation in force since February 2025 expressly covers gender identity and intersex status, with penalties of up to seven years' imprisonment.

Male homosexual conduct ceased to be criminal in Tasmania with effect from 14 May 1997. The Commonwealth Human Rights (Sexual Conduct) Act commenced on 19 December 1994, but Tasmania kept its Criminal Code provisions until faced with a likely adverse outcome in Croome v Tasmania, at which point it repealed them and became the final Australian jurisdiction to do so. The age of consent is 17, a threshold shared only with South Australia.

Identity-document rules are permissive. In April 2019 Tasmania's House of Assembly passed the Marriage Amendments Bill on 10 April 2019, after the Legislative Council had already approved it and after Liberal Speaker Sue Hickey crossed the floor to vote with the Opposition. The reforms make gender on birth certificates optional, remove any requirement that a transgender person undergo surgery for their gender to be recognised, and allow people aged 16 or over to change their registered gender without parental approval. As of 2019 Tasmania also issues 'X' sex descriptors on birth certificates. The Tasmanian Government opposed the amendments and declined to rule out later repeal.

Nothing in the sourced material imposes facility restrictions, medical screening or entry friction on trans travellers to Tasmania. Marriage equality has held nationally since the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Act came into force on 9 December 2017, federal law has recognised same-sex couples as de facto partners since 2009, and Tasmania allows same-sex couples to enter registered domestic partnerships with an optional official ceremony. Same-sex couples have had equal adoption rights in every Australian state and territory since April 2018.

No state-specific incident series or enforcement pattern is documented for Tasmania, and the available evidence for trans equality there is enactment-level rather than case-level.

The national patchwork around Tasmania continues to shift. The Queensland Human Rights Commission has announced better discrimination protections for gender-diverse people as part of that state's discrimination-law reform, and Victoria's Anti-vilification Act 2025 will add gender identity to its covered grounds when it takes effect on 30 June 2026, while New South Wales, the ACT and Victoria cover only sexual orientation in their vilification provisions and the Northern Territory and Western Australia cover neither ground.

Care access for trans minors has tightened in other Australian states, which shapes the national conversation a visitor may encounter. Queensland paused new public-health prescriptions of puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones for under-18s in January 2025, the Queensland Supreme Court ruled that directive unlawful on 27 October 2025, a replacement directive restored substantially the same restrictions on 28 October 2025, and a legal challenge was filed in December 2025. A New South Wales independent review released in September 2024 found puberty blockers safe, effective and reversible while calling for further long-term research.

Detention policy elsewhere in Australia runs on stated rules with attached discretion: Queensland's inspection standards of August 2023 direct that transgender and intersex prisoners are generally housed according to lived or experienced gender, but admission staff keep discretion and people who have undergone sexual reassignment surgery sit outside that identity-based process.

The national climate of contest is visible in the 2019 Tasmanian passage itself, where the gender-marker reforms cleared the lower house only after the Speaker broke with her own party and the government publicly opposed them.

82085004B12086860067424.name: Other Territories
82085004B12086860067424.summary:
Australia treats gender identity as a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act 1984, which was amended by the Sex Discrimination Amendment (Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity and Intersex Status) Act 2013. Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex status is prohibited alongside sex, marital or relationship status, pregnancy and breastfeeding across areas of public life including work, accommodation, education and the provision of goods and services. As a Commonwealth statute applying throughout Australia, including the external territories governed directly by Commonwealth law, this is the anti-discrimination framework a visitor on Norfolk Island, Christmas Island, the Cocos (Keeling) Islands or Jervis Bay territory stands under.

In August 2024 the Federal Court held in Tickle v Gigble that this protection extends to trans women as women, awarding damages against a female-only dating app that had excluded a trans woman member. Reuters reported the outcome on 23 August 2024 as a landmark case in gender-identity discrimination.

None of the territories in this group has its own territory-specific statute covering sexual orientation, gender identity or intersex status, and no divergence from the national framework is documented in the sources. Each instead sits inside a state legislative scheme: Norfolk Island has been incorporated into New South Wales legislation from 1 July 2016 under the Norfolk Island Legislation Amendment Act 2015 and the Territories Legislation Amendment Act 2016, while Christmas Island and the Cocos (Keeling) Islands, the Australian Indian Ocean Territories, are jurisdictions where Western Australian laws apply. Jervis Bay territory stands under the national and New South Wales framework on the same basis.

The federal hate-crime legislation passed in February 2025 (Act 1 of 2025, effective immediately) explicitly covers sex, sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex status, with penalties of up to seven years' imprisonment. Vilification coverage beneath that layer remains uneven across Australia: New South Wales, the ACT and Victoria cover only sexual orientation, South Australia, Tasmania and Queensland also cover gender identity, and the Northern Territory and Western Australia cover neither.

No law in the parent framework confines bathrooms or changing facilities by gender identity, and no border friction has been reported for trans travellers entering Australia or its territories. An 'X' sex descriptor on identity documents is available across the states and territories with concurrent federal protection, and same-sex adult private sexual conduct has been legal nationally since the Human Rights (Sexual Conduct) Act 1994 commenced on 19 December 1994.

Marriage equality has held since the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Act 2017 came into force on 9 December 2017 after a 61.6% Yes result in the national postal survey. Federal law has recognised same-sex couples as de facto partners since 2009, and overseas same-sex marriages are recognised automatically.

Care access is where official policy has tightened, and the tightest measures are in the state layer that governs these territories' neighbouring jurisdictions. Since November 2017 a transgender child could access puberty blockers and hormone treatment without court approval where child, parents and doctors agree, with surgery generally unavailable until 18. In January 2025 the Queensland government paused new prescriptions of puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones for under-18s in public health services, exempting existing patients; the Queensland Supreme Court ruled the directive unlawful on 27 October 2025, and a new ministerial directive reinstated substantially the same restrictions on 28 October 2025 pending reviews, with a legal challenge filed in December 2025. A New South Wales independent review released in September 2024 found puberty blockers safe, effective and reversible while calling for more long-term research.

Detention carries a stated rule with discretion attached in the jurisdictions whose law reaches these territories. Queensland's inspection standards of August 2023, issued under the Inspector of Detention Services Act 2022, direct that transgender and intersex prisoners are generally admitted to facilities corresponding to their lived or experienced gender, but staff retain discretion at admission, and transgender people who have undergone sexual reassignment surgery are excluded from that identity-based process. The 2009 Corrective Services procedure it replaced was assessed as largely ineffective.

14911670B45290909693812.tangentialFactors:
Brazil's national legislature contains organised pressure against the existing framework. OutRight International records that the country's significant LGBTIQ legal advances face repeal pressure in a conservative Congress, so protections that a visitor relies on are contested politically even where they are settled in law.

Political representation of trans people has moved quickly. The first transgender federal legislators, Salabert and Hilton, were elected in 2022, and over 3,000 openly LGBTQ candidates ran in the 2024 municipal elections. In the October 2024 municipal elections close to 1,000 transgender candidates stood across every state of the country and received death threats and intimidation, while the number of trans officeholders tripled compared with the previous cycle.

The comparison class for a visitor arriving from elsewhere in the region is favourable on paper. An OAB/SP guide for expatriates places Brazil among the most progressive jurisdictions in Latin America for LGBTQ protections, covering same-sex marriage under CNJ Resolution 175/2013, joint adoption, name and gender-marker change without surgery, and the criminalisation of homophobia and transphobia as equivalent to racism.

Violence risk is documented independently of the legal text. A May 2024 investigation documented 'boa noite, Cinderela' drink-spiking robberies in which LGBTQIA+ people are targeted in São Paulo nightlife, in a city preparing for a Pride event that draws thousands of tourists. Courts have also applied the anti-discrimination provisions to commercial conduct: the 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing.

Protection machinery has widened. An analysis of case law from 2022 records lower courts pressing the Superior Court of Justice toward unanimously extending the remedies of the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women, bringing trans people within the country's violence-prevention statutes.
