14911670B32365136910534.name: Piaui
14911670B32365136910534.summary:
Piauí stands under Brazil's national framework for LGBTI people, and the source inventory records no state-level deviation from it. A trans visitor's status, documents and family recognition are therefore handled under the same rules that operate everywhere in the country, and Piauí's own courts have engaged with that machinery: a 2021 record documents a gender-recognition judgment issued through the state's judiciary.

Legal gender change requires no surgery, hormones or medical diagnosis, under the Supreme Federal Tribunal ruling of 1 March 2018, and proceeds by self-determination. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since the National Council of Justice resolution of 14 May 2013, carried 14-1, with joint adoption available since 2010 and full adoption rights since 2015. An expat legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide, so entry and family matters are assessed on the same footing as for anyone else.

On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court held discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity to be a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines. Courts have applied the prohibition to commercial conduct: the 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing, affirming the compensation ordered at first instance in Barra Bonita.

No third-gender option exists on identity documents nationwide, but civil-registry entries recording 'non-binary/unspecified' have been possible since 2020, and a Superior Court of Justice ruling of 6 May 2025 permits neutral-gender registry rectification and treats it as precedent. Documents therefore do not yet carry a non-binary marker in the ordinary case, and a visitor whose papers show a marker inconsistent with presentation should expect inspection at entry.

Detention carries a specific regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed. Recognition as LGBTI for these purposes rests on self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing; the judge must set out the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it the general population or a specific wing or cell. The declared preference is recorded, a later change of placement is possible, and transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

Practice does not reliably follow that framework. A peer-reviewed census of travestis and transgender women held in Rio de Janeiro state prisons between April and June 2021 interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates inside eleven units treated as masculine in the metropolitan region. It documents that such inmates are housed in units operated as masculine, with some held in so-called neutral or security units, and treats placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights.

The protective text of the law does not describe what people routinely encounter. OutRight International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records that LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions, and that the country retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people. A May 2024 investigation documented 'boa noite, Cinderela' drink-spiking robberies in which LGBTQIA+ people are targeted in São Paulo nightlife. In the October 2024 municipal elections, close to 1,000 transgender candidates stood across every state of the country and received death threats and intimidation.

Protection machinery has widened in parallel. An analysis of case law from 2022 records lower courts pressing the Superior Court of Justice toward unanimously extending the remedies of the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women, bringing trans people within the country's violence-prevention statutes.

14911670B1613159902410.name: Rondonia
14911670B1613159902410.summary:
Rondônia stands under the national framework of Brazil, where same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since the National Council of Justice Resolution of 14 May 2013, adopted by a 14-1 vote, with joint adoption permitted since 2010 and full marital rights since 2015. The Supreme Federal Tribunal ruling of 1 March 2018 removed surgery, hormone therapy and diagnosis as conditions for legal gender-marker change, and the age of consent is equal regardless of sexual orientation.

On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court held in ADO 26 and MI 4733 that discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity constitute a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, carrying imprisonment of one to five years and fines. Federal anti-discrimination provisions cover sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds, so a trans visitor's documents and entry are assessed under the same rules as anyone else's.

Documents remain the sharpest friction. There is no third-gender option in national identity documents, although civil-registry entries marked non-binary or unspecified have been possible since 2020, and a Superior Court of Justice ruling of 6 May 2025 allows rectification of gender to a neutral marker and treats the decision as precedent. Gender-marker change otherwise proceeds by self-determination.

Risk of violence does not track the statute. Brazil retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, most acutely affecting trans people, and enforcement of the protections is uneven in practice. The advances themselves face repeal pressure from a conservative Congress.

Political visibility is measurable. Salabert and Hilton became the country's first transgender federal legislators in 2022, and more than 3,000 openly LGBTQ candidates stood in the 2024 municipal elections.

14911670B86532577506919.name: Sergipe
14911670B86532577506919.summary:
Sergipe stands under Brazil's national framework. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since the National Council of Justice Resolution of 14 May 2013, adopted on a 14-1 vote; joint adoption has been available since 2010 with full equal rights from 2015; and a person may change their name and gender marker without surgery, hormones or a diagnosis under the Supreme Federal Tribunal ruling of 1 March 2018. A trans visitor's documents and family status are therefore handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry and in matters of marriage and adoption.

On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court held that discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, carrying imprisonment of one to five years and fines. Brazilian courts have applied that provision to commercial conduct: the 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing. An expatriate legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide.

No third-gender option exists in national identity documents. Civil registries have nevertheless been able to record 'non-binary/unspecified' entries since 2020, and a Superior Court of Justice ruling of 6 May 2025 permits rectification of the registry to a neutral gender, established as precedent for lower courts.

The statutory text does not describe what people routinely encounter. OutRight International's country report of 12 March 2026 records that Brazil retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, trans people above all, and that the legal advances face repeal pressure in a conservative Congress. The same report notes that gender-marker change proceeds by self-determination.

Enforcement also varies geographically. The April 2026 law-firm guide reports that major cities including São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Brasília, Belo Horizonte, Curitiba and Florianópolis are broadly welcoming with established legal infrastructure, while smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction despite identical legal rights. Sergipe's smaller municipalities fall on the less-resourced side of that division.

Detention carries a specific regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed. LGBTI status is recognised by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing. A judge fixes the place of deprivation of liberty in a reasoned decision after consulting the person, setting out the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and asking trans, travesti and intersex people which they prefer, and within it whether the general population or a specific wing or cell. The preference is recorded, later changes of placement are possible, and transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

Practice does not reliably follow that framework. A peer-reviewed census carried out between April and June 2021 interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates inside eleven units treated as masculine in one large state's metropolitan prison system, finding that travestis and trans women are held in units operated as masculine, some in so-called neutral or security units, and characterising placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights. Protection machinery has widened in parallel: analysis of case law from 2022 records lower courts pressing the Superior Court of Justice toward unanimously extending the remedies of the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women.

The protective text does not describe routine experience. 14911670B28216513632935.name: Espirito Santo
14911670B28216513632935.summary:
Espirito Santo stands under Brazil's national framework for LGBTI people, which applies uniformly in every state of the country. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since May 2013 under National Council of Justice Resolution 175/2013, binding on all civil registries after a 14-1 vote, and on 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court ruled, in the ADO 26 case, that discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is a crime equivalent to racism under Lei 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines.

A trans visitor entering Espirito Santo is handled on the same footing as anyone else in matters of entry, status and family law. Name and gender-marker changes require no surgery, spousal-visa equality applies, joint adoption has been available since 2015, and LGB people serve openly in the armed forces. Explicit national discrimination protections have been in force since 2019.

The protective framework is thinner in places than it appears. Outright International's 2026 country status records that the 2019 ruling makes discrimination and hate crimes based on sexual orientation and gender identity federally criminal, but that no specific federal anti-discrimination statute exists, and that repeal efforts are active in Congress. The Superior Court of Justice ruled in 2023 that nonbinary people may amend their civil records, while intersex people still lack specific legal protections.

Within Espirito Santo the practical picture splits by settlement size. Larger cities carry established legal infrastructure for name changes, marriage registration and counsel, whereas smaller cities and rural areas carry more social friction for visibly trans people. The state's capital region and its interior municipalities are therefore not equivalent settings for a trans traveller.

14911670B46470234103867.name: Sao Paulo
14911670B46470234103867.summary:
São Paulo state stands under Brazil's national framework, which is applied uniformly across all 27 states. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since May 2013 under National Council of Justice Resolution 175/2013, binding on every civil registry after a 14-1 vote, and joint adoption has been available since 2015. Name and gender-marker changes require no surgery, spousal-visa equality operates on the same footing as for any other traveller, and lesbian, gay and bisexual people serve openly in the armed forces. A trans visitor's documents and status are therefore handled on the ordinary terms at entry and in family matters.

On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court ruled in ADO 26 that discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is a crime equivalent to racism under Lei 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines. Transphobia is prosecuted on that footing, and the provision has been applied to commercial conduct inside the state: the 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing, affirming the compensation ordered at first instance in Barra Bonita. A visitor who faces discriminatory conduct in São Paulo can invoke the same provision.

No specific federal anti-discrimination statute exists; the protection rests on the 2019 ruling and constitutional provisions, and repeal efforts have been tabled in Congress. In 2023 the Superior Court of Justice allowed non-binary people to amend their civil records, while intersex people have no specific legal protections.

The protective text of the law does not describe what people routinely encounter. Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records that LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions. A May 2024 investigation documented 'boa noite, Cinderela' drink-spiking robberies in which LGBTQIA+ people are targeted in São Paulo nightlife, in a city that hosts Pride events drawing thousands of tourists.

Arrest carries a specific and contested regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed. A person is recognised as LGBTI by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing; the judge must set out the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units, ask trans, travesti and intersex people their preference, and record it in a reasoned decision. Placement can be changed later, transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat, LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

Practice does not reliably follow that framework. A peer-reviewed census carried out between April and June 2021 in Rio de Janeiro state prisons interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates inside eleven units treated as masculine, and documents that travestis and trans women are held in masculine-operated units, with some placed in so-called neutral or security units; it treats placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights. Comparable national norms from 2014 and 2020 permit people to be housed where they choose, including in units denominated masculine.

1811400B81659894240990.name: Puducherry
1811400B81659894240990.summary:
Puducherry is a union territory of India with a partial legislature. Legal recognition of gender identity, identity-document rules and welfare policy for transgender people are set principally by the central government in New Delhi, and no Puducherry-specific statute, enforcement series or incident pattern is on file. The framework a visitor meets in Puducherry is therefore the national one.

That framework was rewritten in March 2026. India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill, which amends the 2019 law by removing the right to self-identification, narrowing the statutory definition of transgender person, and limiting legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner and to intersex individuals. The bill also mandates medical certification as a condition of identity recognition. Both houses approved the measure and it awaited presidential assent as of the most recent reporting.

Human Rights Watch, writing on 26 March 2026, calls the amendment a major reversal of the rights affirmed by the Supreme Court's 2014 third-gender ruling and has urged the president not to sign it. The government's stated case is that the narrower definition improves the delivery of welfare schemes. Critics counter that the exclusion catches trans men, trans women and non-binary and gender-fluid people who identify outside the recognised categories, and that compulsory medical certification is an attack on privacy and dignity.

The entry and stay baseline is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and the same court has held that discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity falls within the Article 15 prohibition of discrimination by sex. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had protected trans persons from sexual violence, and trans people interviewed for reporting expressed fear of a rise in assaults as a result.

Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person who had been required to undergo a medical examination by passport authorities. In November 2024 an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel even though she presented her PAN card. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at the station under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have described degrading treatment in custody.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic, while victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. Bans flowing from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating.

Care access is set at the level of Indian states and the centre rather than by Puducherry. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha run transgender welfare boards coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions, and several states provide targeted welfare, housing and healthcare benefits for hijras. Nationally, the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community. In August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.

Intersex minors remain at risk. Reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations, and in April 2019 the Madras High Court ordered the Tamil Nadu government to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.

1811400B55669546485086.name: Lakshadweep
1811400B55669546485086.summary:
Lakshadweep stands under India's national framework. As a union territory without a full legislature, it has no separate trans statute: legal recognition, policing practice and identity-document rules that reach a visitor or resident are set by the central government. No Lakshadweep-specific recognition policy, enforcement series or incident pattern is on file.

Recognition narrowed in March 2026. The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill passed both houses of Parliament and, as of the source dates, awaited presidential assent; Human Rights Watch, writing on 26 March 2026, called it a major reversal of the 2014 rights framework and urged the president not to sign it. The bill amends the 2019 law by removing the right to self-identification affirmed by the Supreme Court's 2014 third-gender ruling, narrowing the statutory definition of a transgender person, and mandating medical certification for identity recognition.

Legal recognition is now limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. The government argues the narrower definition improves delivery of welfare schemes; critics warn it excludes trans men, trans women, non-binary and gender-fluid people, and describe mandatory medical certification as an attack on privacy and dignity. The activist Akkai Padmashali characterises the amendment as criminalising and as an attack on the right to exist. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which the Supreme Court has read to cover gender identity; the Allahabad High Court extended that in 2021 to bar employment discrimination on sexual orientation grounds. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person who had been asked to take a medical examination by passport authorities. In November 2024 an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at the station under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender persons arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic; victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities.

1811400B80305611676067.name: Gujarāt
1811400B80305611676067.summary:
Gujarat stands under the national framework of India. The Parliament of India passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, and the source inventory records no Gujarat-specific legal or enforcement deviation material enough to distinguish the state from the national baseline on trans recognition, documents or policing.

The amendment removes the right to self-identification affirmed by the Supreme Court of India's 2014 judgment and limits legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, together with intersex individuals. Self-identified trans men, trans women and non-binary people fall outside the recognition scheme. Identity recognition now requires medical certification, so a trans traveller's document practice in Gujarat rests on that certification rather than on self-declaration.

Human Rights Watch described the bill as a major setback that strips thousands of people of rights and increases their risk. The bill passed both houses of Parliament and awaits presidential assent, and opposition parties and the LGBTQ community protested its approval. The government argues the change widens access to welfare benefits; critics counter that it excludes many transgender, non-binary and gender-fluid people.

Recognition and treatment remain uneven across India, with continuing discrimination reported in education, healthcare and formal employment. A trans visitor to Gujarat should expect entry, screening and document checks to be governed by this narrowed national recognition scheme, with no state-level safeguard recorded in the sources.

No Sikkim-specific trans statute, enforcement series or incident record is on file. Sikkim stands under India's national framework, which supplies the recognition, document and policing baseline a trans visitor will meet in Gangtok and at entry points elsewhere in the country.

India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, in both houses, and the measure awaits presidential assent. It amends the 2019 Act, removes the right to self-identification affirmed by the Supreme Court's 2014 third-gender judgment, and redefines transgender identity.

Legal recognition under the amended scheme is limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner and to intersex individuals. Self-identified trans men, trans women and non-binary people fall outside the recognition scheme, and medical certification is mandatory for identity recognition. A visitor whose documents reflect a gender marker outside those categories should expect the certification requirement to govern how identity is established at counters in Sikkim as elsewhere in India.

Human Rights Watch described the bill as a major setback that strips thousands of people of rights and increases their risk, and noted that as national law it sets the recognition baseline for visitors and residents across every Indian state and union territory, including this one.

1811400B82358585030651.name: Odisha
1811400B82358585030651.summary:
Odisha has no trans-specific statute of its own. It stands under India's national framework, and that framework narrowed in March 2026: India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill, which removes the right to self-identification affirmed by the Supreme Court's 2014 judgment and limits legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Self-identified trans men, trans women and non-binary people fall outside the recognition scheme, and medical certification is mandatory for identity recognition. Human Rights Watch called the bill a major setback that strips thousands of their rights and increases their risk. As national law it sets the recognition baseline for visitors and residents in every Indian state and union territory, including Odisha.

The amendment cleared both houses of Parliament and, as of 26 March 2026, awaited presidential assent. It redefines transgender identity within the 2019 Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act and removes the self-identification right. Opposition parties and members of the LGBTQ community protested the change. The government argues it makes welfare benefits more accessible; critics, among them rights activists such as Akkai Padmashali, say it excludes transgender, non-binary and gender-fluid people and attacks the right to exist. The Supreme Court's 2014 third-gender ruling remains the reference point for recognition, but recognition remains uneven and discrimination continues in education, healthcare and formal employment.

Entry and stay sit on a mixed baseline. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which courts have interpreted to cover gender identity. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed legal safeguards that had protected trans persons from sexual violence, and trans people fear a rise in assaults because the new code omits the gender-identity-specific offences the old law carried.

Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person who had been asked to take a medical exam by passport authorities. In November 2024 an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at the station under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender persons arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic; victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. Bans on conversion therapy from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating.

Facilities and care access are largely set at state level. Odisha runs a transgender welfare board alongside Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Maharashtra, coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions. Nationally, the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community, and in August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.

Intersex minors remain at risk: reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations, and the Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.

Odisha's provision is best read against neighbouring and peer states rather than against a local statute. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha all maintain transgender welfare boards, and several states provide targeted welfare, housing and healthcare benefits for hijras; Odisha therefore sits inside the more accommodating group of states on paper, even as the national recognition scheme narrowed in March 2026.

Reporting on trans encounters with authority contradicts itself. A foreign government's December 2025 country policy note judges police abuse of LGBT+ people to be limited and non-systemic, while victim interviews documented in June 2024 describe abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. Both readings can hold at once: a pattern that is scattered nationally can still be severe at the point of contact.

Protective judicial orders in India are territorially uneven. The S. Sushma guidelines of June 2021 and the April 2019 order banning sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants were issued by the Madras High Court and direct Tamil Nadu and central bodies, so they do not by themselves bind Odisha's police, hospitals or schools.

1811400B23769854471902.name: Ladākh
1811400B23769854471902.summary:
Ladakh is a union territory of India and stands under India's national framework as rewritten by the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill, which both houses of India's Parliament passed in March 2026. As national law the amendment sets the recognition baseline for a trans visitor in Ladakh, whatever the union territory's own administration does.

The amendment removes the right to self-identification affirmed by the Supreme Court of India's 2014 judgment, limits legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner and to intersex individuals, and mandates medical certification for identity recognition. Self-identified trans men, trans women and non-binary people fall outside the scheme altogether. For a visitor, the practical consequence is that identity-document practice in Ladakh runs through medical certification and category membership rather than self-declaration, and a person who identifies outside those categories has no route to legal recognition while in the territory.

Human Rights Watch described the amendment as a major setback that strips thousands of people of their rights and increases their exposure to abuse. Reporting by BBC News records that the amendment still awaited presidential assent when both houses approved it, that opposition parties and the LGBTQ community protested its passage, and that the government presents the change as widening access to welfare benefits while critics say it excludes transgender, non-binary and gender-fluid people.

Entry and stay sit on a mixed baseline. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court of India in 2018, and courts have read the constitutional prohibition of discrimination on grounds including sex to cover gender identity, with the Allahabad High Court extending that reasoning in 2021 to bar employment discrimination on sexual-orientation grounds. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership anywhere in India, so a trans visitor's partner has no legal standing in Ladakh, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had protected trans persons from sexual violence, and trans people interviewed for reporting say they fear a rise in assaults as a result. Recognition itself remains uneven across India, with continuing discrimination reported in education, healthcare and formal employment, and that national condition travels with a visitor into clinics, schools and workplaces in Ladakh.

HRW calls it a major setback that strips thousands of rights and increases risk. As national law it sets the recognition baseline for visitors and residents across every Indian state and union territory, including this one.

1811400B23769854471902.tangentialFactors:
Identity checkpoints are a recurring source of friction in India and there is no reporting available on how they operate inside Ladakh. In November 2024 an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel even though she presented her PAN card. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person who had been required by passport authorities to take a medical exam, a judgment that bears directly on the new certification requirement. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at a station while claiming to check her gender, and transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have described degrading treatment in custody.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic, while victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. Bans flowing from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine conversion-therapy networks that continue to operate.

Intersex minors remain at risk. Reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations, and the Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants. That order binds Tamil Nadu, not Ladakh.

1811400B37341166588993.name: Rājasthān
1811400B37341166588993.summary:
Rājasthān stands under India's national framework on gender identity, and no state-level deviation from that framework has been sourced. The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill 2026 was passed by both houses of India's Parliament in March 2026 and awaits presidential assent, so the recognition rules a visitor encounters in this state are those of the amended national statute.

The amendment removes the right to self-identification that the 2014 Supreme Court third-gender judgment had established and that the 2019 Act carried forward. Legal recognition is now limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Self-identified trans men, trans women and non-binary people fall outside the recognition scheme entirely, and recognition is tied to medical certification rather than to the applicant's own declaration.

Human Rights Watch described the bill as a major setback on 26 March 2026, stating that it strips thousands of people of rights and increases their exposure to risk. As national law it sets the recognition baseline for visitors and residents in every Indian state and union territory, Rājasthān included.

Recognition remains uneven in practice, and the discrimination the amended regime sits alongside continues in education, healthcare and formal employment across the country. A trans visitor to Rājasthān should therefore expect document encounters governed by medical certification, and should not assume that a self-declared gender marker will be accepted by state authorities.

1811400B49281905528064.name: Mizoram
1811400B49281905528064.summary:
Mizoram stands under India's national framework, which applies directly to the state. India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, replacing the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Presidential assent remained pending as of late March 2026.

Human Rights Watch reported on 26 March 2026 that the amendment removes self-identification, requires medical certification for identity recognition, and reverses the 2014 Supreme Court ruling that had recognised gender identity on the applicant's own assertion. The same report records new offences carrying up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring anyone into being transgender, which Human Rights Watch warns could criminalise the support networks trans people rely on. Of 487,803 transgender persons recorded in the census, only about 32,500 hold identity cards. Human Rights Watch urged the president not to sign the bill.

BBC reporting of 26 March 2026 states that recognition now rests on biological or physical traits alongside traditional identities, with medical boards and district authorities required to certify gender-affirming surgery. The government presents the narrower definition as targeting welfare benefits and anti-trafficking protection; critics warn that it excludes many trans men, trans women and non-binary people. A Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel asked the government to withdraw the bill, describing the removal of self-identification as a setback against the 2014 ruling. India is estimated to have around two million transgender people.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which courts have interpreted to cover gender identity. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed legal safeguards that had protected trans persons from sexual violence, and trans people fear a rise in assaults because the new code omits the gender-identity-specific offences the old law carried.

Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person who had been asked to take a medical examination by passport authorities. In November 2024 an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at the station under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender persons arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic; victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. Bans on conversion therapy from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating.

Facilities and care access are largely set at state level. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha run transgender welfare boards coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions. Nationally, the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community.

Intersex minors remain at risk: reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations, and the Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.

Manipur stands under India's national framework. No Manipur-specific trans statute, recognition scheme, welfare board or enforcement campaign is reported in the sources, and the operative law is the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2019 as amended in 2026.

India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill on 26 March 2026. The amendment removes the self-identification route that the 2019 Act provided and that the Supreme Court's 2014 judgment established, and restricts legal recognition to historically recognised socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, together with intersex persons. Presidential assent remained pending as of late March 2026. Human Rights Watch urged the president not to sign the bill, and a Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel asked the government to withdraw it, describing the removal of self-identification as a setback to the 2014 ruling.

1811400B97532436596698.tangentialFactors:
The 2026 amendment sits against a baseline that is mixed rather than uniformly restrictive. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which courts have read to cover gender identity; the Supreme Court has held that discrimination on sexual orientation and gender identity falls within Article 15, and the Allahabad High Court extended that in 2021 to employment. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the legal safeguards that had protected trans persons from sexual violence, and trans people fear a rise in assaults because the new code omits the gender-identity-specific offences the old law carried.

Protection machinery is unevenly enforced. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. Bans on conversion therapy from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks that still operate.

Facilities and welfare responses vary sharply between Indian states. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha run transgender welfare boards coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions, and several states provide targeted welfare, housing and healthcare benefits for hijras. Whether Manipur operates an equivalent body is not established by the sources.

1811400B3558497485804.name: Uttarākhand
1811400B3558497485804.summary:
Uttarakhand has no trans-specific statute, enforcement series or documented incident pattern of its own. The national framework of India governs encounters with police, identity documents and public services in the state, and nothing in the sourced record shows a divergent state policy.

India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, narrowing the 2019 law. Human Rights Watch, reporting on 26 March 2026, states that the amendment removes self-identification, restricts legal recognition to traditionally recognised groups such as hijra and kinner and to intersex persons, and requires medical certification of identity, reversing the 2014 Supreme Court ruling that had established self-identification. The bill adds offences carrying up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring anyone to be transgender; HRW warns that this could criminalise support networks. Of 487,803 census-recorded transgender persons, about 32,500 hold identity cards. HRW urged the president not to sign the bill, and assent was pending as of late March 2026.

BBC reporting of the same date records that recognition now rests on biological or physical traits alongside traditional identities, with medical boards and district authorities required to certify gender-affirming surgery. The government presents the narrower definition as targeting welfare benefits and anti-trafficking protection; critics warn that it excludes many trans men, trans women and non-binary people. A Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel asked the government to withdraw the bill, calling removal of self-identification a setback against the 2014 ruling. India is estimated to have around two million transgender people.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which courts have interpreted to cover gender identity; the Supreme Court has held that discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity falls within Article 15, and the Allahabad High Court extended that in 2021 to bar employment discrimination on sexual orientation grounds. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed legal safeguards that had protected trans persons from sexual violence, and trans people fear a rise in assaults because the new code omits the gender-identity-specific offences the old law carried.

Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person who had been asked to take a medical exam by passport authorities. In November 2024 an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at the station under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender persons arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic; victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. Bans on conversion therapy from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating.

Facilities and care access are largely set at state level. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha run transgender welfare boards coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions, and several states provide targeted welfare, housing and healthcare benefits for hijras. Nationally, the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community. 1811400B75807316846587.name: Madhya Pradesh
1811400B75807316846587.summary:
Madhya Pradesh has no state-specific transgender statute and no documented state-level enforcement series. Legal uniformity across the country sets the deviation at ±0.02, so a visitor to Madhya Pradesh is assessed against the national framework rather than any provincial rule.

That framework was altered on 25 March 2026, when India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill, approved by both houses and awaiting presidential assent at the time of sourcing. The amendment replaces the self-identification route affirmed by the Supreme Court in 2014 with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Critics warn the narrower definition excludes self-identifying gender-fluid and non-binary people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

Recognition now rests on medical certification. The amendment makes medical-board and district-authority certification mandatory for gender-affirming surgery and conditions identity recognition on medical certification, a direct documents consequence for a trans traveller whose papers rest on that certification. Passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination; the Allahabad High Court granted relief in February 2026.

The amendment adds offences carrying up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring a person to be transgender. People's Union for Civil Liberties warns that these offences echo colonial-era criminalisation of transgender people. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist, while the government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking. The bill was passed amid protests in Mumbai.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

Checkpoint and document friction is documented across modes of travel. A trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender. Transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024. At Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, although she presented a PAN card for verification.

The courts remain the strongest protection machinery. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, followed police harassment of a same-sex couple and issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office's country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

For a visitor, exposure concentrates at checkpoints and in police contact rather than in statute alone: recognition narrowed in March 2026, sexual-violence safeguards were removed in 2024, and abuse at railway, airport and passport encounters was documented in 2024 and 2026, set against high courts that have intervened repeatedly on behalf of trans and LGBT+ people.

1811400B21325138943523.name: Andaman and Nicobar Islands
1811400B21325138943523.summary:
The Andaman and Nicobar Islands is a Union Territory of India and stands under India's national framework for transgender recognition and protection. No territory-specific trans law, enforcement series or incident pattern is on file, so a visitor to the islands is assessed against the national position, which changed materially in March 2026.

India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill on 25 March 2026, approved by both houses and awaiting presidential assent at the time of sourcing. Protests were held in Mumbai on the day of passage. The bill amends the 2019 law and removes the self-identification route to legal recognition that had been affirmed by the Supreme Court in 2014.

Recognition is now limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals, with recognition in practice narrowed to male and female categories plus those traditional identities. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Critics warn the narrower definition excludes self-identifying gender-fluid and non-binary people; rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist. The government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking.

The amended law mandates medical certification, including medical-board and district-authority certification for gender-affirming surgery, and adds offences carrying up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring people to be transgender. The People's Union for Civil Liberties warns these offences echo colonial-era criminalisation of transgender people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which courts have interpreted to cover gender identity. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024: replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Sanhita removed legal safeguards that had protected trans persons from sexual violence, and trans people fear a rise in assaults because the new code omits the gender-identity-specific offences the old law carried.

Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person asked to take a medical exam by passport authorities. In November 2024 an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender persons arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic; victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy. Bans on conversion therapy from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating.

Facilities and care access are largely set at state level. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha run transgender welfare boards coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions. Nationally, the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community. In August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.

Intersex minors remain at risk: reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations, and the Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.

1811400B42025667129192.name: Jammu and Kashmīr
1811400B42025667129192.summary:
Jammu and Kashmīr stands under India's national framework. On 25 March 2026, India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill, approved by both houses and awaiting presidential assent at the time of reporting. The amendment removes the self-identification route established by the Supreme Court's 2014 recognition and carried into the 2019 Act. Legal recognition is limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, to intersex individuals, and to male and female categories. Certification by a medical board and a district authority becomes mandatory, including for gender-affirming surgery. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

The amendment adds offences carrying up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring a person to be transgender. The People's Union for Civil Liberties warns that these provisions echo the colonial-era criminalisation of transgender people. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and as an attack on the right to exist. The government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and as protection from trafficking; critics say it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. The bill was passed amid protests in Mumbai.

The baseline for entry and stay remains mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which courts have interpreted to cover gender identity: the Supreme Court has held that discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity falls within Article 15's prohibition of discrimination by sex, and the Allahabad High Court extended that in 2021 to bar employment discrimination on sexual orientation grounds. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed legal safeguards that had protected trans persons from sexual violence, and trans people fear a rise in assaults because the new code omits the gender-identity-specific offences the old law carried.

Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person who had been required to undergo a medical examination by passport authorities. In November 2024 an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card for identity verification. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at the station under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender persons arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic; victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. Bans on conversion therapy from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating.

10402087B60055985875400.name: Baden-Württemberg
10402087B60055985875400.summary:
Baden-Württemberg stands under Germany's national framework. Federal constitutional and equality protections apply nationwide, identity documents, marriage law and legal gender recognition are uniform across the Länder, and no Land can remove that floor.

Custody placement is the sharpest documented exposure for a trans visitor. German prisons operate under statutory separation with a binary men and women housing model, and the Criminological Research Institute of Lower Saxony (KFN) reports that placement corresponding to a prisoner's gender identity has been practised only in exceptional cases; it runs a research project on the situation of transgender people in prison. The exception is applied inconsistently. In July 2026 a convicted far-right extremist holding a legally recognised female gender entry was transferred from a women's prison to a men's prison after public outcry, authorities citing the safety of prisoners at the women's facility. In the earlier Penelope Frank case, reported by DW in August 2023, a climate activist with a legal male registration faced assignment to a men's prison on conviction, and the reporting described German prisons as offering few safe spaces for trans inmates.

Baden-Württemberg carries the older rule. A constitutional-law analysis published on 18 March 2026 found that placement rules in most Länder have stood unchanged since the 1970s and are now being revised: a new Art. 17 of Rhineland-Palatinate's prison act has been in force since 1 March 2026, and Bavarian, Saxon and Hamburg rules have also recently entered into force, giving a majority of Länder revised provisions. Only Bremen's law explicitly references the registered gender entry, with other Länder doing so implicitly. Baden-Württemberg is not named in the analysis, and its own prison law retains the unrevised 1970s-era placement rules, so a trans visitor taken into custody here stands under the pre-revision regime.

Legal gender recognition on paper is straightforward. The Self-Determination Act, passed in April 2024 by 374 votes to 251, took effect on 1 November 2024 and allows transgender, intersex and non-binary adults to change their legal gender by self-determination with three months' notice, replacing the Transsexuals Act of 1980 whose surgery and sterilisation requirements the Federal Constitutional Court struck down in January 2011. A 'divers' marker has been available on birth certificates, passports and driving licences since 1 January 2019 under the Third Gender Act, but it requires a doctor's statement confirming intersex status and was clarified in April 2019 as applying to intersex people only, not transgender people.

Airport screening has produced a specific documented complaint. The DJ and producer BASHKKA filed a legal complaint under the General Act on Equal Treatment over a screening at Frankfurt Airport on 23 November 2024, stating that officers deliberately disregarded her gender identity in what she called a targeted, degrading act of transphobic harassment; she provided Resident Advisor, reporting in June 2025, a copy of her statement to the airport.

Access to women-protected spaces is contested in the leisure sector. A Deutscher Sauna-Bund guideline issued in January 2025 restricting women's saunas to persons whose primary sex characteristics correspond set off public argument over registered trans women's access after the Self-Determination Act took effect, amid fears that the self-declaration route would be misused.

Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity is prohibited in health services and in education under the General Act on Equal Treatment, in force since 18 August 2006. A nationwide ban on conversion therapy for minors has been in place since May 2020, carrying penalties of up to one year in prison for practitioners and fines of €30,000 for offering, promoting or referring minors to such treatment.

Asylum and admission policy moved against LGBTI protection during 2025. In June the Federal Cabinet proposed designating Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia as safe countries of origin despite LGBTI people facing imprisonment there, and in August the governing coalition announced it would end humanitarian admission programmes, including the Afghanistan scheme for persecuted LGBTI people.

A victim-support infrastructure exists. The German STOP the HATE campaign runs a counselling finder sorted by topic, emergency guidance including an LSBTIQ* crisis line, and a hate-crime knowledge base covering underreporting, evidence preservation, witness support and reporting channels.

10402087B44391416804171.summary:
Bremen stands under the federal framework. The Self-Determination Act (Selbstbestimmungsgesetz, SBGG) passed the Bundestag by 374 votes to 251 and took effect on 1 November 2024, allowing adults over 18 to change their legal gender by self-determination rather than through the previous medical and court pathway; the change is entered in the civil registry, which in Bremen is processed by the city-state's own registry offices. Same-sex marriage has been legal in Germany since 1 October 2017. Bremen has no trans-specific statute or ordinance of its own, and federal criminal law and the General Act on Equal Treatment apply in the city-state without local deviation.

Custody is the sharpest documented exposure. Prison administration is a Land competence, and an analysis published on Verfassungsblog on 18 March 2026 found that all German Länder tie inmate placement to the prisoner's legal gender while § 6(1) SBGG permits state law to override the registry entry. Several Länder have enacted exception clauses, some written abstractly for all inmates and others criticised as targeted at trans prisoners; Bremen has enacted no placement statute of its own, so this national framework is the operative standard for any placement question arising in the city-state.

The exception has been applied in practice. A France24 wire report of 16 July 2026 covers the Liebich case, in which a prisoner was held in a men's prison despite a completed legal gender change. The case prompted Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia to launch a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act, placing the question on the legislative agenda for every Land, including Bremen.

Entry and screening do not turn on gender identity in Bremen, but a documented screening complaint exists elsewhere in Germany: DJ and producer BASHKKA filed a complaint under the General Act on Equal Treatment over a Frankfurt Airport screening of 23 November 2024 in which, as reported by Resident Advisor in June 2025, officers disregarded her gender identity in what she described as targeted transphobic harassment.

Hamburg stands under the federal framework of Germany. 10402087B60782008682549.name: Mecklenburg-Vorpommern
10402087B60782008682549.summary:
The federal Self-Determination Act (Selbstbestimmungsgesetz, SBGG) governs every step of a trans visitor's stay in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. Approved by the federal cabinet in August 2023, passed by the Bundestag in April 2024 by 374 votes to 251 and in force since 1 November 2024, it lets adults over 18 change their legal first name and gender entry by self-declaration with three months' notice and no medical certification. No Mecklenburg-Vorpommern-specific trans statute, placement reform or ordinance is recorded in the sources; the federal framework applies here in full, including to short-term visitors and their documents at check-in and border or identity checks.

Prison placement is the sharpest documented exposure in this state. An analysis published on Verfassungsblog on 18 March 2026 sets out the operative rule under the SBGG: placement follows the prisoner's legal gender entry unless state law provides otherwise, with Länder statutes differing on whether they carry an abstract exception clause or one drafted specifically for trans prisoners. Mecklenburg-Vorpommern is the site of the flashpoint case under that framework, a July 2026 ruling of the Landgericht Neubrandenburg that ordered placement in a men's prison despite the prisoner's completed legal gender change.

The outcome has gone the other way elsewhere in Germany, and the resulting political pressure is live. DW reported on 16 July 2026 that Marla-Svenja Liebich, whose gender entry had been changed to female at the end of 2024 under the Self-Determination Act, was transferred to a men's prison after extradition from Czechia, with authorities citing the safety of prisoners at the women's facility and critics characterising the gender change as an abuse of the law. France24 reported the same day that Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia responded by launching a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act, the statute that applies in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern as in every other Land.

Airport screening has produced a specific documented complaint. The DJ and producer BASHKKA filed a legal complaint under the General Act on Equal Treatment over a screening at Frankfurt Airport on 23 November 2024, in which, according to her account reported by Resident Advisor in June 2025, officers deliberately disregarded her gender identity in what she called a targeted, degrading act of transphobic harassment; she gave the publication a copy of her statement to the airport. Frankfurt is a common entry point for visitors arriving in northern Germany.

The partner baseline is the federal one as well: same-sex marriage with full marital and adoption rights has been available since 1 October 2017, implementing legislation having been passed on 30 June 2017.

Several other Länder have amended their prison statutes in recent years to accommodate legally recognised gender diversity, so the placement picture across Germany is uneven rather than uniform. The Criminological Research Institute of Lower Saxony reads § 170(2) of the Lower Saxony correctional act as the operating rule and reports that placement corresponding to a prisoner's gender identity has been practised only in exceptional cases; it runs a research project on the situation of transgender people in prison. A new § 17 of the Rhineland-Palatinate prison act took effect on 1 March 2026 with no press coverage at all.

Earlier reporting sets the tone for how courts and prosecutors treat trans prisoners. In the Penelope Frank case, covered by DW in August 2023, a climate activist with a legal male registration faced assignment to a men's prison if convicted, and the reporting described German prisons as offering few safe spaces for trans inmates.

Access to women-protected spaces has been contested in the leisure sector since the Self-Determination Act took effect. A Deutscher Sauna-Bund guideline issued in January 2025 restricting women's saunas to persons whose primary sex characteristics correspond set off a public debate about registered trans women's access, and reporting from Berlin on how saunas and similar venues handle trans women after the new law followed months of argument over women-protected spaces and fears that the self-declaration route would be misused.

Asylum and admission policy moved against LGBTI protection during 2025. In June the Federal Cabinet proposed designating Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia as safe countries of origin despite LGBTI people facing imprisonment there, and in August the governing coalition announced it would end humanitarian admission programmes, including the Afghanistan scheme for persecuted LGBTI people.

A victim-support infrastructure exists nationally: the German STOP the HATE campaign runs a counselling finder sorted by topic, emergency guidance including an LSBTIQ* crisis line, and a hate-crime knowledge base covering underreporting, evidence preservation, witness support and reporting channels.

10402087B86022102756745.summary:
North Rhine-Westphalia stands under the German federal framework. Constitutional equality guarantees, the General Act on Equal Treatment, the national identity-document regime and marriage law are uniform across the federation, and criminal equality provisions are federal, so the Land cannot lower that floor. Prison administration is a Land competence, which means North Rhine-Westphalia's own correctional rules govern how a detained visitor is housed, within the limits of federal law.

Legal gender recognition is uniform and straightforward on paper. The Self-Determination Act, passed in April 2024, took effect on 1 November 2024 and allows transgender, intersex and non-binary adults to change their legal gender by self-declaration with three months' notice, replacing the Transsexuals Act of 1980. A 'divers' marker has been available on birth certificates, passports and driving licences since 1 January 2019, but it requires a doctor's statement confirming intersex status and applies to intersex people only, not transgender people.

Custody is the sharpest documented exposure for a trans visitor to North Rhine-Westphalia. German prisons operate under statutory separation built on a binary men-and-women housing model. Under § 6(1) of the Self-Determination Act a person's legal gender entry governs placement in custody unless state law provides otherwise. No North Rhine-Westphalia statute prescribing trans-specific placement rules is on file, so the federal standard is the operative framework in this Land, and how any exception is exercised is unsettled.

Placement corresponding to a prisoner's gender identity has been practised only in exceptional cases. That is the reading the Criminological Research Institute of Lower Saxony gives to § 170(2) of the Lower Saxony correctional act, and the institute runs a research project on the situation of transgender people in prison. Where the exception is applied, outcomes have gone both ways. In the case reported by wire services on 16 July 2026, a prisoner who had completed a legal gender change was held in a men's prison; authorities cited the safety of prisoners at the women's facility.

The federal government's response is contested at the level of the upper chamber. Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia responded to that case by launching an initiative to tighten the Self-Determination Act. Because the Act is federal legislation, any tightening would apply to North Rhine-Westphalia as to every other Land, and no such amendment is on file as of this record.

Constitutional-law analysis of 18 March 2026 examines how Länder house trans prisoners under the Self-Determination Act. It criticises several states' exception clauses for singling out trans inmates, and defends abstractly drafted clauses such as the new § 17 of the Rhineland-Palatinate prison act, which took effect on 1 March 2026. North Rhine-Westphalia has no comparable trans placement statute on file, so the federal default governs here rather than an abstract or trans-specific state clause.
