A guideline issued in January 2025 by the Deutscher Sauna-Bund, restricting women's saunas to persons whose primary sex characteristics correspond, set off a public debate about registered trans women's access and fears that the self-declaration route would be misused. Visitors to saunas and similar venues in North Rhine-Westphalia should expect operator-specific rules rather than a settled standard.

Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity is prohibited in health services and in education under the General Act on Equal Treatment, in force since 18 August 2006. Since May 2020 a nationwide ban on conversion therapy for minors has carried penalties of up to one year in prison for practitioners and fines of €30,000 for offering, promoting or referring minors to such treatment. The Federal Anti-Discrimination Office found that a July 2025 ban on gender-inclusive language imposed by the Education Minister in her own ministry contradicted constitutional equality protection.

Asylum and admission policy moved against LGBTI protection during 2025. In June the Federal Cabinet proposed designating Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia as safe countries of origin despite LGBTI people facing imprisonment there, and in August the governing coalition announced it would end humanitarian admission programmes, including the Afghanistan scheme for persecuted LGBTI people. A trans visitor arriving from a country where homosexuality or trans status is criminalised should not assume humanitarian protection pathways remain open.

The German STOP the HATE campaign runs a counselling finder sorted by topic, emergency guidance including an LSBTIQ* crisis line, and a hate-crime knowledge base covering underreporting, evidence preservation, witness support and reporting channels.

10402087B42728698084544.name: Rheinland-Pfalz
10402087B42728698084544.summary:
Custody placement is the sharpest documented exposure for a trans visitor to Rhineland-Palatinate. German prisons operate under statutory separation with a binary men and women housing model. The Criminological Research Institute of Lower Saxony reads § 170(2) of the Lower Saxony correctional act as the operating rule and reports that placement corresponding to a prisoner's gender identity has been practised only in exceptional cases; it runs a research project on the situation of transgender people in prison. Prison administration is a competence of the individual Länder, so placement practice varies by where an offence is tried.

Rhineland-Palatinate replaced its prison-execution code with a new § 17 of the state correctional act, in force 1 March 2026, which anchors inmate placement to the legally recorded gender entry. The provision pairs that rule with a general, abstract exception clause that is open to all prisoners rather than targeting trans people as such. A constitutional-law commentary of 18 March 2026 reads Rhineland-Palatinate as the state that carried the bloc of Länder past the point of modernising placement rules that had stood unchanged since the 1970s, and raises constitutional doubts about the trans-targeted exception clauses used by other states. No press coverage of the new provision was found.

How exceptions are applied in practice is unsettled and the outcome has gone both ways. In August 2025 the chief prosecutor for Halle stated that Marla-Svenja Liebich, whose gender entry had been changed to female at the end of 2024 under the Self-Determination Act, would serve an 18-month sentence for incitement at Chemnitz women's prison with placement reviewed at intake. Wire reporting of 16 July 2026 covered the outcome: after extradition from Czechia she was held in a men's prison despite her legal gender change. Authorities cited the safety of prisoners at the women's facility, while critics characterised the gender change as an abuse of the self-determination law. The case drove the eastern Länder to launch an initiative in the Bundesrat to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act. In the earlier Penelope Frank case, covered in August 2023, a climate activist with a legal male registration faced assignment to a men's prison if convicted, and the reporting described German prisons as offering few safe spaces for trans inmates.

Legal gender recognition is straightforward on paper. The Self-Determination Act, passed in April 2024 by 374 votes to 251, took effect on 1 November 2024 and allows transgender, intersex and non-binary adults to change their legal gender by self-determination with three months' notice, replacing the Transsexuals Act of 1980, whose surgery and sterilisation requirements the Federal Constitutional Court struck down in January 2011. Since 1 January 2019 a 'divers' marker has been available on birth certificates, passports and driving licences under the Third Gender Act, but it requires a doctor's statement confirming intersex status and was clarified in April 2019 as applying to intersex people only, not transgender people.

Airport screening has produced a specific documented complaint. The DJ and producer BASHKKA filed a legal complaint under the General Act on Equal Treatment over a screening at Frankfurt Airport on 23 November 2024. In her account, reported in June 2025, officers deliberately disregarded her gender identity in what she called a targeted, degrading act of transphobic harassment, and she provided the publication a copy of her statement to the airport.

Access to women-protected spaces in the leisure sector has been contested since the Self-Determination Act took effect on 1 January 2025. A guideline issued in January 2025 by the Deutscher Sauna-Bund, restricting women's saunas to persons whose primary sex characteristics correspond, set off public argument about registered trans women's access, alongside reporting from Berlin on how saunas and similar venues handle trans women under the new law and months of argument over women-protected spaces and fears that the self-declaration route would be misused. Trans people in custody in Berlin have an official information page from the Berlin prison service setting out rules and contacts across the city's facilities; no equivalent Rhineland-Palatinate page was found.

Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity is prohibited in health services and in education under the General Act on Equal Treatment, in force since 18 August 2006. The Federal Anti-Discrimination Office found that a July 2025 ban on gender-inclusive language imposed by the Education Minister in her own ministry contradicted constitutional equality protection. Since May 2020 a nationwide ban on conversion therapy for minors has carried penalties of up to one year in prison for practitioners and fines of €30,000 for offering, promoting or referring minors to such treatment.

Asylum and admission policy moved against LGBTI protection during 2025. In June the Federal Cabinet proposed designating Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia as safe countries of origin despite LGBTI people facing imprisonment there, and in August the governing coalition announced that it would end humanitarian admission programmes, including the Afghanistan scheme for persecuted LGBTI people.

A victim-support infrastructure exists. The German STOP the HATE campaign runs a counselling finder sorted by topic, emergency guidance including an LSBTIQ* crisis line, and a hate-crime knowledge base covering underreporting, evidence preservation, witness support and reporting channels.

10402087B83775792336645.name: Saarland
10402087B83775792336645.summary:
Saarland has no trans-specific statute, ordinance or prison-placement rule of its own. Prison administration is a state competence while equality and criminal law sit at federal level, so a trans visitor in Saarland stands under the German federal position and their exposure tracks that framework.

Custody placement is the sharpest documented exposure. German prisons operate under statutory separation with a binary men-and-women housing model, and the Criminological Research Institute of Lower Saxony reads § 170(2) of the Lower Saxony correctional act as the operating rule under which placement corresponding to a prisoner's gender identity has been practised only in exceptional cases. Under § 6(1) of the Self-Determination Act, in force 1 November 2024, placement follows the legal gender entry unless a state law provides otherwise, and the Verfassungsblog analysis of 18 March 2026 finds no constitutional obligation on a Land to follow that entry. Saarland has legislated nothing, so the default federal rule applies and the outcome rests on administrative discretion.

That discretion has gone against registered gender. On 16 July 2026 France 24 reported that a person convicted of neo-Nazi incitement whose gender entry had been changed to female under the Self-Determination Act was sent to a men's prison after extradition from Czechia, with authorities citing the safety of prisoners at the women's facility and critics characterising the gender change as an abuse of the self-determination law. In the earlier Penelope Frank case of August 2023, DW described German prisons as offering few safe spaces for trans inmates and reported a legal male registration facing assignment to a men's prison if convicted.

Legal gender recognition is straightforward on paper. The Self-Determination Act, passed in April 2024 by 374 votes to 251, took effect on 1 November 2024 and lets transgender, intersex and non-binary adults change their legal gender by self-determination with three months' notice, replacing the Transsexuals Act of 1980 whose surgery and sterilisation requirements the Federal Constitutional Court struck down in January 2011. A 'divers' marker has been available on birth certificates, passports and driving licences since 1 January 2019 under the Third Gender Act, but it requires a doctor's statement confirming intersex status and was clarified in April 2019 as applying to intersex people only.

Entry screening carries a documented complaint. The DJ and producer BASHKKA filed a legal complaint under the General Act on Equal Treatment over a screening at Frankfurt Airport on 23 November 2024, telling Resident Advisor in June 2025 that officers deliberately disregarded her gender identity in what she called a targeted, degrading act of transphobic harassment; she gave the publication a copy of her statement to the airport.

Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited federally in employment, education, health services and the provision of goods and services under the General Act on Equal Treatment, in force since 18 August 2006. Saarland adds a constitutional layer: its state constitution was amended in 2011 so that the anti-discrimination provisions explicitly cover sexual orientation and gender identity, which makes transphobic hate speech prohibited under Saarland law where most of Germany has no such ban.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Germany (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: The page records that Saarland's state constitution was amended in 2011 so that its anti-discrimination provisions explicitly include sexual orientation and gender identity, one of only five Lander constitutions to carry such a clause (Berlin since 1995, Brandenburg since 1992, Bremen since 2001, Saarland since 2011, Thuringia since 1993; Saxony-Anhalt in the public sector since 1997). It further records that Saarland, with Hesse, Berlin, Bremen and Schleswig-Holstein, tabled a joint Bundesrat motion for a ban on conversion therapy, presented in plenary on 12 April 2019, with Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia agreeing and Bavaria offering modified support. sources.title: Transgender rights in Germany (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: The page states that hate speech on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned nationwide in Germany, but that some states have laws banning all forms of discrimination in their constitutions - Berlin, Brandenburg, Bremen, Saarland and Thuringia - and that in those states hate speech based on both sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited. For Saarland this is a jurisdiction-specific enforcement difference: transphobic hate speech is prohibited under the state constitution, unlike in most of Germany, and the federal General Act on Equal Treatment (in force since 18 August 2006) bans discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity in employment, education, health services and the provision of goods and services.

sources.title: Jens Spahn will Pseudotherapien gegen Homosexualität verbieten
sources.summary: Zeit Online (10 April 2019) reports that, parallel to Federal Health Minister Jens Spahn's announced plan to ban so-called conversion therapies, Hesse, Berlin, Bremen, Saarland and Schleswig-Holstein planned to present a joint Bundesrat motion (Entschließungsantrag) for a ban that same week. Saarland is one of the five tabling states in the run-up to the 12 April 2019 Bundesrat plenary presentation recorded on Wikipedia's LGBTQ rights in Germany page; the federal ban was subsequently approved by the Bundestag on 7 May 2020.

10402087B46069870964378.name: Schleswig-Holstein
10402087B46069870964378.summary:
Schleswig-Holstein stands under the German national framework. Legal gender recognition runs through the Self-Determination Act (SBGG), in force since 1 November 2024, under which a prisoner's placement tracks the legal gender entry unless state law provides an exclusion.

No Schleswig-Holstein statute or ordinance specific to trans people is in force. The state has no prison act provision of its own governing the placement of trans prisoners, so the SBGG mechanics and the national July 2026 placement case are the operative rules for a visitor detained here.

Custody placement is the sharpest documented exposure. In July 2026 a German court sent a person convicted of neo-Nazi incitement, whose legal gender had been changed to female under the Self-Determination Act, to a men's prison, amid public outcry over women's-prison safety. The case drove the Länder-level prison-placement law debate and illustrates how placement can diverge from the legal gender entry in practice.

A Verfassungsblog analysis of 18 March 2026 raises constitutional doubts about trans-targeted exception clauses in Länder prison law, though Schleswig-Holstein has not enacted such a clause.

25490228B84620027724461.name: Canarias
25490228B84620027724461.summary:
Canarias stands under Spain's Ley 4/2023 of 28 February 2023, the Law for the real and effective equality of trans people and the guarantee of the rights of LGBTI persons, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado (no. 51) on 1 March 2023 and applied uniformly across all of Spain's autonomous communities. Under Article 43 any person aged 16 or over may rectify the sex marker on their own civil registry entry by simple declaration before the Civil Registry, with no prior medical diagnosis of gender dysphoria and no requirement of two years of medical treatment; corresponding identity documents are adapted to the new marker, and the law's transitory provisions govern rectification applications pending at entry into force.

Self-identification replaced the former diagnostic and treatment pathway, placing Spain alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay in using an administrative route to legal gender change. Recognition is available from age 12 under conditions, and the statute regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16; the age-12 provision proved contentious in the Congress of Deputies.

The same statute bans medically unnecessary normalising surgeries on intersex children before consent, expands access to assisted reproduction, enables parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, strengthens sexuality education, and prohibits LGBTI discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing. Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have been in force since 2005, and legal gender change does not require surgery or sterilisation.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on the gender marker recorded in the civil registry rather than on biological sex, so the registry entry a visitor carries is the operative basis for facility rules in Spain.

There is no free-standing criminal offence of gender-expression-based hate crime: the phrase 'gender expression' appears in no article of the Spanish Criminal Code. The hate-speech aggravating circumstance in Article 22.4 and the penalties of Article 510, one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months, derive from Organic Law 6/2022, while Ley 4/2023 itself reformed offences against sexual freedom, including Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.

Enforcement of the gender-identity aggravation is documented at first-instance level. In July 2026 the Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo applied the transfobia aggravating circumstance for the first time in a misdemeanour case concerning threats sent by WhatsApp to a trans woman, fining the author EUR 300. In a separate case reported on 8 January 2026, a juvenile gang harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park in Valencia to mock them; the only adult defendant received six months' prison and two minors were judged separately.

Beneath the national framework Canarias carries its own protections. Ley 8/2014 of 28 October 2014 prohibits discrimination on gender-identity grounds and recognises trans persons' rights, and the community has allowed trans people to self-declare their legal gender since 2021, one of 14 communities to do so before the national law of 28 February 2023. Canarias is also listed among the communities banning conversion therapies.

The law further mandates public-policy, workplace, health and education measures, and its transitory provisions govern rectification applications pending at entry into force.

Human Rights Watch (16 February 2023) reports the Spanish Congress of Deputies' passage of the Trans Law: legal gender recognition by self-identification through a simple administrative process, replacing the previous requirements of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment. The same law expands access to assisted reproduction, strengthens sexuality education, bans medically unnecessary normalising surgery on intersex children before consent, enables parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, and prohibits LGBTI discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing; children from age 12 can obtain recognition under conditions, a provision that proved contentious. HRW places the reform within European and international standards against disproportionate requirements for legal gender recognition.

A trans traveler therefore stands under a regional anti-discrimination and self-identification regime alongside the 2023 national law.

sources.title: Historia LGBT en el País Vasco (Spanish Wikipedia)
sources.summary: The Basque Parliament passed a law against discrimination on grounds of gender identity and recognising the rights of trans people, dated 2013, which for the first time incorporated an LGTBI perspective into gender-violence prevention in the Basque education system. Institutional markers predating it include the first Basque Pride march in Bilbao in 1978, the legalisation of the activist collective EHGAM in 1983, and the creation of Emakunde, the Basque Women's Institute, in 1988. A 2017 survey by the Basque Youth Observatory reported that 9 in 10 Basque young people favour same-sex marriage and legal change of sex. Osakidetza, the Basque health service, provided assisted reproduction regardless of sexual orientation and reaffirmed that position in 2013. The Basque Country operates its own non-discrimination legal instruments and equality institutions, including Emakunde, within the national framework.

sources.title: Diversidad sexual en España (Spanish Wikipedia)
sources.summary: The earliest documented executions for same-sex acts in the Iberian peninsula occurred in the Kingdom of Navarra. In 1290 a Muslim man was burned in Arguedas for 'yacer con otros'. In 1345 Juce Abolfaça and Simuel Nahamán, two Jews of Olite, were tortured for confessions and burned before a cortege of 20 for the crime of sodomy. For the modern period, Diario de Navarra (12 May 2026) reports that Navarra planned to create an observatory against LGTBI-phobia, a measure placed at the planning stage by that date, which sits in tension with a 2025 observatory report. Ley Foral 8/2017 is not substantively covered in the material. Navarra's standing rests on the national framework, with no substantive regional divergence of its own.

25490228B27950689864224.name: Región de Murcia
25490228B27950689864224.summary:
Región de Murcia stands under Spain's national framework: Ley 4/2023 of 28 February 2023, the Law for the real and effective equality of trans people and the guarantee of the rights of LGBTI persons, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado (BOE no. 51, 1 March 2023) and applied uniformly across Spain's autonomous communities. Title II allows any person aged 16 or over to rectify the sex marker on their civil-registry entry by simple declaration before the Civil Registry, with no prior medical diagnosis or treatment, and provides for the corresponding adaptation of identity documents. This replaced the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis plus two years of medical treatment. Recognition is available from age 12 under conditions, and the statute regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16. Human Rights Watch, reporting on 16 February 2023, placed the reform within European and international standards against disproportionate requirements for legal gender recognition, while noting that the under-16 provision proved contentious.

Ley 4/2023 also mandates public-policy, workplace, health and education measures, and its transitory provisions govern rectification applications pending at entry into force. Other operative provisions ban medically unnecessary normalising surgeries on intersex children before consent, expand access to assisted reproduction, enable parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, strengthen sexuality education, and prohibit discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing. Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have been in force since 2005, and legal gender change does not require surgery or sterilisation.

Access to sex-separated facilities in Spain rests on legal gender self-determination rather than biological sex, so the gender marker recorded in the civil registry is the operative basis for facility rules. This contrasts with the stricter single-sex-space approach adopted in the United Kingdom on biological-sex lines, where restrictions are applied case by case rather than as a blanket ban.

Spain has no free-standing criminal offence of gender-expression-based hate crime: the phrase 'gender expression' appears in no article of the Spanish Criminal Code. The hate-speech aggravating circumstance in Article 22.4 and the penalties of Article 510 (one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months) derive from Organic Law 6/2022. Enforcement of the gender-identity aggravation is documented at first-instance level: in July 2026 a Tribunal de Instancia applied the transfobia aggravating circumstance for the first time in a misdemeanour case concerning threats sent by WhatsApp to a trans woman, fining the author EUR 300, and in a case reported on 8 January 2026 a juvenile gang harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park to mock them, with the only adult defendant receiving six months' prison and two minors judged separately.

Beneath the national layer, the Región de Murcia's own statute is Ley 8/2016 of 27 May 2016 (BOE-A-2016-6170), which prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics in public and private activity in the region and, within its scope, bars any requirement to prove declared gender identity by psychological or medical report.

The regional instrument sits within a wider pattern: autonomous-region LGTBI and trans-equality laws were approved across eight regions in the 2010s, with Murcia listed alongside País Vasco, Andalucía, Galicia, Extremadura, Madrid, Baleares and Aragón. Implementation of Ley 4/2023 falls to the regional government.

Comparatively, Spain's administrative self-declaration regime places it alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay. A 2016 survey of 23 countries ranked Spain the most trans-supportive of the group surveyed and the only country where a majority supported unrestricted legal gender designation change; that ranking is a dated baseline predating the 2023 law.

25490228B86140490400531.name: Extremadura

The procedure is depathologised: no medical diagnosis and no treatment requirement apply, the former age-majority requirement has been removed, and the corresponding identity documents are adapted after the change. Recognition is possible from age 12 under conditions, a provision that provoked political conflict, and the law regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16.

The hate-speech aggravating circumstance in Article 22.4 and the penalties of Article 510, one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months, derive from Organic Law 6/2022, while Ley 4/2023 itself reformed offences against sexual freedom, including Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis. 25490228B94630301010512.name: Castilla-La Mancha
25490228B94630301010512.summary:
Castilla-La Mancha stands under Spain's national framework: Ley 4/2023 of 28 February 2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado, applies uniformly across all autonomous communities, including this one, and the source inventory identifies no facility, expression or assembly restriction enacted at regional level.

Document-relevant provision is national and administrative. Adults may request rectification of the sex entry on their own registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, without prior surgical reassignment, a gender-dysphoria diagnosis or two years of medical treatment; the right is grounded in the free development of personality under Article 10.1 of the Constitution. Recognition is possible from age 12 under conditions, a provision that proved contentious during passage.

Because access to sex-separated facilities rests on the gender marker recorded in the civil registry rather than on biological sex, that registry entry is the operative basis for facility rules in Castilla-La Mancha, in contrast to the stricter single-sex-space approach being adopted in the United Kingdom on biological-sex lines with restrictions applied case by case rather than as a blanket ban.

The national statute defines and sanctions discriminatory conduct and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation, sexual identity, gender expression and sexual characteristics, declares discriminatory contract clauses null and void, obliges discrimination data collection broken down by the covered causes, and mandates measures adapted to rural circumstances. Human Rights Watch (16 February 2023) recorded that the law strengthens protections for unmarried same-sex couples and combats LGBTI discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing.

There is no free-standing criminal offence of gender-expression-based hate crime: the phrase 'gender expression' appears in no article of the Spanish Criminal Code. The hate-speech aggravating circumstance in Article 22.4 and the penalties of Article 510 (one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months) derive from Organic Law 6/2022, while Ley 4/2023 itself reformed offences against sexual freedom, including Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.

Enforcement of the gender-identity aggravation is documented at first-instance level. In July 2026 the Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo applied the transfobia aggravating circumstance for the first time in a misdemeanour case concerning threats sent by WhatsApp to a trans woman, fining the author EUR 300. In a separate case reported on 8 January 2026, a juvenile gang harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park in Valencia to mock them; the only adult defendant received six months' prison and two minors were judged separately.

Other operative provisions of the national statute include a ban on non-consensual normalising surgeries on intersex children, expanded assisted reproduction rules, and strengthened sexuality education. Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have been in force since 2005, and legal gender change does not require surgery or sterilisation.

Comparatively, Spain's administrative self-declaration regime places it alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay. A 2016 23-country survey ranked Spain the most trans-supportive of the group surveyed and the only country where a majority supported unrestricted legal gender designation change, a dated baseline predating the 2023 law.

25490228B88831207743232.summary:
Andalucía stands under Spain's national framework: Ley 4/2023 of 28 February 2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado, applies uniformly across all autonomous communities and governs the regional position. The law covers the real and effective equality of trans persons and the guarantee of LGBTI rights.

Any person aged 16 or over may rectify the gender mention on their own civil registry entry directly before the Civil Registry. The right to the registered change is grounded in the free development of personality under Article 10.1 of the Constitution, and adults may rectify the registered sex entry without prior surgical reassignment. This administrative route replaced the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment. Recognition is possible from age 12 under conditions, a provision that proved contentious during the parliamentary passage of the law.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on the gender marker recorded in the civil registry rather than on biological sex, so the entry obtained through self-declaration is the operative basis for facility rules in Spain. This contrasts with the stricter single-sex-space approach being adopted in the United Kingdom on biological-sex lines, applied case by case rather than as a blanket ban.

The national framework defines and sanctions discriminatory conduct and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation, sexual identity, gender expression and sexual characteristics. It also declares discriminatory contract clauses null and void, obliges collection of discrimination data broken down by the causes covered, and mandates measures adapted to rural circumstances. Human Rights Watch recorded on 16 February 2023 that the law strengthens protections for unmarried same-sex couples and combats LGBTI discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing.

Adults may rectify the registered sex entry without prior surgical reassignment, the right to the registered change being grounded in the free development of personality (art. 10.1 CE). The law further defines and sanctions discriminatory conduct and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation, sexual identity, gender expression and sexual characteristics, declares discriminatory contract clauses null and void, obliges discrimination data collection broken down by the causes covered, and mandates measures adapted to rural circumstances. This national framework governs the regional position.

Human Rights Watch (16 February 2023) on the Spanish Congress's passage of the national Trans Law: legal gender recognition by self-identification through a simple administrative process, replacing the previous gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment requirements; children from age 12 may obtain recognition under conditions, a provision that proved contentious. The law also strengthens protections for unmarried same-sex couples and combats LGBTI discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing. These are the national provisions this autonomous community implements under the same framework.

25490228B88831207743232.tangentialFactors:
There is no free-standing criminal offence of gender-expression-based hate crime in Spain: the phrase appears in no article of the Spanish Criminal Code. The hate-speech aggravating circumstance in Article 22.4 and the penalties of Article 510, one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months, derive from Organic Law 6/2022.

Enforcement of the gender-identity aggravation is documented at first-instance level outside Andalucía. In July 2026 a Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo applied the transfobia aggravating circumstance for the first time in a misdemeanour case over WhatsApp threats sent to a trans woman, fining the author EUR 300. In a case reported on 8 January 2026 in Valencia, a juvenile gang harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park to mock them; the sole adult defendant received six months' prison and two minors were judged separately.

Spain's administrative self-declaration regime places it alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay. A 2016 survey of 23 countries ranked Spain the most trans-supportive of the group surveyed and the only country where a majority supported unrestricted legal gender designation change; that ranking predates the 2023 law.

25490228B88831207743232.localsOnly:
For residents of Andalucía, the rectification procedure runs as an ordinary administrative act before the Civil Registry, with no requirement of a diagnosis, judicial authorisation or medical treatment. The same registry entry governs subsequent dealings with regional Andalucian services that key off the recorded gender marker.

Ley 4/2023 also applies to residents through anti-discrimination duties with a regional operational edge: employers, service providers and public bodies in Andalucía must collect discrimination data broken down by the covered causes, and the statute mandates measures adapted to rural circumstances, relevant to the province's interior. Contracts containing discriminatory clauses are null and void for residents who encounter them in employment, housing or insurance.

Other operative provisions in force for Andalucian residents include the ban on non-consensual normalising surgeries on intersex children, expanded assisted reproduction rules, parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, strengthened sexuality education, and anti-discrimination coverage in healthcare, employment and housing. Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have been in force since 2005, and legal gender change does not require surgery or sterilisation.
25490228B88831207743232.outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory for this record contains national provisions only. No Andalucía-specific Civil Registry office procedure, regional implementing decree, or regional enforcement decision is documented here, so the practical steps a visitor would take in Málaga, Sevilla or Granada beyond the national administrative route remain unresolved and not sourced.

The comparative ranking cited is a 2016 baseline and predates Ley 4/2023; no post-2023 survey of Spanish public opinion is available in this inventory. Likewise, no documented case of a trans visitor being refused facility access on Andalucian territory is sourced, and the enforcement examples recorded here come from Vigo and Valencia, in other autonomous communities.

19177384B98145761763330.name: Catamarca
19177384B98145761763330.summary:
Catamarca is a province of Argentina and stands under the national framework. Argentina's Law 26.743, passed by the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and by the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, was promulgated on 24 May 2012 and permits a change of legal gender without surgery, without hormone treatment and without judicial approval. The United Nations described it at the time as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region. No separate provincial record for Catamarca was located, so the national picture is the baseline a visitor should carry.

That statutory position has been narrowed by executive action rather than by repeal. In February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei issued a decree banning gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy for minors and a second decree governing the housing of transgender people in prison. Legal experts called the first decree illegal and unconstitutional and petitioned the courts to intervene; the outcome of that litigation is not recorded in the sources available here.

The institutional machinery of protection has been dismantled. The federal anti-discrimination institute INADI has been closed, the Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry eliminated, and trans people hired under the public-sector labour-inclusion quota dismissed in 2024. Trans activists in the national capital interviewed on 4 April 2025 said the government's policies had made the community more vulnerable and described the situation as chaotic and desperate; violence, discrimination and poverty affecting trans people are reported as worsened.

Violence reached a documented high in 2025. The National LGBT+ Hate Crimes Observatory recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity during the year, an increase of 62% over the previous year and the highest count in the observatory's ten years of operation, averaging one crime every 38 hours. Trans women and travestis accounted for 62.5% of victims (142 cases) and gay men 22% (50). The report ties the surge to institutional weakening and to state legitimation of discriminatory discourse. Agencia Presentes published the figures on 19 March 2026.

On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán, rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeal court had removed in 2020. The gender-motivated-crime aggravator therefore does not apply in that case as it now stands.

Argentina legalised marriage equality in 2010, the first Latin American country to do so, and anti-discrimination protections exist through national and provincial law. An Outright International country overview updated on 12 March 2026 nonetheless records negative assessments on same-sex relations, on gender recognition and on organisation registration, indicating deterioration.

Violence, discrimination and poverty affecting the trans community are reported as worsened; this region carries no separate reporting, so the national picture stands as its baseline.

Agencia Presentes (19 March 2026) on the National LGBT+ Hate Crimes Observatory's 2025 report: Argentina recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity in 2025, up 62% year on year, the highest count in the observatory's ten years of operation, one crime every 38 hours. The report ties the surge to institutional weakening and state legitimation of discriminatory discourse; this province sits under that national pattern with no separate local record.

19177384B38635755405886.name: Chaco
19177384B38635755405886.summary:
Chaco has no separate provincial statute on legal gender recognition, no provincial criminalisation provision and no provincial enforcement series in the record. A trans visitor to Chaco therefore stands under Argentina's national framework: Law 26.743, promulgated on 24 May 2012, permits a change of legal gender without surgery, without hormone treatment and without judicial approval. The statute was approved by the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and by the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, and the United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action rather than by repeal. In February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei issued a decree banning gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy for minors, and a second decree governing the housing of transgender people in prison. Legal experts called the decree on minors illegal and unconstitutional and a setback for adolescents' rights, and petitioned the courts to intervene; the outcome of that litigation is not recorded in the sources available here.

Protection machinery at national level has been dismantled in ways a visitor would feel. The federal anti-discrimination agency INADI has been closed, the Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry eliminated, and trans people hired under the public-sector labour-inclusion quota dismissed during 2024. The report ties the surge to institutional weakening and state legitimation of discriminatory discourse.

Judicial protection for gender-motivated violence is contested. On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán, but rejected attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeal court had removed in 2020, so the gender-motivated-crime aggravator does not apply in the case as it now stands.

An Outright International country overview updated on 12 March 2026 records negative assessments on same-sex relations, on gender recognition and on organisation registration, indicating deterioration. Argentina legalised marriage equality in 2010 as the first Latin American country to do so, and anti-discrimination protections exist through national and provincial laws.

19177384B69455221212116.name: Chubut
19177384B69455221212116.summary:
Chubut is a province of Argentina and stands under the national framework, which remains among the most permissive legal gender recognition regimes in the world. Law 26.743 was approved by the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and by the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, and promulgated on 24 May 2012. It permits a change of legal gender without surgery, without hormone treatment and without judicial approval, and the United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region. Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and anti-discrimination protections exist through national and provincial laws.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action rather than by repeal of the statute. A decree of 5 February 2025 issued by the government of President Javier Milei restricts minors' access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy, and a second decree governs the housing of transgender people in prison. Legal experts called the decree on minors illegal and unconstitutional and a setback for adolescents' rights, and petitioned the courts to intervene; the outcome of that litigation is not recorded in the sources available here.

Implementation at national level has also deteriorated. Trans people hired under the 1% Trans Labor Quota were dismissed, and INADI, the federal anti-discrimination agency, was abolished, removing the national complaints channel. 19177384B45303095947895.name: Formosa
19177384B45303095947895.summary:
Formosa stands under Argentina's national framework, which remains among the most permissive in the world on paper. Law 26.743, promulgated on 24 May 2012 after passing the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and the Senate 55 to one abstention, allows a change of legal gender without surgery, without hormone treatment and without judicial approval; the United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region, and Argentina legalised marriage equality in 2010 as the first Latin American country to do so.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action rather than by repeal. A decree of 5 February 2025 issued by the government of President Javier Milei restricts minors' access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone treatment, and a second decree governs the housing of transgender people in prisons. Legal experts called the decree on minors illegal and unconstitutional and petitioned the courts to intervene.

Protection machinery has been withdrawn at the same time. Trans people hired under the 1% Trans Labor Quota were dismissed, and the federal anti-discrimination agency INADI was abolished, removing the national body that had handled discrimination complaints.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people reached a documented high in 2025. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity during the year, a ten-year record and a 62% increase on 2024, averaging one every 38 hours. Perpetrators were mostly security-force personnel and unknown assailants in public space, with beatings the main modality. Institutional violence rose from 17 cases in 2024 to 64 in 2025, and 32% of 2025 incidents took place inside police stations or prisons. Forty-three per cent of perpetrators were strangers to their victims.

Trans and travesti sex workers report police violence that has worsened since President Milei took office, and activists say it is worst outside Buenos Aires, in the more conservative interior provinces. Formosa is one of those provinces, and it sits under the national picture with no local reporting infrastructure to generate separate records.

On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán, rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance removed by an appeal court in 2020; the gender-motivated-crime aggravator therefore does not apply in that case as it now stands.

19177384B51705615570562.name: Mendoza
19177384B51705615570562.summary:
Mendoza is a province of Argentina and stands under the national framework. Argentina's Law 26.743, approved by the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and by the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, was promulgated on 24 May 2012 and remains one of the most permissive legal gender recognition regimes in the world. It permits a change of legal gender without surgery, without hormone treatment and without judicial approval, and the United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region. Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and anti-discrimination protection exists through a combination of national and provincial laws.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action rather than by repeal of the statute. A decree of 5 February 2025 restricts minors' access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone treatment, and a second decree governs the housing of transgender people in prison. Legal experts called the decree on minors illegal and unconstitutional and petitioned the courts to intervene; the outcome of that litigation is not recorded in the sources available here.

The national protective machinery has been dismantled in part. The federal anti-discrimination institute INADI was abolished in 2024, and the 1% Trans Labor Quota had its hires dismissed.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people reached a documented high in 2025. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity during the year, a figure reported by Agencia Presentes on 19 March 2026 that represents a 62% increase year on year and a ten-year record, averaging one every 38 hours. Perpetrators were mostly security-force personnel and unknown assailants in public space, with beatings the main modality. Institutional violence rose from 17 cases in 2024 to 64 in 2025, and 32% of 2025 incidents took place in police stations or prisons; 43% of perpetrators were strangers to their victims.

No Mendoza-specific statute, enforcement series or incident pattern for transgender visitors is documented, and the province has no local reporting infrastructure capable of generating separate records. It therefore sits under the national figures rather than producing its own. Activists interviewed in April 2025 by the Washington Blade, dateline Buenos Aires, told the publication that police violence against trans and travesti sex workers has become more common under President Javier Milei and is worse still in interior provinces such as Mendoza that lack strong reporting infrastructure.

On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán, while rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeal court had removed in 2020, with the result that the gender-motivated-crime aggravator does not apply in that case as it now stands.

Trans activists interviewed in April 2025 reported that the law is still formally in force but is no longer guaranteed in practice, pointing to administrative and budgetary measures rather than to any repeal.

Executive action has narrowed the framework. A decree of 5 February 2025 issued by the government of President Javier Milei restricts minors' access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy, and a second decree governs the housing of transgender people in prisons. Legal experts called the decree on minors illegal and unconstitutional and petitioned the courts to intervene; the outcome of that litigation is not recorded in the sources available here.

19177384B47339545206363.name: San Juan
19177384B47339545206363.summary:
San Juan is a province of Argentina and stands under the country's national legal framework. No source records a San Juan-specific departure from that framework on gender recognition, document markers or entry rules, so the province is assessed at the national position.

Argentina's Law 26.743, promulgated on 24 May 2012, remains formally in force. It permits a change of legal gender without surgery, without hormone treatment and without judicial approval, and Argentine identity documents have carried an "X" marker since 2021. Argentina legalised marriage equality in 2010, and the United Nations described the 2012 statute as a pioneering regional step for transgender rights.

The framework has been narrowed by executive decree rather than by repeal of the statute. Decree 62/2025, published on 5 February 2025 under President Javier Milei, amended Article 11 of the Gender Identity Law to bar people under 18 from gender-affirming surgical and hormonal interventions. Decree 61/2025 amended sentencing law to change the placement of transgender detainees. Both apply nationally and reach every province, San Juan included.

Legal experts and LGBT+ organisations called both decrees unconstitutional and warned that abruptly suspending adolescent treatment endangers trans youth, and they filed a judicial challenge to them. Until a court rules, the decrees govern, and transgender visitors who are under 18 should expect the surgical and hormonal prohibitions to apply to them here as anywhere else in Argentina.

Trans activists interviewed in Buenos Aires in April 2025 described the situation facing their community as chaotic and desperate. They reported that the national government eliminated the Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry and dismissed transgender hires made under a federal quota reserving 1% of public-sector posts, which they said is no longer being implemented. The same activists said the 2012 Gender Identity Law remains formally in force but is no longer guaranteed in practice.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people reached a documented high in 2025. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity during the year, a record, averaging one every 38 hours. Agencia Presentes reported the figures on 19 March 2026 and described them as an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina.

On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán. The Court rejected attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance, which an appeal court had removed in 2020, with the result that the gender-motivated-crime aggravator does not apply in the case as it now stands.

19177384B6836410786482.name: Santa Fe
19177384B6836410786482.summary:
Santa Fe province has no trans-specific statute of its own that the source inventory documents. For a trans visitor, the operative legal picture is Argentina's national framework, which extends to every province. Law 26.743, promulgated on 24 May 2012, permits a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval, and has allowed an 'X' marker on the national identity document since 2021.

That statutory position has been narrowed by executive decree. On 5 February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei published DNU 62/2025, amending Article 11 of the 2012 Gender Identity Law to bar under-18s from gender-affirming surgical and hormonal interventions, alongside DNU 61/2025, which alters prison-sentencing law to change the placement of transgender detainees. Legal experts and LGBT+ organisations interviewed by Agencia Presentes called both measures unconstitutional and said the abrupt suspension of adolescent treatments endangers transgender youth; both decrees face judicial challenge and apply to every province.

Enforcement exposure in 2025 was severe. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity over the year, a record, averaging one every 38 hours. Cases in which security-force personnel were the perpetrators rose from 17 to 64, a doubling that materially changes what a trans visitor should expect from police contact.

Trans activists in Buenos Aires interviewed in April 2025, including representatives of organisations named for Diana Sacayán and Lohana Berkins, described a chaotic and desperate situation under the Milei government. They reported that the national Women/Gender/Diversity Ministry was eliminated, that trans hires made under the federal Trans Labor Quota Law covering 1 per cent of public-sector posts were dismissed, and that the quota is no longer being implemented. They also reported that the 2012 Gender Identity Law remains formally in force but is no longer guaranteed in practice.

Santa Fe is nonetheless better documented than most provinces on the violence question: the provincial government publishes violent-death statistics that include transfemicidios and travesticidios, and national registers name provincial transfemicide victims. No provincial enforcement series with a source was found in the inventory.

On judicial protection for gender-motivated killing, Argentina's Supreme Court in April 2025 left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán, while rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeals court had removed in 2020. The gender-motivated aggravation is therefore not currently applied in that line of cases.

19177384B61792957744675.name: Santiago del Estero
19177384B61792957744675.summary:
Santiago del Estero is a province of Argentina and stands under the national framework, which remains one of the most permissive legal gender recognition regimes in the world. Law 26.743 was approved by the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and by the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, promulgated on 24 May 2012, and permits a change of legal gender without surgery, without hormone treatment and without judicial approval. The United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region.

No provincial rule departing from that statute appears in the sources reviewed here, so a trans visitor's identity documents are not gated by medical approval in Santiago del Estero. The 2012 Gender Identity Law remains on the books.

Violence is the operative visitor concern. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio LGBT+ recorded at least 227 bias-motivated crimes against LGBT people in Argentina over 2025, a record and an increase on 2024, averaging one every 38 hours. Agencia Presentes, reporting the figures on 19 March 2026, described the year as an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in the country.

The victims were disproportionately trans. Trans women and travestis accounted for 62.5% of cases (142). Trans men were victims in 18 cases, against 5 in 2024; 13 victims were lesbians and 4 were non-binary people.

Physical violence made up 64.8% of the recorded cases (147). Roughly 32% occurred inside police stations or penal institutions, and cases involving police jumped from 17 in 2024 to 64 in 2025. Institutional settings carry a documented rather than a theoretical exposure here.

The United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region. An adult visitor's identity documents are therefore not gated by medical approval on arrival.

The framework has been narrowed by executive action rather than by repeal. On 5 February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei issued a decree banning gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy for minors, reported by Reuters as a restriction on adolescents' access to those procedures. A second decree governs the housing of transgender people in prison, a provision that bears directly on any trans detainee. Legal experts called the decree on minors illegal and unconstitutional and a setback for adolescents' rights, and petitioned the courts to intervene; the outcome of that litigation is not recorded in the sources available here.

17162690B9130125042960.name: Lower Silesian Voivodeship
17162690B9130125042960.summary:
Lower Silesian Voivodeship stands under the national framework of Poland, and the inventory records no local deviation in law or enforcement that would distinguish this voivodeship from the country as a whole. A trans visitor in Wrocław or anywhere else in the province meets the Polish national position on custody, entry and documents.

Detention is the clearest documented risk. On 13 March 2024 the Association for Legal Intervention published the case of a transgender Vietnamese woman, on hormone therapy since 2018, whom a Polish regional court placed in a guarded centre for male foreigners. Polish law bars such placement wherever a stay would threaten a person's life or health, and wherever the person shows signs of having suffered violence. The Border Guard refused to move or release her despite that statutory bar, and she was freed only after the association applied to the Border Guard Post commander; the page was updated on 28 March 2024.

The March 2024 case sets the framework applied to trans foreigners in Polish immigration detention, and therefore bears directly on any trans visitor detained in this voivodeship. The statutory protection existed in writing and did not operate until a third party invoked it.

Courts have proved willing to intervene. On 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights held that Polish prison authorities violated a trans woman's right to private and family life under Article 8 of the Convention by denying her hormone-replacement therapy in Siedlce prison, awarding EUR 8,000 in damages. The refusal had no reasonable legal grounds and was disproportionate.

The same judgment left the alleged breaches of Article 3 and Article 14 undecided. It binds Poland and governs healthcare for trans people in Polish prisons and detention in every voivodeship, Lower Silesian among them, though placement decisions in custody remain individual and unpredictable in practice.

17162690B67719337891950.name: Opole Voivodeship
17162690B67719337891950.summary:
Opole Voivodeship stands under Poland's national framework, and no voivodeship-level deviation from that framework has been documented.

Detention is the clearest documented risk to a trans visitor in Poland. In a case publicised by the Association for Legal Intervention on 13 March 2024, a Polish regional court placed a transgender Vietnamese woman, on hormone therapy since 2018, in a guarded centre for male foreign nationals. Polish law bars such placement wherever a stay would threaten life or health or the person shows signs of having suffered violence; the Border Guard refused to move or release her. Her hormone therapy was interrupted for three months because the centre would not supply the medication, and she was released only after the Association applied to the Border Guard Post commander and he ordered it. Her documented history of violence and sexual assault indicates that trans women held in these facilities may be exposed to both untreated care needs and vulnerable placement.

Courts have proved willing to intervene. On 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights found that Polish prison authorities violated Article 8 of the Convention by denying a trans woman hormone replacement therapy in Siedlce prison, awarding EUR 8,000 in damages while leaving the alleged Articles 3 and 14 breaches undecided; the refusal was held to have no reasonable legal grounds and to be disproportionate. The judgment binds Poland as a whole and sets the governing standard for trans people's healthcare in Polish prisons and detention in every voivodeship, including Opole. Poland operates no specialised trans prison section, and placement decisions remain individual and unpredictable.

Entry itself is straightforward for many nationalities: Global Affairs Canada's travel advisory notes visa-free entry for tourists staying up to 90 days. The same advisory lists sexual orientation among reported motives for harassment in Poland, alongside physical appearance and foreigner status, and links general LGBTQ2+ travel guidance.

The wider legal environment is in transition. Human Rights Watch describes LGBT-rights reform under the Prime Minister Tusk government as slow and insufficient through 2024. Deputy Justice Minister Smiszek announced a hate-speech law extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation; a March draft Penal Code amendment raising penalties for anti-LGBTI hate speech and violence cleared the Government Legislation Centre in May before approval was postponed, and a second bill followed in late October 2024. The Prosecutor General established a special response team with new guidelines for law enforcement. The status of these bills at the time of travel should be verified rather than assumed.

Recognition of same-sex relationships has moved materially. In June 2024 Justice Minister Bodnar revoked the directive issued by his predecessor Ziobro that had blocked recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad, and in September 2024 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Poland's absence of partnership recognition leaves couples in an illegal vacuum contrary to their rights, calling for a recognition framework.

17162690B16879770934003.name: Silesian Voivodeship
17162690B16879770934003.summary:
Silesian Voivodeship stands under the national framework of Poland, where detention is the sharpest documented risk to a trans visitor. In a case publicised by the Association for Legal Intervention on 13 March 2024, a Polish regional court placed a transgender Vietnamese woman, on hormone therapy since 2018, in a guarded centre for male foreign nationals. The Border Guard refused to move her or release her despite her identifying as a woman and a warning that stopping the medication would cause her harm. After the legal-aid organisation cited Polish law, court rulings and international standards, the Border Guard Commander released her on the ground that continued detention there posed a serious health risk. Her medication had been interrupted for roughly three months.

The case establishes that a detained foreign trans woman in Poland may be held in a male-only facility until the placement is formally challenged, and that release can depend on legal intervention arriving from outside the system. The same case documented her history of violence and sexual assault, indicating that trans women held in these facilities may be exposed to untreated care needs and to victimisation at the same time.

Poland operates no specialised trans prison section, and placement decisions remain individual and unpredictable. On 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights found that Polish prison authorities violated Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights by denying a trans woman hormone replacement therapy while she was imprisoned, despite hormones having been prescribed to her for almost two years, and awarded EUR 8,000 in damages; the Court rejected the Article 3 claim. The ruling establishes that medication denial in Polish custody is litigable and winnable across Europe, though enforcement has required litigation.

Entry itself is straightforward for many nationalities. Global Affairs Canada's travel advisory notes visa-free entry for tourists staying up to 90 days, and lists sexual orientation among reported motives for harassment in Poland alongside physical appearance and foreigner status, with general LGBTQ2+ travel guidance attached.

The surrounding legal environment is in transition. Human Rights Watch describes LGBT-rights reform under the Prime Minister Tusk government as slow and insufficient through 2024. Deputy Justice Minister Smiszek announced a hate-speech law extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation; a March draft Penal Code amendment raising penalties for anti-LGBTI hate speech and violence cleared the Government Legislation Centre in May before approval was postponed, and a second bill followed in late October 2024. The Prosecutor General established a special response team with new guidelines for law enforcement. The status of these bills at the time of travel should be verified rather than assumed.

Recognition of same-sex relationships has moved materially. In June 2024 Justice Minister Bodnar revoked the directive issued by his predecessor Ziobro that had blocked recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad, and in September 2024 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Poland's absence of partnership recognition leaves couples in an illegal vacuum contrary to their rights, calling for a recognition framework.

27671186B81745654473385.name: Cross River
27671186B81745654473385.summary:
Cross River State falls entirely under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 operates in full within the state: same-sex marriage or civil union, and the registration, operation or participation in gay clubs, societies and organisations, or any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, carry up to 14 years' imprisonment nationwide, and the offence reaches anyone who assists, attends or promotes a same-sex relationship or an LGBTQ+ organisation. A visitor who accompanies a partner to a gathering, or who helps organise one, is exposed on the same terms as a resident.

The Criminal Code in force in Cross River separately criminalises sexual activity between men at 14 years' imprisonment and gross indecency between men at 3 years.

Cross River is not among the twelve northern states — Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara — where religious criminal law applies to same-sex acts and the maximum can be death. Within Cross River the exposure is secular and capped at 14 years; crossing into any of those twelve states materially raises it.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's travel advice for Nigeria, reported in August 2026, warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex sexual activity, and of death-penalty risk under religious law in some northern states.

Nigeria offers no anti-discrimination protection to LGBTQ+ people, so there is no official complaint route when a visitor is refused service, threatened or extorted.

Dating apps and social venues carry documented entrapment risk. A nationwide 'kito' scheme lures gay men and trans women to meetings where they are assaulted, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Police profiling produces arbitrary arrest and paid release. The pattern of mass detentions is national: 42 men arrested in Lagos in August 2017, 53 charged in Kaduna in April 2017, more than 100 held after a hotel raid in Delta in June 2018, 67 arrested in Warri in August 2023 and 76 detained in Gombe in October 2023.

Human Rights Watch's 17 August 2010 report on the Nigeria Police Force documents arbitrary arrests, mass 'raid' arrests, prolonged unlawful detention used as a 'cash cow', and extortion backed by threats and physical abuse, with bribery the standard price of release. The report is national in scope and describes the machinery a visitor perceived as gay or trans would meet.

Criminal exposure attaches at the point of entry. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records that same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and that Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

UK travel advice now addresses LGBT+ visitors directly. The Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 advisory for Nigeria, reported by Sahara Reporters (19 August 2026), warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation, of a 14-year jail term under the 2014 Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act, and of possible death-penalty risk under Sharia criminal law in some northern states. Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Police violence against perceived gay people is a routine feature of enforcement. 27671186B56513237316251.name: Oyo
27671186B56513237316251.summary:
Oyo State stands under the national framework of Nigeria, and that framework applies in full to visitors. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 punishes same-sex marriage or civil union, the registering, operating or participating in gay clubs, societies and organisations, and any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, with up to 14 years' imprisonment. The statute reaches participants and guests at same-sex weddings, so attending a private ceremony is itself exposure.

Sexual conduct is separately criminal. Oyo is a southern state governed by the Criminal Code, which penalises sex between men with up to 14 years' imprisonment and gross indecency with up to 3 years. Oyo lies outside the Shari'a regime. Twelve northern states — Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara — apply Shari'a law, under which male same-sex conduct carries a maximum of death.

Nigeria provides no anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and the 2014 statute reaches LGBTI organisations themselves, so advocacy and support provision are criminal acts rather than safeguards.

Enforcement against individuals commonly proceeds through police profiling, entrapment and extortion of people perceived as gay, a practice known locally as "kito". Mass arrests recur across the country: 42 men arrested in Lagos in August 2017, 53 charged in Kaduna in April 2017, more than 100 detained after a hotel raid in Delta in June 2018, and 67 in Warri and 76 in Gombe in 2023.

Dating applications carry a documented abduction and extortion risk. An investigation broadcast on 15 May 2023 found criminal gangs posing as potential dates on popular apps, entraping men, filming them and then extorting, beating and kidnapping them; it interviewed 21 people who had been "kito'd". The same risk reaches gay and transgender app users in Oyo as elsewhere in Nigeria. Victims do not report these crimes to police, for fear of being arrested or assaulted themselves. The investigation also recorded police acting against the extortion gangs, including a commander vowing to hunt down those who blackmail gay people and footage of an officer detaining a suspect — enforcement directed at the blackmailers rather than their victims.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's travel advice for Nigeria warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex conduct, and of death-penalty risk under Shari'a law in northern states.

The statute invalidates any marriage or civil union entered into between persons of the same sex and carries a maximum penalty of up to 14 years' imprisonment. Same-sex sexual activity has been illegal across the country since 1916.

Akwa Ibom stands under that secular national framework. The state lies outside the twelve states operating Shari'a-based criminal codes, so the death-penalty layer does not reach it and the ceiling for same-sex sexual activity in Akwa Ibom is 14 years' imprisonment. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025) records no state-specific enforcement divergence: the national criminal framework applies across all states, and no evidence of a distinct Akwa Ibom enforcement pattern appears in the sources.

The 2014 Act reaches well beyond marriage. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office travel advisory, reported by Sahara Reporters on 19 August 2026, states that the Act also criminalises participants and guests at same-sex weddings, and warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation. Human Rights Watch (October 2016) separately documents that the Act bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have invoked it to justify torture and arbitrary arrest.

Gender identity carries no legal standing in Nigeria. The country has no legal recognition of gender identity, no anti-discrimination protections and no recognition of same-sex relationships. Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed: Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public, and whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Police extortion on suspicion of homosexuality is also documented: in March 2025 Lagos police struck a 24-year-old man in the mouth with a gun butt and released him only after he paid part of a 50,000 naira bribe demanded for looking gay.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing. The FCDO advisory likewise warns of blackmail and intimidation alongside the risk of imprisonment.

The only trans-specific imprisonment case in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

The death penalty for male sodomy is confined to the twelve northern Shari'a states under state Zina provisions. No state-specific protective statute exists in Delta.

Delta has a documented record of mass arrests under this framework. In June 2018 police in Asaba arrested more than 100 party-goers at a hotel on charges that they were gays and lesbians, and by July 2018 they were facing homosexuality-related charges in court. In August 2023 police raided what Wikipedia's overview describes as a gay wedding in Warri, arresting dozens in the case known as the 'Warri 67', of whom 67 were charged to court.

Accounts of the night of 27 August 2023 differ on what occurred. The US State Department's 2023 human rights report, cited in the UK Home Office's June 2025 country policy note, records that Delta police raided a 'white party' organised by the LGBTQI+ community and detained more than 200 individuals, with police alleging the event was a same-sex wedding while some civil society representatives disputed that account. Daily Post reports that officers from Ekpan Division in Uvwie Local Government Area arrested 67 suspects at 9 pm at Teebolus Hotel, Refinery Road, Ekpan, for allegedly conducting and attending a same-sex wedding ceremony between Daniel Pius, 22, and Maxwel Ohwonohwo, 20.

Delta State Police Command spokesman DSP Bright Edafe said the raid followed a confession by a male cross-dresser that he belonged to a gay club and was travelling to a gay marriage ceremony, that the suspects fled on the officers' arrival but 67 were chased and arrested, and that drugs and 'gay marriage ceremonial dresses' were recovered. Edafe said the suspects and exhibits were in custody and efforts continued to arrest fleeing members for possible prosecution. One suspect alleged he had been sexually assaulted by a man at the hotel while intoxicated.

A human rights lawyer based in Warri told the UK Home Office that victims of 'kito' — predatory same-sex assault — under-report for fear of prosecution, which leaves visitors and residents exposed both to the assault and to the machinery used against them. State-level documentation from Delta is thin, and that absence of records does not demonstrate safety.
