Delta-specific entries on the page record that in June 2018 Nigerian police arrested more than 100 party-goers at a hotel in Asaba, Delta State, on charges that they were gays and lesbians, and that by July 2018 they were facing homosexuality-related charges in court; in August 2023 police raided a gay wedding in Warri, Delta State, arresting dozens in the case known as the 'Warri 67', of whom 67 were charged to court following a mass arrest at a party or marriage ceremony. The 2014 statute punishes same-sex unions with up to 14 years' imprisonment in Delta, and no state-specific protective statute exists.

sources.title: Country policy and information note: sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and sex characteristics, Nigeria, June 2025 (accessible) - GOV.UK
sources.summary: The UK Home Office's June 2025 country policy and information note documents the national criminal framework applying across all states: the 2014 statute punishes same-sex unions with up to 14 years' imprisonment, Section 217 of the Criminal Code makes male gross indecency a felony liable to three years' imprisonment, and the death penalty is confined to the twelve northern Shari'a states. Citing the USSD 2023 human rights report, it records that on 27 August 2023 police in Delta State raided a 'white party' organized by the LGBTQI+ community and detained more than 200 individuals, with police alleging the event was a same-sex wedding while some civil society representatives disputed that account. It also quotes a human rights lawyer based in Warri, Delta state, on 'kito' (predatory same-sex assault) victims under-reporting for fear of prosecution. State-level documentation is thin, which does not demonstrate safety.

sources.title: Police arrest 67 gay suspects in Delta hotel - Daily Post Nigeria
sources.summary: Daily Post reports that police officers from Ekpan Division in Uvwie Local Government Area of Delta State arrested 67 suspects on 27 August 2023 at 9 pm at Teebolus Hotel, Refinery Road, Ekpan, for allegedly conducting and attending a same-sex wedding ceremony between Daniel Pius (the groom), 22, and Maxwel Ohwonohwo (the bride), 20. Delta State Police Command spokesman DSP Bright Edafe said the raid followed a male cross-dresser's confession that he was a member of a gay club travelling to a gay marriage ceremony, that the suspects fled on the officers' arrival but 67 were chased and arrested, and that drugs and 'gay marriage ceremonial dresses' were recovered. Edafe said the suspects and exhibits were in custody and efforts continued to arrest fleeing members for possible prosecution, and that one suspect alleged he was sexually assaulted by a man at the hotel while intoxicated. The incident shows the national anti-LGBT framework actively enforced in Delta State (Warri), with incidents frequently framed together with drug allegations.

27671186B95832466049157.name: Rivers
27671186B95832466049157.summary:
Rivers State lies inside Nigeria and takes its governing law from national instruments rather than any local statute. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014, signed by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014, applies there, as does the Nigerian Criminal Code in the form used across the country's southern states. The sources assembled here record no Rivers-specific provision, incident series or enforcement divergence, so a visitor to Port Harcourt should expect the national rules to govern.

The 2014 Act reaches well past marriage. It makes same-sex marriage and civil unions invalid and illegal, and it criminalises registering, operating, participating in or supporting gay clubs, societies or organisations. Human Rights Watch's October 2016 report sets 10 to 14 years' imprisonment for those organisational offences and records that the Act also bans same-sex cohabitation and any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship. UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office travel advice, updated in August 2026, adds that the Act extends to helpers and attendees of same-sex weddings.

In the south, where Rivers sits, the Criminal Code criminalises sex between men with penalties of up to 14 years' imprisonment and treats gross indecency as an offence carrying up to 3 years. Sharia criminalisation in twelve northern Nigerian states reaches same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy punishable by death under state Zina provisions. That northern exposure is not the law in Rivers, but it shapes onward travel inside the country.

One provisional narrowing exists. In 2022 a group of Nigerian human rights organisations and activists sued over Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act, and the court ruled those sections unconstitutional and unenforceable nationwide, removing them as a basis for prosecuting LGBTQ+ organisations and individuals. The ruling does not decriminalise same-sex conduct; the marriage, civil union and cohabitation bans and the wider criminal code remain.

Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people of any kind, and police practice after the 2014 Act has been documented. Human Rights Watch records arbitrary arrest and extortion as commonplace, including eight of the 21 young men arrested but never charged at a birthday party in Ibadan. The same report documents an attack inside Rivers State itself: Daniel, a 21-year-old gay man from Lagos, travelled to Port Harcourt in January 2015 to meet someone he had contacted on Facebook, and was attacked and sexually abused there. He did not report the assault to the police.

The UK travel advisory of August 2026 warns LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty exposure under Sharia law in northern states. A trans or gender-nonconforming visitor to Port Harcourt faces the same criminal framework plus the documented risk of violence and extortion in a country where police have treated gender nonconformity as evidence of criminality.

27671186B95832466049157.tangentialFactors:
Dating apps carry a specific entrapment risk inside Nigeria. The Thomson Reuters Foundation reported in April 2024 on kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and comparable apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Trans people in Nigeria have been killed with apparent official indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on an Abuja highway hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; the police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing. The Dial reported in February 2025 that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Gender expression sits in active legislative contention. Reuters reported in September 2022 that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

The imprisonment of Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), the country's most prominent transgender woman, illustrates detention risk for a trans visitor. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024, was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, and served it in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly debated which prison would hold the crossdresser, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

Extortion of men perceived as gay by police is routine. TimesLIVE reported in March 2025 that Okafor, a 24-year-old stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay.

27671186B2031248555853.name: Kwara
27671186B2031248555853.summary:
Kwara State stands under Nigeria's national framework, with no regional exception recorded. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 (SSMPA), signed in January 2014, applies nationwide and makes same-sex sexual activity punishable by up to 14 years' imprisonment under federal law; the sources describe the Criminal Code as operating in southern states and the Penal Code in northern states.

Kwara is not among the twelve states recorded as having adopted Sharia law — Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara — so no Sharia penal exposure is documented for the Ilorin area, and the federal statute supplies the operative framework.

The Act's reach extends well beyond sexual conduct. It voids same-sex unions and criminalises forming, operating or supporting gay clubs, societies or organisations. Human Rights Watch, in 'Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe' (October 2016), records 10 to 14 years' imprisonment for participating in or supporting such organisations, a ban on same-sex cohabitation, and a ban on public shows of a same-sex amorous relationship.

A 2022 court ruling held Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the SSMPA unconstitutional and unenforceable nationwide. The sources do not state which provisions remain operative or whether the ruling was appealed.

Official foreign guidance aimed at LGBT+ visitors is explicit and current. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's updated Nigeria travel advice, reported by SaharaReporters on 19 August 2026, warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, states that same-sex activity carries up to 14 years' imprisonment, notes that some northern states under Sharia law can prescribe the death penalty, and confirms that the SSMPA reaches helpers and attendees of same-sex weddings.

Trans visitors face lethal violence. The Nigerian transgender TikToker known as 'Abuja Area Mama', aged 33, was murdered in August 2024: her beaten body was found on a highway in Abuja and police opened an investigation. She had been stabbed a year earlier and had feared for her life. The killing occurred in Abuja rather than Kwara, and it illustrates the national pattern rather than a Kwara-specific case.

Enforcement under the SSMPA takes the form of mass arrests and detention, recorded as common especially in northern states, alongside mob attacks, arbitrary arrests, extortion and detentions across the country following the Act's passage. Human Rights Watch documents 21 young men arrested but never charged at an Ibadan birthday gathering. The report covers Nigeria nationally and names no Kwara-specific case; it documents the federal criminalisation and arbitrary enforcement that apply in Kwara.

27671186B96047513549152.name: Kogi
27671186B96047513549152.summary:
Kogi State stands under Nigeria's national framework. The Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act was passed by the House of Representatives on 30 May 2013 and signed into law by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014; entering a same-sex marriage or civil union carries 14 years' imprisonment, and registering, operating or participating in gay clubs, societies and organisations, or making a public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, carries 10 years.

Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that the Act additionally bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests; the penalties it sets run from 10 to 14 years' imprisonment.

The Criminal Code applies separately in Kogi, criminalising sex between men with up to 14 years' imprisonment and gross indecency with up to 3 years. The twelve Shari'a-administering northern states impose harsher penalties, with death penalties applied in Kano and Katsina for lesbianism; non-Shari'a states such as Kogi sit under the 14-year national maximum instead.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) assesses that same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and that Shari'a law in all twelve northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

Official foreign travel guidance aimed at LGBT+ visitors is explicit and current. Sahara Reporters (19 August 2026), reporting the UK FCDO's updated Nigeria travel advice, relays warnings of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation against LGBT+ travellers; same-sex activity is illegal with up to 14 years' imprisonment; some northern states under Shari'a law can prescribe the death penalty; and the Same Sex Marriage Prohibition Act also reaches helpers and attendees of same-sex weddings.

A 2022 ruling by a coalition of Nigerian human rights organisations held that Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the 2013 Act breached the Constitution and could not be enforced anywhere in the country, effectively allowing LGBTQ+ organisations and individuals to exist and organise. No comparable ruling is recorded for the conduct-prohibition or marriage-prohibition provisions, which remain in force.

The Constitution contains no specific protections on sexual orientation, and there are no federal anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people.

Trans visitors face lethal violence. The beaten body of the Abuja trans TikToker 'Abuja Area Mama', a 33-year-old transgender woman, was found on a highway in Abuja in August 2024; BBC News (9 August 2024) reports that police opened an investigation, that she had been stabbed a year earlier, and that she had feared for her life. Mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people are common across Nigeria, including in Kogi, and are especially frequent in northern states.

Plateau State stands under Nigeria's national criminal framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 criminalises same-sex conduct across the country with penalties of up to 14 years' imprisonment, and its reach extends past the couple: helpers who arrange same-sex weddings and attendees who witness them are also exposed. The statute additionally bans cohabitation between same-sex partners and any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, so exposure for a visitor is not limited to sexual conduct.

Sexual orientation and gender expression carry criminal consequences from the moment of entry. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's updated Nigeria travel advice, reported by Sahara Reporters on 19 August 2026, warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, of violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Shari'a law in some northern states.

Plateau is a North Central state with its capital at Jos and a population of around 4.7 million. Two features of its position matter to a trans visitor. Shari'a criminal law does not apply in the state, so the death penalty that state Zina provisions carry in the twelve northern Shari'a states is not the operative risk here; and the sources do not record for Plateau the concentration of arrests and communal tension attributed to the wider North Central zone.

Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the sources record frequent violence against them. A 2022 legal challenge produced a court ruling that Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the Act are unconstitutional and unenforceable in any part of the country; whether that ruling has narrowed practical enforcement is not established by the sources here, and police and administrative practice continues to operate under the Act's terms.

27671186B76680224160916.name: Anambra
27671186B76680224160916.summary:
Anambra State stands under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies nationwide and reaches conduct well beyond marriage: Human Rights Watch reported in October 2014 that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrest.

Anambra lies outside the twelve northern states that apply Shari'a criminal law, so the federal penalties apply here in full and the death-penalty provisions for male sodomy under state Zina rules do not reach this state. Same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law at entry, carrying up to 14 years' imprisonment, and Shari'a provisions in those twelve states criminalise same-sex acts between men and between women.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's updated Nigeria travel advice, reported by SaharaReporters on 19 August 2026, warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation; it states that same-sex activity is illegal with up to 14 years' imprisonment, that some northern states under Shari'a law can prescribe the death penalty, and that the Same Sex Marriage Prohibition Act also reaches helpers and attendees of same-sex weddings.

Nigeria's federal framework, which governs Anambra, criminalises same-sex sexual activity with up to 14 years' imprisonment in the southern portion and under northern secular law, and death in the twelve northern states applying Shari'a law. The Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2013 extends criminalisation to attempted same-sex marriages. LGBTQ+ people in Nigeria have no legal protections and face frequent violence. In 2022 a court ruled Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the 2013 Act unconstitutional and unenforceable in any part of the country.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Trans people in Nigeria face documented killing and official indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; the police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Police violence against perceived gay people is a routine feature of enforcement. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law that produces a climate of hostility independent of its text.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

The only trans-specific imprisonment case surfaced in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, which she served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

27671186B74554005070963.name: Nasarawa
27671186B74554005070963.summary:
Nasarawa State stands under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 (SSMPA) applies across the country and reaches well beyond marriage: Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests.

Criminal exposure attaches at entry. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records that same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and that Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's travel advisory for Nigeria (19 August 2026, carried by Sahara Reporters) warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation. Same-sex sexual activity is illegal and can attract up to 14 years' imprisonment, and the federal law extends to people who arrange, attend or conduct same-sex weddings and to those involved with gay groups or organisations. Some northern states operate Sharia law under which same-sex activity can attract the death penalty, and breaching curfews or movement restrictions risks arrest and detention.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Violence against trans people is documented and enforcement outcomes are weak. On 9 August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama was found along the Katampe–Mabushi expressway in the capital, roughly a year after she had said she feared for her life; police announced an investigation and described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, while the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Formal constitutional guarantees of non-discrimination and of private and family life do not translate into protection in practice. Mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people are common, especially in northern states, and Nigeria offers no statutory protection for LGBTQ+ people; the SSMPA reinforced colonial-era criminalisation.

27671186B49737451005073.summary:
Adamawa State stands under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies across every state of the federation, including to visitors and tourists: entering a same-sex marriage or civil union carries up to 14 years' imprisonment, and 10 years for anyone who administers, witnesses, abets or aides the solemnization of one, or who supports the registration and operation of gay clubs, societies and organisations. Sharia criminal law is the layer that varies by state. The UK government's June 2025 country-policy note and Wikipedia's survey of the statute both identify twelve northern states where sharia penal codes apply to Muslims, with death as the maximum penalty for men: Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara. Adamawa is not on that list, so the sources do not identify it as a sharia state, and the death-penalty exposure reported for northern states does not attach here on the available evidence. Sharia courts elsewhere in the north have imposed at least four death sentences since 2022, none carried out.

Enforcement climate is documented as hostile regardless of which statute is charged. The UK country-policy note records that NGOs document tens of LGBT+ arrests per year nationwide, and that police and the Islamic police subject LGBT+ people to beatings, blackmail, extortion and torture. 27671186B83117616801018.name: Abia
27671186B83117616801018.summary:
Abia is a southern state of Nigeria and stands under the national criminal framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies across the whole country, has been in force since January 2014, and reaches visitors as well as residents. Same-sex sexual acts between men carry up to 14 years' imprisonment under secular law, and a visitor to Abia is exposed to that penalty from the moment of entry.

The statute's reach extends well beyond marriage. Entering a same-sex marriage or civil union is punishable by 14 years' imprisonment; anyone who administers, witnesses, abets or aides the solemnization of one, or who supports the registration, operation and sustenance of gay clubs, societies, organisations, processions or meetings, faces 10 years. Human Rights Watch further records that the Act bans cohabitation between same-sex partners and any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used the law to justify torture and arbitrary arrests.

Sharia criminal law does not reach Abia. It operates only in twelve northern states, Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara, where male sodomy can carry the death penalty under state Zina provisions. At least four Sharia death sentences have been imposed since 2022 and none has been carried out. Abia is not among the twelve, so the federal penalties and the national arrest climate apply there in full without that religious layer.

Sexual orientation and gender identity carry exposure at the border. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025) sets out the framework a visitor to Abia stands under, and the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's travel advice, as reported by SaharaReporters in August 2026, warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, of death-penalty risk under Sharia provisions in some northern states, and of penalties for those who help arrange or attend a same-sex wedding.

Arrest is routine rather than exceptional. The June 2025 country-policy note documents tens of LGBT+ arrests per year across Nigeria, alongside police and Islamic-police harassment that includes beatings, blackmail, extortion and torture. Enforcement is often financial and summary: in March 2025 TimesLIVE reported that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Those affected describe the Act as a weaponised law that produces a climate of hostility independent of its text.

Dating apps are a documented vector for entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) records kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar applications to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing. A trans visitor who uses these platforms in Abia faces the same mechanism, with no local safeguard against it.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reported that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here. Violence against trans people is documented and official response has been slow. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in the national capital hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the Dial recorded in February 2025 that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Detention carries a specific placement problem for trans women. The country's most prominent transgender woman, Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine. She served the term in a maximum-security prison in Lagos and was released on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to official discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the Act reinforced colonial-era criminalisation. A 2022 federal court ruling struck down sections of the Act as unconstitutional, but the core penalties and the enforcement climate described above remain what a visitor to Abia should expect to encounter.

27671186B91150779192485.summary:
Ekiti State operates under Nigeria's uniform national criminalisation framework. Same-sex conduct is criminalised nationwide by the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014, and its reach extends far beyond marriage: Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, carrying 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have invoked the Act to justify torture and arbitrary arrest.

Criminal exposure begins at the border. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records that same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and that Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice, as reported by SaharaReporters (19 August 2026), warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years for same-sex activity, of death-penalty risk under Sharia provisions in some northern states, and confirms that the same-sex marriage law reaches people who help arrange or attend such weddings.

Enforcement inside Ekiti State is documented rather than hypothetical. Human Rights Watch records that on 21 January 2014, days after the SSMPA was passed, Debbie, a 26-year-old transgender woman, was beaten by six men in Ado Ekiti, the state capital, who threatened her with 14 years in prison; the report states she was beaten at least twice over that period. The same report documents a September 2014 arrest at the Faguyi bar in Ado Ekiti, the gay man's third arrest, who was released after two days in detention once he paid 2,000 Naira for himself and 10,000 Naira for a friend, and a 2014 incident in which a 25-year-old gay man was extorted by a state investigator in Ado Ekiti.

Care access carries a documented gap. Debbie was unable to use Ekiti's health services safely and travelled three hours each way to Ibadan for HIV treatment, which indicates that a trans visitor needing routine or urgent care in the state should expect the same problem.

Dating apps are a documented vector for entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) records kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar applications to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised by the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public. Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the SSMPA reinforced colonial-era criminalisation.

27671186B91150779192485.tangentialFactors:
The most prominent case of a trans person in the Nigerian penal system concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), the country's most prominent transgender woman. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, which indicates that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

Trans people in Nigeria face documented killing with slow official response. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Police violence against perceived gay people is a routine feature of enforcement across the country. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law that produces a climate of hostility independent of its text, which is the same dynamic the 2014 Ekiti incidents show.

Health care for trans residents of Ekiti State was not safe to use locally. Debbie, beaten in Ado Ekiti in January 2014, could not use Ekiti health services and travelled three hours each way to Ibadan for HIV treatment, so sustained residents rather than short-term visitors bear the cost of that distance every time care is needed.

Detention in the state has historically ended in payment rather than prosecution. Where trans detainees are held is settled case by case rather than by written policy. 27671186B37873222803025.name: Osun
27671186B37873222803025.summary:
Osun operates inside Nigeria's national criminal framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies across the country, in Osun State as in every other state, and reaches visitors and non-citizens as well as residents. Human Rights Watch (October 2016, 'Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe') records that the statute bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, carrying 10 to 14 years' imprisonment.

The statute binds people beyond the couple. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office travel advisory of 19 August 2026 states that the law also reaches those who arrange or organise same-sex weddings and anyone involved with gay groups. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) assesses that same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment.

A parallel religious criminal law layer in twelve northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions. That layer does not extend to Osun, which sits outside the Sharia states, and the FCDO death-penalty warning is expressly confined to northern states. The federal penalties and the arrest-risk warnings apply in full.

Official foreign guidance aimed at LGBT+ visitors is current and blunt. The FCDO advisory of 19 August 2026 warns travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, and states that same-sex sexual activity is illegal and can attract up to 14 years' imprisonment.

Enforcement rests on appearance and suspicion as much as on evidence. In March 2025 TimesLIVE reported that a 24-year-old man, Okafor, was stopped by Lagos police, struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for 'looking gay'; those affected describe the Act as a weaponised law creating a climate of hostility. Human Rights Watch has documented police torture and arbitrary arrests carried out under the statute.

Trans visitors face lethal violence, official misgendering and impunity. The beaten body of the Abuja trans TikToker 'Abuja Area Mama', a 33-year-old transgender woman, was found on the Katampe-Mabushi expressway in Abuja in August 2024, roughly a year after she had said she feared for her life; police said preliminary investigations showed 'a man fully dressed in female clothing' and the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. In February 2025, six months on, The Dial reported that no suspects had been charged.

Dating applications carry a specific entrapment risk. Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents 'kito' gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and other apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Enforcement also takes the form of mass arrests at social venues, a national pattern rather than a local one. Men arrested in Bauchi in August 2007 were held for several years awaiting a trial that dissolved by the end of 2011; more than 100 party-goers were arrested at a hotel in Asaba in June 2018; 57 young men at Egbeda in Lagos in August 2018; the 'Warri 67' in Warri in August 2023; and 76 people at a party in Gombe state in October 2023. Foreign and domestic guidance should be read against that record when a visitor considers attending any private gathering.

The article notes that despite constitutional guarantees of non-discrimination and private and family life, mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people are common, especially in northern states. This is national-climate evidence bearing on Osun.

UK Foreign Office travel advisory (19 Aug 2026) warns LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, stating that same-sex sexual activity is illegal and can attract up to 14 years' imprisonment, with the law also reaching wedding arrangers and organisers and anyone involved with gay groups. The advisory's Sharia warning applies only to northern states and does not apply in Osun, while the federal penalties and arrest-risk warnings apply in full.

27671186B83252759475924.summary:
Taraba State stands under Nigeria's national criminal framework. The Act also criminalises attending, organising or promoting same-sex weddings and registering or publicly promoting gay groups.

Sharia application is the sharpest variable in the north. The UK Home Office country policy and information note (June 2025, updated April 2026) records that Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions. Taraba is not named among the states that have adopted Sharia, so no Sharia application in Taraba is documented; a visitor crossing into a state that has adopted it faces exposure to those penalties.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Police violence against perceived gay people is a routine feature of enforcement. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. 65028918B98829509874887.name: West Nusa Tenggara
65028918B98829509874887.summary:
West Nusa Tenggara stands under Indonesia's national framework, and no sub-national deviation for this province is recorded: no enacted bylaw, raid, arrest or incident targeting transgender people in West Nusa Tenggara, and no protective legislation for the province. The province is assessed at the national risk level.

Indonesia provides no anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. Parliament passed a new Penal Code in December 2022 that took effect on 2 January 2026 and criminalises consensual sexual activity outside marriage, with penalties reported at up to two years' imprisonment and at up to one year where an immediate family member lodges the complaint. Same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, so the provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside the national morality provisions. Aceh punishes homosexuality under sharia law by flogging or imprisonment, and its penalties apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors; two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025. No equivalent provincial provision for West Nusa Tenggara appears in the sources.

Physical risk is rising nationally. Vigilante mobs are attacking transgender people, and August 2026 coverage reports growing repression of Indonesia's transgender community under the framework that governs West Nusa Tenggara. Reporting in August 2026 ties the surge directly to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 that lists LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism.

Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue. On 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa and arrested 75 people, and Amnesty International stated that the gathering violated no law and called the operation a violation of human rights and privacy. Further raids took place in South Jakarta in February and May 2025.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges and died in custody; his mother in Lima alleges police beat him, and Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes writing or audio-visual material showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment. In March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, the government has blocked websites and apps carrying gay or LGBTQ-related words including Grindr, and a bill to prohibit online content presenting LGBT behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Documents allow only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option. Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval.

65028918B99918739720671.name: Banten
65028918B99918739720671.summary:
Indonesia is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Banten stands under this national framework. Since June 2021 the Indonesian Ministry of Home Affairs has conducted outreach to issue transgender Indonesians with identity papers, including the national identity card (e-KTP), and Banten is named among the nine provinces whose transgender residents have benefited so far. The stated reasoning was that many of those people were undocumented, particularly where families did not approve of their transition. For a trans traveller, this documents that identity-document issuance for transgender people has operated in this province since mid-2021, which bears on document status and enrolment here.

Provincial criminalisation remains in force in two of Indonesia's provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, which criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national-level morality provisions. Banten is not among them. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors; in Aceh two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025.

Physical risk is rising. Vigilante mobs are attacking transgender people, and an August 2026 feature reports growing repression against Indonesia's transgender community. Reporting in August 2026 ties the surge directly to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 that lists LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism, placing them inside national defence policy.

Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue. On 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman; Amnesty International said the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him. Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment; in March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, and the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words, including Grindr. A bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option. Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval. No national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

65028918B13838862025135.name: Central Java
65028918B13838862025135.summary:
Central Java is a province of Indonesia, and a visitor there stands under Indonesia's national legal framework. The sources record no provision specific to Central Java that would alter that position: no criminalisation of gender identity itself, no X marker on identity documents, and no legal recognition of same-sex marriage.

The national penal code was passed by the House of Representatives on 6 December 2022, signed by President Joko Widodo, and took effect on 2 January 2026. It criminalises sexual activity outside marriage, with penalties reported at up to two years' imprisonment under the framework and at up to one year where a complaint is lodged by an immediate family member. The code does not explicitly criminalise same-sex relationships, but because Indonesia does not recognise same-sex marriage, all sexual activity between same-sex couples falls within the outside-marital-sex restriction. Reporting indicates prosecutions under the provision are selective rather than systematic.

Physical risk to transgender visitors is rising. Reporting in August 2026 documents growing repression of Indonesia's transgender community, and other reporting ties a surge in vigilante mob attacks on transgender people to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 listing LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism. Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue: on 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman; Amnesty International said the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him. Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment; in March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, and the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words, including Grindr. A bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option. Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval. No national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

65028918B19721185942402.name: West Kalimantan
65028918B19721185942402.summary:
West Kalimantan records no separate LGBTI legislation and no documented provincial enforcement, so the national framework of Indonesia governs what a trans visitor faces in the province.

Indonesia's penal code, signed in December 2022 and in force from 2 January 2026, penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, the provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Provincial morality laws elsewhere in the country and Aceh's caning punishments, imposed under provincial religious law, form part of the enforcement texture a visitor may encounter on inter-provincial travel. Aceh's penalties apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors; in Aceh two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025.

Physical risk is rising. Vigilante mobs attacked transgender women across Indonesia in a wave of 14-16 July 2026, among them more than 15 trans women who were doused, stripped and beaten in Bogor, with footage of the attack shared online. A presidential decree of October 2025 lists the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture among non-military threats alongside terrorism, radicalism and drug addiction, placing LGBTQ+ people inside national defence policy, and reporting of August 2026 ties the surge in attacks directly to that decree and to officials' public condemnations.

Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue. On 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman; Amnesty International said the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment. In March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words including Grindr, and a bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Documents and screening carry exposure. Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors with no third-gender or X option, and legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery plus a judge's approval. No national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and the Constitution does not address either.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; his mother in Lima was told during a WhatsApp call that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. 65028918B29194895292819.name: Jambi
65028918B29194895292819.summary:
Jambi is a province of Indonesia, and the national framework applies there in full: Indonesia's penal code, national morality provisions, document rules and policing practice govern a visitor in Jambi as they govern anyone else in the country. No Jambi-specific ordinance, protection measure or documented incident against a transgender person was found in the sources reviewed.

The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. A separate source records a maximum of one year, on complaint by an immediate family member.

Same-sex conduct is otherwise not criminalised in private under national law. Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national-level morality provisions. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors, and two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship there in February 2025. Provincial moral laws of this kind remain part of the enforcement texture across Indonesia.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment. In March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words including Grindr, and a bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Physical risk is rising. Vigilante mobs attacked transgender people across Indonesia in a wave of 14 to 16 July 2026, including more than 15 trans women doused, stripped and beaten in Bogor, with footage shared online. Reporting in August 2026 ties the surge directly to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 issued by President Prabowo Subianto, which lists LGBTQ+ people and "the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture" among nonmilitary threats to be monitored and controlled alongside terrorism, radicalism and drug addiction. Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue. 65028918B48178230554278.name: Maluku
65028918B48178230554278.summary:
Maluku stands under Indonesia's national framework. Both sources audited for this province are national in scope, and neither records a Maluku-specific ordinance, police operation, protection scheme or service, so the assessment rests on the national picture those sources document.

The penal code signed on 6 December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and criminalises sexual activity between adults outside marriage. The Human Dignity Trust country profile records a maximum of two years' imprisonment, while the national overview gives up to one year where an immediate family member lodges the complaint. Because Indonesia does not permit same-sex marriage, every sexual act by a same-sex couple falls within the outside-marriage offence. Reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Criminalisation below the national level exists in two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, which penalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women; Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors. Two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in Aceh in February 2025. Maluku has no equivalent provincial provision.

Physical risk is rising across Indonesia. Vigilante mobs are attacking transgender people, and reporting in August 2026 ties the surge to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 that lists LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism, placing them inside national defence policy.

Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue. On 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman; Amnesty International said the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him. Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment; in March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, and the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words, including Grindr. A bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option. Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval. Since June 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs has run outreach issuing transgender Indonesians electronic ID cards, operating in nine provinces, as the document route. No national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and the Constitution is silent on both.

On 14 December 2017 the Constitutional Court rejected, by five votes to four, a petition to criminalise homosexuality. Indonesia voted against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, and a 2023 Pew Research survey found 95% of Indonesians oppose same-sex marriage.

65028918B43243108525571.name: East Java
65028918B43243108525571.summary:
East Java stands under the national framework of Indonesia, a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. East Java has no provincial carve-out from this framework.

Physical risk is carried by the national regime rather than by any East Java-specific rule. Vigilante mobs are attacking transgender people, and reporting in August 2026 ties the surge to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 listing LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism. Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue: on 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman, with Amnesty International stating the gathering violated no law. The Diplomat's August 2026 reporting is national and does not describe East Java specifically.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger anywhere in Indonesia, East Java included. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment; in March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, and the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words, including Grindr. A bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Documents and status: Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option. Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, so a trans visitor travelling on a foreign passport with a changed marker is entering a jurisdiction whose own standard of legal gender change is far stricter. Same-sex couples have no recognised legal relationship of any kind, and no national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. Indonesian law provides no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection on those grounds.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller in Indonesia. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him; Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

East Java specifics are thin but concrete on one point: nothing in East Java civil law barred authorities from placing the trans woman Isa Zega in a women's prison facility by identity, and with no anti-discrimination framework there is no statutory basis on which to contest such a placement. A trans visitor detained in East Java therefore faces custody conditions determined by local practice alone.

65028918B10722647473585.name: Bangka-Belitung Islands
65028918B10722647473585.summary:
Bangka-Belitung Islands stands under the national framework of Indonesia, which is assessed as a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to one year's imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations, and reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. The provision applies in Bangka-Belitung Islands as throughout Indonesia.

No national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and Indonesia has no anti-discrimination or hate-crime provisions for LGBT people. Same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are unrecognised, so no same-sex relationship carries legal recognition anywhere in the country.

Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option. Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, a process that shapes what documents a trans visitor or resident can present at airports, hotels and police checks.

Physical risk is rising across Indonesia. Reporting by The Diplomat in August 2026 describes a transgender community facing growing repression, with vigilante mobs attacking trans people as the government moves to codify anti-LGBT provisions. Reporting in the same period ties the surge in attacks to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 that lists LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism, placing them inside national defence policy.

Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue. On 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman; Amnesty International said the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national morality provisions. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors; in Aceh two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025. A visitor travelling onward from Bangka-Belitung Islands to either province carries the national exposure plus that provincial layer.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him. Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment; in March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, and the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words, including Grindr. A bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Social and institutional hostility is documented at national level. A 2025 Pew figure found 93% of Indonesians rating homosexuality 'morally unacceptable'. The Constitutional Court rejected a petition to criminalise gay sex on 14 December 2017 by 5-4, and Indonesia voted against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2016, 2022 and 2025. No deviation from this national position has been documented in Bangka-Belitung Islands.

15666254B97003483933575.name: Kuala Lumpur
15666254B97003483933575.summary:
Malaysia criminalises same-sex conduct at the federal level. Sections 377A and 377B of the Penal Code 1936 punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" for any person regardless of gender or consent, carrying a maximum of 20 years' imprisonment plus whipping; these provisions are not limited to Malaysian citizens and apply to visitors. Section 377D's "gross indecency" offence carries up to two years. The federal territory of Kuala Lumpur stands directly under this Penal Code, with no local ordinance displacing it, and sodomy has been criminalised in the territory's governing law since 1871.

A second layer applies only to Muslims. Every state and the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya maintain Sharia enactments that criminalise cross-dressing or a man posing as a woman, with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. All 13 states have passed such enactments since the 1980s, and three of them also bar women from posing as men. Enforcement is carried out by state Islamic religious departments, and the enactments contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing. A non-Muslim foreign visitor is therefore outside this layer, but inside the federal one in full.

Litigation has narrowed the state layer without loosening the federal one. The High Court denied a request to declare the Sharia prohibition on cross-dressing unconstitutional. The Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024, both on federalism grounds, leaving Penal Code offences fully intact. A constitutional challenge was still pending as of late 2014, filed after police arrested 16 trans women at a wedding on 8 June 2014.

Enforcement against gender nonconformity is active and publicly sanctioned. In July 2020 the Religious Affairs Minister announced that the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi) had his full licence to carry out its enforcement actions against transgender persons, an order the International Commission of Jurists demanded be revoked. In the case of the trans public figure Nur Sajat, 122 religious officers were mobilised to pursue her for "insulting Islam" before she fled to Thailand and received UNHCR protection.

Raid-based arrest is the documented pattern, and venue raids carry acute exposure risk for foreign visitors. On 28 November 2025 police, Kuala Lumpur City Hall and Jawi raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur, arresting 208 men under section 377B in the largest operation of its kind since 2022. Media had been pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details were leaked; 17 civil servants identified among those arrested were suspended. A magistrate rejected an extension of remand for lack of ground, yet release was delayed, with more than 130 people held at one point, including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Justice For Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid; on 2 December the Home Minister floated revisiting the provisions, and days later police raided another sauna in Penang.

Trans people in Malaysia face lethal violence and official indifference to it. A transgender woman was killed in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in the country in fewer than two months; documentation of that case records police mistreatment and impunity under the heading "The Deceased Can't Speak for Herself".

The wider climate is one of state-backed restriction. Human Rights Watch, working with Justice for Sisters, documented discrimination against LGBT people in August 2022 on the basis of interviews with 73 LGBT people conducted between 2018 and 2021, including people living in Kuala Lumpur; a Kuala Lumpur activist quoted there described regression as a conservative strand of Islam gains ground. Government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, LGBT events and media content are censored, and Islamist opposition has foreclosed reform prospects. There is no same-sex marriage and no anti-discrimination law.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor, the practical exposure is the Penal Code rather than the Sharia enactments. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted; the documented pattern is raid-based arrest and public outing rather than individual stops.

15666254B60207109163985.name: Negeri Sembilan
15666254B60207109163985.summary:
Negeri Sembilan stands under the national framework of Malaysia. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code 1936 punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" for any person regardless of gender or consent, carrying a maximum of 20 years' imprisonment plus whipping. These provisions are not limited to Malaysian citizens and apply to visitors.

Those state offences reach Muslims only, so a non-Muslim foreign visitor in Negeri Sembilan is exposed to the Penal Code rather than to the Sharia layer.

Negeri Sembilan is the state whose cross-dressing offence was struck down on the record. In November 2014 the Court of Appeal declared section 66 of the Syariah Criminal Enactment 1992 of Negeri Sembilan unconstitutional for breaching rights guaranteed by the Federal Constitution. The Federal Court has more recently struck down Sharia criminal-code provisions in Selangor and Kelantan on the ground that state legislatures lack criminal-law power.

15666254B50935235229272.summary:

Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code 1936 criminalise "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" for any person regardless of gender or consent, carrying up to 20 years' imprisonment and whipping; the offence is not limited to Malaysian citizens and applies to foreign visitors. Enforcement is reported as active. The 2021 Nur Sajat case shows the machinery a transgender person can face: a transgender woman was pursued on a religious-affairs arrest warrant, with a search mobilising 122 officers. Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters call for decriminalisation of same-sex conduct and gender diversity in response to the pattern they document.

15666254B8535925993004.name: Sarawak
15666254B8535925993004.summary:
Sarawak stands under Malaysia's national framework. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" for any person regardless of gender or consent, carrying a maximum of 20 years' imprisonment plus whipping, and acts of gross indecency are separately punishable on the same scale. The provisions are not limited to Malaysians and apply to visitors. Sodomy was first criminalised in 1871.

Sarawak is one of the 13 states whose Sharia enactments criminalise cross-dressing or a man posing as a woman, with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. These offences reach Muslims only, so a non-Muslim visitor is not exposed to that layer; enforcement is carried out by the state Islamic religious department, and the enactments contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing.

No legal gender-recognition procedure is recorded for Malaysia, so a trans visitor's documents will carry their original markers at immigration and in any identity check.

Discrimination and violence against LGBT people are regularly reported, with transgender people particularly vulnerable. A study accompanying an August 2022 report interviewed 73 LGBT people across Malaysia between 2018 and 2021 and documented conversion practices, discrimination and violence against them.

Enforcement recorded since the 2018 election includes an October 2022 raid on a Queer Halloween party in Kuala Lumpur in which at least 20 LGBT people were arrested, an August raid on an LGBT venue that netted twenty men, a Terengganu Sharia court ordering a lesbian couple caned, and November 2023 plans in Johor to open conversion-therapy centres. None of these incidents took place in Sarawak, but each arose under the statutes that govern Sarawak, and the raid-based pattern is the exposure a visitor would encounter.

Government-run "rehabilitation" programmes had drawn at least 1,733 attendees as of June 2021. The federal provisions apply in Sarawak in full.
