15666254B54729125478011.name: Putrajaya
15666254B54729125478011.summary:
Putrajaya is a federal territory of Malaysia and the country's administrative capital. It stands under the national framework: Malaysia criminalises both same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity at federal level, and the territory's own Sharia code adds a second layer that reaches Muslims only.

Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code 1936 punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" and acts of "gross indecency" with up to 20 years' imprisonment and whipping. These provisions are not limited to Malaysians and apply to visitors. Sodomy was first criminalised in 1871.

Sharia enactments in all 13 states and in the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya criminalise cross-dressing or "a man posing as a woman", with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. These offences reach Muslims only. State Islamic religious departments enforce them, and the enactments contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing.

No legal gender-recognition procedure is recorded for Malaysia, so a visitor whose passport marker does not match their presentation has no domestic mechanism to align documents before travel.

Litigation has narrowed the Sharia layer without loosening the federal one. A High Court request to declare the cross-dressing prohibition unconstitutional was denied, and the Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds, leaving Penal Code offences fully intact.

Enforcement against gender nonconformity is active and public. Since the 2018 election, documented action includes an October 2022 raid on a Queer Halloween party in Kuala Lumpur with at least 20 LGBT people arrested and an August raid on an LGBT venue that detained twenty men; a Terengganu Sharia court ordered a lesbian couple caned. Discrimination and violence against LGBT people are regularly reported, with transgender people particularly vulnerable.

In July 2020 the Religious Affairs Minister stated that the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi) had his "full licence to carry out its enforcement actions" against transgender persons, an order the International Commission of Jurists demanded be revoked. In the Nur Sajat case, 122 religious officers were mobilised to pursue her for "insulting Islam" before she fled to Thailand and received UNHCR protection.

Queue-and-venue raids carry acute exposure risk for foreign visitors. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur, arresting 208 men under section 377B, the largest operation of its kind since 2022. Media were pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details were leaked; 17 civil servants identified among them were suspended. A magistrate rejected the remand extension as lacking ground, yet release was delayed, with more than 130 people held at one point including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Justice For Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid; on 2 December the Home Minister floated revisiting the provisions, and days later police raided another sauna in Penang.

Trans people in Malaysia face lethal violence and official indifference to it. A transgender woman was killed in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in the country in fewer than two months; documentation of that case records police mistreatment and impunity.

There is no same-sex marriage and no anti-discrimination law.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor, the Putrajaya Sharia cross-dressing offence does not apply, but the federal Penal Code does. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted; the documented pattern is raid-based arrest and public outing rather than individual stops.

15666254B34720353032971.name: Pahang
15666254B34720353032971.summary:
Pahang stands under the national framework of Malaysia. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code 1936 criminalise "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" and acts of "gross indecency", carrying up to 20 years' imprisonment plus whipping. The offences turn on the conduct rather than on gender or consent, so they reach visitors as well as citizens.

Every Malaysian state and the federal territories maintain Sharia enactments that criminalise cross-dressing or "a man posing as a woman", with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. No legal gender-recognition procedure is recorded for Malaysia, and no federal law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. A visitor whose documents do not match their presentation has no statutory protection against being challenged on that basis.

Enforcement across the country concentrates on venues and queues rather than on private conduct. Police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur on 28 November 2025 and arrested 208 men under section 377B; detainees' faces and personal details were published, more than 130 people were held at one point, and 31 foreign nationals were among them until their embassies intervened. For a visitor in Pahang the operative exposure is the federal Penal Code, not a local operation: no Pahang-specific raid, prosecution or arrest is documented in these sources. Discrimination and violence against LGBT people are regularly reported nationally, and transgender people are identified as particularly vulnerable.

Litigation has narrowed the state Sharia layer without loosening the federal one. Trans people in Malaysia face lethal violence. A transgender woman was killed in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in the country in fewer than two months, and documentation of that case records police mistreatment and impunity.

In July 2020 the Religious Affairs Minister said the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department had his "full licence to carry out its enforcement actions" against transgender persons, an order the International Commission of Jurists demanded be revoked; in the Nur Sajat case 122 religious officers were mobilised before she fled to Thailand and received UNHCR protection.

15666254B44964481844598.name: Perlis
15666254B44964481844598.summary:
Perlis stands under Malaysia's federal framework: the Penal Code 1936 applies in the state without modification. Sections 377A and 377B punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" for any person regardless of gender or consent, with acts of gross indecency criminalised alongside them, carrying up to 20 years' imprisonment and whipping. These offences are not limited to Malaysian nationals. The Human Dignity Trust's Malaysia country profile, last updated 16 December 2025, records them in force.

Perlis is one of all 13 states, together with Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya, that maintains Sharia enactments criminalising cross-dressing or "a man posing as a woman", with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. Since the 1980s every state has passed such an enactment, and three also bar women from posing as men. These state offences reach Muslims only. A non-Muslim foreign visitor in Perlis is not exposed to them; a Muslim visitor is, and enforcement rests with the state Islamic religious department.

No legal gender-recognition procedure is recorded for Malaysia, so a visitor whose identity documents do not match their presentation has no domestic process available to align them. Discrimination and violence against LGBT people are regularly reported in the country, and transgender people are documented as particularly vulnerable.

The national framework has been applied through raids and public proceedings since the 2018 election. An October 2022 raid on a Queer Halloween party in Kuala Lumpur produced at least 20 LGBT arrests; a raid on an LGBT venue in August drew twenty men; a Terengganu Sharia court ordered a lesbian couple caned; and in November 2023 Johor authorities announced plans for conversion-therapy centres. Raid operations have publicly identified detainees. None of the sources names a Perlis-specific enforcement case, so what a visitor faces here is the national pattern rather than a documented local record.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor the operative exposure in Perlis is the federal Penal Code and venue-based raids. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted; the documented pattern is raid-based arrest and public outing rather than individual stops.

15666254B92074897121205.name: Penang
15666254B92074897121205.summary:
Penang stands under Malaysia's federal framework. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code criminalise 'carnal intercourse against the order of nature' and acts of 'gross indecency', carrying up to 20 years' imprisonment plus whipping. The offences are not confined to Malaysian citizens, so a foreign visitor in Penang is exposed to them on the same terms as a resident. Sodomy has been criminalised in the territory since 1871.

Sharia enactments add a second, narrower layer. Every one of Malaysia's 13 states and the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya criminalise cross-dressing or 'a man posing as a woman', with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning; three of them also bar women from posing as men. These offences reach Muslims only, so a non-Muslim visitor is not subject to them, and the enactments contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing. Enforcement is carried out by state Islamic religious departments.

Litigation has narrowed the state layer without loosening the federal one. A High Court declined to declare the Sharia prohibition on cross-dressing unconstitutional, and the Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds, leaving the Penal Code offences fully intact. A constitutional challenge was still pending as of late 2014, filed after religious officers and police arrested 16 trans women at a wedding on 8 June 2014.

Enforcement against gender nonconformity is active and publicly authorised. In July 2020 the Religious Affairs Minister announced that the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi) had his 'full licence to carry out its enforcement actions' against transgender persons, an order the International Commission of Jurists demanded be revoked. In the Nur Sajat case, 122 religious officers were mobilised to pursue her for 'insulting Islam' before she fled to Thailand and received UNHCR protection.

The documented pattern of exposure is venue-based raid and public outing rather than individual stops. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur, arresting 208 men under section 377B, the largest operation of its kind since 2022. Media were pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details were published; 17 civil servants identified among them were suspended. A magistrate rejected a remand extension for lack of ground, yet release was delayed, with more than 130 people held at one point including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Justice For Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid; on 2 December the Home Minister floated revisiting the provisions, and days later police raided another sauna, this one in Penang.

Trans people in Malaysia also face lethal violence met with official indifference. A transgender woman was killed in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in the country in fewer than two months; documentation of that case records police mistreatment and impunity under the heading 'The Deceased Can't Speak for Herself'.

The surrounding climate is one of state-backed restriction. Islamist opposition has foreclosed reform prospects, government-funded mukhayyam 'rehabilitation' retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, and LGBT events and media content are censored. There is no same-sex marriage, no legal gender-recognition procedure is recorded for Malaysia, and no law prohibits discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor, the practical exposure in Penang is the Penal Code, not the Sharia enactments. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted; the risk concentrates in raids on venues where attendees are arrested and named.

28173009B80457268982215.summary:
Altai Krai stands under the national framework of Russia, and the sources record no regional deviation: the 2023 prohibition on legal gender recognition and on gender-affirming care, the Supreme Court's designation of the "international LGBT movement" as an extremist organisation, and the expanded "propaganda" statutes apply in full to a visitor in this region.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025, assessment updated 11 June 2025) sets out the baseline a trans visitor here faces. 28173009B16834140201491.name: Republic of Mordovia
28173009B16834140201491.summary:
The Republic of Mordovia stands under the national framework of Russia, which applies in full; the assessment is made at the national level, with no regional deviation identified for Mordovia.

Russia presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes to official documents was signed; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression that, explicitly, includes anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, detention of up to 15 days, and deportation, and national government warnings directed at LGBT travellers say so plainly.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Russia (June 2025) records that same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, while same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023. The 2013 "gay propaganda" statute is punishable by administrative fines or detention of up to 15 days, escalating to up to four years' imprisonment on a repeat offence. Since the 2023 extremist designation of the international LGBT+ movement, participation carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising carries six to ten years.

The same note records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024, and assesses that openly LGBT+ people face societal discrimination that may amount to persecution, with the state able but unwilling to protect them.

Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts have issued 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the "International LGBT Movement" or for displaying its symbols since the 2023 Supreme Court designation, comprising about 98 administrative cases and 3 criminal cases. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges; three publishing-house staff charged under article 282.2 face up to 12 years' imprisonment, and 81 people were convicted in 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols.

No separate Mordovia-specific legal instrument, enforcement record, or service provision affecting transgender visitors was present in the inventory; the national figures above are the operative baseline for a visit to Saransk or elsewhere in the republic.

28173009B71296032393878.name: Kurgan Oblast
28173009B71296032393878.summary:
Kurgan Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, which applies in full and with no identified regional deviation. The dedicated country record identified no deviation material enough to score separately (±0.02), so the oblast is assessed at the national score.

For a trans visitor this framework means that legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care have been banned outright since 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed; gender-transition procedures are banned and gender-marker changes on documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023. Same-sex marriage is banned. Same-sex sexual activity as such is not criminalised.

The Supreme Court's designation of the "international LGBT movement" as an extremist organisation operates nationwide, including in Kurgan Oblast: participation carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising carries six to ten years. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the designated movement or for displaying its symbols as of 30 June 2025, roughly 98 of them administrative and three criminal. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, including three publishing-house staff charged under article 282.2 who face up to 12 years' imprisonment, while 81 people were convicted in 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols.

The 2013 "propaganda" law, expanded in 2022 to cover any public expression including anything "justifying" gender transition, is punishable by administrative fines or detention of up to 15 days, escalating to up to four years' imprisonment on a repeat offence. Enforcement is escalating in volume as well as severity: Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, with fines bringing more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget over the two preceding years.

Foreigners are explicitly at risk. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention.

The Guardian reported on 17 January 2024 that within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night. The Moscow Times (23 June 2025) reported that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, including a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, among them three publishing-house staff charged under article 282.2 who face up to 12 years' imprisonment, while 81 people were convicted in 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols.

The UK Home Office assesses that openly LGBT+ people in Russia face societal discrimination that may amount to persecution, with the state able but unwilling to protect them, and records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024. 28173009B21210279674314.name: Komi Republic
28173009B21210279674314.summary:
The Komi Republic stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation, which extends in full. The sources record no republic-level variation in how these laws operate, and the jurisdiction is assessed at the national score. A trans visitor to Syktyvkar or anywhere else in the Komi Republic faces the same legal position as a trans visitor elsewhere in the country.

Same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned. Gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes to official documents was signed.

The 2013 "gay propaganda" statute is punishable by administrative fines or detention of up to 15 days, escalating to four years' imprisonment on a repeat offence. Since the Supreme Court's 2023 designation of the "international LGBT movement" as an extremist organisation, participation carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising carries six to ten years. The expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression, explicitly including anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who violate these provisions face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation, and foreign government warnings issued to LGBT travellers say so.

Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the designated movement or display of its symbols as of 30 June 2025, roughly 98 administrative and three criminal. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, among them three publishing-house staff charged under article 282.2 who face up to 12 years' imprisonment, while 81 people were convicted in 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols.

Enforcement has grown in volume as well as severity. An independent media outlet reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under the propaganda statutes have increased eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding. Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling, on 17 January 2024, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow; about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. A foreign broadcaster's report of 27 July 2024 followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found. In December 2024 a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

The US State Department travel advisory advises against all travel for all travellers regardless of personal characteristic, citing wrongful detention risk, the war and arbitrary law enforcement. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (v2.0, June 2025, page updated 12 August 2026) records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024, and assesses that openly LGBT+ people face societal discrimination that may amount to persecution, with the state able but unwilling to protect them.

Kostroma Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, which applies in full. The regional assessment identified no deviation from the national position material enough to score separately, so the oblast is assessed at the national score.

Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care have been banned outright since 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed. Gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited, trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned the same year, and same-sex marriage is banned. Same-sex sexual activity as such is not criminalised.

The 2013 propaganda law is punishable by administrative fines or detention of up to 15 days, escalating to up to four years' imprisonment on a repeat offence. The expanded law criminalises any public expression that justifies gender transition. Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation, and national government warnings expressly direct LGBT travellers to that risk.

Since the Supreme Court's 2023 designation of the "international LGBT movement" as an extremist organisation, participation carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising six to ten. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions as of 30 June 2025, about 98 of them administrative and three criminal. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, including three publishing-house staff charged under article 282.2 who face up to 12 years' imprisonment, while 81 people were convicted in 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols.

Enforcement has grown in volume as well as severity. Cases under the propaganda laws have increased eighteenfold over the past decade, and fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding. Within 48 hours of the extremist designation, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 on a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Travel advisories reflect the same position. The US State Department rates Russia Level 4, Do Not Travel, for all travellers regardless of personal characteristic, citing wrongful detention risk, the war and arbitrary law enforcement, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention.

28173009B65133456612022.name: Krasnoyarsk Krai
28173009B65133456612022.summary:
Krasnoyarsk Krai stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation in full. The sources identify no deviation from that framework at the level of Krasnoyarsk Krai material sufficient to score separately, and the division is therefore assessed at the national score.

Under that framework, same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, while same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned outright. Gender-marker changes on official documents are refused, legal gender recognition was banned in 2023, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in the same year.

The 2013 "gay propaganda" statute punishes public expression with administrative fines or detention of up to 15 days, escalating to four years' imprisonment on a repeat offence, and the expanded law reaches material that "justifies" gender transition. Since the Supreme Court's 2023 designation of the "international LGBT movement" as an extremist organisation, participation in it carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising it six to ten years.

Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation, and official national government warnings expressly tell LGBT travellers of this.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024. It assesses that openly LGBT+ people face societal discrimination that may amount to persecution, that the state is able but unwilling to protect them, and it affirms that LGBT+ people constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and advises against all travel for all travellers regardless of personal characteristic, citing wrongful detention risk, the war, and arbitrary law enforcement; the advisory carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts had issued 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the designated "international LGBT movement" or for displaying its symbols, of which about 98 were administrative and three criminal. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges under the designation, including three publishing-house staff charged under article 282.2 who face up to 12 years' imprisonment, while 81 people were convicted in 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols. Human Rights Watch called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

Enforcement is escalating in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under the propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles into the state budget in the two years preceding.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night. Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025 according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025), which reported a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented well outside the major cities. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk in Siberia, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

28173009B46424166303156.name: Rostov Oblast
28173009B46424166303156.summary:
Rostov Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, where the legal position of transgender visitors has been severe since 2023. President Vladimir Putin signed the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents, closing both gender-affirming care and legal gender recognition. The Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation, and the expanded propaganda statute criminalises any public expression that "justifies" gender transition. Same-sex activity is not itself criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned and no specific legal protections exist.

Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, administrative detention of up to 15 days, and deportation. The propaganda law carries administrative fines, with repeat offences punishable by up to four years in prison. Participation in the designated extremist movement carries two to six years and organising six to ten years. The US State Department rates travel to Russia Level 4, Do Not Travel, and its advisory carries warnings addressed to LGBT travellers.

Enforcement is documented at scale. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism convictions tied to the 2023 Supreme Court designation as of 30 June 2025. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges; one died by suicide in pretrial detention and courts sentenced two to prison. In the same period 81 people were found guilty in 98 cases under article 20.3 of the Code of Administrative Offenses for displaying banned symbols, with the organisation's participants exposed to up to 12 years in prison.

Within Rostov Oblast, the practical risk that differs from the national average is access to care. Survey data place the Southern Federal District, which contains Rostov Oblast, at 27% for discrimination by healthcare providers who knew a patient's sexual orientation or gender identity. No Rostov Oblast-specific detention, raid or extremism conviction is documented in the material reviewed for this record.

28173009B55422170414647.name: Khakassia
28173009B55422170414647.summary:
Khakassia, a republic within the Russian Federation, stands under Russia's national legal framework, and the source record shows no sub-national variation in how that framework is applied. Russia prohibits legal gender recognition outright: the law signed by President Vladimir Putin in 2023 bans gender reassignment surgery, bars any change of gender marker on official documents, voids a marriage concluded by a trans person with someone of their same birth sex, and removes the right to adopt from people diagnosed with gender dysphoria. Same-sex marriage is not recognised, trans-specific healthcare has been effectively banned since 2023, and neither residents nor visitors in Khakassia can obtain a recognised legal gender status.

Russia provides no anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, does not designate hate crimes as such, does not treat gender-identity motivation as an aggravating factor in sentencing, and does not officially record hate crimes against the LGBTQ community. A visitor who is subjected to hostility on that basis in Khakassia therefore enters no formal protection or recording machinery at the point of reporting.

Public expression is constrained by the propaganda statutes. The 2013 law targeted material concerning minors; it was expanded in December 2022 to cover all age groups and now reaches content that promotes "non-traditional" sexual relationships, makes minors interested in gender transition, gives minors a "desire to change their sex", or justifies gender transition. More than 180 cases were brought under these provisions in 2023 alone, exceeding the total for 2013 to 2022 combined and producing roughly 26 million rubles in fines; cases have increased eighteenfold over the past decade, and fines brought over 60 million rubles (about $765,300) into the state budget in the two years to mid-2025.

Since the Supreme Court's November 2023 designation of a non-existent "international LGBT movement" as extremist, charges have been brought for displaying the rainbow flag or its colours. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions by 30 June 2025 for alleged participation in that movement or display of its alleged symbols, comprising 98 administrative and 3 criminal cases. At least 20 people faced criminal charges from January 2024, three publishing-house staff charged on 15 May 2025 face up to 12 years, and repeated display of banned symbols carries up to four years in prison. Between March and May 2026, nine LGBTQ organisations, among them the Russian LGBT Network, Coming Out and Centre T, were outlawed as extremist.

The post-designation crackdown was immediate. Within 48 hours of the ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow; about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night. In December 2024 a man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel business was found dead in a pretrial detention facility. Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ life through 2025.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and warns that foreigners found guilty of violating the propaganda law may be detained for up to 15 days and deported. The advisory states that displaying rainbow symbols is a crime. These are country-wide federal rules with no sub-national variation, so they apply identically to a visitor crossing into Khakassia.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression, version 2.0 of June 2025, affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention. The note assesses that LGB people are not generally at real risk of persecution solely for their sexual orientation, while people in the North Caucasus, trans people and public LGBT+ advocates are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. It records that 139 people were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws across Russia between 2022 and 2024.

Coercive conversion practice against trans people is documented: in summer 2021 a transgender woman was lured by relatives to a centre near Novosibirsk and held for nine months, forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour, escaping only after police responded to a phone she had found. For many transgender Russians, emigration has become the only remaining means of living openly.

A 2024 law bans adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that permit gender transitions, a rule with implications for foreign visitors present in Khakassia and for their standing in any adoption-related proceeding.

28173009B50284711669511.name: Tambov Oblast

Tambov Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, where the legal and physical risks for transgender visitors are severe and have worsened since 2022. The 2023 law signed by Putin prohibits gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression that, explicitly, "justifies" gender transition.

Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and official national government advisories tell LGBT travellers as much. The US State Department rates travel to Russia Level 4, Do Not Travel, with warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

Enforcement is live rather than theoretical. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the designated movement or display of its symbols as of 30 June 2025, comprising 98 administrative and 3 criminal cases. At least 20 people faced criminal charges from January 2024, and repeat display of banned symbols carries up to four years in prison.

Custody carries lethal risk. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges connected to an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) judges that trans people and public LGBT+ advocates are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, even where it finds that LGB people are not generally at real risk of persecution solely for their sexual orientation. The note records no Tambov Oblast-specific findings, and no regional divergence is recorded for this oblast.

The Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation, and the expanded "propaganda" law criminalises public expression including anything "justifying" gender transition. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under the propaganda statutes have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget across the two preceding years. 28173009B49563687485750.name: Buryatia
28173009B49563687485750.summary:
Buryatia, an autonomous republic of the Russian Federation, stands under the national framework applied across every Russian region. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) records no region-specific findings: it sets out the conditions in force throughout the country, and those conditions govern what a transgender visitor to Buryatia can expect to face.

Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents took effect; the Home Office notes that trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in the same year. Same-sex activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are prohibited. No discrimination legislation based on sexual orientation or gender identity covers housing, healthcare or employment anywhere in the country.

The expanded "propaganda" statute criminalises public expression that "justifies" gender transition. Offences carry fines of up to 400,000 roubles (about £3,600) for individuals or up to 15 days' detention, and a repeat offence can bring criminal prosecution with up to four years in prison. Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and official national government warnings tell LGBT travellers of this directly.

In November 2023 the Supreme Court designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation, with the ruling entering into force in January 2024. Participation in that movement is punishable by two to six years' imprisonment and organising it by six to ten years. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions tied to the designation as of 30 June 2025: approximately 98 administrative and three criminal.

Enforcement has been sustained rather than sporadic. Between December 2022 and March 2024 at least 139 people were affected by enforcement of anti-LGBT+ laws. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges under the designation, of whom two were sentenced to prison and one died by suicide in pretrial detention; a further 81 people across 98 court cases were found guilty of administrative offences for displaying banned symbols, with fines up to 2,000 roubles and repeat displays punishable under the criminal code by up to four years. On 15 May 2025 investigators charged three publishing-house staff under article 282.2 for selling fiction exploring LGBT themes, an offence carrying up to 12 years.

The Home Office assesses that trans people, publicly active LGBT+ advocates and those in the North Caucasus are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, and affirms that LGBT+ people constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention — the standard applied to UK asylum claims. The US State Department advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers; a foreign-government travel advisory also states that official support is "very limited" in parts of the country.

28173009B49563687485750.tangentialFactors:
The post-designation crackdown moved fast. On 17 January 2024, within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life through 2025, according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025), which reported a queer woman in St Petersburg describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is separately documented. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found. The case is from Siberia rather than Buryatia, but it illustrates the coercion trans people may face from within their own families, including through institutional detention.

Volume as well as severity is rising. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under the propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million roubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding. Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

Mari El is a republic of the Russian Federation and stands under Russia's national framework, which presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention, and deportation, and official national government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers of this.

The UK government country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) sets out the framework under which this division operates. Same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, and the constitution offers no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people. Public expression promoting non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition is punishable under the gay propaganda law by fines or detention of up to 15 days, with repeated offences risking criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment. Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 people in Russia were affected by enforcement of anti-LGBT+ laws through convictions, detentions and extremism prosecutions, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023.

Federal extremism enforcement applies nationwide, Mari El included. Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts had issued 101 extremism-related convictions for participating in the "International LGBT Movement" or displaying its alleged symbols, with charges brought under both the administrative and criminal codes. The same report records 81 people convicted across 98 court cases since January 2024 for administrative offences involving those symbols, mostly for posts on social media. The 2023 Supreme Court designation that enabled these prosecutions carries penalties of up to 12 years in prison and builds on the 2013 gay propaganda law.

Enforcement is rising in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding. The Guardian reported on 17 January 2024 that within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Physical coercion and death in custody are documented. The Associated Press reported in December 2024 that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility. BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 that a transgender woman was lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

28173009B3082792446388.name: Nenets Autonomous Okrug
28173009B3082792446388.summary:

It records that consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised, while same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned; that the Supreme Court designated the international LGBT+ movement an extremist organisation in November 2023; that at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement between 2022 and 2024; and that trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023. A visitor whose documents carry a marker inconsistent with their presentation has no lawful route to reconciliation inside the country and no access to trans-specific care. 28173009B27844369294009.name: Novosibirsk Oblast
28173009B27844369294009.summary:
Novosibirsk Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, where legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care have been banned since 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and changes of gender marker on official documents was signed. The Supreme Court designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation in November 2023, the expanded propaganda law reaches expression that "justifies" gender transition, and same-sex marriage is prohibited. A trans visitor has no route to corrected documents, no marriage-based partner status, and no lawful public expression of the legal aspect of their identity.

Foreign nationals who breach these provisions face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation, and official national government travel guidance warns LGBT travellers of exactly that. The US State Department rates travel to Russia Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the designated "international LGBT movement" or for displaying its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, with defendants facing up to 12 years in prison, and called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia. The same report documents 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024 of administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying banned LGBT symbols, mostly on social media. These totals are national figures that cover Novosibirsk Oblast; the report records no case specific to the oblast.

Enforcement is escalating in volume as well as severity. Cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding, Meduza reported on 19 June 2025. Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's designation, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night, The Guardian reported on 17 January 2024.

Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025), which reported a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (v2.0, June 2025, page updated 12 August 2026) records a Novosibirsk court fining the Elton John Bar 500,000 rubles (about £4,598) for promoting LGBTI propaganda through a rainbow flag, after the bar appeared in a video by LGBT+ activist blogger Karen Shainyan. The same note records that 2022–2024 enforcement affected at least 139 people, with individual "gay propaganda" fines reaching 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or 15 days' detention, and affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented within the oblast's wider region. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk in Siberia, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

28173009B3932420572168.name: Oryol Oblast
28173009B3932420572168.summary:
Oryol Oblast stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation, which presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors and has deteriorated sharply since 2022. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when Vladimir Putin signed the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents. The propaganda statutes and the extremist-designation regime apply in Oryol Oblast exactly as they do in every other region of the country.

The expanded propaganda law criminalises any public expression of LGBT identity and, explicitly, anything that "justifies" gender transition. Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and official national government warnings directed at LGBT travellers state this plainly. The US State Department rates travel to Russia Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings addressed specifically to LGBT travellers.

The Supreme Court designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation in November 2023. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for participation in that movement or for displaying its symbols as of 30 June 2025, with defendants facing up to 12 years in prison and charges brought under both the administrative and criminal codes. The same organisation documented 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024 of administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying banned LGBT symbols, most of them posted on social media. Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) is the framework against which Oryol Oblast is assessed. Consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised, while same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned. At least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement between 2022 and 2024, "gay propaganda" carries fines of up to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or 15 days' detention for individuals, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023. The note contains no information specific to Oryol Oblast beyond that national framework, and it affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented alongside the statutory penalties. BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 that a transgender woman, lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

28173009B8796515134902.name: Saint Petersburg
28173009B8796515134902.summary:
Visitors in every region stand under the national framework: since 2023 legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care are banned nationwide, and the propaganda and 'extremist movement' laws apply in every region.

Mixed record: the dismembered remains of a gender-nonconforming person who sold sex and was murdered in the region (26 February 2025) were found in the city, and the case was prosecuted - arrest within days, a strict-regime colony sentence of 11 years on 9 September 2025 - although press coverage was mocking and misgendered. the country's most European city; window-to-Europe legacy, underground scene. Assessed relative to the national picture in Russia.

sources.summary: The UK Home Office country policy and information note on SOGI for Russia (June 2025) names Moscow and St Petersburg as the large urban centres where survey data suggests LGBT+ people feel more able to be open and where relocation may be a reasonable option. A 2023 Coming Out and Sphere Foundation survey found 57% of St Petersburg respondents out to most friends, 19% to most relatives and 24% to classmates or colleagues, against Moscow at 50%/15%/19%. The note records two St Petersburg policewomen fired for allegedly flirting on social media, and an August 2024 Citizens' Watch/Sphere Foundation study of enforcement of the 'propaganda' articles whose respondents included 13% living in St Petersburg. Nationally, same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, the LGBT+ movement was designated 'extremist' in November 2023, and at least 139 individuals were affected by enforcement in 2022-2024.

Human Rights Watch (30 June 2025) reports that Russian courts have issued 101 'extremism'-related convictions connected to the 'International LGBT Movement' since its November 2023 designation, with defendants facing up to 12 years in prison. A further 81 people in 98 cases have been found guilty since January 2024 of article 20.3 administrative offences for displaying banned LGBT symbols, mostly on social media. St Petersburg appears in the article only in a photo caption for the 'X St.Petersburg Pride' rally of 3 August 2019.

sources.title: Vitaly Milonov - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's biography of Vitaly Milonov documents the city-level origin of the anti-LGBT law a trans visitor to Saint Petersburg stands under. As a member of the Saint Petersburg Legislative Assembly (2007-2016), he is recorded as the principal sponsor of the legislation criminalising 'homosexual propaganda directed toward minors', the city ban enacted in 2012 that the New York Times report 'Anti-Gay Law Stirs Fears in Russia' (29 February 2012) covered. The page quotes his statement that he fully intended to catch Madonna committing a possible offence under it when she visited the city. It also records Milonov stating in 2013 that gay athletes could be arrested at the 2014 Sochi Winter Olympics if they promoted homosexuality to minors, and his protests against the city's Side by Side LGBT film festival in November 2013.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Russia - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's country overview of LGBTQ rights in Russia supplies the federal framework Saint Petersburg is assessed under: a 2013 law criminalises distributing 'propaganda' of 'non-traditional sexual relationships' among minors, with fines up to 5,000 roubles for citizens, 50,000 for officials, and 1 million roubles plus up to 90 days' suspension for organisations, while foreigners face up to 15 days' detention, a fine up to 100,000 roubles and deportation. Ten regions including Saint Petersburg (2012) enacted regional versions of the ban before the federal law, and Saint Petersburg removed its regional law in 2014, leaving the federal statute in force there. A July 2023 law bans gender transition outright, prohibiting both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition. A 2010 European Court of Human Rights ruling fined Russia over the systematic refusal of pride-event permits.

28173009B31773571872137.name: Smolensk Oblast
28173009B31773571872137.summary:
Smolensk Oblast stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation. The source inventory contains no oblast-specific trans-related evidence: the UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression for Russia (June 2025) sets out the national position and offers no information specific to this division, so a visitor's assessment here is the national picture as it applies in Smolensk Oblast.

Russia presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned the same year. Gender transition and same-sex marriage are prohibited nationally, while consensual same-sex activity is not itself criminalised. These statutes operate in Smolensk Oblast exactly as they do elsewhere in the country.

The Supreme Court designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation in November 2023. The expanded "propaganda" law criminalises public expression, explicitly including anything justifying gender transition. Foreigners who breach these laws face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation, and the US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, carrying warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

Human Rights Watch recorded, as of 30 June 2025, 101 extremism-related convictions for participation in the designated international LGBT movement or for displaying its symbols, with defendants facing up to 12 years in prison. The same reporting counted 81 people found guilty across 98 cases since January 2024 of administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying banned LGBT symbols, most of them posted on social media. Charges have been brought under both the administrative and the criminal codes.

Enforcement has grown in volume as well as severity. Cases under the propaganda laws have increased eighteenfold over the past decade, and fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles into the state budget over two years. Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's designation, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where roughly 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night.

28173009B5502896824563.name: Lipetsk Oblast
28173009B5502896824563.summary:
Lipetsk Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia. Trans-related criminalisation in Russia is legislated centrally and enforced through national courts and security bodies, and the two assessments relied on here — the UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) and Human Rights Watch's reporting of 30 June 2025 — contain no information specific to this oblast beyond that national framework. The national picture therefore governs what a trans visitor to Lipetsk can expect to face.

The Home Office note sets the baseline: consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised in Russia, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023. The Supreme Court designated the international LGBT+ movement an extremist organisation in November 2023. Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement, with 'gay propaganda' fines for individuals reaching 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or 15 days' detention. The note records no detail for Lipetsk Oblast beyond these national provisions.

Human Rights Watch records the human cost of the November 2023 designation. Russian courts issued 101 extremism-related convictions for participation in the 'International LGBT Movement' or for displaying its symbols, with defendants facing up to 12 years in prison. The same organisation documented 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024 of administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying banned LGBT symbols, most of them posted on social media. Human Rights Watch's article likewise carries no division-specific detail, and its national enforcement baseline underpins the score applied to Lipetsk Oblast.

Two distinct charging tracks therefore operate across the country and, by extension, in Lipetsk Oblast: criminal extremism proceedings carrying long custodial sentences, and administrative proceedings under article 20.3 that require only the display of a symbol and that most commonly arise from social media activity rather than conduct observed in public.

28173009B2185273376578.name: Magadan Oblast
28173009B2185273376578.summary:
Magadan Oblast stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation, and every source consulted treats that framework as applying uniformly across the country. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) sets out that framework, and none of its findings are specific to Magadan Oblast. A visitor to Magadan Oblast faces the same legal exposure as a visitor to Moscow or Vladivostok.

Consensual same-sex activity is not itself a criminal offence in Russia, while same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned. The 2023 law prohibits gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in the same year. The Supreme Court designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation in November 2023. The expanded propaganda statutes criminalise any public expression, including anything explicitly justifying gender transition.

The practical consequence for a transgender visitor is that no document can be brought into alignment with their gender presentation. Any police stop, hotel registration, bank or transport identity check reads as a mismatch between presentation and papers. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention, and deportation, and official national government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers of this.

Enforcement is documented at national scale. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for participation in the designated movement or for displaying its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, with defendants facing up to 12 years in prison. The same organisation documented 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024 of administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying banned LGBT symbols, mostly on social media. The UK Home Office note records at least 139 individuals affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement between 2022 and 2024.

Volume has risen alongside severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under the propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles into the state budget in the two years preceding. Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night. In December 2024 a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is separately documented. A transgender woman was lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

28173009B42697300509311.name: Ulyanovsk Oblast
28173009B42697300509311.summary:
Ulyanovsk Oblast stands under the Russian national framework, which applies in full and offers no regional deviation material enough to score separately. Same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised in Russia, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023. For a visitor this means an identity document carrying an outdated marker cannot be corrected before or during travel, so any police, hotel or transport identity check reads a mismatch.

The 2013 'gay propaganda' law carries administrative fines of up to 400,000 rubles for individuals or detention of up to 15 days, with repeated offences escalating to criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment. The expanded statute reaches public expression that 'justifies' gender transition, and foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, detention and deportation.

Since the November 2023 Supreme Court 'extremist' designation of the international LGBT+ movement, participation carries 2 to 6 years and organising 6 to 10 years' imprisonment under Article 282.2. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 'extremism'-related convictions, about 98 administrative and 3 criminal, for alleged participation in the designated movement or displaying its symbols as of 30 June 2025; between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, including three publishing-house staff charged in May 2025 who each face up to 12 years' imprisonment, and 81 people were found guilty in 98 administrative cases under Article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols.

Citing an October 2024 OVD-Info report, the UK Home Office records that Ilya Zhuravlev, former head of the dialysis centre in Inza in the Ulyanovsk region, was detained in August 2024 on charges of participating in the activities of the 'extremist' 'LGBT movement' (Part 2 of Article 282.2) and coercion of a person to a sexual act (Part 1 of Article 133). Human Rights Watch separately reports that in March 2025 a Ulyanovsk-region doctor facing a maximum of one year's imprisonment for alleged sexual coercion was also prosecuted for 'involving' another man in the 'LGBT movement' and received a three-year sentence.

The UK Home Office note records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024 and assesses that openly LGBT+ people are likely to face discriminatory treatment that, by its nature or repetition, may amount to persecution, with the state able but unwilling to provide protection. The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

The 2013 'gay propaganda' statute is punishable by administrative fines of up to 400,000 rubles for individuals or detention of up to 15 days, with a repeated offence escalating to criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment. Since the Supreme Court's November 2023 designation of the international LGBT+ movement as extremist, participation carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising carries six to ten years under Article 282.2. Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, detention of up to 15 days, and deportation, and official national government warnings state this expressly to LGBT travellers.

Enforcement operates at volume. 28173009B47279883421777.name: Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug
28173009B47279883421777.summary:
Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation. The federal statutes governing gender identity and sexual orientation apply within the okrug unaltered, and no regional deviation from the national position has been identified, so the national assessment governs what a visitor faces here.

Same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised in Russia, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are both banned. Gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023, so a visitor's papers cannot be brought into line with their presentation: any police, hotel or transport identity check reads a mismatch that no supporting document can resolve, and no lawful route to obtain gender-affirming care exists during a stay.

The 2013 "gay propaganda" statute is punishable by administrative fines of up to 400,000 rubles for individuals or detention of up to 15 days, with repeated offences escalating to criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment. Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, short detention and deportation, and the expanded law reaches public expression that justifies gender transition.

Since the November 2023 Supreme Court designation of the international LGBT+ movement as extremist, participation carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising carries six to ten years under Article 282.2. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions arising from that designation as of 30 June 2025, of which about 98 were administrative and three criminal.

The volume of extremism cases is now substantial. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges connected to the designation, including three publishing-house staff charged in May 2025 under Article 282.2 who each face up to 12 years' imprisonment. A further 81 people were found guilty across 98 administrative cases under Article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols, meaning symbol display alone has produced convictions.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Russia (SOGI, June 2025) records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024, and assesses that openly LGBT+ people are likely to face discriminatory treatment that, by its nature or repetition, may amount to persecution. Its assessment that the state is able but not willing to provide protection sets the standard applied to UK asylum claims, and it affirms that LGBT+ people constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention.

28173009B30008444211385.summary:
The Altai Republic stands under the national framework of Russia, and no sub-national deviation from that framework has been identified in the sources; the territory is therefore assessed at the national score. Within the republic, Russia's laws apply in full: legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited, and same-sex marriage is banned, while same-sex sexual activity itself is not criminalised.

The expanded propaganda statute criminalises public expression that, explicitly, justifies gender transition. Penalties reach administrative fines of up to 400,000 rubles for individuals or detention of up to 15 days, with repeated offences escalating to criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, do not travel, for all travellers regardless of personal characteristic, citing wrongful detention, active war and arbitrary law enforcement.

28173009B57398385788417.name: Kalmykia
28173009B57398385788417.summary:
Kalmykia, an autonomous republic of the Russian Federation, is assessed under the UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression for Russia (version 2.0, June 2025). That note records that consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised in Russia, while same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned and the constitution offers no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people. The note contains no Kalmykia-specific information; the national framework sets the standard for what a transgender visitor to the republic should expect.

Legal gender recognition is prohibited outright. The law signed by President Vladimir Putin in 2023 bans gender reassignment surgery and any change of gender marker on official documents, voids a marriage concluded by a trans person with someone of their same birth sex, and removes the right to adopt from people diagnosed with gender dysphoria. Trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned the same year. A 2024 law additionally bars adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that permit gender transitions.

Public expression is constrained by the propaganda statutes, which since their December 2022 expansion reach material promoting "non-traditional" sexual relationships, making minors interested in gender transition, or giving minors a "desire to change their sex"; the provisions cover speech that justifies gender transition. Penalties reach fines of up to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or up to 15 days' detention, and repeated offences risk criminal prosecution. The UK Home Office note records that at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement between 2022 and 2024. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions as of 30 June 2025, with sentences of up to 12 years in prison, for participation in that movement or display of its symbols. The same organisation documented 81 people found guilty in 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 since January 2024 for displaying banned symbols, mostly on social media. Within 48 hours of the designation, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow, and between March and May 2026 nine LGBTQ organisations were outlawed as extremist.

Russia provides no anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, does not designate hate crimes as such, does not treat gender-identity or sexual-orientation motivation as an aggravating factor, and does not officially record hate crimes against the LGBTQ community. Coercive conversion practice against trans people is documented: a transgender woman was lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a centre near Novosibirsk and held for nine months, forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour.

The UK Home Office note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, the assessment standard for UK asylum claims. Reporting published in June 2024 profiles transgender Russians caught between leaving and staying, and analysis from August 2024 describes the court-driven purge and mass emigration of LGBT Russians; for many, emigration has become the only remaining means of living openly.
