28173009B70023447378008.name: Kamchatka Krai
28173009B70023447378008.summary:
Kamchatka Krai stands under the national framework of Russia. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) is the standard against which claims concerning Kamchatka Krai are assessed, and the note carries no Kamchatka-specific material; the findings below are therefore national findings applied to the territory.

Transgender visitors face several overlapping grounds of legal exposure. Consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised in Russia, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, and the Russian constitution offers no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people. Public expression 'promoting' non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition is punishable under the 'gay propaganda' law by fines of up to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or up to 15 days' detention, with repeated offences risking criminal prosecution. The expanded statute reaches anything 'justifying' gender transition, which places a trans visitor's ordinary self-description at risk.

Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed; trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned the same year. A visitor whose documents already carry a changed marker has no route to update or replace paperwork in Russia, and no lawful route to care.

Foreigners who breach these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and official Russian government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers of this. The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

Enforcement has grown sharply since the Supreme Court designated the 'international LGBT movement' an extremist organisation in November 2023. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for participating in that movement or displaying its symbols as of 30 June 2025, with sentences of up to 12 years in prison. Human Rights Watch also documented 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024 of administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols, most of them on social media, and counted 257 'gay propaganda' penalties in 2023-24 against 22 in 2021-22. The UK Home Office records that at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement between 2022 and 2024.

The response to the designation was immediate and physical. Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow: about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face the wall, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night (The Guardian, 17 January 2024). The Associated Press reported in December 2024 that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed 'Ada', a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found. The case occurred outside Kamchatka Krai but evidences the coercion pattern available to those acting against trans people within Russia.

Protection machinery exists on paper and at the border of the asylum system. The UK Home Office country policy note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims. Human Rights Watch called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

28173009B40138449315491.name: Kaliningrad
28173009B40138449315491.summary:
Kaliningrad has no division-specific transgender evidence in the surviving sources. A visitor to Kaliningrad stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation as it operates across the whole country, and that framework has tightened markedly since 2022.

Legal gender recognition is prohibited outright. The law signed by President Vladimir Putin in 2023 bans gender reassignment surgery, bars any change of gender marker on official documents, voids a marriage concluded by a trans person with someone of their same birth sex, and removes the right to adopt from people diagnosed with gender dysphoria. Trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned the same year. Consensual same-sex activity is not itself criminalised, but same-sex marriage is prohibited and the constitution offers no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people. Russia provides no anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, does not designate hate crimes as such, does not treat gender-identity or sexual-orientation motivation as an aggravating factor in sentencing, and does not officially record hate crimes against the LGBT+ community.

Public expression is constrained by the propaganda statutes. The 2013 law targeted material concerning minors; it was expanded in December 2022 to cover all age groups and now reaches content promoting "non-traditional" sexual relationships, making minors interested in gender transition, or giving minors a "desire to change their sex", as well as speech that justifies gender transition. Penalties reach fines of up to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or up to 15 days' detention, with repeat offences risking criminal prosecution. Enforcement has risen steeply: 257 propaganda penalties were imposed in 2023-24 against 22 in 2021-22, and more than 180 cases were brought under the provisions in 2023 alone, exceeding the total for 2013 to 2022 combined.

Since the Supreme Court's November 2023 designation of a non-existent "international LGBT movement" as extremist, charges have been brought for displaying the rainbow flag or its colours. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in that movement or display of its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, with sentences of up to 12 years in prison and charges drawn from both the administrative and criminal codes. The same reporting documents 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024 of administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols, mostly on social media. Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement.

The post-designation crackdown was immediate. Within 48 hours of the ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow; about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night. Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ life through 2025. In December 2024 a man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel business was found dead in a pretrial detention facility. Between March and May 2026 nine LGBTQ organisations, among them the Russian LGBT Network, Coming Out and Centre T, were outlawed as extremist.

Coercive conversion practice against trans people is documented. A transgender woman was lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a centre near Novosibirsk and held for nine months, forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour, escaping only after police responded to a phone she had found.

Entry carries explicit warnings for LGBT travellers. The US State Department advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and includes language relevant to LGBT travellers. The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression, version 2.0 of June 2025, affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims. For many transgender Russians emigration has become the only remaining means of living openly.

Residents of Kaliningrad live under the same statutory text as the rest of Russia, including the 2023 prohibition on legal gender recognition, the 2022 expansion of the propaganda provisions to all age groups, and the November 2023 extremism designation. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions as of 30 June 2025 and 81 people found guilty in 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 since January 2024, mostly for posting banned symbols on social media.

Same-sex relationships between consenting adults are lawful, but same-sex marriage is banned and the marriage of a trans person is voided under the 2023 law. People diagnosed with gender dysphoria lose the right to adopt. There is no anti-discrimination protection, no hate-crime designation, and no official recording of hate crimes against the community.

Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement. In the two years to mid-2025, fines under the propaganda provisions exceeded 60 million rubles. Trans-specific healthcare has been effectively unavailable through legal channels since 2023, and coercive detentions by relatives have been documented, most extensively in the 2021 case near Novosibirsk in which a transgender woman was held for nine months.

Nine LGBTQ organisations, among them the Russian LGBT Network, Coming Out and Centre T, were outlawed as extremist between March and May 2026, which restricts the support machinery available to residents.

28173009B46831765844996.name: Primorsky Krai
28173009B46831765844996.summary:
Primorsky Krai stands under the legal framework of the Russian Federation. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) is the framework against which this division is assessed, and it contains no division-specific information: a trans visitor to Primorsky Krai therefore faces the position that operates throughout Russia, administered by national security and court structures rather than by the regional administration.

Consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised under Russian law, but same-sex marriage is prohibited and gender transition is banned. The Russian constitution offers no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023, so a trans visitor cannot obtain gender-affirming care or corrected identity documents here.

Public expression 'promoting' non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition is punishable under the 'gay propaganda' law by fines of up to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or up to 15 days' detention, with repeated offences risking criminal prosecution. Foreign nationals who breach these provisions face arrest, detention and deportation.

Enforcement is documented at national scale. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 'extremism'-related convictions for participating in the 'International LGBT Movement' or displaying its symbols since the Supreme Court's November 2023 designation, with sentences of up to 12 years in prison. The same organisation documented 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024 of administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols, most of them on social media, and 257 'gay propaganda' penalties imposed in 2023-24 against 22 in 2021-22.

Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement in Russia. Neither the Home Office note nor the Human Rights Watch reporting identifies enforcement specific to Primorsky Krai, and the assessment here is set at the national level accordingly.

28173009B30250450380208.name: Bashkortostan
28173009B30250450380208.summary:
The Republic of Bashkortostan stands under Russia's national legal framework, and every source available here is national in scope. No reporting specific to Bashkortostan was located, so a transgender visitor should expect the national regime to apply unchanged.

Gender transition is prohibited in law. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression for Russia (version 2.0, June 2025, page updated 12 August 2026) records that same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, while same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, and that trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023.

Public expression itself is an offence. The 'gay propaganda' statute covers any public expression 'promoting' non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition, and expressly includes displaying rainbow symbols. Individuals face fines of up to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or detention of up to 15 days; a repeated offence can bring up to four years' imprisonment.

Foreigners are not exempt from these provisions. The US State Department advises against all travel to Russia regardless of personal characteristics, and warns that foreigners found guilty under the propaganda law may be arrested, detained for up to 15 days and deported. It states plainly that displaying certain symbols, including the rainbow flag, is a crime.

Since November 2023, when the Supreme Court designated the international LGBT+ movement an 'extremist' organisation, participation in that movement or display of its symbols has carried penalties of up to twelve years in prison under the extremism provisions.

76434192B57942368908249.name: Free State
76434192B57942368908249.summary:
The Free State province of the Republic of South Africa stands under the national framework set by the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, which prohibits unfair discrimination on the grounds of sex, gender and sexual orientation. The Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act (PEPUDA) gives effect to that guarantee through the Equality Court. South Africa was the first country in the world to bar sexual-orientation discrimination, doing so in 1996, and the Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act of 2024 explicitly extends protection to gender identity and sex characteristics alongside sexual orientation.

Partner status is recognised for a trans visitor travelling with a spouse. The Constitutional Court's judgment of December 2005 compelled Parliament to act, and the Civil Union Act was passed in November 2006 with a National Assembly vote of 229 to 41, legalising same-sex marriage nationwide.

Legal gender recognition is available under the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act of 2003, which permits a change of sex status in the population registry and therefore on identity documents and passports on proof of medical treatment such as hormone therapy, without requiring surgery. The route nonetheless requires medical evidence, a pathologising standard that locks some people out of recognition, and its binary sex classification excludes non-binary people; reform toward self-determination is pending but not in force. Where documents do not match presentation, trans people face humiliation, denial of service and threats of arrest for alleged fraud. A 2024 Gender Dynamix report documents a trans woman met with police mockery and refused when she attempted to file a domestic-violence complaint after producing her identity document.

Detention carries elevated and now-litigated risk. On 10 November 2025 the High Court of South Africa, Gauteng Local Division, sitting as an Equality Court, delivered judgment in Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre (case 2024/070075), a challenge against the Department of Correctional Services. The court held that refusing a transgender inmate feminising attire and she/her pronouns, restricting her gender expression, and denying state-funded gender-affirming hormone therapy constituted unfair discrimination, and that gender-affirming health care forms part of the constitutional right to adequate medical treatment under section 35(2)(e). The South African Human Rights Commission's National Preventive Mechanism welcomed the ruling on 14 November 2025, describing its OPCAT monitoring mandate over places of deprivation of liberty and the Department's argument that the therapy was cosmetic. Correctional Services already had a standard operating procedure for transgender prisoners before the ruling, but reporting in August 2025 recorded that rights organisations doubt whether it is implemented in practice.

Violence risk is documented and ongoing. On 26 December 2024 Aobakwe Mahlobo, a 23-year-old trans woman and make-up artist, survived an unprovoked hate-crime assault at a tavern in Tshwane that left her with severe facial injuries and lasting physical and emotional scars; she spoke out publicly and an arrest was reported. OUT LGBT Well-being's rights watch for December 2024 recorded five LGBTQIA+ murders that month, and violence disproportionately affects Black lesbian, trans and gender-nonconforming people in townships.

Access to gender-affirming care is uneven and concentrated in the main cities, so trans people in the Free State must travel long distances to reach it; private treatment costs hundreds of thousands of rands and public waiting lists are long. Activists in East London delivered a memorandum to Frere Hospital over treatment delays running to a year. Academic analysis published in 2024 concludes that trans people do not in practice experience equal protection in access to gender-segregated bathrooms, so restroom and changing-room disputes remain foreseeable for visitors.

The Justice Department's National Task Team, established in 2011, and the 2014 National Intervention Strategy for LGBTI Communities address hate crimes against LGBT people. No Free State-specific trans source was surfaced, so this record rests on the national framework.

Human-rights commission / National Preventive Mechanism media statement (14 November 2025): welcomes the 10 November 2025 High Court ruling in Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre (case 2024/070075); describes the OPCAT monitoring mandate over places of deprivation of liberty, the inmate's account (initially allowed to express her gender, later restricted from feminine clothing and make-up, misgendered, denied prescribed hormone therapy, DCS arguing it was cosmetic), and the court's finding that gender-affirming healthcare forms part of adequate medical treatment under section 35(2)(e) of the Constitution.

76434192B57942368908249.blindSummary:
The state/province stands under the national framework set by the Constitution of 1996, which prohibits unfair discrimination on the grounds of sex, gender and sexual orientation. The Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act gives effect to that guarantee through the Equality Court. The country was the first in the world to bar sexual-orientation discrimination, doing so in 1996, and the Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act of 2024 explicitly extends protection to gender identity and sex characteristics alongside sexual orientation.

Partner status is recognised for a trans visitor travelling with a spouse. The Constitutional Court's judgment of December 2005 compelled Parliament to act, and the Civil Union Act was passed in November 2006 with a National Assembly vote of 229 to 41, legalising same-sex marriage nationwide.

Legal gender recognition is available under the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act of 2003, which permits a change of sex status in the population registry and therefore on identity documents and passports on proof of medical treatment such as hormone therapy, without requiring surgery. The route nonetheless requires medical evidence, a pathologising standard that locks some people out of recognition, and its binary sex classification excludes non-binary people; reform toward self-determination is pending but not in force. Where documents do not match presentation, trans people face humiliation, denial of service and threats of arrest for alleged fraud. A 2024 report documents a trans woman met with police mockery and refused when she attempted to file a domestic-violence complaint after producing her identity document.

Detention carries elevated and now-litigated risk. On 10 November 2025 the national High Court, sitting as an Equality Court, delivered judgment in a challenge against the national correctional-services department (case 2024/070075). The court held that refusing a transgender inmate feminising attire and she/her pronouns, restricting her gender expression, and denying state-funded gender-affirming hormone therapy constituted unfair discrimination, and that gender-affirming health care forms part of the constitutional right to adequate medical treatment under section 35(2)(e). The national human rights commission's National Preventive Mechanism welcomed the ruling on 14 November 2025, describing its OPCAT monitoring mandate over places of deprivation of liberty and the department's argument that the therapy was cosmetic. The correctional-services department already had a standard operating procedure for transgender prisoners before the ruling, but reporting in August 2025 recorded that rights organisations doubt whether it is implemented in practice.

Violence risk is documented and ongoing. On 26 December 2024 a 23-year-old trans woman and make-up artist survived an unprovoked hate-crime assault at a tavern in a neighbouring city that left her with severe facial injuries and lasting physical and emotional scars; she spoke out publicly and an arrest was reported. An LGBTQIA+ rights watch for December 2024 recorded five murders that month, and violence disproportionately affects Black lesbian, trans and gender-nonconforming people in townships.

Access to gender-affirming care is uneven and concentrated in the main cities, so trans people in the state/province must travel long distances to reach it; private treatment costs hundreds of thousands of rands and public waiting lists are long. Activists in one city delivered a memorandum to a public hospital over treatment delays running to a year. Academic analysis published in 2024 concludes that trans people do not in practice experience equal protection in access to gender-segregated bathrooms, so restroom and changing-room disputes remain foreseeable for visitors.

The national justice department's National Task Team, established in 2011, and the 2014 National Intervention Strategy for LGBTI Communities address hate crimes against LGBT people. No state/province-specific trans source was surfaced, so this record rests on the national framework.

19338628B5758982491638.name: Centre-Val de Loire
19338628B5758982491638.summary:
Centre-Val de Loire stands under France's national framework. Criminal law, the custody rules of the French Criminal Procedure Code, anti-discrimination law, identity-document rules and the law on marriage apply uniformly across French regions, and no source in the inventory records a departure specific to this region.

For a trans visitor the operative exposure is custodial. Article D248 of the French Criminal Procedure Code requires men and women to be held in separate establishments, and placement follows the gender inscribed on identity documents rather than lived gender. Trans women whose documents are marked male — the majority, who have not undergone sex-reassignment surgery — are therefore held in men's facilities. Each establishment then improvises its own arrangement: special units, or isolation that restricts contact with other inmates.

Adeline Hazan, controller-general of places of deprivation of liberty, has stated that transgender detainees, overwhelmingly women, are the group that suffers the most in prison. A BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 records a detainee recalling inmates shouting "We don't want any women here!" alongside threats of violence, and describes the case of American trans woman Kara B. held in conditions Hazan called worrying.

The CGLPL, France's national preventive mechanism, issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty, following its opinion of 30 June 2010. It found that serious violations of trans detainees' fundamental rights persist in adult prisons, while none were noted in mental-health establishments, closed educational centres or juvenile detention centres. The review covered some forty transgender detainees, with interviews including eight trans women and one trans man, and inspection visits at the Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse-Seysses prisons and the Toulouse central police station.

At entry points, trans women have faced questioning of their identity documents in public. Giovanna Rincon's first-person account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of routine humiliation by French border police at the airport, questioned in front of other travellers, documenting identity-document friction for trans travellers arriving in France.

The Défenseur des droits issued a new framework decision on trans rights, confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony. It cites the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and sets out official guidance for service providers.

For partner recognition, the legal baseline dates from the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013; CNN reported France's first same-sex wedding on 29 May 2013, performed days after the law took effect.

19338628B74392602121343.name: Grand Est
19338628B74392602121343.summary:
Grand Est stands under the national framework of France. Identity documents, anti-discrimination law, criminal law and marriage law apply uniformly across the region, and the sources record no regional deviation from the national position on transgender rights.

Custody is the sharpest exposure. Article D248 of the French Criminal Procedure Code requires men and women to be held in separate establishments, so a trans woman whose identity documents record a male sex, which is the case for the vast majority who have not had sex-reassignment surgery, is placed in a men's facility. A BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 records a detainee hearing other inmates shout "We don't want any women here!" alongside threats of violence. Adeline Hazan, controller-general of places of deprivation of liberty, states that transgender detainees, overwhelmingly women, are the group that suffers the most in prison; the same feature documents an American trans woman, Kara B., held in conditions Hazan described as worrying.

The national custodial-inspection authority, the CGLPL, issued an opinion of 25 May 2021, following its opinion of 30 June 2010, recording the persistence of serious violations of the fundamental rights of transgender detainees in adult prisons. No such violations were noted in mental-health establishments, closed educational centres or juvenile detention centres. The review covered the situations of some forty transgender detainees, with interviews including eight trans women and one trans man, and inspection visits at the Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse-Seysses prisons and the Toulouse central police station. None of those establishments lies in Grand Est, so the region carries no inspection finding of its own; the national pattern is what a detainee held here would encounter.

At entry points, trans women have faced questioning of their identity documents in public. Giovanna Rincon's first-person account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of questioning by French border police at an airport, conducted in front of other travellers, documenting identity-document friction for trans travellers arriving in France.

The Défenseur des droits issued a new framework decision on trans rights confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony. It cites the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and sets out official guidance for service providers.

For partner recognition, the legal baseline dates from the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013; CNN reported France's first same-sex wedding on 29 May 2013, performed days after the law took effect.

A bill approved by the Senate on 6 November 2015 and by the National Assembly on 24 May 2016 was signed into law on 18 November 2016 and took effect on 1 January 2017; it abolished the sex-reassignment-surgery and forced-sterilisation requirements, rejected a Senate amendment that would have demanded proof of medical treatment, and requires going before a court rather than any medical intervention. Penal Code article 225-1 has covered gender identity since an 18 November 2016 amendment that replaced the term sexual identity, itself protected since 2012.

The Défenseur des droits issued a new framework decision on trans rights, confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony. sources.summary: France legalised same-sex marriage and full adoption in 2013, and civil solidarity pacts have existed since 1999. Penal Code article 225-1 has covered 'gender identity' since an 18 November 2016 amendment that replaced 'sexual identity', protected since 2012, and homophobic hate speech has carried penalties up to EUR 45,000 and/or one year's imprisonment since a 31 December 2004 amendment. 19338628B22604203385446.name: Corse
19338628B22604203385446.summary:
Corse stands under the national framework of France. French law on identity documents, criminal procedure, anti-discrimination, marriage and criminal law applies uniformly across metropolitan and overseas regions, and no Corse-specific finding on transgender detainees, border checks or hate violence appears in the sources; the national mechanisms documented below apply on the island unchanged.

Detention is the setting where the risk is documented most concretely. Article D248 of the Criminal Procedure Code mandates separate establishments for men and women, so placement follows the sex inscribed on identity documents and trans women are typically held in men's facilities. As of 1 November 2016 there were 13 transgender detainees held across eight establishments, most of them at Fleury-Mérogis. Each facility improvises within that rule, using special units or isolation that restricts contact with other inmates.

A BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 profiles Paola, an Argentine trans woman transferred to a men's facility in 2014, where she was met with shouts of "We don't want any women here" despite a passport listing her as female, because French law does not recognise her Argentine legal gender for placement purposes. The same reporting documents inconsistent access to treatment and a 2,000-euro symbolic damages award over detention conditions, with the justice minister pressed to amend Article D248.

The Contrôleur général des lieux de privation de liberté (CGLPL), France's national preventive mechanism, issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 on the care of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty, building on referrals received since 2010 and a 2010 opinion on transsexual prisoners. Inspections cited include Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse-Seysses prisons and the Toulouse central police station, with evidence from eight transgender women. The opinion documents discrimination, stigmatisation and health and social-care blind spots, and recommends policies to combat the discrimination and exclusion they face, referencing law n° 2016-1547 of 18 November 2016 on justice modernisation and prison transfers and the "racism, antisemitism, LGBT and discrimination" referents appointed since 2018. The CGLPL reports persistent serious violations of trans detainees' rights across the prisons it inspected.

At entry points, trans women have faced questioning of their identity documents in public. Giovanna Rincon's first-person account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of routine humiliation by French border police at the airport, questioned in front of other travellers, documenting identity-document friction for trans travellers arriving in France.

The Défenseur des droits issued a new framework decision on trans rights, confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony. It cites the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and sets out official guidance for service providers.

For partner recognition, the legal baseline dates from the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013; CNN reported France's first same-sex wedding on 29 May 2013, performed days after the law took effect.

36201628B45254163682963.name: Mimaropa
36201628B45254163682963.summary:
Mimaropa region has no documented provincial or municipal ordinance criminalising transgender expression, cross-dressing or facility use; the framework that governs a trans visitor is that of the Philippines. Same-sex relations are legal, no provision of national law criminalises a person for being transgender, and public homophobic and transphobic slurs are punishable under the Safe Spaces Act.

Legal gender recognition is not available administratively. The 2001 Clerical Error Law (RA 9048) blocks correction of the gender marker on a birth certificate, leaving a court order as the only route, and the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery. A bill filed by trans Filipinos would let applicants, including consenting minors, choose markers other than male or female such as X or non-binary; it had not been enacted as of the reports, and allies planned to endorse it to the 20th Congress on 28 July.

No national SOGI anti-discrimination statute is in force. The SOGIE Equality Bill, also called the SOGIESC Equality Bill, has been pending in Congress for about 25 years, since 2000, with the latest version filed as Senate Bill 1600; it would prohibit denial of admission, denial of public and health services, and infliction of physical harm or verbal abuse based on sexual orientation, gender identity, expression and sex characteristics. The protections in force form a patchwork: SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinances at barangay, city, municipal and provincial level, plus sectoral statutes including Republic Act 11166 on discrimination tied to HIV status, sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, the Magna Carta for Public Social Workers (fines of 20,000 to 40,000 pesos and/or up to one year's imprisonment for SOGIE harassment), and the Magna Carta of Women and the Safe Spaces Act, which punish transphobic, homophobic and misogynistic slurs and ridicule with fines of 1,000 to 10,000 pesos, up to 30 days' penalty and a sensitivity seminar.

Violence against trans people is documented and recent. On 23 June 2025 two killings occurred the same day: 18-year-old trans woman Kierra Apostol, a Cagayan State University business-management student, was found dead in a Cagayan province river with signs of physical assault, days after being reported missing, and a criminology student who admitted driving her surrendered to police while denying involvement; separately, trans woman and former activist-journalist Ali Macalintal was shot by an unidentified gunman inside an acupuncture clinic in General Santos. In May 2025 a foreign national was arrested for raping a trans woman in Batangas, and in April 2024 the drag artist Taylor Sheesh was struck on stage by a man from the crowd at a concert in Bayambang, Pangasinan, after which the town mayor publicly apologised to the LGBTQ+ community. Bahaghari and other groups cited the June 2025 cases as an urgent reason to pass the bill. The Commission on Human Rights has described that year's killings of trans people as a disturbing pattern of transfemicide.

Public presentation is restricted in some localities. Marawi City banned men from appearing in public in female attire, makeup or earrings in December 2004, and Kabacan in Cotabato prohibited cross-dressing and homosexual relations for Muslims in November 2019 under penalty of imprisonment. Gender-diverse people have been refused entry and service by establishments, and cross-dressers and transgender people may be excluded from private and public spaces with little or no legal consequence. After the 2017 Marawi siege, people perceived as LGBTQ were at times harassed in displacement camps.

A 2026 travel-risk assessment scores Manila at 69 of 100, 'Generally Safe', for LGBTQ+ travellers overall, but 62 for trans travellers, in the 'Exercise Caution' band; the same assessment scores HIV-positive travellers at 81. Public opinion lags behind the legal position: a 2018 SWS survey found only 22% of Filipinos supported same-sex civil unions and a majority opposed trans women's access to women's toilets.

The Safe Spaces Act criminalises homophobic and transphobic slurs; the Anti-Bullying Act and the Gender-Responsive Basic Education Policy (reiterated 2022, June designated Pride Month) cover sexual orientation and gender identity in schools; Executive Orders No. 100 (2019) and No. 51 (2023) creating the national Diversity and Inclusion Program remain unimplemented as of 2025.

The 2001 Clerical Error Law (RA 9048) blocks correction of the gender marker on a birth certificate, leaving a court order as the only route, and the Supreme Court held in a 2008 decision that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery. A bill filed by trans applicants would let applicants, including consenting minors, choose markers other than male or female such as X or non-binary; it had not been enacted as of the reports, and allies planned to endorse it to the 20th Congress on 28 July.

No national SOGI anti-discrimination statute is in force. The SOGIE Equality Bill, also called the SOGIESC Equality Bill, has been pending in the national legislature for about 25 years, since 2000, with the latest version filed as Senate Bill 1600; it would prohibit denial of admission, denial of public and health services, and infliction of physical harm or verbal abuse based on sexual orientation, gender identity, expression and sex characteristics. The protections in force form a patchwork: SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinances at local government, city, municipal and provincial level, plus sectoral statutes including a national act on discrimination tied to HIV status, sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, a public social workers statute (fines of 20,000 to 40,000 pesos and/or up to one year's imprisonment for SOGIE harassment), and a women's statute and the Safe Spaces Act, which punish transphobic, homophobic and misogynistic slurs and ridicule with fines of 1,000 to 10,000 pesos, up to 30 days' penalty and a sensitivity seminar.

Violence against trans people is documented and recent. On 23 June 2025 two killings occurred the same day: an 18-year-old trans woman university student was found dead in a river in a northern province with signs of physical assault, days after being reported missing, and a criminology student who admitted driving her surrendered to police while denying involvement; separately, a trans woman and former activist-journalist was shot by an unidentified gunman inside an acupuncture clinic in a southern city. In May 2025 a foreign national was arrested for raping a trans woman in a southern province, and in April 2024 a drag artist was struck on stage by a man from the crowd at a concert in a northern town, after which the town mayor publicly apologised to the LGBTQ+ community. LGBT groups cited the June 2025 cases as an urgent reason to pass the bill. The national human rights commission has described that year's killings of trans people as a disturbing pattern of transfemicide.

Public presentation is restricted in some localities. A southern city banned men from appearing in public in female attire, makeup or earrings in December 2004, and a town in a southern province prohibited cross-dressing and homosexual relations for Muslims in November 2019 under penalty of imprisonment. Gender-diverse people have been refused entry and service by establishments, and cross-dressers and transgender people may be excluded from private and public spaces with little or no legal consequence. After a 2017 siege in the southern city, people perceived as LGBTQ were at times harassed in displacement camps.

A 2026 travel-risk assessment scores the national capital at 69 of 100, 'Generally Safe', for LGBTQ+ travellers overall, but 62 for trans travellers, in the 'Exercise Caution' band; the same assessment scores HIV-positive travellers at 81. Public opinion lags behind the legal position: a 2018 survey found only 22% of the population supported same-sex civil unions and a majority opposed trans women's access to women's toilets.

36201628B47773222326566.name: Zamboanga Peninsula
36201628B47773222326566.summary:
The Zamboanga Peninsula stands under the national framework of the Philippines. Consensual same-sex relations are legal and no provision of national law criminalises a person for being transgender, but legal gender recognition is unavailable: the Clerical Error Law (RA 9048, 2001) forecloses an administrative birth-certificate sex change, leaving a court order as the only route, and the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery. The Family Code defines marriage as between a man and a woman, so same-sex marriage is not recognised, and no national anti-discrimination statute covers sexual orientation or gender identity.

The local legal floor in this division is set in part by Zamboanga City, the peninsula's regional center, which enacted its own anti-discrimination ordinance in 2020 and is named among the more than 20 local governments with such ordinances. Non-discrimination ordinances operate at barangay, city, municipal and provincial levels across the country. The other provinces and cities of the peninsula are not sourced individually, so equivalent protection outside Zamboanga City is unresolved.

Violence against trans women is documented and recent. On 23 June 2025 Kierra Apostol, an 18-year-old trans woman and student at Cagayan State University in Peñablanca, was found dead in a river in Cagayan province with visible signs of physical assault; a person who admitted picking her up the previous night surrendered to police and denied killing her. The same day Ali Macalintal, a trans activist and former journalist, was shot by an unidentified gunman inside an acupuncture clinic in General Santos, and Shalani Dolina was killed in Caloocan earlier in 2025. The Commission on Human Rights has described the trans killings recorded in a single year as a disturbing pattern of transfemicide. All three killings occurred outside this peninsula, but they are the clearest available indication of what a trans visitor to the country should expect.

Detention strips away most of what protection exists on paper. Transgender women are held with male inmates according to birth sex. At Manila City Jail, arrivals to the male dormitory have their heads shaved, and safety is organised through inmate hierarchies and informal same-sex 'weddings' with male inmates rather than through policy. The Bureau of Jail Management and Penology's documented response at Davao City Jail is administrative segregation, transferring LGBT detainees in batches to the City Jail Annex 'to prevent abuse' alongside persons with disabilities, the sick and senior citizens, with three LGBT groupings housed there since the annex was established. These facilities are outside the peninsula; no jail practice specific to the peninsula is sourced.

Public space is governed by statute rather than by identity. The Safe Spaces Act 2019 criminalises homophobic and transphobic slurs, with fines of PHP 1,000 to 10,000, up to 30 days' penalty and a sensitivity seminar. A 2018 Social Weather Stations survey found a majority of Filipinos opposed trans women's access to women's toilets, a division of shared facilities a trans visitor may be challenged over. The SOGIE Equality Bill has been filed repeatedly since 1999 and has never passed; campaigners cite its 25-year blockage as the direct reason two killings in June 2025 produced no legislative remedy, and the latest version was filed in 2022 as House Bill 5551 and Senate Bill 1600.

36201628B13149248482964.blindSummary:
The region stands under the national framework of the country. Consensual same-sex relations are legal nationwide and no provision of national law criminalises a person for being transgender, but there is no route to legal gender recognition: a 2001 clerical-error law forecloses an administrative birth-certificate sex change, and in a 2008 Supreme Court ruling the court held that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery. The national family code confines marriage to a man and a woman, and no national statute prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity; the SOGIE Equality Bill has been filed repeatedly in the national legislature since 1999 without passage.

Protection in the region rests on local instruments rather than national law. Non-discrimination ordinances exist at village, city, municipal and state/province level, alongside sectoral statutes: a 2019 statute punishes homophobic and transphobic slurs, and a 2013 anti-bullying law extends SOGI coverage to basic education. Within the region, one state/province lying wholly inside it enacted a state/province-wide sexual-orientation and gender-identity anti-discrimination ordinance in 2022, one of nine state/provinces nationwide to do so; a trans visitor elsewhere in the region has no sourced equivalent to rely on, and the ordinance's reach stops at the state/province boundary.

Public opinion, not statute, governs everyday exposure. A 2018 national survey found only 22% of the population supported same-sex civil unions, and a majority opposed trans women's access to women's toilets, a finding that bears directly on facilities use and public presentation in the region even where ordinances are silent. Diversity-and-inclusion executive orders issued in 2019 and amended in 2023 exist on paper but had not been implemented as of 2025, so the formal protection machinery does not operate in practice.

No source provides a finding specific to the region on violence, detention placement, healthcare access or police conduct. The regional assessment therefore rests on the national framework and on that state/province's ordinance as the single local data point.

36201628B29919658129037.name: Eastern Visayas
36201628B29919658129037.summary:
Eastern Visayas, six provinces in the eastern central Philippines, stands under the national framework of the Philippines, which applies uniformly across the region; the sources record no regional deviation from that framework, and the region is assessed at the national position.

Consensual same-sex relations are legal nationwide and no provision of national law criminalises a person for being transgender; same-sex conduct has never been criminalised. An international overview updated 12 March 2026 confirms the position for the Philippines: same-sex conduct legal, and no legal gender recognition pathway of any kind.

Transgender visitors should expect their documents to be read as issued. No administrative legal gender recognition process exists: the Clerical Error Law (RA 9048, 2001) bars an administrative birth-certificate sex change, leaving a court order as the only route, and the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery. A mismatch between presentation and the sex marker on a passport or birth certificate therefore has no domestic legal remedy during a visit.

Marriage equality does not exist. The Family Code defines marriage as between a man and a woman, so a foreign same-sex marriage has no recognition in Philippine family law.

No national SOGI anti-discrimination statute is in force. National legislation on the subject has been filed since 1999 without enactment, and the SOGIE Equality Bill has remained pending in Congress since the 2000s. Protection instead comes from a patchwork of local anti-discrimination ordinances enacted at barangay, city, municipal and provincial levels elsewhere in the country, alongside sectoral statutes: Republic Act 11166 bars discrimination tied to HIV status, sexual orientation, gender identity and expression; the Safe Spaces Act, the Magna Carta of Women and the Magna Carta for Public Social Workers penalise SOGIE-based harassment and slurs with fines and, in the social-workers statute, up to one year's imprisonment. Visitors have no standing under local ordinances, and coverage in any given Eastern Visayas town cannot be assumed from the national picture.

Facilities remain contested. A 2018 Social Weather Stations survey found a majority of respondents opposed transgender women's use of women's toilets, an attitude that shapes how establishments in the region are likely to treat a trans woman asking for gendered facilities.

Executive measures exist on paper without effect. Executive Order 100, signed 17 December 2019, created a Diversity and Inclusion Program, and Executive Order 51 of 2023 added a special LGBTQIA+ affairs committee; neither had been implemented as of 2025.

Violence against trans people is documented nationally and recent. On 23 June 2025 the body of 18-year-old trans woman Kierra Apostol, found with signs of physical assault, was recovered from a river in Peñablanca, Cagayan, after she had been reported missing on 22 June; her mother had reported the disappearance to local police. The case fell in Cagayan Valley rather than Eastern Visayas and is cited here as evidence of national climate. The national LGBT alliance Bahaghari's chairperson described the killing as part of a pattern of violence against Filipino trans women and renewed calls for the SOGIESC Equality Bill; the Commission on Human Rights has separately described that year's killings of trans people as a disturbing pattern of transfemicide.

Detention carries acute risk for anyone remanded or arrested. Transgender women and gay men are held in ordinary male dormitories in Philippine jails, where head-shaving on arrival can be mandatory and safety depends on inmate hierarchies rather than policy; there is no gender-matched placement, and official practice instead takes the form of administrative segregation by the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology.

Local ordinances elsewhere in the country restrict gender presentation in public: Marawi City banned men from appearing in public in female attire, makeup or earrings in December 2004, and Kabacan in Cotabato prohibited cross-dressing and homosexual relations for Muslims in November 2019 under penalty of imprisonment. Gender-diverse people have been refused entry and service by establishments with little or no legal consequence.

sources.summary: Outright International's Philippines country overview (updated 12 March 2026): same-sex conduct legal nationwide; no legal gender recognition (still required: no LGR pathway); Executive Order 100 s.2019 (signed 17 Dec 2019) created a Diversity and Inclusion Program, amended by EO 51 s.2023 to add a special LGBTQIA+ affairs committee, neither implemented as of 2025; anti-discrimination ordinances exist at barangay, city, municipal and provincial levels but national legislation filed since 1999 has not been enacted; a 2018 Social Weather Stations survey found 22% support for same-sex civil unions and a majority opposed trans women's access to women's toilets.

Alternative-media report (26 June 2025): an 18-year-old trans woman, Kierra Apostol, was found dead with signs of physical assault in a river in Peñablanca, Cagayan province on 23 June 2025 after being missing since 22 June; her mother reported the disappearance to local police; Bahaghari (national LGBT alliance) chairperson called the killing part of a pattern of violence against Filipino trans women and renewed calls for the SOGIESC Equality Bill. Case is in Cagayan Valley region, not Eastern Visayas — national-climate evidence.

sources.summary: Wikipedia's LGBTQ rights in the Philippines page supplies the national legal framework applied in Eastern Visayas, where national law applies uniformly across the region's six provinces. It records two Eastern-Visayas datapoints: in Northern Samar, two of the province's 24 municipalities were reported (circa 2012) to be run by openly LGBTQ mayors, and Leyte is among the provinces listed as having LGBTQ elected officials. The national baseline set out there is that no general anti-discrimination law exists at national level while numerous LGU-level SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinances exist elsewhere in the country, transgender people may not change their legal gender, same-sex marriage is not recognized (the Family Code defines marriage as between 'a man and a woman'), and the SOGIE Equality Bill has remained pending in Congress since the 2000s. Eastern Visayas shows local LGBTQ political participation but no legal deviation from the national position.

Political visibility of LGBTQ people in Eastern Visayas is high but does not alter the legal position. In Northern Samar, two of the province's 24 municipalities were reported around 2012 to be run by openly LGBTQ mayors, and Leyte is among the provinces listed as having LGBTQ elected officials. Elected representation has not produced a regional anti-discrimination ordinance or any other documented deviation from national law.

36201628B97761566458517.name: Northern Mindanao
36201628B97761566458517.summary:
Northern Mindanao stands under the national framework of the Philippines. Same-sex relations are lawful and no provision of national law criminalises a person for being transgender, but the country has no national anti-discrimination statute covering sexual orientation and gender identity: the SOGIE Equality Bill has been filed and stalled in Congress since 2000, roughly 25 years, and a comparable bill first filed in 1999 has not been enacted. The binding protections a visitor can rely on are therefore sub-national ordinances, sectoral statutes and the courts.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable. The Clerical Error Law (RA 9048, 2001) bars an administrative birth-certificate sex change, and the Supreme Court's 2008 ruling in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan held that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery, leaving a court order as the only route. Same-sex marriage is not recognised; the Family Code confines marriage to a man and a woman, and Quezon City's 2023 Right to Care Card is a municipal health-decision mechanism rather than partner recognition.

Local protection across Mindanao is thin. Citing MindaNews of 24 June 2019, the national reference material reports that only four local government units across the entire island had passed pro-LGBT ordinances by mid-2019. Documentation for Northern Mindanao specifically is sparse, so the absence of a regional signal does not establish that no divergence exists. Lanao del Norte, within the region, has adjacent Muslim personal-law courts operating.

Executive machinery exists on paper. Executive Order 100 s.2019, signed 17 December 2019, created a Diversity and Inclusion Program, and Executive Order 51 s.2023 amended it to add a special LGBTQIA+ affairs committee; neither was implemented as of 2025. Anti-discrimination ordinances do exist at barangay, city, municipal and provincial levels elsewhere in the country, which gives a visitor some sub-national recourse, but they are uneven.

Public attitudes constrain how protections are used. A 2018 Social Weather Stations survey found 22% support for same-sex civil unions and a majority opposed trans women's access to women's toilets, a divide that bears directly on which facilities a trans visitor can safely enter.

Violence against trans people is documented and recent at national level. On 23 June 2025 Kierra Apostol, an 18-year-old trans woman, was found dead with signs of physical assault in a river in Peñablanca, Cagayan province, after going missing on 22 June; her mother had reported the disappearance to local police. The killing occurred in the Cagayan Valley region rather than Northern Mindanao, and Bahaghari's national alliance chairperson cited it as part of a pattern of violence against Filipino trans women and as reason to renew calls for the SOGIESC Equality Bill.

36201628B90061603712355.name: Davao Region
36201628B90061603712355.summary:
The Davao Region records no separate regional legislation. A visitor to the region stands under the national framework of the Philippines together with any local ordinance of Davao City, the region's administrative center, which passed a non-discrimination ordinance in 2012 covering LGBT people, minorities and persons with disabilities.

Same-sex conduct is legal nationwide, same-sex relations have never been criminalised, and no provision of national law criminalises a person for being transgender. A 2026 travel-risk assessment scores the capital at 69 of 100 for LGBTQ+ travellers overall and 81 for HIV-positive travellers, but 62 for trans travellers, which falls in the 'Exercise Caution' band rather than 'Generally Safe'.

No administrative legal gender recognition process exists. The Clerical Error Law (RA 9048, 2001) bars an administrative birth-certificate sex change, and the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery, leaving a court order as the only route. A trans visitor's identity documents therefore cannot be brought into line with their presentation.

Marriage equality and civil unions have no national recognition. The Family Code defines marriage as between a man and a woman, and the SOGIE Equality Bill has been repeatedly filed in Congress without enactment, with national legislation on the subject pending since 1999.

No national SOGI anti-discrimination statute is in force, and national protection runs only in the basic-education context. Local government non-discrimination ordinances fill part of the gap: anti-discrimination ordinances exist at barangay, city, municipal and provincial levels across the country, and Davao City's 2012 ordinance is among them.

Executive measures exist on paper without effect. Executive Order 100, signed 17 December 2019, created a Diversity and Inclusion Program, and Executive Order 51 of 2023 amended it to add a special LGBTQIA+ affairs committee; neither had been implemented as of 2025.

Public attitudes constrain day-to-day use of space. A 2018 Social Weather Stations survey found 22 per cent support for same-sex civil unions and a majority opposed trans women's access to women's toilets, which bears directly on restroom access for a trans visitor.

Detention carries acute risk and the region has its own practice. Transgender women and gay men are held in ordinary male dormitories in Philippine jails, where there is no gender-matched placement, head-shaving on arrival is mandatory in the male dorm of Manila City Jail, and safety depends on inmate hierarchies rather than policy. In Davao, the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology transfers LGBT detainees in batches to the City Jail Annex alongside persons with disabilities, the sick and senior citizens, to prevent abuse.

Violence against trans people is documented and recent. In June 2025 two killings occurred within days: 18-year-old trans woman Kierra Apostol was found dead in a Cagayan river on 23 June, and a trans woman former journalist and activist was shot inside a clinic in General Santos the same day. A foreign national was arrested in May 2025 for raping a trans woman in Batangas, and in April 2024 the drag artist Taylor Sheesh was struck on stage at a concert in Bayambang, Pangasinan. The Commission on Human Rights has described that year's killings of trans people as a disturbing pattern of transfemicide.

Establishment practice can exclude gender-diverse people regardless of ordinance. Gender-diverse people have been refused entry and service, and cross-dressers and transgender people may be excluded from private and public spaces with little or no legal consequence.

There is no national anti-discrimination law; protection exists only in the basic-education context, with non-discrimination coverage left to local ordinances. Transgender people cannot change their legal gender. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised, the Family Code defining marriage as between a man and a woman, and the SOGIE Equality Bill has been filed repeatedly without enactment. Among the localities with a non-discrimination ordinance is Butuan City (2016), the capital of Caraga.

36201628B99380759663697.blindSummary:
The state/province records no region-specific law or regulation bearing on trans people. A visitor there stands under the national framework of the country, where same-sex conduct is legal nationwide and no provision of law criminalises a person for being transgender. The state/province entry in the sourced reference material carries no separate finding on LGBT rights, so the national position governs in full.

Identity documents cannot be brought into line with a trans visitor's presentation. There is no administrative legal gender recognition: a clerical-error statute forecloses an administrative birth-certificate sex change, and a 2008 supreme court holding states that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery. A court order is the only route, so the marker a visitor carries at hotels, checkpoints and counters will remain the one assigned at birth. A bill filed by trans nationals would permit applicants, including consenting minors, to choose markers other than male or female, such as X or non-binary; it had not been enacted as of the reports.

No national SOGI anti-discrimination statute is in force. The equality bill has been pending in the national legislature since 2000 without passage, and national legislation on the subject filed since 1999 has not been enacted. Protection against discrimination exists only as a patchwork of local ordinances at barangay, city, municipal and provincial level, plus sectoral statutes. Among the localities with a non-discrimination ordinance is the capital of the state/province, adopted in 2016; a visitor's protection therefore varies sharply by which city or municipality they are in. A national health statute separately prohibits discrimination tied to HIV status, sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and a safe-spaces statute and a women's statute punish transphobic and homophobic slurs with fines and, in some cases, a sensitivity seminar.

Violence against trans people is documented and recent at national level. In June 2025 two killings occurred within days: an 18-year-old trans woman was found dead in a river on 23 June, and a trans woman former journalist and activist was shot inside a clinic in a southern city the same day. In May 2025 a foreign national was arrested for raping a trans woman in a province south of the capital. The national human rights commission has described that year's killings of trans people as a disturbing pattern of transfemicide.

Public presentation can attract official and private restriction. One city banned men from appearing in public in female attire, makeup or earrings in December 2004, and a town in another province prohibited cross-dressing for members of one religious community in November 2019 under penalty of imprisonment. Gender-diverse people have been refused entry and service by establishments with little or no legal consequence. A 2018 national survey found a majority opposed trans women's access to women's toilets, an attitude that shapes how such refusals are received locally.

Executive measures exist on paper without effect. An executive order signed 17 December 2019 created a diversity and inclusion program, amended by a further order in 2023 to add a special LGBTQIA+ affairs committee; neither was implemented as of 2025.

Marriage equality does not exist. The national family code defines marriage between a man and a woman, and same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised nationally.

36201628B99380759663697.tangentialFactors:
Caraga's profile is a regional illustration of a national pattern rather than an exception: the Philippines decriminalised same-sex conduct and has never criminalised trans identity, yet leaves recognition and protection to a patchwork of local measures. A 2026 travel-risk assessment scores Manila at 69 of 100, 'Generally Safe', for LGBTQ+ travellers overall, but 62 for trans travellers, which falls in the 'Exercise Caution' band; the same assessment scores HIV-positive travellers at 81. The gap between the general and trans-specific scores indicates that a trans visitor faces a measurably higher risk profile than an LGB traveller in the same setting.

Detention carries acute risk nationwide. Transgender women and gay men are held in ordinary male dormitories, including Manila City Jail, where head-sharing on arrival is mandatory for the male dorm and safety depends on inmate hierarchies rather than policy. There is no gender-matched placement; the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology in Davao instead transfers LGBT detainees in batches to a city jail annex alongside persons with disabilities, the sick and senior citizens, to prevent abuse. A trans visitor detained in Caraga should expect placement by birth-assigned sex.

Social visibility is high and cuts both ways. Long-standing gender-diversity traditions with local names such as bakla and tomboy sit alongside prominent Pride events, nightlife and substantial LGBTQ+ media presence. Openly gay and bisexual people have been permitted in the armed forces since 2009 and transgender people since 2017, with uniform policy following the legal gender recorded on the birth certificate. The lawyers' Code of Professional Responsibility was updated in 2023 to bar discrimination against clients on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity. In June 2023 Quezon City launched the country's first Right to Care Card, letting registered LGBTQ couples make medical and health decisions for each other, initially in government-owned hospitals.

36201628B99380759663697.localsOnly:
Residents of Caraga live under the same national framework as visitors, but the local ordinance layer matters more to them. Butuan City, Caraga's capital, adopted a non-discrimination ordinance in 2016, one of a set covering eight provinces and 32 cities and municipalities nationwide. National protection remains absent: the SOGIE Equality Bill has been pending in Congress for roughly 25 years, and the protections that do exist form a patchwork of local ordinances and sectoral statutes, including the Magna Carta for Public Social Workers, which penalises SOGIE harassment with a fine of 20,000 to 40,000 pesos and/or up to one year's imprisonment.

Legal gender recognition requires a court order, since the Clerical Error Law forecloses the administrative route and Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) bars change even after gender-affirming surgery. A resident's birth-certificate marker therefore governs uniform policy in the armed forces and, in practice, placement in detention. The Bureau of Jail Management and Penology's batch-transfer practice in Davao is the nearest thing to an official accommodation, and it is segregation rather than gender-matched placement.

Local opinion is not uniformly supportive. A 2018 Social Weather Stations survey found 22% support for same-sex civil unions and a majority opposed trans women's access to women's toilets. Executive Order 100 s.2019 and its 2023 amendment created a Diversity and Inclusion Program and a special LGBTQIA+ affairs committee, but neither was implemented as of 2025.

36201628B99380759663697.outOfScopeNotes:
Two items in the source inventory remain unresolved. The first is whether any Caraga city or province outside Butuan City has adopted a SOGIE or non-discrimination ordinance; the inventory names only Butuan for this region, and the wider national count of eight provinces and 32 cities and municipalities is not broken down by region. The second is whether the trans-specific travel-risk scores (69 and 62 for Manila) have any regional equivalent for Caraga; none is sourced, so the Manila figures are used as a national proxy and may not reflect conditions in Butuan or elsewhere in the region.

The status of the gender-marker bill is stated as of the reports, with allies planning to endorse it to the 20 Congress on 28 July; whether it has advanced since is not sourced here. The Wikipedia entry for Caraga itself records no usable finding on LGBT rights, so the region-specific layer of this dossier rests on the absence of a recorded regulation rather than on an affirmative statement that none exists.

47653553B40993810137393.name: RegiÃ³n de Antofagasta
47653553B40993810137393.summary:
RegiÃ³n de Antofagasta stands under Chile's national legal framework. Gender identity recognition rests on Gender Identity Law 21,120, in force since 27 December 2019, which lets adults change their registered name and sex on request to the Civil Registry without therapy or surgery. The 2012 Zamudio Law prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, was extended to gender expression in 2018, and treats hate-crime motivation as an aggravating criminal circumstance. Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022, and birth certificates offer a third sex option for intersex children.

The Outright International Chile country dossier, published 12 March 2026, records no Antofagasta-specific legal, incident or enforcement finding and carries no division-specific information. A visitor to the region therefore has no regionally sourced account of how these national rules are applied, or enforced, on the ground.

Nationally documented abuse is rising, and the rise is concentrated outside the two largest urban regions. Movilh's XXIV annual report (HECHOS 2025, published March 2026) records 3,620 cases and complaints of discrimination in 2025, a 27.1% increase and the highest figure in 24 years. Fourteen of Chile's 16 regions recorded increases; only ValparaÃ­so (-17.56%) and Metropolitana (-14.35%) fell.

Antofagasta accounts for 2.09% of nationally documented abuse cases, a year-on-year rise of 45.45% in 2025 and the second-largest regional increase after La AraucanÃ­a (+150%). Movilh reads the shift as hostility expanding into regions with less public debate on sexual and gender diversity. The region's 2024 share is not reproduced in this edition, so the base for the percentage change is not stated in the source.

sources.summary: The Outright International Chile country dossier (published March 12, 2026) contains no Antofagasta-specific legal, incident or enforcement finding, and carries no division-specific information. Its findings are national: same-sex marriage and adoption legal since March 2022; the hate-crime law covering sexual orientation and gender identity since 2012; legal gender recognition by self-determination since 2019; a third sex option on birth certificates since 2006. In the 2025-26 rollback, the Chilean congress excluded the Gender Identity Support Program (PAIG) from the 2026 budget bill, an action condemned by civil society groups and the national ombuds for children.

Movilh's XXIV annual report (HECHOS 2025, published March 2026) places Antofagasta at 2.09% of nationally documented abuse cases in its national regional table, a +45.45% year-on-year rise in 2025 and the second-largest regional increase after La Araucania (+150%). Nationally the report records 3,620 cases and complaints of discrimination in 2025 (+27.1%, the highest in 24 years), with only Valparaiso (-17.56%) and Metropolitana (-14.35%) falling while the other 14 regions rose. Movilh reads the shift as hatred expanding into regions with less public debate. The 2024 Antofagasta share is not reproduced in this 2025 edition.

47653553B40993810137393.tangentialFactors:
Chile's national politics are running a rollback effort alongside the protections now on the books. In November 2025 Congress defunded the Ministry of Social Development's Gender Identity Support Program through the 2026 Budget Law, a step the Outright International dossier places within the 2025-26 rollback and which civil society groups and the national ombudsperson for children condemned. The Ministry of Health-run programme continues to provide support in medical centres.

On 15 May 2025 the Chamber of Deputies approved the CEI 57 commission report, 56 votes to 30 with 6 abstentions. Its recommendations, non-binding, would eliminate the Gender Identity Support Program, restrict minors' progressive autonomy, ban hormonal treatment for minors and repeal the circular protecting gender identity in schools.

Regional comparisons in the Movilh table point in different directions: La AraucanÃ­a rose 150%, roughly three times Antofagasta's 45.45%, while ValparaÃ­so and Metropolitana declined. The two regions with the largest documented caseloads are the two that fell, which is consistent with Movilh's reading that documented hostility is spreading outward rather than concentrating in the capital.

Residents of Antofagasta use the same gender recognition process as the rest of Chile. Adults apply to the Civil Registry; people aged 14 to 18 apply to family courts with psychosocial and family-context antecedents. On 9 April 2025 the Constitutional Court declared the 'over 14 years old' wording inapplicable as unconstitutional in a case brought by the mother of a 10-year-old trans girl, and that ruling applies only to that case.

Health care is a resident-level entitlement with contested edges. The public health system has funded sex reassignment surgery and hormone therapy since 2013, and a 2011 Ministry of Health circular obliges all care centres to register transgender patients by their social name. Circular 7 of June 2024 suggested deferring the start of new gonadotropin-releasing hormone blockers and cross-sex hormone therapy in adolescents until national guidelines are published, while the Medical College noted that physicians may still prescribe. On 9 January 2025 the Constitutional Court, by seven votes to three, annulled section 46 of the 2025 Budget Law, which had barred the Ministry of Health from financing hormone therapies for trans children and adolescents. The Crece con Orgullo programme has run since 2023 for children and adolescents aged 3 to 17.

Detention carries specific rules nationally. GendarmerÃ­a de Chile's national director signed a protocol guaranteeing the gender identity of trans detainees, providing placement by assumed gender, segmented housing and entry examinations, with a standing committee of GendarmerÃ­a and undersecretariat representatives overseeing implementation, including access rules for trans visitors.

Migration rules also reference gender identity. The Migration and Immigration Law of 11 April 2021 bans arbitrary discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity and offers protection to LGBT immigrants seeking asylum. Article 10 provides that recognised asylum seekers may be granted complementary protection, and no foreigner holding complementary protection may be expelled or returned to a country where their right to life, physical integrity or personal freedom is at risk on grounds including sexual orientation or gender identity.

Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022, civil unions since 2015, and birth certificates have offered a third sex option for intersex children since 2006.

Outright International's Chile country dossier, published 12 March 2026, records no Atacama-specific legal, incident or enforcement finding and no division-level information, so the region is assessed at the national score. The dossier's Chile findings match the national framework: self-determination legal gender recognition since 2019, marriage and adoption since March 2022, hate-crime coverage of sexual orientation and gender identity since 2012, and the third sex option since 2006.

Movilh's XXIV annual report (HECHOS 2025, published March 2026) places Atacama at 1.83% of nationally documented abuse cases, a year-on-year rise of 7.69%. Only Valparaíso (-17.56%) and Metropolitana (-14.35%) fell, while the other 14 regions rose, and Movilh reads the shift as hatred expanding into regions with less public debate. Atacama's share is therefore a small but rising fraction of a national total that is itself rising steeply.

Two Atacama-specific positives appear in the same report. The Municipality of Atacama convened the commune's first Pride march, and Atacama and Puerto Varas became the first regions to hold Pride marches during 2025, expanding the movement's territorial visibility.

Transphobic violence remains documented nationally. A young trans man was murdered in 2023 in a killing covered up for 24 hours and described in national reporting as Chile's largest hate crime, the perpetrator an acquaintance who confessed. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for close to an hour at a Santiago hotel, where the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim.

Entry and removal rules reference gender identity. The Migration and Immigration Law of 11 April 2021 bans arbitrary discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity and offers protection to LGBT immigrants seeking asylum. Article 10 provides that recognised asylum seekers may be granted complementary protection, and no foreigner holding complementary protection may be expelled or returned to a country where their right to life, physical integrity or personal freedom is at risk on grounds including sexual orientation or gender identity.

Detention carries specific rules. Gendarmería de Chile's national director signed a protocol guaranteeing the gender identity of trans detainees, providing placement by assumed gender, segmented housing and entry examinations, with a standing committee of Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives overseeing implementation, including access rules for trans visitors.

Restrictive proposals are active but non-binding. On 15 May 2025 the Chamber of Deputies approved the CEI 57 commission report, 56 votes to 30 with 6 abstentions, a non-binding recommendation to eliminate the Gender Identity Support Program, restrict minors' progressive autonomy, ban hormonal treatment for minors and repeal the circular protecting gender identity in schools.
