Región de Los Lagos stands under Chile's national framework: Gender Identity Law 21,120, in force since 27 December 2019, applies in the region on the same terms as elsewhere in the country. Adults may change their registered name and sex on request to the Civil Registry without therapy or surgery. People aged 14 to 18 must apply to family courts with psychosocial and family-context antecedents, and those under 14 cannot use the law, though the statute recognises them as transgender. On 9 April 2025 the Constitutional Court declared the 'over 14 years old' wording inapplicable as unconstitutional in a case brought by the mother of a 10-year-old trans girl, and that ruling applies only to that case.

Discrimination and hate-motivated offending are governed nationally. The 2012 Zamudio Law prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, was extended to gender expression in 2018, and treats hate-crime motivation as an aggravating criminal circumstance. Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022, civil unions since 2015, and birth certificates offer a third sex option for intersex children, a provision in place since 2006.

Transphobic violence remains documented at national level. A young trans man was murdered in 2023 in a killing covered up for 24 hours and described in national reporting as Chile's largest hate crime; the perpetrator, an acquaintance, confessed. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for close to an hour at a Santiago hotel, where the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim.

Detention carries specific rules across the prison system. Gendarmería de Chile's national director signed a protocol guaranteeing the gender identity of trans detainees, providing placement by assumed gender, segmented housing and entry examinations, with a standing committee of Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives overseeing implementation, including access rules for trans visitors.

Care access follows national policy. The public health system has funded sex reassignment surgery and hormone therapy since 2013, and a 2011 Ministry of Health circular obliges all care centres to register transgender patients by their social name. Circular 7 of June 2024 suggested deferring the initiation of new gonadotropin-releasing hormone blockers and cross-sex hormone therapy in adolescents until national guidelines are published; the Medical College noted that physicians may still prescribe. On 9 January 2025 the Constitutional Court, by seven votes to three, annulled section 46 of the 2025 Budget Law, which had barred the Ministry of Health from financing hormone therapies for trans children and adolescents.

Entry and removal rules reference gender identity. The Migration and Immigration Law of 11 April 2021 bans arbitrary discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity and offers protection to LGBT immigrants seeking asylum. Article 10 provides that recognised asylum seekers may be granted complementary protection, and no foreigner holding complementary protection may be expelled or returned to a country where their right to life, physical integrity or personal freedom is at risk on grounds including sexual orientation or gender identity.

47653553B65340542415201.blindSummary:
This state/province stands under the national framework of the country, where legal gender recognition has operated since the national Gender Identity Law 21,120 came into force on 27 December 2019. Adults may change their registered name and sex on request to the Civil Registry without therapy or sex-reassignment surgery, so a traveller's papers can be brought into line with their presentation. People aged 14 to 18 must apply to family courts with psychosocial and family-context antecedents. Those under 14 cannot use the law, although the statute recognises them as transgender; on 9 April 2025 the national Constitutional Court declared the 'over 14 years old' wording inapplicable as unconstitutional in a case brought by the mother of a 10-year-old trans girl, and that ruling applies only to that case. Birth certificates offer a third sex option for intersex children.

Anti-discrimination protection rests on the national anti-discrimination law of 2012, which covers sexual orientation and gender identity, was extended to gender expression in 2018, and treats hate-crime motivation as an aggravating criminal circumstance; individuals may also file anti-discrimination lawsuits. Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since 10 March 2022, under a law approved on 9 December 2021, following civil unions available since 2015.

Entry and removal rules reference gender identity. The national migration law of 11 April 2021 bans arbitrary discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity and offers protection to LGBT immigrants seeking asylum. Its tenth article provides that recognised asylum seekers may be granted complementary protection, and no foreigner holding complementary protection may be expelled or returned to a country where their right to life, physical integrity or personal freedom is at risk on grounds including sexual orientation or gender identity.

Detention carries specific rules. The director of the national prison authority signed a protocol guaranteeing the gender identity of trans detainees, providing placement by assumed gender, segmented housing and entry examinations, with a standing committee of prison-authority and undersecretariat representatives overseeing implementation, including access rules for trans visitors.

Access to care is established at national level. The public health system has funded sex reassignment surgery and hormone therapy since 2013, and a 2011 health-ministry circular obliges care centres to register transgender patients by their social name. A circular of June 2024 suggested deferring the initiation of new gonadotropin-releasing hormone blockers and cross-sex hormone therapy in adolescents until national guidelines are published, and the national medical college noted that physicians may still prescribe. On 9 January 2025 the national Constitutional Court, by seven votes to three, annulled a section of the 2025 Budget Law that had barred the health ministry from financing hormone therapies for trans children and adolescents. In November 2025 the national legislature defunded the social development ministry's gender identity support programme through the 2026 Budget Law, but the health-ministry-run programme continues to provide support in medical centres; a support programme for children and adolescents aged 3 to 17 has operated since 2023.

Transphobic violence remains documented. A young trans man was murdered in 2023 in a killing covered up for 24 hours and described in national reporting as the country's largest hate crime; the perpetrator, an acquaintance, confessed. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for close to an hour at a hotel in the capital, where the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim.

Restrictive proposals are active but non-binding. On 15 May 2025 the lower house of the national legislature approved a parliamentary commission report, 56 votes to 30 with 6 abstentions, a non-binding recommendation to eliminate the gender identity support programme, restrict minors' progressive autonomy, ban hormonal treatment for minors and repeal the circular protecting gender identity in schools.

68945753B85747362819570.name: Gangwon
68945753B85747362819570.summary:
Gangwon province stands under the national framework of South Korea. Consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal, and gender identity and gender expression are not offences in civilian life. The criminalising provision that survives, Military Criminal Act article 92-6, reaches consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, and the Constitutional Court upheld it in 2023. No Gangwon-specific ordinance, police practice or enforcement pattern targeting trans visitors is documented in these sources, so the rules a visitor meets in the province are the national ones.

Transgender people are excluded from South Korean military service altogether, and the state's sharpest documented harm to a trans person sits in that domain. Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su was compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after a military panel classified the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a physical or mental handicap; she died by suicide in March 2021. The Daejeon District Court ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021, and in March 2024 the Defence Ministry recognised her death as in the line of duty.

Legal gender recognition no longer depends on surgery. On 8 May 2024 a regional court in Yeongdong approved changing the registered sex from male to female for five applicants who had not undergone sex-reassignment surgery, holding that it is against the law to determine gender change based on surgery and that judicial guidelines requiring surgery are now reference only, not criteria. The court stated that every human being has the right to form their character and live a life according to their gender identity. That ruling is the standard applied in Gangwon, and no province-specific gender-recognition case is documented here.

Restroom access is settled in the visitor's favour at national level and no Gangwon incident contradicts it. On 2 July 2024 a court ruled, and on 22 July 2024 the Seoul appellate court dismissed the state's appeal to finalise the matter, that police advice telling a person transitioning from male to female, who had obtained court approval for a family-register gender change in 2020, to avoid women's public restrooms infringed her personal rights; the award was 300,000 won against a claim of 3 million won, and the court held that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right. A 2021 Daegu District Court, Pohang branch award of 7 million won against a beauty academy that prohibited a transgender student from using its restroom forms part of the same national standard. No specific incident in Gangwon is documented.

Practical exposure persists despite that standard. A 2021 National Human Rights Commission of Korea survey of 591 transgender respondents found that 41% used a restroom of a different gender, 39% avoided food and drink and 36% forwent restroom use altogether. Research from the youth LGBTQ+ centre DDing Dong, presented on 20 March 2024, shows trans teenagers avoid school restrooms for fear of being outed; a 16-year-old trans girl at a boys' school reported holding it in and leaving school early.

Healthcare carries an official blind spot identified from within the state. In November 2023 the National Human Rights Commission of Korea flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation after the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, reasoning that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

South Korean national law does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, and same-sex couples cannot jointly adopt children. There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, a gap that shapes what recourse a trans visitor has if refused service, housing or transport. LGBTI organisations can register, though an NGO won registration litigation at the Seoul Metropolitan Court in March 2017 and the government appealed onward, which Human Rights Watch described as years of bureaucratic obstruction.

Violence and hostility concentrate at public events and in everyday life. In Incheon a Pride event ended in violence when about 1,000 Christian protestors attacked participants, with organisers later filing charges against pastors and accusing police of inaction; at Busan's 2018 Pride some 2,000 police were deployed to protect 15,000 attendees from violent anti-gay protesters. During the May 2020 Itaewon COVID-19 cluster, contact tracing outed LGBTQ people and doxing and online harassment rose. A 2018 study found 51.5% of transgender adults faced harsh discrimination in the past year.

A state/province within the country stands under the national framework. Consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal and gender identity or gender expression is not criminalised in civilian life, but the military criminal code article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment; the Constitutional Court upheld the provision in 2023, and transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

The punitive edge of that regime is documented. In 2017 the military charged 32 personnel in what an international human rights organisation described as a gay witch hunt, and a soldier received six months for consensual sex. A staff sergeant was compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after a panel treated the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a handicap; she died by suicide in March 2021. A district court ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021, and in March 2024 the defence ministry recognised her death as in the line of duty.

Legal gender recognition no longer depends on surgery. On 8 May 2024 a regional court approved changing the registered sex from male to female for five transgender applicants without sex-reassignment surgery, holding that conditioning a gender change on surgery is contrary to law and that judicial guidelines once treated as criteria are now reference only; the court stated that every person has the right to form their character and live according to their gender identity. On 24 November 2022 the Supreme Court ruled en banc that transgender people with minor children may be legally recognised provided they are unmarried, overturning an eleven-year-old precedent, itself an extension of a 2011 ruling that had required applicants to be over 20, single and childless.

Relationship recognition remains closed. The country does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, and same-sex couples cannot jointly adopt; the 2024 Constitutional Court ruling on same-sex partners' healthcare rights is the principal advance in that area. No comprehensive anti-discrimination law covers sexual orientation or gender identity. LGBTI organisations can register, but an NGO's registration win at a metropolitan court in March 2017 drew a government appeal and years of bureaucratic obstruction, as a global human rights group described it.

Restroom access is a live legal and institutional problem. A national newspaper report of 22 July 2024 records that an appellate court dismissed the state's appeal and finalised a 300,000 won damages award against a claim of 3 million won, holding that police advice telling a person who had obtained family-register approval to change sex in 2020 to avoid women's public restrooms infringed personal rights, and that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right. A 2021 national human rights commission survey of 591 transgender respondents found 41% avoiding facilities out of fear. Research presented by a youth LGBTQ+ centre on 20 March 2024 shows trans teenagers avoiding school restrooms to avoid being outed; a 16-year-old trans girl at a boys' school reported holding in and leaving early.

Healthcare carries an official blind spot identified from within the state. In November 2023 the national human rights commission flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation after the national health ministry refused to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, reasoning that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

Violence concentrates at public events. At a Pride event in a west-coast city about 1,000 Christian protestors attacked participants, after which organisers filed charges against pastors and accused police of inaction; a southern port city's 2018 Pride required some 2,000 police to protect 15,000 attendees from violent anti-gay protesters. During the May 2020 outbreak cluster in a capital-district entertainment area, contact tracing outed LGBTQ people, doxing and online harassment rose, and a trans-male bartender told an American news outlet he felt unsafe walking the street in the absence of a nondiscrimination bill.

Discrimination is measured at scale. A 2014 finding recorded that 54% of LGBTQ youths were harassed by classmates; 16.1% of outed LGBTQ people were recommended conversion therapy, with 65.4% reporting harm and 94% psychological trauma; a 2018 study found 51.5% of transgender adults facing harsh discrimination in the preceding year. A peer-reviewed nationwide survey published on 27 June 2025, covering 585 transgender and non-binary young adults, mapped milestones and stigmatisation across life stages and documented a pervasive discrimination burden at school, work and in transition-related care. A global human rights group's 2025 country report describes a comparatively positive record on free media and civil society alongside persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people.

68945753B46109248456415.name: Gwangju
68945753B46109248456415.summary:
Gwangju stands under South Korea's national framework. Gender identity and gender expression are not criminalised in civilian life, and consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal. The exception is the armed forces: Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, the Constitutional Court upheld the provision in 2023, and enforcement has been punitive. In 2017 the military charged 32 personnel in what Amnesty International described as a gay witch hunt, and a gay soldier received a six-month prison sentence for consensual sex. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

The sharpest documented trans-specific harm is the case of Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su, compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after a military panel classified the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a physical or mental handicap. She died by suicide in March 2021. The Daejeon District Court ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021, and in March 2024 the Defence Ministry recognised her death as in the line of duty.

Legal gender recognition is available and the surgical prerequisite has fallen away. On 8 May 2024 a regional court in Yeongdong approved changing the registered sex from male to female for five transgender applicants without sex-reassignment surgery, holding that conditioning gender change on surgery is against the law and that court guidelines requiring surgery are now reference rather than criteria; the court stated that every human being has the right to form their character and live a life according to their gender identity. On 24 November 2022 the Supreme Court ruled en banc that transgender individuals with minor children can have their gender legally recognised provided they are not married, overturning an 11-year-old precedent that uniformly denied recognition to trans parents of minors.

South Korean national law does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, and same-sex couples cannot jointly adopt children. A 2024 Constitutional Court ruling on same-sex partners' healthcare rights is the main advance in that area. There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity; an NGO won registration litigation at the Seoul Metropolitan Court in March 2017 and the government appealed onward, which Human Rights Watch described as years of bureaucratic obstruction.

Restroom access is the most concrete on-the-ground protection for a visitor. On 22 July 2024 a Seoul appellate court dismissed the state's appeal and finalised a 300,000 won damages award on a 3 million won claim, holding that police advice telling a person transitioning from male to female, whose family-register gender change a court had approved in 2020, to avoid women's public restrooms infringed personal rights; the court held that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right. The first-instance judgment had issued on 2 July 2024 from the Seoul Central District Court with no appeal on that point. A 2021 National Human Rights Commission of Korea survey of 591 transgender respondents found that 41% avoided facilities out of fear.

Facility avoidance extends to schools. Research from the youth LGBTQ+ centre DDing Dong, presented on 20 March 2024, shows trans teenagers avoid school restrooms for fear of being outed; a 16-year-old trans girl at a boys' school reported holding it in and leaving school early, and researchers urged legal and institutional reform for safer school environments.

Healthcare carries an official blind spot identified from within the state. In November 2023 the National Human Rights Commission of Korea flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation after the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, reasoning that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

Documented violence and hostility concentrate at public events and in everyday life. In Incheon a Pride event ended in violence when about 1,000 Christian protestors attacked participants, and organisers later filed charges against pastors and accused police of inaction; at Busan's 2018 Pride some 2,000 police were deployed to protect 15,000 attendees from violent anti-gay protesters. A 2014 finding recorded that 54% of LGBTQ Korean youths were harassed by classmates; 16.1% of outed LGBTQ people were recommended conversion therapy, with 65.4% reporting harm and 94% psychological trauma, and a 2018 study found 51.5% of transgender adults faced harsh discrimination in the past year. During the May 2020 Itaewon COVID-19 cluster, contact tracing outed LGBTQ people and doxing and online harassment rose; a trans-male bartender told NBC News he felt threatened walking on the street absent a nondiscrimination bill.

A peer-reviewed nationwide survey published on 27 June 2025 in Epidemiology and Health, covering 585 transgender and non-binary young adults, mapped key milestones and stigmatisation across life stages and documented a pervasive discrimination burden at school, work and in transition-related care. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 describes an overall relatively positive record on free media and civil society alongside persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people.

1875124B91024374055933.name: La Libertad
1875124B91024374055933.summary:
La Libertad region stands under Peru's national framework. Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents requires restroom entry to be determined by 'biological sex', barring trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their gender identity, and the same package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'. Vague child-protection articles in that law, including a ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, leaving Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected, and its co-author, trans journalist and human-rights defender Gianna Camacho, stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry; between 2020 and 2023, 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed. In December 2025 three police officers were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history. Two protective developments are on record: in June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, and in July 2025 a Lima constitutional court ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

La Libertad appears in the Public Ministry's Observatory of Criminality study of intentional deaths of LGTB people in Peru between 2012 and 2021, which recorded 84 criminal complaints involving 88 victims and 72 identified suspects. Fifty-eight per cent of the deaths were concentrated in six fiscal districts: Lima (12), La Libertad (10), Lima Norte (10), Lima Este (7), Lima Sur (6) and Callao (6). La Libertad therefore ranks second in absolute count, level with Lima Norte and behind Lima, making it one of the two highest-burden jurisdictions outside the capital.

The Regional Government of La Libertad adopted Ordenanza Regional N.° 009-2024-GRLL-CR of 6 September 2024, promoting labour inclusion of travesti, transsexual and transgender persons in the region. It declares that every such person has the right to formal, dignified and productive work in equitable and satisfactory conditions without discrimination on grounds of gender identity and/or its expression, and recognises the trans community as a group in a situation of vulnerability in La Libertad.

The study was developed with the Justice Ministry human-rights office and the University Cayetano Heredia LGTB-rights observatory with UNDP support, and yielded recommendations including training criminal prosecutors on LGTB-victim identification and monitoring systems.

1875124B58976419670313.name: Tacna
1875124B58976419670313.summary:
The Tacna region stands under Peru's national framework. Peru does not criminalise consensual same-sex sexual activity, which has been lawful since the 1924 Penal Code; the 1863 code had criminalised sodomy with penalties comparable to rape. The age of consent is 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation under a 2012 Constitutional Court decision and applies to trans and cisgender youth alike. Trans identity itself is not an offence.

Legal protection against discrimination and hate crime on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is absent. Government Decree Nº 1323 criminalised such discrimination with effect from 7 January 2017 through Articles 46 and 323 of the Penal Code; Congress voted 66–29 in May 2017 to strip those provisions, President Kuczynski's veto stood at that point, and the protections were subsequently removed as the Penal Code was reworked. Peru is one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage. The repeal was carried by Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members arguing the President lacked authority to issue the decree, following an April Constitutional Committee vote and a petition carrying one million signatures. Investigators may still label a killing a hate crime, but that label carries no separate legal consequence; anti-trans violence is prosecuted as ordinary homicide.

Legal recognition of gender is partial. Transgender Peruvians may change their legal name to match their gender identity, but no gender-identity-recognition statute is in force. The Constitutional Court barred gender-marker changes on national identity documents in 2014, then reversed itself in a ruling of 21 October 2016 published 8 November, permitting gender change through a judicial process without sex-reassignment surgery. A Gender Identity Law covering legal gender change without surgery and access to identity documents was introduced on 4 November 2016 and remained pending in the legislature as of March 2021.

Access to public facilities matching gender identity is restricted by law. Law 32331, enacted 13 May 2025, bars trans people from using public restrooms according to their gender identity, and also bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'. The underlying bills, 6505/2023-CR and 8457/2023-CR, were presented by legislators including Jorge Montoya and Muñante of Honor y Democracia, and the committee approved the dictamen unanimously for plenary on 20 February 2025. The IDEHPUCP human-rights institute of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru finds the restriction openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by barring access to facilities matching their identity, implicitly casting trans people as harassment risks; it invokes Inter-American Court of Human Rights Advisory Opinion OC-24/17, under which gender identity falls within protected personal autonomy and states must guarantee trans people's full rights. The institute also records dehumanising comparisons made by congressman Lizarzaburu on the floor.

The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents extends the restriction. Human Rights Watch reports that it mandates public-restroom entry be determined by 'biological sex', which bars trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their identity; that its vaguely worded child-protection articles, notably Article 4 on media and advertising and Article 5, enable censorship of identity-related, artistic and educational content; and that the minimum sentence for obscenity rose from three to four years. Human Rights Watch characterises child protection as a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

A trans woman was killed in Tacna in April 2025. Marcia Paucara Cora, 48, was found dead in a hostel room in central Tacna on 19 April 2025; the autopsy recorded death by mechanical asphyxia through compression of the airways. She had entered the hostel, the Los 5 Titos on Arias y Aragüez street, with a man who registered under a false identity and left alone about two hours later carrying a white bag. She was initially processed as an unidentified body and identified through the hostel's cameras. Police analysed surveillance footage inside and outside the hostel to trace the escape route, and as of 21 May 2025 no suspect had been identified. Her family and local LGTBIQ+ collectives held a vigil on Friday 23 May demanding justice, describing the killing as the reflection of a structural system of violence that silences trans lives. The Public Prosecutor's Office identified 84 criminal complaints on LGTB deaths between January 2012 and May 2021, of which 55.8% of victims were gay men and 36.4% trans women.

Violence against trans people is rising and recorded figures understate it. A July 2024 report finds hate crimes increasing in Peru with trans women most affected, and co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans human-rights defender and journalist, states that the recorded numbers are only a sub-registry. A 2012 Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia study found that 70% of trans women in Lima and Callao work in sex work, a documented exposure factor for police and public violence.

The torture and rape of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, ended in conviction on 15 December 2025: police officers Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León received 17 years' imprisonment, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It is Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Hostility is also institutional. Outright International reports that public institutions themselves contribute to anti-LGBTIQ discrimination; in July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, struck an anti-equality decree as unconstitutional; and an April 2025 law on foreign funding of NGOs lets authorities revoke registrations on 'public order and security' grounds, which risks being weaponised against queer organising. In April 2025 the television presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed the first openly-lesbian congresswoman, Susel Paredes, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

Tacna is a border city with heavy transit, and the hostel in the Paucara Cora case was in the central district, the kind of short-stay accommodation where a visitor is registered under whatever identity is given at the desk. Restroom restrictions and the biological-sex rule were adopted in April and May 2025, while the Azul Rojas Marín judgment of 15 December 2025 shows litigation can still produce accountability after decades. Both directions of movement are live, and neither settles what a trans visitor will encounter at a hotel desk, a police station, or a clinic.

The report designates Barranquilla and Soledad as territories with high threat levels for this population. It also reports that threats meet near-total impunity, with 99.8% of cases never advancing past the investigation stage.

The same report places Atlántico inside a national pattern: 270 LGBTIQ+ victims recorded in 2025, a 63% increase over the 165 recorded in 2024, equivalent to one killing every 32 hours. Violence is documented as a continuum running from discrimination through intrafamily violence (1,531 cases), sexual violence (628 cases) and threats (1,184 victims) to homicide and impunity, with territorial expansion of the violence into corridors of the illegal economy where state presence is weak, and an insufficient state response.

Some of the targeting is organised. In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, stating that "all will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". In Caquetá, flyer campaigns announce a "social cleansing" of "drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots"; trans salon owner Tatiana Cespedes was forced to move twice after death threats from armed men, and trans women in the department have few options beyond sex work. Killings of queer Colombians continued after the Millerey case, described in reporting as calculated brutality persisting amid the country's decades-long civil conflict.

13589884B36646919284035.name: Caldas
13589884B36646919284035.summary:
Caldas stands under the national framework of Colombia, where legal gender recognition rests on self-recognition. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition without a surgical requirement, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025.

The legal framework is assessed against a national pattern of lethal violence. Hate crimes killed 13 trans people in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025. On 14 April 2025 national reporting described Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman beaten in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia, filmed by onlookers and thrown into a creek, who died of a second cardiac arrest the following afternoon with no one arrested; her death provoked national outrage and mobilisations against transphobia. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025, and more than 40 transgender women were killed in 2023, with 41 trans women killed in 2023 and a further eight between February and April 2024.

Some of the targeting is organised. In Guajira, armed groups have circulated flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, stating that "all will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". In Caquetá, flyer campaigns announce a "social cleansing" of "drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots"; armed groups gave trans salon owner Tatiana Cespedes one week to leave town or be killed, and trans women in the department have few options beyond sex work. An activist quoted in the investigation states that the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide, recording the killings as ordinary cases.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity; the UN Human Rights Committee noted concern. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015.

Access to facilities and custody are covered by court order and administrative decree. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.

No finding specific to Caldas on law, enforcement practice or incidents affecting trans people appears in the sources available. The reporting carried here is national in scope or concerns other departments, and nothing in it marks Caldas as materially safer or more dangerous than the national picture.

13589884B75246552958907.name: Meta
13589884B75246552958907.summary:
Meta Department, a southern Colombian department in which an armed-conflict displacement dynamic persists, stands under Colombia's national framework. Consensual same-sex activity has been legal since 1981, the Constitutional Court legalised same-sex marriage in April 2016, same-sex couples have held full adoption rights since 2015, and a 2011 law bans discrimination based on sexual orientation. A national LGBTI policy addresses rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and states that national entities may not refuse to recognise them.

Legal gender recognition has been available since 1993 on the basis of self-recognition and without psychiatric or physical evaluations. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. National identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025, and a comprehensive trans law remained under legislative consideration in 2025.

The formal framework meets a rising national pattern of violence. On 6 August 2025 an international broadcaster reported a wave of anti-LGBTQ attacks across Colombia, covered through the case of Sara Millerey, 32, who on 5 April 2025 was filmed flailing in a creek outside Medellín in Bello, Antioquia, with fractured legs, arms and hands, before she drowned; her mother Sandra Borja said "They killed her for being who she was." President Petro ordered an urgent investigation. Thirteen trans people were killed in the first quarter of 2025, and the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025.

Some of the targeting is organised by armed groups. An international investigation published on 30 July 2024 documents groups in Caquetá giving trans salon owner Tatiana Cespedes one week to leave town or be killed and circulating "social cleansing" flyers against trans women; she was forced to move twice. The same investigation quotes an activist saying the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide and records these killings as ordinary cases, and reports 41 trans women killed in Colombia in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024. In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, stating that "all will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans".

No source in the inventory supplies a department-level record for Meta Department. Its entry rests on the national armed-group violence and displacement baseline and on the national legal provisions above, which is the layer a visitor there is governed by.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity; the UN Human Rights Committee noted concern. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.

Access to facilities and custody are covered by court order and administrative decree. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.

13589884B23733272568917.name: Cundinamarca
13589884B23733272568917.summary:
Cundinamarca is a department of Colombia and stands directly under the national legal framework. The source inventory carries no finding on law, enforcement practice or recorded incidents specific to this department, so a visitor's expectations rest on how the national rules apply and on the national enforcement record.

Legal gender recognition runs through an administrative channel rather than a court. Since 1993 a person may change the gender marker on a Colombian birth certificate, with current options of F, M, NB (no binario) and T (transgénero); the process is notarial and requires no surgery and no court ruling, and the sources state that it applies equally in Cundinamarca. Decree 0732 of 2026, signed by outgoing justice minister Jorge Iván Cuervo on 9 July 2026, obliges public notaries to complete the request within five business days, makes the first request and any simultaneous name change free of charge, and shields the change history from public disclosure.

The non-binary marker exists by court order. The Constitutional Court's 4 February 2022 ruling ordered the government to offer the NB option to everyone and to ask Congress to amend the relevant laws, and since August 2023 passports issued within Colombia offer three gender options: male, female and X.

Documentary practice has not always matched the rules. A 2016 report, Cartografía de derechos trans in Colombia, by OutRight Action International, El Aquelarre Trans and PAIIS, documented notaries refusing to process name changes and recommended ending the psychiatric pathologisation of transgender identity.

Violence risk is documented nationally rather than for this department. In 2023, 41 trans women were killed in Colombia, with a further eight between February and April 2024. Armed groups in Caquetá gave trans woman Tatiana Cespedes one week to leave town or be killed and circulated 'social cleansing' flyers against trans women. Reporting of 6 August 2025 covers the wave of attacks against LGBTQ+ people following the killing of Sara Millerey. The inventory contains no Cundinamarca-specific incident data.

13589884B56780975975491.name: Tolima
13589884B56780975975491.summary:
Tolima is a department of Colombia, and a trans visitor here stands under the national framework. Since the rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement, national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025, marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015.

That framework sits alongside lethal violence. On 14 April 2025 El País reported the case of Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman beaten in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia, filmed by onlookers and thrown into a creek, who died of a second cardiac arrest the following afternoon. No one had been arrested in the case at the time of reporting. Her death provoked national outrage and mobilisations against transphobia.

The scale of the killing is national. Hate crimes killed 13 trans people in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025, a figure that anchors the risk assessment for Tolima because the sourced material contains no Tolima-specific information.

Some of the targeting is organised and displacement-driven. The Guardian's investigation of 30 July 2024 documents armed groups in Caquetá giving trans woman Tatiana Cespedes one week to leave town or be killed, and circulating "social cleansing" flyers against trans women. The same investigation quotes an activist stating that the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide and records those killings as ordinary cases, and reports 41 trans women killed in Colombia in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024. Again, the report contains no Tolima-specific information.

The assessment for Tolima therefore rests on the national transfemicide picture and on violence patterns documented in other departments rather than on evidence from this department itself.

The national legal framework and the national violence record move in opposite directions, and a visitor to Tolima should treat them as separate layers. Identification, marriage and adoption rights are settled nationally, while the risk of lethal assault is set by a conflict-adjacent armed-group environment documented in other departments.

Two departments supply the comparative picture. Antioquia, where Sara Millerey was attacked in Bello in April 2025, shows targeted assault in an urban setting with onlookers filming rather than intervening. Caquetá, where armed groups issued death deadlines and "social cleansing" flyers in 2024, shows organised campaigns that push trans women out of towns and, for many, into sex work as the only available income. Neither department is Tolima, and neither report establishes that the same actors operate there.

The recording practice of the prosecutor's office is itself a turbulence factor: an activist cited in the Guardian investigation states that transfemicide is not recognised as such and that such killings are recorded as ordinary cases, which affects how quickly a visitor can expect a killing to be investigated as a hate crime.

Colombia's decades-long internal conflict remains the background condition for the organised violence, and the 2023 and 2024 death totals cited in the sources are national counts, not counts for any single department.

13589884B76435085510886.name: Cesar
13589884B76435085510886.summary:
Cesar operates under Colombia's national legal framework, and no Cesar-specific finding on trans law, enforcement practice or incidents is available for this department. The rules a trans visitor therefore faces in Cesar are the national ones, which are among the more developed in the region on paper and considerably weaker in application.

Legal gender recognition rests on self-recognition. Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 recognises recognition without a surgical requirement, and since a rule change approved in June 2015 the sex marker on government identification has been changed by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. The official who defended that change described those examinations as profoundly invasive of privacy rights and rooted in unacceptable prejudice. No court ruling and no surgery are required, and the process applies equally in Cesar.

Marker options are F, M, NB (no binario) and T (transgénero) on the birth certificate. The Constitutional Court's ruling of 4 February 2022 ordered the government to offer the nonbinary option to everyone and to ask Congress to amend the relevant laws. Decree 0732 of 2026, signed by the outgoing justice minister on 9 July 2026, obliges public notaries to complete the request within five business days, makes the first request free of charge when combined with a simultaneous name change, and shields the change history from public disclosure. Since August 2023, passports issued within Colombia offer three gender options: male, female and X.

Bureaucratic friction remains the practical obstacle. A 2016 report, Cartografía de derechos trans en Colombia, by OutRight Action International, El Aquelarre Trans and PAIIS, documented notaries refusing to process name changes and recommended ending the psychiatric pathologisation of transgender identity. Nothing in the inventory indicates whether notarial practice in Cesar differs from the national pattern of refusals.

Lethal violence runs alongside the formal framework. On 5 April 2025 a video showed Sara Millerey, 32, flailing in a creek outside Medellín in Bello, Antioquia, unable to swim with fractured legs, arms and hands, before she drowned; her mother said she was killed for being who she was, the president ordered an urgent investigation, and solidarity events were held in several cities. Thirteen trans people were killed in the first quarter of 2025, the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025, and more than 40 transgender women were killed in 2023. A Guardian investigation of 30 July 2024 reported 41 trans women killed in Colombia in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024, and quoted an activist stating that the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide, recording the killings as ordinary cases. A CNN report of 6 August 2025 described a wave of attacks on LGBTQ+ people across the country following the Millerey killing. None of these sources names Cesar.

Some of the targeting is organised. In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, stating that all will be military targets, including trans people. In Caquetá, flyer campaigns announce a social cleansing of drug addicts, prostitutes and gay men; trans salon owner Tatiana Cespedes was given a week to leave town or be killed and has been forced to move twice, and trans women in the department have few options beyond sex work. Killings of queer Colombians continued after the Millerey case, described in reporting as calculated brutality persisting amid the country's decades-long civil conflict.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity; the UN Human Rights Committee noted concern. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015.

Access to facilities and custody are covered by court order and administrative decree. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.

13589884B85940101840667.name: Magdalena
13589884B85940101840667.summary:
Magdalena department stands under the national framework of Colombia. Consensual same-sex activity has been legal since 1981, Congress passed a law banning discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation in 2011, and Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition with no surgical requirement. Since a rule change approved in June 2015 a trans Colombian changes the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a declaration before a notary; the earlier route, in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments, no longer applies. National identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025. Same-sex marriage has been available since April 2016, full adoption rights for same-sex couples since 2015, and transgender people have been permitted to serve openly in the armed forces since 2015.

No finding specific to Magdalena on law, enforcement practice, facilities or incidents affecting trans people appears in the sourced material. The reference article on Magdalena Department records no department-specific trans finding, and national reporting on attacks against LGBTQ+ people published on 6 August 2025, after the killing of Sara Millerey, carries no Magdalena-specific information either.

The national baseline a visitor is assessed against is lethal violence. Colombia recorded 41 trans women killed in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025, and 13 trans people were killed in the first quarter of 2025. On 5 April 2025 a 28-second video circulated showing Sara Millerey, 32, flailing in a creek outside Medellín in Bello, Antioquia, unable to swim with fractured legs, arms and hands, before she drowned; her mother Sandra Borja stated that "They killed her for being who she was." President Petro ordered an urgent investigation and solidarity events were held in several cities.

Some of that targeting is organised. The Guardian reported on 30 July 2024 that armed groups in Caquetá gave trans woman Tatiana Cespedes one week to leave town or be killed and circulated "social cleansing" flyers against trans women; the same investigation quotes an activist stating that the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide and records the killings as ordinary cases. In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, listing trans people among those described as military targets. Caquetá and Guajira stand as department-level examples of a documented national pattern; the sources supply no equivalent reporting for Magdalena.

Protection machinery exists and has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity, and the UN Human Rights Committee noted concern. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with killings rising.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office.

Access to facilities and custody are governed by court order and administrative decree. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (guards at a Cali mall) and T-301 of 2004 (police at the Santa Marta boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since ruled on the treatment of trans detainees. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.

Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 recognises recognition without a surgical requirement, and identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025.

That legal position does not contain the violence. On 4 April 2025 Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia; the assault was filmed and the video went viral on 5 April, and she died of cardiac arrest that afternoon. Police interrogated local residents, and even after the president ordered an urgent investigation no one had been arrested as of 14 April 2025. Her mother Sandra Borja said: "They killed her for being who she was." Thirteen trans people were killed by hate in the first quarter of 2025. The pattern a visitor should expect nationally is that lethal anti-trans violence can occur in daylight, be filmed, and leave the perpetrator unarrested.

Some of the targeting is territorial and organised. In Caquetá department armed groups have run a "social cleansing" campaign, distributing flyers on the street and via WhatsApp that name "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets. A trans woman and local election candidate was told by three armed men she had one week to leave town, hid for a week, then fled at night; a second trans woman said a friend had been killed. Eight trans women were killed in Colombia between February and April 2024, and 41 in 2023. Discrimination limits trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015.

Access to premises and to detention are governed by court order and decree. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since ruled on the treatment of trans detainees. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.

Protection machinery exists without having closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with killings rising.

13589884B66570655136682.name: La Guajira
13589884B66570655136682.summary:
La Guajira stands under the national framework of Colombia, which is among the most developed in Latin America and is what a trans visitor in this frontier department meets directly. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement. Marriage equality has been available since 2016, adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025.

The source inventory identifies no La Guajira-specific legal, document, entry, screening, facilities or care finding that departs from that national position, and no enforcement deviation material enough to score separately; the department is assessed at the national score.

What distinguishes La Guajira is who controls conduct on the ground. The department sits in the country's frontier belt where "orden público" regimes mean armed groups rather than departmental police effectively regulate conduct. In March 2024 armed groups in Guajira posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans".

A 2025 report by Caribe Afirmativo documents the territorial expansion of violence and the insufficiency of the state response, with trans women displaced from such departments because of their gender identity by the same armed actors that displace others. National context reaching this department: the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025, and one count recorded 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025 alone.

Targeted violence continues in ordinary urban settings as well. Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in Bello, Antioquia, near Medellín in April 2025; a video of the assault went viral from 5 April showing her with fractured limbs in a creek unable to swim, before she drowned. Her mother Sandra Borja stated, "They killed her for being who she was". President Petro ordered an urgent investigation and solidarity events were held in several cities.

The courts have also intervened directly in detention: a Colombian court ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.

13589884B67034552102836.summary:
Guainía department lies in Colombia's frontier 'orden público' belt, where armed groups rather than departmental police effectively regulate day-to-day conduct. No department-specific legal or enforcement deviation is on record for Guainía, so formal exposure is assessed against the national framework and its enforcement record.

That framework is among the most developed in Latin America. Adults can change legal gender before a notary with a free simultaneous name change on first request.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses on presenting a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.

13589884B79790550435280.name: Cauca
13589884B79790550435280.summary:
Cauca department stands under Colombia's national framework for sexual-orientation and gender-identity law. The sources assembled for this record contain no Cauca-specific statute, court ruling or documented incident: Human Rights Watch's Colombia country page records no finding for Cauca, and the CNN 'As Equals' follow-up of 6 August 2025 on killings of LGBTQ+ people (https://www.cnn.com/2025/08/06/americas/colombia-lgbtq-attacks-sara-millerey-as-equals-intl-latam) describes no incident in the department. What a trans visitor faces in Cauca is therefore the national floor, plus the national patterns of violence that the sources place across the country's departments.

That floor is comparatively developed. Consensual same-sex relations have been legal since 1981; Congress passed a national ban on discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation in 2011; the Constitutional Court legalised same-sex marriage in April 2016, with the country's first same-sex wedding taking place in Cali on 24 May 2016; and adoption by same-sex couples has been available since 2015.

Legal gender recognition rests on self-recognition, a basis recognised in Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 and carrying no surgical requirement. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Birth certificates offer F, M, NB and T markers, and national identification documents have carried 'trans' and 'non-binary' markers since November 2025.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office.

Access to premises and to detention facilities is covered by court order and administrative decree. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees.

The violence picture is the part of the assessment that carries real weight for a visitor. The pattern of armed-group 'social cleansing' campaigns documented in neighbouring departments applies to Cauca, and the national kill figures apply: 41 transgender women were killed in 2023, eight between February and April 2024, and 13 trans people in the first quarter of 2025, with the Attorney General's Office recording 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025. Sara Millerey, 32, drowned in a creek outside Medellín in Bello, Antioquia on 5 April 2025 after being thrown in unable to swim with fractured legs, arms and hands; her mother Sandra Borja said: 'They killed her for being who she was.' Reporting after that case describes gangs linked to queer and transgender deaths and killings that did not stop in its wake.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity, and the UN Human Rights Committee noted concern. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.

13589884B16144547040567.name: Caquetá
13589884B16144547040567.summary:
Caquetá is a department of Colombia and stands under the national framework of Colombia, which is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition with no surgical requirement, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025. A comprehensive trans law remained under legislative consideration in 2025.

Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. A couple presenting a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office is entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as a heterosexual spouse.

Access to public and commercial premises rests on Constitutional Court judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk). A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.

Within Caquetá, organised armed groups run a "social cleansing" campaign. Flyers distributed on the streets and via WhatsApp name "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets, and further campaigns announce a cleansing of "drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots". A trans woman and local election candidate was told by three armed men she had one week to leave town, hid for a week, then fled at night; a second trans woman said a friend of hers had been killed. Trans salon owner Tatiana Cespedes was forced to move twice after death threats from armed men. Discrimination limits trans women in the department mainly to hairdressing or sex work.

Lethal anti-trans violence is a national pattern that a visitor to Caquetá faces. On 4 April 2025 Sara Millerey, 32, was attacked in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia; the assault was filmed and the video went viral on 5 April, and she died of cardiac arrest that afternoon. Police interrogated local residents but no arrests followed even after President Petro ordered an urgent investigation, and her mother Sandra Borja said: "They killed her for being who she was." Thirteen trans people were killed in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025, the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025, more than 40 transgender women were killed in 2023, and eight trans women were killed between February and April 2024.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity; the UN Human Rights Committee noted concern. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.

Huila department stands under the national framework of Colombia, where the legal position a trans visitor meets is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Huila itself carries one documented constitutional protection. In ruling T-268 of 2000 the Constitutional Court permitted a gay pride parade in Neiva, the department's capital, after the Mayor of Neiva had previously prevented it, establishing constitutional protection for public expression of sexual orientation within the department. Nothing in the sourced material marks Huila as diverging from the national framework.
