13589884B18807997781037.name: Archipiélago de San Andrés, Providencia y Santa Catalina
13589884B18807997781037.summary:
The Archipiélago de San Andrés, Providencia y Santa Catalina is a department of Colombia and stands under the national framework. The legal framework a trans visitor meets in Colombia is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. The official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice".

Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition, without a surgical requirement. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025. The courts have also intervened directly in detention: a Colombian court ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.

The gap between that framework and enforcement is severe. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025 alone. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms and commitment to equality while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected, and that widespread discrimination and violence against LGBT people must be addressed urgently as killings rise.

Targeted killings of trans people continue in ordinary urban settings. On 4 April 2025 Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia. The assault was filmed and the video went viral on 5 April; she died of cardiac arrest that afternoon. Police interrogated local residents, and no one had been arrested even after President Petro ordered an urgent investigation. Her mother Sandra Borja stated, "They killed her for being who she was", and solidarity events were held in several cities. One report counted 13 trans people killed by hate in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025, and the same reporting records the stabbing death of a trans woman sleeping rough.

Some of this violence has been prosecuted as an international crime rather than ordinary homicide. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against these individuals constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity. The UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern.

The source inventory records no incident, law or enforcement finding specific to Archipiélago de San Andrés, Providencia y Santa Catalina. A trans visitor to the islands is therefore assessed against the national position: the recognition framework set out above, and a national pattern of lethal anti-trans violence in which no arrest was recorded even after an investigation was ordered at the highest level.

1875124B3772980127380.name: Puno
1875124B3772980127380.summary:
Puno is a department of Peru, and every legal measure bearing on trans visitors there is national in scope. The sources record no Puno-specific application, exemption, local ordinance or documented enforcement practice; what follows is the Peruvian framework as it binds the department.

Consensual same-sex sexual activity has been lawful since the 1924 Penal Code, which replaced an 1863 code that had criminalised sodomy at penalties comparable to rape. The age of consent is 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation under a 2012 Constitutional Court decision, and applies to trans and cisgender youth alike. Trans identity itself is not an offence.

Legal protection against discrimination and hate crime on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is absent. Government Decree Nº 1323 criminalised such discrimination with effect from 7 January 2017 through Articles 46 and 323 of the Penal Code; Congress voted 66–29 in May 2017 to strip those provisions, President Kuczynski's veto stood at that point, and the protections were subsequently removed as the Penal Code was reworked. Peru is one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage.

Access to public facilities matching gender identity is restricted by law. Law 32331, enacted 13 May 2025, bars trans people from using public restrooms according to their gender identity. Its underlying bills 6506 and 8457/2023-CR were presented by congressmen Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante of Honor y Democracia. The Women and Family Commission approved a merged draft unanimously on 20 February 2025, barring entry to restrooms that do not correspond to birth sex while allowing exceptions for custody situations, required medical attention, and accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, and banning so-called ambiguous bathroom signage. The bill's stated trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint over gendered restroom labels at Jorge Chávez airport.

On 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved the bill and exempted it from a second vote. Its article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their biological sex, subject to narrow listed exceptions. A legal analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte of the IDEHPUCP human-rights institute at the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, dated 15 April 2025, holds that the provision violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. The authors state that the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors.

LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho called the measure discriminatory and warned that restroom access would come to depend on security staff's personal judgment, including identity-document checks, and noted that there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. IDEHPUCP finds the restriction openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by barring access to facilities matching their identity, implicitly casting trans people as harassment risks, and invokes Inter-American Court of Human Rights Advisory Opinion OC-24/17, under which gender identity falls within protected personal autonomy and states must guarantee trans people's full rights. The institute also records dehumanising comparisons made by congressman Lizarzaburu on the floor.

The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents extends the restriction. Human Rights Watch reports that it mandates public-restroom entry be determined by biological sex, which bars trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their identity; that its vaguely worded child-protection articles, notably Article 4 on media and advertising and Article 5, enable censorship of identity-related, artistic and educational content; and that the minimum sentence for obscenity rose from three to four years. Human Rights Watch characterises child protection as a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

Violence against trans people is rising and recorded figures understate it. A July 2024 report finds hate crimes increasing in Peru with trans women most affected, and co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans human-rights defender and journalist, states that the recorded numbers are only a sub-registry. A 2012 Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia study found that 70% of trans women in Lima and Callao work in sex work, a documented exposure factor for police and public violence.

The torture and rape of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, ended in conviction on 15 December 2025: police officers Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León received 17 years' imprisonment, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It is Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Legal recognition of gender is partially available. Transgender Peruvians may change their legal name to match their gender identity. In 2014 the Constitutional Court barred gender-marker changes on national identity documents, then reversed itself in a ruling of 21 October 2016 published 8 November, permitting gender change through a judicial process without sex-reassignment surgery. A Gender Identity Law covering legal gender change without surgery and access to passports and other identity documents matching gender identity was introduced on 4 November 2016 and remained pending in the legislature as of March 2021.

Healthcare classifications have shifted in both directions. In May 2024 the government decreed transsexualism a mental health problem in order to cover trans healthcare; after protests, MINSA revised the term to gender discordance in June 2024 for health-insurance classification purposes, and in June 2024 health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described by Human Rights Watch as a step toward dignity for trans patients. Conversion therapy is banned in Peru for medical professionals, and in May 2024 MINSA reiterated that sexual orientation and gender identity are not diseases, a protection with direct bearing on trans and LGBTQ minors exposed to such practices.

Hostility is also institutional. Outright International reports that public institutions themselves contribute to anti-LGBTIQ discrimination; in July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, struck an anti-equality decree as unconstitutional; and an April 2025 law on foreign funding of NGOs lets authorities revoke registrations on public order and security grounds, which risks being weaponised against queer organising. In April 2025 the television presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed the first openly-lesbian congresswoman, Susel Paredes, telling her to go use the men's room.

No source in the inventory reports any incident, arrest, prosecution or complaint arising under Law 32331 or the April 2025 sexual-integrity law in Puno, so the department's practical risk profile is inferred from national law alone.

1875124B3772980127380.localsOnly:
Transgender Peruvians may change their legal name to match their gender identity, and since the Constitutional Court ruling of 21 October 2016, published 8 November that year, gender markers on national identity documents may be changed through a judicial process without sex-reassignment surgery.

Health-insurance classification moved from transsexualism, decreed in May 2024 to secure coverage of trans healthcare, to gender discordance in June 2024 after protests, and in June 2024 health authorities stripped pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official guidance.

Conversion therapy is prohibited for medical professionals in Peru, and MINSA stated in May 2024 that sexual orientation and gender identity are not diseases.

A 2012 Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia study found 70% of trans women in Lima and Callao work in sex work, an exposure factor documented for police and public violence.

The IDEHPUCP institute of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru provides legal analysis and challenge capacity on gender-identity claims, and an activist constitutional challenge succeeded in July 2025 when a Lima court struck an anti-equality decree as unconstitutional.

An April 2025 law on foreign funding of NGOs permits registration revocation on public order and security grounds, a mechanism that constrains the funding base of queer organisations.

1875124B82769317880582.name: Tumbes
1875124B82769317880582.summary:
Tumbes stands under Peru's national framework: trans identity is not criminalised, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising. There is no documented local mitigation for this border department, and the national restroom rule applies to public facilities including transport hubs, which matters because the bill was triggered by a July 2023 social-media complaint about gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chávez airport.

On 20 February 2025 the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by Jorge Montoya of Honor y Democracia and Alejandro Muñante, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex, with exceptions for custody, where medical attention is required, or accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, plus a ban on 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho called the measure discriminatory, warning that bathroom access would come to depend on security staff's personal judgment, including ID checks, and noted there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms.

On 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved and exempted from second vote the bill, whose article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', save for narrow listed exceptions. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights; IDEHPUCP's analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte argues the Peruvian provision violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, resting on a stigmatising stereotype that implicitly presents trans people as likely restroom harassers while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors.

Enforcement reaches private life: a consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy, and on television presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'. The same legislative package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected, and its co-author Gianna Camacho stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry; between 2020 and 2023, 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed, trans women most affected. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack; it was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history.

Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, leaving Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law. Two protective developments are on record: in June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, and in July 2025 a Lima constitutional court ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional after an activist legal challenge.

Speech and association are also constrained. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years; Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

1875124B64829338827261.name: Piura
1875124B64829338827261.summary:
Piura has no statute, enforcement record or incident specific to trans visitors in the sources; the national framework of Peru is the whole of what is documented, and it binds Piura as national legislation. Nothing in the record marks Piura as an aggravation of, or a refuge from, that framework, and no local mitigation is documented.

The central mechanism is a national restriction on restroom access. On 20 February 2025 the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a draft opinion merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, which bars trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex. Exceptions cover custody, cases where medical attention is required, and accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, and the draft bans 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The measure was prompted by a July 2023 social-media complaint about gendered restroom labels at Jorge Chávez airport, and stood at committee stage in February 2025.

On 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved the bill and exempted it from a second vote. Its article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', with narrow listed exceptions. The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents carries that requirement into force, including for trans youth, and the same legislative package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'. The law governs Piura as national law.

The legal analysis of IDEHPUCP by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte holds that the provision violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. Its stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse, they argue, rests on a stigmatising stereotype that implicitly presents trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors. LGBTI activist Gianna Camacho adds that bathroom access would come to depend on the personal judgment of security staff, including identity-document checks, and states that there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms.

Hate-crime protection for LGBT people is absent from the Penal Code. Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip those provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The result leaves Peru one of only three countries in South America, alongside Paraguay and Guyana, without LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in the country with trans women most affected, and its co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stated that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry. Between 2020 and 2023, 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed, trans women most affected.

In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was the country's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Enforcement of the restriction reaches private as well as public settings. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

1875124B61751373376494.name: Lambayeque
1875124B61751373376494.summary:
Lambayeque has no trans-specific ordinance, municipal rule or documented pattern of local enforcement on record; a trans visitor in this department is bound throughout by Peru's national framework. Trans identity is not criminalised in Peru, so being trans is not itself an offence. The operative constraints are the national restriction on shared public facilities, the absence of hate-crime coverage for LGBT people in the Penal Code, and a documented level of violence against trans women.

The facility restriction was adopted in stages during 2025. On 20 February 2025 the congressional Comision de Mujer y Familia approved by unanimity a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Munante, prohibiting any person from entering a public sanitary facility designated for the sex opposite to their birth sex, with narrow exceptions covering custody and situations where presence is required, such as accompanying minors, elderly people or people with disabilities; the text would also oblige venues not to post ambiguous restroom signs. At that date the text still required plenary backing. On 2 April 2025 the plenary of Congress approved the dictamen and waived a second vote on the 'Ley que fortalece el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los ninos y adolescentes', whose Article 5.1 carries the prohibition. Infobae Peru reports the trigger as a July 2023 complaint about gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chavez international airport.

The restriction reaches ordinary venues in Lambayeque as it does anywhere in Peru, and its enforcement would rest on security staff checking the national identity document to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender, according to activist Gianna Camacho, quoted by Infobae Peru. A consumer-protection body has already declined to intervene on the same logic: SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022 dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against the gym chain SmartFit, which assigned restroom use to the sex recorded in her identity document.

Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the hate-crime provisions of the new Penal Code, and the state's crime-registration systems do not incorporate sexual orientation or gender identity, so hate crimes cannot be prosecuted as such. Assault against a trans visitor would therefore be charged as ordinary assault.

Violence against trans people is recorded at national level and the figures are substantial. The annual report of the Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI of Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia records 54 assassinations of LGBTI people and 170 rights-violation cases between 2020 and 2023; the homicide victims were 30 trans women, 23 gay men and one lesbian. Nineteen killings occurred in 2023 alone, 12 of them trans women, and the killers were not identified in 26 of the 54 homicides, including 13 of the 19 in 2023. In February 2023 Rubi Torres Silvano, a 31-year-old trans sex worker, was kidnapped from central Lima by the 'Los Gallegos' extortion gang and shot some 30 times in Carabayllo, days after Priscila Aguado Huatuco was shot; two killers were arrested in March 2023.

1875124B1797874831789.name: Amazonas
1875124B1797874831789.summary:
Amazonas stands under Peru's national framework: the department has no documented trans-specific regional law, ordinance or enforcement pattern, and none of the sources covering this territory contain Amazonas-specific content. What a trans visitor faces in Amazonas is the national statute book, national policing and national monitoring data.

Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities. On 20 February 2025 the Comision de Mujer y Familia of the Congress approved by unanimity a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Munante, prohibiting any person from entering or using public sanitary facilities designated for the sex opposite to their birth sex. The exceptions are narrow: custody, and cases where required, including accompanying minors, elderly people or people with disabilities. Venues would also be obliged not to post ambiguous restroom signs. The text still required plenary backing at that date, and the reported trigger was a July 2023 complaint over gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chavez international airport. Activist Gianna Camacho argued that the measure is discriminatory and that enforcement would rest on security staff checking the DNI to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender.

On 2 April 2025 the plenary of Congress approved and waived a second vote on the dictamen of the Ley que fortalece el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los ninos y adolescentes, whose Article 5.1 prohibits persons from entering or using public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than their birth sex. The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, in an analysis of 15 April 2025 by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte, reads Article 5 as a direct breach of equality and non-discrimination under Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors. The same legislative package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'.

The restriction reaches private as well as public life. INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022 dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against the gym chain SmartFit, which grounded bathroom assignment on the sex recorded in the DNI. Gender-identity recognition in Peru remains long, costly and invasive, so the document a visitor carries will generally carry the sex marker assigned at birth. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. The annual report of the Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI of Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia recorded 54 killings of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases between 2020 and 2023; the homicide victims were 30 trans women, 23 gay men and one lesbian. Nineteen killings occurred in 2023 alone, 12 of them trans women, and the killers were not identified in 26 of the 54 homicides, including 13 of the 19 in 2023. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected, and its co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry. The state has not incorporated sexual orientation or gender identity into its crime-registration systems, so hate crimes cannot be prosecuted as such.

One case illustrates the pattern of violence and the delay of remedy. In February 2023 the trans sex worker Rubi Torres Silvano, 31, was kidnapped from central Lima by the 'Los Gallegos' extortion gang and killed in Carabayllo with some 30 gunshots; Priscila Aguado Huatuco, 30, had been shot days earlier. Two killers were arrested in March 2023. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code. Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome left Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. IDEHPUCP found the bathroom provision openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by barring access to facilities matching their gender identity, implicitly framing them as harassment risks, and recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Speech and association are also constrained. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

Its Article 5.1 prohibits any person from entering or using a public sanitary facility designated for a sex other than their birth sex. The provision applies in Huánuco as elsewhere, since the statute is national and carries no regional opt-out.

The IDEHPUCP legal analysis of 15 April 2025, written by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte, reads Article 5 as a direct breach of Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. The facilities restriction moved through Congress in two steps in 2025: a committee-stage dictamen approved unanimously on 20 February, then plenary approval on 2 April with the second vote waived. The February text carried exceptions for custody and for accompanying minors, elderly people or people with disabilities; the analysis of the enacted Article 5.1 reproduced by IDEHPUCP states the prohibition without those carve-outs, so a visitor should not assume an exception will be honoured at a restroom door.

Gianna Camacho's objection is operational rather than formal: a restroom ban enforced through DNI checks by private security means the practical test is a document inspection, not a legal proceeding. The same dynamic appears in the SmartFit resolution, where a private company set bathroom assignment from the sex recorded on the identity card and a consumer-protection body declined to intervene.

Recorded killings of trans women account for 30 of 54 TLGBI homicides in the 2020–2023 period and 12 of 19 in 2023, which makes trans women the consistently most affected group in the national totals. The proportion of homicides with no identified killer, 26 of 54 overall and 13 of 19 in 2023, indicates that a substantial share of these deaths remain unpunished regardless of motive.

The absence of sexual orientation and gender identity fields in the state's crime-registration systems means the absence of recorded hate-crime convictions cannot be read as an absence of bias-motivated violence. The Rubi Torres Silvano case was processed as an ordinary killing and extortion matter, with two arrests in March 2023, and no hate-crime charge was available.

Residents of Huánuco who need gender identity recognised on official documents face a national process that IDEHPUCP describes as long, costly and invasive. Until that recognition is completed, the sex recorded on the DNI governs which restroom a person may use on private and public premises, and the 2025 statute now backs that assignment for public sanitary facilities.

Because Article 5.1 of the April 2025 law is a national statute, its application in Huánuco's shopping centres, health facilities, transport terminals and municipal buildings follows the national text, and a local authority has no power to exempt those premises.

1875124B19837374654956.name: Pasco
1875124B19837374654956.summary:
Pasco department has no documented trans-specific regional law, ordinance or enforcement pattern on record. It stands under the national framework of Peru, where trans identity is not criminalised, but where the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, repealed hate-crime protection for LGBT people from the Penal Code, and presided over rising recorded violence against trans women.

On 20 February 2025 the congressional Comisión de Mujer y Familia approved by unanimity a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Munante, prohibiting any person from entering or using a public sanitary facility designated for a sex other than their birth sex. The text carries narrow exceptions for custody situations and where entry is otherwise required, including accompanying minors, elderly people or people with disabilities, and would oblige venues not to post ambiguous restroom signs. The measure still required plenary backing at that point, and its reported trigger was a July 2023 complaint about gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chávez international airport.

Trans journalist and human-rights defender Gianna Camacho argues the measure is discriminatory and that enforcement would fall to security staff checking the DNI to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender.

On 2 April 2025 the plenary of Congress approved and waived a second vote on the dictamen of the Ley que fortalece el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los niños y adolescentes, enacted in April 2025, whose Article 5.1 prohibits entering or using public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than a person's birth sex. The same legislative package bars inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'.

The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru reads Article 5 as a direct breach of equality and non-discrimination under Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors. The institute has documented trans people barred from public restrooms and recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights.

Enforcement of the restriction reaches private as well as public life. SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022 dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against the gym chain SmartFit, where bathroom assignment was grounded on the sex recorded in the DNI. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected, and its co-author Camacho stressed that recorded figures are only a sub-registry. Between 2020 and 2023, 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed, trans women most affected. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reached through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome left Peru one of only three countries in the subregion, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Speech and association are also constrained. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

1875124B73300566086976.name: El Callao
1875124B73300566086976.summary:
El Callao, the department containing Peru's principal international gateway, stands under the national framework. No department-specific trans law, ordinance, incident series or enforcement finding appears in the sources, so what a trans visitor faces in El Callao is what Peru's national rules deliver. Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but its Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising.

The governing instrument is the April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents. Its Article 5.1 prohibits any person from entering or using a public sanitary facility designated for a sex other than their birth sex, with narrow exceptions for custody and for cases where required, including accompanying minors, elderly people or people with disabilities. The same package obliges venues not to post ambiguous restroom signs and bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'. A visitor who is visibly trans should expect to be refused entry to gendered facilities across the country, including at airports, hotels, shopping centres and public buildings.

The provision was fast-tracked. On 20 February 2025 the congressional Comisión de Mujer y Familia approved by unanimity a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Munante, which still required plenary backing. On 2 April 2025 the plenary approved the dictamen and waived a second vote. The reported trigger was a July 2023 complaint about gendered restroom labels at Jorge Chávez international airport, the country's main port of entry for international visitors.

The Inter-American human-rights framework points the other way. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru reads Article 5.1 as a direct breach of equality and non-discrimination under Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors.

Enforcement reaches private life as well as public facilities. Consumer-protection body INDECOPI dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against the gym chain SmartFit in Resolution 0735-2022, where the company grounded bathroom assignment on the sex recorded in the national identity card. Activist and journalist Gianna Camacho argues that enforcement of the 2025 ban would rest on security staff checking the identity card to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender. Gender-identity recognition in Peru remains long, costly and invasive, so many trans people, including visitors, cannot obtain documents matching their presentation.

Hostility has been voiced from national platforms. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'. A congressman, Lizarzaburu, made dehumanising comparisons on the floor of Congress, as recorded by IDEHPUCP.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI of Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia recorded 54 killings of LGBT people and 170 rights-violation cases between 2020 and 2023; the homicide victims were 30 trans women, 23 gay men and one lesbian. Nineteen killings occurred in 2023 alone, twelve of them trans women, and perpetrators were not identified in 26 of the 54 homicides, including 13 of the 19 in 2023. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising with trans women most affected, and its co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stressed that recorded figures are only a sub-registry.

Named cases illustrate the risk. In February 2023 the trans sex worker Rubi Torres Silvano, 31, was kidnapped from central Lima by the 'Los Gallegos' extortion gang and killed in Carabayllo with some 30 gunshots. Priscila Aguado Huatuco, 30, was shot days earlier; two killers were arrested in March 2023. Trans women engaged in sex work face elevated exposure to organised extortion and lethal violence.

Legal recourse is slow but not absent. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reached through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Hate-crime coverage is absent. Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. Peru is now one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law. The state has not incorporated sexual orientation or gender identity into its crime-registration systems, so hate crimes cannot be prosecuted as such.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Speech and association are constrained. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

1875124B80189625477090.blindSummary:
The state/province stands under the national framework of the country. The country does not criminalise trans identity, but the national legislature has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the penal code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising. Any trans visitor to the state/province is subject to these national rules rather than to a regional regime of its own.

On 2 April 2025 the national legislative plenary approved, and exempted from a second vote, the bill whose article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex'. The exceptions are narrow: custody situations, places where medical attention is required, and accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities. The provision binds public facilities throughout the state/province.

The legislative route to that ban ran through the women and family committee, which on 20 February 2025 unanimously approved a merged draft of two bills introduced by two members of the national legislature. The stated trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint over gendered restroom labels at the country's main international airport. The same committee draft barred trans people from restrooms not matching their birth sex, set the exceptions listed above, and prohibited 'ambiguous' bathroom signage.

An LGBTI activist warned at that stage that restroom access would be left to the personal judgment of security staff, including whether to demand identity checks, and noted that there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. Her warning bears on how the rule is applied at a door in the state/province, where a guard's discretion rather than a document decides entry.

The human-rights institute of a national Catholic university, in an analysis by two legal researchers dated 15 April 2025, holds that article 5 violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the country's constitution and article 1.1 of the regional human-rights convention. The authors state that the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors. The same institute found the provision implicitly frames trans and non-binary people as harassment risks and recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of the national legislature by one of its members.

The same legislative package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity' alongside other 'ambiguous' restroom wording. Its vague child-protection articles, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people. These speech and signage restrictions apply to hotels, restaurants, shops and municipal buildings in the state/province.

Enforcement reaches private life as well as public facilities. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy. On television, a presenter on a national channel publicly harassed the country's first openly lesbian member of the national legislature, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

The national legislature voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new penal code's hate-crime provisions, with two right-wing parliamentary groups carrying the repeal after an April committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The country is one of only three states in the subregion lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law, so a visitor assaulted in the state/province on grounds of gender identity has no hate-crime provision to invoke.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in the country with trans women most affected, and its co-author, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry. Between 2020 and 2023, 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed, trans women most affected.

In December 2025 three police officers were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was the country's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and the regional human-rights court's first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the Court through the regional human-rights commission. The same court had held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 the national health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings, including clinics in the state/province. In July 2025 a constitutional court in the national capital, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

The department stands under Peru's national framework, so what a trans visitor to Junín encounters is set in Lima: Peru does not criminalise trans identity or consensual same-sex activity, but the national legislature has legislated directly against trans people's use of public facilities, the Penal Code carries no hate-crime or discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and recorded violence against trans women is rising.

The restriction on restrooms was adopted in stages. Law 32331, enacted 13 May 2025, carries the ban into force nationally and also prohibits inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'.

The exceptions are narrow: custody situations, cases requiring medical attention, and accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities. The stated trigger for the bills was a July 2023 social-media complaint about gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chávez airport. The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents extends the logic, mandating that public-restroom entry be determined by 'biological sex' and thereby barring trans youth as well as adults from facilities matching their identity; Human Rights Watch reports that its vaguely worded child-protection provisions, notably Article 4 on media and advertising and Article 5, enable censorship of identity-related, artistic and educational content, and that the minimum sentence for obscenity rose from three to four years.

She notes there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. Recorded anti-LGBTI violence is high and, per the report's co-author, understated: national figures for 2020-2023 count 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases, with trans women more than half the homicide victims at 30, against 23 gay men and one lesbian. In February 2023 the trans sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano, 31, was abducted by a gang in central Lima and killed in Carabayllo with about 30 gunshots as part of an extortion scheme.

1875124B25343038633883.name: Ica
1875124B25343038633883.summary:
Peru does not criminalise consensual same-sex sexual activity or trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising. Ica stands under this national framework.

On 20 February 2025 the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a draft opinion merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex, with narrow exceptions for custody, medical attention, or accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, plus a ban on 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The stated trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint about gendered restroom labels at Jorge Chávez airport. On 2 April 2025 the Plenary approved and exempted from second vote the bill, whose article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex' save for the listed exceptions. Law 32331, enacted 13 May 2025, codifies the restriction and also bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'.

Law 32331 also bars trans people from using public restrooms according to their gender identity, a state-imposed limit on daily movement that can intensify hostile interactions in transit spaces. The IDEHPUCP human-rights institute of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, in analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte of 15 April 2025, argues the law violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, and that its stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors. The institute also invokes Inter-American Court of Human Rights Advisory Opinion OC-24/17, under which gender identity falls within protected personal autonomy and states must guarantee trans people's full rights, and records dehumanising comparisons made by congressman Lizarzaburu on the floor.

LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho warns that bathroom access under the measure would depend on security staff's personal judgment, including ID checks, and notes there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms.

The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents extends the restriction. Human Rights Watch reports that it mandates public-restroom entry be determined by 'biological sex', barring trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their identity; that its vaguely worded child-protection articles, notably Article 4 on media and advertising and Article 5, enable censorship of identity-related, artistic and educational content; and that the minimum sentence for obscenity rose from three to four years. Human Rights Watch characterises child protection as a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

Legal protection against discrimination and hate crime on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is absent. Government Decree Nº 1323 criminalised such discrimination with effect from 7 January 2017 through Articles 46 and 323 of the Penal Code; Congress voted 66–29 in May 2017 to strip those provisions, President Kuczynski's veto stood at that point, and the protections were subsequently removed as the Penal Code was reworked. Peru is one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage.

Violence against trans people is rising and recorded figures understate it. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI annual report, covered by Agencia Presentes on 22 July 2024, records 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases in Peru over 2020-2023, with trans women more than half the homicide victims (30), followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian. Killings rose to 19 in 2023 (12 trans women) from 13 in 2022, 10 in 2021 and 12 in 2020, many committed with multiple gunshots or stabbings. The 170 violation cases include state violence and incitement to discrimination, with 61 denuncias in 2020. The report also recounts the February 2023 gang abduction of trans sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano, 31, in central Lima and her killing in Carabayllo with about 30 gunshots as part of an extortion scheme. Co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans human-rights defender and journalist, states the recorded numbers are only a sub-registry. A 2012 Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia study found that 70% of trans women in Lima and Callao work in sex work, a documented exposure factor for police and public violence.

The torture and rape of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, ended in conviction on 15 December 2025: police officers Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León received 17 years' imprisonment, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It is Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Legal recognition of gender is partially available. Transgender Peruvians may change their legal name to match their gender identity. In 2014 the Constitutional Court barred gender-marker changes on national identity documents, then reversed itself in a ruling of 21 October 2016 published 8 November, permitting gender change through a judicial process without sex-reassignment surgery. A Gender Identity Law covering legal gender change without surgery and access to passports and other identity documents matching gender identity was introduced on 4 November 2016 and remained pending in the legislature as of March 2021.

Healthcare classifications have shifted in both directions. In May 2024 the government decreed 'transsexualism' a mental health problem in order to cover trans healthcare; after protests, MINSA revised the term to 'gender discordance' in June 2024 for health-insurance classification purposes, and in June 2024 health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described by Human Rights Watch as a step toward dignity for trans patients. Conversion therapy is banned in Peru for medical professionals, and in May 2024 MINSA reiterated that sexual orientation and gender identity are not diseases, a protection with direct bearing on trans and LGBTQ minors exposed to such practices.

Hostility is also institutional. Outright International reports that public institutions themselves contribute to anti-LGBTIQ discrimination; in July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, struck an anti-equality decree as unconstitutional; and an April 2025 law on foreign funding of NGOs lets authorities revoke registrations on 'public order and security' grounds, which risks being weaponised against queer organising. In April 2025 the television presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed the first openly-lesbian congresswoman, Susel Paredes, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

The bathroom legislation's stated trigger, a July 2023 social-media complaint about restroom labels at Jorge Chávez airport in Lima, indicates that ordinary visibility of trans-inclusive signage can prompt national restrictive legislation, a pattern relevant to any visitor expecting to encounter inclusive facilities elsewhere in Peru.

Peru's position as one of only three South American countries, alongside Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage places the country at the restrictive end of its regional comparators, and neighbouring jurisdictions may offer stronger formal protections than Peru does.

The Azul Rojas Marín conviction, reached through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights and decided by the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, shows that regional human-rights machinery remains a functioning avenue for redress where domestic institutions fail, a channel also available to visitors who are victims of discrimination-based violence.

UN reporting cited in the same analysis shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors.

The legislative trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint about restroom labels at the country's main international airport. A trans activist and journalist who co-authored the July 2024 violence report calls the measure discriminatory and warns that bathroom access would come to depend on the personal judgment of security staff, including identity checks, noting that there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. The bill was still at committee stage as of February 2025 in the sources available here.

Hate-crime and anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is absent. A government decree had criminalised such discrimination from 7 January 2017 through articles 46 and 323 of the Penal Code, but the legislature voted 66–29 in May 2017 to strip the provisions and the protections were removed as the Penal Code was reworked, leaving the country one of only three states in the subregion, with two neighbouring jurisdictions, without LGBT anti-discrimination coverage.

Recorded violence is rising and understated. A national rights observatory's annual report, covered by a national news agency on 22 July 2024, records 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases across the country in 2020–2023, with trans women accounting for more than half the homicide victims (30), ahead of 23 gay men and one lesbian. Killings rose to 19 in 2023, of which 12 were trans women, from 13 in 2022, 10 in 2021 and 12 in 2020, many committed with cruelty such as multiple gunshots and stabbings; the 170 violation cases include violence by the state and incitement to discrimination, with 61 complaints filed in 2020. The report's co-author states that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry.

One 2023 case illustrates the pattern: in February 2023 a trans sex worker, 31, was abducted by a gang in the capital and killed in a northern district of the same metropolitan area with about 30 gunshots as part of an extortion scheme. A 2012 university study found that 70% of trans women in the capital and its neighbouring province work in sex work, a documented exposure factor for police and public violence.

1875124B2667580847298.name: Madre de Dios
1875124B2667580847298.summary:
Madre de Dios has no distinct trans-specific law, ordinance, incident series or enforcement record in the material reviewed for this dossier; the national framework therefore governs what a trans visitor to the department faces. Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, removed hate-crime protection for LGBT people from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women continues to rise.

Restroom access is restricted nationally. On 20 February 2025 the congressional Women and Family Commission approved unanimously a merged dictamen of bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante of Honor y Democracia, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex. The text lists narrow exceptions for custody, required medical attention, and accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, and bans 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The bill followed a July 2023 social-media complaint about gendered restroom labels at Jorge Chávez airport.

On 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved the text and exempted it from a second vote. Its article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex'. The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents carries the same requirement into force for trans people, including trans youth, and the legislative package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'.

Enforcement is expected to rest on the judgement of individual security staff. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho warns that access to restrooms would depend on staff discretion, including checks of identity documents, and notes that there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. The restriction reaches private life as well: a consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy, and on television the presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV told Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, to 'go use the men's room'.

The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, in an analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte, holds that the restroom provision violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. The institute states that the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype that implicitly presents trans people as likely restroom harassers, and cites UN reporting showing that trans people are more often victims than aggressors. It also recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI annual report records 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases across Peru for 2020-2023, with trans women accounting for more than half the homicide victims (30), followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian. Killings rose to 19 in 2023, 12 of them trans women, from 13 in 2022, 10 in 2021 and 12 in 2020, many committed with cruelty. The 170 violation cases include state violence and incitement to discrimination, with 61 complaints recorded in 2020. A 2024 report on rising hate crimes found trans women most affected, and its co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stated that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry.

One case sets a legal precedent for the region. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

1875124B5984096006894.summary:
Cusco stands under the national framework of Peru. Consensual same-sex sexual activity has been lawful since the 1924 Penal Code, trans identity is not an offence, and the age of consent is 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation under a 2012 Constitutional Court decision. The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents extends the restriction. Human Rights Watch characterises child protection as a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

No sub-national trans law, ordinance, incident series or enforcement finding could be located for this state/province; all sources attached to this jurisdiction are national in scope, and every binding rule below applies here as elsewhere in the country.

Consensual same-sex sexual activity has been lawful since the 1924 Penal Code, trans identity is not an offence, and the age of consent is 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation under a 2012 Constitutional Court decision.

Legal protection against discrimination and hate crime on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is absent. Government Decree Nº 1323 criminalised such discrimination with effect from 7 January 2017 through Articles 46 and 323 of the Penal Code, but Congress voted 66–29 in May 2017 to strip those provisions, the President's veto stood at that point, and the protections were removed as the Penal Code was reworked. The country is one of only three states in the subregion, with two neighbours, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage; the repeal was carried by governing-party members arguing the President lacked authority to issue the decree, following an April Constitutional Committee vote and a petition carrying one million signatures.

Access to public facilities matching gender identity is restricted by law. Law 32331, enacted 13 May 2025, bars trans people from using public restrooms according to their gender identity. The underlying bills, 6505/2023-CR and 8457/2023-CR, presented by legislators from an opposition bloc, also ban inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'; the committee approved the dictamen unanimously for plenary on 20 February 2025, with exceptions for custody, medical need, or accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities. The trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint over a major airport's gendered restroom labels. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho called the measure discriminatory, warning that bathroom access would come to depend on security staff's personal judgment, including ID checks, and noted there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms.

On 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved and exempted from second vote the bill, whose article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', save for narrow listed exceptions. The authors say the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype implicitly presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors. The institute also invokes an Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion under which gender identity falls within protected personal autonomy and states must guarantee trans people's full rights, and records dehumanising comparisons made by a congressman on the floor.

The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents extends the restriction. Human Rights Watch reports that it mandates public-restroom entry be determined by 'biological sex', barring trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their identity; that its vaguely worded child-protection articles, notably Article 4 on media and advertising and Article 5, enable censorship of identity-related, artistic and educational content; and that the minimum sentence for obscenity rose from three to four years. Human Rights Watch characterises child protection as a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

Violence against trans people is rising and recorded figures understate it. A national observatory's annual report, covered by a local news agency on 22 July 2024, records 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases over 2020–2023, with trans women more than half the homicide victims (30), followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian. Killings rose to 19 in 2023 (12 trans women) from 13 in 2022, 10 in 2021 and 12 in 2020, many committed with cruelty, including multiple gunshots and stabbings. The 170 violation cases include government violence and incitement to discrimination, with 61 denuncias in 2020. The report recounts the February 2023 gang abduction of trans sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano, 31, in the capital and her killing in a northern district with about 30 gunshots as part of an extortion scheme. Co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans human-rights defender and journalist, states the recorded numbers are only a sub-registry. A 2012 university study found that 70% of trans women in the capital region work in sex work, a documented exposure factor for police and public violence.

The torture and rape of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, ended in conviction on 15 December 2025: three police officers received 17 years' imprisonment, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It is the country's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Legal recognition of gender is partially available. Transgender residents may change their legal name to match their gender identity. In 2014 the Constitutional Court barred gender-marker changes on national identity documents, then reversed itself in a ruling of 21 October 2016 published 8 November, permitting gender change through a judicial process without sex-reassignment surgery. A Gender Identity Law covering legal gender change without surgery and access to passports and other identity documents matching gender identity was introduced on 4 November 2016 and remained pending in the legislature as of March 2021.

Healthcare classifications have shifted in both directions. In May 2024 the government decreed 'transsexualism' a mental health problem in order to cover trans healthcare; after protests, the health ministry revised the term to 'gender discordance' in June 2024 for health-insurance classification purposes, and in June 2024 health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described by Human Rights Watch as a step toward dignity for trans patients. Outright International reports that public institutions themselves contribute to anti-LGBTIQ discrimination; in July 2025 a capital-city constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, struck an anti-equality decree as unconstitutional; and an April 2025 law on foreign funding of NGOs lets authorities revoke registrations on 'public order and security' grounds, which risks being weaponised against queer organising. In April 2025 a television presenter of a capital-based channel publicly harassed the first openly-lesbian congresswoman, Susel Paredes, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.
