1875124B63771233756824.summary:
Apurímac stands under the national framework of Peru. No Apurímac-specific trans statute, ordinance or enforcement finding appears in the sources attached to this record, so the rules a visitor faces in the department are Peru's national laws and the national patterns of their application.

Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities. Bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by congressmen Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, were merged and approved unanimously by the congressional Women and Family Commission on 20 February 2025. The measure bars trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their sex at birth, with exceptions only for custody, situations requiring medical attention, or accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, and it bans 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The bill followed a July 2023 social-media complaint about gendered restroom labels at Jorge Chávez airport.

On 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved the bill and exempted it from a second vote. Its article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', save for the narrow listed exceptions. The Inter-American institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, in an analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte, holds that this directly violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, and that the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors. The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents, which contains the bathroom mandate and also bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity', applies throughout Peru including Apurímac.

LGBTI activist Gianna Camacho, cited on the commission's February 2025 approval, warns that bathroom access would come to depend on security staff's personal judgment, including identity-document checks, and states that there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. The restriction reaches private as well as public life: a consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy, and on television presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV told Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, to 'go use the men's room'.

Violence against trans people in Peru is documented and rising. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI annual report, covered by Agencia Presentes on 22 July 2024, records 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases over 2020–2023, with trans women more than half the homicide victims (30), followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian. Killings rose to 19 in 2023 (12 trans women) from 13 in 2022, 10 in 2021 and 12 in 2020, many committed with cruelty. The 170 violation cases include state violence and incitement to discrimination, with 61 complaints recorded in 2020 alone.

One case marks the limits and the possibility of protection. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code. Congress voted in 2017 to strip the protections from the new code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. Peru is one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights.

Speech and association are constrained by the same legislative package. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years; Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people. 1875124B76579830071892.name: Ayacucho
1875124B76579830071892.summary:
Ayacucho stands under Peru's national framework. No department-specific trans statute, ordinance, enforcement action or incident series for Ayacucho appears in the sources, and all attached material is national in scope, so the operative facts for a visitor to the region are the national ones.

Peru does not criminalise trans identity or consensual same-sex sexual activity, lawful since the 1924 Penal Code, and the age of consent is 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation under a 2012 Constitutional Court decision. Legal protection against discrimination and hate crime on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is absent: Government Decree Nº 1323 had criminalised such discrimination from 7 January 2017 through Articles 46 and 323 of the Penal Code, Congress voted 66–29 in May 2017 to strip those provisions, and the protections were subsequently removed as the Penal Code was reworked. Peru is one of only three countries in South America, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage.

Access to public facilities matching gender identity is restricted by law. The congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved on 20 February 2025 a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by congressmen Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, and the Plenary approved it and exempted it from a second vote on 2 April 2025. Its article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their biological sex, with exceptions only for custody, where medical attention is required, or for accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities; it also bans ambiguous bathroom signage. The stated trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint about gendered restroom labels at Jorge Chávez airport.

Law 32331, enacted 13 May 2025, bars trans people from using public restrooms according to their gender identity and bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'. The IDEHPUCP human-rights institute of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru finds the restriction openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by barring access to facilities matching their identity, implicitly casting trans people as harassment risks, and it invokes Inter-American Court of Human Rights Advisory Opinion OC-24/17, under which gender identity falls within protected personal autonomy and states must guarantee trans people's full rights. The institute also records dehumanising comparisons made by congressman Lizarzaburu on the floor.

Legal analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte of IDEHPUCP of 15 April 2025 argues that article 5 violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, and that the stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype implicitly presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho warns that bathroom access would come to depend on security staff's personal judgment, including identity checks, and notes there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms.

The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents extends the restriction. Human Rights Watch reports that it mandates public-restroom entry be determined by biological sex, barring trans people including trans youth from facilities matching their identity; that its vaguely worded child-protection articles, notably Article 4 on media and advertising and Article 5, enable censorship of identity-related, artistic and educational content; and that the minimum sentence for obscenity rose from three to four years. Human Rights Watch characterises child protection as a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

Violence against trans people is rising and recorded figures understate it. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI annual report, covered on 22 July 2024, records 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases over 2020–2023, with trans women more than half the homicide victims (30), followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian. Killings rose to 19 in 2023, 12 of them trans women, from 13 in 2022, 10 in 2021 and 12 in 2020, many committed with cruelty, and the violation cases include state violence and incitement to discrimination, with 61 denuncias in 2020. The report recounts the February 2023 gang abduction of trans sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano, 31, in central Lima and her killing in Carabayllo with about 30 gunshots as part of an extortion scheme. A July 2024 report finds hate crimes increasing with trans women most affected, and co-author Gianna Camacho states that recorded numbers are only a sub-registry.

The torture and rape of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, ended in conviction on 15 December 2025: police officers Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León received 17 years' imprisonment, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It is Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Transgender Peruvians may change their legal name to match their gender identity. In 2014 the Constitutional Court barred gender-marker changes on national identity documents, then reversed itself in a ruling of 21 October 2016 published 8 November, permitting gender change through a judicial process without sex-reassignment surgery. A Gender Identity Law covering legal gender change without surgery and access to passports and other identity documents matching gender identity was introduced on 4 November 2016 and remained pending in the legislature as of March 2021.

Healthcare classifications have shifted in both directions. In May 2024 the government decreed transsexualism a mental health problem in order to cover trans healthcare; after protests, MINSA revised the term to gender discordance in June 2024 for health-insurance classification purposes, and in June 2024 health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described by Human Rights Watch as a step toward dignity for trans patients.

Conversion therapy is banned in Peru for medical professionals, and in May 2024 MINSA reiterated that sexual orientation and gender identity are not diseases, a protection with direct bearing on trans and LGBTQ minors exposed to such practices. Residents nevertheless live without statutory anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection, since the Penal Code provisions introduced by Decree Nº 1323 were removed.

Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising.

1875124B48847835594727.name: Moquegua
1875124B48847835594727.summary:
Moquegua department stands under Peru's national framework. Consensual same-sex activity has not been criminalised since the 1924 Penal Code, trans identity is not an offence, and the age of consent is 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation under a 2012 Constitutional Court decision. No Moquegua-specific trans statute, municipal ordinance, court finding or enforcement action appears in the sources; the national rules described below bind the department directly.

Two legislative stages restrict which public restrooms a trans visitor may use. On 20 February 2025 the Congress' Commission on Women and Family approved without dissent a dictamen covering bills 6506 and 8457, barring entry to public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than one's birth sex, with exceptions limited to custody, medical care, or accompanying an adult, a child under 12 or a disabled person, and requiring unambiguous signage; at publication the measure still awaited plenary backing. Trans-rights activist Gianna Camacho called it discriminatory and warned that security staff would apply their own criteria, for example by demanding a DNI at the door.

On 2 April 2025 the Congress plenary approved, exempt from a second vote, the law strengthening the right to sexual integrity of children and adolescents. Its Article 5 bars anyone whose biological sex does not match the facility's intended sex from public sanitary facilities, with exceptions only for accompanying or assisting minors, patients or people with specific needs. An analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte of the IDEHPUCP institute at the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru (15 April 2025) states that the measure implicitly brands trans people as more likely to enter bathrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors, conditions basic rights on verifiable 'biological sex', and violates equality, non-discrimination and gender self-determination; the same institute's published position invokes Inter-American Court of Human Rights Advisory Opinion OC-24/17, under which gender identity falls within protected personal autonomy. The authors note that Congress had already banned inclusive language and again rejected equal marriage.

Recorded violence against trans people is rising and the figures understate it. The TLGBI Rights Observatory's annual report, covered by Agencia Presentes on 22 July 2024, records 54 killings of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases in Peru between 2020 and 2023, with trans women the most affected. The report recounts the February 2023 kidnapping of trans woman Rubí Torres Silvano, 31, in central Lima and her murder in Carabayllo with approximately 30 shots at the hands of the 'Los Gallegos' gang; the bodies showed gunshot wounds, stab wounds and throat-slitting indicating extreme hate. These national figures describe the risk environment a trans visitor to Moquegua enters, and no departmental breakdown is available.

Peru also has documented protection machinery of first-instance significance. The torture and rape of trans activist Azul Rojas Marín ended on 15 December 2025 with 17 years' imprisonment for police officers Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, the country's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region.

1875124B48847835594727.tangentialFactors:
Peru is one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, without LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in law. Government Decree Nº 1323 had criminalised discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity from 7 January 2017 through Articles 46 and 323 of the Penal Code; Congress voted 66–29 in May 2017 to strip the provisions, President Kuczynski's veto stood at that point, and the protections were removed as the Penal Code was reworked, the repeal carried by Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members after an April Constitutional Committee vote and a petition carrying one million signatures.

Human Rights Watch reports that the April 2025 sexual-integrity law also mandates that public-restroom entry be determined by 'biological sex', applies to trans youth, and contains vaguely worded child-protection provisions, notably Article 4 on media and advertising and Article 5, that enable censorship of identity-related, artistic and educational content, while the minimum sentence for obscenity rose from three to four years. Human Rights Watch characterises child protection as a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

Institutional hostility is documented alongside the legislative measures. Outright International reports that public institutions themselves contribute to anti-LGBTIQ discrimination; in July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, struck an anti-equality decree as unconstitutional; and an April 2025 law on foreign funding of NGOs lets authorities revoke registrations on 'public order and security' grounds, a power that risks being used against queer organising. In April 2025 television presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed the first openly-lesbian congresswoman, Susel Paredes, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

Co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans human-rights defender and journalist, states that recorded hate-crime numbers are only a sub-registry.

Legal recognition of gender is partially available to Peruvian residents. Transgender Peruvians may change their legal name to match their gender identity. In 2014 the Constitutional Court barred gender-marker changes on national identity documents, then reversed itself in a ruling of 21 October 2016 published 8 November, permitting gender change through a judicial process without sex-reassignment surgery. A Gender Identity Law covering legal gender change without surgery and access to passports and other identity documents matching gender identity was introduced on 4 November 2016 and remained pending in the legislature as of March 2021.

Healthcare classification has shifted in both directions. In May 2024 the government decreed 'transsexualism' a mental health problem in order to cover trans healthcare; after protests, MINSA revised the term to 'gender discordance' in June 2024 for health-insurance classification purposes, and in June 2024 health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described by Human Rights Watch as a step toward dignity for trans patients. Conversion therapy is banned for medical professionals, and in May 2024 MINSA reiterated that sexual orientation and gender identity are not diseases, a protection with direct bearing on trans and LGBTQ minors exposed to such practices.

Residents live under the same national statutes described for visitors, including the sexual-integrity law's restroom provision and the absence of Penal Code hate-crime coverage, and they additionally face the identity-document and health-insurance procedures above.

25984515B95172477822815.name: Adana
25984515B95172477822815.summary:
Adana Province has no provision of its own on gender identity, documentation, policing or facilities, and the source record carries no local enforcement data for the province. A trans visitor to Adana is therefore dealing with the Turkish national framework, set at national level and applied here without a provincial overlay.

The statutory baseline is permissive on its face. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1858 under the Ottoman penal code, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, the year gender reassignment surgery became lawful. A passport whose marker was changed at home or abroad can be presented without that change itself constituting an offence.

The protections around that baseline are thin. Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no direct discrimination protection for gender identity; the European Commission's 2025 report found legal protection insufficient and out of line with the EU acquis. Same-sex relationships receive no legal recognition: marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are all unavailable, and same-sex couples cannot adopt jointly or as individuals. LGBTQ people are barred from serving openly in the military.

The direction of travel is toward criminalisation. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked draft omnibus justice reform, the 11th Judicial Package, would enable criminal charges against LGBT people in Türkiye, a rollback HRW described as among the most alarming in decades; Istanbul activists held a press conference against it on 28 October 2025. The package applies countrywide if adopted, with no province-specific provisions, and whether it has since been enacted is unresolved in the sources. The parent framework's own exposure points are internal rather than at the border: foreigners must carry original photo ID at transit checkpoints, with fines of up to 3,000 in local currency and warnings of detention for non-compliance, and in August 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women in Beyoğlu while they were walking, shopping or sitting in cafés, holding them for background checks with no charge laid.

Detention is organised by registered sex rather than gender identity, and Turkish prisons subject LGBTI+ detainees to arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto isolation and restricted healthcare, with no policy or staff training to identify LGBTI+ needs. If hormone replacement therapy is needed during a stay, it is not covered by the government healthcare system and must be obtained and paid for privately.

25984515B90872828599679.name: Adıyaman
25984515B90872828599679.summary:
Adıyaman Province stands under the national framework of Türkiye, which presents a structured and documented danger to trans visitors. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in a single year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, with 299 detention decisions: 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record, alongside systematic attacks on the privacy of LGBT people. The source inventory contains no Adıyaman-specific carve-out from any of this. The provisions that govern a visitor's exposure in the province are national.

The government has repeatedly framed its position as protecting "the family" and "public morals", language Human Rights Watch identifies as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma of LGBT people. Under that framing a leaked draft omnibus justice reform, the 11th Judicial Package, would enable criminal charges against LGBT people countrywide. Human Rights Watch described it on 29 October 2025 as one of the most alarming rollbacks of rights in decades, and Istanbul activists held a press conference against it on 28 October 2025. The measure had not been passed when reported, but its pending status has not prevented authorities from acting as though the prohibitions were already in force.

Street-level enforcement illustrates that gap. Police stop trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés and hold them for "General Information Gathering" (GBT) background checks before release; legal experts cited in the reporting argue such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One detained woman stated that police took no fines but documented her anyway, adding that the new law had not yet been passed even as enforcement was already being applied. Foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints are required to produce original identity documents, which creates a direct outing risk for anyone whose appearance does not match their passport gender marker.

Türkiye requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. For a trans visitor, any checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Violence against trans people in Türkiye is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, and transgender individuals were disproportionately affected.

Trans prisoners are held by registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at a women's prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in six provinces demanded an independent investigation, and accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case, raised in parliament by an opposition MP on 12 December 2025, confirmed that Türkiye places trans prisoners according to their registered sex, a trans man having been held in a women's prison, and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. A country prison profile prepared with a civil society association and using ILGA World data documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. There is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

25984515B26209284550223.name: Afyonkarahisar
25984515B26209284550223.summary:
Afyonkarahisar has no distinct legal or policing regime on LGBTI+ matters. The province stands entirely under Turkey's national framework, and the draft omnibus justice package reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025 contains no Afyonkarahisar-specific provision. A visitor in the province is subject to the same national statutes, the same identity-document requirements at checkpoints and the same street-level policing practice documented elsewhere in Turkey.

The leaked draft of Türkiye's 11th Judicial Package would open the way to criminal charges against LGBT people. Conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality, including its so-called promotion, would carry up to three years in prison. Participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies would carry up to four years; because same-sex marriage is not legal in Turkey, such ceremonies are by definition symbolic and any attendance is exposed. Human Rights Watch describes the package as one of the most alarming rollbacks of rights in decades.

The same draft restricts gender-affirming care. It would raise the surgery age from 18 to 25 and make permanent infertility mandatory. Medical professionals would face fines or up to seven years for care outside the new limits, and transgender patients up to three years, a combination that would push transition care into underground settings.

Kaos GL's 2025 report, A Major Siege against LGBTI+ People in 2025: Hostility Turned into State Policy, records six right-to-life violations across the country, three of them logged as hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected. It documents 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, up from 51 the previous year, most linked to peaceful assembly, alongside 336 violations of assembly and 313 violations of liberty. The liberty figure is a roughly 2.5-fold increase made up mostly of detentions, and the report also records event-specific bans and violent police attacks on peaceful gatherings.

The counts in that report are drawn from media and civil-society monitoring because the Turkish state keeps no official hate-crime statistics. The report contains no Afyonkarahisar-specific finding; it describes the country-wide framework that governs the province.

25984515B39003465173278.name: Ağrı
25984515B39003465173278.summary:
Ağrı stands under the national legal framework of Türkiye; the source inventory records no province-specific statute, ordinance or incident series applying to the province. What a trans visitor encounters in Ağrı is Turkish national law and national police practice.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked draft of Türkiye's omnibus 11th Judicial Package would open the way to criminal charges against LGBT people, described there as one of the most alarming rollbacks of rights in decades. Conduct deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality', including its so-called 'promotion', would carry up to three years in prison, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies up to four years. Same-sex marriage is not legal in Türkiye, so such ceremonies are symbolic by definition. The package contains no provision naming Ağrı.

The same draft would restrict gender-affirming care: the surgery age raised from 18 to 25, permanent infertility made mandatory, medical professionals fined or imprisoned for up to seven years, and transgender patients imprisoned for up to three years for care falling outside the new limits. Human Rights Watch warns this would push transition treatment into underground settings. A trans visitor seeking or already receiving hormone therapy should expect that any care sought in Türkiye now sits under these proposed constraints.

Kaos GL's report 'A Major Siege against LGBTI+ People in 2025: Hostility Turned into State Policy' records six right-to-life violations in 2025, three of them counted as hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected. Because the state keeps no official hate-crime statistics, these figures are compiled from media and civil-society reports. The same report documents 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, up from 51 the previous year, mostly linked to peaceful assembly, alongside 336 assembly violations and 313 liberty violations — the liberty figure roughly 2.5 times the prior total, driven mostly by detentions — together with event-specific bans and violent police attacks on peaceful gatherings.

Kaos GL presents this hostility as institutionalised under 'Year of the Family' instructions issued to public institutions, accompanied by hate speech from senior officials, censored broadcasts and cancelled artistic events. The report frames these as national practice rather than provincial choice, and no Ağrı-specific finding appears in it.

25984515B97476213604692.name: Antalya
25984515B97476213604692.summary:
Antalya stands under the national framework of Turkey, which has no visa, entry or border rule specific to LGBTQ travellers; the documented exposure points lie inside the country rather than at the frontier. Foreigners must carry original photo ID at transit checkpoints in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and warnings of detention for non-compliance. That requirement intersects with identity checks on the street: in August 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women while they were walking, shopping or sitting in cafés in Beyoğlu, held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station and released them after 'General Information Gathering' background checks. Legal experts quoted by bianet argue those checks breach Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Nothing was fined in that incident, but names and details were recorded.

Criminalisation by statute had not been enacted when Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025, but a leaked draft omnibus law then before the government, the 11th Judicial Package, would amend the Turkish penal and civil codes to criminalise behaviour deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality'. It would criminalise taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony with penalties of up to four years in prison, raise the minimum age for gender-affirming health care including surgery from 18 to 25 on condition of permanent infertility, and punish health professionals who perform such care. Human Rights Watch calls it one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades; 15 Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association oppose the draft. Whether the package has since passed is unresolved in the sources.

The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 records 313 violations over the year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, dominated by 299 detention decisions — 256 taken on the record and 43 off it — alongside systematic attacks on the privacy of LGBT people. Turkish Minute's coverage of the same report counts six deaths linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. Kaos GL's report launch, where findings were presented by lawyer Kerem Dikmen, states that anti-LGBTI+ hostility became institutionalised as explicit state policy: senior officials' hate speech and instructions issued to public institutions under a 'Year of the Family' banner created a climate that encouraged human-rights violations, and regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricted freedom of expression and artistic freedom.

Policing asymmetry is documented at the level of individual cases. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy by a 17-year-old; the attacker was released while the victim herself was referred for arrest, which activists describe as evidence of a state hate policy. On 1 December 2025 the transgender prisoner Poyraz was found dead in his cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara, and rights groups demanded an independent investigation and changes to detention practices affecting transgender prisoners. Four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, medical staff arrived after prolonged delay, prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison only two days later, witness statements were not taken, and an opposition MP raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025.

Trans visitors who are detained are held in facilities organised by registered sex rather than gender identity, and Turkish prisons subject LGBTI+ detainees to arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto isolation and restricted healthcare. Some prisoners refuse hospital transfers for fear of other male inmates. No policy or staff training exists to identify LGBTI+ needs, complaints are ineffective and can provoke further violence, and transfers are frequent. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through the year, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

Protection machinery is thin. Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity, and no direct discrimination protection for gender identity; the European Commission's 2025 report found legal protection insufficient and out of line with the EU acquis, while noting official permissions granted to demonstrations promoting exclusion. If medication is needed during a stay, hormone replacement therapy is not covered by the government healthcare system, so trans visitors must obtain and pay for it privately.

25984515B1602304411378.name: Artvin
25984515B1602304411378.summary:
Artvin stands under the national framework of Turkey, where hostility toward trans people has been organised into documented state policy rather than left as residual prejudice. Kaos GL's LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025, launched under the title "A major siege against LGBTI+ people in 2025: Hostility turned into state policy", recorded 313 violations in a single year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, alongside 299 detention decisions — 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record — and systematic attacks on the privacy of LGBT people. The launch presentation by lawyer Kerem Dikmen set out how senior officials' hate speech and instructions issued to public institutions under a "Year of the Family" banner created a climate that encouraged violations, with regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricting freedom of expression and artistic freedom.

A draft omnibus law, the 11th Judicial Package, was reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025. It would amend the Turkish penal and civil codes to criminalise behaviour deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality", criminalise taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony with penalties of up to four years in prison, raise the minimum age for gender-affirming health care including surgery from 18 to 25 with a requirement of permanent infertility, and punish health professionals who perform such care. Human Rights Watch calls it one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades; 15 Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association oppose the draft. The measure had not been passed when reported, but its pending status has not prevented authorities from acting as though the prohibitions were already in force.

The Erdoğan government has repeatedly framed its position as protecting "the family" and "public morals", language Human Rights Watch identifies as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma of LGBT people. Street-level enforcement illustrates the gap between the draft's status and its application: in 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" (GBT) background checks before release, with legal experts arguing that such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that no fines were issued but that the police documented them anyway, and that enforcement was already being applied to her before any new law had passed.

Foreign visitors face a direct outing risk at these interactions. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. Any checkpoint stop is an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, a detention asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Prison conditions form part of the same regime. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025, and the case confirmed that Turkey places trans prisoners according to their registered sex, a trans man having been held in a women's prison. Rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation, reporting that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case was raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025, placing custody conditions for trans prisoners under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

Pride events remain flashpoints. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia and entrenching discrimination against LGBT people and their allies.

25984515B63739470532168.name: Aydın
25984515B63739470532168.summary:
Aydın province stands under the framework that applies across Turkey, and that framework now places documented LGBT people under sustained legal jeopardy. Aydın has no separate regime: the criminal-law, identification-document and health-recording rules set out below are national and operate in the province's clinics, police stations and street checkpoints alike.

As of 29 October 2025 the government had before it a draft omnibus package, reported by Human Rights Watch as the '11th Judicial Package', that would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise behaviour deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality'. The draft criminalises taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony with penalties of up to four years in prison, raises the minimum age for gender-affirming health care including surgery from 18 to 25 and conditions it on mandatory permanent infertility, and punishes health professionals who perform such care. Human Rights Watch describes it as one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades; 15 Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association oppose the draft. The measure had not been passed when reported, but authorities have been acting as though the prohibitions were already in force.

Document checks are the sharpest everyday risk for a visitor. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for 'General Information Gathering' (GBT) background checks before release; legal experts cited in the reporting argue those checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women stopped stated that no fines were issued but that she was documented anyway. Any stop in Aydın is an occasion on which a passport can be compared against presentation, and for a visitor whose appearance does not match the gender marker in their documents the interaction is an immediate outing risk.

Official records now mark trans status in clinical settings. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added 'gender reassignment' as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the 'other' gender option and required e-reports to be issued. Every clinical encounter can therefore leave a documented marker of a trans patient's status, restricting access to transition care and creating a record that can surface in any subsequent official process.

Hostility is documented policy rather than residual prejudice. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025, launched under the title 'A major siege against LGBTI+ people in 2025: Hostility turned into state policy' and presented by lawyer Kerem Dikmen, records 313 violations in a single year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, alongside 299 detention decisions, 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record. The report documents senior officials' hate speech, instructions issued to public institutions under a 'Year of the Family' banner, and regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricting freedom of expression and artistic freedom, creating a climate that encouraged human-rights violations.

Violence against trans people is lethal and the state response asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, a detention asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate.

25984515B55384476443375.summary:
Balıkesir is a province of Turkey and stands under the national framework, in which the documented exposure points for a trans visitor lie inside the country rather than at the frontier. Turkey has no visa, entry or border rule specific to LGBTQ travellers. Criminalisation by statute had not been enacted when Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025, but a leaked draft omnibus law then before the government, the 11th Judicial Package, would amend the Turkish penal and civil codes to criminalise behaviour deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality'. It would criminalise taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony with penalties of up to four years in prison, raise the minimum age for gender-affirming health care including surgery from 18 to 25 on condition of mandatory permanent infertility, and punish health professionals who perform such care. Whether the package has since passed is unresolved in the sources.

Hostility at this scale is recorded as organised state policy. Kaos GL's LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 records 313 violations over the year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, dominated by 299 detention decisions, 256 taken on the record and 43 taken off it, alongside systematic attacks on the privacy of LGBT people. Turkish Minute's coverage of the same report counts six deaths linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. At the report's launch, lawyer Kerem Dikmen presented findings showing that anti-LGBTI+ hostility became institutionalised as explicit state policy, with senior officials' hate speech and instructions issued to public institutions under a 'Year of the Family' banner creating a climate that encouraged human-rights violations, and regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricting freedom of expression and artistic freedom.

Policing asymmetry is documented at the level of individual cases. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy by a 17-year-old; the attacker was released while the victim herself was referred for arrest, which activists describe as evidence of a state hate policy. On 1 December 2025 the transgender prisoner Poyraz was found dead in his cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara. Accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers state that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived after prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison only two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. An opposition MP raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025, and rights groups demanded an independent investigation and changes to detention practices affecting transgender prisoners.

A trans visitor who is detained is held in facilities organised by registered sex rather than gender identity. Turkish prisons subject LGBTI+ detainees to arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto isolation and restricted healthcare, and some prisoners refuse hospital transfers for fear of other male inmates. Hostility at this scale is recorded as national policy. A national LGBTI+ rights organisation's human rights report for 2025 records 313 violations over the year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, dominated by 299 detention decisions, 256 taken on the record and 43 taken off it, alongside systematic attacks on the privacy of LGBT people. Press coverage of the same report counts six deaths linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. At the report's launch, a lawyer presented findings showing that anti-LGBTI+ hostility became institutionalised as explicit national policy, with senior officials' hate speech and instructions issued to public institutions under a 'Year of the Family' banner creating a climate that encouraged human-rights violations, and regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricting freedom of expression and artistic freedom.

Policing asymmetry is documented at the level of individual cases. In August 2024 a trans woman was knifed in a district of a major city by a 17-year-old; the attacker was released while the victim herself was referred for arrest, which activists describe as evidence of a national hate policy. On 1 December 2025 a transgender prisoner was found dead in her cell at a women's prison near the capital. Accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers state that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived after prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison only two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. A trans visitor who is detained is held in facilities organised by registered sex rather than gender identity. Prisons subject LGBTI+ detainees to arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto isolation and restricted healthcare, and some prisoners refuse hospital transfers for fear of other male inmates. No policy or staff training exists to identify LGBTI+ needs, complaints are ineffective and can provoke further violence, and transfers are frequent. Monitoring of a major city's 2025 Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through the year, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

A regional oversight body's 2025 report found legal protection insufficient and out of line with the regional legal order, while noting official permissions granted to demonstrations promoting exclusion. Hormone replacement therapy is not covered by the national healthcare system, so a trans visitor who needs medication during a stay must obtain and pay for it privately. No province-specific enforcement record, local detention practice or facility provision is sourced for this dossier; the state/province's exposure follows the national pattern described above.

25984515B40051660631000.name: Aksaray
25984515B40051660631000.summary:
Aksaray stands under the national framework of Turkey, where hostility toward trans people has been formalised as state policy rather than left to residual prejudice. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in a single year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, alongside 299 detention decisions — 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record — together with systematic attacks on the privacy of LGBT people.

A leaked draft omnibus justice package from October 2025, the 11th Judicial Package, would amend the Turkish penal and civil codes to criminalise behaviour deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality'. It would criminalise taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony with penalties of up to four years in prison, raise the minimum age for gender-affirming health care including surgery from 18 to 25 with a requirement of permanent infertility, and punish health professionals who perform such care. Human Rights Watch calls it one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades; 15 Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association oppose the draft. The measure had not been passed when reported, but its pending status has not prevented authorities from acting as though the prohibitions were already in force.

Street-level enforcement in Istanbul illustrates that point. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" (GBT) background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue that such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that the police took no fines but documented them anyway, adding that the new law had not yet been passed even as enforcement was already being applied to them. Foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints are required to produce original identity documents, which creates a direct outing risk for anyone whose appearance does not match their passport gender marker.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, and transgender individuals were disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest. Activists treat that detention asymmetry as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Pride events remain flashpoints. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia and entrenching discrimination against LGBT people and their allies.

The passport-carrying rule for foreigners compounds these risks. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. For a trans visitor, any checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Trans prisoners are held by registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Turkish rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation, and accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case, raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025, confirmed that Turkey places trans prisoners according to their registered sex — a trans man had been held in a women's prison — and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. There is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care, with online framing contested as an "LGBT opening".

The underlying pattern is longstanding. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. That report predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited here as historical evidence of the regime's depth rather than as a statement of current law.

25984515B679661827679.name: Batman
25984515B679661827679.summary:
Batman province stands under the national framework of Turkey, where hostility toward trans people has been formalised as state policy rather than left as residual prejudice. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in a single year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, including 299 detention decisions — 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record — alongside systematic intrusion into the privacy of LGBT people.

A leaked draft omnibus justice package circulated in October 2025, the 11th Judicial Package, would amend the Turkish penal and civil codes to criminalise behaviour deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality. The draft would criminalise taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony with penalties of up to four years in prison, raise the minimum age for gender-affirming health care including surgery from 18 to 25 on a requirement of permanent infertility, and punish health professionals who carry out such care. Human Rights Watch called the draft one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades, and 15 Turkish LGBT groups together with the Turkish Medical Association oppose it. The measure had not been passed when reported, but authorities have acted as though the prohibitions were already in force.

Kaos GL's 2025 report, A major siege against LGBTI+ people in 2025: Hostility turned into state policy, found that anti-LGBTI+ hostility has become institutionalised as explicit policy. Senior officials' hate speech and instructions issued to public institutions under a Year of the Family banner created a climate that encouraged human-rights violations, while regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricted freedom of expression and artistic freedom. The findings were presented by lawyer Kerem Dikmen at the report launch.

Street-level enforcement shows how that framework operates against individuals. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafes in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for General Information Gathering background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue that such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One detained woman stated that police issued no fines but documented them anyway, and observed that the new law had not yet passed even as enforcement was applied to her.

Foreign visitors stopped at such checkpoints must produce original identity documents, and Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. For a trans visitor, any checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents are compared against presentation.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response is asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of them classified by rights organisations as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, a detention asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate. Monitoring by the Truth Justice Memory Center of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025.

Trans prisoners are placed by registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Coordinated by Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın, rights groups demanded an independent investigation, and accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. Opposition MP Sevda Karaca raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025, confirming that a trans man had been held in a women's prison and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. There is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added gender reassignment as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the other option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

The underlying pattern is longstanding. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. That report predates the legal changes made after 2018 and stands as historical evidence of the regime's depth rather than a statement of current law.

One of the women detained stated that police took no fines but documented them anyway, adding that the new law had not yet been passed even as enforcement was already being applied to them. Foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints are required to produce original identity documents, creating a direct outing risk for anyone whose appearance does not match their passport gender marker.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest. Activists treat that detention asymmetry as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. For a trans visitor, any checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Trans prisoners are held by registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation; accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added 'gender reassignment' as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the 'other' option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

Pride events remain flashpoints. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

25984515B39892287187022.summary:
Bilecik province stands under the legal and administrative framework of Türkiye, and the sources carried for this record contain no Bilecik-specific statute, municipal ordinance or documented local enforcement practice. Whatever variation exists at provincial level is undocumented here, so a visitor to Bilecik should expect the national picture to apply without local modification.

The most consequential measure bearing on trans visitors is the leaked draft omnibus justice package reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025. Senior officials' hate speech, instructions issued to public institutions under a "Year of the Family" banner, and regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricting freedom of expression and artistic freedom together created what the report describes as a climate encouraging human-rights violations. For a trans visitor this is the operating environment behind any checkpoint, hospital or public-space interaction in Bilecik.

25984515B19802935753104.name: Bitlis
25984515B19802935753104.summary:
Bitlis province stands under the national framework of Türkiye, which presents a structured and documented danger to trans visitors, driven by hostility that has become formal state policy rather than residual prejudice. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in a single year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, with 299 detention decisions — 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record — together with systematic attacks on the privacy of LGBT people.

On 29 October 2025 Human Rights Watch reported a leaked draft omnibus law, the 11th Judicial Package, that would amend the Turkish penal and civil codes to criminalise behaviour deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality'. The draft would criminalise taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony with penalties of up to four years in prison, raise the minimum age for gender-affirming health care including surgery from 18 to 25 and require permanent infertility as a condition, and punish health professionals who perform such care. Human Rights Watch called it one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades; 15 Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association oppose the draft. It had not been passed when reported, but its pending status has not prevented authorities from acting as though the prohibitions were already in force.

The Erdoğan government has repeatedly framed its position as protecting "the family" and "public morals", language Human Rights Watch identifies as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma of LGBT people. Kaos GL's 2025 report, launched under the title "A major siege against LGBTI+ people in 2025: Hostility turned into state policy", documents that anti-LGBTI+ hostility became institutionalised as explicit state policy: senior officials' hate speech and instructions issued to public institutions under a "Year of the Family" banner created a climate that encouraged human-rights violations, and regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricted freedom of expression and artistic freedom. The findings were presented by lawyer Kerem Dikmen at the launch.

Street-level enforcement in Istanbul illustrates how the pending draft is already being applied. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" (GBT) background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue that such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that the police took no fines but documented them anyway, adding that the new law had not yet been passed even as enforcement was already being applied to them. Foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints are required to produce original identity documents, which creates a direct outing risk for anyone whose appearance does not match their passport gender marker.

The passport-carrying rule compounds that risk nationwide. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. For a trans visitor, any checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, and transgender individuals were disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest. Activists treat that detention asymmetry as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Pride events remain flashpoints. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia and entrenching discrimination against LGBT people and their allies.

Trans prisoners are held by registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation, and accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case, raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025, confirmed that Turkey places trans prisoners according to their registered sex — a trans man had been held in a women's prison — and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. There is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care, with online framing contested as an "LGBT opening".

The underlying pattern is longstanding. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. That report predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited here as historical evidence of the regime's depth rather than as a statement of current law.
