25984515B90474549897215.name: Burdur
25984515B90474549897215.summary:
Burdur Province stands under Türkiye's national legal and policing framework, which leaves no separate provincial regime for a visitor to rely on. The Turkish Criminal Code and the national police powers that accompany it apply in full within the province, and the risks described below are national in scope rather than local quirks of Burdur.

The most consequential pending measure is the leaked 11th Judicial Package, described by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025. The draft would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise conduct deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality', with penalties of up to three years in prison, and would criminalise taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony with penalties of up to four years. It would also raise the minimum age for gender-affirming health care, including surgery, from 18 to 25 and require proof of permanent infertility, and would punish health professionals who perform such care. Human Rights Watch calls the draft one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades; 15 Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association oppose it. The package had not been adopted when reported.

The gap between draft text and enforcement practice is the operational risk for a trans visitor. In 2025 police in the Beyoğlu district of Istanbul stopped roughly twenty trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for 'General Information Gathering' (GBT) background checks before release. No fines were issued, but the women were documented. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue that such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One detainee stated that the new law had not yet been passed even as enforcement was already being applied to her. Foreign nationals stopped at these checkpoints must produce original identity documents, which creates a direct outing risk wherever appearance and passport gender marker diverge.

Hostility has been formalised as state policy rather than left to residual prejudice. The Kaos GL report 'A major siege against LGBTI+ people in 2025: Hostility turned into state policy', launched by lawyer Kerem Dikmen, documents anti-LGBTI+ hostility becoming institutionalised: senior officials' hate speech, instructions issued to public institutions under a 'Year of the Family' banner creating a climate that encouraged human-rights violations, and regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricting freedom of expression and artistic freedom. The same organisation's LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in a single year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, alongside 299 detention decisions, 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record.

Violence against trans people in Türkiye is lethal and the state response is asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 a trans woman was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest. Activists treat that detention asymmetry as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Carrying documents is itself a checkpoint risk. Türkiye requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. Every checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Prison conditions matter for any trans visitor who is detained. Trans prisoners are held according to registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation; accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. Opposition MP Sevda Karaca raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025, confirming that a trans man had been held in a women's prison and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025. The Prison Insider country profile, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners, binary and heteronormative administration with no policy or staff training to identify LGBT prisoners' needs, transfers that disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints mechanisms that are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added 'gender reassignment' as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the 'other' option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

Pride events remain flashpoints. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

25984515B3524648625362.summary:
Çankırı province stands under the national framework of Turkey, which presents a structured and documented danger to trans visitors. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025, published 24 February 2026, finds that hostility toward LGBT people became explicit state policy during the year, driven by "Year of the Family" instructions issued to public institutions from senior officials.

Kaos GL documented 313 violations of the right to liberty in 2025, roughly two and a half times the previous year's total, most of them detentions. It also recorded 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, up from 51, and six right-to-life violations, three of which were classified as hate-motivated killings, with trans people most affected.

Turkey's state keeps no official hate-crime statistics, so the monitoring data rely on media coverage rather than government records. The report is national in scope and records no province-specific enforcement or incidents in Çankırı.

A leaked draft of Türkiye's 11th Judicial Package, reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025, would amend penal-code article 225 to punish conduct "contrary to biological sex" with up to three years in prison. The same draft would allow charges against anyone taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony, carrying up to four years.

Under civil-code article 40, the draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25 and impose a permanent-infertility mandate. Providers could face fines and up to seven years in prison, patients up to three years. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association objected, and Human Rights Watch has called for the draft's withdrawal.

25984515B57743432888015.name: Çorum
25984515B57743432888015.summary:
Çorum province stands under the national framework applicable across Türkiye, and that framework presents a structured and documented danger to trans visitors. The sources assembled for this province record no Çorum-specific enforcement actions or incidents; the findings below are national, and they are what a visitor to Çorum would be subject to.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked draft of Türkiye's 11th Judicial Package would amend penal-code article 225 to punish conduct "contrary to biological sex" with up to three years in prison, and would allow charges against anyone taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony, carrying up to four years. Under civil-code article 40 the same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25 and impose a permanent-infertility mandate, with providers facing fines and up to seven years and patients up to three years. Fifteen LGBTI+ organisations and the Turkish Medical Association objected, and Human Rights Watch called for withdrawal. Whether the package has been enacted remains unresolved in the sources.

Criminalisation by statute had not been enacted when Human Rights Watch reported, but the reform sits within a broader authoritarian drift in which the government has repeatedly framed LGBTI+ life as a threat to the family and to public morals. Kaos GL's LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025, published 24 February 2026, finds that hostility hardened into explicit state policy over the year under "Year of the Family" instructions.

The same report documents 313 right-to-liberty violations across 2025, about two and a half times the previous year and mostly detentions, alongside 89 torture and ill-treatment violations, up from 51, and six right-to-life violations of which three were hate-motivated killings, with transgender people the group most affected. Türkiye keeps no official hate-crime statistics, so these figures rest on media monitoring rather than state records, which means the true scale is not established.

Identity checks on the street are a direct visitor risk. In August 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women while they were walking, shopping or sitting in cafés in Beyoğlu, held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station and released them after "General Information Gathering" background checks. Legal experts quoted by bianet argue those checks breach Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Nothing was fined; names and details were recorded, and officers applied a regime that had not been enacted. Foreigners must separately carry original photo ID at transit checkpoints in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and warnings of detention for non-compliance.

Policing asymmetry is documented at the level of individual cases. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy by a 17-year-old; the attacker was released while the victim herself was referred for arrest, which activists describe as evidence of a state hate policy. On 1 December 2025 the transgender prisoner Poyraz was found dead in his cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara. Accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers state that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, medical staff arrived after prolonged delay, prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison only two days later, and witness statements were not taken; an opposition MP raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025.

Trans visitors who are detained are held in facilities organised by registered sex rather than gender identity. Turkish prisons subject LGBTI+ detainees to arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto isolation and restricted healthcare; some prisoners refuse hospital transfers for fear of other male inmates. No policy or staff training exists to identify LGBTI+ needs, complaints mechanisms are ineffective and can provoke further violence, and transfers are frequent.

Protection machinery is thin. Türkiye has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity, and no direct discrimination protection for gender identity. The European Commission's 2025 report found legal protection insufficient and out of line with the EU acquis, while noting official permissions granted to demonstrations promoting exclusion. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through the year, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia. If medication is needed during a stay, hormone replacement therapy is not covered by the government healthcare system, so trans visitors must obtain and pay for it privately.

The state's own evidentiary gap shapes how the risk can be assessed. 25984515B87415935832289.name: Düzce
25984515B87415935832289.summary:
Düzce stands under the national framework of Turkey, where hostility toward trans people has been converted into documented state practice. The province's own record yields no distinct local finding, so the assessment below rests on the nationwide regime a visitor to Düzce is subject to, including at police checkpoints, in medical facilities and in document controls that apply equally in interior provinces.

Turkish law itself is not the immediate hazard. Consensual same-sex activity has been legal since the 1858 Ottoman penal code, and legal gender change has been available since 1988. Turkish marriage law, however, gives same-sex relationships no recognition and provides no civil unions, domestic partnerships or joint adoption, and no comprehensive statute bans discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity. LGBT people are barred from open service in the armed forces.

The immediate hazard is a draft law. The leaked 11th Judicial Package omnibus draft, reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025, would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment. The same package would sharply restrict gender-affirming healthcare by imposing a minimum age of 25 and onerous eligibility conditions, and would allow criminal charges against both trans people and the professionals providing their care. The government's stated justification is protecting "the family" and "public morals". The package also carries unrelated measures such as longer child sentences and online-content removal.

Enforcement has outpaced legislation. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" (GBT) background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue that such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that the police took no fines but documented them anyway, adding that the new law had not yet been passed even as enforcement was already being applied to them. Foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints are required to produce original identity documents, which creates a direct outing risk for anyone whose appearance does not match their passport gender marker.

The passport-carrying rule compounds these risks. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. For a trans visitor, any checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, and transgender individuals were disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest. Activists treat that detention asymmetry as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Pride events remain flashpoints. Amnesty International recorded that Pride events and LGBTQ gatherings were repeatedly disallowed in 2024 and 2025, with police detaining participants. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

Trans prisoners are held by registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Turkish rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation, and accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case, raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025, confirmed that Turkey places trans prisoners according to their registered sex, a trans man having been held in a women's prison.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. There is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

In early 2026 Turkish media reported that the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex'; that provision was not included in that year's judicial reform package. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in a single year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, with 299 detention decisions, 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record.

The underlying pattern is longstanding. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people, and is cited here as historical evidence of the regime's depth rather than as a statement of current law.

25984515B68163725002210.name: Edirne
25984515B68163725002210.summary:
Edirne Province falls entirely under the national law of Türkiye. The sources reviewed contain no Edirne-specific policing, document, facility or violence findings, so the province is assessed here through the national framework, which is documented as hostile and is tightening rather than loosening.

Türkiye presents a structured and documented danger to trans visitors. A national LGBTI+ human rights report recorded 313 violations in 2025, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, including 299 detention decisions, of which 43 were taken off the record. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of them classified by rights organisations as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected.

Enforcement is already operating ahead of legislation. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women in streets, shops and cafés and held them at a central police station for "General Information Gathering" background checks before release. Legal experts cited in that reporting argue such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One woman detained stated that no fines were issued but that the police documented those stopped anyway, and that a law which had not been passed was being applied to them regardless. Foreign visitors stopped at such checkpoints must produce original identity documents, creating a direct outing risk where appearance does not match the passport gender marker.

Carrying rules raise the frequency of those encounters. Türkiye requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention for non-compliance. Every checkpoint interaction is a point at which documents can be compared against presentation.

A leaked draft of the 11th Judicial Package, reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025, would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" with up to three years' imprisonment. The same package would raise eligibility for gender-affirming healthcare to a minimum age of 25 under onerous conditions and would expose both trans people and the professionals treating them to criminal charges, with fines and sentences for providers and up to three years for patients. The government's stated justification is protecting "the family" and "public morals". The package was reported as a draft and is recorded here as pending; its pending status has not prevented authorities from acting as though equivalent prohibitions were already in force.

Transition-related care is being restricted through regulation as well as statute. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a provincial circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording an "other" option and required electronic reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

Prison placement follows registered sex. A transgender prisoner was found dead in a cell at a women's prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025, with rights groups demanding an independent investigation; accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case, raised in parliament on 12 December 2025, confirmed that Türkiye places trans prisoners by registered sex, including a trans man held in a women's prison. The Prison Insider country profile, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted healthcare access, refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners, an absence of policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, a binary and heteronormative administration, transfers that disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints procedures that are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Pride events remain flashpoints. Pride was disallowed in 2024 and in 2025, with police detaining participants, and monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through the year. The European Commission's Türkiye Report 2025 concludes that the country's laws and their implementation do not properly protect LGBTQ people.

25984515B73855241915553.name: Elazığ
25984515B73855241915553.summary:
Elazığ province stands under the national framework of Turkey, where homosexuality has been decriminalised since 1858 and gender-reassignment surgery has been legal since 1988, and where discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is prohibited in law. The same framework withholds recognition of same-sex relationships, marriage, civil unions and same-sex adoption, and bars LGBTI people from serving openly in the military. In ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking Turkey placed 47th of 49, ahead only of Azerbaijan and Russia.

Legislative risk is live rather than hypothetical. A leaked omnibus draft law dated 29 October 2025, the 11th Judicial Package, would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" with penalties of up to three years, would sharply restrict gender-affirming healthcare by imposing a minimum age of 25 and onerous eligibility conditions, and would allow criminal charges against both trans people and the professionals providing their care. The government's stated justification is protecting "the family" and "public morals". The package also carries unrelated measures, including longer sentences for child offences and online-content removal. Whether it has since been enacted is unresolved in the sources.

Hostility is not confined to statute. On 19 December 2022 an anti-LGBT hate rally was held at Elazığ's Cumhuriyet (Republic) Square under a banner reading "LGBT sapkınlıktır" ("LGBT is perversion"), with the participation of ruling AKP deputy mayor Nazif Bilginoğlu. The rally statement denounced consensual same-sex relationships and "homosexual marriage" as a "revolting loss of reason" in Western states, deployed the terms "perverse" and "degenerate mentality", and tied gender and sexual themes to Turkey's denunciation of the Istanbul Convention. The event records state-facilitated, locally active anti-LGBT mobilisation in this province, which bears directly on what a visibly LGBTQ traveller can expect on the ground.

Since 2015 the Turkish authorities have repeatedly banned and forcibly dispersed Pride marches, using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions. In early 2026 the government was considering criminalising public advocacy of "behaviour contrary to biological sex and general morality", extending the same framing beyond private conduct to speech.

25984515B50530672954016.name: Erzurum
25984515B50530672954016.summary:
Erzurum province lies wholly inside Türkiye's national legal framework. No provincial regime applies to trans visitors: the penal code, the civil code, Health Ministry regulations and the police practices documented in Istanbul and Ankara operate identically in Erzurum.

Homosexuality has been decriminalised in Türkiye since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, the same year gender-reassignment surgery was legalised. That statutory position is the baseline a trans visitor enters on.

The trajectory runs the other way. A leaked draft of the 11th Judicial Package, reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025, would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" with penalties of up to three years, would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming healthcare to 25 under onerous eligibility conditions, and would allow criminal charges against both trans people and the professionals providing their care. The government's stated justification is protection of "the family" and "public morals". The package also carries unrelated measures including longer sentences for children and online-content removal.

Recognition is withheld across the board. Same-sex marriage, civil unions and joint adoption are not recognised, LGBTQ people are barred from openly serving in the military, and no comprehensive national law bans discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking placed Türkiye 47th out of 49 countries.

Public assembly is the sharpest exposure point. Pride events have been banned in Istanbul and most other cities in most years since 2015, with police deploying tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against participants. A court case seeking to close the association Lambda Istanbul was overruled by the Constitutional Court, which kept the association open.

25984515B57889067347253.name: Hakkâri
25984515B57889067347253.summary:
Hakkâri Province stands under Turkey's national framework: there is no separate provincial layer of trans-specific law, and Turkey has no visa, entry or border rule specific to LGBTQ travellers. The documented exposure points lie inside the country rather than at the frontier. Foreigners must carry original photo ID at transit checkpoints, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and warnings of detention for non-compliance; in August 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women while they were walking, shopping or sitting in cafés in Beyoğlu, held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station and released them after background checks that legal experts quoted by bianet argue breach Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Nothing was fined in that episode, but names and details were recorded.

Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence in Turkey since the Ottoman Empire's 1858 penal code, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, with gender-reassignment surgery legal from that year subject to court approval. Criminalisation by statute had not been enacted when Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025, but a leaked omnibus draft then before the government, the 11th Judicial Package, would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise LGBT conduct deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' with up to 3 years' imprisonment, criminalise same-sex ceremonies with up to 4 years, raise the age for gender-affirming healthcare to 25 with mandatory infertility and multiple-evaluation conditions, and punish providers with fines and up to 7 years' imprisonment; 15 LGBT groups and the national medical association object. Whether the package has since passed is unresolved in the sources.

The framework offers a trans visitor little protective depth. Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no direct discrimination protection for gender identity; the European Commission's 2025 report found legal protection insufficient and out of line with the EU acquis, while noting official permissions granted to demonstrations promoting exclusion. The country recognises no same-sex relationships: marriage is defined by law as a union between a man and a woman, which makes same-sex marriage legally impossible though not criminalised, and marriage eligibility turns on the gender recorded in a person's civil-registry entry rather than on trans status.

Hostility is recorded at the level of aggregate state action. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 documents 313 violations over the year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, dominated by 299 detention decisions — 256 on the record and 43 off it — alongside systematic attacks on the privacy of LGBT people. Turkish Minute's coverage of the same report counts six deaths linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected.

Policing asymmetry recurs in individual cases. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy by a 17-year-old; the attacker was released while the victim herself was referred for arrest, which activists describe as evidence of a state hate policy. On 1 December 2025 the transgender prisoner Poyraz was found dead in his cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara, and rights groups demanded an independent investigation and changes to detention practices affecting transgender prisoners. Accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers state that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived after prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison only two days later, and that witness statements were not taken; an opposition MP raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025.

Trans visitors who are detained are held in facilities organised by registered sex rather than gender identity, and Turkish prisons subject LGBTI+ detainees to arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto isolation and restricted healthcare. Some prisoners refuse hospital transfers for fear of other male inmates. No policy or staff training exists to identify LGBTI+ needs, complaints are ineffective and can provoke further violence, and transfers are frequent.

Event attendance carries its own exposure. Police have banned Pride events in Istanbul and other cities in most years since 2015, deploying tear gas and water cannons, and Amnesty International has reported restrictions and excessive force in 2015 and 2024. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through the year, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

If medication is needed during a stay, hormone replacement therapy is not covered by the government healthcare system, so trans visitors must obtain and pay for it privately. No trans-specific finding was documented for Hakkâri Province itself; any divergence from the national baseline there is a matter of security practice and social climate rather than provincial law.

An international human rights organisation reported on 29 October 2025 on a leaked omnibus draft, an eleventh judicial package, which would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise LGBT conduct deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' with up to 3 years' imprisonment, criminalise same-sex ceremonies with up to 4 years, raise the age for gender-affirming healthcare to 25 subject to mandatory infertility and multiple-evaluation conditions, and punish providers with fines and up to 7 years' imprisonment. Fifteen LGBT groups and the national medical association objected. A second international human rights organisation records that three draft packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025, which would criminalise expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible, and that they were ultimately not submitted to parliament. A February 2026 press report states that the government was considering a law criminalising publicly encouraging 'behavior contrary to biological sex' with one to three years' imprisonment, and that this was not included in the 2026 omnibus bill, the twelfth judicial package.

The general document requirement is the sharpest routine exposure. Foreigners must carry original photo ID at transit checkpoints in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 units of national currency and warnings of detention for non-compliance. In August 2025 police in the largest city stopped roughly 20 trans women while they were walking, shopping or sitting in cafés in a central district, held them at a police station on the main square and released them after 'General Information Gathering' background checks. Legal experts quoted by a national press agency argue those checks breach Article 5 of a regional human rights convention. One detainee's account records that nothing was fined, but names and details were taken, and that officers were applying a regime that had not been enacted.

Detention carries trans-specific harm. Visitors who are detained are held in facilities organised by registered sex rather than gender identity, and prisons subject LGBTI+ detainees to arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto isolation and restricted healthcare. No policy or staff training exists to identify LGBTI+ needs, complaints are ineffective and can provoke further violence, and transfers are frequent.

Medical continuity is a private cost. Hormone replacement therapy is not covered by the government healthcare system, so a trans visitor who needs medication during a stay must obtain and pay for it privately.

Protection machinery is thin. The country has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity, and no direct discrimination protection for gender identity. An interstate commission's 2025 report found legal protection insufficient and out of line with the regional legal framework, while noting official permissions granted to demonstrations promoting exclusion.

25984515B9026957888422.summary:
Isparta province stands under the national framework of Turkey. The sources behind this record contain no Isparta-specific statute, incident, police action or court case, so the assessment below sets out national law and national enforcement as they apply in Isparta alongside every other province.

A leaked omnibus draft known as the 11th Judicial Package, reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025, would amend Turkey's penal and civil codes to criminalise conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality at up to three years' imprisonment, and would criminalise same-sex ceremonies at up to four years. The same package would raise the age for gender-affirming healthcare to 25, condition it on infertility and repeated evaluations, and expose medical providers to fines and up to seven years in prison. Fifteen LGBT groups and the national medical association object to it.

Amnesty International's Türkiye country report for 2025/26 records that three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025. Had they entered force they would criminalise expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible. None was ultimately submitted to parliament. The absence of enacted statutes has not restrained enforcement: the report describes 2025 as an unprecedented assault on LGBTI people in legislative form.

Public assembly is the sharpest point of contact between a trans visitor and Turkish policing. In June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful force, and more than 90 people were arbitrarily detained. In November a court overturned an Istanbul governorate ban as disproportionate and unlawful, yet prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches were still running at the end of the year. In December 2025 an Izmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, finding that it had acted outside its stated purpose and shared obscene images incompatible with the law. Istanbul and Izmir stand here as examples of a pattern the sources record nationally rather than as isolated local events.

The baseline law is more permissive than the enforcement climate. 25984515B58862484177861.name: Kahramanmaraş
25984515B58862484177861.summary:
Kahramanmaraş province operates under Turkish national law, and the source inventory records no Kahramanmaraş-specific statute, incident, or court case concerning trans people. What a trans visitor faces in the province is the national framework as it functions elsewhere in Türkiye, which is documented as a structured and deliberate state campaign against LGBT people rather than residual prejudice.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked draft of Türkiye's 11th Judicial Package would amend the penal code to imprison for up to three years anyone who incites or promotes conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality, criminalise participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with penalties of up to four years, and restrict gender-affirming healthcare to people aged 25 and over under a requirement of permanent infertility, exposing providers to fines and up to seven years and patients to up to three years in prison. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association objected. The package is national legislation and would apply in Kahramanmaraş; it had not been enacted when reported.

Enforcement has run ahead of the statute. In Istanbul's Beyoğlu district on 31 July 2025, police detained trans women for identity checks, recording their names and filming videos of the stops. That incident falls outside Kahramanmaraş, but it evidences national practice: identity-document checks are used against trans people on the street and in commercial premises, with detentions for background-check purposes and no charge required. Türkiye also requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and detention warnings for non-compliance. For a visitor whose appearance does not match the passport gender marker, every checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which presentation and documents are compared.

Kaos GL's 2025 record, A Major Siege against LGBTI+ People, counts 313 liberty violations in one year, roughly two and a half times the previous year, mostly detentions, alongside 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, up from 51 and mostly linked to peaceful assembly, and six right-to-life violations of which three were recorded as hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected. Because the Turkish state keeps no hate-crime statistics, these figures are compiled from media and civil-society reporting. The same documentation describes hostility institutionalised under instructions to public institutions for an officially designated Year of the Family, hate speech from senior officials, and artistic events cancelled or banned. These describe national practice, not a provincial choice, and the source records no Kahramanmaraş-specific finding.

Two further national layers bear on a visitor's exposure. Prisoners are placed by registered sex, so trans people are held in gendered facilities that do not correspond to their gender, with arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement, and restricted healthcare documented by the Prison Insider country profile. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added gender reassignment as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording an 'other' option and required electronic reports, which risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

Karabük province stands under the national framework of the Republic of Turkey, which presents a structured and documented danger to trans visitors. As of 29 October 2025 a leaked omnibus measure known as the 11th Judicial Package was before the government. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of them classified by rights organisations as hate killings, and transgender people were disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, an asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate.

25984515B11362042972294.name: Kırıkkale
25984515B11362042972294.summary:
Kırıkkale is a conservative, military-industrial province with no province-specific statute, ordinance or incident series in the record. A trans visitor here stands under the national framework of Turkey, and that framework has tightened rather than loosened.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked draft omnibus reform, the 11th Judicial Package, would amend the penal code so that acting 'contrary to biological sex and general morality', or promoting such conduct, carries up to three years in prison through an amendment to article 225 on indecent acts. The same draft would restrict gender-affirming healthcare to people aged 25 and over under onerous eligibility criteria, and would expose both trans people and the professionals who treat them to criminal charges. Human Rights Watch described the package as one of the decade's most alarming rights rollbacks and urged its withdrawal. Whether it has since been enacted is unresolved in the sources.

Amnesty International's Report 2025/26 records three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people made public during 2025. They would have criminalised any expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and made legal gender recognition nearly impossible. The packages were not submitted to parliament. A February 2026 newspaper report separately describes a proposal under government consideration that would criminalise publicly encouraging 'behavior contrary to biological sex', with a sentence of one to three years.

There is no visa, entry or border rule specific to LGBTQ travellers. The visitor-facing document risk is general: foreigners must carry original photo ID at transit checkpoints in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and warnings of detention for non-compliance. That requirement intersects with street-level identity checks. In August 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women while they were walking, shopping or sitting in cafés in Beyoğlu, held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station and released them after 'General Information Gathering' background checks. Legal experts quoted by bianet argue those checks breach Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Nothing was fined, but names and details were recorded.

Event attendance carries its own exposure. In June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, and over 90 people were arbitrarily detained. In November a court overturned an Istanbul governorate ban as 'disproportionate' and 'unlawful', while prosecutions involving 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. In most years authorities have banned Pride events in Istanbul and other cities, and police have used tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against participants who defied the bans.

Detention conditions bear directly on a trans visitor who is held. Turkish prisons place detainees by registered sex rather than gender identity and subject LGBTI+ prisoners to arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto isolation and restricted healthcare, with no policy or staff training to identify LGBTI+ needs. On 1 December 2025 the transgender prisoner Poyraz was found dead in his cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara, and rights groups demanded an independent investigation and changes to detention practices affecting transgender prisoners. If hormone replacement therapy is needed during a stay, it is not covered by the government healthcare system, so trans visitors must obtain and pay for it privately.

HRW called it one of the most alarming rights rollbacks of the decade and urged withdrawal.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Turkey - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's national 'LGBT rights in Turkey' page is the framework every Turkish province, Kırıkkale included, stands under: homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, but Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Openly LGBTQ people are barred from serving in the military: the armed forces' health regulation defines homosexuality as a 'psychosexual' illness making members unfit for service, and conscripts who declare their homosexuality have to provide photographic proof. Same-sex marriage is not recognised; a 2012 constitutional-writing request to include it was rejected by both the AKP and the MHP. Authorities have banned Pride events in Istanbul and other cities in most years and police have used tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against participants who defied the bans; on 14 June 2019 the 7th Izmir Pride, the 3rd Antalya Pride and the 27th Istanbul Pride were banned by the cities' governors. The page also records a February 2026 newspaper report that the government was considering a law criminalising publicly encouraging 'behavior contrary to biological sex', with a sentence of one to three years in prison.

In November a court overturned a ban in Istanbul governorate as 'disproportionate' and 'unlawful', though prosecutions involving 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. In December 2025 an Izmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling it had engaged in activities outside its stated purpose and shared 'obscene' images incompatible with the law. 25984515B11362042972294.blindSummary:
Kırıkkale is a conservative, military-industrial province with no province-specific statute, ordinance or incident series in the record. A trans visitor here stands under the national framework of the country, and that framework has tightened rather than loosened.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked draft omnibus reform, a draft judicial reform package, would amend the penal code so that acting 'contrary to biological sex and general morality', or promoting such conduct, carries up to three years in prison through an amendment to article 225 on indecent acts. The same draft would restrict gender-affirming healthcare to people aged 25 and over under onerous eligibility criteria, and would expose both trans people and the professionals who treat them to criminal charges. Human Rights Watch described the package as one of the decade's most alarming rights rollbacks and urged its withdrawal. Whether it has since been enacted is unresolved in the sources.

Amnesty International's Report 2025/26 records three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people made public during 2025. They would have criminalised any expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and made legal gender recognition nearly impossible. The packages were not submitted to parliament. A February 2026 newspaper report separately describes a proposal under government consideration that would criminalise publicly encouraging 'behavior contrary to biological sex', with a sentence of one to three years.

There is no visa, entry or border rule specific to LGBTQ travellers. The visitor-facing document risk is general: foreigners must carry original photo ID at transit checkpoints in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 in the local currency and warnings of detention for non-compliance. That requirement intersects with street-level identity checks. In August 2025 police in the country's largest city stopped roughly 20 trans women while they were walking, shopping or sitting in cafés, held them at a central police station and released them after 'General Information Gathering' background checks. Legal experts quoted by a domestic human-rights publication argue those checks breach Article 5 of the regional human-rights convention. Nothing was fined, but names and details were recorded.

Event attendance carries its own exposure. In June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the largest city's LGBTI and trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, and over 90 people were arbitrarily detained. In November a court overturned a governorate ban as 'disproportionate' and 'unlawful', while prosecutions involving 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. In most years authorities have banned Pride events in the largest city and in other provinces, and police have used tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against participants who defied the bans.

Detention conditions bear directly on a trans visitor who is held. Prisons place detainees by registered sex rather than gender identity and subject LGBTI+ prisoners to arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto isolation and restricted healthcare, with no policy or staff training to identify LGBTI+ needs. On 1 December 2025 the transgender prisoner Poyraz was found dead in his cell at a women's prison near the capital, and rights groups demanded an independent investigation and changes to detention practices affecting transgender prisoners. If hormone replacement therapy is needed during a stay, it is not covered by the government healthcare system, so trans visitors must obtain and pay for it privately.

The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 records 313 violations over the year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, dominated by 299 detention decisions, 256 taken on the record and 43 off it, alongside systematic attacks on the privacy of LGBT people. Turkish Minute's coverage of the same report counts six deaths linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. Hostility of this scale is best read as state policy rather than residual prejudice.

Policing asymmetry is documented at the level of individual cases. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy by a 17-year-old; the attacker was released while the victim herself was referred for arrest, which activists describe as evidence of a state hate policy.

The circumstances of Poyraz's death are disputed by officials and contested by witnesses. Accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers state that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived after prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison only two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. An opposition MP raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025.

Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through the year, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia. The Erdoğan government has repeatedly justified restrictive measures as protecting 'the family' and 'public morals', and the draft legislative package sits within a broader authoritarian drift.

The European Commission's 2025 report found legal protection against discrimination insufficient and out of line with the EU acquis, while noting official permissions granted to demonstrations promoting exclusion.

25984515B10334298996421.name: Kırklareli
25984515B10334298996421.summary:
Kırklareli Province has no province-specific statute, ordinance or incident series in the record. The position of a trans visitor in Kırklareli is set entirely by the national framework that governs every province of Turkey, and no Kırklareli-specific deviation from that framework is documented.

Turkey has no visa, entry or border rule specific to LGBTQ travellers; the documented exposure points lie inside the country rather than at the frontier. The visitor-facing document risk is general: foreigners must carry original photo ID at transit checkpoints in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and warnings of detention for non-compliance. That requirement intersects with street-level identity checks. In August 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women while they were walking, shopping or sitting in cafés in Beyoğlu, held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station and released them after background checks recorded as 'General Information Gathering'. Legal experts quoted by bianet argue those checks breach Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One detainee's account captures the practical position: nothing was fined, but names and details were recorded.

The statutory baseline is mixed on its face and hostile in operation. Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence in Turkey since the Ottoman Empire adopted a new penal code in 1858, and trans people have been able to change their legal gender, following surgery, since 1988. Criminalisation by statute had not been enacted when Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025, but a leaked draft omnibus reform then before the government, the 11th Judicial Package, would amend the penal code so that acting 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' or promoting it carries up to three years in prison through an amendment to article 225 on 'indecent acts'. The same package would restrict gender-affirming healthcare to people aged 25 and over under onerous eligibility rules and allow criminal charges against trans people and the professionals who treat them, justified as protecting 'the family' and 'public morals'. Human Rights Watch called it one of the most alarming rights rollbacks of the decade and urged withdrawal. Whether the package has since passed is unresolved in the sources.

Protection machinery is thin. Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity, and no direct discrimination protection for gender identity; the European Commission's 2025 report found legal protection insufficient and out of line with the EU acquis. LGBTQ people are barred from serving openly in the military, and same-sex relationships receive no legal recognition in the form of marriage, civil union or adoption.

Hostility is recorded at the scale of aggregate data. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 documents 313 violations over the year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, dominated by 299 detention decisions, 256 taken on the record and 43 off it, alongside systematic attacks on the privacy of LGBT people. Turkish Minute's coverage of the same report counts six deaths linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. The Erdoğan government has repeatedly used 'the family' and 'public morals' framing to legitimise stigmatisation, and the draft reform sits within a broader authoritarian drift.

Policing asymmetry is documented through individual cases. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy by a 17-year-old; the attacker was released while the victim herself was referred for arrest, which activists describe as evidence of a state hate policy. On 1 December 2025 the transgender prisoner Poyraz was found dead in his cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara, and rights groups demanded an independent investigation and changes to detention practices affecting transgender prisoners. Accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers state that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived after prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison only two days later, and that witness statements were not taken; an opposition MP raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025.

Detainees are held in facilities organised by registered sex rather than gender identity, and Turkish prisons subject LGBTI+ detainees to arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto isolation and restricted healthcare. Some prisoners refuse hospital transfers for fear of other male inmates. No policy or staff training exists to identify LGBTI+ needs, complaints are ineffective and can provoke further violence, and transfers are frequent. Event attendance carries its own exposure: authorities have banned Pride events in Istanbul and most other cities in most years since 2015, using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions, and monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through the year, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia. In ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking Turkey placed 47th out of 49 assessed countries.

If medication is needed during a stay, hormone replacement therapy is not covered by the government healthcare system, so trans visitors must obtain and pay for it privately.

25984515B83185192232063.name: Kırşehir
25984515B83185192232063.summary:
Kırşehir stands under Turkish state law. National legislation sets what a trans or LGBTQ visitor to the province can expect to face, and the sources document no province-specific statute, municipal ordinance, police practice or incident arising from Kırşehir itself. Turkey has no visa, entry or border rule specific to LGBTQ travellers, so the exposure points lie inside the country rather than at the frontier.

The baseline is a decriminalisation that does not amount to a rights framework. Homosexuality has not been an offence in Turkey since the Ottoman Empire adopted a new penal code in 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender, following surgery, since 1988. Against that baseline, Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity and no direct legal protection for gender identity; LGBTQ people are barred from serving openly in the military; and same-sex relationships receive no legal recognition, whether marriage, civil union or adoption. In ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking Turkey placed 47th of 49 assessed countries.

The most serious statutory threat is a leaked draft omnibus reform, the 11th Judicial Package, described by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025. The package would amend article 225 of the penal code on indecent acts so that acting "contrary to biological sex and general morality", or promoting such conduct, carries up to three years in prison. It would restrict gender-affirming healthcare to people aged 25 and over under onerous eligibility rules, and open criminal charges against trans people and the professionals who treat them. The stated justifications are the protection of "the family" and "public morals". Human Rights Watch called it one of the most alarming human-rights rollbacks of the decade and urged the government to withdraw it. Whether the package has since been enacted is unresolved in the sources.

Kaos GL's LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025, presented on 24 February 2026 as "The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People", finds that hostility toward LGBTI+ people became explicit state policy over the year. Targeting of LGBTI+ people as "deviant" or "a threat" by the president and senior officials raised the motivation of officials and impunity for attacks by third parties, and the new Family Ministry became the implementing ministry. One LGBTI+ rights organisation was closed, platforms and broadcasters were penalised or withdrew material, and artistic events were cancelled. The report records 313 violations of the right to liberty in 2025, about two and a half times the previous year's total and mostly detentions; 89 torture and ill-treatment violations against 51 the previous year, largely during assemblies; and six violations of the right to life, three of them hate-motivated killings, with trans people most affected.

State hostility reaches street-level identity checks. In 2025 about 20 trans women in Istanbul's Beyoğlu district were rounded up for identity checks and taken to a police station, where their names were recorded and videos were filmed and no official reason was given. One detainee's account, reported alongside the detentions, describes officers already applying a regime that had not been enacted: nothing was fined, but names and personal details were logged. Legal experts quoted by bianet argue that such background checks breach Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. For a trans visitor, this intersects with the general requirement that foreigners carry original photo ID at transit checkpoints in holiday destinations, where non-compliance carries fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and warnings of detention.

Detainees are held in facilities organised by registered sex rather than gender identity, and Turkish prisons subject LGBTI+ detainees to arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto isolation and restricted healthcare. Some prisoners refuse hospital transfers for fear of other male inmates. No policy or staff training exists to identify LGBTI+ needs, complaints procedures are ineffective and can provoke further violence, and transfers between facilities are frequent.

Policing asymmetry is documented at the level of individual cases. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy by a 17-year-old; the attacker was released while the victim herself was referred for arrest, which activists describe as evidence of a state hate policy. On 1 December 2025 the transgender prisoner Poyraz was found dead in his cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara, and rights groups demanded an independent investigation and changes to detention practices affecting transgender prisoners. Accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers state that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived after prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison only two days later, and that witness statements were not taken; an opposition MP raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025.

Attendance at Pride events carries its own exposure. Authorities have banned Pride events in Istanbul and other cities in most years since 2015, using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against participants. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through the year, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

If medication is needed during a stay, hormone replacement therapy is not covered by the government healthcare system, so trans visitors must obtain and pay for it privately.

25984515B86381770870747.name: Kocaeli
25984515B86381770870747.summary:
Kocaeli is a province of Turkey and stands under the national framework set out for the country. No statute, court decision, enforcement incident or provincial documentation specific to Kocaeli appears in the sources, so the assessment below describes the national regime a visitor to Kocaeli is subject to.

A leaked omnibus draft, the 11th Judicial Package, reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025, would amend the penal code to criminalise conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality with up to three years' prison, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years. The same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care, including surgery, from 18 to 25, with mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals. Healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison, and trans people receiving care deemed illegal up to three years. Human Rights Watch warns the package would force treatment underground and expose people to arrest and pretrial detention. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft.

Hostility toward LGBTI+ people has become explicit state policy, according to Kaos GL's 2025 monitoring review. Public institutions received "Year of the Family" instructions, an LGBTI+ association was closed with criminal cases opened against 11 of its members, and artistic events were cancelled or banned.

Kaos GL recorded roughly 313 violations in 2025, about two and a half times the previous year's total, alongside 299 detention decisions. Six violations of the right to life were recorded, three of them hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected group. Torture and ill-treatment violations rose to 89 from 51 the prior year, and freedom-of-expression violations rose from 216 to 540.

25984515B47044460443496.name: Kütahya
25984515B47044460443496.summary:
Kütahya province stands under the national framework of the Republic of Turkey, and no Kütahya-specific evidence of trans-specific enforcement, violence or legal practice was located in the source inventory. What a trans visitor to Kütahya faces is the national regime as it is applied across the country's interior provinces, where a conservative social environment compounds a legal order that offers no comprehensive protection on grounds of gender identity.

The baseline is mixed on its face. Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence in Turkey since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988. There is nonetheless no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, openly LGBTQ people are barred from serving in the military, and same-sex marriage, civil unions, domestic partnerships and joint adoption are not recognised.

Legislative pressure is documented and specific. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked omnibus judicial package would amend the penal code so that acts "contrary to biological sex and general morality" carry up to 3 years' imprisonment, with same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies carrying up to 4 years. The same package would amend the civil code to raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25, require infertility and evaluation at a government-approved hospital, and imprison care providers for up to 7 years and trans patients for up to 3 years.

Three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025 and were ultimately not submitted to parliament. Amnesty International's 2025 reporting states that they would have criminalised the expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and made legal gender recognition nearly impossible. The distance between drafting and enactment has not stopped coercive action: in June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful force, more than 90 people were arbitrarily detained, and prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches were still continuing at the end of the year.

Courts and police have moved on the same reasoning without new legislation. In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling that it had shared "obscene" images incompatible with "society's moral values" that could encourage or promote LGBTI identities. Pride parades have been banned by local authorities since 2015. Reporting from 2026 shows the direction of travel remains unsettled: a judicial reform package passed that year dropped provisions discriminating against LGBTQ people and made symbolic same-sex weddings possible, though these carry no legal marital status; earlier in 2026 the government considered but did not include legislation criminalising public advocacy of "behaviour contrary to biological sex"; and in September 2026 police detained dozens in raids on gay bars and the homes of LGBTQ+ activists under a "Decade of Family and Population" crackdown.

25984515B80837210717778.name: Malatya
25984515B80837210717778.summary:
Malatya province falls entirely under Turkey's national legal framework. No statute, police directive, court decision or incident specific to Malatya appears in the sources consulted, so the position of a trans visitor in the province is the position the central authorities have constructed nationally.

There is no visa, entry or border rule specific to LGBTQ travellers; the documented exposure points lie inside the country rather than at the frontier. The visitor-facing document risk is general: foreigners must carry original photo ID at transit checkpoints in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and warnings of detention for non-compliance. In practice that requirement meets street-level identity checks. In August 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women while they were walking, shopping or sitting in cafés in Beyoğlu, held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station and released them after "General Information Gathering" background checks. Legal experts quoted by bianet argue those checks breach Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Nothing was fined, but names and details were recorded.

Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence in Turkey since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988. No comprehensive law prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and there is no direct discrimination protection for gender identity. Openly LGBTQ people are barred from serving in the military. Same-sex marriage, civil unions, domestic partnerships and joint adoption are not recognised.

The most consequential visitor-facing item is the leaked omnibus "11th Judicial Package", reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025. It would amend penal-code article 225 so that acts "contrary to biological sex and general morality" carry up to three years' imprisonment and same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies up to four years; amend civil-code article 40 ("Changing Sex") to raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25, add a mandatory infertility condition and require evaluation by a government-approved hospital; and imprison care providers for up to seven years and trans patients for up to three years. Amnesty International records that three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025, which would criminalise expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible, but were ultimately not submitted to parliament. Human Rights Watch states criminalisation by statute had not been enacted as of that date, framed as protecting "the family" and "public morals".

The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 records 313 violations over the year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, dominated by 299 detention decisions, 256 taken on the record and 43 off it, alongside systematic attacks on the privacy of LGBT people. Coverage of the same report counts six deaths linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. Hostility at this scale is recorded as state policy rather than residual prejudice.

Policing asymmetry is documented case by case. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy by a 17-year-old; the attacker was released while the victim herself was referred for arrest, which activists describe as evidence of a state hate policy. On 1 December 2025 the transgender prisoner Poyraz was found dead in his cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara. Accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers state that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived after prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison only two days later, and that witness statements were not taken; an opposition MP raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025.

Trans visitors who are detained are held in facilities organised by registered sex rather than gender identity. Turkish prisons subject LGBTI+ detainees to arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto isolation and restricted healthcare; some prisoners refuse hospital transfers for fear of other male inmates. No policy or staff training exists to identify LGBTI+ needs, complaints are ineffective and can provoke further violence, and transfers are frequent.

Public visibility carries its own exposure. Pride parades have been banned by local authorities since 2015, with Istanbul's 2015–2018 parades banned and dispersed. In June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, and over 90 people were arbitrarily detained; prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through the year, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia. In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling that it had shared "obscene" images incompatible with "society's moral values" that could "encourage or promote" LGBTI identities. In September 2026 police detained dozens in raids on gay bar and the homes of LGBTQ+ activists under a "Decade of Family and Population" crackdown.

Protection machinery is thin. The European Commission's 2025 report found legal protection insufficient and out of line with the EU acquis, while noting official permissions granted to demonstrations promoting exclusion. If medication is needed during a stay, hormone replacement therapy is not covered by the government healthcare system, so trans visitors must obtain and pay for it privately.
