25984515B80837210717778.blindSummary:
The state/province falls entirely under the country's national legal framework. No statute, police directive, court decision or incident specific to this state/province appears in the sources consulted, so the position of a trans visitor is the position the central authorities have constructed nationally.

There is no visa, entry or border rule specific to LGBTQ travellers; the documented exposure points lie inside the country rather than at the frontier. The visitor-facing document risk is general: foreigners must carry original photo ID at transit checkpoints in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 units of local currency and warnings of detention for non-compliance. In practice that requirement meets street-level identity checks. In August 2025 police in the largest city stopped roughly 20 trans women while they were walking, shopping or sitting in cafés, held them at a police station and released them after "General Information Gathering" background checks. Legal experts quoted by a domestic rights outlet argue those checks breach Article 5 of an international human rights convention. Nothing was fined, but names and details were recorded.

Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence in the country since the historic penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988. No comprehensive law prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and there is no direct discrimination protection for gender identity. Openly LGBTQ people are barred from serving in the military. Same-sex marriage, civil unions, domestic partnerships and joint adoption are not recognised.

The most consequential visitor-facing item is a leaked omnibus judicial package, reported by an international human rights organisation on 29 October 2025. It would amend the penal code so that acts "contrary to biological sex and general morality" carry up to three years' imprisonment and same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies up to four years; amend the civil code provision on changing sex to raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25, add a mandatory infertility condition and require evaluation by a government-approved hospital; and imprison care providers for up to seven years and trans patients for up to three years. A separate international organisation records that three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025, which would criminalise expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible, but were ultimately not submitted to parliament. The first organisation states criminalisation by statute had not been enacted as of that date, framed as protecting "the family" and "public morals".

A national LGBTI+ human rights report for 2025 records 313 violations over the year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, dominated by 299 detention decisions, 256 taken on the record and 43 off it, alongside systematic attacks on the privacy of LGBT people. Coverage of the same report counts six deaths linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. Hostility at this scale is recorded as state policy rather than residual prejudice.

Policing asymmetry is documented case by case. In August 2024 a trans woman was knifed in a neighbourhood of the largest city by a 17-year-old; the attacker was released while the victim herself was referred for arrest, which activists describe as evidence of a national hate policy. On 1 December 2025 a transgender prisoner was found dead in a cell at a women's prison. Accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers state that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived after prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison only two days later, and that witness statements were not taken; an opposition MP raised the case in the national legislature on 12 December 2025.

Trans visitors who are detained are held in facilities organised by registered sex rather than gender identity. Prisons subject LGBTI+ detainees to arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto isolation and restricted healthcare; some prisoners refuse hospital transfers for fear of other male inmates. No policy or staff training exists to identify LGBTI+ needs, complaints are ineffective and can provoke further violence, and transfers are frequent.

Public visibility carries its own exposure. Pride parades have been banned by local authorities since 2015, with the largest city's 2015–2018 parades banned and dispersed. In June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against that city's LGBTI and Trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, and over 90 people were arbitrarily detained; prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. Monitoring of that city's 2025 Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through the year, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia. In December 2025 a court in another city ordered the dissolution of a young LGBTI+ association, ruling that it had shared "obscene" images incompatible with "society's moral values" that could "encourage or promote" LGBTI identities. In September 2026 police detained dozens in raids on gay bars and the homes of LGBTQ+ activists under a family-and-population campaign.

Protection machinery is thin. A regional body's 2025 report found legal protection insufficient and out of line with the regional legal framework, while noting official permissions granted to demonstrations promoting exclusion. If medication is needed during a stay, hormone replacement therapy is not covered by the government healthcare system, so trans visitors must obtain and pay for it privately.

25984515B19932594956901.name: Manisa
25984515B19932594956901.summary:
Manisa falls under Turkey's national legal and security framework. The sources behind this record contain no statute, incident, police action or court decision specific to Manisa, so a trans visitor's exposure in this province is the national position. The nearest named provincial action is in İzmir, where a court ordered the Young LGBTI+ Association dissolved in December 2025.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked omnibus 11th Judicial Package would amend penal-code article 225 so that acts deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' carry up to three years' imprisonment, and same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies up to four years. The same package would amend civil-code article 40 ('Changing Sex') to raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25, add mandatory infertility conditions and government-approved hospital evaluation, and imprison care providers for up to seven years and trans patients for up to three years. The package is national legislation and would apply in Manisa on enactment.

The baseline law is more permissive than the drafting. Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence in Turkey since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and trans people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988. No comprehensive law prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised; marriage eligibility turns on the gender recorded in the civil registry, so a trans person who has legally changed the registered gender may marry a partner of the opposite registered gender. Openly LGBTQ people are barred from the military.

Enforcement against assembly and expression has been sustained. Since 2015 Turkish authorities have banned pride events in most years, using tear gas, water cannon and mass detentions against those who defied the bans. Amnesty International's Report 2025/26 records that in June 2025 the authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and trans pride marches, that police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful force, that more than 90 people were arbitrarily detained, that three activists were remanded in prison on 29 June and released on 8 August pending trial, and that prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches were continuing at year's end. In ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow ranking Turkey placed 47th of 49.

Care access tightened during 2025. In June 2025 Turkey's medicines agency banned prescription and supply of hormones for gender-affirming procedures for people under 21, despite existing law permitting access from 18. Three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025, criminalising expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and making legal gender recognition nearly impossible, but none were ultimately submitted to parliament.

Two further developments are recorded for 2026. A February 2026 press report described legislation considering criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex' with one to three years in prison; that measure was not included in the 2026 omnibus, the 12th judicial package. In September 2026 coordinated raids under the 'My Family is Safe' crackdown involved 162 suspects, 9 associations and 13 businesses.

25984515B30119007363221.summary:
No measure, incident or institution specific to Mardin concerning transgender visitors is recorded in this edition's sources. Mardin province stands under the national framework of Türkiye, and no local authority in the province is documented adding bans, checkpoints or enforcement programmes of its own. What a trans visitor to Mardin faces is that national framework as it is applied by police, prosecutors and hospitals across the country.

The most consequential legal threat is pending rather than settled. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked omnibus, the 11th Judicial Package, would amend penal-code article 225 so that acts described as contrary to biological sex and general morality carry up to three years' imprisonment, and same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies up to four years. The same package would amend civil-code article 40, Changing Sex, to raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from eighteen to twenty-five, impose mandatory infertility conditions and evaluation at a government-approved hospital, and imprison care providers for up to seven years and trans patients for up to three. The package is national in scope. Authorities have repeatedly acted as though prohibitions of this kind were already in force while the legislation remained unpassed.

The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in one year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, alongside 299 detention decisions — 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record — and systematic intrusions on the privacy of LGBT people. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly twenty trans women in streets, shops and cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for General Information Gathering (GBT) background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women stopped stated that police took no fines but documented her anyway. Foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints must produce original identity documents, creating a direct outing risk where appearance does not match the passport gender marker. Türkiye separately requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention for non-compliance.

Public assembly is prohibited rather than merely discouraged. Amnesty International's Report 2025/26 records that in June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and trans pride marches, that police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful force, that more than ninety people were arbitrarily detained, that three activists were remanded in prison on 29 June and released on 8 August pending trial, and that prosecutions of ninety-two people for participating in pride marches were still running at year's end. Pride events have been banned in most years since 2015, with tear gas, water cannon and mass detentions used against those who defied the bans, and monitoring by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week.

Violence against trans people is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, a detention asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Transition-related care is tightening at administrative level. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added gender reassignment as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the other option on such reports and required electronic reports to be issued, risking profiling of trans patients in official records. In June 2025 the health ministry's medicines agency banned prescription and supply of hormones for gender-affirming procedures for people under twenty-one, despite existing law permitting access from eighteen. 25984515B33535290178113.name: Mersin
25984515B33535290178113.summary:
Mersin province records no local statute, police programme or administrative ban directed at transgender visitors in this edition's sources. What a trans visitor to Mersin faces is the national framework of Türkiye, applied here without any provincial counterweight: no local authority in Mersin is documented adding protection, and none is documented adding restriction of its own.

Under Türkiye's national law the position on legal gender is unchanged since 1988. A person may change registered gender only after sex-reassignment surgery, a medical examination and court permission. There is no comprehensive statute prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no remedy exists against the denial of housing, employment or public service on those grounds. Same-sex marriage, civil unions and adoption are unavailable. Because Turkish marriage law determines eligibility by the gender recorded in a person's civil registry rather than by trans status, an individual who has legally changed registered gender may marry a partner of the opposite registered gender.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked omnibus "11th Judicial Package" would amend penal-code article 225 so that acts "contrary to biological sex and general morality" carry up to 3 years' imprisonment, with same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies carrying up to 4 years. The same package would amend civil-code article 40, "Changing Sex", raising the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25 and requiring infertility and evaluation at a government-approved hospital. Care providers would face imprisonment of up to 7 years and trans patients up to 3 years. The document is national in scope and contains no Mersin-specific content.

A subsequent judicial reform package passed in 2026, with provisions discriminating against LGBTQ people removed from the bill. The enacted measure nonetheless makes symbolic same-sex weddings possible, ceremonies that carry no legal marital status.

The Erdoğan government and religious conservative opposition parties regularly use discriminatory speech amounting to hate speech against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender communities on the pretext of promoting family values, which Human Rights Watch states puts LGBT people at great risk. Istanbul Pride was banned for the tenth consecutive year, and many cities across the country impose similar bans on LGBT assembly. The same national ban pattern applies to visible LGBT assembly in Mersin-area cities.

25984515B57226385500606.blindSummary:

An international human rights organisation reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked omnibus measure, a judicial package, would amend penal-code article 225 so that acts "contrary to biological sex and general morality" carry up to three years' imprisonment and same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies up to four years. The same draft would amend a civil-code article governing legal sex change, raising the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25 and adding mandatory infertility evaluation and approval by an approved hospital, while imprisoning care providers for up to seven years and trans patients for up to three.

The draft applied to the whole country and contained no provision specific to the state/province. Reporting on it did not establish whether the measure had been enacted or remained pending, and its status is treated here as unresolved. Rights organisations have separately noted that authorities have in practice behaved as though prohibitions of this kind were already operative.

Entry and movement bring document exposure. The country requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 in local currency for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. Police stops for background checks are a routine instrument: in 2025 officers in the largest city held roughly twenty trans women stopped in streets, shops and cafés for checks before release, with no fines imposed but records taken. Foreign visitors stopped at such checkpoints must produce original identity documents, so any stop is an occasion on which a passport gender marker can be compared against presentation.

Discriminatory enforcement operates nationwide rather than regionally. A World Report covering 2023 records that the head of government made anti-LGBT hate speech a core part of its election campaign, that the ninth successive ban on Pride week events in the largest city in June was accompanied by police arrests of those who attempted to assemble, that local authorities around the country have increasingly cancelled concerts by artists openly supportive of LGBT rights, and that the national broadcast regulator justified fines on digital platforms for LGBT-related content as violations of "societal and cultural values." Authorities also ban LGBT group events regularly and arbitrarily. These patterns govern what any visible LGBT assembly in the state/province's resort towns can expect.

There is no comprehensive law in the country prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. Same-sex marriage, civil unions and adoption are unavailable. Because marriage law determines eligibility by the gender recorded in a person's civil registry rather than by trans status, a person who has legally changed registered gender may marry a partner of the opposite registered gender.

Violence against trans people in the country is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 a trans woman was knifed in a neighbourhood of the largest city by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest.

Transition-related care is tightening. A health ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a provincial health directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required electronic reports to be issued, a change that risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to care.

25984515B88478081264350.name: Muş
25984515B88478081264350.summary:
Muş province stands under the national legal framework of Türkiye. No Muş-specific ordinance, arrest, incident or court decision is documented for the province, so what a trans visitor faces in Muş is what the national sources record for the country as a whole.

The statutory baseline is permissive in narrow terms and hostile in every operative one. Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and legal gender recognition has been available since 1988, but no comprehensive law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and same-sex marriage is not recognised. A visitor's marriage, partnership or transition status therefore carries no protective weight in dealings with Turkish authorities.

Criminalisation is pending rather than enacted, and that distinction has not slowed enforcement. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked draft judicial-reform package, the 11th Judicial Reform, would pave the way for criminal charges against LGBT people, described as one of the most alarming rights rollbacks in decades; activists held a press conference in Istanbul on 28 October 2025 against the provisions targeting LGBT people. Amnesty International's Report 2025/26 records three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people made public during 2025, an unprecedented assault that would criminalise expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible, none of which was submitted to parliament. Press reports in early 2026 stated that the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of "behaviour contrary to biological sex"; that provision was ultimately not included in that year's judicial reform package.

Street-level enforcement is already running ahead of statute. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue that such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that police took no fines but documented them anyway, and that the new law had not yet been passed even as it was being applied to them. Foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints are required to produce original identity documents, creating a direct outing risk for anyone whose appearance does not match their passport gender marker.

Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. For a trans visitor, every checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Pride events are flashpoints and have been since 2015, when local authorities began repeatedly banning and forcibly dispersing Pride marches; police used water cannon and tear gas on the 2015 and 2016 Istanbul parades. In June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, over 90 people were arbitrarily detained, and prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in a single year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, with 299 detention decisions, 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record.

Detention carries documented danger for trans people. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025, and the case, raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025, confirmed that Turkey places trans prisoners according to their registered sex, a trans man having been held in a women's prison. Custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

25984515B18723924091225.name: Nevşehir
25984515B18723924091225.summary:
Nevşehir province operates under Turkey's national legal framework. No province-specific ordinance, incident or court decision has been recorded for Nevşehir, and the sources supporting this record are national in scope; the assessment below is therefore the national picture as it would be encountered in a tourist district of Cappadocia, where a tourism economy sits alongside regional conservatism.

The legal baseline is mixed but thin. Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988. No comprehensive law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, so a trans visitor who is refused service, turned away or stopped has no statutory complaint to make. Same-sex marriage is not recognised, so marriage or partnership status carries no weight in Turkey.

Criminalisation by statute has not been enacted, but the exposure is live. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked draft judicial-reform package, the 11th Judicial Reform, would pave the way for criminal charges against LGBT people, described as one of the most alarming rights rollbacks in decades; activists held a press conference in Istanbul on 28 October 2025 against the provisions. Amnesty International's Türkiye country report (Report 2025/26) records that three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025, which would criminalise expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible; these were ultimately not submitted to parliament. Press reports in early 2026 said the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex', but that provision was not included in the year's judicial reform package. Whether any package has since passed is unresolved in the sources.

Entry and document rules are general rather than LGBTQ-specific: Turkey has no visa, entry or border rule targeting LGBT travellers, but foreigners must carry original photo ID at transit checkpoints in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and warnings of detention for non-compliance. For a trans visitor this intersects with street-level identity checks: in August 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women while walking, shopping or sitting in cafés in Beyoğlu, held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station and released them after 'General Information Gathering' background checks. Legal experts quoted by bianet argue those checks breach Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One detainee's account: nothing was fined, but names and details were recorded, and officers were applying a regime that had not been enacted.

Hostility is documented at scale. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 records 313 violations over the year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, dominated by 299 detention decisions — 256 on the record and 43 off it — alongside systematic attacks on LGBT privacy. Turkish Minute's coverage of the same report counts six deaths linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. Amnesty documents that in June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful force, over 90 people were arbitrarily detained, and prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through the year, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia. Since 2015 local authorities have repeatedly banned and forcibly dispersed Pride marches, with police using water cannon and tear gas on the 2015 and 2016 Istanbul parades.

Policing asymmetry is documented at the level of individual cases. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy by a 17-year-old; the attacker was released while the victim herself was referred for arrest, which activists describe as evidence of a state hate policy. On 1 December 2025 the transgender prisoner Poyraz was found dead in his cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara, and rights groups demanded an independent investigation and changes to detention practices affecting transgender prisoners. Accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers state that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived after prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison only two days later, and that witness statements were not taken; an opposition MP raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025. In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling that it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values' that could 'encourage or promote' LGBTI identities.

Detention conditions carry specific risk for trans visitors. Those detained are held in facilities organised by registered sex rather than gender identity, and Turkish prisons subject LGBTI+ detainees to arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto isolation and restricted healthcare. Some prisoners refuse hospital transfers for fear of other male inmates. No policy or staff training exists to identify LGBTI+ needs, complaints are ineffective and can provoke further violence, and transfers are frequent.

Openly LGBTI people are barred from military service: conscripts who declare their homosexuality are classed under a definition of homosexuality as a 'psychosexual illness', must provide photographic proof, and risk their 'unfit report' being made public. This bears on trans visitors only if they are subject to Turkish conscription, which foreign tourists are not.

Protection machinery is thin. The European Commission's 2025 report found legal protection insufficient and out of line with the EU acquis, while noting official permissions granted to demonstrations promoting exclusion. If medication is needed during a stay, hormone replacement therapy is not covered by the government healthcare system, so trans visitors must obtain and pay for it privately.

25984515B59741408878569.name: Niğde
25984515B59741408878569.summary:
Niğde Province stands under the national framework of Turkey, which presents a structured and documented danger to trans visitors. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in a single year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, alongside 299 detention decisions, 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record, and systematic attacks on the privacy of LGBT people.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked draft judicial-reform package, the 11th Judicial Reform, would pave the way for criminal charges against LGBT people and described it as one of the most alarming rights rollbacks in decades. Activists held a press conference in Istanbul on 28 October 2025 against the provisions targeting LGBT people.

Amnesty International's Türkiye country report (Report 2025/26) records that three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025, an assault that would criminalise expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible. The packages were ultimately not submitted to parliament. A February 2026 press report of draft legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex' with one to three years in prison was not included in the 12th judicial package, whose passage removed provisions discriminating against LGBTQ people and made symbolic same-sex weddings possible.

There is no comprehensive law in Turkey prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Same-sex marriage, civil unions, domestic partnerships and joint adoption are not recognised, so a visitor travelling with a spouse or partner has no legal status for that relationship on arrival. Homosexuality has been decriminalised since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and legal gender recognition has been available since 1988, meaning a trans visitor's documents may already carry a marker matching their presentation, or may not.

LGBTQ people are barred from serving openly in the Turkish military: the armed forces' health regulation defines homosexuality as a 'psychosexual illness', conscripts who declare it must provide photographic proof, and those receiving an 'unfit report' may face later discrimination in public life. Conscription does not apply to foreign visitors, but the classification signals the official medical framing a trans person may encounter.

Pride events have been banned in Istanbul and other cities in most years since 2015, with police using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions. Amnesty International records that in June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, and over 90 people were arbitrarily detained; prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association after ruling it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values'. A court case to close Lambda Istanbul was overruled by the Constitutional Court.

ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking placed Turkey 47th out of 49 countries, a position consistent with the enforcement pattern above rather than an isolated year.

25984515B15602000155844.name: Ordu
25984515B15602000155844.summary:
Turkey presents a structured and documented danger to trans visitors, driven by hostility that has become formal state policy rather than residual prejudice. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in a single year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, with 299 detention decisions — 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record — together with systematic attacks on the privacy of LGBT people. This national framework applies identically in Ordu Province, and no local authority in Ordu is recorded adding bans or screening of its own.

No province-specific measure, enforcement programme or institution concerning trans visitors is documented for Ordu in this edition's sources. The source covering Ordu Province itself yielded no usable finding, so what governs a trans visitor to Ordu is the national framework of Turkey alone.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked draft judicial-reform package, the 11th Judicial Reform, would pave the way for criminal charges against LGBT people, describing it as one of the most alarming rights rollbacks in decades; activists held a press conference in Istanbul on 28 October 2025 against the provisions targeting LGBT people. Amnesty International's Türkiye country report (Report 2025/26) records that three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025, an unprecedented assault that would criminalise expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible, but that they were ultimately not submitted to parliament. The Erdoğan government frames its position as protecting "the family" and "public morals", language Human Rights Watch identifies as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma of LGBT people; the pending status of the drafts has not prevented authorities from acting as though the prohibitions were already in force.

Street-level enforcement illustrates that point. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" (GBT) background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue that such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that the police took no fines but documented them anyway, adding that the new law had not yet been passed even as enforcement was already being applied to them. Foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints are required to produce original identity documents, which creates a direct outing risk for anyone whose appearance does not match their passport gender marker.

The passport-carrying rule for foreigners compounds these risks. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. For a trans visitor, any checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Homosexuality has been legal in Turkey since the Ottoman penal code of 1958, and that legality has not translated into safety. Violence against trans people is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric: six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest. Activists treat that detention asymmetry as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Pride events remain flashpoints. In June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, and over 90 people were arbitrarily detained. Prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end, and in December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association after ruling it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values'. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

Trans prisoners are held by registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches demanded an independent investigation, and accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case, raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025, confirmed that Turkey places trans prisoners according to their registered sex — a trans man had been held in a women's prison.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. There is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

The underlying pattern is longstanding. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. That report predates the legal changes made after 2018 and stands as historical evidence of the regime's depth rather than as a statement of current law.

25984515B63638727958144.name: Osmaniye
25984515B63638727958144.summary:
Osmaniye province has no trans-specific ordinance, enforcement programme or local institution in the sourced material. A trans visitor to Osmaniye stands under the national framework of Türkiye, which applies here without local modification.

The baseline national position is mixed. Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and legal gender change has been available since 1988. No comprehensive statute prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and same-sex marriage is not recognised.

Legislative pressure has been sustained. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked draft judicial-reform package, the 11th Judicial Reform, would pave the way to criminal charges against LGBT people, describing it as among the most alarming rights rollbacks in decades; LGBT activists held a press conference in Istanbul on 28 October 2025 against the provisions targeting LGBT people. Amnesty International recorded three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people made public during 2025, an unprecedented assault that would criminalise any expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible to obtain. None of the three was submitted to parliament. In 2026 the draft package's LGBTI-discriminatory provisions were removed, and a February 2026 press report described a proposed law criminalising publicly encouraging "behaviour contrary to biological sex" with one to three years in prison; that measure was not included in the 12th judicial package.

Enforcement has not waited for legislation. Since 2015 authorities have banned Pride events in Istanbul and other cities in most years, using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against participants who defied the bans. In June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans Pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, and more than 90 people were arbitrarily detained; prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches were still continuing at the end of the year.

Association and expression are also constrained. In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling that it had shared "obscene" images on social media incompatible with "society's moral values" and that these could "encourage or promote" LGBTI identities.

Openly LGBTQ people are barred from military service. Conscripts who declare their homosexuality are classified under a definition of homosexuality as a "psychosexual illness", must provide photographic proof, and risk their "unfit report" leaking publicly.

Transition-related care is restricted. In June 2025 the Turkish Medicines and Medical Devices Agency, part of the Ministry of Health, banned the prescription and supply of hormones for gender-affirming procedures for people under 21.

In December an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling it had shared 'obscene' images on social media that were incompatible with 'society's moral values' and could 'encourage or promote' LGBTI identities. The report also records three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people made public during 2025 - an unprecedented assault that would criminalize any expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible to obtain - though they were ultimately not submitted to parliament. In June 2025 the Turkish Medicines and Medical Devices Agency (Ministry of Health) banned the prescription and supply of hormones for gender-affirming procedures for people under 21.

The province has no trans-specific ordinance, enforcement programme or local institution in the sourced material. A trans visitor to the province stands under the national framework of the country, which applies here without local modification.

The baseline national position is mixed. Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since a historic-era penal code of 1858, and legal gender change has been available since 1988. No comprehensive statute prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and same-sex marriage is not recognised.

Legislative pressure has been sustained. An international rights organisation reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked draft judicial-reform package, the 11th Judicial Reform, would pave the way to criminal charges against LGBT people, describing it as among the most alarming rights rollbacks in decades; LGBT activists held a press conference in the largest city on 28 October 2025 against the provisions targeting LGBT people. A second international rights organisation recorded three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people made public during 2025, an unprecedented assault that would criminalise any expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible to obtain. Since 2015 authorities have banned Pride events in the largest city and other urban centres in most years, using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against participants who defied the bans. Association and expression are also constrained. In December 2025 a court in a coastal city ordered the dissolution of a young LGBTI+ association, ruling that it had shared "obscene" images on social media incompatible with "society's moral values" and that these could "encourage or promote" LGBTI identities.

Openly LGBTQ people are barred from military service. Conscripts who declare their homosexuality are classified under a definition of homosexuality as a "psychosexual illness", must provide photographic proof, and risk their "unfit report" leaking publicly.

Transition-related care is restricted. In June 2025 the national medicines regulator, part of the health ministry, banned the prescription and supply of hormones for gender-affirming procedures for people under 21.

The national backdrop a trans visitor carries into Osmaniye includes documented street-level and custodial risk. Kaos GL's LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in one year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, with 299 detention decisions, of which 43 were taken off the record.

Checkpoint interaction is the principal outing vector. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for formal warnings of detention for non-compliance. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped around 20 trans women in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" background checks before release; legal experts cited in the reporting argue such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One detained woman stated that no fines were issued but the women were documented anyway.

Violence remains lethal and the state response asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest.

Custody conditions add a further layer. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025, and Turkey places trans prisoners according to their registered sex, with a trans man held in a women's prison. Prison Insider's country profile, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners.

25984515B47778459062669.name: Rize
25984515B47778459062669.summary:
No Rize-specific measure, enforcement programme or institution concerning transgender visitors is documented in the sourced material. A trans visitor to Rize Province stands under Turkey's national framework in full: the province applies Turkish law and Turkish policing practice, and the findings below are the national picture that a visitor crosses into.

That framework has moved toward criminalisation without the prohibitions yet being on the books. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked 11th Judicial Reform package would pave the way for criminal charges against LGBT people, calling it one of the most alarming rights rollbacks in decades; activists held a press conference in Istanbul on 28 October 2025 against its provisions. Amnesty International's Türkiye country report for 2025/26 records three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people made public during 2025, an assault that would criminalise any expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible to obtain. None of the three was submitted to parliament.

The legislative position shifted again in 2026. The discriminatory LGBTI provisions of the draft judicial package were removed, and a February 2026 press report described a separate proposed law criminalising publicly encouraging "behaviour contrary to biological sex" with one to three years in prison; that proposal was not included in the 2026 omnibus bill, the 12th judicial package. A visitor therefore faces a regime in which prohibitions are proposed, dropped and re-proposed within months, while street-level enforcement continues on the strength of administrative and discretionary powers rather than a new statute.

The baseline law is comparatively permissive on its face. Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence in Turkey since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988. There is, however, no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and same-sex marriage is not recognised. The absence of a discrimination statute removes the ordinary route by which a visitor or resident would challenge differential treatment by police, hotels, clinics or transport operators.

Openly LGBTQ people are barred from military service. Conscripts who declare their homosexuality are classified under a definition of homosexuality as a "psychosexual illness", must provide photographic proof of their claims, and risk their "unfit report" leaking publicly. This affects Turkish citizens rather than visitors, but it evidences the official classification of queer identity as pathology that shapes how state institutions treat gender variance generally.

Pride events remain the most visible flashpoint. Authorities have banned Pride events in Istanbul and other cities in most years since 2015, using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against participants who defied the bans. In June 2025 the authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, and more than 90 people were arbitrarily detained; prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches were still running at year's end. In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling that it had shared "obscene" images on social media incompatible with "society's moral values" and that it could "encourage or promote" LGBTI identities.

Transition-related care is tightening. In June 2025 the Turkish Medicines and Medical Devices Agency, under the Ministry of Health, banned the prescription and supply of hormones for gender-affirming procedures for people under 21. A visitor who depends on uninterrupted hormone supply should treat Turkish pharmacies as an unreliable source for anyone under that threshold, and should carry an adequate personal supply with documentation.

Checkpoint practice is the sharpest document risk. Under the national framework, Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women in 2025 in Beyoğlu streets, shops and cafés and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" (GBT) background checks before release; legal experts cited argue such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights, and one detainee recorded that no fine was issued but she was documented anyway, with the unpassed law already being applied to her. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. Any checkpoint interaction is thus an occasion on which a passport is compared against presentation, and a mismatch is a direct outing risk.

The broader record indicates that hostility is a documented state posture rather than residual prejudice. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in a single year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, with 299 detention decisions — 256 through formal channels and 43 off the record. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, with transgender people disproportionately affected. Monitoring by the Truth Justice Memory Center of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

25984515B47778459062669.tangentialFactors:
The Erdoğan government has repeatedly framed its position as protecting "the family" and "public morals", language Human Rights Watch identifies as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma of LGBT people. Rize, on Turkey's Black Sea coast, sits in a socially conservative region where that framing is unlikely to be countered by local counter-messaging, but the sourced material records no Rize-specific mobilisation, protest or official statement in either direction.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim herself was referred for arrest, a detention asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate.

The historical depth of the pattern predates the current legislative cycle. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. It predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as evidence of the regime's depth rather than as a statement of current law.

Documented deterioration across the period is measurable rather than impressionistic: three draft packages in 2025, a hormonal prescribing ban in June 2025, blanket Pride bans with mass detentions in June 2025, an association dissolved in December 2025, and the Sincan Women's Prison death of the transgender prisoner Poyraz on 1 December 2025, which opposition MP Sevda Karaca raised in parliament on 12 December 2025. The counter-current — removal of the discriminatory provisions in 2026 and the omission of the February 2026 proposal from the omnibus bill — shows legislative outcomes remaining unsettled while administrative measures hold.
25984515B47778459062669.blindTangential:
The pending nature of the draft packages is itself a live risk factor: three separate packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025 without being tabled, and the February 2026 proposal on public encouragement of conduct "contrary to biological sex" circulated as a press report rather than an enacted measure. Enforcement rhetoric and administrative action have repeatedly run ahead of statute.

Openly LGBTQ people are barred from national military service. Conscripts who declare homosexuality are assessed under a definition treating it as a "psychosexual illness", must supply photographic proof, and risk an "unfit report" leaking publicly, which is a documented outing channel relevant to any trans or gender-nonconforming man of conscription age.

The documented pattern of detention is asymmetric in its handling of victims. Rights reporting cited within the national framework describes a trans woman knifed in one of the largest cities in August 2024 whose attacker was released while she herself was referred for arrest, and six deaths linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified by rights organisations as hate killings.

The 2025 national report cited in the national framework counted 313 violations in one year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, alongside 299 detention decisions, of which 43 were taken off the record.

Legal gender recognition has been available to Turkish citizens since 1988, but Amnesty International's 2025/26 reporting notes that the draft packages would have made it nearly impossible to obtain, and the current route is under active political pressure.

Residents face the June 2025 Ministry of Health agency ban on prescription and supply of hormones for gender-affirming procedures for people under 21, alongside a Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025 — following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports — barring hospitals from recording the "other" option and requiring e-reports to be issued, which risks profiling trans patients in official records.

Trans prisoners are held by registered sex in gendered facilities: a transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025, and the case confirmed in parliament that a trans man had been held in a women's prison. Rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation; accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered two days later, and that witness statements were not taken.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners, no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, a binary and heteronormative administration, transfers that frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints processes that are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Openly LGBTQ Turkish citizens are barred from military service under a classification of homosexuality as a "psychosexual illness", with photographic proof required and an "unfit report" at risk of public leakage. Same-sex marriage is not recognised, and there is no comprehensive anti-discrimination statute covering sexual orientation or gender identity.

25984515B30494634933389.name: Sakarya
25984515B30494634933389.summary:
Sakarya is a province in Turkey's Marmara region and stands under the national framework: no Sakarya-specific statute, enforcement programme or local ban concerning transgender visitors is documented in the sources assembled here, and nationwide provisions govern the province's residents and visitors alike.

Turkey has no visa, entry or border rule specific to LGBTQ travellers, so the documented exposure points lie inside the country rather than at the frontier. The visitor-facing document risk is general: foreigners must carry original photo ID at transit checkpoints in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and warnings of detention for non-compliance. That requirement intersects with identity checks on the street. In August 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women while they were walking, shopping or sitting in cafés in Beyoğlu, held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station and released them after 'General Information Gathering' background checks. Legal experts quoted by bianet argue those checks breach Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The statutory baseline is permissive on its face. Homosexuality has been decriminalised since 1858 and sex-reassignment surgery has been legal since 1988, but legal gender recognition still requires a court's permission under Civil Code Article 40, with the applicant at least 18, unmarried and holding a medical report from a state-designated hospital. No province-specific rule applies to Sakarya; these provisions govern nationwide.

The most consequential pending measure is the leaked 11th Judicial Package, a 66-page draft amending the Turkish Penal Code, the Civil Code and six other laws, leaked to Turkish media in mid-October 2025 and analysed by Amnesty International in a November 2025 factsheet. Human Rights Watch's release of 29 October 2025 sets out its terms: conduct deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' would carry up to three years' imprisonment, and participation in same-sex ceremonies up to four years. It is the third set of proposed legal amendments targeting LGBTI+ rights during 2025, the earlier two having stalled in Parliament. Whether the package has since passed is unresolved in the sources.

For trans visitors and residents the draft's care and recognition provisions carry the sharpest practical consequences. It would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25 while adding mandatory infertility and multi-evaluation hurdles, imprison providers for up to seven years and patients for up to three, and would raise the minimum age for legal gender recognition procedures from 18 to 25 with further conditions attached. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association object. What a trans visitor to Siirt faces is the country-wide regime, applied by national ministries, provincial governors and police stations that operate the same powers throughout the country.

That framework is structured and documented rather than residual prejudice. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in a single year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, with 299 detention decisions, 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of them classified by rights organisations as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. Foreign visitors stopped at checkpoints must produce original identity documents, and Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention, so any police interaction is an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked 11th Judicial Package would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality, carrying up to three years' imprisonment, with participation in same-sex ceremonies punishable by up to four years. The same package would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from eighteen to twenty-five, attach mandatory infertility and multiple-evaluation conditions to transition care, and imprison providers by up to seven years and patients by up to three years. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association object to the measure. A parallel proposal to criminalise publicly encouraging behaviour contrary to biological sex, with a one-to-three-year sentence, was ultimately not included in the 12th judicial package.

Enforcement already runs ahead of legislation. Amnesty International's Türkiye country report (Report 2025/26) records that in June 2025 blanket bans were issued against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans pride marches, that police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful force, that more than 90 people were arbitrarily detained, and that prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches were still continuing at year's end. In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling that it had shared obscene images incompatible with society's moral values. The same report records three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people made public during 2025, which would criminalise LGBTI identity expression and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible; none was ultimately submitted to parliament.

Historically, homosexuality was decriminalised in 1858 under the Ottoman penal code and legal gender change has been possible in Turkey since 1988, but same-sex marriage is not recognised and LGBT people are barred from serving openly in the military. 25984515B33997294820892.name: Sivas
25984515B33997294820892.summary:
No Sivas-specific statute, enforcement programme, incident or institution concerning transgender visitors is documented in the sources assembled for this edition. The province of Sivas stands under the national framework of Türkiye, and no local authority in Sivas is recorded adding prohibitions of its own.

That national framework includes a draft legislative threat at the level of penalty. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that the leaked 11th Judicial Package would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality, carrying up to three years' imprisonment, with participation in same-sex marriage ceremonies or celebrations carrying up to four years. The same package would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from eighteen to twenty-five, attach mandatory infertility conditions and repeated evaluation hurdles, and imprison providers of such care for up to seven years and patients for up to three. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association objected.

The baseline recorded for Türkiye is that homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and that trans people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, subject to sex reassignment surgery, medical examination and court permission. There is no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Openly LGBTQ people are barred from Turkish military service. A health regulation defines homosexuality as a 'psychosexual illness', conscripts who declare it must provide photographic proof, and the resulting 'unfit report' can leak and fuel later discrimination in public life. Anyone subject to conscription or its documentation carries that record forward.

Same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not recognised. When the 12th judicial reform package passed in 2026 the anti-LGBTQ provisions were removed from the bill, leaving only symbolic same-sex weddings possible; the outcome of the 11th Judicial Package as of the sources' reporting is separate and unresolved.

Enforcement climate is set by national-level decisions that provincial authorities in Sivas apply as elsewhere. Amnesty International's Report 2025/26 records that in June 2025 the authorities issued blanket bans against the LGBTI and Trans Pride marches in Istanbul, that police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force and that over 90 people were arbitrarily detained. Three activists were remanded in prison on 29 June 2025 under Law No. 2911 and released on 8 August pending trial, and prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches were still running at year's end.

In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling that it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values' that could 'encourage or promote' LGBTI identities. Since 2015 authorities have banned Pride events in Istanbul and other cities in most years, with police using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against participants who defied the bans.

Two further national indicators bear on expectations. Press reports in early 2026 stated that the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex'. Türkiye placed 47th of 49 countries in ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking.

25984515B20532508270601.name: Tokat
25984515B20532508270601.summary:
Tokat province has no trans-specific statute, enforcement pattern or incident documentation of its own. The national framework of Türkiye governs in Tokat as in every other province, and the absence of local records is recorded as absence of documented divergence rather than as evidence of local permissiveness.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked draft 11th Judicial Package would amend penal-code article 225 to criminalise conduct "contrary to biological sex and general morality" with up to three years' imprisonment, raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care to 25, and expose trans people, care providers, civil-society organisations and journalists to charges. The same package would penalise same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years' imprisonment and advances under a "Year of the Family" framing.

Legal gender recognition has been available in Türkiye since 1988, conditional on surgery and court approval. The country has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and same-sex marriage, civil unions and adoption are unavailable.

Marriage eligibility is determined by the gender recorded in the civil registry rather than by trans status, so a person who has legally changed registered gender may marry a partner of the opposite registered gender. When a 12th judicial reform package passed in 2026, provisions discriminating against LGBTQ people were removed from the bill, leaving same-sex weddings possible only as symbolic ceremonies with no legal marital status.

Visible LGBT assembly is policed nationwide. Authorities have banned Pride events in Istanbul and other cities in most years since 2015, with police using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against those who attempt to assemble. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025, covering 2024, records that the government and religious-conservative opposition parties regularly use discriminatory speech amounting to hate speech against LGBT communities on the pretext of promoting family values, and that Istanbul Pride was banned for the tenth consecutive year while many cities imposed similar bans. Any visible LGBT assembly in Tokat province would be policed under this same framework.

25984515B1589724669162.name: Trabzon
25984515B1589724669162.summary:
Trabzon province generates no trans-specific statute, enforcement pattern or incident documentation in the available record. What is recorded for Trabzon is the absence of any documented divergence from the national position, which is not a finding of safety: the Turkish national framework extends to Trabzon in full, and a visitor to the province should expect the same legal exposure, document checks and detention practice documented elsewhere in Turkey.

Turkey has no currently enacted criminal statute directed at trans identity or same-sex conduct, but a leaked omnibus reform draft reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025 would change that position substantially. The draft, identified as the 11th Judicial Package, would amend the penal code to punish conduct "contrary to biological sex" with up to three years' imprisonment, and would punish participation in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony with up to four years. It would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care including surgery from 18 to 25, require permanent infertility assessment and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals, and expose both healthcare professionals who provide such care and their patients to criminal prosecution, with pretrial detention possible. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft, and Human Rights Watch called for its withdrawal. The measure had not been passed when reported.

Kaos GL's Human Rights Report 2025, titled "The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People", finds that hostility toward LGBTI+ people has become explicit state policy, with instructions issued to public institutions under the "Year of the Family" banner. The report documents 6 right-to-life violations including 3 hate-motivated killings, with transgender people the most affected group. It records 89 torture and ill-treatment violations, a striking increase on the prior year, and 313 right-to-liberty violations — roughly two and a half times the previous year's total — comprising 299 detention decisions. Freedom-of-expression violations rose from 216 to 540, and 40 right-to-association violations included the first closure of an LGBTI+ association in many years.

25984515B1589724669162.tangentialFactors:
The national pattern is one of enforcement running ahead of legislation. Human Rights Watch's framing of the draft package as a threat while it remains unpassed reflects a documented reality in which authorities act on prohibitions before they are enacted: in 2025 Istanbul police stopped around 20 trans women in the Beyoğlu district, in streets, shops and cafés, and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" background checks before release, with legal experts cited arguing those checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One detainee reported that no fines were issued but that the women were documented anyway.

Document presentation is the principal checkpoint risk for a foreign visitor. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention for non-compliance. Any checkpoint interaction is therefore an occasion on which passport details can be compared against presentation, and Trabzon's position on a major domestic tourism and pilgrimage route does not insulate a visitor from that exposure.

Lethal violence is documented at national level. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified by rights organisations as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, an asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Prison placement follows registered sex. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025, in a case raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025 and confirming that Turkey places trans prisoners according to their registered sex, with a trans man held in a women's prison. Pride events remain flashpoints: monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

Transition-related care is tightening through administrative channels as well as legislation. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording an "other" option and required electronic reports to be issued, risking the profiling of trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care. The same restriction applies at health facilities in Trabzon.
