For residents, the Kaos GL findings describe an operating environment rather than a set of isolated incidents. Instructions issued to public institutions under the "Year of the Family" banner converted hostility into administrative practice, and the report's counts — 6 right-to-life violations with 3 hate-motivated killings, 89 torture and ill-treatment violations, 313 liberty violations with 299 detention decisions, expression violations rising from 216 to 540, and 40 association violations — indicate the scale of routine contact with state machinery. The first closure of an LGBTI+ association in many years signals that formal organising carries a new class of risk.

Detained LGBT people in Turkey face segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. No policy or staff training exists to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints mechanisms are ineffective and can attract further violence.

The death of the transgender prisoner Poyraz at Sincan Women's Prison on 1 December 2025 drew a coordinated response from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanding an independent investigation. Accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken.

The Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025 affects residents directly by removing the "other" option from hospital records and requiring electronic medical-board reports that name gender reassignment, with online framing of the change contested as an "LGBT opening".

25984515B95251525471141.name: Uşak
25984515B95251525471141.summary:
Uşak is a province of Turkey, and trans visitors to Uşak stand under the national framework documented across the country. No province-specific trans-related source exists for Uşak, so the absence of a documented local ban or local incident is not evidence of permissiveness; the national pattern is the operative expectation.

Turkey's danger to trans visitors is structured and documented rather than residual prejudice. Kaos GL's 2025 review, "The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People," finds hostility toward LGBTI+ people converted into explicit state policy, with "Year of the Family" instructions issued to public institutions, the closure of an LGBTI+ rights organisation for the first time in years, restrictions on expression and artistic freedom, and events cancelled or banned.

The same monitoring counted 313 liberty violations in 2025, roughly two and a half times the previous year's total, alongside 299 detention decisions, 89 torture or ill-treatment violations (up from 51 the prior year), 6 right-to-life violations including 3 hate-motivated killings in which trans people were the most affected, private-life violations rising from 16 to 67 including obstruction of trans people's hormone therapy, and 61 travel bans.

A leaked omnibus draft, the "11th Judicial Package," reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025, would amend the Turkish penal code to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" with up to three years in prison, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years. The draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care including surgery from 18 to 25, conditioned on mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals; healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison and patients up to three years, with possible pretrial detention. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft, and Human Rights Watch warns it would force treatment underground and leave LGBT people in constant fear of arrest.

Street-level enforcement already operates as though such prohibitions were in force. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" (GBT) background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that police took no fines but documented them anyway, adding that the new law had not yet been passed even as enforcement was already being applied to them.

Foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints are required to produce original identity documents, creating a direct outing risk for anyone whose appearance does not match their passport gender marker. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. Any checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest. Activists treat that detention asymmetry as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Pride events remain flashpoints. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia and entrenching discrimination against LGBT people and their allies.

Trans prisoners are held by registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation; accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case, raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025, confirmed that Turkey places trans prisoners according to their registered sex, a trans man having been held in a women's prison, and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. There is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

The underlying pattern is longstanding. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. That report predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as historical evidence of the regime's depth rather than as a statement of current law.

25984515B28392380114016.name: Van
25984515B28392380114016.summary:
Van is a province of Turkey and stands under the national framework: the Turkish penal code, migration rules, health regulations and prison administration apply here in full. No trans-specific statute, enforcement pattern or incident documentation exists for Van itself, and that absence is recorded as absence of documented divergence rather than as local permissiveness.

A leaked omnibus draft identified by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025 as the "11th Judicial Package" would amend the Turkish penal code to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" with up to three years in prison, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years. The same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care, including surgery, from 18 to 25, conditioned on mandatory permanent infertility assessment and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals. Healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison, and patients up to three years, with pretrial detention possible. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft; Human Rights Watch warns it would force treatment underground and leave LGBT people in constant fear of arrest. The measure had not been enacted as reported, but authorities have applied its prohibitions as though already in force.

Kaos GL's 2025 national monitoring, "The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People", records hostility toward LGBTI+ people as explicit state policy: "Year of the Family" instructions issued to public institutions, the closure of an LGBTI+ rights organisation for the first time in years, restrictions on expression and artistic freedom, and events cancelled or banned. The same review documents six right-to-life violations including three hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected; 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, up from 51 the previous year; 313 liberty violations, roughly two and a half times the prior year, carrying 299 detention decisions; private-life violations rising from 16 to 67, among them obstruction of trans people's hormone therapy; and 61 travel bans.

Two parent-layer rules bear directly on a visitor in Van. Foreign nationals are required to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints country-wide, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention for non-compliance, so any checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents are compared against presentation. Police stops for background checks have been used against trans women in public spaces in Istanbul in 2025, with detainees documented even where no fine was imposed.

Care and custody conditions are tightening at the same time. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025 barred hospitals from recording the "other" option on reports and required electronic reports to be issued, a change that risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care. Trans prisoners are placed according to registered sex: a trans man had been held in a women's prison, and the death of a transgender prisoner at Sincan Women's Prison on 1 December 2025 prompted demands from rights groups for an independent investigation, with accounts of delayed medical response, prosecutors entering two days later, and witnesses not interviewed. The case was raised in parliament on 12 December 2025.

25984515B28392380114016.tangentialFactors:
Van's status as a province with no locally documented incidents makes it an illustration of the national pattern rather than an exception to it. The provincial record carries the country-level regime unchanged: the draft criminalising package, the monitoring totals, the identification checkpoints and the prison placement rules all reach Van through the same statutory and administrative channels that apply in Istanbul or Ankara.

The relationship between drafting and enforcement is asymmetric. The 11th Judicial Package remained a draft as of its October 2025 reporting, yet trans women stopped by police in 2025 stated that officers applied the new law's logic before any statute had been passed. 25984515B19658467647683.name: Yozgat
25984515B19658467647683.summary:
Yozgat province has no trans-specific statute, enforcement series or incident pattern documented in the sources. That absence records an absence of evidence of divergence from Turkey's national position rather than local safety: the national rules set out below reach Yozgat unchanged.

Turkey has no visa, entry or border rule specific to LGBTQ travellers, and the documented exposure points lie inside the country rather than at the frontier. The visitor-facing document risk is general: foreigners must carry original photo ID at transit checkpoints in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and warnings of detention for non-compliance. That requirement intersects with identity checks on the street. In August 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women while they were walking, shopping or sitting in cafés in Beyoğlu, held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station and released them after 'General Information Gathering' background checks. Legal experts quoted by bianet argue those checks breach Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One detainee's account captures the practical position: nothing was fined, but names and details were recorded, and officers were already applying a regime that had not been enacted.

Criminalisation by statute had not been enacted when Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025, but a leaked omnibus draft then before the government, the 11th Judicial Package, would amend the Turkish penal code to criminalise conduct deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' with up to three years in prison, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years. The same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care including surgery from 18 to 25, behind mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals. Healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison, patients up to three years, with pretrial detention possible. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft, and Human Rights Watch warns it would force treatment underground and leave LGBT people in constant fear of arrest. Whether the package has since passed is unresolved in the sources.

Hostility toward LGBTI+ people in Turkey has hardened into explicit state policy. Kaos GL's 2025 review, 'The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People', records 'Year of the Family' instructions issued to public institutions and, for the first time in years, the closure of an LGBTI+ rights organisation, with expression and artistic freedom restricted and events cancelled or banned. The review counts 313 liberty violations over the year, roughly two and a half times the previous total, alongside 299 detention decisions; 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, up from 51 the prior year; 6 right-to-life violations including 3 hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected; private-life violations rising from 16 to 67, including obstruction of trans people's hormone therapy; and 61 travel bans. Turkish Minute's coverage of the same report counts six deaths linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified as hate killings.

Trans visitors who are detained are held in facilities organised by registered sex rather than gender identity, and Turkish prisons subject LGBTI+ detainees to arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto isolation and restricted healthcare. Some prisoners refuse hospital transfers for fear of other male inmates. No policy or staff training exists to identify LGBTI+ needs, complaints are ineffective and can provoke further violence, and transfers are frequent.

Policing asymmetry is documented at the level of individual cases. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy by a 17-year-old; the attacker was released while the victim herself was referred for arrest, which activists describe as evidence of a state hate policy. Comparable asymmetry recurs in custody: on 1 December 2025 the transgender prisoner Poyraz was found dead in his cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara, and rights groups demanded an independent investigation and changes to detention practices affecting transgender prisoners. Accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers state that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived after prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison only two days later, and that witness statements were not taken; an opposition MP raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025.

Event attendance carries its own exposure. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through the year, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

Protection machinery is thin. Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity, and no direct discrimination protection for gender identity. The European Commission's 2025 report found legal protection insufficient and out of line with the EU acquis, while noting official permissions granted to demonstrations promoting exclusion. If medication is needed during a stay, hormone replacement therapy is not covered by the government healthcare system, so trans visitors must obtain and pay for it privately.

25984515B19658467647683.blindSummary:
The state/province has no trans-specific statute, enforcement series or incident pattern documented in the sources. That absence records an absence of evidence of divergence from the country's national position rather than local safety: the national rules set out below reach the state/province unchanged.

The country has no visa, entry or border rule specific to LGBTQ travellers, and the documented exposure points lie inside the country rather than at the frontier. The visitor-facing document risk is general: foreigners must carry original photo ID at transit checkpoints in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 units of the national currency and warnings of detention for non-compliance. That requirement intersects with identity checks on the street. In August 2025 police in the country's largest city stopped roughly 20 trans women while they were walking, shopping or sitting in cafés in a central district, held them at a police station in the same area and released them after 'General Information Gathering' background checks. Legal experts quoted by a domestic rights outlet argue those checks breach Article 5 of a regional human-rights convention. One detainee's account captures the practical position: nothing was fined, but names and details were recorded, and officers were already applying a regime that had not been enacted.

Criminalisation by statute had not been enacted when an international human-rights organisation reported on 29 October 2025, but a leaked omnibus draft then before the government, an 11th judicial package, would amend the penal code to criminalise conduct deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' with up to three years in prison, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years. The same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care including surgery from 18 to 25, behind mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at state-approved hospitals. Healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison, patients up to three years, with pretrial detention possible. Fifteen LGBT groups and a national medical association opposed the draft, and the international human-rights organisation warns it would force treatment underground and leave LGBT people in constant fear of arrest. Whether the package has since passed is unresolved in the sources.

Hostility toward LGBTI+ people in the country has hardened into explicit state policy. The national monitor's 2025 review, 'The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People', records 'Year of the Family' instructions issued to public institutions and, for the first time in years, the closure of an LGBTI+ rights organisation, with expression and artistic freedom restricted and events cancelled or banned. The review counts 313 liberty violations over the year, roughly two and a half times the previous total, alongside 299 detention decisions; 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, up from 51 the prior year; 6 right-to-life violations including 3 hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected; private-life violations rising from 16 to 67, including obstruction of trans people's hormone therapy; and 61 travel bans. Domestic press coverage of the same report counts six deaths linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified as hate killings.

Trans visitors who are detained are held in facilities organised by registered sex rather than gender identity, and prisons subject LGBTI+ detainees to arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto isolation and restricted healthcare. Some prisoners refuse hospital transfers for fear of other inmates of a different registered sex. No policy or staff training exists to identify LGBTI+ needs, complaints are ineffective and can provoke further violence, and transfers are frequent.

Policing asymmetry is documented at the level of individual cases. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in a district of the largest city by a 17-year-old; the attacker was released while the victim herself was referred for arrest, which activists describe as evidence of a national hate policy. Comparable asymmetry recurs in custody: on 1 December 2025 the transgender prisoner Poyraz was found dead in his cell at a women's prison near the capital, and rights groups demanded an independent investigation and changes to detention practices affecting transgender prisoners. Accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers state that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived after prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison only two days later, and that witness statements were not taken; an opposition MP raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025.

Event attendance carries its own exposure. Monitoring of the 2025 trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week in the largest city found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through the year, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

Protection machinery is thin. The country has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity, and no direct discrimination protection for gender identity. A regional rights body's 2025 report found legal protection insufficient and out of line with the applicable regional standards, while noting official permissions granted to demonstrations promoting exclusion. 25984515B35512619552530.name: Şanlıurfa
25984515B35512619552530.summary:
Şanlıurfa is a province of Turkey and stands under the Turkish national framework. The source inventory assembled for this province contains no trans-specific material for Şanlıurfa itself: no statute, enforcement action, facility or recorded incident. A trans visitor to the province should therefore expect the national regime described here.

Turkey has no visa, entry or border rule specific to LGBTQ travellers; the documented exposure points lie inside the country. Foreigners must carry original photo ID at transit checkpoints in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and warnings of detention for non-compliance. That requirement intersects with street-level identity checks: in August 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women while they were walking, shopping or sitting in cafés in Beyoğlu, held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station and released them after background checks recorded under 'General Information Gathering'. Legal experts quoted by bianet argue those checks breach Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Nothing was fined in that episode, but names and details were recorded.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 on a leaked omnibus draft, the 11th Judicial Package, that would amend the Turkish penal code to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" with up to three years in prison, and to criminalise participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years. The same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care, surgery included, from 18 to 25, behind mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals; healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison and patients up to three years, with pretrial detention possible. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft, and Human Rights Watch warned it would force treatment underground and leave LGBT people in constant fear of arrest. As of that reporting the draft had not been enacted; whether it has since passed is unresolved in the sources.

Criminalisation by statute therefore had not been enacted when the package was reported, but it sits inside a broader official framing: the Erdoğan government has repeatedly used protection of "the family" and "public morals" to legitimise stigmatisation. Kaos GL's 2025 review, "The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People", finds that hostility toward LGBTI+ people became explicit state policy, with 'Year of the Family' instructions issued to public institutions and the closure of an LGBTI+ rights organisation for the first time in years, expression and artistic freedom restricted and events cancelled or banned.

The same Kaos GL monitoring records 313 liberty violations over the year, about two and a half times the previous year, comprising 299 detention decisions (256 taken on the record, 43 off it); 89 torture and ill-treatment violations, up from 51 the prior year; private-life violations rising from 16 to 67, including obstruction of trans people's hormone therapy; 61 travel bans; and six right-to-life violations, of which three were hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected. Turkish Minute's coverage of the report counts six deaths linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected.

Hostility of this scale is documented at the level of individual cases. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy by a 17-year-old; the attacker was released while the victim herself was referred for arrest, which activists describe as evidence of a state hate policy. On 1 December 2025 the transgender prisoner Poyraz was found dead in his cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara, and rights groups demanded an independent investigation and changes to detention practices affecting transgender prisoners. Accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers state that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived after prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison only two days later, and that witness statements were not taken; an opposition MP raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025.

Detained trans visitors are held in facilities organised by registered sex rather than gender identity, and Turkish prisons subject LGBTI+ detainees to arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto isolation and restricted healthcare. Some prisoners refuse hospital transfers for fear of other male inmates. No policy or staff training exists to identify LGBTI+ needs, complaints are ineffective and can provoke further violence, and transfers are frequent.

Event attendance carries its own exposure: monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through the year, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

Protection machinery is thin. Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity, and no direct discrimination protection for gender identity; the European Commission's 2025 report found legal protection insufficient and out of line with the EU acquis, while noting official permissions granted to demonstrations promoting exclusion. Hormone replacement therapy is not covered by the government healthcare system, so trans visitors must obtain and pay for it privately during a stay.

19177384B49506124846693.name: Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires
19177384B49506124846693.summary:
Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires stands under Argentina's national framework, which remains among the most permissive in the world for legal gender recognition. Law 26.743 passed the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and the Senate by 55 votes to one abstention on 9 May 2012, was promulgated on 24 May 2012, and allows a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval. The United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region, and Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action rather than by repeal of the statute. Emergency decree DNU 62/2025, published in February 2025, modified Article 11 of the Gender Identity Law to prohibit gender-affirming interventions for people under 18, which Reuters reported as a ban on surgery and hormone therapy for adolescents. Decree DNU 61/2025, published the same month, re-regulates the housing of transgender people deprived of liberty and invites the provinces and the City of Buenos Aires to adhere; it prohibits people who have legally changed gender from being held in women's prisons when they are detained for sexual offences or violence against women. FALGBT and legal experts call both decrees illegal and unconstitutional and are seeking judicial intervention. The outcome of that litigation is not recorded in the sources available here.

The national administration has eliminated the Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry, closed the National Institute Against Discrimination, Xenophobia and Racism (INADI), dismissed trans people hired under the Trans Labor Quota Law, which reserved at least 1% of public-sector jobs, and has moved to restrict the 12-year-old Gender Identity Law.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people reached a documented high in 2025. Argentina recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity during the year, a 62% rise on the previous year and a ten-year record of one crime every 38 hours. Agencia Presentes data published on 19 March 2026 shows that 32% of the crimes occurred in police stations and penal facilities, that security-force violence multiplied from 17 cases in 2024 to 64 in 2025, and that trans women and travestis concentrated 62.5% of victims, 142 cases. Most perpetrators were security personnel and unknown assailants.

Buenos Aires-based activists told the Washington Blade on 10 April 2025 that police violence against trans and travesti sex workers has become more common since the current government took office, with harassment and hate speech rising nationally. Activists from organisations named for Diana Sacayán, stabbed to death in 2015, and for Lohana Berkins said the government's policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence and described the situation as chaotic and desperate.

On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán. The Court rejected attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance, which an appeal court had removed in 2020, with the result that the gender-motivated-crime aggravator is not applied in the case as it now stands.

An Outright International country overview updated on 12 March 2026 records negative assessments on same-sex relations, on gender recognition and on organisation registration, indicating deterioration, even though anti-discrimination protections exist through national and provincial laws.

14911670B90188072957077.name: Santa Catarina
14911670B90188072957077.summary:
Santa Catarina stands under the national framework of Brazil. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2013 under National Council of Justice Resolution 175/2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change, and joint and second-parent adoption were confirmed by the Supreme Federal Tribunal in RE 846.102 (2015). A visitor's entry, documents and family status are therefore handled on the same footing as any other traveller's.

Discrimination and hate crimes on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds are punishable as equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989 following the Supreme Federal Tribunal's 2019 ruling in ADO 26. Foreign same-sex spouses and partners are treated identically in visa and residence categories, including the spousal residence permit, and foreign same-sex marriages are recognised for immigration purposes.

Santa Catarina's own constitution carries an anti-discrimination clause dating to 2002 that lists sexual orientation among the protected grounds, yet as of 2019 it does not address discrimination against transgender people. Trans-specific protection in the state rests on the national constitutional and criminal provisions rather than on the wording of the state charter.

Since 2020 people in Santa Catarina have obtained documents recording non-binary gender through the courts or notarial offices, although no specific law prescribes this. The Superior Court of Justice has ruled that non-binary people may amend their civil registry to reflect their gender identity, and gender-marker changes proceed without surgery.

Courts in the state have applied family protection to foreign partners. In Florianópolis, judge M. C. F. Ribeiro da Silva of the 1st Civil Court blocked immigration authorities from deporting an Italian citizen who had lived over ten years in a stable relationship with a lesbian Brazilian.

A legal guide updated 5 April 2026 names Florianópolis among Brazil's broadly welcoming major cities, with active LGBTQ+ communities, pride events and legal infrastructure accustomed to processing same-sex marriages, adoptions and name or gender-marker changes. Smaller cities and rural areas of Santa Catarina may present more social friction, though legal rights are identical nationwide.

The wider national environment remains contested. A deeply conservative Congress has generated a surge of anti-LGBTIQ proposals, including efforts to repeal the marriage equality recognised by the Supreme Court in 2013, while constitutional guarantees and federal criminal provisions continue to apply nationwide and cover visitors in Santa Catarina.

On health care, the government reinstated the National LGBTI+ Health Technical Committee in September 2025, a participatory mechanism dissolved in 2019, for shaping and monitoring inclusive public-health policy.

82249235B24619009834807.name: British Columbia
82249235B24619009834807.summary:
British Columbia stands under the Canadian framework. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation and hate-propaganda provisions of the Criminal Code, both carried by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017. Section 15 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms applies in British Columbia, and courts have applied these protections consistently. Sexual orientation has been a protected ground federally since 1996. No province or territory restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities, and entry into Canada carries no trans-specific friction for visitors.

British Columbia has no hostile provincial legislation addressing trans people. It was the first jurisdiction in Canada to write sexual orientation into its human-rights code, in 1992, and is routinely assessed as the country's most progressive province on LGBT issues. A 2021 Criminal Code amendment, in force since 2022, made Canada the first country in North America to statutorily ban conversion therapy nationwide for both minors and adults; that ban applies in British Columbia.

Legal gender recognition operates largely on self-declaration. Transgender people may change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules, and federally issued identity documents can carry an X marker. Provincial human rights machinery is available to visitors and residents who face discrimination in the province.

National hate-crime data shows a mixed picture. A Statistics Canada release of 30 March 2026 covering police-reported hate crime in 2024 records 4,882 incidents, up 1% from 2023 after a 34% rise between 2022 and 2023, and a 169% increase since 2018, with the population rate down 2% to 11.9 per 100,000. Incidents targeting sexual orientation fell 26% to 658, while religion-motivated incidents were essentially stable at 1,342. The release breaks out sexual orientation as a motivation category rather than gender identity, and it contains no British Columbia breakdown, so trans-specific hate-crime volume in the province is not established by this dataset.

Conditions inside correctional institutions are the weakest point in the record. Federal policy is that transgender prisoners are to be placed in correctional facilities according to their gender identity, and transgender prisoners held for more than 12 continuous months are to be considered for sex-reassignment surgery. Litigation has tested both placement and care: lawyer Barbara findlay represented the transgender prisoner Synthia Kavanagh in a case over gender-affirming medical treatment and placement in a women's institution. A 2022 report alleged that gender-diverse prisoners face a pattern of abuse and discrimination in Canadian jails and are more likely to be victims of sexual assault, while a 2022 study of Nova Scotia correctional officers found them generally mindful of trans-prisoner safety and security, with some concerns about risk to other prisoners. These concerns bear on a trans visitor only if the visitor is detained.

47653553B5611469222723.name: RegiÃ³n de ValparaÃ­so
47653553B5611469222723.summary:
Región de Valparaíso stands under the national framework of Chile. Legal gender recognition rests on Gender Identity Law 21,120, in force since 27 December 2019: adults may change their registered name and sex on request to the Civil Registry without therapy or surgery, while applicants aged 14 to 18 must apply to family courts with psychosocial and family-context antecedents. People under 14 cannot use the statute, which nevertheless recognises them as transgender. On 9 April 2025 the Constitutional Court declared the 'over 14 years old' wording inapplicable as unconstitutional in a case brought by the mother of a 10-year-old trans girl, and that ruling applies only to that case.

The 2012 Zamudio Law prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, was extended to gender expression in 2018, and treats hate-crime motivation as an aggravating criminal circumstance. Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022, civil unions since 2015, and birth certificates have offered a third sex option for intersex children since 2006. No legal ban exists on medically unnecessary interventions on intersex minors; the Health Minister published non-binding intersex-affirming guidance in 2023.

Transphobic violence remains documented nationally. A young trans man was murdered in 2023 in a killing covered up for 24 hours and described in national reporting as Chile's largest hate crime, with an acquaintance perpetrator confessing. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held for close to an hour at a Santiago hotel, where the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim.

Detention carries specific rules. The national director of Gendarmería de Chile signed a protocol guaranteeing the gender identity of trans detainees, providing placement by assumed gender, segmented housing and entry examinations, with a standing committee of Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives overseeing implementation, including access rules for trans visitors.

The public health system has funded sex reassignment surgery and hormone therapy since 2013, and a 2011 Ministry of Health circular obliges all care centres to register transgender patients by their social name. Circular 7 of June 2024 suggested deferring the initiation of new gonadotropin-releasing hormone blockers and cross-sex hormone therapy in adolescents until national guidelines are published, and the Medical College noted that physicians may still prescribe. On 9 January 2025 the Constitutional Court, by seven votes to three, annulled section 46 of the 2025 Budget Law, which had barred the Ministry of Health from financing hormone therapies for trans children and adolescents. In November 2025 Congress defunded the Ministry of Social Development's Gender Identity Support Program through the 2026 Budget Law, while the Ministry of Health-run programme continues to provide support in medical centres; the Crece con Orgullo programme has operated since 2023 for children and adolescents aged 3 to 17.

Entry and removal rules reference gender identity. The Migration and Immigration Law of 11 April 2021 bans arbitrary discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity and offers protection to LGBT immigrants seeking asylum. Article 10 provides that recognised asylum seekers may be granted complementary protection, and no foreigner holding complementary protection may be expelled or returned to a country where their right to life, physical integrity or personal freedom is at risk on grounds including sexual orientation or gender identity.

Regional conditions in Región de Valparaíso are not benign. Movilh's XXIV Annual Human Rights Report records that the region concentrated 51.32% of national recorded anti-LGBTI discrimination cases in 2024, an increase of 80.93% over 2023. In 2025 recorded cases fell only in Valparaíso and Metropolitana while all other regions rose; Movilh reads this pattern as the decentralisation of hate toward territories where LGBTIQ themes have less visibility.

Restrictive proposals are active but non-binding. On 15 May 2025 the Chamber of Deputies approved the CEI 57 commission report, 56 votes to 30 with 6 abstentions, a non-binding recommendation to eliminate the Gender Identity Support Program, restrict minors' progressive autonomy, ban hormonal treatment for minors and repeal the circular protecting gender identity in schools.

13589884B3780741375954.name: Antioquia
13589884B3780741375954.summary:
Antioquia department stands under Colombia's national legal framework, among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement, and national identification documents carry trans and non-binary markers from November 2025. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office.

Access to premises is protected by court order. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees.

Antioquia is also a site of lethal violence. On 5 April 2025 a 28-second video went viral showing 32-year-old Sara Millerey González Borja beaten and thrown into a waterway in Bello, in broad daylight while onlookers filmed; she could not swim and drowned. Her mother Sandra Borja said: "They killed her for being who she was." President Gustavo Petro ordered an urgent investigation and protests were held in several cities. She was the third LGBTQ person killed in Bello in 2025; the first two victims were gay men.

Treatment and official conduct compounded the case. A clinic reportedly did not treat Millerey as an emergency "because she didn't get shot", and she died of cardiac arrest the following afternoon. Medellín's city hall was criticised for using her pre-transition name.

Killings continue at scale. Thirteen trans people were killed in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025 alone, and the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025. More than 40 transgender women were killed in 2023, with eight more between February and April 2024, national figures that also cover Antioquia.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity; the UN Human Rights Committee noted concern. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.

13589884B40908771570386.name: Bogota Capital District
13589884B40908771570386.summary:
Bogotá Capital District stands under Colombia's national framework, which the sources describe as among the most developed in Latin America for trans legal recognition. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender change on the basis of self-recognition without surgical or psychiatric requirements, reinforced by a 2012 Constitutional Court ruling allowing change through the civil registry without family court authorisation; since a rule change approved in June 2015 that route runs through a notary rather than judicially ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. National identification documents carry four markers, female (F), male (M), trans (T) and non-binary (NB), available on the national identity card from November 2025; rulings T-033 of 2022 and T-527 of 2024 further protected the right to gender identity and its recording.

Consensual same-sex activity has been legal in Colombia since 1981. The Constitutional Court legalised same-sex marriage in April 2016, making Colombia the fourth Latin American country to do so, and adoption equality for same-sex couples followed in November 2015. A 2011 law bans discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation.

Despite these protections, prejudice and discrimination against LGBTI people remain present in a considerable part of the Colombian population, a context relevant to a visibly gender-nonconforming person in central Bogotá. Lethal violence is documented: on 4 April 2025 Sara Millerey, 32, a trans woman, was beaten and thrown into a creek in Bello, Antioquia, and died; the killing prompted a presidential call to investigate and vigils in several cities. Thirteen trans people were killed nationwide in the first quarter of 2025, and CNN reported in August 2025 on continuing attacks against LGBTQ people in the country in the wake of the Millerey case.

Facilities and detention are addressed by court order. A 2012 ruling allowed a transgender woman to choose her own hairstyle and makeup in prison. Bogotá's public life includes large pride parades counted among the country's major LGBTQ events, and Washington Post reporting describes thriving gay neighbourhoods in the city. Claudia López Hernández became the first openly gay person to serve as mayor of Bogotá.

25490228B43154843394848.name: Comunidad de Madrid
25490228B43154843394848.summary:
Madrid is one of Europe's principal LGBT urban centres. The Chueca district anchors the city's LGBT life, the annual MADO Pride in late June or early July draws millions of attendees, and daily life offers substantial anonymity for LGBT visitors. The same source records that homophobic and transphobic discrimination and violence remain significant problems in the city, and that marginalised groups including trans people and migrants face additional barriers.

Documents presented in Madrid stand under Ley 4/2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado on 28 February 2023, which establishes real and effective equality for trans persons and guarantees LGTBI rights. Under Article 43 any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own civil registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, an administrative self-identification route that replaced the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis plus two years of medical treatment. Recognition is possible from age 12 under conditions, the law regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16, and legal gender change does not require surgery or sterilisation.

The Comunidad de Madrid was among the first Spanish regions to adopt its own gender-identity law, passing it in 2016 alongside the Islas Baleares and the Región de Murcia and following Extremadura in 2015. That regional statute was later amended by Ley 17/2023, and regional rules of this kind must comply with the national framework set by Ley 4/2023, which fixes the statutory floor a trans visitor to the region stands under.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on legal gender self-determination rather than on biological sex, so the gender marker recorded in the civil registry is the operative basis for facility rules in Spain. This contrasts with the stricter single-sex-space approach being adopted in the United Kingdom on biological-sex lines, with restrictions applied case by case rather than as a blanket ban.

There is no free-standing criminal offence of gender-expression-based hate crime: the phrase 'gender expression' appears in no article of the Spanish Criminal Code. The hate-speech aggravating circumstance in Article 22.4 and the penalties of Article 510, one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months, derive from Organic Law 6/2022, while Ley 4/2023 itself reformed offences against sexual freedom, including Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis. A Spanish criminal-law firm's analysis sets out what Ley 4/2023 does and does not do alongside the discrimination aggravating factor of Article 22.4 covering gender identity and expression motives and the hate offences of Article 510 as extended to trans and LGBTI people.

Enforcement of the gender-identity aggravation is documented at first-instance level, though the cases on record come from outside the region. In July 2026 the Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo applied the transfobia aggravating circumstance for the first time in a misdemeanour case concerning threats sent by WhatsApp to a trans woman, fining the author EUR 300. In a separate case reported on 8 January 2026, a juvenile gang harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park in Valencia to mock them; the only adult defendant received six months' prison and two minors were judged separately.

The national statute also bans non-consensual normalising surgeries on intersex children, expands assisted reproduction rules, provides parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, strengthens sexuality education, and imposes anti-discrimination measures covering healthcare, employment and housing. Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have been in force since 2005.

Local support machinery recorded for the city includes COGAM, founded in 1986 and the city's most influential LGBT organisation, the municipal Oficina de Atención a la Diversidad Sexual y de Género, and Arcopoli, which works against discrimination and violence.

19338628B30439183828151.name: Bourgogne-Franche-Comté
19338628B30439183828151.summary:
Bourgogne-Franche-Comté stands under the French national framework. Rules on identity documents, anti-discrimination, criminal law, marriage and legal gender recognition are set by national statute and apply uniformly across metropolitan and overseas regions, so the legal position a trans visitor faces in this region is the one that applies elsewhere in France.

Detention carries the sharpest documented risk. France has no statutory rule governing where a trans prisoner is held: placement follows the gender inscribed on identity documents, and each facility improvises, using special units or isolation that restricts contact with other inmates. A BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 describes trans women incarcerated on that basis as falling into a legal grey area and being punished beyond their alleged crimes, with accounts of heightened assault vulnerability and suicide risk under those arrangements.

The national custodial-inspection authority, the CGLPL, issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty, drawing on roughly 40 referrals received since 2010. It found serious violations of fundamental rights persisting across all places of detention, including placement by birth sex, isolation and exposure during strip searches, and recorded no marked improvement since its 2010 opinion despite the 2016 gender-recognition reform. Its recommendations also cover intersex and non-binary detainees.

The national preventive mechanism told the Association for the Prevention of Torture that a further opinion was necessary precisely because the 2010 opinion produced no marked improvement, because the gender-recognition law and its terminology had changed, and because coverage now extends to intersex and non-binary detainees. The findings rest on a decade of letters from detained trans people and identify structural problems in the isolation of vulnerable detainees and in suicide prevention.

That practice remained current through 2025. Louna, a trans woman detained for opposing the A69 motorway works, has been held since mid-October 2024 in the Tarbes men's prison and kept in isolation since October. Her incarceration was raised before the Keeper of the Seals in oral question no. 219 in the French National Assembly, which argued that the case exposes a prison system unable to guarantee conditions for trans detainees.

At entry points, trans women have faced questioning of their identity documents in public. Giovanna Rincon's first-person account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of routine humiliation by French border police at an airport, questioned in front of other travellers, documenting identity-document friction for trans travellers arriving in France.

The Défenseur des droits issued a new framework decision on trans rights confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony. It cites the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and sets out official guidance for service providers.

The baseline for partner recognition dates from the marriage-equality law of 17 May 2013, which opened marriage to same-sex couples; international television coverage recorded France's first same-sex wedding on 29 May 2013, days after the law took effect.

Within the region, the documented restriction concerns public assembly rather than trans status as such. The Côte-d'Or prefecture banned the Dijon Pride march from the city centre in June 2025, an event with over a decade of local history: pride marches have been organised in the Bourgogne cities of Chalon-sur-Saône, Dijon and Auxerre since 2013, in the national context of marches spreading to provincial cities from 1994 to 1995 onward. The ban is an exception against the national legal baseline rather than the regional rule.

19338628B36302232233914.name: Hauts-de-France
19338628B36302232233914.summary:
Visitors in Hauts-de-France stand under France's national framework: criminal law, identity-document rules, anti-discrimination law and marriage law apply uniformly across the region, and the country's oversight bodies record the same pattern of risk everywhere.

Prison placement is the region's documented contact point with trans-visitor risk. Under Article D248 of the criminal-procedure code men and women must be held in separate establishments, but placement follows the legal gender inscribed on identity documents, so trans women still recorded as male are held in all-male facilities. Controller-general Adeline Hazan, the national detention inspector-general, identifies transgender detainees as the group that suffers the most in prison.

The BuzzFeed News investigation of 12 January 2018 documents that practice in the region directly. Paola, transferred in 2014 to Lille's northern correctional facility, was met by detainees shouting "We don't want any women here!", was attacked with a knife by a fellow inmate and spent two days in solitary confinement. The same investigation records Kara B. held under conditions described as worrying after her 2016 Paris protest trial, and a Ministry of Justice count of 13 transgender detainees across eight facilities as of 1 November 2016.

The national custodial-inspection authority, the CGLPL, issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 covering every place of deprivation of liberty and built from referrals received since 2010. It finds that assignment to establishments or wards is based exclusively on civil status, so the vast majority of transgender people are held in institutions or wards that do not correspond to their gender identity, and that searches of people whose civil-status sex does not match their identity add constraints such as isolation. It recommends guaranteeing every transgender detainee the possibility of choosing the sex of searching officers and of their ward, bars identity-based isolation, requires continuity of medical and hormone care with free choice of doctor, urges research funding, and faults the administration for not translating the 2016 justice-modernisation law (n° 2016-1547 of 18 November 2016) into prison rules.

At entry points, trans women have faced questioning of their identity documents in public. Giovanna Rincon's first-person account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of routine humiliation by French border police at the airport, questioned in front of other travellers, documenting identity-document friction for trans travellers arriving in France.

The Défenseur des droits issued a new framework decision on trans rights, confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony. It cites the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and sets out official guidance for service providers.

For partner recognition, the legal baseline dates from the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013; CNN reported France's first same-sex wedding on 29 May 2013, performed days after the law took effect.

Trans women still legally marked male are therefore held in men's facilities, and each establishment decides for itself between a special unit and isolation. A national press investigation of January 2018 documents the consequences: an Argentine trans woman whose passport listed her as female spent three days in a men's facility in Lille while inmates threatened her, including an attempt to attack her with a knife. As of 1 November 2016 France held 13 transgender detainees, and damages awarded for one detainee's conditions of detention amounted to a symbolic 2,000 euros. The investigation records no Occitanie-specific event, and its national custody framework applies unchanged in this department.

Its visits covered the Toulouse-Seysses prison and the Toulouse central police station, and its findings concern eight transgender women held in those Toulouse facilities. 65028918B14696209246677.name: Jakarta Special Capital Region
65028918B14696209246677.summary:
The Jakarta Special Capital Region stands under the national framework of Indonesia, which is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, this provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national-level morality provisions. In Aceh, where Sharia law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025; those punishments reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors.

Venue raids are a standing enforcement instrument. On 22 June 2025, Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena described the operation as a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and stated that the gathering violated no law.

There is a directly documented death of a trans traveler in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022. During a WhatsApp call, his mother in Lima was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody; his mother alleges that police beat him, while Indonesian police have denied that violence was used.

Official policy frames LGBTQ+ people as a security matter. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists nonmilitary threats and places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled. Reporting from August 2026 ties that framing to a wave of vigilante attacks on transgender women, with mobs attacking trans people as the government codifies anti-LGBTQ+ attitudes into law. Commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.

Jakarta is the most heavily raided venue in Indonesia for LGBTQ+ gatherings, and the capital's raid series is the clearest documented instance of the national pattern. Police arrested 141 people over a "gay sex party" in Jakarta in May 2017, detained 144 at the Atlantis Gym sauna on 21 May 2017 with ten subsequently charged, and arrested 51 at a Central Jakarta sauna in October 2017 with six charged. All of those cases were pursued under the pornography law.

The same pattern continues in the current period. Police detained 56 people at a hotel in South Jakarta on 1 February 2025, nine at another South Jakarta hotel on 24 May 2025, and 75 at a private villa near the capital on 22 June 2025. Offences charged in these operations can carry up to 15 years' imprisonment under Indonesia's broadly worded Pornography Law.

Arrests in these raids are made without naming detainees and without judicial proceedings, according to Amnesty International's 24 June 2025 press release. Amnesty International Indonesia's deputy director called the villa operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy that exemplifies the hostile environment for LGBTI people in Indonesia, and demanded the release of those arrested.

There is no LGBT-specific statute and no general anti-discrimination law in Indonesia, so police action in Jakarta operates on pornography and morality provisions rather than any LGBT-specific offence. A visitor therefore faces exposure through broadly worded national laws applied at the discretion of police, not through a named prohibition.

1811400B15614733245507.name: Mahārāshtra
1811400B15614733245507.summary:
The national framework applies in Maharashtra as it does across India. India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026; the bill amends the 2019 law, removes the right to self-identification, limits legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner and to intersex people, and makes medical certification a condition of recognition. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. The BBC reports that the bill was approved by both houses of Parliament and awaits presidential assent, and that it reverses the Supreme Court of India's 2014 ruling on third gender and self-determination.

Human Rights Watch, in a news release of 26 March 2026, calls the amendment a huge setback. It objects to the new offences of "coercing or alluring" a person to be transgender, provisions it describes as reminiscent of colonial-era laws that punished transgender people for presenting dressed as women.

Identification documents are a narrow channel. India's last census recorded 487,803 transgender persons, while only about 32,500 hold the identity cards on which access to social security depends.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court of India in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which courts have interpreted to cover gender identity. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed legal safeguards that had protected trans persons from sexual violence, and trans people fear a rise in assaults because the new code omits the gender-identity-specific offences the old law carried.

Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person who had been asked to take a medical examination by passport authorities. In November 2024 an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card for identity verification. 1811400B23625213884851.name: Delhi
1811400B23625213884851.summary:
Delhi stands under India's national framework. India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, replacing the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme.

Human Rights Watch reported on 26 March 2026 that the bill removes the right to self-identification, limits legal recognition to those historically accepted socio-cultural groups and intersex people, mandates medical certification, and creates "coercing or alluring" offences that could criminalise the support systems trans people rely on. Human Rights Watch calls the bill a major reversal of hard-won rights and has urged the president not to sign it.

BBC News reported that the amendment bill has been approved by both houses of Parliament and now awaits presidential assent, reversing the 2014 Supreme Court ruling that established the right to self-identify. A Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel has asked the government to reconsider the bill, citing privacy-and-dignity challenges. The government argues the narrower definition will make welfare benefits, job reservations and healthcare support more targeted while strengthening protections against exploitation and trafficking.

India's last census recorded 487,803 transgender persons, but only about 32,500 hold the identity cards essential for accessing social security. This national documentation gap bears directly on Delhi as the capital, where identity verification at checkpoints is a recurring point of friction.

At a press conference in Delhi, activist Grace Banu stated that the community sought "recognition without invasion" and "rights without humiliation". Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist.

Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which the Supreme Court has held covers gender identity and sexual orientation under Article 15. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership in India, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024: replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed legal safeguards that had protected trans persons from sexual violence, and trans people fear a rise in assaults because the new code omits the gender-identity-specific offences the old law carried.

Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person who had been asked to take a medical exam by passport authorities. In November 2024 an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at the station under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender persons arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic; victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. Bans on conversion therapy from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating.

Facilities and care access are largely set at state level. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha run transgender welfare boards coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions. Nationally, the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community. In August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.

Intersex minors remain at risk: reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations, and the Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.
