68945753B55100681051852.name: Seoul
68945753B55100681051852.summary:
Seoul stands under South Korea's national framework. The country does not criminalise gender identity or gender expression in civilian life; consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal. The exception is the armed forces, where Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, a provision the Constitutional Court upheld in 2023. Enforcement has been punitive: in 2017 the military charged 32 personnel in what Amnesty International described as a gay witch hunt, and a gay soldier received a six-month prison sentence. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

The sharpest documented harm to a trans person in the armed forces is the case of Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su, compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after a military panel classified the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a physical or mental handicap. She died by suicide in March 2021. The Daejeon District Court ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021, and in March 2024 the Defence Ministry recognised her death as in the line of duty.

Restroom access is a live legal issue in Seoul. On 2 July 2024 the Seoul Central District Court, presiding judge Chung In-jae, dismissed the state's appeal and made final a ruling holding that police advice telling an LGBT person mid-legal-transition to avoid public restrooms for a while infringed personal rights. The court awarded the plaintiff 300,000 won of the 3 million won claimed, stating that the right to comfortably use restrooms is a fundamental and universal human right. The decision became final after neither party appealed.

The same problem appears in everyday practice. A 2021 National Human Rights Commission of Korea survey of 591 transgender respondents found that 41% used another-gender restrooms out of fear of mistreatment, 39% avoided food and drink to reduce the need, and 36% forwent restroom use altogether. A 2021 Pohang branch of the Daegu District Court ruling awarded 7 million won in damages against an academy that barred a trans student's restroom use.

Legal gender recognition is available and the surgical condition is falling away. On 8 May 2024 a court in Yeongdong approved male-to-female gender-marker changes for five transgender people without sex reassignment surgery, holding that it is against the law to determine gender change based on surgery and that every human being has the right to live according to their gender identity. The national court guidelines that previously required surgery have been downgraded to reference-only status, though some courts still apply them. The ruling sits outside Seoul and bears on Seoul as evidence of the national judicial trend. Earlier precedent had required persons seeking gender-affirming care to be over 20, single and without children, and on 24 November 2022 the Supreme Court ruled en banc that transgender individuals with minor children can have their gender legally recognised provided they are not married.

South Korean national law does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, and same-sex couples cannot jointly adopt children. There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity. The government's position on care was tested in November 2023, when the National Human Rights Commission of Korea identified a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation after the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, saying that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

Violence concentrates at public events. In Incheon a Pride event ended in violence when about 1,000 Christian protestors attacked participants, and organisers later filed charges against pastors and accused police of inaction; at Busan's 2018 Pride some 2,000 police were deployed to protect 15,000 attendees from violent anti-gay protesters. In Seoul, the May 2020 Itaewon COVID-19 cluster saw contact tracing out LGBTQ people, after which doxing and online harassment rose; a trans-male bartender told NBC News he felt threatened walking on the street absent a nondiscrimination bill.

Discrimination burden is documented across life stages. A 2014 finding recorded that 54% of LGBTQ Korean youths were harassed by classmates, 16.1% of outed LGBTQ people were recommended conversion therapy, with 65.4% reporting harm and 94% psychological trauma, and a 2018 study found 51.5% of transgender adults faced harsh discrimination in the past year. Research from the youth LGBTQ+ centre DDing Dong, presented on 20 March 2024, shows trans teenagers avoid school restrooms for fear of being outed; a 16-year-old trans girl at a boys' school reported holding it in and leaving school early. A peer-reviewed nationwide survey published on 27 June 2025 in Epidemiology and Health, covering 585 transgender and non-binary young adults, documented a pervasive discrimination burden at school, work and in transition-related care. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 describes an overall relatively positive record on free media and civil society alongside persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people.

A district court ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021, and in March 2024 the defence ministry recognised her death as in the line of duty.

On 2 July 2024 the local district court dismissed the state's appeal and made final a ruling holding that police advice telling an LGBT person mid-legal-transition to avoid public restrooms for a while infringed personal rights. The court awarded the plaintiff 300,000 won of the 3 million won claimed, stating that the right to comfortably use restrooms is a fundamental and universal human right. The decision became final after neither party appealed.

A 2021 national human rights commission survey of 591 transgender respondents found that 41% used another-gender restrooms out of fear of mistreatment, 39% avoided food and drink to reduce the need, and 36% forwent restroom use altogether. 31927357B30293642818187.name: Quintana Roo
31927357B30293642818187.summary:
Quintana Roo stands under the national framework of Mexico, where extending legal gender recognition to trans people remains the central unfinished task of equality law. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of Mexico's 32 states had legislated an administrative recognition procedure by that date, while six states (Aguascalientes, Chiapas, Durango, Querétaro, Tabasco and Tamaulipas) had reformed nothing, leaving trans residents carrying documents permanently mismatched to their lived identity.

The same Human Rights Watch feature documents coercive detention and border scrutiny as risks for travellers whose documents contradict their presentation, hazards that fall hardest where recognition procedures are absent or obstructed. Quintana Roo enacted legal gender recognition in 2020, so a trans visitor's papers are not automatically a point of friction at the state level, although national reporting indicates that formal recognition does not guarantee consistent treatment.

Partnership and family rights are settled in Quintana Roo. Same-sex marriage has been permitted in the state since 2012: two marriages performed in Kantunilkín in November 2011 were annulled by the governor in April 2012 and reinstated on 3 May 2012 once the state conceded that its Civil Code sets no gender requirement. The Quintana Roo congress legalized adoption by same-sex couples in August 2022. Nationally, same-sex marriage has been legal since 2009.

The state penal code punishes crimes motivated by sexual orientation or gender as hate crimes, and Quintana Roo ratified the 2011 federal constitutional ban on sexual-orientation discrimination.

Quintana Roo banned conversion practices on 15 December 2023, following the example set by Morelos. Both legislatures approved initiatives prohibiting and sanctioning 'Esfuerzos para Corregir la Orientación Sexual e Identidad de Género' (ECOSIG), commonly called conversion therapies. Penalties run to two to six years in prison and fines of 1,000 to 2,000 times the daily UMA value for those who carry out such practices, and the reform applies across the state, including the tourist corridors of Cancún and the Riviera Maya.

Violence against trans people nationally gives the legal picture its context. Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to the 100 recorded in another country in the region. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that all LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.

31927357B30293642818187.tangentialFactors:
Partnership recognition is settled nationally: same-sex marriage has been legal across Mexico since 2009, with Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction. Cancún is counted among the country's principal gay-tourism destinations, which shapes the commercial surface a visitor meets without altering the legal framework described above.

Violence against trans people intensified over the year to mid-2024. AP reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City; the killings drew LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months. Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100.

One legislature has moved to close a specific gap. Mexico City's Congress approved the 'Paola Buenrostro law' in July 2024, criminalising transfemicide; the statute takes its name from a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished, and activists describe the law as critical to their sense of safety.

Inter-American authorities have pressed the same point. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that all LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.

Where recognition is delayed, the consequences are concrete. The Human Rights Watch report 'I Just Want to Contribute to Society' (6 March 2024) found that delays and refusals in name and gender recognition in Tabasco leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying everyday discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police, set against killings including a trans woman found dead in the Carrizal River in August 2023.

Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice; the analysis explicitly cautions that its earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

15666254B89722251658211.name: Selangor
15666254B89722251658211.summary:
Selangor is a state of Malaysia and stands under the Malaysian national framework. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature", covering oral and anal sex, with up to twenty years' imprisonment plus whipping, regardless of the gender of the participants, whether the act is consensual, or whether it takes place in private. Section 377D adds an undefined "gross indecency" offence carrying up to two years. The Human Dignity Trust country profile, last updated 16 December 2025, records that these provisions have been enforced in recent years, apply to both men and women, are usable against transgender people, and are not confined to Malaysian citizens, so they reach foreign visitors in Selangor. Non-Muslim visitors fall under the federal Penal Code alone.

Selangor maintains a state Sharia layer above the federal code. The Syariah Criminal Offences Enactment 1995 criminalises cross-dressing and a man posing as a woman, alongside liwat and musahaqah, with penalties reaching three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. These offences bind Muslims only, and enforcement rests with the Selangor Islamic Religious Department. Because the enactment contains no definition of transgender dress, the boundary between acceptable and offending presentation is set by officers on the ground.

Enforcement in Selangor is active and documented. A Selangor Sharia court sentenced five men to six or seven months' imprisonment with six strokes of the cane. At least 1,733 people had attended state "rehabilitation programmes" as of June 2021, under a crackdown on LGBT people running since the 2018 general election; Human Rights Watch and Justice For Sisters found that such programmes internalise discrimination and foment self-hatred among those ordered into them.

The case of Nur Sajat shows how far Selangor authorities will go to enforce gender norms. She is a transgender woman and cosmetics entrepreneur who in 2021 failed to appear in a Selangor court to answer criminal charges for "insulting Islam" brought on the basis of her attire. The state religious department issued a warrant for her arrest, announced that it had mobilised 122 religious-affairs officers to hunt her down, and later sought her extradition from Thailand. She was permitted to remain under UNHCR protection and has since settled in Australia.

Violence against transgender women in the state is lethal. A trans woman was killed in Klang, Selangor, in June 2019, the third such killing of a trans woman in Malaysia in fewer than two months, and killings of this kind have gone unpunished.

The Federal Court struck down provisions of the Syariah Criminal Offences Enactment 1995 in 2021 as exceeding the power of the state legislature. The ruling turned on which legislature may enact the offence rather than on the substance of the prohibition, and nothing under the federal Penal Code was decriminalised; cross-dressing and same-sex conduct remain chargeable in Selangor through the federal sections and the surviving state provisions.

The national framework also governs entry, relationships and remedies. There is no explicit visa rule for transgender visitors; the closest documented statement of entry policy is a 2001 declaration by then-Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad that Malaysia would deport any visiting foreign cabinet minister or diplomat who is gay. Same-sex marriage and any form of partner recognition are unavailable, and Malaysian law provides no protection against discrimination or hate crimes on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation.

Sharia state enactments criminalise cross-dressing and "males posing as females". In Selangor, the Federal Court struck down provisions of the Syariah Criminal Offences Enactment 1995 as exceeding state power (2021). State authorities issued an arrest warrant for a trans businesswoman who failed to appear in court and announced the deployment of 122 religious-affairs officers (the Sajat case). 15666254B42356713390762.name: Johor
15666254B42356713390762.summary:
Johor is one of Malaysia's thirteen states and stands under the national framework: federal law criminalises same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity across the country, and the state layer adds Sharia offences that reach Muslims alone. Sections 377A to 377D of the federal Penal Code, in force in Johor, punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" and "outrages on decency" with up to twenty years' imprisonment plus whipping. The provisions cover oral and anal sex, apply to men and women alike, reach acts that are consensual and private, and are not confined to Malaysian citizens.

Johor's Sharia enactment sits alongside that federal layer, prohibiting cross-dressing and "males posing as females" together with liwat and musahaqah, with penalties reaching three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. These offences apply only to Muslims; a non-Muslim visitor falls under the federal Penal Code alone. The enactments contain no legal definition of transgender dress, so the boundary between compliant and offending presentation is set by officers on the ground.

In November 2023 the Johor state government announced plans to establish conversion-therapy centres to "rehabilitate" LGBT people. The announcement sits within a nationwide crackdown that has run since the 2018 general election: at least 1,733 people had attended state "rehabilitation programmes" as of June 2021. A visitor who comes to the attention of Johor's religious authorities as gender-nonconforming can therefore expect to be routed into a religious intervention rather than a purely legal process.

Enforcement is discretionary rather than systematic. Consenting adults in private are rarely prosecuted under the federal sections, but that discretion is not a legal protection and has been withdrawn at moments of political pressure, most visibly in the mass venue raids documented elsewhere in Malaysia since 2018. There is no explicit visa or entry rule keyed to gender identity; the nearest documented statement of entry policy is a 2001 declaration by then-Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad that Malaysia would deport any visiting foreign cabinet minister or diplomat who is gay.

Malaysian law provides no protection against discrimination or hate crimes on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation, and same-sex marriage and partner recognition are unavailable nationwide. Legal challenges have failed to remove the framework: the Federal Court struck down a Selangor cross-dressing provision in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds only, and nothing under the federal Penal Code has been decriminalised.

15666254B45695250728659.name: Malacca
15666254B45695250728659.summary:
Malacca is one of the thirteen states of Malaysia and stands under the Malaysian national framework. A visitor to Malacca who is neither a Malaysian citizen nor a Muslim is exposed to the federal Penal Code alone; the state Sharia enactments reach only Muslims.

The Human Dignity Trust Malaysia country profile, last updated 2024, reports that sections 377A and 377B of the Federal Penal Code 1936 criminalise same-sex sexual activity with a maximum penalty of twenty years' imprisonment and whipping, and that section 377D, "outrages on decency", criminalises gross indecency in terms that can be used to target transgender people. State Sharia enactments, including in Malacca, additionally criminalise cross-dressing for Muslims.

That profile records evidence of the law being enforced in recent years and a crackdown on the LGBT community since the 2018 election. It documents a high-profile 2021 case of a prominent transgender woman fleeing the country following threats of arrest, and it reports consistent discrimination and violence in which transgender people are particularly vulnerable to physical and verbal abuse.

Human Rights Watch, in a report published on 10 August 2022 produced with the organisation Justice for Sisters, documents government-sponsored discrimination against LGBT people in Malaysia. The report cites the federal penal code punishment of up to twenty years' imprisonment for oral and anal sex, and Sharia codes, including those of the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya, that typically criminalise same-sex activity and gender nonconformity. It details conversion and rehabilitation programmes, officials shutting down events, and the 2021 prosecution of the transgender woman Nur Sajat in the state of Selangor.

The HRW report concludes that pervasive antipathy toward sexual and gender diversity influences law enforcement and judicial outcomes. For a transgender visitor this matters because the discretion to charge under section 377D and the state cross-dressing provisions is exercised by officers working within that antipathy, and neither source records a Malacca-specific case against which to gauge how the discretion is used locally.

27671186B76269877687363.name: Abuja Federal Capital Territory
27671186B76269877687363.summary:
Abuja Federal Capital Territory stands under Nigeria's national framework with no territorial carve-out. Nigeria criminalises same-sex conduct nationally under the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 (SSMPA), and the law reaches far beyond marriage: Human Rights Watch (October 2016) documents that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests.

Sexual orientation and gender identity carry criminal exposure at entry. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, while Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions. Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed: Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public, and whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Abuja itself is the site of a documented trans-specific killing. On 8 August 2024 the beaten, bruised body of 33-year-old transgender TikToker "Abuja Area Mama" was found along the Katampe-Mabushi expressway in the Banex/Wuse II area, hours after she posted a final video, having previously expressed fear for her life. A police statement described the victim as "a man fully dressed in female clothing with no means of identification". Abuja police chief Benneth Igweh ordered a "thorough and discreet" investigation; The Dial (February 2025) records that six months later no suspects had been charged. A petition of nearly 6,000 signatures demands that her murder be investigated as a hate crime.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice for Nigeria, as reported by Sahara Reporters (19 August 2026), warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states. The advisory extends the law to people who help arrange or conduct same-sex marriages and to activities involving gay groups and organisations, and warns that breaching curfews or movement restrictions could expose travellers to arrest and detention.

Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people. Although Nigerian laws guarantee freedom from discrimination, mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people are common, especially in northern states.

1875124B65618634887963.name: Lima
1875124B65618634887963.summary:
Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising. The national framework binds Lima directly: the Congress that enacted these measures sits and operates in the capital, and its provisions apply throughout the department and the metropolitan area.

On 2 April 2025 the Plenary of Congress approved, exempt from a second vote, the fused bills 6505/2023-CR and 8457/2023-CR, promulgated as the April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents. Article 5 prohibits entry to and use of public sanitary facilities by any person whose biological sex does not match the sex for which the facility is designated, with listed exceptions, barring trans people including trans youth from facilities matching their gender identity. The provision followed a February 2025 unanimous approval by the Congress Women and Family Commission of the Muñante initiative presented by Jorge Montoya of Honor y Democracia, which still required plenary backing at that point. The same text bars inclusive signage, including the wording the international airport Jorge Chávez in Lima had installed, reading "for all persons with female identity" and "male identity", and the wider package bans signage of the kind "women in their diversity".

Enforcement of the restriction reaches private and public life. LGBTIQ activist Gianna Camacho, co-author of a 2024 report on hate crimes and a trans journalist and human-rights defender, states that the rule would reduce to security staff demanding a DNI on their own judgement of whether a woman entering a restroom is trans. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to "go use the men's room".

The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, analysing the text on 15 April 2025, calls article 5 direct legislation conditioning basic rights on a "biological sex" and a violation of the equality and non-discrimination principle, and finds the rule openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by implicitly framing them as harassment risks. IDEHPUCP also recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights.

Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome left Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. The TLGBI Rights Observatory annual report, covered on 22 July 2024, recorded 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 reports of rights violations between 2020 and 2023; more than half of the dead were trans women (30), followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian. The year 2023 saw the most homicides (19), and no suspects were identified in 26 of the 54 killings. The same reporting states that hate crimes in Peru are rising with trans women most affected, and Camacho stresses that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry. Peru has no official system recording victims' sexual orientation, and hate crimes go unsanctioned.

Lima has seen lethal anti-trans violence: on 12 February 2023 the transgender sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano, aged 31, was kidnapped from jirón Chancay in central Lima by the "Los Gallegos" extortion gang, who killed her with roughly 30 gunshots.

In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Speech and association are constrained. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

1875124B43998217738279.name: Municipalidad Metropolitana de Lima
1875124B43998217738279.summary:
Lima stands under the national framework of Peru: trans identity is not criminalised, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising. The Metropolitan Municipality of Lima sets none of these rules itself; a trans visitor to the capital is governed by national statute and by the enforcement practice of national agencies and private security operating in the city.

On 20 February 2025 the Congressional Women and Family Commission approved unanimously, for plenary debate, a bill barring trans people from public bathrooms of the sex that does not match their biological sex at birth. The same text obliges public premises to remove "ambiguous" signage of the kind Jorge Chávez international airport had displayed, wording such as "for all persons with female identity" and "for all persons with male identity". The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents then mandated that restroom entry be determined by biological sex, extending the bar to trans youth, and the wider legislative package bans inclusive signage such as "women in their diversity".

Enforcement is expected to reach individuals at the door. Activist and journalist Gianna Camacho warns that the restriction will be applied through identity-card (DNI) checks carried out by security staff deciding who may enter a restroom, a screening practice she describes as discriminatory and grounded in prejudice rather than in any observed conduct.

Violence against trans people in Peru is documented and under-recorded. An Observatory report covering 2020 to 2023 counted 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 reported rights violations, with trans women the most affected group at 30 of the 54 killed; 19 homicides were recorded in 2023 alone, and in 26 of the killings no suspects were identified. The state maintains no system recording the sexual orientation or gender identity of victims of killing, so official counts understate the pattern.

The capital illustrates that pattern. On 12 February 2023 members of the "Los Gallegos" gang kidnapped trans sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano, aged 31, from jirón Chancay in central Lima; she was killed with roughly 30 gunshots.

25984515B47806653651907.name: Ankara
25984515B47806653651907.summary:
Ankara stands within Turkey's national framework, where the documented exposure for a trans visitor lies inside the country rather than at the border. Turkey has no visa, entry or border rule specific to LGBTQ travellers. The visitor-facing document risk is general: foreigners must carry original photo ID at transit checkpoints in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and warnings of detention for non-compliance. That requirement intersects with street-level identity checks — in August 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women while they were walking, shopping or sitting in cafés in Beyoğlu, held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station and released them after 'General Information Gathering' background checks. Legal experts quoted by bianet argue those checks breach Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Nothing was fined in that episode, but names and details were recorded.

Criminalisation by statute had not been enacted when Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025, but the leaked draft '11th Judicial Package' then before the government would amend the Turkish penal code to criminalise conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality with up to three years' prison, and penalise participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years. The same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care including surgery from 18 to 25, with mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals. Healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years' prison, trans people receiving care deemed illegal up to three years, and courts could order pretrial detention. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft. Whether the package has since passed is unresolved in the sources.

Kaos GL's annual report, 'The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People', launched in 2025, finds that hostility toward LGBTI+ people became explicit state policy, centred on the presidency and implemented through the Ministry of Family. It records censorship of broadcasts, cancellation or banning of artistic events, and the closure of an LGBTI+ association for the first time in years with criminal cases opened against 11 of its members. The report documents six violations of the right to life during the year, three recorded as hate-motivated, with transgender people the most affected, and a rise in torture and ill-treatment violations to 89 from 51 the previous year.

The scale of documented hostility extends beyond official acts. The same reporting cycle records 313 violations over the year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, dominated by 299 detention decisions — 256 taken on the record and 43 off it — alongside systematic attacks on the privacy of LGBT people. Turkish Minute's coverage counts six deaths linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. The state keeps no official hate-crime statistics.

Policing asymmetry recurs in individual cases. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy by a 17-year-old; the attacker was released while the victim herself was referred for arrest, which activists describe as evidence of a state hate policy. On 1 December 2025 the transgender prisoner Poyraz was found dead in his cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara, and rights groups demanded an independent investigation and changes to detention practices affecting transgender prisoners. Accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers state that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived after prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison only two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. An opposition MP raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025.

Detained visitors are held in facilities organised by registered sex rather than gender identity, and Turkish prisons subject LGBTI+ detainees to arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto isolation and restricted healthcare. Some prisoners refuse hospital transfers for fear of other male inmates. No policy or staff training exists to identify LGBTI+ needs, complaints are ineffective and can provoke further violence, and transfers are frequent. Event attendance carries its own exposure: monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through the year, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

Protection machinery is thin. Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity, and no direct discrimination protection for gender identity. The European Commission's 2025 report found legal protection insufficient and out of line with the EU acquis, while noting official permissions granted to demonstrations promoting exclusion. Hormone replacement therapy is not covered by the government healthcare system, so trans visitors must obtain and pay for it privately during a stay.

25984515B12971548112787.name: Eskişehir
25984515B12971548112787.summary:
Eskişehir stands under the national framework applicable in Turkey, where hostility toward trans people has been formalised as state policy rather than residual prejudice. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked 11th Judicial Package would amend the penal and civil codes with articles criminalising behaviour "contrary to biological sex and general morality" and its "promotion", carrying up to three years' prison through an amendment to the indecent-acts provision. The same package would impose sharp restrictions on gender-affirming care, including a minimum age of 25 and onerous eligibility requirements, and could expose trans people, care providers, civil-society organisations and journalists to charges. The government justified the measures as protecting "the family and public morals".

The national baseline is mixed. Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, subject to surgery, medical examination and court permission. There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law, and same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not recognised. In ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking Turkey placed 47th of 49 countries.

Eskişehir has its own documented record of suppression. In June 2021 police blocked the first Eskişehir pride parade, showing that even in this university city local authorities have moved against the local Pride event. Duvar English reports that officers reached the planned meeting area hours before the scheduled start and carried out identity checks; organisers were not permitted to hold a press meeting or conduct the parade, and police detained 20 people on the grounds of "viololving the ban on the march". The intervention came days after police actions against Pride events in Istanbul and Ankara.

Pride bans are a national pattern, not a local aberration. Since 2015 authorities have banned Pride events in most years and participants have faced police attacks, with Turkish authorities citing security concerns and public order. Trans visitors attending events in Eskişehir should expect identity checks, refusal of assembly permissions and detention on ban-violation grounds.

25984515B63001774148772.name: Gaziantep
25984515B63001774148772.summary:
Gaziantep stands under the national framework of Turkey in full, with no documented local divergence in either direction: a visibly trans visitor to the province faces the same legal exposure, the same document checks and the same enforcement climate as elsewhere in the country, applied by provincial authorities under national law.

The most serious pending threat is a leaked 11th Judicial Package reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025. It would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise behaviour "contrary to biological sex and general morality" and its "promotion", carrying up to three years' imprisonment through an amended indecent-acts provision, and would sharply restrict gender-affirming care through a minimum age of 25 and onerous eligibility requirements. Human Rights Watch states the package could support charges against trans people themselves, against care providers, civil-society organisations and journalists, and that the government justified it as protecting "the family and public morals".

The national baseline itself has not changed: homosexuality has not been an offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and legal gender recognition has been available since 1988 subject to surgery, medical examination and court permission. There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law, and same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not recognised. In ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking Turkey placed 47th of 49 countries.

Enforcement against LGBT people is active and documented. Amnesty International's Report 2025/26 records that in June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the LGBTI and Trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful force, and over 90 people were arbitrarily detained. Three activists were remanded in prison on 29 June 2025 under Law No. 2911 and released on 8 August pending trial, while prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association over allegedly "obscene" images incompatible with "society's moral values". These are the meeting-and-demonstrations and speech exposures a visibly trans visitor would face anywhere in Turkey, including Gaziantep.

In early 2026 Turkish media reported the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of "behaviour contrary to biological sex"; that provision was ultimately not included in that year's judicial reform package. Pride events have been banned in most years since 2015, with participants facing police attacks.

25984515B63001774148772.tangentialFactors:
Checkpoint interactions carry a direct outing risk: Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. Any stop is an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Street-level enforcement already operates ahead of legislation. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women in Beyoğlu and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" (GBT) checks before release; legal experts cited argue such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One detainee stated police took no fines but documented them anyway, and that the new law had not yet passed even as enforcement was already applied to them.

Violence against trans people is lethal and the state response asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest.

The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in one year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, with 299 detention decisions — 256 through formal channels and 43 off the record.
25984515B63001774148772.localsOnly:
Trans prisoners are held by registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation; accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case, raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025, confirmed that Turkey places trans prisoners according to their registered sex — a trans man had been held in a women's prison.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. There is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

25984515B18786507826220.name: İstanbul
25984515B18786507826220.summary:
İstanbul stands under the national framework in force across Turkey, where hostility toward LGBTI+ people has been formalised as state policy. Kaos GL's 2025 annual report, "The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People", records that pattern operating in the city directly, including intensified practices of sealing or closing the homes of LGBTI+ residents that obstruct access to housing.

The same monitoring counts six violations of the right to life across Turkey in 2025, three of them recorded as hate-motivated, with trans people the group most affected. Torture and ill-treatment violations nearly doubled, rising to 89 from 51. One LGBTI+ association was closed and criminal cases were opened against 11 of its members. The state keeps no official hate-crime statistics, so these figures rest on civil-society monitoring rather than on government record-keeping.

Stop-and-check policing of trans women is documented in the city centre. On 31 July 2025 police in the Beyoğlu district rounded up around 20 trans women for identity-document checks, recorded their names and filmed them; the reporting describes the operation as profiling. A foreign visitor stopped in such an interaction must produce original documents, which places passport details alongside presentation in front of officers.

The Governorship of İstanbul has denied permission for and locally banned pride parades on security and public-order grounds since 2015, and water cannon was used against marchers on 29 June 2015. 25984515B59477790330217.name: İzmir
25984515B59477790330217.summary:
İzmir stands under the national framework of Turkey. Turkey has no visa, entry or border rule specific to LGBTQ travellers, so the visitor-facing exposure lies inside the country. Foreigners must carry original photo ID at transit checkpoints in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and warnings of detention for non-compliance. That general requirement intersects with identity checks aimed at trans people on the street: bianet reports that on 31 July 2025 trans women in a large-city entertainment district were subjected to mass identity-document roundups, with names recorded and videos taken and no official reason given. In August 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women while they were walking, shopping or sitting in cafés in Beyoğlu, held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station and released them after 'General Information Gathering' background checks; legal experts quoted by bianet argue those checks breach Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Nothing was fined in that episode, but names and details were recorded.

Criminalisation by statute had not been enacted when Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025, but a leaked draft of Türkiye's omnibus 11th Judicial Package then before the government would amend the penal code to criminalise conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality and its promotion with up to three years' prison, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years. The draft would amend civil code article 40 to raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care including surgery from 18 to 25, with mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals. Healthcare professionals performing deemed-illegal interventions would face fines and up to seven years' prison, trans people receiving such care up to three years, with courts able to order pretrial detention. Fifteen Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft, and Human Rights Watch warns it would force treatment into unregulated underground settings. Whether the package has since passed is unresolved in the sources.

Kaos GL's report 'A Major Siege against LGBTI+ People in 2025: Hostility Turned into State Policy' finds that hostility toward LGBTI+ people became explicit state policy. It records 313 violations of the right to liberty in 2025, roughly two and a half times the previous year, citing detentions, arrests and criminal cases against Pride participants as the main reasons, alongside 89 torture or ill-treatment violations and six right-to-life violations, three of them recorded as hate-motivated killings with trans people the most affected. For the first time in many years an LGBTI+ association was closed and criminal cases were opened against 11 of its members for human rights advocacy.

Policing asymmetry is documented at the level of individual cases. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy by a 17-year-old; the attacker was released while the victim herself was referred for arrest, which activists describe as evidence of a state hate policy. On 1 December 2025 the transgender prisoner Poyraz was found dead in his cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara. Accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers state that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived after prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison only two days later, and that witness statements were not taken; an opposition MP raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025.

Trans visitors who are detained are held in facilities organised by registered sex rather than gender identity, and Turkish prisons subject LGBTI+ detainees to arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto isolation and restricted healthcare. Some prisoners refuse hospital transfers for fear of other male inmates. No policy or staff training exists to identify LGBTI+ needs, complaints are ineffective and can provoke further violence, and transfers are frequent. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through the year, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

Protection machinery is thin. Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity, and no direct discrimination protection for gender identity. The European Commission's 2025 report found legal protection insufficient and out of line with the EU acquis, while noting official permissions granted to demonstrations promoting exclusion. If medication is needed during a stay, hormone replacement therapy is not covered by the government healthcare system, so trans visitors must obtain and pay for it privately.

66186276B86072070009793.name: Puerto Rico
66186276B86072070009793.summary:
Puerto Rico is a United States territory, and the United States federal framework applies on the island in full: federal statutes, executive orders and agency procedure govern entry, documents, screening, federally funded care and federal custody. Puerto Rico's own legislation does not soften that framework, and in the area of trans medical care it sharpens it.

United States travel documents record sex assigned at birth, and Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, eliminated the X marker, so a trans visitor arriving on United States documents may present a marker that does not match their appearance at inspection. Entry scrutiny is tightened further for one category of traveller: in February 2025 the United States State Department announced visa denials for trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sports.

Airport screening at Puerto Rico's airports follows federal Transportation Security Administration procedure. All luggage is screened and may be hand-searched. Prosthetics, including breast forms, are treated as medically necessary equipment rather than liquids, so they fall outside the three-liquid rule and are allowed through the checkpoint after screening. Published guidance for trans travellers advises packing strategies that reduce the likelihood of invasive searches.

In July 2025 Puerto Rico banned gender-affirming care for anyone under 21, barred public funding for that care, and set penalties of up to 15 years in prison, a $50,000 fine and permanent loss of medical licences for doctors who violate the ban. The Puerto Rico LGBTQ+ Federation announced plans to challenge the ban in court.

The care law was pushed through non-public hearings and is written with deliberate vagueness, so doctors and affirming parents who facilitate hormone treatment or top surgery risk prosecution. It mandates campaigns by the Education and Health departments on the risks of trans-affirming care. Health Secretary Ramos Otero proposed amendments that would have allowed puberty blockers and the continuation of existing hormone treatment, but the text as enacted stands as the most restrictive care law in any United States jurisdiction according to the report documenting it.

Puerto Rico amended its hate crime statutes in 2002 to include sexual orientation and gender identity as protected characteristics, and the territory is also covered by the United States federal Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act. The first hate crime charges in Puerto Rico's history were brought in 2020, after Sean Díaz de León and Juan Pagán Bonilla were charged in the murder of two transgender women on 22 April 2020; Bonilla confessed to the killings. In January 2021 Governor Pedro Pierluisi declared a state of emergency over ongoing murders, assaults and rape of transgender individuals on the island.

Anti-discrimination coverage remains partial. The 2013 law that passed (Senate Bill 238, signed 29 May 2013) was amended in the House to apply only to employment discrimination, so public facilities, housing, transit and business transactions are not covered by it. An earlier bill, House Bill 1725, passed the House 43-6 in November 2009 with wider coverage but the Senate held no hearings and took no action after Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz said it would not be approved.

Marriage recognition for same-sex couples in Puerto Rico was obtained through the federal courts: four couples joined the federal lawsuit filed in March 2014, with Lambda Legal and Puerto Rico Para Todas intervening, and plaintiffs included a couple married in Canada in 2007 and another married in New York in 2012, one of them a former National Guard member.

Under Executive Order 14168, which directs United States federal agencies to recognise only two sexes, the Bureau of Prisons houses transgender inmates by sex assigned at birth rather than asserted gender identity, a rule that governs any federal custody in Puerto Rico. The ACLU said it had received reports that transgender women were being transferred to men's prisons, told they would be, or moved to solitary confinement, and the Bureau of Prisons stopped reporting how many transgender people it holds. Advocates say the order contravenes the Prison Rape Elimination Act requirement that trans inmates' housing be decided by individual safety assessment.

sources.summary: Puerto Rico's sodomy ban was upheld by the Puerto Rico Supreme Court in 2002, but after the U.S. Supreme Court's Lawrence v. Texas ruling in 2003 struck down all state and territorial sodomy statutes for consensual private acts, Puerto Rico amended its Penal Code in 2004 to remove private, non-commercial sexual activity between consenting adults from the statute. In July 2025 Puerto Rico banned gender-affirming care for anyone under 21, barred public funding for it, and threatened doctors who violate the ban with up to 15 years in prison, a $50,000 fine, and permanent loss of their licenses; the Puerto Rico LGBTQ+ Federation announced plans to challenge the ban in court. An anti-discrimination bill (House Bill 1725) passed the House 43-6 in November 2009 and would have barred discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in employment, public transportation and public facilities, business transactions and housing, but the Senate held no hearings and took no action after Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz said it would not be approved. The 2013 law that did pass (Senate Bill 238, signed 29 May 2013) was amended in the House to apply only to employment discrimination, so public facilities remain uncovered. A 2017 religious freedom bill that would have let public businesses legally discriminate against LGBTQ people was vetoed by Governor Ricardo Rosselló in February 2018, and a similar 2019 bill was withdrawn by Rosselló on 13 June 2019 after House approval amid protests. Puerto Rico amended its hate crime statutes in 2002 to include sexual orientation and gender identity as protected characteristics, and the territory is also covered by the U.S. federal Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act. 2020 was the first year anyone in Puerto Rico was charged with a hate crime: Sean Díaz de León and Juan Pagán Bonilla were charged after Bonilla confessed that he and Díaz de León murdered two transgender women on 22 April 2020. In January 2021 Governor Pedro Pierluisi declared a state of emergency over ongoing murders, assaults and rape of transgender individuals on the island. In 2013 the legislature passed House Bill 488 (signed 29 May 2013) extending domestic violence protections to all households regardless of sexual orientation and gender identity.

SYN-ASM.name: American Samoa
SYN-ASM.summary:
American Samoa is an unincorporated United States territory and stands under the full federal entry-and-documents regime. Federal executive orders reach the territory through federal agencies: EO 14168 on binary sex classification in documents, federal facilities and care funding; EO 14187 on gender-affirming care funding; and EO 14201 on athletic participation, the last paired with a State Department visa restriction carrying an SWS25 marker.

Since the January 2025 executive order, all United States identity documents reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department has stopped processing X-marker passports and markers that do not match sex assigned at birth; new and renewed passports are issued only as M or F on the basis of supporting documents; and passports already carrying an X marker remain valid until expiry. The X marker, available from 2022, has been eliminated for new applicants. The policy is challenged in federal courts, and the ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs; trans and nonbinary travelers report passports confiscated or blocked, with some stranded abroad.

Same-sex marriage remains formally contested in the territory. The Fono Senate voted down a bill that would have outlawed same-sex marriage in March 2003, after the House judiciary committee recommended killing it. In 2015 American Samoa was the only United States territory whose attorney general said applicability of the federal marriage ruling was still under review, while Puerto Rico, the US Virgin Islands, Guam and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands moved to apply it. In January 2016 a district court judge confirmed by the Senate told legislators he had not read Obergefell and that the district court did not deal with the ruling. A 2026 law review article by two attorneys practising in American Samoa concludes that Obergefell does apply and that the territory would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied, while recording that no same-sex couple has applied to date; the litigation path runs through the High Court of American Samoa against the Territorial Registrar, then the United States Department of the Interior. As of mid-2024 the local ban was still treated on-island as operative, with its constitutional durability an open question under academic study.

Trans-specific violence and protection machinery are documented. In September 2023 the United States Justice Department settled an employment-discrimination case against the American Samoa Government over harassment of a transgender employee; a June 2023 federal civil action cited a hostile work environment in a transgender woman's lawsuit against the territorial government over her gender identity; and in February 2023 a 51-year-old man was charged with sexual abuse of a 16-year-old transgender teen.

Local cultural context shapes daily expectations. The Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa, formed in 2010, frames fa'afafine as a recognised and integral part of traditional Samoan culture; reserved public behaviour is expected of people of all orientations, and homosexuality is widely accepted within Samoan culture compared with neighbouring Pacific states.

sources.summary: The UH Manoa libraries research guide on Pacific gender identities, last updated 2026-07-23, states that the Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa (SOFIAS) was formed in 2010 by merging the American Samoa Island Queens Association and the American 7s Association, explicitly re-anchored to cultural pride: 'we are fa'afafine Samoa'. It defines fa'afafine as born male but embodying both male and female traits, 'a recognized and integral part of traditional Samoan culture', and frames colonial suppression followed by contemporary reclaiming of Pacific gender identities.

Out Traveler 'Ask the Expert' column (Ed Salvato, 2009-07-01) answering a honeymoon question about American Samoa: the two Samoan nations share the fa'amatai chiefly system; ASM's ~57,000 residents across seven islands/atolls; 'Samoan culture tends toward traditionalism, and reserved behavior by people of all orientations is expected', yet 'unlike the homophobia rampant in Fiji, homosexuality is a widely accepted part of Samoan culture', with Western gay men reportedly courted by fa'afafine transgender locals and by officially straight men; local artist Dan Taulapapa McMullin calls the Samoan islands 'the homeland of fa'afafine culture'; ASM hotels skew business-travel (Tradewinds, Pago Pago).

The Independent (2015-07-10): American Samoa was then the only US territory unsure whether the 2015 federal marriage ruling applied — its AG said applicability was 'still being reviewed... I don't know' while Puerto Rico, USVI, Guam and CNMI moved to apply it; no licence applications had been made.

sources.title: American Samoa Senate rejects bill outlawing same sex marriages (RNZ Pacific)
sources.summary: American Samoa's Fono Senate voted down a bill that would have outlawed same-sex marriage in March 2003, after the House judiciary committee recommended the bill be killed. The bill was introduced by Representative Sua Carl Schuster, who wanted to preempt the kind of marriage lawsuits then unfolding in US states. At the committee hearing, fa'afafine resident Tifanny Poutasi testified that Samoan fa'afafine 'don't believe in marriages with other men', describing them as men expressing femininity through dress and speech who do not seek same-sex marriage, citing Christian upbringing. The territory therefore deliberately declined a formal marriage ban before Obergefell, and the hearing records contemporaneous local fa'afafine views on the question.

sources.title: American Samoa judge objects to same sex marriage (RNZ Pacific)
sources.summary: In January 2016 the American Samoa Senate unanimously confirmed former territory Attorney General Fiti Alexander Sunia as District Court judge, filling the seat left by Judge John Ward II's retirement. At his confirmation hearing Senator Tauolo Manaia Fruean, a retired associate judge of the High Court of American Samoa, asked whether Sunia had read Obergefell; Sunia replied he had not read the US Supreme Court decision and that the district court 'doesn't deal with this ruling', and said he would not perform weddings for same-sex couples unless local laws are changed. The exchange shows that eighteen months after Obergefell the territory's judiciary was operating on the premise that the ruling did not automatically apply.

sources.title: The Ambiguity that Isn't: Why Same-Sex Marriage Is Legal in American Samoa (Harootunian & Lawrence, American University JGSPL vol 33 iss 2 (2026) pp 163-207)
sources.summary: 2026 law review article by two attorneys practicing in American Samoa (American Samoa Legal Aid, with Freedom From Religion Foundation) concluding that Obergefell DOES apply in the territory despite local officials' statements, and that American Samoa would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied. It records that to date no same-sex couple has applied for a marriage license in the territory, and lays out the litigation roadmap: the High Court of American Samoa first (defendant the Territorial Registrar), then the US Department of the Interior. The article is the most recent dated authority on whether the 2015 ruling is operative in American Samoa, and it separates the law as written from the practical reality.

sources.title: Survey conducted on-island focuses on local same sex marriage ban (Samoa News, Asi Andrew Fa'asau, Pago Pago)
sources.summary: Samoa News reported in July 2024 an on-island survey by Dr Daniel Hall, a constitutional and comparative law professor at Miami University, testing whether American Samoa's same-sex marriage ban would survive a challenge under the 14th Amendment. The survey also probes cultural dimensions bearing on the question (collectivistic vs individualistic orientation; linear vs polychronic time). As of mid-2024, nine years after Obergefell and more than a year after the Respect for Marriage Act obliged recognition of outside marriages (Dec 13 2022), the local ban is treated on-island as operative and its constitutional durability as an open question.

USA TODAY (7 Mar 2025): Trump executive order requires all US identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; ACLU sued the State Department for seven plaintiffs; trans/nonbinary travelers report passports confiscated or blocked, leaving some stranded abroad.

Lambda Legal's FAQ sets out passport and identity-document rules for TGNCNBI people under the current federal policy change: which documents to consider, how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the current status of document updates.

HRC (updated 2025): since Jan 2025 executive order, new/renewed US passports show sex assigned at birth regardless of gender identity or name change; the 'X' marker (available since 2022) eliminated; policy challenged in federal courts -- current passport posture for trans US travelers.

Condé Nast Traveler (Feb 2025) reports that the State Department stopped processing X-marker passports and markers not matching sex assigned at birth; existing X-marker passports remain valid until expiration; new applications are processed only as M or F per supporting documents.

SYN-GUM.name: Guam
SYN-GUM.summary:
Guam stands under the full United States federal framework as an unincorporated United States territory. United States passports and other federal travel documents reflect sex assigned at birth, and the X gender marker was eliminated by a January 2025 executive order, so a trans visitor travelling on United States documents faces a mismatch between document and presentation at entry.

Screening at Guam's airport follows Transport Security Administration procedure, which applies in Guam as a United States territory. The agency's body-scanner and pat-down protocols can disclose a trans traveller's status to officers. Travellers may request an alternative screening method and escalate problems on the spot, and most trans travellers pass screening without incident. Guidance for trans travellers also addresses pre-flight packing and handling document and screening mismatches.

The January 2025 executive order halting federal funding for gender-affirming care reaches federally funded institutions in Guam, so access to that care during a visit can be constrained by federal policy rather than local practice.

A separate January 2025 executive order bans transgender troops from serving openly and directs the Secretary of Defense to submit an implementation plan within 30 days; the order frames trans identity as "radical gender ideology." It applies in Guam, which hosts a large permanent United States military presence, and indicates the federal posture a visitor can expect from official institutions on the island.

On partner recognition, chief judge Frances M Tydingco-Gatewood struck down Guam's prohibition on same-sex marriage in June 2015 following an April 2015 lawsuit by Loretta Pangelinan and Kathleen Aguero, who had been denied a marriage licence. The ruling took effect at 8am on Tuesday 9 June 2015, making Guam the first United States territory to recognise same-sex marriage.

SYN-VIR.name: United States Virgin Islands
SYN-VIR.summary:
The U.S. Virgin Islands stands under the full United States federal framework, and that framework governs what a trans visitor meets at the border. United States travel documents reflect sex assigned at birth, and the X marker was eliminated by executive order in January 2025, so a visitor arriving on United States documents carries an identification that does not match their presentation at entry.

Airport screening follows federal procedure. Transportation Security Administration body scanners can flag trans bodies and lead to secondary screening and pat-downs; travellers may request alternative screening and may decline the scanner. The agency's know-your-rights guidance extends to United States nationals travelling to and from the territory on the same terms as mainland travellers, including what may and may not be carried in hand baggage under the federal screening framework.

The January 2025 executive order halting federal funding for gender-affirming care reaches federally funded institutions in the territory, so access to that care during a visit cannot be assumed.

Territorial law adds a layer of protection. The U.S. Virgin Islands human-rights statute prohibits discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation and gender identity, and in March 2017 the territory's Attorney General issued an official interpretation that the anti-discrimination law applies to transgender students, extending that protection explicitly into the education setting.

Relationship status is settled. In 2015 the Superior Court of the U.S. Virgin Islands struck down the refusal of marriage licences to same-sex couples as unconstitutional, and later federal recognition settled the question nationwide, so a married couple can rely on their marriage in the territory. The historic sodomy statute, applicable to the territory since 1957, has been replaced and is no longer in force.

SYN-MNP.name: Northern Mariana Islands
SYN-MNP.summary:
The Northern Mariana Islands is a US commonwealth and stands under the national framework of the United States for travel documents, immigration and airport screening. United States passports and entry documents reflect sex assigned at birth, and the X marker option was eliminated by the January 2025 executive order, so a trans visitor travelling on United States documents presents a gender marker that may not match presentation at the port of entry.

Screening at the airport follows federal procedure, and the order halting federal funding for gender-affirming care reaches federally funded institutions in the territory, so access to such care during a visit cannot be assumed. In February 2025 the United States State Department additionally announced visa denials for trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sports.

Consensual same-sex conduct is not criminalised, and same-sex marriage has been legal since 2015 under Obergefell v. Hodges; the first same-sex marriage on Saipan was officiated on 27 July 2015. Adoption has been available to same-sex couples since 2015.

Commonwealth law provides for enhanced sentencing in hate-motivated crimes: CNMI Public Law 22-32, signed in January 2023, amends the Commonwealth Code with criteria covering offences motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity. This is the principal commonwealth-level protection with direct bearing on gender-identity-motivated violence.

Legal gender change is permitted in the Northern Mariana Islands provided the applicant has undergone the specified medical process, which means identity documents can be brought into line with presentation, subject to that medical requirement.

Wider protection remains thin. As of 27 September 2026 the Movement Advancement Project scored the territory's sexual orientation policy at 3.5 of 22 and its gender identity policy at minus 2 of 25, an overall rating of 1.5 of 47, classified as Low with a Negative gender-identity score. There is no comprehensive commonwealth nondiscrimination statute covering gender identity; recourse beyond federal EEOC complaint channels is limited, and commonwealth-level protections extend to government employees only.
